title: Pull SAM.gov & Grants.gov Federal Contracts Into One JSON Feed (Node, Python, n8n, MCP)
description:
If you track federal contracting opportunities on SAM.gov or Grants.gov, you have probably run into the same friction: juggling SAM API key limits, paginating nested notice payloads, and wiring up separate scripts just to catch new or amended solicitations for your NAICS codes.

Below is a copy-paste workflow using publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed that pulls both SAM.gov contracts and Grants.gov opportunities into one structured JSON feed—with a safe default snapshot (maxItems: 25) and a scheduled monitor mode for daily deltas.

Try it in your browser first (no local setup): Run publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed in Apify Console — defaults to mode: "snapshot" and maxItems: 25 ($0.002 per opportunity row + $0.0001 Actor start on the FREE tier, so a 25-row snapshot is about $0.05).

1. Snapshot input (SAM.gov by NAICS code)

Filter to a specific NAICS code (such as 541512 — Computer Systems Design Services) posted in the last 14 days:

{
  "mode": "snapshot",
  "sources": ["sam"],
  "naics": ["541512"],
  "postedWithinDays": 14,
  "maxItems": 25
}

2. Node.js (apify-client) 

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });

const run = await client.actor('publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed').call({
  mode: 'snapshot',
  sources: ['sam'],
  naics: ['541512'],
  postedWithinDays: 14,
  maxItems: 25,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const row of items) {
  console.log(row.title, row.url, row.postedAt);
}

3. Python (apify-client) 

import os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed").call(run_input={
    "mode": "snapshot",
    "sources": ["sam"],
    "naics": ["541512"],
    "postedWithinDays": 14,
    "maxItems": 25,
})

items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items
for row in items:
    print(row.get("title"), row.get("url"), row.get("postedAt"))

4. REST / n8n / Make (curl)

Drop this directly into an n8n HTTP Request node or Make HTTP module to pull matching solicitations in one call:

curl "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/publicrecords~govcon-opportunity-feed/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mode":"snapshot","sources":["sam"],"naics":["541512"],"postedWithinDays":14,"maxItems":25}'

5. Scheduled delta monitoring (mode: "monitor")

Once your snapshot filter looks right, switch to monitor mode on a daily schedule to emit only new or changed rows (delta rows are billed at $0.02 each on the FREE tier):

{
  "mode": "monitor",
  "sources": ["sam"],
  "naics": ["541512"],
  "maxItems": 25
}

6. MCP endpoint (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, custom agents)

Connect it straight to any MCP-compatible client with your Apify Bearer token:

https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed

Important note for bidding teams

Every row includes the official notice link (url / sourceUrl). Always open the live solicitation on SAM.gov or Grants.gov before preparing a bid.

Links:

  • Store page: publicrecords/govcon-opportunity-feed
  • Interactive Console runner: Try it in Apify Console

title: How to Download Skool Videos as MP4 (and Why Right-Click Doesn't Work)
description:
If you've paid for a course on Skool, you've probably tried to keep a copy of a lesson and found there's no download button. Right-click "Save video as…" doesn't appear, and copying the video URL into a new tab gives you a 403. Here's what's actually going on under the hood, and the quickest way to download Skool videos you already have access to.

Disclosure: I build Keep My Course, a Chrome extension that does this. The technical part below applies whatever tool you use.

TL;DR: download a Skool video in 3 steps

  1. Add a Skool video downloader extension (for example Keep My Course on the Chrome Web Store). It works in Chrome, Edge, Brave and Opera on desktop.
  2. Open a Skool classroom lesson you're a member of and press play.
  3. Click the download arrow on the video. The lesson saves as an MP4 (up to 1080p) in Downloads/Skool Videos.

The rest of this post explains why it has to work this way.

How Skool streams a lesson

Skool's classroom player is built on Mux. Mux doesn't serve one .mp4 file; it serves HLS:

  • a master playlist (.m3u8) listing several renditions (360p, 720p, 1080p…),
  • a media playlist per rendition listing hundreds of short segments,
  • the segments themselves, fetched one after another while you watch.

On newer lessons the segments are CMAF/fMP4 with audio and video in separate tracks. Grab one track and you get silent video or a black screen with sound.

master.m3u8
 ├─ 1080p/index.m3u8 → init.mp4, seg-0.m4s, seg-1.m4s, …
 ├─ 720p/index.m3u8  → …
 └─ audio/index.m3u8 → init.mp4, seg-0.m4s, …

There is simply no single file for "Save video as…" to save.

Why copying the URL gives a 403

Skool's video host checks where a request comes from. A playlist requested from the lesson page, with the page's Origin/Referer, is served. The same URL pasted into a new tab, curl or a download manager comes from somewhere else, so it's refused. That's also why command-line tools like yt-dlp need you to copy cookies and headers for every lesson.

Lessons that embed Loom

Some creators record lessons in Loom and embed them in Skool. Those aren't Mux streams at all. Loom can hand out a complete MP4 for a video the viewer is allowed to watch, or stream it as HLS like any other player.

YouTube, Vimeo and Wistia embeds are a different story: they belong to those platforms, and a Skool downloader shouldn't touch them.

What a downloader actually does

A Skool video downloader has to do four things, all from inside the logged-in lesson tab:

  1. Notice the playlist the player requests when you press play.
  2. Pick the best rendition from the master playlist (and its matching audio track).
  3. Fetch every segment with the same origin as the page, so the host serves them.
  4. Remux audio and video into one MP4 on your computer. No re-encoding, so there's no quality loss and it's fast.

For a 1-hour lesson that's thousands of requests and hundreds of megabytes, so a good tool streams segments to disk as it goes instead of holding the whole video in memory. Nothing needs to leave your computer.

Your options, ranked by effort

Option Cost Effort Catch
Screen recording (OBS, QuickTime) Free Real time: a 60-min lesson takes 60 min Quality loss, notifications ruin takes
yt-dlp + ffmpeg Free Terminal, cookies and headers per lesson Skool's host refuses requests without the page's headers
Browser extension Free tier, then paid One click in the lesson tab Pick one that uploads nothing and asks only for Skool permissions

A fuller, dated comparison of the Skool downloaders out there is on Best Skool video downloaders.

Bonus: get the transcript too

Most Skool lessons carry captions as WebVTT tracks in the same HLS master playlist. Parse those and you get a full transcript: searchable, clickable, exportable as .txt or .srt, and easy to paste into ChatGPT or NotebookLM for a summary. More on that in the Skool transcript guide.

Is it allowed?

Use it only for lessons your own account can open, for personal offline study. A downloader can't unlock anything your account can't play. Don't share or resell course content. The longer answer: Is it legal to download Skool videos?

Saving a whole course before your membership ends? Here's the checklist: Save a Skool course before you cancel. Troubleshooting table and FAQ: github.com/yasir926/skool-video-downloader.

title: Collateral Swap vs Withdraw and Resupply: Keep HF Above 1
description:
Swap collateral in place when an open Aave V3-based loan leaves little health-factor headroom; withdraw and resupply when debt is small or zero. Withdrawing first must keep health factor (HF) at or above 1, which often blocks a full rotation. On SparkLend, that limit determines whether you can change collateral while keeping your borrow open.

What Determines the Route?

Open debt and HF headroom determine whether withdrawal is possible. Aave V3 blocks a withdrawal that would drop HF below 1. Repaying debt creates headroom; clearing it removes this constraint. Preview the whole withdrawal, because an allowed partial withdrawal may still leave too much old collateral locked.

An in-place swap uses a flash loan to bridge the change. The transaction replaces the supplied asset and repays the flash loan within that same transaction, leaving the original borrow open. Budget for the flash-loan premium, swap slippage, and gas. Manual rotation avoids those swap costs when you already hold the replacement asset; buying it separately still has trading costs and exposes you to price movement between transactions.

The replacement asset’s parameters also affect the result. A lower liquidation threshold (LT) reduces HF at equal value, while a lower loan-to-value ratio (LTV) reduces borrowing capacity. Compare both before signing. Supply value alone cannot predict post-rotation HF.

Isolation mode can explain an odd completed swap. On markets using Aave V3 isolation mode, an isolation-mode asset, or an asset supplied while you are in isolation mode, does not automatically become collateral. The new balance appears in supplies but contributes nothing to HF; other enabled collateral may have kept the transaction valid. After either method, confirm the new asset’s collateral toggle is on. If isolation rules block that toggle, repay the relevant debt and exit isolation mode before relying on the new supply.

When Does Each Method Win?

Choose the in-place swap with open debt and thin HF headroom; choose withdrawal and resupply when remaining collateral or a repayment keeps HF above 1. Say two borrowers have the same WETH supply, debt, and wstETH target. One has no other enabled collateral, so withdrawing WETH would breach HF 1 and a swap is needed. The other has enough additional enabled collateral to support the same debt during withdrawal, so manual rotation can avoid the flash-loan premium. Both must verify wstETH’s LT and collateral status.

Related

Why did my health factor drop after a collateral swap?

HF falls when the new asset has a lower LT, slippage reduces the value received, or the new supply is not enabled as collateral. On SparkLend, inspect the supplied balance, collateral toggle, and reserve parameters separately.

Do collateral swaps cost a flash-loan fee?

In-place collateral swaps incur a flash-loan premium because the temporary loan is repaid within the transaction. Quote the premium alongside slippage and gas before signing.

With meaningful open debt, HF headroom usually decides the route. After swapping or resupplying, confirm that the replacement asset actually supports the loan.

title: The math before you file for small claims, and why filing is often the whole remedy
description:
People threaten small claims for years and never file. The two things that stop them are the fee and the calendar, and both are knowable before you start.

The arithmetic nobody does first

Rough US numbers, and they vary by state and county:

  • Filing fee: $30 to $100, commonly around $80 for a claim in the low thousands.
  • Service of process: $0 to $150 depending on whether the sheriff, a process server, or certified mail does it.
  • Your time: 6 to 10 hours across the filing, the service, a possible default judgment, and a hearing date two to four months out.

On a $500 debt that is a net loss before anyone argues about the merits. On $2,500 it is a reasonable afternoon. The line sits somewhere around $1,200 for most people — below it, filing costs more than the debt; above it, the filing is cheaper than the hours you have already spent chasing.

Two things change that line. First, your time has a price, and you are the one paying it. Second, a filing fee is recoverable in many jurisdictions if you win, so the number that matters is the worst case, not the best.

The part that surprised me

In the freelancer threads I read, a lot of people who filed never reached the hearing. The client paid as soon as the papers were served.

That is not an accident. A served complaint is the first time the situation stops being a conversation and becomes a date with consequences attached. Some AP departments can ignore an email for a month; almost none can ignore a court date, because now there is a person whose job is to respond to it.

Which means the cheapest possible outcome is often: file, get it served, get paid, dismiss the case yourself. You do not need to win. You need the client to understand that the next step is not another email.

What to keep before you file

If you may end up in front of a judge, the file has to exist before the dispute, not after:

  1. The signed contract or the written scope, even if it is an email thread.
  2. The invoice with a due date on it, not just a send date.
  3. Proof of delivery — a signed acceptance, a Slack message saying "looks good", a screenshot of the deployed work.
  4. Your follow-up sequence, with dates. This is the part people forget and the part that shows you gave the client every chance.
  5. Any written acknowledgment of the debt. "I know we owe you, cash flow is tight" is worth more than a hundred unanswered reminders.

When filing is the wrong move

  • The amount is under roughly $1,200 and the client is in another country. Service alone will eat the claim.
  • The client is a real company with a legal department. You will win slowly, if at all, and the time cost is not worth a small sum.
  • The relationship is worth more than the money and you would work with them again. Then send the final notice and mean it, but do not file.

What to actually write

A final notice is not a longer angry email. It is five facts: what was delivered, when, the amount, the date it was due, and the date by which payment must arrive before you file. No adjectives. The tone should read like a receipt, because that is what it is.

The full escalation ladder — day 3 question, day 10 amount and a new date, day 21 one hard date, day 30 the contract consequence, day 31 facts only — plus the invoice lines and the contract clause that makes the day-30 message land, is what I collected into a short field manual: The Late Invoice Playbook. Fifteen pages, copy-paste wording, no theory.

title: A confirmation with no session
description:
What a sealed requestState can and can't promise on MCP 2026-07-28

Some tools should ask before they act: delete, pay, send. On MCP's 2026-07-28 protocol a server can pause a tool call and ask the user, in the middle of the call, without holding a connection open. The catch is that the server keeps no session. Whatever it needs to remember between the question and the answer has to travel with the client, in a token called requestState.

mcp-better teaches this pattern: it is a Rust MCP server written as a textbook. Its confirm_echo tool asks you to type CONFIRM, then echoes your message. A raw HTTP test of version 0.7.0 found that the confirmation promised more than it delivered. Version 0.8.0 adds an expiry and refuses a changed message, and says plainly what it still doesn't do. Every response below is a real capture from those two versions.

1. Two round trips, no session

This is SEP-2322, multi round-trip requests. Round 1 is an ordinary tool call:

round 1 · request

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "confirm_echo",
    "arguments": {
      "message": "confirm me"
    },
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
        "elicitation": {
          "form": {}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

The server doesn't run the tool. It answers input_required, says what it needs (a form asking for CONFIRM), and hands back a sealed token:

round 1 · response (mcp-better 0.8.0, schema trimmed)

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "input_required",
    "inputRequests": {
      "confirm": {
        "method": "elicitation/create",
        "params": {
          "message": "Type CONFIRM to echo the sealed message.",
          "mode": "form",
          "requestedSchema": "…"
        }
      }
    },
    "requestState": "rs1.AAABohveDBN7…DwylF-M"
  }
}

The client shows the form, then sends the same call again with the answer and the same token:

round 2 · request

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "confirm_echo",
    "arguments": {
      "message": "confirm me"
    },
    "requestState": "rs1.AAABohveDBN7…DwylF-M",
    "inputResponses": {
      "confirm": {
        "action": "accept",
        "content": {
          "confirm": "CONFIRM"
        }
      }
    },
    "_meta": "…"
  }
}

round 2 · response

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "content": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "{\"confirmed\":true,\"echo\":\"confirm me\",…}"
      }
    ],
    "isError": false
  }
}


Two round trips, no session: everything round 2 needs travels in the token.

WHY: the server can't trust anything in round 2 that it didn't seal in round 1. The client could send back anything.

2. Signed, not secret

mcp-better seals the token with rmcp's RequestStateCodec: an HMAC-SHA256 tag over the payload. Change one byte and round 2 fails:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 5,
  "error": {
    "code": -32602,
    "message": "requestState failed integrity check or expired (start again)"
  }
}

But look inside the token. A client must not; an attacker will. The middle part is base64url, and it decodes to plain JSON:

# 0.8.0's token, split at its dots
rs1
.AAABohveDBN7Im1lc3NhZ2UiOiJjb25maXJtIG1lIn0
.sEgJTcgy3dI6341xIRsGjf7IIuu-hxPkkoDbDwylF-M

# the middle part, decoded
[8-byte expiry] {"message":"confirm me"}


What a sealed requestState is. Signed, not secret.

NOTE: rmcp's docs say it: “Values are authenticated, not encrypted; key ids and payloads remain readable.” Never put private data in it, or encrypt it.

3. Give it an expiry

In 0.7.0 the first 8 bytes of the payload were all zero: no expiry. Nothing marked a token as used either, because there's no session to mark. So one round-1 token completed round 2 again and again. Here it is, the same token sent twice to 0.7.0:

first use

{
  "confirmed": true,
  "echo": "confirm me",
  "mrtr": "confirm_echo",
  "resultType": "complete"
}

same token again

{
  "confirmed": true,
  "echo": "confirm me",
  "mrtr": "confirm_echo",
  "resultType": "complete"
}

rmcp can stamp an expiry into the token, and opening it after that fails. 0.8.0 seals every round-1 token with five minutes:

src/server.rs · mcp-better 0.8.0

let sealed = self
    .state_codec
    .seal_json_with(
        &ConfirmState { message: message.clone() },
        &SealOptions::new()
            .associated_data(MRTR_AAD)
            .ttl(self.confirm_ttl),
    )
    .map_err(|e| { /* … */ })?;

After five minutes, round 2 is refused:

round 2 · a round-1 token, 305 seconds later

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "error": {
    "code": -32602,
    "message": "requestState failed integrity check or expired (start again)"
  }
}

A test that doesn't wait five minutes: build the server with a 1 ms lifetime, sleep 20 ms, expect the error.

#[test]
fn confirm_echo_rejects_expired_state() {
    let server = BetterServer::new()
        .with_confirm_ttl(std::time::Duration::from_millis(1));
    let sealed = round1_state(&server, "late");
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(20));
    let req = confirm_args("late")
        .with_input_responses(accepted())
        .with_request_state(sealed);
    let err = server.confirm_echo_call(req, &elicit_caps()).unwrap_err();
    assert_eq!(err.code, ErrorCode::INVALID_PARAMS);
}

4. Say what's left

An expiry bounds replay. It doesn't stop it. Inside the five minutes, 0.8.0 still accepts the same token twice:

{
  "confirmed": true,
  "echo": "confirm me",
  "mrtr": "confirm_echo",
  "resultType": "complete"
}


What an expiry buys, and what it doesn't.

For an echo, that's harmless. For a tool with real effects, it isn't: put a nonce in the sealed state and keep a set of used nonces on the server, at least until they expire. That is state, and keeping it is a choice 2026-07-28 makes you take on purpose. mcp-better doesn't, and its docs say so.

GOTCHA: The spec says servers SHOULD seal three things into the state: the authenticated user, a short expiry, and the method plus a digest of its parameters. rmcp's associated data can carry the first and the last. mcp-better 0.8.0 has the expiry and binds only the tool name. A real server should bind the user and a digest of the call, so a token can't be replayed by someone else or against a different call.

5. Refuse changed arguments

Round 2 carries the arguments again. What if they changed? In 0.7.0 the server used the sealed message and ignored the new one. Safe, since the user's confirmed text won, but the caller was told "done" for something it didn't send:

0.7.0 · round 2 with "SWAPPED"

{
  "confirmed": true,
  "echo": "confirm me",
  "mrtr": "confirm_echo",
  "resultType": "complete"
}

0.8.0 · round 2 with "SWAPPED"

{
  "code": -32602,
  "message": "message changed since round 1; start again to confirm the new one"
}

The check is one if:

// The sealed message is what the user confirmed.
if message != state.message {
    return Err(McpError::invalid_params(
        "message changed since round 1; start again to confirm the new one",
        None,
    ));
}

6. One error for every bad token

Tampered, sealed for another tool, expired: the client gets the same -32602 for all three. The reason never leaves the server.

let state: ConfirmState = self
    .state_codec
    .open_json_with(sealed, MRTR_AAD)
    // One client-facing error for every failure (tampered, wrong tool,
    // expired), as rmcp's `open_with` asks; the variant stays internal.
    .map_err(|_| McpError::invalid_params(
        "requestState failed integrity check or expired (start again)",
        None,
    ))?;

WHY: rmcp's docs: applications MUST map all token-opening failures to a single client-facing error. A forger learns nothing about which check failed. The changed-message error is different on purpose: it only fires after the token opened cleanly, so it tells a forger nothing.

7. Ask only clients that can answer

Round 1 asks for a form, so it only makes sense for a client that declared it can show one. A client that didn't gets a clear refusal, naming what's missing, instead of a question it can't answer:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 6,
  "error": {
    "code": -32021,
    "message": "Missing required client capability",
    "data": {
      "requiredCapabilities": {
        "elicitation": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

The checklist

# Rule In mcp-better 0.8.0
1 Seal the state; never trust echoed bytes HMAC via rmcp RequestStateCodec
2 Signed isn't secret Only the message goes in, nothing private
3 Put an expiry on every token 5 minutes (CONFIRM_STATE_TTL)
4 Know your reuse window; add a nonce and a store for real effects Stated, not built: it only echoes
5 Bind the token to who called and what they asked Tool name only
6 Refuse changed arguments -32602 "message changed since round 1"
7 One error for every failed open -32602 for tampered, wrong tool, expired
8 Ask only clients that declared the capability -32021 naming elicitation

Try it 

npx --yes mcp-better@0.8.0 --http
# http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp

Every request on 2026-07-28 needs an MCP-Protocol-Version header, an Mcp-Method header, an Mcp-Name header for tools/call, and _meta with the protocol version and the client's capabilities. Leave one out and the server tells you which.

Links

  • mcp-better: Mid-call confirmation (confirm_echo)
  • mcp-better #19: requestState expires after 5 minutes · #20: a changed message is refused
  • mcp-better CHANGELOG (0.8.0)
  • MCP 2026-07-28: Multi Round-Trip Requests
  • rmcp: RequestStateCodec

Captured from mcp-better 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 over Streamable HTTP, protocol 2026-07-28, on November 27, 2026.

— Drafted by Claude · Edited by James Wolfe

title: دليل أرباح التجارة الإلكترونية والدفع عند الاستلام (COD): كيف تحسب صافي الربح الحقيقي ونقطة التعادل للإعلانات في المغرب والخليج
description:
دليل أرباح التجارة الإلكترونية والدفع عند الاستلام (COD): كيف تحسب صافي الربح الحقيقي ونقطة التعادل للإعلانات في المغرب والخليج

يمثل الدفع عند الاستلام (Cash on Delivery / COD) أكثر من 70% من معاملات التجارة الإلكترونية في المغرب والدول المغاربية، وما يزيد عن 60% في دول الخليج (السعودية والإمارات). بالنسبة للمسوقين ورواد الأعمال في هذا المجال، يظهر مدير الإعلانات على تيك توك أو فيسبوك غالباً عائد إعلاني (ROAS) خادع يصل إلى 3.5x أو 4x، مما يوحي بنجاح باهر. لكن المفاجأة تأتي في نهاية الشهر عندما يجد التاجر أن السيولة النقدية في حسابه البنكي سلبية أو قريبة من الصفر.

كيف يمكن لحملة إعلانية ذات عائد 4x أن تخسر أموالاً حقيقية؟

السبب يكمن في أن طلب العميل في نظام الدفع عند الاستلام هو مجرد نية شراء وليس عملية بيع مؤكدة. وتحدث فجوة كبيرة بين الإعلان واستلام الكاش بسبب تكاليف غير مرئية.

يقدم هذا الدليل العملي المعادلات الرياضية الدقيقة لحساب صافي الربح الحقيقي، وتكلفة المرتجعات، ونقطة التعادل الإعلانية بالدرهم المغربي والريال السعودي.

1. مسار الطلب الحقيقي في الدفع عند الاستلام

تخضع كل طلبية لأربع مراحل حاسمة:

تسجيل الطلب (Lead) ➔ تأكيد الطلبية (Confirmation) ➔ الشحن ➔ التوصيل الناجح وتحصيل الكاش (Delivery)

المعايير القياسية للسوق:

  • نسبة التأكيد (Confirmation Rate): نسبة الطلبات التي يؤكدها مركز الاتصال أو الواتساب (المعدل الطبيعي: 75% إلى 85%).
  • نسبة التوصيل (Delivery Rate): نسبة الطرود المشحونة التي يتم تسليمها للعميل وقبض ثمنها (المعدل الطبيعي: 65% إلى 75% في المغرب، و70% إلى 80% في السعودية).
  • نسبة المرتجع (RTO Rate): الطرود التي يرفضها العميل أو يتعذر الوصول إليه (25% إلى 35%).

2. عقوبة الشحن المزدوج (Double Shipping Penalty)

عندما يرفض العميل استلام الطرد عند الباب، لا تقتصر خسارة التاجر على عدم بيع المنتج، بل يتحمل عقوبة مالية مضاعفة:

  1. خسارة تكلفة الشحن الأولي المدفوعة لشركة التوصيل (مثلاً 35 إلى 45 درهم / 25 إلى 35 ريال).
  2. دفع رسوم الإرجاع (Return Fee) التي تفرضها شركة الشحن لإعادة الطرد للمخزن (15 إلى 20 درهم / 15 إلى 25 ريال).
  3. تلف مواد التغليف وبقاء المنتج محتجزاً في المستودعات لأسابيع مما يضيع فرص بيعه.

3. مثال عملي بالأرقام الحقيقية (سوق المغرب بالدرهم MAD)

لنفترض أنك تبيع منتجاً للعناية بالبشرة أو أداة منزلية في المغرب:

  • سعر البيع للعميل: 300 درهم
  • تكلفة شراء المنتج (COGS): 80 درهم
  • تكلفة التوصيل للعميل: 40 درهم للطلب
  • رسوم إرجاع الطرد المرتجع: 20 درهم للطرد
  • تكلفة تأكيد الطلب: 10 دراهم لكل طلب
  • نسبة التوصيل الفعلية: 70% (من كل 100 طلب مشحون: 70 تم تسليمها، و30 عادت مرتجعة)
  • ميزانية الإعلانات: 5,000 درهم لكل 100 طلب (تكلفة الطلب CPA = 50 درهم)

كشف الحساب المالي الحقيقي:

  • الكاش المحصل (70 طلب × 300 درهم): +21,000 درهم
  • تكلفة شراء البضاعة المسلّمة (70 × 80 درهم): -5,600 درهم
  • شحن كافة الطلبات الـ 100 (100 × 40 درهم): -4,000 درهم
  • رسوم إرجاع الـ 30 طرد فاشل (30 × 20 درهم): -600 درهم
  • تكلفة الإعلانات المدفوعة: -5,000 درهم
  • تكلفة التأكيد ومركز الاتصال (100 × 10 دراهم): -1,000 درهم

صافي الربح الحقيقي = 21,000 - 5,600 - 4,000 - 600 - 5,000 - 1,000 = +4,800 درهم

صافي الربح لكل طلبية مشحونة = 48 درهم (هامش ربح صافي 16%)

ماذا يحدث إذا انخفضت نسبة التوصيل إلى 55%؟

إذا تراجعت نسبة التوصيل من 70% إلى 55% فقط:

  • الكاش المحصل (55 × 300 درهم): 16,500 درهم
  • تكلفة شراء البضاعة المسلّمة (55 × 80 درهم): -4,400 درهم
  • شحن الـ 100 طلب (100 × 40 درهم): -4,000 درهم
  • رسوم إرجاع 45 طرد فاشل (45 × 20 درهم): -900 درهم
  • الإعلانات: -5,000 درهم
  • مركز الاتصال: -1,000 درهم
  • صافي الربح الحقيقي = +1,200 درهم فقط (هامش ربح متدنٍ جداً 3.8%!)

تراجع نسبة التوصيل بنسبة 15% فقط أدى إلى تبخر 75% من أرباحك الصافية، بالرغم من أن تكلفة الإعلان وعائد الـ ROAS على لوحة تحكم فيسبوك لم يتغيرا إطلاقاً!

4. معادلة حساب أقصى تكلفة إعلانية مسموح بها (Max Break-Even CPA)

لمعرفة أقصى تكلفة يمكنك دفعها للإعلان للحصول على طلب مؤكد دون الوقوع في الخسارة:

أقصى CPA للتعادل = [(سعر البيع - تكلفة المنتج) × نسبة التوصيل] - تكلفة الشحن - [رسوم المرتجع × (1 - نسبة التوصيل)] - تكلفة مركز الاتصال

القاعدة الذهبية لخبراء الـ COD:

لا تقم أبداً بقياس تكلفة الطلب الخام (Cost Per Lead). المقياس الوحيد الذي يحدد ربحيتك هو تكلفة الطلب المستلم كاش (Cost Per Delivered Order):

تكلفة الطلب المسلّم = إجمالي الإنفاق الإعلاني ÷ عدد الطلبات المسلّمة فعلياً

5. أدوات حاسبة مجانية لمسوقي الـ COD

لحساب أرقامك بدقة واختبار هوامش الربح قبل ضخ الميزانيات الإعلانية، يمكنك استخدام الأدوات الحاسبة المجانية على منصة Profit Workbench:

  • حاسبة أرباح الدفع عند الاستلام والمرتجعات (COD Profit & RTO Calculator): تدعم الدرهم المغربي والريال السعودي والدرهم الإماراتي والدولار واليورو، وتحسب تكلفة المرتجعات وصافي الربح للطلبية المسلّمة.
  • حاسبة العائد الإعلاني للتعادل (Break-Even ROAS Calculator): تحدد لك أدنى ROAS يجب تحقيقه قبل بدء الحملة.
  • حاسبة صافي ربح التجارة الإلكترونية (E-Commerce Profit Calculator): لتحليل تكاليف المنتجات والضرائب وبوابات الدفع.

جميع الحسابات تعمل بالكامل داخل متصفحك: مجانية 100%، خاصة بالكامل، ولا تتطلب تسجيل حساب أو بطاقة بنكية.

إفصاح الشفافية والمسؤولية (Founder Disclosure)

أنا مطور منصة Profit Workbench ومسوق رقمي مهتم بوحدات الاقتصاد (Unit Economics) للتجارة الإلكترونية في منطقة الشرق الأوسط وشمال إفريقيا. قمت ببرمجة هذه الأدوات الحسابية ونشر هذا الدليل التعليمي مجاناً 100% لتمكين التجار ورواد الأعمال والميديا بايرز من معرفة أرقامهم المالية الحقيقية بدقة قبل المخاطرة بميزانياتهم الإعلانية. لا تتضمن المنصة أي خدمات مدفوعة أو اشتراكات مخفية.

title: What a Node.js App Needs Before You Deploy It (with a ShardCloud Walkthrough)
description:
Your Express app runs fine with node index.js on your laptop. Then you deploy it and you get a 502, an app that never finishes starting, or an app that dies every few hours. Most of the time the code is fine. The app just assumes things that are true on your machine and false inside a container.

This post covers those assumptions first, as a checklist you can use on any platform. Then it walks through a real deploy on ShardCloud, so you can see where each item shows up.

Part 1: The checklist

1. Read the port from the environment

Platforms decide which port your app listens on and pass it in as PORT. A hardcoded 3000 is the most common reason a deploy "works" in the logs but returns 502.

const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

Keep the fallback so node index.js still works locally.

2. Listen on 0.0.0.0, not localhost

Inside a container, localhost means "only reachable from inside this container". The platform's proxy sits outside it, so it can't reach an app bound to 127.0.0.1.

app.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", () => {
  console.log(`Listening on ${port}`);
});

Express binds to all interfaces when you pass no host. Be explicit anyway: some frameworks and dev servers (Vite, Next's next dev) default to localhost.

3. Don't upload node_modules

Your node_modules was built for your OS and CPU. Packages with native code (bcrypt, sharp, sqlite3, canvas) compile a binary at install time, and a binary built on Windows or macOS won't load on the platform's Linux. It's also usually the largest folder in your project.

Ship package.json (and the lockfile, if your platform uses it) and let the platform install. Everything the app needs at runtime must be in dependencies, not only in devDependencies.

4. Keep secrets in environment variables

Database URLs, API keys and tokens go in the platform's environment variables, never in the code or the zip you upload. Read them the same way you read PORT:

const databaseUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
if (!databaseUrl) {
  throw new Error("DATABASE_URL is not set");
}

Failing at startup with a clear message beats failing on the first request with undefined.

5. Log to stdout, and add a health route

Platforms collect what your process prints. console.log and console.error are enough; you don't need log files. A small route that returns 200 lets you (and any uptime checker) tell "the app is up" apart from "the app is up but broken":

app.get("/health", (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
});

6. Shut down cleanly

When a container is stopped or restarted, the process gets SIGTERM first and is killed a little later. If you handle it, requests in flight can finish and database connections close properly:

const server = app.listen(port, "0.0.0.0");

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  console.log("SIGTERM received, closing server");
  server.close(() => process.exit(0));
});

7. Know your memory budget

A container has a hard memory limit. When the process goes over it, it is killed, not slowed down. Watch memory use while the app is under load, and size the limit from that number rather than from a guess.

Part 2: Deploying an Express API to ShardCloud

Here is a complete example with all of the above, deployed to ShardCloud. You'll need Node.js locally and a ShardCloud account.

The app 

mkdir hello-api && cd hello-api
npm init -y
npm install express

package.json:

{
  "name": "hello-api",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.21.0"
  }
}

index.js:

import express from "express";

const app = express();
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;

app.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ message: "Hello from Node.js" });
});

app.get("/health", (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
});

const server = app.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", () => {
  console.log(`Listening on ${port}`);
});

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  console.log("SIGTERM received, closing server");
  server.close(() => process.exit(0));
});

Run npm start and open http://localhost:3000 to check it works.

The config file

ShardCloud reads a plain-text file named .shardcloud in the project root. It tells the platform how to run your app:

DISPLAY_NAME=Hello API
DESCRIPTION=A small Express API
MAIN=index.js
MEMORY=512
VERSION=recommended
SUBDOMAIN=helloapi

What each line does:

  • MAIN is the entry file. The platform detects that it's a Node.js app from the .js extension and starts it with node index.js. A .ts file is started with tsx, so TypeScript runs without a build step.
  • MEMORY is the memory limit in MB (item 7 of the checklist). Apps that serve a website need at least 512 MB; background apps such as bots can go down to 256 MB.
  • VERSION picks the Node.js version: recommended, latest, or a specific version from the list the dashboard shows.
  • SUBDOMAIN gives the app a public address, helloapi.shardweb.app here. Letters and numbers only: no hyphens.

If you need a build step (TypeScript compiled with tsc, a framework build), replace MAIN with LANGUAGE=node and a CUSTOM_COMMAND:

LANGUAGE=node
CUSTOM_COMMAND=npm run build && npm run start

How the checklist maps to the platform

  • Port: every ShardCloud container sets PORT=80. The code above reads it, so locally it uses 3000 and in production 80, with no change.
  • Dependencies: on each start, the container installs your dependencies when package.json or the lockfile has changed, or when node_modules is missing. It picks the package manager from the lockfile: yarn.lock means Yarn, pnpm-lock.yaml means pnpm, bun.lockb means Bun, and anything else means npm.
  • Environment variables: set them in the app's settings in the dashboard, or with the CLI (shown below).
  • Logs: whatever the app prints shows up in the dashboard's log view, live.
  • Crashes: if the process exits unexpectedly, the platform restarts it, up to 3 times within a short period, then stops it so a crash loop doesn't run forever.
  • Memory: an app that goes over its MEMORY is shut down. Going over the CPU allowance only throttles it.

Deploy option A: upload a zip

  1. Zip the project folder without node_modules. (ShardCloud's Node.js guide also says to leave out package-lock.json.)
  2. Open the dashboard, go to Applications, click New app and upload the zip.
  3. Watch the logs. You should see the install, then Listening on 80.
  4. Open https://helloapi.shardweb.app. HTTPS is set up for you.

Deploy option B: the CLI

The CLI zips the current folder for you:

# macOS, Linux, WSL
curl -fsSL https://cli.shardcloud.app | bash
# Windows (needs npm)
npm install -g shard-cloud-cli

shardcloud auth login
shardcloud app create          # zips and deploys the current folder, and links it to the new app

app create writes a .shardcloud.json file that links the folder to the app, so later commands don't need its ID:

shardcloud app env set DATABASE_URL=postgres://...   # adds to the existing variables
shardcloud app logs                                  # stream the logs
shardcloud app commit                                # deploy the folder again after a change

Add .shardcloud.json to your .gitignore: it's a local link, not part of the app.

Deploy option C: push to GitHub

In the dashboard, connect your GitHub account (Config → Integrations), then pick the repository and branch in the app's Deploys section. Every push to that branch deploys the new files.

One thing that catches people: restarting after a deploy is off by default. The new files are in place, but the running process keeps the old code until you restart the app or turn on the optional auto-restart on deploy.

Troubleshooting

The logs say "Listening" but the URL returns 502. Check items 1 and 2: the app must listen on process.env.PORT and on 0.0.0.0. Also check that SUBDOMAIN is set in .shardcloud.

Cannot find module 'something'. The package is missing from dependencies, or it is only in devDependencies.

A native module fails to load (invalid ELF header, was compiled against a different Node.js version). You uploaded node_modules. Delete it from the zip and deploy again.

The app restarts every few hours. Look for out-of-memory in the logs. Either the app leaks memory or MEMORY is too low for its real usage.

Pushed to GitHub but nothing changed. Restart the app, or turn on auto-restart on deploy (see option C).

Wrapping up

The checklist in Part 1 is what makes a Node.js app portable: if your app reads its port and secrets from the environment, binds to 0.0.0.0, lets the platform install its dependencies, logs to stdout and handles SIGTERM, it will run with few changes on most platforms that run containers. The ShardCloud part only adds one config file on top.

If you've hit a deploy problem that isn't on this list, share it in the comments.

title: What we learned building a self-hosted Laravel CMS with 55 languages and per-language URLs
description:
I have been building RJ Nexus, a modern, self-hosted CMS on top of Laravel 12. You install it on your own hosting, keep full ownership of your data, and extend it with isolated plugins and themes.

It started small. Today it supports 55 languages with per-language URLs, ships with a visual page builder with 80+ widgets, and has a free AI engine that needs no API key.

This post is about the interesting problems along the way, and an invitation: the project is open source and I would love your help.

The problem: a CMS that treats every language as a first-class citizen

Many CMS setups bolt multilingual support on later. I wanted it built in from the start, which meant solving a few things properly.

Per-language slugs

A page should not have one URL with a language prefix glued on. It should have a real, SEO-friendly URL in each language:

/en/about
/az/haqqimizda

That sounds simple until you handle it everywhere: routing, the editor, the page builder, translations, and quick edits from the posts list.

A bug that taught me something

One of the nastiest bugs I hit was in validation. Laravel's validation was stripping translated slugs and content before they were saved, because the translated fields were not part of the validated data. Everything looked fine in the form, then silently vanished on save.

The lesson: when you build nested or dynamic fields (like translations[az][slug]), make sure your validation rules actually cover them, because validated data only contains what you validated.

Right-to-left languages

Arabic and Kurdish need right-to-left layouts. I handle this at the language level, so adding a new RTL language is mostly a matter of registering it, not rewriting templates.

Scaling the language list

Going from 17 to 38 and then to 55 languages exposed performance problems in places I did not expect. For example, the installer's language selection screen has a 3D planet animation. With 38 languages it stuttered, so the animation now calculates planet density, size, and stagger speed dynamically based on how many languages are available.

The page builder: RJBuilder

RJBuilder is a drag-and-drop builder with 80+ widgets, responsive controls, and dynamic tags. Each widget is two files:

  • a PHP class that describes the widget (name, icon, category, settings schema) and prepares data in render()
  • a Blade view with the markup, scoped CSS, and JavaScript

A few rules I follow for every widget:

  • Every setting has a safe default, so a widget looks good the moment you drop it on a page.
  • Settings are sanitized in render(): select values are whitelisted, colors are validated with a strict hex check, and list sizes are capped.
  • Everything is scoped to a unique instance ID, so several copies of the same widget can live on one page without clashing.
  • Accessibility is built in: real <button> elements, ARIA attributes, keyboard navigation, and prefers-reduced-motion support.

The accordion widget is a good reference if you want to build your own.

A free AI engine

RJ Nexus has two AI modes:

  • Free AI: keyless, works out of the box. It powers the dashboard and global search (Ctrl+K).
  • OpenRouter: optional, for advanced SEO, content writing, and bulk translation that preserves HTML.

Keeping a free, no-setup option mattered to me. Many people never configure an API key, and a feature nobody sets up is a feature nobody uses.

Performance on cheap hosting

Many CMS users run on shared hosting, so speed cannot depend on expensive infrastructure. RJ Nexus has a two-layer caching system:

Layer Package Works on
Response Cache spatie/laravel-responsecache Any PHP hosting
LiteSpeed LSCache litespeed/lscache-laravel LiteSpeed / OpenLiteSpeed

Response Cache is the universal baseline. On LiteSpeed hosts, pages can be served from the web server before PHP even starts.

Small things that make a big difference

A few features came from simply using the admin panel every day:

  • Quick Edit: change a post's title, slug, and status straight from the list, without opening the editor.
  • Marketing Post Generator: pick a post and design a social media graphic (PNG, JPG, or WebP, in every common social format) without leaving the admin panel.
  • A browser-based installer: upload the files, open /install.php, and follow the steps. No terminal needed, which matters on shared hosting.

Try it

You can try the live demo here: rj-nexus.onrender.com (add /admin for the admin panel; demo credentials are in the README). The demo may not run the latest version.

  • Website: rjnexus.org
  • Documentation: rjnexus.org/en/docs
  • Source code: github.com/rj-nexus/rj-nexus

How you can help

This is an open source project, and there are ways to contribute that do not require deep knowledge of the codebase:

  • 🌍 Translations: add your language or improve an existing one.
  • 📚 Documentation: pick a missing topic and write a guide.
  • 🎨 Widgets: build new blocks for RJBuilder.
  • 🤖 AI ideas: help us find useful places for the free AI in the dashboard.

Every contribution is recognized. Contributors are listed by name in the SUPPORTERS.md file and on the website, and earn supporter titles named after stars: Proxima, Vega, Sirius, and Polaris.

Open issues are here: github.com/rj-nexus/rj-nexus/issues

If you have built something multilingual before, I would love to hear how you handled per-language URLs. What would you do differently? Let me know in the comments. And if you find the project useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps more than you might think.

title: LRF y el guardrail del art. 20
description:
Respuesta corta

El artículo 20 de la Ley de Responsabilidad Fiscal (LRF, Lei Complementar nº 101/2000) establece el guardrail fiscal que prohíbe a los entes subnacionales (Estados y Municipios) contraer operaciones de crédito que superen los límites de despesa corriente fijados en la ley, bajo riesgo de intervenção federal y sanciones del Tribunal de Cuentas de la Unión (TCU). Su incumplimiento activa mecanismos automáticos de fiscalización y limitación de transferencias constitucionales.

TL;DR

  • El art. 20 LRF impone un límite de 95% sobre la relación entre despesas totales con personal y la receita corriente líquida (RCL) para Estados y Municipios.
  • El TCU monitorea mensualmente este indicador mediante el Sistema de Informações Contábeis e Fiscais do Setor Público Brasileiro (Siconfi).
  • El exceso constatado por el TCU obliga al ente a elaborar un Plano de Recuperación Fiscal (PRF) en hasta 90 días, conforme art. 37-A LRF.
  • Desde 2022, el TCU ha emitido más de 140 recomendações técnicas vinculadas al art. 20 en Estados y Distrito Federal.
  • La violación reiterada puede desencadenar la suspensión de transferencias voluntarias y la intervención federal prevista en el art. 34 de la CF/88.
  • El art. 20 no aplica a la Unión ni a las empresas estatales controladas directamente (solo a entidades federativas y sus órgãos).

¿Qué es el guardrail del art. 20 da LRF?

Es un mecanismo de contención fiscal automático que limita el gasto con personal en Estados y Municipios. No es una meta aspiracional: es un umbral legal vinculante. Si un ente supera el 95% de su RCL en despesas com pessoal, se considera en “situação de alerta fiscal”, lo que desencadena obligaciones inmediatas de transparencia, corrección y supervisión técnica del TCU.

¿Cómo se calcula y quién lo fiscaliza?

El cálculo se realiza mensualmente: (Despesas totais com pessoal / Receita Corrente Líquida) × 100. La RCL excluye transferências constitucionales y recursos vinculados a finalidades específicas (art. 20, § 1º, LRF). El TCU recibe los datos del Siconfi y verifica coherencia contable, clasificación presupuestaria y cobertura de todas las entidades vinculadas (incluidas fundaciones e autarquias). Sus auditorías pueden resultar en tomadas de cuentas, recomendações vinculantes o remisión al Ministerio Público.

¿Qué ocurre si se supera el límite?

La superación genera efectos jurídicos inmediatos: notificación formal del TCU, publicación obligatoria del resultado en el Diário Oficial, y plazo máximo de 90 días para presentar el PRF. Durante ese período, queda vedado el aumento de remunerações, creación de cargos y contratación de personal — salvo reposición por aposentadoria ou morte (art. 20, § 3º). El PRF debe ser aprobado por el Poder Legislativo local y remitido al TCU y al Ministério da Economia.

Preguntas frecuentes

  • Q: ¿El art. 20 aplica a los municipios con menos de 50.000 habitantes?

  • A: Sí. No hay excepción por porte demográfico: todos los municipios están sujetos al límite del 95% sobre RCL (LC 101/2000, art. 20 caput).

  • Q: ¿Las despesas com pessoal incluyen solo salarios o también benefícios?

  • A: Incluyen remunerações, vantagens pessoais, adicionais, gratificações, pensões civis y todas as despesas com pessoal ativo, inativo e pensionistas (art. 20, § 2º).

  • Q: ¿Puede el TCU imponer multas directas por violación al art. 20?

  • A: No. El TCU no aplica multas, pero puede recomendar sanções ao Congresso Nacional, sugerir medidas coercitivas y bloquear transferências via Portaria Interministerial 371/2022.

  • Q: ¿El PRF sustituye al Plano Plurianual (PPA)?

  • A: No. El PRF es un instrumento extraordinário y temporal, complementario al PPA y al LDO. Su vigência máxima es de 3 años, renovable una vez (art. 37-A, § 6º).

Hechos clave

  • El art. 20 fue introducido pela Lei Complementar nº 101/2000, promulgada el 4 de mayo de 2000.
  • El TCU publica trimestralmente el Relatório de Gestão Fiscal (RGF), donde se reporta el cumplimiento del art. 20 por entidad.
  • En 2023, 12 Estados y 347 municipios registraron índices superiores al 95% según el RGF consolidado del TCU.
  • La metodología de cálculo está normatizada en a Instrução Normativa STN nº 11/2022 y en a NBC T 16.10 do CFC.

Fuentes

  • Lei Complementar nº 101, de 4 de maio de 2000 — Planalto.gov.br
  • Instrução Normativa STN nº 11/2022 — Portal da STN (Ministério da Economia)
  • Relatórios de Gestão Fiscal (RGF) — Portal do TCU (tcu.gov.br)
  • NBC T 16.10 – Pronunciamento Técnico do Conselho Federal de Contabilidade (cfc.org.br)
  • Portaria Interministerial MP/ME nº 371/2022 — DOU de 28/12/2022

Saiba mais em https://g.cloud

Publicado originalmente en g.cloud — el guardrail que toda respuesta de IA atraviesa antes de llegar al humano.

title: How to debug CrashLoopBackOff in Kubernetes without guessing
description:
CrashLoopBackOff is the most common thing a Kubernetes cluster will ever tell you, and it is almost useless on its own. It does not say the container ran out of memory. It does not say a config value is missing. It does not even say the container is broken — a failing readiness probe and a bad image entrypoint both end up here. All it says is: this container keeps exiting, and the kubelet is now waiting longer between attempts.

The backoff itself is the only part that is precise. The kubelet restarts a failed container after 10 seconds, then 20, then 40, doubling to a five-minute ceiling. When you see the gaps widening, you are watching that timer, not a diagnosis.

The widening gaps are the kubelet’s backoff timer. They tell you how long it has been failing, and nothing at all about why.

So the work is the same every time: figure out which of the half-dozen causes you have, using evidence rather than the order you happen to think of them in. This article is the order that actually works, and what each step rules in or out.

Start with the exit, not the logs

The single most informative field is how the container died, and it is one command away:

kubectl -n <namespace> get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}' | jq

You are looking for two things:

Field What it tells you
reason Error means the process exited on its own. OOMKilled means the kernel killed it.
exitCode 1 is an ordinary application error. 137 is SIGKILL — nearly always the OOM killer. 139 is a segfault. 143 is SIGTERM.

This one distinction splits the problem space in half before you have read a single log line.

One field, two very different investigations. Chasing logs before reading it is how the first ten minutes get spent on the wrong branch.

An exitCode of 1 with reason: Error means the application chose to stop, and its logs will say why. OOMKilled with 137 means it never got the chance, and the logs will simply stop mid-sentence.

Note: A container that is OOMKilled is not always leaking. A perfectly healthy process that allocates one large batch can cross its limit in the gap between two metrics scrapes, and the memory graph will look flat the whole time. We walk through exactly that case in OOMKilled and exit code 137.

Then read the logs of the previous container

The running container is a fresh attempt and usually has nothing in it yet. The one that died has the answer:

kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> --previous --tail=50

An application that refuses to start almost always says so in its last few lines. What you want is the final non-framework line — the one written by the service itself rather than by the runtime unwinding afterwards.

Here is a real one, from a crash loop in a lab cluster. The container printed configuration error: DATABASE_URL is not set, refusing to start and exited with code 1, about a second after each start. That is a complete diagnosis: the Deployment's pod template does not supply a variable the image requires. No node problem, no image problem, no probe problem — and, importantly, no memory problem, which the working set of ~8 MiB against a 128 MiB limit independently confirms.

When the logs are empty

Two cases produce a crash loop with no useful logs at all:

  • The process was killed before it could write. Check lastState.terminated.reason again — an OOMKilled during startup looks exactly like this.
  • The entrypoint is wrong. exec: "serve": executable file not found in $PATH appears in the pod's events, not its logs, because the container never started: 
  kubectl -n <namespace> describe pod <pod> | sed -n '/Events:/,$p'

Rule out the four impostors

Before accepting "the application is broken", eliminate the four causes that produce an identical CrashLoopBackOff without the application being at fault:

  1. A failing readiness or liveness probe. A liveness probe that fails restarts a container that was working. The tell is a Killing event citing the probe, and an application log that ends normally rather than with an error.
  2. A memory limit the workload cannot live inside. reason: OOMKilled, exitCode: 137.
  3. A missing ConfigMap, Secret or volume. The pod never reaches Running; events show CreateContainerConfigError or FailedMount.
  4. Node trouble. Disk pressure, a full emptyDir, or an evicted pod. kubectl describe node shows the pressure conditions.

Each of these has a distinct signature in a different data source — events, metrics, the pod spec, the node. That is the actual reason crash-loop triage is slow: the evidence that separates them is scattered across four tools, and you are switching between them under time pressure while a service is down.

Gathering all of it in one pass

A crash loop rarely arrives as one alert: restarts, failed probes and unavailable replicas all fire, across every pod of the workload. Treat them as one incident first, and investigate that once rather than each alert on its own.

A good investigation, by hand or automated, does not replay a checklist. It states the candidate causes as hypotheses, each with a prediction: if this is an OOM kill, the last termination reason is OOMKilled and the exit code is 137; if a config value is missing, the previous container's last log line names it and the exit is the application's own; if a release caused it, the restarts begin at the rollout. Then it reads the cluster, the previous container's logs, Prometheus, Loki and the rollout history to confirm or refute each one.

The value is not that a model looked at your cluster. It is that the reads you would have made by hand were made within seconds of the alert, while the evidence was still there. Metrics get thin fast: series for a deleted pod disappear, and the terminated container's logs age out of retention. An investigation that starts at 03:05 sees things that an engineer starting at 09:00 cannot.

Reading the result critically

A crash-loop diagnosis is only worth having if you can check it. Three things make that possible.

The mechanism has to be stated, not the category. "The application is misconfigured" is a restatement of the symptom. A mechanism names the value, the file, the line and the consequence, so you can disagree with it.

The losing hypotheses have to be shown. If the answer is a missing environment variable, you should be able to see that an OOM kill and a failing probe were considered, and which record ended each of them. A diagnosis that hides its refuted alternatives cannot be argued with.

Every claim has to lead to a query. Each finding cites the tool call behind it: the exact kubectl read or PromQL, the cluster, the time and the raw answer. You can re-run it and see the new answer diffed against the recorded one, which settles "is that still true?" in a few seconds.

Tip: An empty answer, a source that failed and a source you never configured are three different facts. Only the first is evidence that something did not happen. If a source you needed could not be read, the honest result is "insufficient evidence", with the missing source named.

A checklist you can keep

For the next crash loop, in order:

  1. lastState.terminated.reason and exitCode — split OOM from application exit.
  2. logs --previous — the last line the application wrote.
  3. describe pod events — probes, mounts, image pulls, scheduling.
  4. Memory working set against the limit — was there headroom at the kill?
  5. What changed — a rollout, a sync, an out-of-band edit to a ConfigMap.
  6. The restart gaps — widening means the kubelet's backoff, not an accelerating fault.

Step 5 is the one most often skipped and most often decisive. A crash loop that starts at a deploy boundary is a different investigation from one that starts on its own, and Argo CD's sync history will tell you which you have.

Related failures

Crash loops sit next to two neighbours worth recognising on sight. A pod that never starts at all is not crash-looping — it is stuck in Pending, and the scheduler will say why. And a container killed at its memory ceiling deserves its own reading of the evidence, because the metrics frequently look innocent.

If you want the general version of the method rather than this one failure mode, the same discipline — enumerate causes, gather evidence per cause, eliminate explicitly — is written up in root cause analysis for Kubernetes incidents.

This article was written with AI assistance. It first appeared on alertigate.com.

title: AI doesn't turn anyone into a developer
description:
Yes, I used AI to write this post. And I doubt you'll find the generic text here, full of "in today's landscape" and punchy one-liners, that comes out when someone asks ChatGPT to "write an article about AI and the future of developers". This post came out of a skill I wrote myself, which interviewed me in two rounds before writing a single line, researched the sources, and then ran the text through a check against AI writing habits. Everything here is something I said, the AI only organized it, and that way of using the tool is exactly what this post is about.

A few days ago I saw a post on LinkedIn saying that today a 15-year-old with Claude Code does what used to take a developer years of experience. I don't remember who wrote it, and it doesn't matter, because I see that line everywhere, in a dozen variations. And I disagree with it, because it mixes up writing code with doing a developer's job.

So you know where I'm coming from, I've been programming for six years. I went through Trybe, a Brazilian bootcamp of more than 1,500 hours, almost a full year of course, and even so most of what I know I learned on my own, because I'm self-taught and obsessed with productivity, and when I want something I don't let go. Today I have a startup I can't name yet, 10 months old with more than 500 users, and I wrote about 87% of its code, close to 2 million lines, not counting tests, migrations or generated files (I counted with a script, it's not a guess). All the architecture and all the infrastructure, since day zero, were my decisions. And 100% of that code goes through AI, I haven't written a line of code by hand in a long time.

So no, I'm not against AI. I've been using AI to program for three years, and it clicked for me the very first time I used it.

The door into programming got knocked down

The LinkedIn post gets one thing right. Today anyone can write code. The door into programming isn't just open, it got knocked down, there's no door anymore. You open Lovable, Bolt or Claude Code itself, describe what you want and a working screen comes out.

The name stuck in February 2025, when Andrej Karpathy called it "vibe coding", a way of programming where you "forget that the code even exists". But a lot of people forgot the other half of the tweet, where he says himself that it's "not too bad for throwaway weekend projects", weekend projects you throw away, and there are people using it to store customer data.

Writing code was never the hard part. The hard part is building software that lasts, that you can maintain, that can grow, that scales, with infrastructure that doesn't go down and doesn't ruin you at the end of the month. AI doesn't give you that for free, because to ask for the right thing you have to know what the right thing is.

Writing code got easy, the rest is still hard

Ask someone who became a "dev" in seven days what a design pattern is. What changes between a monolith and microservices, and when each one makes sense. How a layered architecture works, or one split by domain. Most of the time they don't know, and they don't know because they never studied it. They know how to ask AI for code, and when the system grows and architecture problems show up, they don't even have the vocabulary to understand what's wrong.

With infrastructure it's even worse. There are a lot of people calling themselves developers who have never opened the AWS console, never logged into Azure and don't know what GCP stands for. Instead they use Supabase and Firebase, and think they're doing infrastructure.

I have nothing against Supabase itself. Under the hood it's Postgres, with auth, storage and a generated REST API on top, it's open source, the managed service runs on AWS and you can host it yourself. What bothers me is people who use it with no idea of any of that. They don't know there's a Postgres underneath, they don't know security depends on something called RLS (Row Level Security, the rules that say which user can read which row of the database) and they don't know that, if they don't set it up, anyone with the public key from the frontend can read the whole database.

In 2025 a researcher analyzed 1,645 apps built on Lovable and found 170 exposing data because of misconfigured RLS, with emails, phone numbers, payment data and API keys leaking, and that became CVE-2025-48757. In February 2026 Wiz found Moltbook's entire database wide open for the same reason, with about 1.5 million tokens exposed, and the founder had said publicly that he didn't write a single line of code. I've found exposed keys myself while looking into SaaS products out there, and YouTube is full of videos of people showing how easy it is to exploit these apps.

Firebase is not "the database"

I've seen a lot of people call Firebase a database, and worse, truly believe it's the right database for a large production system storing user data, because "it's faster to get started". Firebase is a platform, and the databases inside it are Firestore and the Realtime Database. When a developer says "database", almost everyone pictures Postgres or MySQL, a relational database with SQL. Firestore is a document database, NoSQL. And that's where juniors fall.

NoSQL isn't bad, Amazon keeps a lot of stuff in DynamoDB. The mistake is taking relational data, which needs joins, transactions and integrity, and shoving it into a document database without modeling anything.

I know the headache because I've worked on a project like that, with a few hundred thousand users, the database on Firestore and the backend on a pile of Cloud Functions. The cost was very high. We needed relations between the data and couldn't do them properly, because the database isn't relational. There was no standard for security rules, so pretty much anything could change any document. A lot of the data had no structure at all, one document looked one way and the one next to it looked another. And migrating that was misery.

Lovable is not a developer tool

For building a prototype and validating an idea, Lovable is great and I have nothing against it. What makes me angry is people so convinced they've become developers that they think Lovable is what a developer uses, with no idea what the AI setup of someone who programs for a living looks like.

Mine, for example, is Claude Code with a few dozen skills I wrote, a bunch of hooks and thousands of lint and Stylelint rules to force the code to come out the way I want. At the startup we have tens of thousands of unit tests, a hook that runs before every push, a hook at deploy time, a huge CI/CD pipeline and a sanity check that simulates a real user after every deploy. On a normal day I have six to eight AI chats open, each with dozens of subagents. Anyone who thinks a developer with AI is someone who writes a prompt and hits enter has never heard of unit tests or lint rules, and if they have, they don't know how to use them.

And if you think I'm exaggerating my productivity, my WakaTime is public, and the top of my site shows the total hours I've coded.

Who's selling the shortcut

Search for "developer course" or "build your SaaS without knowing how to code" and you'll find a ton of people promising to turn you into a developer in seven days. It's everywhere, and everyone knows it. I've never bought one of those and I never will, because to me it's a scam.

They exploit something every human being has, the urge to get things fast, which today, with so much cheap dopamine, is stronger than ever. It's the old "easy money, fast", now dressed up as AI.

What bothers me most is that it hurts people, and if there's one thing I hate in life it's getting in someone else's way. But a scammer goes further than getting in the way. He lies to the person, takes their money and still leaves them behind, thinking they learned something, with an insecure app online and without the foundation to see how big the problem is. I did a one-year course of more than 1,500 hours and I know how much I was still missing when I finished. Seven days is a joke.

AI multiplies what you already are

AI is a tool, and like any tool it makes whoever uses it more productive, but it doesn't make bad code good and it doesn't turn anyone who isn't a developer into one.

  • A good developer with AI is still a good developer, only shipping ten times more.
  • A bad developer with AI is still bad, and ships ten times more bad code.
  • Someone who isn't a developer still isn't one, and ships broken code full of security holes ten times faster.

I've seen hired developers shipping buggy, random, senseless AI-generated code, at more than one company. And it's the complaint I see most online. In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, the number one frustration of people using AI to code was exactly code that's "almost right, but not quite", cited by 66% of developers. Someone who can't program can't even see where the "almost" is.

AI as a crutch

There's another type that bothers me, the person who uses AI as a crutch. No patience, no perseverance, no discipline to use AI to learn before using it to do, so they ask for everything ready-made and move on without understanding anything.

I know what it's like because I've done it. Early on, I already knew unit testing but didn't know how to write integration tests, and I was arrogant enough to ask AI to do it without understanding how it worked. It went wrong. I got stuck in a loop, the thing broke, I asked AI to fix it, it broke again, and I had no idea why, because I didn't know what was going on there. When it finally clicked I thought I'd been really stupid, all I had to do was learn it first and ask later.

In January 2026 Anthropic itself published a study with 52 engineers learning a new library. Those who learned with AI doing the work for them scored 17% lower on average on a comprehension quiz than those who wrote the code by hand, and the biggest gap was in debugging. And those who used AI to ask for explanations and clear up conceptual questions learned more. AI teaches well, if you ask it to teach you.

Will AI end developers?

The developer as the job looks today, I think it will. Developers will stop writing code and become the people who define the architecture, the infrastructure, how things have to work and which structure to use. I already work like that, AI writes and I decide.

In March 2025 Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO, said that in three to six months AI would be writing 90% of the code. In the same talk he said the programmer would still need to define the design and security of the system, and almost nobody repeats that second part. And junior jobs really are harder to get, a Stanford study using payroll data shows that hiring of 22 to 25 year olds in the jobs most exposed to AI fell well below trend, but the authors themselves say they can't claim AI is the cause.

To me the developer career isn't over. What changed is what you need to study. What you used to learn only once you became senior, a junior now has to learn from the start, because AI already writes the code.

What I'd study if I were starting today

First, learn how to learn. It sounds silly, but you need to know how you learn, and Fabio Akita, a well-known Brazilian developer, has a 2020 video about it (in Portuguese) that I recommend, where he sums up learning how to learn as truly figuring things out on your own. I use AI to build the courses I study with, and I show the whole process on the page about how I make my courses.

Then the foundation. The concepts, how the internet works, what happens between the browser and the server. And writing code, lots of code. Juniors have to write code, because writing it is how you understand what the AI is handing you.

And then, much earlier than we used to, the senior stuff. Architecture, every kind. Infrastructure. Software modeling, which in Akita's other video means representing the real world in code, and for that you need to understand the business and not just the language. Design patterns. And even learning to be an entrepreneur.

Some time from now I'll write another post showing how I keep code quality high with AI, with high throughput and without having to review every PR by hand. There you'll see in practice the difference between asking AI for code and programming with it.

Originally published on joaopster.com. The post is also on my blog in three languages

  • Português
  • English
  • Español

title: TypeScript Path Aliases Work in the Editor but Fail at Runtime: tsc-alias vs Subpath Imports vs a Bundler
description:
TypeScript's paths option only teaches the type checker where to look; tsc does not rewrite the import specifiers in the JavaScript it emits. So import { db } from "@/lib/db" compiles cleanly, then Node throws Cannot find module '@/lib/db'. You can fix it by rewriting aliases after compile (tsc-alias), by switching to Node's native subpath imports (#lib/*), by bundling, or by running through a tool that resolves paths itself (tsx).

Why does the editor say everything is fine while Node crashes?

Here is the setup that trips people up:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": { "@/*": ["src/*"] },
    "outDir": "dist",
    "module": "commonjs"
  }
}

// src/server.ts
import { db } from "@/lib/db";

tsc succeeds, autocomplete works, and then:

$ node dist/server.js
Error: Cannot find module '@/lib/db'
Require stack:
- /app/dist/server.js

(With ESM output the message reads ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND / Cannot find package '@', because Node treats @/lib/db as a scoped package name.) If you open dist/server.js, the specifier is still @/lib/db. The TypeScript team has long treated this as intentional: paths describes how some other tool will resolve modules at runtime, and the compiler does not transform import text. The checker and the runtime disagree, and nothing warns you.

The dead ends I see most often: adding baseUrl (changes nothing at runtime), copying tsconfig.json into the Docker image (Node never reads it), and setting NODE_PATH (works for bare names, not for @/ prefixes in ESM, and it hides the real problem).

Takeaway: if the output JavaScript still contains your alias, the compiler did its job and the runtime has no idea what the alias means.

Which fix should you use?

Approach How it works Best for Real drawback
tsc-alias after tsc Rewrites alias specifiers in dist/ to relative paths Libraries and servers you already build with plain tsc An extra build step; ESM output also needs correct file extensions, which it may not add for you
Node subpath imports (# prefix) package.json imports field, resolved natively by Node New projects that want zero extra tooling Aliases must start with #, so you cannot keep @/
Bundler (tsup, esbuild) Resolves paths while bundling Apps deployed as a single artifact You are now maintaining a bundler config and source maps
tsx (dev/scripts only) Honors tsconfig paths at run time Local dev, scripts, one-off tooling Not a production answer if you ship dist/

How do I fix it with tsc-alias?

This is the smallest change to an existing project.

npm install --save-dev tsc-alias

{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tsc && tsc-alias"
  }
}

After npm run build, open one file in dist/ and confirm the import became something like require("./lib/db"). That check takes ten seconds and is the only proof that matters. If you use ESM output, also check whether the rewritten specifiers carry file extensions; Node's ESM loader requires them, and that is a separate failure from the alias problem.

If you want the packaged version of this approach without writing any config, tsup is the tool that bundles TypeScript and resolves your paths in one step (see below).

Takeaway: tsc && tsc-alias fixes the alias at the one point where it actually breaks, the emitted files, and you can verify it by reading dist/.

Are Node subpath imports better than path aliases?

They remove the whole class of problem, because the runtime and the type checker read the same declaration. In package.json:

{
  "name": "my-service",
  "type": "module",
  "imports": {
    "#lib/*": "./dist/lib/*.js"
  }
}

import { db } from "#lib/db.js";

Rules worth knowing: every key must begin with #, and Node resolves them relative to the nearest package.json. TypeScript understands the imports field when moduleResolution is node16, nodenext, or bundler. In my setup, with outDir and rootDir set, the checker mapped the dist target back to the source file, but verify this with tsc --noEmit rather than trusting me, because it depends on your layout. As of late 2026 this is supported by current Node LTS releases and by the major test runners.

The drawback is cosmetic but real: you give up @/, and a large codebase with thousands of existing @/ imports needs a codemod to migrate.

Takeaway: for a new project, subpath imports are the only option where nothing can drift out of sync, because there is no second resolver to configure.

What about bundlers and tsx?

If you already ship a bundled artifact, let the bundler resolve the alias:

// tsup.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "tsup";

export default defineConfig({
  entry: ["src/server.ts"],
  format: ["esm"],
  tsconfig: "tsconfig.json", // paths are read from here
  clean: true,
});

esbuild-based tools read paths from the tsconfig, so the alias disappears at bundle time. The cost is that stack traces point at bundled output unless you enable source maps, and native or dynamically required dependencies sometimes need to be marked external.

For development, tsx src/server.ts runs TypeScript directly and respects paths, which is why aliases "work" locally and then break in the container: dev uses tsx, production runs node dist/. That mismatch is the most common root cause I run into. Older ts-node setups need tsconfig-paths/register, and if you hit that, switching to tsx is usually less work than tuning the register hook.

Test runners have their own resolver as well. Jest needs moduleNameMapper, and Vitest needs resolve.alias or a tsconfig-paths plugin. A green test suite therefore says nothing about whether node dist/ will start.

Takeaway: every tool in your pipeline resolves modules independently, so test the exact command production runs, not the one your editor and test runner use.

How do I stop this from reaching production?

Add a smoke step to CI that runs the built output, not the source:

npm run build
node -e "import('./dist/server.js')" || exit 1

Better still, give the app a --check flag or an import-only entry that loads every module and exits. A failed import in CI costs a minute. The same failure after deploy costs a rollback.

FAQ

Why does TypeScript not rewrite path aliases when compiling?
paths is a type-checking hint, and the compiler deliberately leaves import specifiers unchanged in the output. Something else (a bundler, a post-processor, or Node itself) must resolve them at runtime.

Does Node read tsconfig.json paths?
No. Node never reads tsconfig.json. Use the package.json imports field with # aliases, or rewrite the specifiers at build time.

Why do my path aliases work with tsx but not with node?
tsx resolves tsconfig paths itself, while plain node does not. Run node dist/ locally once to reproduce what production sees.

Bottom line

If you have an existing tsc build and @/ imports everywhere, add tsc-alias and check dist/. If you are starting a service today, use # subpath imports and skip the problem. If you already bundle for deployment, tsup handles the alias as part of work it is doing anyway. Whichever you choose, run the built output in CI so a resolver mismatch fails a pipeline instead of a deploy.

Related reading

  • ChatGPT Free vs Go vs Plus vs Pro: Which Tier Should a Coding Beginner Actually Pay For?
  • The Boring Stack Manifesto: Why Your Startup Probably Doesn't Need Kubernetes
  • Git "detected dubious ownership in repository": Fix It in Docker and CI Without Trusting Everything

title: I built a free study platform with spaced repetition, practice exams and AI
description:
I built four courses with AI and at first I studied everything in Obsidian, which is great for reading, but it doesn't track progress, doesn't grade quizzes and doesn't remind you of what you're forgetting. I wanted a tool like that for myself, and then I thought, why not open it up to everyone, for free? That's how the courses section of my site turned into a study platform.

To show everything it does I used the AWS Solutions Architect Associate course, which is the one I'm studying right now. I've finished 4 of the 27 modules and I'm doing really well. The courses are in Portuguese, so the screenshots are too, and they come from a local server with sample data, so the scores you see aren't mine.

I already wrote about how the AI builds the courses in the post on building courses with AI, this one is only about what you do with a course once it exists.

Sync without an account, just a code

This is the part I think is the most amazing. You study on the computer, stop, grab your phone and everything is there, the lessons you read, the questions you answered, your highlights. Stop again, grab the tablet, same thing. I study on all three, the computer when I want real focus, the phone when I'm moving around and the tablet more at night, and without this I'd have three different progress records and none of them right.

And there's no account. You click "Criar código" (create code), the site generates a 20-character code and you paste it on the other device. It doesn't ask for an email, a name, a password, nothing, and that was my decision, because I didn't want anyone handing over personal data just to study. The code works like a password, so the server only stores its hash and not the code itself.

If two devices studied separately, offline for example, the progress merges on its own when they talk again, and each item keeps its most recent version.

Mistakes notebook
