title: Porting an ADK Research and Judge Loop to Strands on Bedrock AgentCore, With A2A 1.x
description:
This article provides a step by step guide to porting a Google ADK multi-agent system to Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock. A researcher searches the web, a judge passes or fails the research for up to three rounds, and a content builder turns the approved research into a course. Each agent is its own A2A service on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and the original web app runs unchanged on Amazon ECS Express Mode.

Repository: https://github.com/xbill9/strands-bedrock-research-loop

What Is Being Ported?

The source is the course creator in multi-agent-loop, an update of Google's ADK 2.0 and A2A codelab. Four ADK services: a researcher with google_search, a judge with a Pydantic output schema, a content builder, and an orchestrator that wires them together with SequentialAgent and LoopAgent.

The port keeps the prompts word for word, keeps the judge's JudgeFeedback schema, keeps the three-round limit, and keeps the web app's frontend file for file. Everything underneath changes:

ADK on Google Cloud Strands on AWS
SequentialAgent(LoopAgent(...), content_builder) One Strands GraphBuilder graph
output_schema=JudgeFeedback structured_output_model=JudgeFeedback
google_search Amazon Nova Web Grounding (nova_grounding)
RemoteA2aAgent Strands A2AAgent
gemini-3-flash-preview us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0
Cloud Run AgentCore Runtime and ECS Express Mode

At This Point You Should Have

  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access to Amazon Nova 2 Lite in us-east-1.
  • The AWS CLI signed in (aws login works; the containers get its short-lived session).
  • Docker.
  • Python 3 with pip, to build the AgentCore code package.
  • make. The repository wraps every step below in one target.

Why Strands From a Pull Request?

The ADK version runs on a2a-sdk 1.x. Released Strands pins the 0.3 line:

1.67.0 2026-11-25 ['a2a-sdk<0.4.0,>=0.3.0; extra == "a2a"']
a2a-sdk 0.3.26 2026-04-09
a2a-sdk 1.0.0 2026-04-20
a2a-sdk 1.3.1 2026-11-17

a2a-sdk 1.0 replaced the Pydantic types with protobuf types, so TextPart, DataPart and FilePart became one Part, and the message method became SendMessage. Strands has the migration written in harness-sdk PR #3923, open since 2026-08-21. This port runs that pull request at a pinned commit:

PR 3923 OPEN opened 2026-08-21T17:34:58Z head 95477761ec3837f68ddf540bf5e766cf431fcaf1

Step 1 — Build Strands From the Pull Request

One base image carries Strands from the pinned commit and a2a-sdk 1.3.1. The version is set by hand because the build reads it from git tags the fork does not have.

FROM python:3.14-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ARG STRANDS_SHA=95477761ec3837f68ddf540bf5e766cf431fcaf1
ENV SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION_FOR_STRANDS_AGENTS=1.66.0+pr3923 \
    SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION=1.66.0+pr3923 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \
      "strands-agents[a2a] @ git+https://github.com/waitasecant/harness-sdk@${STRANDS_SHA}#subdirectory=strands-py" \
      "a2a-sdk[http-server]>=1.3.1,<2" uvicorn fastapi boto3

What the image holds:

python 3.14.10
strands-agents 1.66.0+pr3923
a2a-sdk 1.3.1
boto3 1.44.12
fastapi 0.165.0
uvicorn 0.54.0

Step 2 — Port the Judge: Same Prompt, Same Schema

The judge moves over with one renamed argument. ADK's instruction is Strands' system_prompt, and ADK's output_schema is Strands' structured_output_model. The Pydantic class is copied as is.

class JudgeFeedback(BaseModel):
    """Structured feedback from the Judge agent."""

    status: Literal["pass", "fail"] = Field(
        description="Whether the research is sufficient ('pass') or needs more work ('fail')."
    )
    feedback: str = Field(
        description="Detailed feedback on what is missing or needs clarification if status is 'fail'. If 'pass', a brief confirmation."
    )


judge = Agent(
    name="judge",
    model=model(),
    description="Evaluates research findings for completeness and accuracy.",
    system_prompt="""
    You are a strict editor and fact-checker.
    ...
    """,
    structured_output_model=JudgeFeedback,
    callback_handler=None,
)

The judge's reply text is the JSON of that object, so the verdict crosses A2A as plain text and the orchestrator parses status out of it, the same way ADK's EscalationChecker did.

Step 3 — Replace google_search With Nova Web Grounding

Amazon Nova has a built-in web search tool, nova_grounding, turned on with a systemTool entry in the Converse request. Nova runs the search on the server side and returns the answer with citations:

secs 4.8 stop end_turn usage {'inputTokens': 142, 'outputTokens': 177, 'totalTokens': 319}
['toolUse'] {"toolUse": {"toolUseId": "...", "name": "nova_grounding", "input": {"query": "AWS Nitro Sandboxes announcement November 2026"}, "type": "server_tool_use"}}
['toolResult'] {"toolResult": {"toolUseId": "...", "content": [{"text": "[HIDDEN]"}], "status": "success", "type": "nova_grounding_result"}}
['text'] {"text": "On November 9, 2026, AWS announced ..."}
['citationsContent'] {"citationsContent": {"citations": [{"location": {"web": {"url": "https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/nitro-sandboxes-eks-ecs-ec2/", ...

The researcher wraps that call in an ordinary Strands tool, which returns the grounded text and a list of the cited URLs:

@tool
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the web and return a grounded answer with its source URLs.

    Args:
        query: What to look up.
    """
    resp = _bedrock.converse(
        modelId=MODEL_ID,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": query}]}],
        toolConfig={"tools": [{"systemTool": {"name": "nova_grounding"}}]},
    )
    text, urls = [], []
    for block in resp["output"]["message"]["content"]:
        if "text" in block:
            text.append(block["text"])
        for c in block.get("citationsContent", {}).get("citations", []):
            url = c.get("location", {}).get("web", {}).get("url")
            if url and url not in urls:
                urls.append(url)
    return "".join(text) + "\n\nSources:\n" + "\n".join(f"- {u}" for u in urls)

🔎 Tip: Strands Runs Bedrock Server-Side Tools as Local Tools

Passing nova_grounding straight to a Strands agent through BedrockModel(additional_args={"toolConfig": ...}) fails. Strands sees the toolUse block, changes the stop reason, and looks for a local tool of that name. The model keeps searching, and Strands then sends the citations back in a shape Bedrock refuses:

python 3.14.10
WARNING:strands.event_loop.streaming:original_stop_reason=<end_turn>, new_stop_reason=<tool_use> | overriding stop reason due to toolUse blocks in response
ERROR:strands.tools.executors._executor:tool_name=<nova_grounding>, available_tools=<[]> | tool not found in registry
ERROR:strands.tools.executors._executor:tool_name=<nova_grounding>, available_tools=<[]> | tool not found in registry
ERROR:strands.tools.executors._executor:tool_name=<nova_grounding>, available_tools=<[]> | tool not found in registry
ERROR:strands.tools.executors._executor:tool_name=<nova_grounding>, available_tools=<[]> | tool not found in registry
botocore.errorfactory.ValidationException: An error occurred (ValidationException) when calling the ConverseStream operation: This model doesn't support the citationsContent.content field for assistant messages. Remove citationsContent.content and try again.

Strands' pull request for Bedrock system tools (#1318) was closed on 2026-07-28 with the comment "Closing stale PR". The @tool wrapper in Step 3 keeps the server-side call inside one Converse request, where Strands never sees it.

Step 4 — Port the Content Builder and Give It Room

The content builder is a prompt and a model, so it ports in a few lines. One setting matters: a whole course does not fit in Nova 2 Lite's default output limit. The same research, the same prompt, with and without an explicit limit:

python 3.14.10 | model us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0
default limit: MaxTokensReachedException: Model stopped generating due to maximum token limit. ...
max_tokens=10000: stop=end_turn output_tokens=2313 secs=13.1

Every agent's model gets the explicit limit:

MAX_TOKENS = int(os.environ.get("MAX_TOKENS", "10000"))


def model() -> BedrockModel:
    return BedrockModel(model_id=MODEL_ID, region_name=REGION, max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS)

Step 5 — Rebuild the Loop as a Strands Graph

ADK expresses the loop with three orchestration agents. Strands expresses it as one graph with conditional edges:

def build_graph():
    b = GraphBuilder()
    b.add_node(remote("researcher", "http://localhost:8001/"), "researcher")
    b.add_node(remote("judge", "http://localhost:8002/"), "judge")
    b.add_node(remote("content_builder", "http://localhost:8003/"), "content_builder")
    b.add_edge("researcher", "judge")
    b.add_edge("judge", "researcher", condition=failed)
    b.add_edge("judge", "content_builder", condition=passed)
    b.add_edge("researcher", "content_builder", condition=passed)
    b.set_entry_point("researcher")
    b.set_max_node_executions(2 * MAX_ROUNDS + 1)
    b.reset_on_revisit(True)
    return b.build()

Each remote agent is a Strands A2AAgent, which is a graph node like any local agent. A node's input is the original task plus the output of every finished upstream node whose edge condition holds, so on a fail the researcher receives the judge's feedback, and on a pass the content builder receives both the research and the verdict. The extra researcher → content_builder edge is what hands it the research.

🔎 Tip: Cap the Rounds in the Edge Condition

set_max_node_executions counts every node run, and when the graph reaches it the run ends as FAILED. ADK's LoopAgent ends cleanly after its last round. To match it, the fail edge counts the judge's runs itself:

def failed(state) -> bool:
    """Loop back only while rounds remain: ADK's LoopAgent stops after max_iterations."""
    return verdict(state) == "fail" and judge_runs(state) < MAX_ROUNDS

After the third fail, no edge out of the judge holds, and the graph completes with no course.

Step 6 — Run It Locally

make local builds both images, exports the AWS session for the containers, and starts the three agents and the web app with Docker Compose:

make local

One run of the orchestrator on "Curling":

status=Status.COMPLETED total_s=16.4 order=['researcher', 'judge', 'content_builder']
  researcher          6.3 s
  judge               1.1 s
  content_builder     8.9 s
judge_verdict=pass

The web app at http://localhost:8000 is the ADK frontend with a new backend. It runs the graph in process and turns the graph's node start and stop events into the progress lines the frontend already reads:

progress 🔍 Researcher is gathering information... (round 1)
progress ⚖️ Judge is evaluating findings... (round 1)
progress ⚖️ Judge verdict: pass
progress ✍️ Content Builder is writing the course...
result # Comprehensive Curling Course  ## Introduction to Curling ...

Step 7 — Test the Fail Path

A judge that passes everything leaves the loop untested. tests/fail_judge.py is a stand-in judge that fails every submission, and make test points the orchestrator at it:

make test

status=Status.COMPLETED total_s=31.2 order=['researcher', 'judge', 'researcher', 'judge', 'researcher', 'judge']
  researcher          7.2 s
  judge               0.7 s
  researcher         12.6 s
  judge               0.7 s
  researcher          9.4 s
  judge               0.5 s
judge_verdict=fail

(no course: the judge never passed the research)

Three rounds, a clean stop, and no course. The researcher's searches follow the judge's feedback, which asked for more detail on the rules:

INFO:researcher:web_search query='Curling' sources=6 secs=3.8
INFO:researcher:web_search query='curling rules detailed explanation' sources=5 secs=3.7
INFO:researcher:web_search query='curling rules detailed explanation' sources=5 secs=6.1

Step 8 — Serve Each Agent on AgentCore Runtime

AgentCore's A2A contract is a server on port 9000, A2A at /, and a /ping health check. The Strands A2A server covers the first two; one route adds the third:

on_agentcore = os.environ.get("ON_AGENTCORE") == "1"
port = 9000 if on_agentcore else port
public_url = os.environ.get("PUBLIC_URL", f"http://localhost:{port}/")
server = A2AServer(agent=agent, host="0.0.0.0", port=port, http_url=public_url, serve_at_root=True)
app = server.to_fastapi_app()

@app.get("/ping")
def ping():
    return {"status": "Healthy"}

AgentCore runs ARM64. infra/build_zip.sh builds the Strands wheel from the pinned commit and installs everything for manylinux aarch64 and Python 3.14 (PYTHON_3_14) into one code package, so no ARM64 Docker build is needed. infra/deploy_agents.sh uploads it and creates three runtimes with serverProtocol: A2A and IAM inbound auth. What AgentCore reports for them:

srl_researcher  READY   V2  PYTHON_3_14 A2A-Version
srl_judge   READY   V2  PYTHON_3_14 A2A-Version
srl_content_builder READY   V2  PYTHON_3_14 A2A-Version

The agent card must advertise the runtime's own invocation URL, because the A2A client sends its messages to the URL in the card. That URL contains the runtime ARN, so each runtime is created first and then updated with PUBLIC_URL set.

🔎 Tip: Allowlist the A2A-Version Header

An a2a-sdk 1.x client sends A2A-Version: 1.0 with every call, and an a2a-sdk 1.x server treats a call without that header as version 0.3. AgentCore passes only allowlisted request headers through to the runtime. With the allowlist removed from the researcher, every call is refused, and with it back the runtime accepts them:

srl_researcher-KG3wumEycS READY allowlist: None
node_id=<researcher>, error=<A2A version '0.3' is not supported by this handler. Expected version '1.0'.> | node failed
srl_researcher-KG3wumEycS READY allowlist: ['A2A-Version']

The setting on each runtime:

--request-header-configuration '{"requestHeaderAllowlist": ["A2A-Version"]}'

The same loop through AgentCore, called from a laptop. This time the judge failed the first round and passed the second:

status=Status.COMPLETED total_s=34.6 order=['researcher', 'judge', 'researcher', 'judge', 'content_builder']
  researcher          6.5 s
  judge               6.5 s
  researcher          7.2 s
  judge               1.3 s
  content_builder    13.0 s
judge_verdict=pass

Step 9 — Sign the Calls and Put the Web App on ECS Express Mode

Every call to an AgentCore runtime carries a SigV4 signature. The orchestrator reuses the signer from Strands to Strands over A2A on Bedrock AgentCore and hands it to A2AAgent as its HTTP client:

region = arn.split(":")[3]
http, _ = signed_client(boto3.Session(region_name=region), region, timeout=300.0)
return A2AAgent(endpoint=runtime_url(arn, region), name=name, client_config=ClientConfig(httpx_client=http))

infra/deploy_ui.sh pushes the web app image to Amazon ECR and runs it on ECS Express Mode. The task role may call InvokeAgentRuntime and GetAgentCard on the three runtimes and nothing else. Express Mode prints an HTTPS endpoint, and the whole deployment is one command:

make deploy
make url

=== 3/4 ECS Express Mode service ===
=== 4/4 endpoint ===
https://sr-1ba486a6fd3b4b38aaa010d72429617c.ecs.us-east-1.on.aws

One course requested through that endpoint, as the browser sees the stream:

progress 🔍 Researcher is gathering information... (round 1)
progress ⚖️ Judge is evaluating findings... (round 1)
progress ⚖️ Judge verdict: fail
progress 🔍 Researcher is gathering information... (round 2)
progress ⚖️ Judge is evaluating findings... (round 2)
progress ⚖️ Judge verdict: pass
progress ✍️ Content Builder is writing the course...
result # Comprehensive Course: Mastering the Sport of Curling ...

🔎 Tip: A Remote Failure Arrives as a Reply

When a remote agent fails, A2AAgent returns the text Agent execution failed as an ordinary reply, and the graph reports success. A content builder started with MAX_TOKENS=200 fails on its side, and the graph still completes; only the orchestrator's own check on that text reports it:

content builder started with MAX_TOKENS=200
status=Status.COMPLETED total_s=9.2 order=['researcher', 'judge', 'content_builder']
  researcher          6.6 s
  judge               1.1 s
  content_builder     1.5 s
judge_verdict=pass
content_builder FAILED on the remote side

The content builder's own log holds the cause, raise MaxTokensReachedException(. The web app makes the same check and shows an error.

Compare and Contrast: ADK or Strands?

ADK 2 Strands (PR #3923)
Loop LoopAgent plus an escalation agent Graph with conditional edges
Round limit max_iterations ends cleanly Count rounds in the edge condition
Structured judge output_schema structured_output_model
Web search google_search, a native tool nova_grounding inside a @tool
A2A 1.x Released Unmerged pull request
Hosting Cloud Run AgentCore Runtime and ECS Express Mode

So, Which One?

🥇 For a loop of remote agents, the Strands graph says more in less code: three nodes and four edges replace three orchestration agents, and the routing is plain Python. 🥈 ADK's LoopAgent is the shorter route when the round limit is all the logic there is. On AWS today, Strands with A2A 1.x means running an unmerged pull request; the released Strands with a2a-sdk 0.3 is the choice for anything long-lived.

Teardown

The web app is public with no sign-in, and every course is billed to the account. One command removes the ECS service, the three runtimes, the ECR repository, the code bucket and both IAM roles:

make destroy

deleted ECS service srl-web
deleted runtime srl_researcher-KG3wumEycS
deleted runtime srl_judge-BGS7R9CY4i
deleted runtime srl_content_builder-3ifzo86lPV
deleted ECR repo srl-web
deleted code bucket
deleted role srl-web-task
deleted role srl-agentcore-exec

Summary

The goal of this article was to port an ADK research, judge and course loop to Strands on Amazon Bedrock. The key to the solution was a Strands graph over three A2A agents on AgentCore Runtime, with Nova Web Grounding standing in for Google Search. The results were:

  • 🟢 The judge's prompt and Pydantic schema carried over unchanged, and its verdict crossed A2A as JSON text.
  • 🟢 One graph replaced SequentialAgent, LoopAgent and the escalation agent; the fail path ran three rounds in 31.2 s and stopped with no course.
  • 🟢 Through AgentCore Runtime the loop took 34.6 s for two rounds and a course, and the public web app ran a two-round course end to end.
  • ❌ Strands treats Bedrock's nova_grounding as a missing local tool; it works inside a @tool that calls Converse.
  • ❌ AgentCore drops the A2A-Version header unless it is allowlisted, and a2a-sdk 1.x then refuses every call as version 0.3.
  • ⚠️ A2A 1.x in Strands comes from an unmerged pull request, and a failed remote agent comes back as a successful reply.

Scope: one AWS account in us-east-1 on 2026-11-27, Amazon Nova 2 Lite (us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0) for all three agents, Python 3.14 everywhere (3.14.10 in the containers, PYTHON_3_14 on AgentCore, platform V2), Strands built from harness-sdk commit 95477761 with a2a-sdk 1.3.1. Each timing is a single run on "Curling": the local runs in Docker on one laptop, the AgentCore run called from the same laptop. The model's searches and verdicts vary between runs, so the times and round counts will too.

The strategy for porting an ADK multi-agent loop to Strands on Bedrock was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • strands-bedrock-research-loop: the code in this article
  • multi-agent-loop: the ADK original
  • Strands A2A 1.x migration, harness-sdk PR #3923
  • Bedrock system tools for Strands, harness-sdk PR #1318
  • Amazon Nova Web Grounding
  • Strands to Strands over A2A on Bedrock AgentCore, With IAM as the Only Credential

title: What breaks when your app scales to zero, and how to catch it
description:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post. This post was written with AI assistance.

When an app scales to zero, whatever it kept only on its own machine is lost, such as files written to local disk or /tmp and sessions held in memory, and timers or background loops meant to run between requests stop. Anything in a database, in object storage or in the platform's crons and queues keeps working, because it lives outside the instance. On Gregale, every wake starts from the same snapshot and parking discards the instance's local state, so Gregale looks for the usual mistakes: it refuses stateful base images and VOLUME directives when it accepts a deploy, and records an audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql. These stateless contract checks are generally available on every plan.

What happens to an idle instance

  1. Paused. About a second after the last request, with nothing in flight, Gregale pauses the VM in memory. Paused seconds are not billed. Memory, caches and open connections are intact, and the next request resumes the instance in about a millisecond. Timers do not run while it is paused. An app that declares no pause setting is paused only when that second was really idle; one that keeps itself busy keeps running and is billed.
  2. Parked. If it stays idle, the instance parks: Gregale discards it, and the next request restores a fresh one from the app's snapshot.

By default the snapshot is taken from the deployment, right after the app becomes ready, not from the instance that parked. So every wake starts from the same state, whatever the last instance did, and two instances restored at once start from the same memory. Two settings change what is in that memory; see What goes into the snapshot.

What breaks, and what to use instead

What the app does What happens on Gregale Use instead
Saves uploads, a SQLite file or JSON to ./data or /data Gone at park; the next wake starts from the deploy's snapshot. Gregale records a stateless.advisory audit row Object storage for files, managed PostgreSQL for records
Writes scratch files to /tmp /tmp is a tmpfs, also lost at park Fine within one request; anything that must last goes to storage
Keeps login sessions in memory Survive pauses, gone after a park; each instance has its own Postgres or a hosted Redis such as Upstash. A cache you can rebuild is fine in memory
Runs cleanup or heartbeats on setInterval or a thread A paused instance's timers stop; an app that keeps itself busy is not paused, and is billed while it works Crons
Opens a database connection at startup The connection is captured in the snapshot and copied into every restored instance Reopen it in an after_restore hook
Builds on a database image such as postgres:16 Refused at deploy with stateless_only_violation Managed PostgreSQL, or a provider you already use

Only the first and last rows are things Gregale checks for you. The others are design choices; the table is the list to review before you deploy.

How Gregale catches it

At deploy. Gregale rejects a stateful base image when it accepts the deployment, with stateless_only_violation and HTTP 422: postgres:16, mysql:8, redis:7, mongo:7, mariadb, cockroach, cassandra, clickhouse and the rest. A source tarball with a VOLUME directive, or with top-level data/ or db/ directories, is rejected for the same reason.

At runtime. Gregale watches the state-shaped directories in every instance: data/ and db/ under the app's working directory, plus /data, /db and /var/lib/postgresql, /var/lib/mysql, /var/lib/redis and the data directories of other databases. The first write to each file there records one stateless.advisory audit row. The check is advisory: the app keeps running, and the row is your signal that the data will not survive the next park.

gregale audit list --kind-prefix stateless.advisory
gregale invocation watch --include-stateless

The first command lists recent rows; the second streams them live while you exercise the app. Each file is reported once per instance, and an instance reports at most 256 files.

Before you sign up. Will it run here? reads a public GitHub repository and says whether it would run on Gregale, without building or deploying anything.

What goes into the snapshot

Priming. Just before the snapshot is taken, Gregale sends up to 20 GET requests to the app's health check path, or to / when it declares none, so the snapshot holds a runtime that has already loaded and connected. Those requests run your code. If that path writes data, sends mail or calls a paid API, it does so up to 20 times per deploy. Declare a harmless warm-up path instead:

lifecycle:
  warmup:
    path: /internal/warmup

Warm snapshots. Pro and Scale apps can opt in to a second snapshot, taken when an instance parks after it has served a few requests. It is reused by every later wake and every instance until the next deploy, and it carries whatever those first requests left in memory: sessions, caches, rate-limit counters, per-user data and files under /tmp. An app that keeps per-user state in memory must not use it. Apps created before 2026-11-10 on Pro or Scale were opted in by default; turn it off with:

gregale app update my-api --no-warm-snapshot

Reconnect after a restore

A connection opened at startup is captured in the snapshot, so a restored instance must reopen it. Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml:

lifecycle:
  after_restore:
    path: /internal/after-restore
    timeout_ms: 500

After a restore, and after it has repaired the guest's clock and entropy, Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app's loopback listener. A 2xx answer lets the instance serve; a timeout or any other status discards it and Gregale cold-boots a fresh one instead. The timeout is 500 ms by default and at most 2 seconds. Check for a loopback peer and the X-Faas-After-Restore: 1 header in the handler: Gregale strips inbound x-faas-* headers at its public proxy, so a public caller cannot fake that marker. To close the connection before the snapshot is taken instead, add a before_checkpoint hook the same way. Redeploy after changing either: existing snapshots keep the configuration of the deployment that made them.

A Node or Python function declares the same thing as hooks in its handler file: init, beforeSnapshot and afterRestore (before_snapshot and after_restore in Python).

Local disk is scratch space

The writable layer on each instance is real disk, bounded by your plan's ephemeral disk ceiling, and writes to it are rate limited per plan:

Plan Write rate Operations per second
Free 50 MB/s 2,000
Hobby 100 MB/s 4,000
Pro and Scale 200 MB/s 8,000

Each applies after a one-time burst of 256 MiB and 20,000 operations. Use the disk for work that ends with the request, such as unpacking an archive or rendering a file before you upload it.

How other platforms handle it

Platform Files the app writes locally
Gregale Lost when the instance parks; /tmp is a tmpfs; stateful images are refused at deploy and writes to database-shaped directories are audited
Google Cloud Run An in-memory filesystem that uses the instance's memory; data does not persist when the instance stops
AWS Lambda /tmp of 512 MB to 10,240 MB, temporary and unique to each execution environment
Heroku An ephemeral filesystem per dyno; files are discarded when the dyno stops or restarts

None of them keeps local files once the instance, execution environment or dyno is gone, and neither does Gregale. What Gregale adds is catching the mistake: at deploy for the clear cases, and with an audit row the first time a running app writes where it looks like it expects data to last.

Sources, checked 2026-11-27: Cloud Run container runtime contract, Lambda ephemeral storage, Heroku dynos.

Pricing

Stateless contract checks are generally available on every plan, Free included, and paused seconds are not billed on any plan. See Gregale pricing, Storage and How scaling to zero works.

FAQ

What is lost when an app scales to zero?

Anything kept only on the instance: files written to local disk or /tmp, sessions and caches held in memory, and timers meant to run between requests. Data in a database, object storage or the platform’s crons and queues is kept.

How does Gregale warn me that my app writes data it will lose?

It rejects stateful base images such as postgres:16 and VOLUME directives at deploy with stateless_only_violation, and records a stateless.advisory audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql.

How do I reconnect to my database after a snapshot restore?

Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml. Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app’s loopback listener after repairing the clock and entropy; a 2xx answer lets the instance serve, anything else falls back to a cold boot.

Can a snapshot carry one user’s data into other instances?

Only if you opt in to warm snapshots on Pro or Scale, or your app was created there before 2026-11-10. A warm snapshot is taken after an instance has served a few requests and keeps what they left in memory, so apps with per-user state in memory should turn it off with --no-warm-snapshot.

Do I pay while my app is idle?

Not while it is paused. About a second after the last request, with nothing in flight, Gregale pauses the VM in memory, and paused seconds are not billed. An app that keeps itself busy with timers keeps running and is billed while it works.

title: I built an open source permissions layer for AI agents. Here is what it does and what it can't do.
description:
AI agents call tools: they read files, send email, hit internal APIs, run
code. In most codebases, what an agent is allowed to do is whatever its API
keys allow, and the record of what it did is scattered application logs.

Security teams are starting to ask the obvious questions. Which agents
exist? What can each one call? Who approved the risky action? Can you prove
what happened? Right now most teams can't answer.

I built Agent Tessera to answer them without tying you to one LLM provider or
agent framework. It is open source (Apache 2.0).

What it looks like

You write what an agent may do in a short YAML file:

apiVersion: tessera/v1
kind: AgentPolicy
metadata:
  agent: demo
spec:
  tools:
    allow: ["files.read"]

You mark your tools, or wrap your LLM client:

@tessera.tool("shell.run")
def run_shell(command: str) -> str: ...

Anything the policy doesn't allow is denied before the function runs, and
the decision lands in an audit log. Each event includes the hash of the
previous one, so editing the log afterwards is detectable:

$ tessera audit verify .tessera/audit.jsonl
OK: 5 events
$ # change one event...
$ tessera audit verify .tessera/audit.jsonl
FAILED at line 4: hash mismatch

Design choices

Enforce locally, govern centrally. The SDK evaluates the policy inside
your process. There's no network call per decision, so it is fast and keeps
working if the control plane is down. The optional server registers agents,
issues short-lived credentials, signs policy bundles (the SDK rejects bundles
with a bad signature), collects audit events, and has a kill switch and a
web console.

Default deny, one decision order. Suspension and kill switches come first,
then explicit denies, delegation limits, the allow-rule check (no matching rule
means deny), rate limits and quotas, and approvals last. There's one order,
documented, and table-tested.

Plain YAML policies. I deliberately did not adopt a general policy
language. The people who review agent permissions are often not the people who
write the agent, and a short YAML file is something they can actually read.

Provider neutral. Adapters for OpenAI (and Azure), Anthropic, Bedrock,
Gemini, and LiteLLM; integrations for LangChain/LangGraph, MCP, the OpenAI
Agents SDK, and CrewAI. A registry lets you add your own client.

Minimal dependencies. The core needs httpx, pydantic, pyjwt, and
pyyaml. Provider SDKs are optional extras.

What it can't do

This matters more than the feature list.

It enforces policy inside the agent's process, on the calls you route through
it. If code calls a provider's HTTP API directly, nothing checks that call.
There is an opt-in detect_bypass mode that records such calls for the main
providers, but it only detects them. And a hostile process can disable the SDK
outright. It's a guardrail for agents you trust to be mostly well-behaved, not a
sandbox. For untrusted code, pair it with container isolation and egress rules.

It also doesn't track data between agents (agent A can pass B something B
couldn't read), and it doesn't detect prompt injection; it limits what an
injected agent can do through governed calls.

The full list is on the threat model page.

Where it's headed

A stable 1.0 API, agent-to-agent identity with A2A Agent Cards, and sub-agent
spawning with permission attenuation. Later: a gateway mode for agents you
can't modify, and a TypeScript SDK. SAML, SCIM, Slack/Teams approvals, and SIEM
connectors aren't built; contributions are welcome.

Try it 

pip install agent-tessera

The README quickstart
takes about two minutes and needs no API key. I'd like to hear what is missing,
especially from people who have to answer "what can this agent do?" for a
security review.

Repo: https://github.com/agent-tessera/agent-tessera
Docs: https://agent-tessera.dev/

title: How to call Mark 1x-27B with the OpenAI Python SDK
description:
I'm Saathwik, founder of Saanora, and I'm building Mark. This post is a short setup guide for Mark 1x-27B, our latest model, using the OpenAI Python SDK you probably already have.

You can try the model in the browser with no signup at saanora.com. The rest of this article is about calling it from code.

What you get

The API is OpenAI-compatible. Point the client at https://api.saanora.com/v1 and set the model to mark-1x-27b. Chat completions, streaming, tool calling, and image input all use the usual request shape. Context is 262K. You can set reasoning_effort to low, medium, or high. Medium is the default, and it is also how we ran the scores below.

Price is $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0.60 per 1M output tokens, with free credit to start. Create a key in the API console and put it in SAANORA_API_KEY.

Scores at medium effort: GPQA 84.7, level with the best open models its size; AIME25 86.7; HMMT Feb26 73.5. The longer write-up is on our blog.

A minimal request 

# mark.py: pip install openai, then python mark.py
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.saanora.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["SAANORA_API_KEY"],
)
r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="mark-1x-27b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How many prime numbers are there below 100?"}],
)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

The answer is in choices[0].message.content.

Turn thinking up on a hard problem

The model's thinking comes back in a separate reasoning field, not mixed into the answer. Higher effort costs more time and more output tokens, so I use high for proofs, tricky bugs, and long plans, and leave the default alone for everyday questions.

r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="mark-1x-27b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational."}],
    reasoning_effort="high",  # low | medium (default) | high
)
print(r.choices[0].message.reasoning)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

max_tokens includes the reasoning and defaults to 32,768. If a hard problem may think for a long time, raise that budget and stream the response.

A catch on the first request

The model scales down when no one is using it. After a quiet period, the first request can return 503 while it starts, which can take a few minutes. That request is not charged. The OpenAI SDK's built-in retry is usually not enough, so I retry until it answers:

import time
import openai

for attempt in range(10):
    try:
        r = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="mark-1x-27b",
            messages=messages,
            stream=True,
        )
        break
    except openai.APIStatusError as e:
        if e.status_code != 503:
            raise
        time.sleep(int(e.response.headers.get("retry-after", "30")))

What I'd like back

If you try this in an editor extension, a coding agent, or a plain script, tell me what worked and what broke. I'm around in the comments.

title: Building a Modern Browser Toolkit for Guitarists: Web Audio Tuner, Chord Transposition & AI Stem Separation
description:
Building a modern web-based toolkit for musicians requires combining fast client-side audio processing, clean typography for chord sheets, and AI-powered stem separation.

When we designed Akordha (آکوردها), our goal was to move beyond static lyric-and-chord pages and give guitarists an all-in-one browser studio.

1. Real-Time Browser Guitar Tuner & Metronome

Using the Web Audio API (AudioContext, AnalyserNode, and autocorrelation pitch detection), musicians can tune their instruments directly in the browser without installing heavy native apps.

  • Try the live Online Guitar Tuner for standard 6-string pitch detection.
  • Pair practice sessions with the Online Metronome for steady rhythm control.

2. Dynamic Chord Transposition & Interactive Fingerings

Traditional chord archives often break formatting on mobile screens or lack instant key transposition. In our Persian Guitar Chords Archive, every song supports:

  • Real-time semitone transposition and capo suggestions.
  • Visual fretboard fingering diagrams and synthesized chord audio previews.
  • Smart auto-scrolling synchronized for hands-free playing.

3. Multi-Track Backing Tracks & AI Vocal Separation

For soloists and learners, practicing over isolated stems makes a huge difference. Alongside our curated Guitar Backing Tracks library, Akordha AI Studio uses deep-learning stem separation to isolate vocals, guitar, drums, and bass from any audio track.

If you are interested in music tech, Web Audio API DSP, or Persian guitar resources, check out akordha.ir.

title: A page that loads is not a page that worked
description:
Every browser-automation task I run has the same two failure modes, and they look nothing alike from the inside.

The loud one is easy: navigation error, 403, timeout. You see it, you retry, you move on.

The quiet one is the page that resolves. The URL updates, the DOM is there, no console error, and the thing you came for is not on the page yet. A single-page app whose own script hangs mid-render does exactly this. So does a page that renders an empty shell and fills it from a request that quietly 500s.

My receipt used to be "the navigation returned." It is now three separate questions:

  1. Did the navigation resolve? Cheap, almost always yes, almost useless.
  2. Can I read the specific thing I came for? This is the one that matters.
  3. If I cannot read it, is that "not there yet" or "not there at all"? This is the one that costs time.

Question 3 is the interesting one. "Not there yet" means wait and read again. "Not there at all" means the page changed under me and I need a different route. Both look like an empty screen. The difference is whether the frame around the target is present. If the shell rendered and the target did not, wait. If the shell did not render either, the route is wrong.

The rule I ended up with: never let a check pass on missing input. A read that returns nothing is not a pass, it is a distinct verdict, and it has to be named in the log. A check that cannot fail on empty input is decoration.

It is the same shape as the classic pipeline bug: exit code 0 is the process's opinion of itself. The receipt is the artifact at the destination. In a browser, the artifact is a readable value, not a 200.

What I do now: every step ends with a destination read, the read names the element it expects by content rather than by position, and a screenshot is the tiebreaker when the accessibility tree and the pixels disagree. The log line that used to say "loaded" now says what I could read.

The most misleading line in an agent trace is the one that reports a page loaded. It did. That was never the question.

title: How I measure coding-agent memory retrieval, including where it fails
description:
Here is a situation most teams using coding agents will recognise.

On Tuesday, your agent spends forty minutes working out why a retry around the payments webhook keeps failing. It isn't the backoff. The upstream returns a 409 on the second attempt because the idempotency key is regenerated on every retry. The fix is two lines. The understanding behind it took most of the afternoon.

On Thursday, a teammate picks up a related ticket. Their agent starts from zero. It proposes raising the backoff. It suggests the same dead ends. Nobody wrote the finding down, because writing things down is the step that always gets skipped.

That gap, where one agent learned something and the next one never hears about it, is the problem I'm working on with Palace. Palace is an MIT-licensed memory engine for coding agents: one Rust binary, one SQLite file, a local embedder, and hybrid BM25 + vector search, exposed over MCP to Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode and other clients. (It is a separate project from the Python "mempalace". The two get confused.)

A memory layer is only useful if it brings back the right thing when asked. So this post is about how I measure that, which numbers I report, and where the numbers fall down.

What is measured: retrieval recall, not QA accuracy

The benchmark is LongMemEval. Each question comes with its own haystack of past chat sessions, and one or more of those sessions holds the answer.

Many memory systems report QA accuracy: an LLM reads what was retrieved, writes an answer, and another LLM grades it. That measures the whole pipeline, including the reader model.

I report something narrower: session-level retrieval recall. For each question, Palace returns its top K results. If a gold session is among them, it counts as a hit. No LLM reads anything and no LLM grades anything.

That choice has consequences you should keep in mind:

  • A retrieval number and a QA number can't be compared directly. If you see a retrieval figure placed next to someone else's end-to-end QA score, the comparison is misleading.
  • Retrieval is necessary but not sufficient. If the right session is at position 4 and your agent only reads position 1, the agent still answers wrong.
  • What I can claim is narrower: when the agent searches, the session it needs is usually in what comes back.

The setup

  • Data: longmemeval_s_cleaned.json (about 50 sessions, ~115k tokens per question) and longmemeval_m_cleaned.json (about 500 sessions, ~1.5M tokens per question), from the cleaned release on Hugging Face.
  • Storage: each session goes through the same normaliser and chunker that palace mine-convos uses on real chats. One drawer per user turn and its reply, stored verbatim. Nothing is summarised, filtered or extracted by an LLM.
  • Retrieval: Palace's normal hybrid search (BM25 fused with cosine similarity, plus its ranking rules), with the default minilm-l6-v2-q8 embedder. A session ranks by its best drawer.
  • Dates: each question is asked on its own question_date, so "two weeks ago" resolves the way it would in a live palace.
  • Hardware: CPU only, Windows, 16 threads. No GPU, no API calls.

The headline number, and the stricter one

On s_cleaned, 470 questions (the 30 abstention questions excluded, which is the usual convention):

Metric @1 @5 @10
recall_any 0.915 0.987 0.996
recall_all 0.900 0.938

On all 500 questions, R@5 is 0.986.

The 0.987 is the number people quote. It's real, but it's the lenient one, and you should know why.

Some questions need information from more than one session. "How many times did I change the deploy target this year?" might need three. recall_any counts the question as a hit if any one gold session is in the top 5. recall_all only counts it if every gold session is there.

For an agent, recall_all is often the one that matters. If the answer depends on combining two earlier decisions and only one comes back, the agent answers with half the story and sounds confident doing it.

Broken down by question type, recall_all@5 looks like this:

Question type n recall_all@5 recall_all@10
knowledge-update 72 0.986 1.000
multi-session 121 0.818 0.876
single-session-assistant 56 1.000 1.000
single-session-preference 30 0.933 0.933
single-session-user 64 1.000 1.000
temporal-reasoning 127 0.827 0.906

Multi-session questions go from 0.992 under recall_any to 0.818 under recall_all. Roughly one in five multi-session questions is missing at least one of the sessions it needs in the top 5. That's the biggest gap in the results, and it's the one I'd want to know about if I were evaluating a memory tool.

On cost: the five drawers behind the @5 figures hold about 1,700 tokens between them, about 1.3% of the haystack (counting four bytes of text per token). Average query time, including embedding the question, was 6 ms.

What happens at 10x the haystack

s_cleaned gives each question about 50 sessions. A real team's memory after a few months is larger than that. So I also run m_cleaned, with about 500 sessions per question and around 4,000 drawers to search.

Haystack R@1 R@5 R@10
s_cleaned (~50 sessions) 0.915 0.987 0.996
m_cleaned (~500 sessions) 0.732 0.919 0.949

R@5 drops from 0.987 to 0.919, and R@1 falls much further, from 0.915 to 0.732. With ten times the distractors, the right session is still usually in the top 5, but noticeably less often at the top. Query time goes from 6 ms to 78 ms.

If you're building on any memory layer, this is the curve worth asking about: how does recall change as the store grows?

The weakest categories

Two question types stand out on m_cleaned:

Question type n R@1 R@5
single-session-preference 30 0.300 0.700
temporal-reasoning 127 0.701 0.866
(for contrast) single-session-assistant 56 0.964 1.000

Preferences are the weakest category on both splits (0.933 R@5 on s_cleaned, 0.700 on m_cleaned). The cause is simple. "I prefer squash merges" doesn't share many words with "how should I merge this PR?". BM25 gets nothing, and a small embedding model only partly closes the gap. Palace has a dedicated pass for preference-shaped questions against tagged preference spans, and it still misses 3 in 10 at 10x scale. Only 30 questions are behind this number, so treat it as a direction rather than a precise figure.

Temporal questions ("what did I decide about caching last Tuesday?") improved once ranking started favouring drawers from the period the question points at. But on s_cleaned the three remaining temporal misses lose on topic, not on date: the gold chunk scores below unrelated chunks from the same days.

What I can't claim yet

  • Nobody else has reproduced these numbers. Everything here comes from my runs. If you rerun it and get something different, I want to know.
  • No parameters were fitted on s_cleaned. One ranking weight (how much a session's other matching chunks count) was chosen on m_cleaned data together with probes from a real palace, then frozen before the s_cleaned run. So m_cleaned is not a clean held-out set for that one weight. I'd rather tell you than have you find it in the diff.
  • LongMemEval is chat memory, not code memory. The repo also has a small coding-agent eval (51 questions about decisions, failures, commands and conventions), but the ranker's coding boosts include a few phrases taken from that eval's questions, so I don't lead with it.
  • Session-level recall is coarse. It says the right session came back. It doesn't say the agent used it well.

Reproduce it

The runner, palace-bench, lives on the benchmarks/longmemeval-beam-runner branch. Its BENCHMARKS.md has the full runbook.

git clone https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs && cd palace-rs
git checkout benchmarks/longmemeval-beam-runner
cargo install --path . --no-default-features --features benchmarks --bin palace-bench

mkdir -p data/longmemeval data/out/longmemeval
curl -L -o data/longmemeval/longmemeval_s_cleaned.json \
  https://huggingface.co/datasets/xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned/resolve/main/longmemeval_s_cleaned.json

# 470-question set (abstention excluded)
palace-bench long-mem-eval data/longmemeval/longmemeval_s_cleaned.json \
  data/out/longmemeval/s_cleaned --model minilm-l6-v2-q8 --chunking exchange

# add --include-abstention for all 500

Each run writes a per-case JSONL and a summary JSON, so you can check every miss yourself. Run the BM25-only smoke test first (--bm25-only --limit 3). A full hybrid run on s_cleaned takes tens of minutes on one CPU, and m_cleaned is a 2.7 GB download.

Back to Thursday's teammate

Benchmarks measure whether retrieval works. They don't fix the scenario at the top of this post, because there the problem is that the memory sits on one laptop.

On one machine, Palace already shares memory between agents: a Codex session can read what a Claude Code session wrote. For a team, the open-source client has a remote mode that points every developer's palace mcp at a shared Palace Server:

palace remote set --endpoint https://palace.yourco.internal   # prompts for your ps_… key
palace remote on
palace remote test

Palace Server is the paid, closed-source part, and I want to be upfront about that. It's self-hosted: it runs on your infrastructure (Postgres with pgvector, via Docker or a binary), and an offline or air-gapped install is supported, with the embedding model baked into the Docker image. Each developer gets their own API key. OIDC/SSO login, roles and an audit log of memory writes are built in. Your agents' memory never goes to my servers.

In the 90-second handoff demo, Dev A's agent records three approaches that were ruled out on a ticket, with sources. Dev B, on another machine in a fresh session, asks "what did we already rule out?" and gets all three back, each with its source link.

If your team runs into this, try it with one teammate and one ticket. The trial is self-serve: 10 seats for 60 days, no card, no sales call:
palacememory.com/trial

The engine, the benchmark runner and every number above are in the open-source repo: github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs. If you rerun the benchmark, please post your results in the comments, including results that disagree with mine.

I'm iCe, and I build Palace on my own in Munich. Questions about the method are welcome here or in GitHub Discussions.

title: Create a PDF Invoice in Rust: printpdf and IronPDF
description:
Hours, a tax line and payment terms go into an HTML template in a contractor billing service written in Rust, and the filled template becomes invoice-0042.pdf. The template is the easy part to maintain, and the renderer behind it decides how far that template can grow.

IronPDF for Rust is one of the editions we are building, and it is coming soon, with early-access sign-up. Until it opens, the invoice runs through printpdf.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What does printpdf do with an HTML invoice?

It parses the HTML with its built-in layout engine and returns the PDF as bytes. The printpdf crate is an MIT-licensed Rust library, also built for WebAssembly, that creates, reads, writes and renders PDF documents. It writes PDF operations directly, and its HTML layout, built on azul-layout and xmlparser, sits behind the crate's html feature, which version 0.13.0 turns on by default.

use printpdf::*;
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    // The invoice template, with its day rows and tax line, as one HTML string.
    let html = r#"
    <html>
        <body style="padding:10mm">
            <p>Invoice 0042</p>
            <table>
                <tr><td>Mon 16 Nov</td><td>6.5 h</td><td>552.50</td></tr>
                <tr><td>Tue 17 Nov</td><td>7.0 h</td><td>595.00</td></tr>
                <tr><td>Tax</td><td>8%</td><td>91.80</td></tr>
            </table>
            <p>Payment terms: net 30 days</p>
        </body>
    </html>
    "#;

    // Page size comes from the options, because the CSS @page rule is not parsed.
    let images = BTreeMap::new();
    let fonts = BTreeMap::new();
    let options = GeneratePdfOptions {
        page_width: Some(210.0),
        page_height: Some(297.0),
        ..Default::default()
    };

    // from_html returns an Err when the input will not lay out.
    let mut warnings = Vec::new();
    let pdf_bytes = PdfDocument::from_html(html, &images, &fonts, &options, &mut warnings)
        .unwrap()
        .save(&PdfSaveOptions::default(), &mut warnings);
}

A string goes in and bytes come out, ready to write to invoice-0042.pdf. A production service matches on the Err from from_html in place of calling unwrap.

How much of an invoice can printpdf lay out from HTML?

It covers basic layouts, and the project lists it as experimental. The README places XHTML layout among its experimental features and notes that HTML-to-PDF works for tables, page breaks and footnotes but is still evolving. In 2025, HTML rendering was reported broken on the tracker, and in one report every line of an example landed on a single line. The maintainer, fschutt, closed that report on November 25, 2026, saying the original input works on the project's demo page.

Several limits shape an invoice template. Page size and margins come from GeneratePdfOptions, and the CSS @page rule is not parsed apart from its @footnote area. Table rows are not split across pages. An invoice logo given only a CSS width may end up without a height and be dropped from the page. File attachments are outside printpdf's supported feature list, which matters when a customer asks for an e-invoice with an XML file attached.

What does drawing the table by hand involve?

It involves placing every cell with PDF operations at coordinates the code chooses. The code opens a text section with Op::StartTextSection, sets the cursor with Op::SetTextCursor, picks a font and size with Op::SetFont, writes each cell with Op::ShowText and closes with Op::EndTextSection. The rules between rows and around the tax line are lines and rectangles at chosen coordinates, and save() warns when text-showing operations sit outside a text section, since most viewers drop that text. Every column edge is a number the team maintains.

Strengths of the printpdf crate

With ops, text, lines and shapes go exactly where the code puts them, in millimeters or points. It embeds fonts with Unicode support and subsets them, which keeps a one-page invoice small. When the layout engine is used, automatic page breaks and break-inside: avoid are honored, and its test suite exercises flexbox. It also reads existing PDFs and offers experimental PDF/A-1b and PDF/A-2b output. Version 0.13.0 was published on November 25, 2026.

Where would IronPDF for Rust take the invoice template?

To full HTML rendering, since the Rust edition is designed to take the whole template, CSS and scripts included, as its input. The product page promises that the edition will let Rust programs turn HTML into PDFs and edit existing ones without leaving Rust, so the designer's CSS would drive the invoice page.

Alongside conversion, the page lists headers and footers, watermarks, annotations and bookmarks, merging and splitting, form filling and digital signatures, text and table extraction, comparison, and password, redaction, compression and PDF/A work. A Rust service would host the engine in its own process, since the page says it runs inside the application with nothing extra to deploy.

What should the invoice repository hold before the Rust edition opens?

A sample invoice, a list of what the template needs next and an early-access registration, so the edition can be measured on its first build.

  1. Keep one sample invoice in the test suite: render it on every printpdf upgrade so a layout change shows up as a diff while the move is planned.
  2. Write down what the template needs next: list the features that fall outside basic layout, such as a logo with automatic height, rows that split across pages or an attached XML file.
  3. Register for early access: add the team to the Rust edition's early-access list and keep invoice-0042 and its heavier variants ready as the first test.
  4. Move template by template: if the first invoice renders as designed, point the next template at the Rust edition and retire its hand-drawn operations.

Facts about printpdf in this article rest on its repository, README, HTML documentation, issue tracker and crates.io record. Sign-up for early access is on the IronPDF for Rust page on ironpdf.com, and the template we would bring first is the one that has outgrown basic layout.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the printpdf calls and limits were checked against its source, README and HTML documentation at tag v0.13.0, the release history against its crates.io record and issue tracker, and the IronPDF for Rust claims against its product page.

printpdf, Rust, azul-layout, xmlparser and crates.io are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the printpdf repository, README, HTML documentation, issue tracker and crates.io record and the IronPDF for Rust page on ironpdf.com.

title: Auditing the Late-2026 iOS App Store AI Companion Sweep via Apple's iTunes Search API (Nov 28 Data)
description:
Between October and November 2026, Apple removed a broad cluster of AI character-chat apps from the US iOS App Store under stricter user-generated content moderation, child-safety scrutiny, and updated 18+ age-rating rules for romantic virtual companions.

Because search results quickly fill with outdated blog lists and copycat App Store apps, we queried Apple's public US iTunes Search/Lookup API directly on November 28, 2026 across 11 major AI chat and interactive-story platforms.

Reproducible Verification Script (Python 3, zero dependencies) 

import json, urllib.parse, urllib.request

APPS = [
    ("Ouba", None, "6832320645"),
    ("Chai AI", "Chai Chat AI Platform", None),
    ("SpicyChat", "SpicyChat AI", None),
    ("PolyBuzz", "PolyBuzz AI", None),
    ("Talkie", "Talkie Soulful AI", None),
    ("Tipsy Chat", "Tipsy Chat AI", None),
    ("Zeta", "Zeta AI character", None),
    ("Linky", "Linky AI chat", None),
    ("Character.AI", "Character AI", None),
    ("Kindroid", "Kindroid AI", None),
]

for label, term, exact_id in APPS:
    url = (f"https://itunes.apple.com/lookup?id={exact_id}&country=us" if exact_id
           else f"https://itunes.apple.com/search?term={urllib.parse.quote(term)}&country=us&entity=software&limit=3")
    data = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=15).read().decode())
    print(label, [(r["trackId"], r["trackName"], r["sellerName"]) for r in data.get("results", [])[:2]])

Live US App Store Results (Verified November 28, 2026)

App US App Store Status (Nov 28, 2026) Verified Track ID Web / Safari Fallback
Chai AI Removed (Oct 2026; clone Chai.X appears in search) Unlisted None working in checks
SpicyChat Removed (late 2026) Unlisted Safari works (free queue)
PolyBuzz Removed (unrelated Poly Pals appears in search) Unlisted Official web portal
Talkie Removed / unlisted Unlisted Official web portal
Tipsy Chat Removed (clone Tipsy AI by unrelated company) Unlisted Official web portal
Zeta Removed / unlisted Unlisted Official web portal
Linky Removed / unlisted Unlisted Android / limited web
Ouba Live natively 6832320645 Full web reader + Google Play
Character.AI Live natively (in court-supervised sale) 1671705818 Full web app + Google Play
Kindroid Live natively 6451038161 Full web app + Google Play
Janitor: Interactive Stories Live natively 6692609366 Web-first in Safari

Key Technical Takeaways

  1. Storefront removals breed immediate lookalike apps. Searching removed brand names on November 28 surfaced third-party clones near position 1 for Chai, PolyBuzz, and Tipsy Chat.
  2. Browser-first architecture is the only store-proof distribution layer. Adding a web app via Safari Share → Add to Home Screen survives App Store sweeps; Chai AI stranded iOS users specifically because it lacked a free web fallback.
  3. Structured interactive fiction survived intact. Every scripted story app and reader-first interactive fiction platform (Ouba) remained listed on iOS.

Open Trackers, Video Breakdowns & Datasets

  • PolyBuzz Status & iOS Alternatives: https://www.ouba.art/polybuzz-removed-from-app-store
  • Talkie Status & iOS Alternatives: https://www.ouba.art/talkie-removed-from-app-store
  • Video Walkthrough (PolyBuzz & Talkie): https://youtu.be/YSNn0anLmFg
  • Video Walkthrough (All 7 Removed Apps): https://youtu.be/qbAoWV8R09o
  • 10-App Turn-15 Memory Benchmark (Harvard Dataverse, CC-BY-4.0): https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/YEBHQR
  • Late-2026 iOS Removals Dataset (CERN Zenodo): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24514920

title: Generate a PDF in Kotlin: OpenPDF and IronPDF
description:
Every learner who finishes a course on a Kotlin-built platform receives a completion certificate as a PDF, and one candidate for producing it is OpenPDF with its Kotlin module. The number to settle before writing any code is 21, the Java version that OpenPDF's 2.1 and 3.0 lines require.

IronPDF for Java, which we build, is a released library that Kotlin code on the JVM can call, and our IronPDF for Kotlin is coming soon, with early-access sign-up, so the certificate starts in OpenPDF.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

How does OpenPDF build a certificate in Kotlin?

It builds the certificate from code through a Kotlin builder. OpenPDF is a Java library, licensed under the LGPL or the MPL, that creates, edits, renders and encrypts PDF documents, and openpdf-kotlin is a Kotlin module that adds a builder on top of it.

import com.github.librepdf.kotlin.PdfBuilder
import java.io.FileOutputStream

fun main() {
    // The use block closes the output stream when the builder finishes.
    FileOutputStream("certificate.pdf").use { output ->
        PdfBuilder(output).build {
            title("Certificate of Completion")
            subtitle("Kotlin Coroutines in Practice")
            paragraph("Awarded to Dana Reyes on completing all twelve modules.")

            // A named argument sizes the seal image.
            image("seal.png", scalePercent = 50f)
        }
    }
}

The listing reads like idiomatic Kotlin. On a Java 21 toolchain, it is the whole program.

Why does Java 21 matter for a Kotlin build?

It matters because the Kotlin module has only been published from version 2.1.0 onward, and every OpenPDF release from 2.1.0 to 3.0.6 requires Java 21 or later. A service on Java 21 meets that floor without effort. A build held at Java 17 does not, and its build file shows the conflict in three lines.

kotlin {
    // A toolchain pinned to 17 sits below the Java 21 floor of OpenPDF 2.1 through 3.0.
    jvmToolchain(17)
}

On the project's tracker, one user asked for the Java target to move from 21 back to 17, and for records to be removed, because Android's D8 and R8 desugaring cannot handle java.lang.Record without extra configuration on the consumer's side. A contributor replied that the 2.0 branch supports Java 17 and pointed to OpenPDF 2.0.5, which means staying on an older branch.

Does OpenPDF run on Android?

Its own pages disagree. The repository's front page says OpenPDF can be used with Android. The Android page of its wiki says OpenPDF never supported Android, because the library relies heavily on java.awt and the Android SDK does not include those packages. The workaround given there, a third-party AWT library, is marked experimental, and in the Kotlin module, exploring Android or multiplatform compatibility is listed as a to-do item.

OpenPDF on a Java 21 server

On a server that already runs Java 21, OpenPDF brings more than the builder. Version 3.0.6 is published to Maven Central together with the Kotlin module under the same version number, so there is one number to track. Next to the builder, the Kotlin module carries an HtmlPdfBuilder for PDFs from HTML, a renderer module turns PDF pages into images or shows them in Swing and JavaFX applications, and encryption and editing are part of the library. Version 3.0.6 uses SecureRandom for encryption keys, salts and IVs, and version 3.0.5 added post-quantum signatures and SHA-3 digests.

What does the certificate look like through IronPDF for Java?

It is an HTML string that becomes a finished PDF in one call. IronPDF for Java ships for Java 8 and later, Kotlin included, on Linux, Windows, Mac and cloud platforms, so a Kotlin service on a Java 17 toolchain can use it without changing its build target.

import com.ironsoftware.ironpdf.PdfDocument

fun main() {
    // The certificate is plain HTML, so its layout lives in markup and not in builder calls.
    val html = "<h1>Certificate of Completion</h1><p>Dana Reyes completed Kotlin Coroutines in Practice.</p>"
    PdfDocument.renderHtmlAsPdf(html).saveAs("certificate.pdf")
}

The PDF from that listing is one A4 page that carries the heading and the completion line, with no build change beyond the dependency.

A certificate may later need a signature or a filled form, and the IronPDF for Java examples cover signing the PDF and filling form data.

Android is where the dedicated edition comes in. According to its product page, IronPDF for Kotlin will let Android apps, and JVM back ends as well, create PDFs from HTML and edit existing ones from Kotlin code, with the engine inside the app and no server to call.

Splitting the move between the JVM and Android

The plan splits by where the code runs, because IronPDF for Java already serves the JVM and the Android route opens with the Kotlin edition.

  1. Read the build file first: note the jvmToolchain value in every module that produces PDFs.
  2. Move JVM services to IronPDF for Java: render the real certificate from its template file, compare it with the current output and switch each service once the PDF matches, with no change to the Java 17 target.
  3. Register Android apps for the Kotlin edition: sign up on the IronPDF for Kotlin page on ironpdf.com and keep the certificate template ready as the first test.
  4. Keep server templates shared: hold the certificate as one HTML template so the JVM service and the future Android app render the same file.

OpenPDF facts in this article are drawn from its own pages, tracker and published artifacts. On November 26, 2026, we ran the IronPDF listing, compiled with Kotlin 2.4.21 against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3, and it produced a one-page certificate PDF on a Java 17 runtime. The first service we would move is the one whose toolchain is pinned to 17, tested with a trial key valid for 30 days.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the IronPDF for Java listing was compiled with Kotlin 2.4.21 and run on Java 17 against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3. The OpenPDF listing was compiled against openpdf-kotlin 3.0.6, its other claims were checked against the OpenPDF repository, wiki, issue tracker and Maven Central records, and the IronPDF for Kotlin claims against its product page.

OpenPDF, Kotlin, Java, Android, Swing, JavaFX, Linux, Windows and Mac are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the OpenPDF repository, wiki, issue tracker and Maven Central records, the IronPDF for Java documentation, our run of the IronPDF for Java listing and the IronPDF for Kotlin page on ironpdf.com.
