title: Why I started a VPS host in Egypt
description:
I run NileVPS, a small VPS hosting service based in Egypt, started in 2026.

Why I started it

A lot of local customers - developers and small businesses - needed simple VPS hosting they could actually pay for. International cards do not work for everyone here, so from day one we accepted crypto payments (BTC, ETH, LTC, USDT).

The stack

We resell Hetzner cloud infrastructure. Servers are KVM virtual machines on NVMe storage, in Germany (Falkenstein, Nuremberg), Finland (Helsinki), the USA (Ashburn, Hillsboro) and Singapore. Customers can run Linux or Windows Server (RDP), and the Windows license is included - that removes a cost people usually discover too late.

What customers ask for most

Two things come up again and again: Windows RDP that just works, and paying with crypto without hassle. Both are first-class on NileVPS, not afterthoughts.

The site is nilevps.com - pricing is listed there. I would honestly love feedback on the site and the order flow. Contact: support@nilevps.com

title: Supabase Backup and Restore: Dumps, Gaps and a Test Plan
description:
A Supabase backup comes from two places: the daily backup Supabase takes on paid plans, which restores inside the dashboard, and a dump you take with the CLI, which restores into any project. Most teams rely on the first and skip the second. Own both, and run the second one at least once.

This guide is for founders and developers running a live product on Supabase, including Lovable apps that use their own Supabase project. It covers where the backups live, the CLI commands from Supabase's own guide, what a restore leaves out and a drill you can run in an afternoon. It adds to our general guide to database backups for startups, which covers how much data you can afford to lose. This one stays on Supabase. Plan details, prices and commands come from Supabase's documentation and pricing page, read on 16 November 2026.

Key takeaways

  • Pro projects keep 7 days of daily backups and Team projects keep 14. Free projects have no backup retention, and Supabase recommends regular exports with supabase db dump.
  • Supabase's documentation says physical backups are not available for download, so a dump you take yourself is the only copy that leaves the platform.
  • Three dump files (roles, schema and data) and one psql command restore a database into a new project.
  • A database backup leaves out Storage files, Edge Functions, auth settings, API keys and custom role passwords. Each needs its own copy.
  • Lovable Cloud keeps its own backups outside your Supabase dashboard, so check which backend your Lovable app uses before you trust either set.

Where do Supabase backups live, and what do they cover?

They live in the dashboard under Database, then Backups, for Pro, Team and Enterprise projects. Free projects get none. Each plan keeps a different number of daily backups, and point-in-time recovery is a separate add-on.

Plan Daily backups Kept for What to add
Free Not included Nothing Export with supabase db dump and keep the file off-site, as Supabase recommends
Pro Yes 7 days Your own dump
Team Yes 14 days Your own dump
Enterprise Yes Up to 30 days Your own dump

Supabase's pricing page lists Pro from $25 a month and Team from $599 a month. Our guide to Supabase pricing works through what a real app costs on each plan.

Can you download a daily backup?

On a current project, the documentation says no. Projects on Postgres 15.8.1.079 and newer use physical backups, and Supabase's backups documentation says physical backups are not available for direct download. The dashboard restore guide covers older projects that still use logical backups. If your project is newer, the daily backup is a restore point inside Supabase and the dump in the next section is the copy you can hold yourself.

What does point-in-time recovery change?

It replaces daily backups with a restore to a moment you choose. Supabase archives write-ahead log files every two minutes by default, which gives a worst-case recovery point of two minutes. The add-on costs about $100 a month for each 7 days of retention, so 14 days costs about $200 and 28 days about $400. Enabling it stops the daily backups. A point-in-time restore replaces the current database, so Supabase advises that you restore to a new project first if you want to keep the current state.

How do you back up a Supabase database with the CLI?

Run three supabase db dump commands against your project's connection string, one each for roles, schema and data. The machine that runs them needs the Supabase CLI, Docker Desktop and the Postgres client tools that include psql.

Copy the connection string from Connect in the dashboard. Reset the database password in Database Settings if you do not have it. Use the direct connection string. If your network has no IPv6 and the project has no IPv4 add-on, use the session pooler string instead. The direct string looks like this:

postgresql://postgres:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@db.[PROJECT-REF].supabase.co:5432/postgres

Supabase's backup and restore guide gives these commands:

supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f roles.sql --role-only
supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f schema.sql
supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f data.sql --use-copy --data-only -x "storage.buckets_vectors" -x "storage.vector_indexes"

The roles file holds cluster roles. The schema file holds your tables, functions and policies. The data file holds the rows as COPY statements. The CLI reference says a default dump leaves out the schemas Supabase manages, such as auth and storage.

These commands use the --remote flag from the current CLI reference. Version 2 of the CLI, still common on laptops, takes --db-url in its place. The reference says --db-url still works in version 3 and goes away in version 4. Run supabase --version before you paste a command from any guide.

How often should the dump run?

Daily matches the platform's own schedule. Run the three commands from a scheduled job on a small server or a CI schedule, then copy the files to storage in a different account from the one that holds your Supabase organization. A dump that lands in the same account protects you from a bad query and leaves you exposed to a suspended account. Supabase removes a project's backups when you delete the project, so the second copy carries the most value in that case.

The Management API lists the backups the platform holds:

export SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-access-token"
export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/database/backups"

Call it from the same scheduled job and raise an alert when the newest backup is more than a day old.

How do you restore a Supabase backup into a new project?

Create a new project, enable the extensions and webhooks the old one used, and run one psql command that loads the three files in a single transaction. A new project leaves the original untouched, which makes it the safer default for every restore.

  1. Create the new project in the dashboard.
  2. Enable Database Webhooks if the old database used them, and enable any non-default extensions it used.
  3. Copy the new project's connection string and database password.
  4. Run the restore, with the new connection string in place of [CONNECTION_STRING]: 
psql \
  --single-transaction \
  --variable ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  --file roles.sql \
  --file schema.sql \
  --command 'SET session_replication_role = replica' \
  --file data.sql \
  --dbname [CONNECTION_STRING]

5. If the old database used replication for Realtime, enable the publications again under Database, then Publications.

The --single-transaction and ON_ERROR_STOP flags make the restore all or nothing. A failure rolls everything back and leaves no half-loaded database. Setting session_replication_role to replica switches triggers off during the load, which Supabase's guide gives as the way to stop columns being encrypted twice. Supabase offers a Restore to a new project action in the dashboard, described in its Duplicate Project documentation, and that route copies the encryption root key for you.

Which restore errors should you expect?

  • Permission errors on supabase_admin. Open schema.sql and comment out the lines that contain ALTER ... OWNER TO "supabase_admin".
  • A grant error on cli_login_postgres. The message reads permission denied to grant role "postgres". Open roles.sql and comment out the GRANT "postgres" TO "cli_login_postgres" line.
  • Custom roles that cannot log in. Daily backups leave out the passwords of custom roles, so set each one by hand with alter user "YOUR_USER" with password 'SOME_NEW_PASSWORD';.
  • Vault secrets and encrypted columns that cannot be read. A backup holds encrypted data without the root key, and a new project starts with its own key. Copy the old project's key across with the pgsodium endpoint in Supabase's guide before you pause or delete the old project, because the endpoint returns the key while the project is active.

What does a Supabase backup leave out?

It leaves out everything that sits outside the Postgres tables. Copy each item below on the same schedule as the dump.

Item What the backup holds What you do
Storage files Metadata about the objects. A restore shows the buckets and file records and leaves the files themselves missing. Copy the buckets with the supabase-js script in Supabase's guide.
Edge Functions Nothing Run supabase functions download NAME --remote=your_project_ref, then deploy to the target. The download skips import maps and deno.json files.
Auth settings and API keys Nothing Write down every setting and rebuild it in the new project.
Realtime settings, extensions and read replicas Nothing Enable them again by hand.
Custom role passwords Left out by design Reset them after the restore.
Migration history Left out of the three files Dump the supabase_migrations schema in a second run with --schema supabase_migrations.

If you changed the auth or storage schemas, for example by adding a trigger or a policy, the guide tells you to restore those changes on their own and shows how to capture them with supabase db diff against the old project. Our guide to securing Supabase Storage buckets covers the access rules that go with the files.

What about Lovable apps?

It depends on which backend the app uses. A Lovable Cloud app runs on a Supabase project that Lovable manages. That project does not appear in your Supabase dashboard, so the Supabase backups page does not apply to it. If your Lovable app connects to your own Supabase project, everything above applies.

For Lovable Cloud, Lovable's backup documentation says Lovable takes one backup per day and keeps about 14 days of them. A backup covers the database, so files in storage stay as they are. A restore reverts the schema as well as the data, which means your app's code can stop matching the database if the schema changed after the backup. The database is unavailable for a few minutes while the restore runs.

You can export the database too. Lovable exports databases up to 15 GB, caps the export file at 5 GB and allows one export every 24 hours. The file is a compressed PostgreSQL archive that needs pg_restore from PostgreSQL 16 or newer tools. Download it and store it away from Lovable, because removing the database deletes the export along with the rest of your storage. Our guide to a Lovable Cloud to Supabase migration walks through the restore into your own project.

How do you test a Supabase restore?

Restore your latest dump into a scratch project, compare it with production, sign in as a test user and write down how long it took. The first run takes an afternoon and turns a guessed recovery time into a measured one.

  1. Run the three dump commands against production and note the start and end time.
  2. Create a scratch Supabase project and enable the same extensions.
  3. Run the psql restore and note how long it takes.
  4. Compare row counts on the tables that matter most, in production and in the scratch project: 
select 'public.orders' as table_name, count(*) from public.orders
union all
select 'public.profiles', count(*) from public.profiles;

Replace both names with your own tables.

5. Point a staging copy of the app at the scratch project, sign in as a test user and read one record. Open an uploaded file too. It will be missing unless you copied the Storage objects, and that gap is the finding the drill exists to catch.

6. Write the total minutes next to the recovery time you set, then delete the scratch project. Delete the scratch project and nothing else, because deleting a Supabase project removes its backups.

Which mistakes break a Supabase restore?

  • Launching on the Free plan with no export, then assuming the platform holds a backup.
  • Pasting a --remote command into a version 2 CLI, and losing an hour to the flag error.
  • Keeping every copy in one account, so a suspended account takes the database and the backups together.
  • Pausing or deleting the old project before copying the Vault root key.
  • Restoring a point-in-time backup over production without restoring to a new project first.

Frequently asked questions

Does Supabase back up free projects?

No. The pricing page lists backup retention as not included on the Free plan. Supabase's documentation says daily backups cover Pro, Team and Enterprise projects and recommends that Free projects export their data with supabase db dump and keep off-site copies.

Can I restore a Supabase backup into a different project?

Yes. The three-file dump restores into any project you create with the psql command above. The dashboard offers a Restore to a new project action as well, and that route copies the encryption root key for you.

Do Supabase backups include Storage files?

No. The database holds metadata about stored objects, and a restore does not bring back objects you deleted after the backup. Copy buckets with your own script on the same schedule as the dump.

How long does a Supabase restore take?

Supabase says the project is inaccessible during a restore and that downtime grows with the size of the database. It gives no fixed figure. The drill above gives you the number for your own database.

What happens to backups when I delete a project?

Supabase removes the project's data for good, including backups stored in S3, and you cannot undo it. Keep a dump in another account before you delete anything.

Make your next backup one you can restore

Take a dump you can open, copy the files and functions the dump leaves out, store everything away from the account that runs the database, and restore it once into a scratch project. If you would rather have a senior engineer set this up and run the first restore with you, talk to us about our backend and API development work.

Originally published on the AlgoSmiths blog. AlgoSmiths builds web, mobile and AI products on fixed-price contracts, and takes apps built with Lovable, Bolt or Cursor to production. See our services.

title: Patches Welcome #8: Korean Filenames Arrived as Scattered Consonants on Windows
description:
Send a file named 오삐한테-예전.txt from macOS to Windows via LocalSend. What arrives is a filename of decomposed jamo: individual consonants and vowels floating apart instead of composed syllables. The file opens fine. The name is unreadable.

Why macOS sends broken Korean

macOS (HFS+ and APFS) stores filenames in Unicode NFD, the decomposed form. The Korean syllable 오 (U+C624) becomes three separate codepoints: ㅇ (U+110B) + ㅗ (U+1169). On macOS this renders correctly because the OS recomposes on display. Windows doesn't. It renders each codepoint individually, so you see scattered jamo.

This isn't a Korean-only problem. Latin accented characters hit the same thing: résumé.txt sent from macOS can arrive as résumé.txt with combining diacritics on Windows, though most Windows fonts handle Latin combining marks well enough that users don't notice. Korean is where it's visible.

Where the fix goes

LocalSend's Rust core has a sanitize_with() function in packages/core/src/util/filename.rs. Every file save routes through it: direct transfers, folder transfers, gallery-cache saves, SAF paths. One choke point. That's where NFC normalization belongs.

I added unicode-normalization = "0.1" to the Rust crate (mature dependency, 100M+ downloads on crates.io) and a single .nfc().collect::<String>() call at the top of sanitize_with(). The is_valid() function now rejects non-NFC names too, so the invariant between validation and sanitization holds.

use unicode_normalization::UnicodeNormalization;

let name: String = name.nfc().collect();

157 additions, 10 deletions. Most of that is tests and an integration test in v2_server.rs. The core logic change is two lines.

The dependency question

Adding a crate to a 10K-star project isn't free. I considered doing NFC normalization by hand, but Unicode normalization tables are 30K+ entries and the edge cases around Hangul Jamo composition are well-documented traps. unicode-normalization is the standard Rust answer. It's what rustc itself uses internally. I called this out in the PR and the maintainers agreed.

What NFC means here

NFC (Canonical Decomposition followed by Canonical Composition) is the W3C recommendation. It's what Windows, Linux, and most web systems expect. macOS is the outlier. Normalizing on receive at the file-save boundary is the correct place: you want the filename the recipient sees to match what the sender typed, regardless of which OS is doing the rendering.

I tested with cargo test (19 tests, 0 failures) but the manual macOS-to-Windows transfer I couldn't do myself. I don't have a Windows machine on my desk. The PR has a manual test plan checkbox for it; someone on the LocalSend team verified before merge.

PR #3683 · Issue #3676 · localsend/localsend

title: how did the export get order 2 and miss order 1?
description:
If I saw this query in a pull request, my first question would be “When do we save the checkpoint?”

SELECT id, order_ref
FROM order_events
WHERE id > $1
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100;

The worker sends a batch of orders to a reporting database, waits for the write to succeed, then saves the last ID it sent. Next time around, it picks up from there.

“After the write succeeds” sounds like a good answer. I could easily move on to the next file. But there’s another question worth asking. When we save ID 2, how do we know we’ve already seen ID 1?

Two terminals are enough to see it

Open two psql sessions against the same database. In terminal A, create this table with autocommit on.

CREATE TABLE order_events (
    id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    order_ref text NOT NULL,
    exported_at timestamptz
);

Now start a transaction in A and leave it open after the insert.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO order_events (order_ref) VALUES ('order-A') RETURNING id;
-- 1

Switch to terminal B. Leave autocommit on, insert a second order, then run the query the worker would run on its first poll.

INSERT INTO order_events (order_ref) VALUES ('order-B') RETURNING id;
-- 2

SELECT id, order_ref FROM order_events WHERE id > 0 ORDER BY id;
-- 2 | order-B

That’s the whole batch. The worker sends order-B and saves 2.

Now go back to A and run COMMIT. If you open the table, you’ll see both orders. If you run the worker’s next query, WHERE id > 2, you’ll get neither. Restarting the worker just gives you a fresh process reading the same checkpoint.

Both inserts succeed. The worker succeeds too. The mistake is assuming that a higher ID means every lower ID has already committed. Nobody lost a connection. Both writes succeeded. Postgres assigned 1 first, but the transaction holding 2 committed first. Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, that was the only order the worker could see when it polled.

What I’d put in the pull request

For this single-worker export, I’d track which rows still need to reach the report.

SELECT id, order_ref
FROM order_events
WHERE exported_at IS NULL
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100;

I’d keep ORDER BY id. It’s handy for choosing a batch. The difference is that when order-A finally commits, it still has exported_at IS NULL, so the next poll picks it up.

That leaves one awkward moment. The reporting database accepts the order, then the worker dies before it can set exported_at. On restart it sends the order again. I’d give the reporting table a unique constraint on source_event_id and use ON CONFLICT (source_event_id) DO NOTHING. Then it’s safe to retry that insert and mark the source row as exported after the reporting transaction commits.

The test I’d want in that PR is almost exactly the terminal exercise. Hold A open, commit B, run the worker, commit A, run it again. Then check that the report contains both orders exactly once.

You could insert ten thousand orders one after another and miss this bug. Two orders are enough, as long as you let the second one finish first.

title: My Node binary lived in my home directory. The process that needed it never read .bashrc.
description:
I run a small operation on one ARM VPS: a static dashboard served by nginx, a few scheduled jobs, a publishing CLI, and an agent process that calls all of it. Node was installed early, because two of those tools are written in JavaScript.

This week I needed to answer a simple question about that machine: from inside a process that does not start a login shell, can it find node? My terminal said yes. It had been saying yes for months. The answer from the other side was different, and the gap between the two answers is the subject of this post.

A PATH belongs to a process, not to the machine

PATH is inherited. A process gets its environment from whoever spawned it, and only a login or interactive shell reads .profile and .bashrc to build that value. A systemd unit, a crontab line, an ssh host command, and any daemon that shells out with a minimal environment get whatever their parent had, which is usually a short list like /usr/bin:/bin.

I reproduced it rather than waiting for a job to fail:

$ env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin node -v
env: 'node': No such file or directory
$ echo $?
127

Same machine, same user, same disk. The difference is that env -i throws away my environment and keeps only the base directories. My terminal was not special. It just carried a longer list, assembled by files that this process never reads.

The binary was under my home directory

I did not install Node from a distribution package. I extracted the release tarball under ~/.hermes/tools, next to the other toolchains I keep there, so an upgrade is a directory swap:

$ ls -d ~/.hermes/tools/node-*
/home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64
/home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.7.0-linux-arm64
$ ~/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/node -v
v26.12.1

That path only exists for a process whose PATH includes it, and nothing outside my shell adds it. Which means the binary was installed, executable and correct, and simultaneously invisible to half the machine. Both statements were true at once, and only one of them showed up in my terminal.

One detail that mattered when I first set this up: the box is ARM. uname -m answers aarch64, so the build to download is the linux-arm64 one. The default download link for Linux is x64, and the kernel rejects that binary at exec time with Exec format error, which looks like a corrupt download until you check the architecture.

Putting the binary where the system already looks

The fix I applied was to create symlinks in /usr/local/bin, a directory that is on the base PATH of every process on this box, including the short one above:

$ sudo ln -s /home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
$ sudo ln -s /home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/npm  /usr/local/bin/npm
$ sudo ln -s /home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/npx  /usr/local/bin/npx

$ ls -l /usr/local/bin/node
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 60 Oct 22 01:04 /usr/local/bin/node -> /home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/node

$ env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin node -v
v26.12.1

The same command that failed a moment earlier now answers, because the name resolves from a directory every process already searches. No environment file to source, no absolute path to remember in each script.

There was a second reason for the symlink: the failing caller was not a script I control. It was a desktop relay and a couple of helpers that open a non-login SSH session. Fixing the environment of each one would have been four changes in four places, and the fifth caller would still have been broken.

What the symlink costs

The link points into a versioned directory, so an upgrade means recreating it. If I extract node-26.13.x and delete 26.12.1, /usr/local/bin/node becomes a dangling link, and every process that depended on it fails at once while my interactive shell keeps working, because my PATH also lists the tools directory directly.

That split is the part worth designing around. type -a node in my shell prints two entries for one program, one from the symlink and one from the directory entry:

$ type -a node
node is /usr/local/bin/node
node is /home/ubuntu/.hermes/tools/node-26.12.1-linux-arm64/bin/node

Two resolutions, one of them a symlink to the other. Remove the symlink and my shell still finds a node; remove the directory and the whole box loses it. The older 26.7.0 tree is still sitting on disk at 148 MB, which is the other half of this: versioned directories accumulate until someone removes them, and the only thing that makes the removal safe is knowing which names resolve to them.

The check that makes upgrades boring is one line before the upgrade and one after:

readlink -f "$(command -v node)"   # prints the real path, not the link
node -v

If the resolved path is not the version I just installed, the upgrade did not take effect for the processes that matter.

The same problem, one directory over

While measuring this I found the second half of it. My integration CLI is a symlink in ~/.local/bin:

$ ls -l ~/.local/bin/composio
lrwxrwxrwx 1 ubuntu ubuntu 31 Sep 29 23:23 /home/ubuntu/.local/bin/composio -> /home/ubuntu/.composio/composio

That directory is not on the system manager's default path. Asking the user-level systemd manager for its environment shows the full picture:

$ systemctl --user show-environment | grep PATH
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games:/snap/bin

~/.local/bin is absent. Any unit started by that manager, without an explicit Environment=PATH, inherits this list. A unit whose ExecStart calls composio by name starts with 203/EXEC and tells you nothing about why. My interactive shell has the directory and never notices.

Two fixes work. Either call the absolute path in the unit:

[Service]
ExecStart=/home/ubuntu/.local/bin/composio run -f /home/ubuntu/job.js

or set the environment explicitly, which documents the dependency inside the unit instead of leaving it in a shell profile:

[Service]
Environment=PATH=/home/ubuntu/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
ExecStart=composio run -f /home/ubuntu/job.js

The first is easier to audit: the unit file names the binary. The second is easier when the program spawns helpers of its own. Either way the value lives with the code that needs it, not in a file the process does not read.

How I check a process I cannot open a shell in

Three readings cover most cases, and none of them require guessing:

# what a minimal environment sees
env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin node -v

# what a running process actually has
tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<pid>/environ | grep -E '^(PATH|HOME)='

# what the manager would hand to a new unit
systemctl --user show-environment

When the process is a script I own, the cheapest habit is to log the answer at the top of the run, before any work happens:

import os, shutil, sys

print("python", sys.version.split()[0], "node", shutil.which("node"), flush=True)
if shutil.which("node") is None:
    raise SystemExit("node not on PATH for this process: " + os.environ.get("PATH", ""))

A job that fails with the resolved path and the PATH it searched saves the next hour. A job that fails with command not found in the middle of a pipeline sends you to the wrong layer, because the shell reports the missing name and hides the environment behind it.

The rule I keep

Anything a machine invokes has to resolve from that machine's PATH, not from mine. My terminal is one process among dozens, and it is the only one that reads the files where I keep the extra directories. A binary under $HOME, a symlink in ~/.local/bin, a variable exported in .bashrc: all of them are conveniences for interactive use until they are made reachable from the base path or named by absolute path where they are called.

Se você já perdeu tempo com um comando que funciona no seu terminal e falha no serviço que roda a mesma coisa, conta nos comentários qual era a diferença de ambiente. Escrevo em português também, então respondo na língua que você preferir.

title: Gate a Solana bot swap with a pre-trade token risk check
description:
Most Solana bots send the swap first and look at risk later. A better default is a hard gate: call a token check, apply a few thresholds, and skip the trade when the mint fails.

I published a small open-source starter that does exactly that, in zero-dependency Python (stdlib urllib) and TypeScript (Node 18+ fetch): egnaro9/mind-the-mint-starter. It uses the same HTTP check as the free website at mindthemint.com.

This is a heuristic risk screen, not financial advice, and not an audit. Scores are risk signals, not buy or sell calls.

Get a free 100-check key

Website checks stay free and unlimited, with no signup. The HTTP API is for bots and needs a key. You can issue a free 100-check trial key (one per network every 30 days) in one click on mindthemint.com or mindthemint.com/docs, or with:

curl -X POST https://mindthemint.com/v1/trial-key
export MINDTHEMINT_API_KEY="your_trial_key"

Do not commit the key.

Call the check

The live contract is a single GET, with the key in the X-API-Key header:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $MINDTHEMINT_API_KEY" \
  https://mindthemint.com/v1/check/JUPyiwrYJFskUPiHa7hkeR8VUtAeFoSYbKedZNsDvCN

A successful body includes risk_score (0 to 100), risk_level, flags, and a heuristics object with mint_authority_active, freeze_authority_active, and top10_holder_pct. Full examples live in the API docs and in the repo fixture.

Default guardrails and exit codes

The starter blocks a mint when any of these are true:

  • risk_score is at or above 25
  • mint authority is active
  • freeze authority is active
  • top10_holder_pct is above 80

Override them with flags or env vars (--max-risk-score, --max-top10-pct, --allow-mint-authority, --allow-freeze-authority).

Exit codes are simple to wire into a bot:

Code Meaning
0 Token passed your thresholds
2 Token was blocked
1 Error (missing key, HTTP 401/402/429, or a network failure)

Drop it in before the swap

Python:

python python/check_token.py JUPyiwrYJFskUPiHa7hkeR8VUtAeFoSYbKedZNsDvCN

Or import the same functions your CLI uses:

import os
from check_token import fetch_check, evaluate

mint = "JUPyiwrYJFskUPiHa7hkeR8VUtAeFoSYbKedZNsDvCN"
payload = fetch_check(mint, os.environ["MINDTHEMINT_API_KEY"])
decision = evaluate(payload)
if not decision["passed"]:
    print("skip trade:", "; ".join(decision["reasons"]))
    raise SystemExit(2)
# continue with your swap

The TypeScript filter is a drop-in match (typescript/checkToken.ts in the repo).

A real dry-run on the JUP fixture

The repo ships tests/fixtures/jup_pass.json, shaped like a live Mind the Mint check of JUP captured on 27 November 2026. This dry run used that fixture only. It did not call the API or spend a credit:

$ python python/check_token.py --fixture tests/fixtures/jup_pass.json
PASS  JUP (JUPyiwrYJFskUPiHa7hkeR8VUtAeFoSYbKedZNsDvCN)
  risk_score        23 low  (block at 25+)
  mint_authority    inactive
  freeze_authority  inactive
  top10_holder_pct  64.61  (max 80)
  credits_remaining 99
  summary: Top holders look like one entity split across wallets accounting for 64.61% of supply, and top 10 holders control 64.61%. Mint and freeze authorities are inactive, liquidity is 3.54 million USD, and pair age is 24744.19 hours. This is not a buy signal. The score does not cover the team, social channels, off-chain custody, or later changes to the mint.

JUP passes these defaults because the score is 23, both authorities are inactive, and top-10 concentration is 64.61%, under the 80 cap. A high score, an active mint or freeze authority, or a more concentrated holder set exits 2 and should skip the swap.

Clone it here: github.com/egnaro9/mind-the-mint-starter. Run a free website check at mindthemint.com, or read the API docs. Built by Erik Hill. MIT licensed. Not financial advice.
