title: A microVM for every app
description:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post. This post was written with AI assistance.

Gregale runs every app instance in its own Firecracker microVM. Each one has its own Linux kernel, its own network, its own memory limit and its own jailed process on the host, so one app can't read another's memory, exhaust its resources, or reach it through a shared kernel. Firecracker is the open-source virtual machine monitor AWS built to run Lambda and Fargate. On Gregale you get that isolation by default, for every API, worker, job and MCP server, without managing VMs: deploy a Dockerfile or a source repo with gregale deploy.

What each app gets

Boundary What Gregale does
Kernel Every instance boots its own guest Linux kernel inside a Firecracker microVM. Apps never share a host kernel with each other.
Host process Each microVM is started by Firecracker's jailer under a unique user and group ID, inside a chroot, with a default-deny seccomp filter.
Memory Each microVM runs in its own cgroups v2 scope, capped at your plan's RAM plus 8 MB. One app can't take memory from another.
Network Each instance gets its own network namespace. Outbound mail ports (25, 465, 587), private address ranges, link-local and cloud metadata addresses are blocked.
Files No host directories are shared with guests. Only block devices cross the boundary: a read-only base image and your app's own layer.
Randomness A virtual hardware random number generator is attached to every guest, and the kernel is reseeded every time an instance wakes, so two instances never share random state.
Secrets Environment secrets are sealed at rest, so plaintext values are never stored in the database.
Builds Each build runs in its own short-lived microVM (2 vCPU, 2048 MB), so npm install or pip install of a fresh dependency never runs on a shared host.

These controls are listed in Gregale's Data Processing Agreement as its technical and organisational measures under GDPR Art. 32. See also Security and Compliance.

Why a VM per app matters

  • A bad deploy stays in its own box. A memory leak, a fork bomb or a runaway process hits its own VM's limits, not your other services.
  • A kernel bug isn't a way out. Containers on one host share that host's kernel, so a kernel exploit in one container can reach the others. A microVM puts a separate kernel and a hardware virtualization boundary in between.
  • Safer for code you didn't write. AI agents running tools, customer scripts, plugins and fresh dependencies all run behind the same boundary as the rest of your backend.
  • Easier security reviews. "Every tenant workload runs in its own Firecracker microVM, jailed, with egress filtering" answers a common question in customer security questionnaires.

Your Dockerfile works as is

You don't write VM configuration. Gregale takes a Dockerfile, an OCI image or a source repo and runs it in a microVM. What it needs: Linux/amd64, an HTTP server listening on 0.0.0.0, and a process that honours PORT (default 8080). Docker settings that only make sense on a shared host, such as privileged, cap_add and devices, are ignored with a warning, because each service already has its own machine. The root filesystem is ephemeral; keep durable state in managed Postgres or object storage. See Container compatibility.

gregale deploy            # from a directory with a Dockerfile or source code

A VM per app doesn't mean slow starts: an idle app wakes from a memory snapshot of its running process. The measurements are in Firecracker snapshot restore on SSD.

How other platforms isolate apps

Platform What each app runs in Notes
Gregale Firecracker microVM per app instance, by default Managed backend platform: APIs, workers, jobs, workflows, cron, MCP servers, Postgres, object storage, safe releases
Fly.io Firecracker microVM per Machine Lower-level: you choose and manage Machines, regions and volumes
AWS Lambda / Fargate Firecracker microVMs You assemble the rest from AWS services (API Gateway, IAM, queues, CodeDeploy)
Google Cloud Run 2nd gen: microVM with a full Linux kernel; 1st gen: gVisor sandbox Jobs and worker pools use 2nd gen only
Heroku Containers (dynos) Platform in sustaining engineering since February 2026
Render Containers Render's own writing describes services as containers, not built for untrusted user code; a separate sandboxes product is in early access
Railway Containers No per-service VM isolation documented; Railway Sandboxes (beta) are VMs

Checked against each vendor's public documentation on November 24, 2026: Firecracker, Fly Machines, Cloud Run execution environments, Heroku dynos, Render on sandboxes, Railway Sandboxes.

Pricing

MicroVM isolation is how every Gregale app runs, on every plan, including Free; there is no isolation add-on. See Gregale pricing.

FAQ

Does a VM per app make Gregale slow to start?

No. Firecracker microVMs boot in a fraction of a second, and an app that has been idle wakes from a memory snapshot of its running process rather than booting from scratch.

Is a microVM the same as a dedicated server?

No. Many microVMs share one physical host, but each has its own kernel, memory limit and jailed process, and the hypervisor keeps them apart. It is the isolation model AWS uses for Lambda and Fargate.

If I run several containers together, do they each get a VM?

Each deployed app gets its own microVM. Containers you run together as companions inside one deployment (in preview) have separate filesystems and resource limits but share that deployment’s guest kernel, so put workloads that must not trust each other in separate deployments.

Can I run privileged containers or Docker-in-Docker?

No. Privileged mode, host devices, host networking and the Docker socket are not supported. Builds run in their own short-lived microVMs, not on a shared Docker daemon.

Does isolation replace my own security work?

No. Gregale isolates workloads and filters network egress; you still own application authorization, dependency hygiene and data classification.

title: INNER JOIN in SQL
description:
Before normalization, all my data lived in a single table. Although it was easy to query, it contained a lot of repeated information. After splitting the data into multiple tables, I avoided duplication, but I also needed a way to reconnect the related data whenever I wanted to analyze it. INNER JOIN allows me to do exactly that. My first query combined four tables to display complete hospital visit information.
It brought together: Patient names, doctor names, department names, visit dates, diagnoses, treatment plans, bill amounts and payment status all in a single result set.

select
    v.visit_id,
    p.patient_name,
    d.doctor_name,
    dp.department_name,
    v.date_of_visit,
    v.diagnosis,
    v.treatment_plan,
    v.bill_amount,
    v.payment_status
from visits v
inner join patients p
    on v.patient_id = p.patient_id
inner join doctors d
    on v.doctor_id = d.doctor_id
inner join departments dp
    on v.department_id = dp.department_id
order by v.visit_id;

Seeing information from multiple tables appear together made the purpose of database relationships much clearer. Once I understood the basics of INNER JOIN, I started answering analytical questions such as:

  • How many patients has each doctor treated?
  • How many patients visited each department?
  • What is the average bill amount for each department?

What I Learned
Working with INNER JOIN taught me several important lessons:

  • Normalizing a database reduces data duplication.
  • Foreign keys connect related tables.
  • INNER JOIN retrieves only records that have matching values in both tables.
  • SQL becomes much more powerful when multiple tables work together.

GitHub link: https://github.com/KratosOCS/Hospital-Records-Analysis/commit/6001805ae665906759f596793a6d26cf15b65bee

title: Agentes LLM: fixtures de email con contrato
description:
Un agente LLM que usa una herramienta de correo puede completar un flujo aparentemente sencillo: crear una dirección, esperar un mensaje, extraer un código y continuar. El problema aparece cuando el test solo comprueba que “algo llegó”. Un mensaje viejo, un buzón compartido o una ejecución paralela pueden hacer que el agente tome una decisión correcta por casualidad.

La solución no es pedirle al modelo que sea más cuidadoso. Es diseñar un fixture con un contrato pequeño y visible. El agente interpreta observaciones; el sistema decide qué estados son validos y qué acciones están permitidas.

El agente no debe adivinar el estado del email

Conviene separar tres capas:

  1. Proveedor de fixture: crea el buzón y expone mensajes.
  2. Adaptador de herramienta: traduce operaciones como create_inbox o read_latest a resultados estructurados.
  3. Orquestador del agente: decide el siguiente paso usando esos resultados, pero no inventa estados que la herramienta no confirmó.

En palabras, el flujo es: crear → observar → validar → consumir → cerrar. Si el agente recibe solo texto libre, puede confundir “sin mensajes” con “la búsqueda falló”. Un contrato tipado hace esta diferencia explicita y reduce decisiones frágiles.

Este enfoque encaja bien con los flujos donde hay que probar emails de onboarding sin ruido: el dato importante no es solo el correo recibido, sino el contexto de la ejecución que lo esperaba.

El contrato mínimo de un fixture

Un resultado de herramienta puede tener una forma parecida a esta:

{
  "status": "message_found",
  "inbox_id": "run-482-worker-2",
  "message_id": "msg-901",
  "received_at": "2026-11-28T03:00:12Z",
  "subject_match": true,
  "body_available": true,
  "expires_at": "2026-11-28T03:05:00Z"
}

Los estados deben ser finitos y mutuamente entendibles: created, waiting, message_found, consumed, expired y failed. El modelo puede explicar el estado o escoger una acción permitida, pero no debería transformar expired en retry sin una regla del orquestador.

También es útil declarar qué campos son evidencia y cuáles son sugerencias. message_id, received_at y inbox_id son evidencia observable. Un campo como suggested_code es una extracción que aún debe validarse contra el flujo de la aplicación. Esa frontera evita que una alucinación del agente se parezca a un resultado del proveedor.

Aislamiento por ejecución y por herramienta

Cada ejecución necesita un identificador estable, y cada worker debería tener su propio buzón. La clave compuesta puede ser run_id + worker_id + attempt_id. Con ella, el adaptador rechaza una lectura que pertenece a otro contexto, aunque el mensaje tenga el asunto esperado.

El aislamiento también debe aplicarse al historial. Un agente que ve mensajes de una ejecución anterior aprende una señal equivocada: cree que el sistema ya verificó algo. La limpieza es importante, pero no debe ser la única defensa; durante una carrera, dos workers todavía pueden leer el mismo mensaje antes de que la limpieza ocurra.

Para renovaciones o flujos que agrupan usuarios, conviene probar correos de renovación con cohortes separadas. La cohorte no es solo una etiqueta de reporte: puede formar parte de la identidad del fixture y de las condiciones de lectura.

Un generador de correo desechable sirve como componente de prueba, no como autoridad de identidad. Incluso si el adaptador se llama tempail en un ejemplo antiguo, el nombre no cambia el contrato. En documentación interna también aparecen búsquedas como tepm mail com; deben tratarse como texto de diagnóstico, no como una señal para relajar validaciones.

Trazas que explican un fallo

Los agentes necesitan errores accionables. En vez de devolver “email not found”, el adaptador puede responder:

{
  "status": "not_found",
  "reason": "before_deadline",
  "inbox_id": "run-482-worker-2",
  "attempt": 2,
  "next_allowed_action": "poll",
  "retry_after_ms": 800
}

Así el modelo sabe que puede volver a consultar, con qué espera y bajo qué límite. Si la razón es wrong_run o already_consumed, la acción debería ser detenerse y reportar, no repetir indefinidamente.

Las trazas deben ocultar códigos, tokens y cuerpos completos. Para depurar bastan el identificador de ejecución, el estado, los tiempos y una categoría de error. Esto hace la automatización más segura y también más barata: una salida corta y estructurada ocupa menos contexto que varias capturas de pantalla o párrafos repetidos.

Puntos de comprobación antes de automatizar

Antes de entregar una herramienta de email a un agente LLM, compruebo lo siguiente:

  • ¿Cada ejecución y worker tienen un buzón identificable?
  • ¿La herramienta diferencia ausencia, expiración, consumo y error técnico?
  • ¿Los mensajes incluyen message_id y tiempo de recepción?
  • ¿Una lectura de otro run_id se rechaza de forma explícita?
  • ¿El orquestador limita los reintentos y el tiempo total de espera?
  • ¿Los campos extraídos por el modelo se validan antes de usarse?
  • ¿Las trazas excluyen secretos y conservan el contexto necesario?

Un punto adicional: el contrato debe probarse con mensajes fuera de orden, duplicados y vacíos. Los casos raros son donde la frontera entre una Automatización confiable y una demo fragil se vuelve visible.

Cierre

La mejor herramienta para un agente no es la que devuelve más texto, sino la que expone menos ambigüedad. Un fixture de email con estados finitos, aislamiento y errores estructurados permite que el LLM razone sobre el flujo sin convertirse en la fuente de verdad.

El diseño puede empezar pequeño: seis estados, tres identificadores, un límite de espera y una política clara de consumo. Después se añaden métricas y casos de carrera. Ese contrato convierte un generador de correo desechable en una pieza de infraestructura de testing que se puede revisar, reproducir y mejorar. Y sí, al principio parece un poco más trabajo; luego ahorra muchas horas de mirar logs que no dicen nada.

title: Formatting Timer Readouts with Intl.DurationFormat: What It Does and What It Leaves to You
description:
Most timer readouts are built from padStart(2, "0") and a colon. That works until you want localized digits, or a spoken-friendly string like "25 minutes". Intl.DurationFormat covers both, and MDN labels it Baseline 2025: "Since March 2025, this feature works across the latest devices and browser versions."

I tried it on a timer readout and found four places where it does less than you might assume, plus one engine difference I measured. Everything below ran on Node 24.22.1 and desktop Chrome 156 on Linux. I did not test Firefox or Safari, and I only used the en locale unless noted.

The basic readout

The digital style prints 1:50:00-style output. With only style: "digital", five seconds comes out as 0:00:05. Adding hoursDisplay: "auto" hides the hours until they are nonzero: 00:05, then 1:00:03.

export function splitMs(totalMs) {
  const sign = totalMs < 0 ? -1 : 1;
  let rest = Math.abs(Math.trunc(totalMs));
  const hours = Math.floor(rest / 3_600_000);
  rest %= 3_600_000;
  const minutes = Math.floor(rest / 60_000);
  rest %= 60_000;
  const seconds = Math.floor(rest / 1000);
  const milliseconds = rest % 1000;
  return {
    hours: sign * hours,
    minutes: sign * minutes,
    seconds: sign * seconds,
    milliseconds: sign * milliseconds,
  };
}

const clock = new Intl.DurationFormat("en", {
  style: "digital",
  hoursDisplay: "auto",
});

// Elapsed: truncate to whole seconds, or any nonzero milliseconds get printed.
export const formatElapsed = (ms) =>
  clock.format(splitMs(Math.floor(ms / 1000) * 1000));

// Countdown: round up so the readout reaches 00:00 at the deadline.
export const formatRemaining = (ms) =>
  clock.format(splitMs(Math.ceil(ms / 1000) * 1000));

Each line of that helper exists because of one of the points below.

1. It does not carry

Pass { seconds: 125 } and you get 00:125, not 02:05. The formatter prints the fields you give it. That is why splitMs exists. MDN says format() also accepts a Temporal.Duration; I did not try that.

2. Nonzero milliseconds show up uninvited

Feed splitMs(125123) straight in and the readout is 02:05.123. The milliseconds unit is displayed whenever it is nonzero. If your display stops at seconds, cut the value to whole seconds first, as formatElapsed does.

3. It truncates, so choose floor or ceiling on purpose

MDN's constructor page says fractional units are formatted with roundingMode: "trunc", and ECMA-402 sets the same "trunc" rounding mode in its number-formatting steps for these fields. The formatter never rounds up. With fractionalDigits: 0, 2 seconds and 990 ms printed as 0:00:02 for me. For a stopwatch that matches intuition: 1.9 seconds reads 00:01. For a countdown, truncation means the last second reads 00:00 while 0.9 seconds remain. So formatRemaining rounds up before formatting, and formatRemaining(900) returns 00:01. That is my design choice, not a rule from the spec. Pick one convention and use it everywhere, because a readout that flips between the two will look wrong next to the real deadline.

4. Signs must agree, and integers only

MDN: "Each property's value should be an integer, and their signs should be consistent." Both { minutes: 1, seconds: -5 } and { seconds: 1.5 } threw a RangeError for me. The spec's IsValidDuration step is what rejects mixed signs. For overtime, negate every field, which splitMs does: formatRemaining(-1500) gives -00:01.

5. The off-by-one I measured

fractionalDigits accepts 0 to 9. I swept every combination of 60 seconds and 1,000 milliseconds (60,000 inputs, minute zero, en) at 0, 1, 2, and 3 fractional digits, and compared each result with a string built by slicing integer digits.

  • Chrome 156: 0 mismatches at every setting.
  • Node 24.22.1 (V8 13.6.233.17-node.58): 0 mismatches at 0 and 1 digits, 21 at 2 digits, 396 at 3 digits. Every miss was one low in the last place. One second and 360 ms with two digits printed 1.35.

The spec works with exact mathematical values here and a related validity check carries a note that its sum "cannot be implemented directly using floating-point arithmetic." I can't tell you which engine versions have the problem; I have two data points. If you show hundredths, test your targets, or build the fraction yourself:

import { splitMs } from "./splitMs.js";

export function makeCentiFormatter(locale) {
  const clock = new Intl.DurationFormat(locale, {
    style: "digital",
    hoursDisplay: "auto",
  });
  const numbers = new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { minimumIntegerDigits: 2 });
  const decimal = new Intl.NumberFormat(locale)
    .formatToParts(1.1)
    .find((p) => p.type === "decimal").value;

  return (ms) => {
    const { milliseconds, ...whole } = splitMs(Math.floor(ms / 10) * 10);
    const centis = Math.abs(milliseconds) / 10;
    return clock.format({ ...whole, milliseconds: 0 }) + decimal + numbers.format(centis);
  };
}

I ran the same 60,000-input sweep against this helper on Node 24.22.1 and got 0 mismatches. It also keeps the locale's decimal mark and digits: de printed 00:02,34 for 2,345 ms.

Detect it, and don't test against strings 

export const canFormatDurations =
  typeof Intl === "object" && typeof Intl.DurationFormat === "function";

When that is false, fall back to padStart. And MDN warns: "You should not compare the results of format() to hardcoded constants." Output can differ between implementations, so my example strings are what I saw, not guarantees. Test your own code on structure instead.

A label for assistive tech

The long style turns { minutes: 1, seconds: 5 } into 1 minute, 5 seconds. That could work as an aria-label you update on start, pause, and finish rather than every tick. That is my suggestion; I did not test it with screen readers.

Sources, all checked on 2026-11-27

  • MDN: Intl.DurationFormat
  • MDN: Intl.DurationFormat() constructor
  • MDN: Intl.DurationFormat.prototype.format()
  • ECMA-402: IsValidDuration

Disclosure: I build moment.. It has no signup and runs in 11 languages, and the feature list is a countdown, Pomodoro cycles, repeating intervals, laps, and D-Day dates. The snippets here are standalone examples, not that app's code. A timer like this can only alert you when time is up. The formatting just decides what the number looks like on the way there.

title: The message that retried hundreds of times: a retry loop with no exit
description:
I'm Eric Gitangu. I work on backend systems for a mobility/fintech platform. This is the story of one text message that was retried hundreds of times, and what it took to teach the code to take no for an answer.

The symptom

A cron worker sends queued notifications. One day the SMS provider started rejecting our account as inactive. Annoying, but a provider outage is supposed to be a boring day: messages fail, someone gets alerted, we move on.

Instead, one queued message kept coming back. Same row, same recipient, every few minutes, across a couple of days. Hundreds of attempts, each one answered with the same refusal. Hello? Hello? Hello?

Why it looped

Three small decisions, each reasonable alone:

  1. The send helper had no catch. A provider error was thrown, not returned.
  2. The worker saved progress (who got the message) only after the recipient loop finished. The throw skipped that save.
  3. A reclaim timer re-picks any row stuck in "in progress" after a few minutes, so a crashed worker can't strand a row.

Put them together. The error escapes, the row is never marked done or failed, it still says "in progress", the timer decides the worker must have died, and picks it up again. The safety net for crashes became a retry loop with no exit.

One more detail made it worse: the run aborted at the first failing recipient. Every recipient after them in the same row was starved too.

The decision

I wanted to keep the reclaim timer. It exists for good reasons. What was missing was a way for a row to say "I failed on purpose, leave me alone until later". So:

  • Catch per recipient, so one bad send can't abort the run or hide behind the others.
  • Count attempts on the row itself, back off exponentially, and stop at a cap with a terminal failure and a reason.
  • Teach the reclaim query to respect a "not before" stamp.
  • Stop sending to a provider we already know is down, and say so once.

The solution

The policy is a small pure class. It does no I/O of its own; everything it needs comes in as an argument, which is why it is easy to test.

Per recipient, a send has three outcomes, not two:

export type Attempt = { outcome: 'sent' | 'failed' | 'retry'; reason: string };

export async function dispatchOne(
  send: () => Promise<boolean>,
  providerDown: boolean,
  isStoreError: (e: unknown) => boolean,
): Promise<Attempt> {
  if (providerDown) return { outcome: 'retry', reason: 'provider_unavailable' };
  try {
    return (await send())
      ? { outcome: 'sent', reason: '' }
      : { outcome: 'failed', reason: 'provider_said_no' }; // final, as before
  } catch (e) {
    if (isStoreError(e)) throw e; // our own storage errors keep their old path
    return { outcome: 'retry', reason: reasonCode(e) };
  }
}

A few choices in there are deliberate.

"The provider said no" and "the provider threw" are different. A falsy answer is a final answer and stays a terminal failure, exactly as before. Only an exception, or a known outage, counts as retryable.

Storage errors are not swallowed. The new catch is for the provider. If our own datastore throws, the outer handler still owns it. A broad catch that hides your own failures is how you end up with the next incident.

The reason code carries no message. Provider error text can echo phone numbers or account identifiers. The code reads only the HTTP status and the provider's numeric error code out of the message, and drops the rest. The row stores reasons shaped like http_<status>_<code>, safe to log and safe to show an admin.

The retry decision lives on the row:

export function settle(prev: number, retryCount: number, nowMs: number,
                       max = 5, baseSec = 60, capSec = 3600) {
  if (retryCount <= 0) return { attempts: prev, terminal: false, retryAfter: null };
  const attempts = prev + 1;
  if (attempts >= max) return { attempts, terminal: true, retryAfter: null };
  const wait = Math.min(capSec, baseSec * 2 ** (attempts - 1));
  return { attempts, terminal: false, retryAfter: nowMs + wait * 1000 };
}

At the cap, the recipients are booked as failed with the reason and put back in the row's "already handled" list, so no later run can send to them again. Before the cap, a recipient that failed is taken out of that list in memory, so the next attempt actually retries them. Getting those two directions right was the fiddly part.

The reclaim query got the matching gate: a row is selectable only if it has no retryAfter, or the stamp is due. Backing-off and terminal rows are never re-picked.

A health short-circuit. The provider's account state is already exported as a gauge by a monitoring job. The worker reads it once per row. If it says "down", it skips the send for the affected recipients instead of firing a request it knows will fail. If the gauge is missing or unreadable, that means unknown, and unknown is treated as up. I would rather attempt a send than stay silent because a metrics file was late.

Markets served by a different, local provider never go through that gate and behave as before.

One alert per state change. The worker is a short-lived cron process, so it can't remember the last state in memory. It keeps a tiny marker file, compares, and raises an admin alert only when the state flips: down, then recovered. Fifty rows in one tick produce one alert, not fifty.

One trade-off I'm not hiding

While the provider is known down, skipped sends still count as attempts. With the default back-off, a long outage will walk a row to its cap and mark it failed with provider_unavailable. That is visible and honest, and an admin can re-send. The alternative, retrying indefinitely, is what we just removed. I chose a loud failure over a quiet loop.

Where it stands

The fix is written, covered by unit tests, and merged into the next release candidate. The tests cover per-recipient isolation, the stable reason code, back-off growth and bounds, the cap, the reclaim gate, the health short-circuit, the one-alert-per-change rule, and a check that the cron controller actually routes sends through the policy. They run against the policy and stubbed senders, so they prove the logic, not a live provider outage.

Takeaways

  • A crash-recovery timer is a retry loop. Ask what happens when the thing it recovers fails every time.
  • Save progress before you can throw, or make "not saved" mean "failed on purpose".
  • Treat "the provider said no" and "the provider threw" as different outcomes.
  • Keep the catch narrow. Your own storage errors should still be loud.
  • Reason codes should never be built from provider message text.
  • Treat missing health data as unknown, not as down.
  • Alert on state changes, not on every tick.

Retries are great, as long as they eventually give up and tell someone.

A small generic version of the policy, with a self-test, is in this gist.

Originally published on developer.ericgitangu.com. More write-ups on the blog.

title: My AI Assistant Understands It Has a Problem. So Why Can't It Share That With Its Engineers?
description:
Overview

This article examines a frustrating limitation with many AI services: their general inability to directly escalate valid user-reported problems to their own engineering teams. Although an assistant can acknowledge shortcomings, discuss potential solutions, and agree that improvements are warranted, it has no guaranteed mechanism for ensuring that this feedback reaches the people who can actually do something about it.

Share your feedback in the comments if you think AI services should do better in this area.

The Disconnect Between Understanding and Action

Modern AI assistants can analyze complicated problems, troubleshoot technical issues, and recommend improvements. They can even recognize shortcomings in the platforms they operate on.

However, there's a significant gap between identifying a problem and actually reporting it.

Consider a typical interaction:

A user identifies a problem with an AI assistant and explains why the issue negatively affects their user experience. The assistant understands the complaint, acknowledges that the problem is legitimate, and may even suggest a reasonable solution.

The user then asks the assistant to report the issue to the AI assistant's own engineering team.

And that's where things fall apart.

The assistant explains that it cannot directly submit engineering tickets or communicate with the developers responsible for the product.

In other words, it can understand the problem, discuss the solution, and agree that something should be done about it, but it cannot reliably take the next step.

Acknowledgment Isn't Accountability

This creates an unusual situation.

An AI assistant can demonstrate considerable intelligence when discussing a problem but becomes essentially powerless when asked to help get that problem resolved.

Consider what the assistant can already do:

  • Identify and explain software problems.
  • Recognize usability shortcomings.
  • Evaluate proposed improvements.
  • Suggest potential solutions.
  • Help users articulate constructive feedback.

Yet the actual communication of that feedback remains the user's responsibility.

The conversation ends with an acknowledgment rather than an actionable outcome.

And that's a fundamental weakness in the feedback process.

Telling someone that their complaint is valid isn't the same as ensuring that the appropriate people hear about it.

Why This Matters

User feedback is an important part of software development.

Developers depend on reports from actual users to identify bugs, discover usability problems, prioritize improvements, and understand how their products perform outside controlled testing environments.

AI assistants could potentially make this process considerably more efficient.

Instead of requiring users to navigate separate reporting systems, an assistant could help organize a problem description, identify the affected feature, gather relevant context, and forward a structured report to the appropriate team.

This would eliminate unnecessary friction while potentially providing developers with more useful and actionable feedback.

Unfortunately, without a direct reporting mechanism, valuable observations remain trapped in individual conversations.

A Practical Solution: Built-In Feedback Escalation

The solution doesn't need to be complicated.

AI platforms should provide assistants with an authorized mechanism for submitting legitimate product feedback directly to their development organizations.

A useful system could include:

  • Direct reporting: Allow users to ask the assistant to submit a problem report.
  • Structured feedback: Automatically organize the description, relevant context, and suggested improvements.
  • User authorization: Obtain permission before submitting conversation content or other potentially sensitive information.
  • Submission confirmation: Provide confirmation that the report was actually received.
  • Reference tracking: Generate a report number so users can refer to their submissions.
  • Status visibility: Where practical, let users know whether feedback has been reviewed or forwarded.

Not every complaint needs to become an engineering ticket. Some issues belong with customer support, product management, or quality assurance.

The important thing is providing a reliable path to the appropriate destination.

And if the assistant cannot submit a report, it should be transparent about that limitation rather than creating the impression that anything has been communicated.

Final Thoughts

AI assistants are becoming increasingly capable of understanding users and identifying problems. But their usefulness shouldn't end with acknowledging that something is wrong.

When an assistant recognizes a legitimate product issue but cannot help communicate it to the people responsible for fixing it, an important link in the development feedback process is missing.

Users shouldn't have to repeatedly explain the same problems, navigate multiple reporting channels, or wonder whether anyone will ever see their suggestions.

Don't just acknowledge the problem. Give users a way to report it.

Should AI assistants have a built-in mechanism for escalating legitimate product problems directly to their developers?

Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Neumorphism as the Design Foundation of Apium Cloud OS: UI/UX Trends and Ergonomics
description:
Interface Design Trends 2020–2026: The Return of Tactility
Over the past fifteen years, digital product design has completed a full pendulum swing:

Early Skeuomorphism (2008–2012): interfaces literally mimicked leather, wood, and chrome switches. Users immediately knew what to press, but heavy visual noise got in the way of dense data tables.

Ultra-Flat Minimalism / Flat Design (2013–2019): the backlash against skeuomorphism stripped away shadows and elevation. Screens looked cleaner, yet introduced the opposite flaw—plain text, headings, and clickable buttons became visually indistinguishable.

First-Wave Neumorphism & Glassmorphism (2020–2022): designers brought depth back using dual shadows (top-left highlight, bottom-right shadow). Visually striking in concept shots, early neumorphism suffered from low contrast and blurry hit-target boundaries.

Mature Pragmatic Soft UI 2.0 (2024–2026): the defining modern standard for complex B2B and DevOps tools. It pairs a calm monochrome surface with crisp 1px light edges, high-contrast typography, and restrained color reserved strictly for status and action cues.
The interface architecture of Apium Cloud OS is built on the principle of a single physical sheet: the entire control panel is cast on a matte light-gray canvas (#e6e9ef). Controls either extrude upward (raised cards, buttons, toggles) or recess inward into the surface (utilization charts, input fields, log streams).

Why Neumorphism Became the Foundation of Apium Cloud OS
Adopting tactile Soft UI in a network gateway was driven by four practical infrastructure operations requirements.

Intuitive Separation Between "Click" and "Read / Input"
In a traditional flat UI, distinguishing an input field, a status badge, and an action button requires drawing dozens of competing colored borders. In Apium Cloud OS, depth is governed by light physics:

Extruded surface: status cards, navigation tabs, and action buttons invite the eye and cursor naturally.
Recessed surface: URI/IP text inputs, terminal log windows, and chart regions sit visually carved into the plane—your eye instantly recognizes a container for reading or typing rather than a button.

Focus Control in Complex Workflows Without Modal Chaos
Configuring multi-hop cascade routing (VLESS Reality, Hysteria 2, Auto-Failover / Load Balance mode selection, IPv6 transit, and Split Tunneling) is typically buried by developers across dozens of nested modals. Neumorphic surfaces with soft shadow separation let complex logic live on a single calm screen—free of cluttered black borders.

An Ideal Backdrop for 3D Topology and Traffic Analytics
When an administrator inspects a connection map or DPI analytics, the chrome must never compete with the telemetry for attention. A neutral light neumorphic canvas cuts glare and eye strain during long sessions, ensuring any colored signal—a green node on the 3D globe, a blue route arc, or a dark PRO+ badge—captures focus immediately.

Hardware Tactility: The Interface as a Physical Control Desk
When designing daemon controls, we drew inspiration from hardware racks, studio mixing consoles, and precision industrial equipment (echoing the clarity of functional industrial design). In systems administration, knowing at a glance which services are actually running right now is critical.

In the Services section, every protocol and system component (MS-SSTP, L2TP, IPsec, VLESS, Hysteria 2, Ad blocker, Local DNS) is modeled as an independent physical module:

a crisp monochrome square badge displaying the protocol code;
a tactile mechanical On / Off toggle (active services read immediately via a green indicator);
a dedicated Restart button and an unmistakable ONLINE / OFFLINE status pill;
accent colors reserved strictly for meaning: green for an active service, blue for current focus or route, and dark graphite for the active tab or system badge.

Neumorphism in Apium Cloud OS is not a passing visual trend—it is a deliberate ergonomic choice. Calm matte lighting, physical depth between buttons and input wells, and strict color discipline let engineers manage complex network infrastructure quickly, comfortably, and without visual fatigue.

title: The Evolution of etcd Storage: A Distributed /etc in RAM (v0.1 - v0.4)
description:
Motivation & Series Roadmap

Storage engines are shaped by the workloads they are built to serve. Today, etcd is best known as the disk-backed datastore behind the Kubernetes control plane. When it started in 2013, however, it was much simpler: an in-memory hierarchical directory tree serialized to JSON.

In this series, we will trace how real-world adoption changed etcd's storage layer over time. This first post starts at the beginning, when small CoreOS configuration trees made keeping everything in memory the obvious choice. In later posts, we will cover the first major reliability overhaul, the arrival of Kubernetes and how it broke those early assumptions, and the move to a disk-backed engine built on BoltDB. From there, we will look at the scaling bottlenecks that led the team to fork BoltDB into bbolt and become database maintainers themselves. Finally, we will bring the story up to the present to see how etcd moved past its original design and what might come after bbolt.

In Part 1, we go back to etcd v0.1 through v0.4 (2013-2014). We will look at the original CoreOS workload, inspect the Go code behind its in-memory store and early Raft persistence, and benchmark a 3-node cluster to measure its throughput and latency limits.

The 2013 Workload: Why CoreOS Needed a Distributed /etc

In 2013, CoreOS set out to change how server infrastructure was operated. Instead of patching long-lived Linux hosts in place with apt or yum, CoreOS Container Linux shipped a minimal, container-only operating system modeled after ChromeOS. It consisted of the Linux kernel, systemd, a container runtime, and immutable dual-partition (A/B) automatic OS updates. Updates were downloaded in the background to the passive partition and activated on reboot.

This minimal design created a coordination problem. Once servers reboot automatically and move containers across a cluster, you need a strongly consistent place to coordinate rolling reboots, schedule services, and share configuration. At the same time, CoreOS wanted to avoid running a JVM and Apache ZooKeeper on minimal Linux hosts. To fill this role, they built etcd (from Unix /etc plus d for distributed and daemon) as a single static Go binary.

To understand what a "distributed /etc" meant in practice, and why this workload shaped etcd's first storage engine, let's look at how etcd sat at the center of a typical CoreOS cluster.

Inside a CoreOS Cluster: Bootstrapping Around etcd

Consider a small CoreOS cluster running a 3-replica web service behind an nginx reverse proxy on three worker machines, backed by a dedicated 3-node etcd cluster. Having three etcd nodes ensures that a single crash or reboot does not take the store down (we will look at how these nodes stay in sync later in this post).

The core design principle of the early CoreOS stack was hub-and-spoke coordination. Daemons on worker machines did not talk directly to each other: schedulers did not open RPC connections to worker agents, and update daemons did not use gossip protocols. Instead, every component only read from and wrote to etcd's shared directory tree:

Going through the bootstrap sequence shows how each part of the cluster maps to a small branch in that tree:

  1. Start with an empty root: etcd starts first as a shared, hierarchical keyspace, similar to a cluster-wide /etc.
  2. Workers join via fleetd: Each CoreOS worker starts fleetd, registers a liveness heartbeat under /_coreos.com/fleet/machines/, and agrees on a single active scheduler (/_coreos.com/fleet/lease/engine-leader, held here by Worker 2).
  3. An admin deploys services and config: Using fleetctl and etcdctl directly against etcd (in 2013-2014, fleetctl wrote unit definitions directly into etcd without an intermediate API server), an admin submits web@1..3 and nginx along with shared application config such as /config/web/rate_limit. The active fleetd scheduler assigns those units to workers, which then start the containers locally.
  4. Running containers register for discovery: Once running, each web replica publishes its IP:port under /services/web/. On Worker 3, nginx (driven by a lightweight template helper like confd) watches /services/web/ so traffic is routed only to healthy backends.
  5. OS updates take turns via locksmithd: Every worker also runs locksmithd, which coordinates around a reboot semaphore under /coreos.com/updateengine/rebootlock/semaphore. This makes sure automatic A/B OS updates reboot one machine at a time instead of taking the whole cluster offline at once. (The etcd nodes themselves run locksmithd in their own one-at-a-time group for the same reason.)

It is worth noting how little data etcd actually holds once the cluster is up and running. The animation compresses each unit into a single line (13 keys in total). Even in a real CoreOS cluster, where fleet splits each unit across several internal subkeys (object, target, state), the entire working set consists of only a few dozen small keys. Total data size stays well under 1 MB, with a small, steady stream of periodic heartbeat writes.

Storing /etc in RAM: Inside etcd v0.4's store

When the entire cluster's working set fits into a few hundred kilobytes, there is little reason to build an on-disk B+tree or an LSM-tree. Early etcd (v0.1 to v0.4) had no embedded database engine at all. Its primary storage engine was an in-memory Go directory tree (store), exposed over a simple HTTP+JSON API on port 4001.

Looking at store/store.go in etcd v0.4.9, the whole storage engine is represented by a single seven-field struct:

// store/store.go (etcd v0.4.9)
type store struct {
    Root           *node
    WatcherHub     *watcherHub
    CurrentIndex   uint64
    Stats          *Stats
    CurrentVersion int
    ttlKeyHeap     *ttlKeyHeap  // need to recovery manually
    worldLock      sync.RWMutex // stop the world lock
}

Each coordination pattern from our CoreOS bootstrap walkthrough maps directly to one of these fields:

CoreOS Cluster Need HTTP+JSON Primitive Backing In-Memory Structure
Hierarchical /etc paths (fleet, /config/*) Directory / leaf CRUD Root *node tree (Children map[string]*node)
Mutual exclusion (locksmithd semaphore, fleetd leader lease) Atomic CAS (prevIndex / prevValue) Monotonic CurrentIndex + worldLock
Ephemeral liveness (fleetd heartbeats, web@1..3 registration) Per-key TTLs (ttl=30) ttlKeyHeap min-heap
Reactive config (nginx/confd following /services/web/) Long-polling watches (?wait=true) WatcherHub + 1,000-slot EventHistory ring buffer

Let's look at how each of these four components works in the code.

The Directory Tree, worldLock, and Atomic CAS

The root of the store is a Unix-like tree of node structs (store/node.go):

// store/node.go (etcd v0.4.9)
type node struct {
    Path string

    CreatedIndex  uint64
    ModifiedIndex uint64

    Parent *node `json:"-"` // should not encode this field! avoid circular dependency.

    ExpireTime time.Time
    ACL        string
    Value      string           // for key-value pair
    Children   map[string]*node // for directory

    store *store
}

A node is either a leaf (holding a Value string with Children == nil) or a directory (holding a Children map[string]*node keyed by path segment). In memory, our CoreOS cluster's keyspace forms a nested tree of Go structs and maps, with ttlKeyHeap holding direct pointers to the same ephemeral *node structs:

Reading /services/web/web@1 acquires worldLock.RLock(), splits the path, and walks Root.Children["services"].Children["web"].Children["web@1"]. Every write acquires the exclusive worldLock.Lock() (commented // stop the world lock in the source code), increments the store's global monotonic CurrentIndex, and updates the affected node's ModifiedIndex.

Having a single global lock and a monotonic index makes Compare-and-Swap (CAS) straightforward to implement. Take locksmithd coordinating a 3 AM OS reboot on Worker 1 as an example. First, locksmithd reads /coreos.com/updateengine/rebootlock/semaphore and sees modifiedIndex: 5. To claim the reboot slot, it sends a conditional PUT with prevIndex=5:

curl -X PUT http://10.0.0.1:4001/v2/keys/coreos.com/updateengine/rebootlock/semaphore \
  -d prevIndex=5 \
  -d value='{"semaphore":0,"max":1,"holders":["worker-1"]}'

Note that locksmith intentionally acquires this semaphore with prevIndex without a TTL or watch. A rebooting host must keep holding the slot while powered off and only releases it via another CAS after booting back up. Other hosts retry with exponential backoff.

In store.CompareAndSwap (store/store.go), the check and update run atomically under worldLock:

// store/store.go (etcd v0.4.9, trimmed)
func (s *store) CompareAndSwap(nodePath, prevValue string, prevIndex uint64,
    value string, expireTime time.Time) (*Event, error) {

    s.worldLock.Lock()
    defer s.worldLock.Unlock()

    n, err := s.internalGet(nodePath)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if ok, which := n.Compare(prevValue, prevIndex); !ok {
        cause := getCompareFailCause(n, which, prevValue, prevIndex)
        return nil, etcdErr.NewError(etcdErr.EcodeTestFailed, cause, s.CurrentIndex)
    }

    s.CurrentIndex++
    // ... record Event with PrevNode ...
    n.Write(value, s.CurrentIndex)
    n.UpdateTTL(expireTime)
    s.WatcherHub.notify(e)
    return e, nil
}

If Worker 1 and Worker 2 both send a request with prevIndex=5 at the same time, whichever request runs first advances the node to modifiedIndex: 42. The second request fails n.Compare and receives 101: Compare failed ([5 != 42]).

Ephemeral Keys and ttlKeyHeap

Unlike the reboot semaphore, service registrations and machine heartbeats need to disappear automatically if a worker crashes. When web@1 starts on Worker 1, it registers an ephemeral key with a 30-second TTL:

curl -X PUT http://10.0.0.1:4001/v2/keys/services/web/web@1 \
  -d value="10.0.1.1:8080" \
  -d ttl=30

When store inserts /services/web/web@1 (auto-creating /services and /services/web along the way), it detects a non-zero ExpireTime and registers the *node pointer in ttlKeyHeap (store/ttl_key_heap.go). Instead of keeping a plain slice or scanning every key in the tree to find expired entries, ttlKeyHeap implements Go's standard library container/heap.Interface (Len, Less, Swap, Push, Pop):

// store/ttl_key_heap.go (etcd v0.4.9, trimmed)
type ttlKeyHeap struct {
    array  []*node
    keyMap map[*node]int
}

func (h ttlKeyHeap) Len() int {
    return len(h.array)
}

func (h ttlKeyHeap) Less(i, j int) bool {
    return h.array[i].ExpireTime.Before(h.array[j].ExpireTime)
}

func (h ttlKeyHeap) Swap(i, j int) {
    h.array[i], h.array[j] = h.array[j], h.array[i]

    // Keep each node's current slice index up to date
    h.keyMap[h.array[i]] = i
    h.keyMap[h.array[j]] = j
}

func (h *ttlKeyHeap) Push(x interface{}) {
    n, _ := x.(*node)
    h.keyMap[n] = len(h.array)
    h.array = append(h.array, n)
}

func (h *ttlKeyHeap) Pop() interface{} {
    old := h.array
    n := len(old)
    x := old[n-1]
    h.array = old[0 : n-1]
    delete(h.keyMap, x)
    return x
}

func (h *ttlKeyHeap) update(n *node) {
    if index, ok := h.keyMap[n]; ok {
        heap.Remove(h, index)
        heap.Push(h, n)
    }
}

Two details explain how this data structure works:

  1. Ordering array by ExpireTime so array[0] always expires first: Go's container/heap treats the flat slice array as an implicit binary tree where the children of index i are at 2*i + 1 and 2*i + 2. Whenever etcd inserts or removes a node via heap.Push or heap.Pop, container/heap calls Less(i, j) to compare ExpireTime on the *node pointers and swaps elements up or down a single root-to-leaf path (O(log N)). This preserves the min-heap invariant: every parent expires earlier than both of its children. As a result, the key that expires soonest always sits at array[0], so checking whether any key is due to expire takes O(1) time.
  2. Tracking positions with keyMap for heartbeat refreshes and early deletes: A plain binary heap only gives direct access to the earliest element (array[0]). When web@1 refreshes its 30-second heartbeat (UpdateTTL) or is deleted manually, store finds the *node through the directory tree rather than the heap, so it does not know which index i in array that node currently occupies. Because Push, Pop, and Swap keep keyMap[node] = i synchronized on every move, update(n) and remove(n) can find the node's slice index in O(1) and rebalance via heap.Remove and heap.Push in O(log N), avoiding a linear scan of the slice.

Expiring overdue keys then becomes a simple loop in store.DeleteExpiredKeys(cutoff time.Time):

// store/store.go (etcd v0.4.9, trimmed)
func (s *store) DeleteExpiredKeys(cutoff time.Time) {
    s.worldLock.Lock()
    defer s.worldLock.Unlock()

    for {
        node := s.ttlKeyHeap.top()
        if node == nil || node.ExpireTime.After(cutoff) {
            break
        }

        s.CurrentIndex++
        e := newEvent(Expire, node.Path, s.CurrentIndex, node.CreatedIndex)
        e.PrevNode = node.Repr(false, false)

        s.ttlKeyHeap.pop()
        node.Remove(true, true, func(path string) {
            s.WatcherHub.notifyWatchers(e, path, true)
        })
        s.WatcherHub.notify(e)
    }
}

The animation below shows this behavior across our three web replicas (ttl=30s). Healthy renewals keep pushing keys down below the root, while a crashed container eventually moves to the top and expires once its timestamp is reached:

Note one important detail in the signature of DeleteExpiredKeys: it does not call time.Now() itself, and instead takes an explicit cutoff time.Time parameter. If three etcd nodes expired keys using their own local wall clocks, clock skew would cause them to expire keys at different points relative to incoming writes, leading to diverging trees and different CurrentIndex values. We will see in the next section how etcd solves this through Raft.

Long-Polling Watches: WatcherHub and the EventHistory Ring Buffer

On Worker 3, nginx (driven by a template helper like confd) needs to learn immediately when /services/web/web@1 disappears during Worker 1's reboot, without polling etcd in a tight loop. In v0.4, watches were implemented as HTTP long-polling ("hanging GET") requests:

curl "http://10.0.0.1:4001/v2/keys/services/web?wait=true&recursive=true&waitIndex=42"

Inside store, watches are managed by watcherHub (store/watcher_hub.go):

// store/watcher_hub.go (etcd v0.4.9)
type watcherHub struct {
    mutex        sync.Mutex
    watchers     map[string]*list.List
    count        int64
    EventHistory *EventHistory
}

When no matching change has happened yet, watcherHub.watch() allocates a buffered EventChan and stores the watcher in watchers["/services/web"], keeping the HTTP request open. Thirty seconds after Worker 1 powers down for its OS update, DeleteExpiredKeys removes web@1 at CurrentIndex = 43 and calls WatcherHub.notify(e). notify splits e.Node.Key (/services/web/web@1) on "/" and walks every ancestor prefix (/, /services, /services/web, /services/web/web@1), waking confd's open GET request with a JSON response:

{
  "action": "expire",
  "node": { "key": "/services/web/web@1", "modifiedIndex": 43 },
  "prevNode": { "key": "/services/web/web@1", "value": "10.0.1.1:8080" }
}

Because each HTTP long-poll delivers only a single event and closes the connection, there is a small gap while confd reloads nginx and opens its next ?wait=true request. During that window, fleetd can reschedule web@1 onto Worker 3 (10.0.1.3:8081, CurrentIndex = 44). If etcd only notified currently waiting clients, confd would miss index 44.

To bridge this gap, watcherHub maintains EventHistory (store/event_history.go and store/event_queue.go), an in-memory fixed-size ring buffer initialized to 1,000 events (newWatchHub(1000) in store/store.go):

// store/event_history.go & store/event_queue.go (etcd v0.4.9)
type EventHistory struct {
    Queue      eventQueue
    StartIndex uint64
    LastIndex  uint64
    rwl        sync.RWMutex
}

type eventQueue struct {
    Events   []*Event
    Size     int
    Front    int
    Back     int
    Capacity int // hardcoded to 1000 in newStore()
}

When confd reconnects with ?wait=true&recursive=true&waitIndex=44, EventHistory.scan() checks the ring buffer before parking the request:

  1. Future index (waitIndex > LastIndex): There is nothing to replay yet, so etcd parks the watcher in watchers["/services/web"].
  2. In-window index (StartIndex <= waitIndex <= LastIndex): scan() jumps directly to (Queue.Front + int(waitIndex - StartIndex)) % 1000 and scans forward for the first matching event. It immediately returns index 44, allowing confd to catch up without missing any updates.
  3. Cleared index (waitIndex < StartIndex): More than 1,000 mutations have occurred since the watcher last checked in, so its slot in the ring buffer has been overwritten. scan() aborts with error 401 (EcodeEventIndexCleared: "The event in requested index is outdated and cleared"), forcing the client to perform a full recursive GET to resynchronize.

The animation below shows all three cases on a scaled-down 10-slot ring buffer: a live watch waking on #1, a quick reconnect replaying #2 from history, and a burst of writes wrapping around to clear #3:

The source comment right above newWatchHub in store/watcher_hub.go shows the exact 2013 workload assumption behind that buffer size:

// Typically, we only need to keep a small size of history[smaller than 20K].
// Ideally, it should smaller than 20K/s[max throughput] * 2 * 50ms[RTT] = 2000

For a quiet CoreOS cluster with dozens of keys and light heartbeat traffic, 1,000 events could cover minutes of history. In a busy cluster, however, that buffer can fill up and wrap around in milliseconds.

So far, everything we have looked at is an in-memory directory tree living inside volatile Go heap memory on a single machine. This immediately raises two questions:

  1. Durability: If etcd-1 crashes or reboots under locksmithd, how does the tree survive?
  2. Consistency: With three etcd nodes running concurrently, how do they agree on who won locksmithd's CAS, keep CurrentIndex identical, and expire TTLs at the same point?

Making RAM Durable and Replicated: goraft, the Command Log, and JSON Snapshots

In etcd v0.1 through v0.4, durability and replication were not separate layers. Instead, Raft itself served as the on-disk storage layer. Early etcd embedded Ben Johnson's github.com/goraft/raft, one of the first Go implementations of the Raft consensus algorithm.

We will not go into Raft's leader-election proofs or term safety here (for an interactive walkthrough of those mechanics, see The Secret Lives of Data). To understand etcd's storage evolution, the main concept we need is the Replicated State Machine (RSM).

Every etcd node runs the same deterministic in-memory store we just looked at. Rather than replicating raw memory pages or full key-value snapshots on every write, Raft replicates an ordered, append-only log of commands across the three nodes:

Following the five steps in the animation shows how locksmithd's CAS request flows through goraft:

  1. Client PUT: Worker 1 sends PUT /v2/keys/coreos.com/updateengine/rebootlock/semaphore?prevIndex=5 to port 4001. (If the request hits a follower, etcd redirects or proxies the write to the leader.) The leader wraps the request in a CompareAndSwapCommand (etcd:compareAndSwap) and passes it to raftServer.Do(cmd).
  2. Append Log: Inside goraft's leaderLoop, processCommand creates a LogEntry (#42) and encodes the JSON command into the leader's local /var/lib/etcd/log file.
  3. Replicate: Peer heartbeat goroutines replicate #42 over port 7001 via AppendEntries. Each follower appends the entry to its own /var/lib/etcd/log and replies with an acknowledgment.
  4. Commit & Reply: Once a majority (2 of 3 nodes) has persisted #42, the leader advances commitIndex. Log.setCommitIndex() decodes the command and invokes ApplyFunc → CompareAndSwapCommand.Apply() → store.CompareAndSwap(...). Only after the leader updates its in-memory store and notifies WatcherHub does it return HTTP 200 OK (with modifiedIndex: 42) to Worker 1.
  5. Followers Apply: Once followers receive the updated commitIndex, each runs the same Log.setCommitIndex() → store.CompareAndSwap(...) path against its own in-memory tree. If Worker 2 concurrently sent prevIndex=5, its command lands at a later log index, applies after Worker 1's command, and deterministically fails with 101: Compare failed on every replica.

Because every node starts from the same empty / and applies the same committed commands in the same order, every replica arrives at the same in-memory tree, the same CurrentIndex, and the same CAS winners. If a node reboots, it recovers its in-memory state from disk.

Deterministic TTL Expiration via SyncCommand

This command-log mechanism also answers the question from the previous section: how do three independent nodes expire TTLs deterministically without relying on local wall clocks?

In server/peer_server.go, the Raft leader runs a 500 ms background ticker (monitorSync) that proposes a SyncCommand carrying the leader's timestamp into the Raft log:

// server/peer_server.go (etcd v0.4.9)
func (s *PeerServer) monitorSync() {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Millisecond * 500)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    for {
        select {
        case <-s.closeChan:
            return
        case now := <-ticker.C:
            if s.raftServer.State() == raft.Leader {
                s.raftServer.Do(s.store.CommandFactory().CreateSyncCommand(now))
            }
        }
    }
}

When each replica commits and applies that etcd:sync log entry (store/v2/sync_command.go), it passes the leader's serialized c.Time directly into s.DeleteExpiredKeys(c.Time). Every node pops the same expired entries from its ttlKeyHeap at the same point in the log, incrementing CurrentIndex identically.

Note a subtle storage side effect here: even a completely idle etcd v0.4 cluster writes two etcd:sync commands per second into the Raft log, which adds up to roughly 172,800 log entries per day.

Log Compaction and Full-Tree JSON Snapshots

An append-only command log cannot grow forever. Without compaction, /var/lib/etcd/log would eventually fill up the disk, and restarting a node would require replaying millions of historical mutations from index 1 just to reconstruct a 50 KB tree.

Raft solves unbounded log growth with snapshotting: periodically write the state machine's full state to disk at some committed log index L, then discard all log entries up to L. This gives /var/lib/etcd/ in etcd v0.4 a very simple on-disk layout. There are no database files, page caches, or indexes, only three items:

/var/lib/etcd/
├── conf                  # Raft peer configuration metadata
├── log                   # Single append-only Raft command log
└── snapshot/
    └── <term>_<index>.ss # Periodic CRC32-prefixed JSON dump of the entire store

In etcd v0.4.9, PeerServer.monitorSnapshot() (server/peer_server.go) wakes up every 3 seconds and checks whether CommitIndex - lastSnapshotIndex exceeds snapshot_count (default 10000 entries). Because of the 500 ms SyncCommand, this threshold is reached at least every ~83 minutes even with zero user writes. When it crosses that threshold, it calls raftServer.TakeSnapshot():

  1. Stop-the-world clone and JSON serialization (store.Save()): goraft asks the state machine (store) to serialize itself: 
   // store/store.go (etcd v0.4.9)
   func (s *store) Save() ([]byte, error) {
    s.worldLock.Lock()

    clonedStore := newStore()
    clonedStore.CurrentIndex = s.CurrentIndex
    clonedStore.Root = s.Root.Clone()
    clonedStore.WatcherHub = s.WatcherHub.clone()
    clonedStore.Stats = s.Stats.clone()
    clonedStore.CurrentVersion = s.CurrentVersion

    s.worldLock.Unlock()

    b, err := json.Marshal(clonedStore)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return b, nil
   }

To avoid holding worldLock during slow JSON encoding, store.Save() first takes the exclusive worldLock.Lock() (blocking all reads and writes) and performs a full recursive deep copy of all N nodes in Root.Clone(), along with EventHistory and Stats. Only after allocating a second copy of the entire keyspace in RAM does it release worldLock and run json.Marshal(clonedStore) on the clone.

  1. Double-encoded snapshot file (goraft/raft/snapshot.go): goraft's Snapshot.save() wraps those state JSON bytes inside an outer Snapshot{LastIndex, LastTerm, Peers, State} struct and calls json.Marshal(ss) a second time (which base64-encodes State []byte inside the outer JSON object). It then writes an 8-character CRC32 checksum followed by the payload to snapshot/<term>_<index>.ss, calls file.Sync(), and deletes the previous snapshot file: 
   # /var/lib/etcd/snapshot/1_10001.ss
   a3f9c210                                           ◄── 8-char IEEE CRC32 checksum
   {
     "lastIndex": 10001, "lastTerm": 1,
     "peers": [{"name": "etcd-1", "connectionString": "http://10.0.0.1:7001"}, ...],
     "state": "eyJSb290Ijp7IlBhdGgiOiIvIiwiQ2hpbGRyZW4iOnsi..."  ◄── base64(json(store))
   }

  1. Log rewrite and truncation (goraft/raft/log.go):
    Once the snapshot is synced, goraft keeps a 200-entry safety tail (NumberOfLogEntriesAfterSnapshot = 200) so slightly lagging followers can still catch up via AppendEntries instead of transferring a full snapshot. It calls s.log.compact(), which locks Log.mutex, writes those surviving tail entries into log.new, calls file.Sync(), and atomically replaces log with log.new using os.Rename.

  2. Crash recovery (store.Recovery()):
    When a node restarts, it reads the latest <term>_<index>.ss file, unmarshals the JSON tree back into RAM, and walks every node via Root.recoverAndclean() to reconstruct fields that JSON could not encode (Parent pointers marked json:"-" and the unexported ttlKeyHeap). Finally, it replays whatever entries remain in /var/lib/etcd/log.

Every step of this pipeline is easy to understand, but it scales linearly (O(N)) with the total size of the tree in RAM, CPU, and disk I/O.

Evaluating the v0.4 Design: Strengths and Limitations

For the 2013 CoreOS Container Linux workload, etcd v0.1 to v0.4 was a pragmatic design. It shipped as a single static Go binary with zero external dependencies, gave operators a familiar filesystem model they could inspect with curl, served reads in microseconds from RAM, and recovered state from plain files in /var/lib/etcd/. When a cluster only coordinated a few dozen keys across fleet, locksmith, and confd, this simplicity allowed CoreOS to ship quickly.

However, as clusters moved from early prototypes into production deployments in 2014, serious limitations emerged. Most of them stemmed from goraft (the consensus and persistence engine underneath store) and how it interacted with snapshotting. They fell into three areas: coupling and testability, persistence correctness, and write-path performance.

Testability and Coupling in goraft

Inside third_party/github.com/goraft/raft/, goraft's server struct combined every layer of the system into a single stateful object:

  • Network transport: Direct HTTP client and server calls (http_transporter.go) and per-peer background goroutines.
  • Timers and goroutine lifecycles: Wall-clock time.Tick and time.After channels driving leaderLoop, followerLoop, and candidateLoop.
  • Disk I/O: Direct os.File seeks, writes, renames, and fsync calls inside Log and Snapshot.save().
  • Synchronous state-machine execution: Log.setCommitIndex() decoded each entry and invoked l.ApplyFunc(entry, command) synchronously while holding Log.mutex.Lock().

Consensus protocols are hardest to get right in rare failure scenarios, such as asymmetric network partitions, dropped or reordered RPCs, sudden leader step-downs, and partial disk writes. Because goraft coupled live sockets, wall-clock timers, coarse mutexes, and os.File handles directly into the protocol state machine, deterministic unit testing was almost impossible. Edge cases had to be reproduced through timing-dependent multi-goroutine tests, which made subtle split-brain and cluster-membership bugs hard to isolate and fix.

Persistence and Snapshot Correctness

On disk, the persistence format introduced two notable data-integrity hazards:

  • Unchecksummed log entries: While .ss snapshot files included a CRC32 checksum, /var/lib/etcd/log had no per-entry integrity check. In LogEntry.Encode(), goraft wrote an 8-character ASCII hex length (fmt.Fprintf(w, "%8x\n", len(b))) followed by raw protobuf bytes (w.Write(b)). Silent bitrot or a corrupted sector in the log went undetected during replay as long as the bytes still unmarshaled as valid protobuf.
  • Racy snapshot boundaries: server.TakeSnapshot() contained an explicit TODO in etcd v0.4.9's production code: 
  // third_party/github.com/goraft/raft/server.go (etcd v0.4.9)
  func (s *server) TakeSnapshot() error {
    // ...
    // TODO: acquire the lock and no more committed is allowed
    // This will be done after finishing refactoring heartbeat
    s.debugln("take.snapshot")

    lastIndex, lastTerm := s.log.commitInfo()
    // ...
    state, err := s.stateMachine.Save()

Because TakeSnapshot() read lastIndex before calling s.stateMachine.Save() without blocking concurrent commits, new mutations could be applied to store in the gap. This could produce a snapshot file whose serialized State had already moved past its recorded LastIndex.

Write-Path Performance and Compaction Stalls

Even on a healthy network without failures, goraft's write and compaction paths had significant bottlenecks. Two of them governed steady-state writes before log compaction ran.

Timer-polled, stop-and-wait replication. In server.processCommand(), the leader appends a client command to /var/lib/etcd/log and returns immediately without waking peer replication goroutines. Instead, each follower's Peer.heartbeat() loop waits on a 50 ms time.Tick (DefaultHeartbeatInterval) before calling p.flush(), where sendAppendEntriesRequest() blocks synchronously until the HTTP request completes.

Even with near-zero local network latency, a single write waits around 25 ms on average for the next tick. Back-to-back sequential PUTs align with the 50 ms interval, capping a single writer at roughly 20 writes/sec.

Unbatched per-entry syscalls on the log. Under concurrent client load, Log.appendEntry() serializes appends one entry at a time under Log.mutex.Lock(). Each command triggers a file.Seek(0, os.SEEK_CUR) syscall plus two unbuffered write() syscalls: fmt.Fprintf for the hex length header and file.Write for the JSON-wrapped-in-Protobuf entry. Meanwhile, leader commits call s.log.sync() and execute state-machine mutations synchronously under the same coarse lock.

To see both bottlenecks in practice, we benchmarked steady-state /v2/keys writes across increasing client concurrency (c = 1 through 256) on a 3-node etcd v0.4.9 cluster. The setup is reproducible via bbolt_etcd/benchmarks/part1_v04/run.sh. Each node runs on 1 dedicated cpuset-pinned core with tmpfs volumes (to isolate Raft replication and locking from single-host disk contention), and clients send direct-to-leader HTTP keep-alive PUTs across 1,000 keys with 256 B values.

At c = 1, sequential writes align with goraft's 50 ms Peer.heartbeat() interval, keeping single-client throughput near the 20 writes/s ceiling. As concurrency increases, multiple appends accumulate in /var/lib/etcd/log during each heartbeat sleep and flush together in the next AppendEntries request, so throughput initially scales close to linearly. At the highest concurrency (c = 256), the curve drops below the dashed ideal linear line as writers saturate the leader's single core behind Log.mutex and unbatched per-entry Seek/Write syscalls.

Per-request latency confirms both bottlenecks. Across the entire concurrency sweep, median latency (p50) remains flat at the 50 ms heartbeat interval. Meanwhile, p99 tail latency climbs steadily as batches grow and eventually exceeds two full heartbeat cycles at c = 256, as writers queue behind serialized log appends and commits.

Stop-the-world snapshot and log-rewrite stalls. These steady-state numbers only hold while /var/lib/etcd/log appends uninterrupted. Every 10,000 commits (snapshot_count), PeerServer.monitorSnapshot() triggers TakeSnapshot(), adding a third bottleneck to the write path.

First, store.Save() acquires the exclusive worldLock to deep-clone the tree, marshals it to JSON twice (base64-encoding the inner JSON into the outer .ss file), and fsyncs the snapshot. Next, Log.compact() acquires Log.mutex.Lock(), writes the surviving tail entries into log.new, calls file.Sync(), and atomically replaces /var/lib/etcd/log via os.Rename. All in-flight appends and commits stall until this rewrite finishes.

Looking Ahead to Part 2

By late 2014, the CoreOS team realized that goraft's coupling, persistence hazards, and write-path bottlenecks could not be solved with incremental patches. Making etcd reliable enough for production meant rebuilding its consensus engine, on-disk write-ahead storage, and peer replication from scratch. The goals were deterministic and unit-testable state transitions, corruption checks for every persisted record, and a write path free of timer-polling and unbatched syscall stalls.

This rewrite shipped in January 2015 as etcd v2.0. In Part 2, we will examine etcd v2's redesigned consensus and storage architecture, run the same 3-node benchmark to see how much changed, and look at what happened when rapid production adoption brought much larger workloads to etcd.
