title: Write-Ahead Log vs Append-Only Event Log: Two Logs With Opposite Jobs
description:
Both structures are files that only grow. Both are written sequentially, both are read in order, and both are described as "the log." That shared vocabulary hides a deep difference in intent. One exists to make a single write atomic and durable, and it is deleted the moment its job is done. The other exists to preserve a record forever, and it is the source of truth rather than a temporary aid. Confusing them leads to systems that keep the wrong data too long or throw away the right data too soon.

A write-ahead log is a crash-recovery device that records an intended change before applying it and is discarded once the change is safe, while an append-only event log is a permanent history whose retained entries are the product itself.

That distinction determines retention, readers, ordering guarantees, and what happens when the disk fills up. It also explains why the two are often used together in the same system.

Part One: What each log is for

A write-ahead log, usually shortened to WAL, solves the torn-write problem. A database page is larger than a disk sector, so a crash can leave a page half updated. The WAL records the change as a small, sequential entry before the data page is modified. If the process dies, the database replays committed entries from the log and ignores incomplete ones. This is the foundation of atomicity and durability in almost every relational engine. Because the log is only needed until the changed pages are flushed, it is periodically truncated or recycled.
An append-only event log solves a different problem: how does a system remember everything that happened so that other systems can reconstruct state? Events are immutable business facts — an order was placed, a seat was reserved, a temperature crossed a threshold. Producers append; consumers read from an offset and never modify old records. Retention is measured in days, months, or forever. The log is not a helper for a write; it is the ledger from which derived views, caches, and downstream services are built.

The physical similarity is real. But a WAL cares about the state of one page at one instant, while an event log cares about the ordering of facts across a whole system over time.

Part Two: The cost of keeping records

Run the numbers on a busy service. Suppose a database processes 50,000 writes per second, each producing a 200-byte WAL record. That is 10 megabytes per second, or roughly 36 gigabytes an hour. If checkpointing flushes pages every five minutes, the active WAL stays around three gigabytes — small enough to keep on local NVMe and cheap to replay after a crash. Now take an event log for the same service generating 8,000 business events per second at 1 kilobyte each: about 8 megabytes a second, or 700 gigabytes a day. Keeping ninety days means roughly 63 terabytes before replication. With three replicas that is close to 200 terabytes of storage, a figure that turns retention policy into a budget line rather than a default.

These orders of magnitude explain the design split. The WAL can afford to be fast and small because it throws data away. The event log must be partitioned, compressed, and tiered to cold storage because its value grows with its history. The global stream-processing and event-streaming platform market is now measured in several billions of dollars annually, and most of that spend is really a storage bill wearing a software label.

A WAL is cheap because it is throwaway, while an event log is expensive because it is retained, so the moment you start keeping a recovery log for analysis you have quietly built a second database with none of a database's lifecycle controls.

The practical rule follows: give each log an owner and a retention policy. The WAL belongs to the storage engine. The event log belongs to the organization.

Part Three: Where each design breaks

A write-ahead log breaks when replay is slow. After a crash, a database with a large uncheckpointed WAL may spend minutes applying records before it accepts connections. Teams tune checkpoint frequency to balance recovery time against write amplification: flushing too often wears devices, flushing too rarely lengthens outages. The WAL also cannot answer business questions. It records physical changes, not intentions, and its format is private to the engine. Trying to build analytics on it is a classic mistake.

An append-only event log breaks when events are wrong. Because records are immutable, a badly designed event cannot be quietly corrected; the fix is a compensating event, and every consumer must understand compensation. Late-arriving data complicates ordering: an event about yesterday that arrives today may need to be inserted into a stream that consumers have already processed. Schemas also drift. Without versioning, a field rename breaks consumers months later. And because every consumer replays from an offset, a slow or buggy consumer can fall arbitrarily far behind, forcing the platform to retain data longer than planned.

Treating the WAL as an event source almost always fails. WAL entries are physical, engine-specific, and subject to truncation. They describe how a row changed, not why. The "why" is the part that future systems need.

Part Four: An everyday analogy

Imagine a bakery. The write-ahead log is the baker's order slip written before the bread goes in the oven: "two rye, one sourdough." If the power cuts and the baker forgets what was in the oven, the slip tells them what was supposed to happen. Once the bread is baked and sold, the slip is thrown away. Nobody keeps last Tuesday's slip to understand the bakery; it was an aid to getting through the moment.

The append-only event log is the bakery's ledger: "Tuesday, 7:04, two rye sold to the corner cafe." That line is never erased. The accountant sums it for revenue, the supply manager reads it to order flour, and the owner looks back a year later to see which bread sold in winter. The ledger is not an aid to baking — it is the memory of the business. A bakery that throws away its ledger to save paper has made the same error as a team that truncates its events to save storage.

What is actually transferable

The first lesson is to ask what a log is allowed to forget. If forgetting is the point, treat it as recovery infrastructure: keep it local, keep it short, and tune it for replay speed. If forgetting is unacceptable, treat it as data infrastructure: replicate it, version its schema, define retention explicitly, and budget for cold storage.

The second lesson is that the two patterns compose. A database writes a WAL to survive crashes and also emits business events to a durable log for everyone else. Trying to merge the roles produces a WAL that is too large to replay and an event stream that is too physical to use. Keeping them separate costs more machinery but makes each one honest about its job.

The write-ahead log and the append-only event log are both sequential files, but one is a short-lived promise that a write will survive and the other is a long-lived memory of what occurred, and a system needs to know which promise it is making before it picks a retention policy.

Name them differently in your diagrams. The wording will save you an argument during the next outage.

title: Curved ramps in a 2D physics engine, and the ball that looked like it was being hit 500 times a second
description:
I build Soliton, a physics engine in Rust that compiles to WebAssembly and runs in the browser. It powers 151 interactive simulations of school physics, and a sandbox where you build your own.

Someone sent me a video: a block slides down a curved ramp and hits a second block sitting on a spring, with a pendulum hanging under it. Could Soliton do that?

Almost. It had no curves.

This post is about adding them properly. It covers:

  • why a chain of flat pieces is the wrong answer,
  • representing a curve so the engine can be exact about it,
  • contact between a curve and a ball, and between a curve and a box,
  • testing it all against textbook physics,
  • and the two bugs those tests caught, one of them in the solver itself.

Try it first: open the sandbox and press U to drop a curved ramp. Free, no sign-up.

Why not just chain flat pieces?

The obvious way to fake a curve is a polyline: lots of short straight segments. It looks fine. It behaves badly.

A box sliding over a polyline meets a tiny corner at every joint. Each one is a small collision. It loses a little speed, judders, and sometimes snags outright. Make the pieces smaller and you get more corners, not fewer.

So curves had to become a real shape in the engine.

The representation: a turtle path

A track is a list of pieces. Each one starts where the last ended, heading the same way:

pub enum TrackPiece {
    /// Straight ahead for this many metres.
    Line(f64),
    /// Turn through `angle` radians on a circle: positive left, negative right.
    Arc { radius: f64, angle: f64 },
    /// A sharp turn on the spot: a floor meeting a wall, a ledge dropping away.
    Corner(f64),
}

Because each piece leaves in the direction the previous one was heading, the tangent is continuous at every join by construction, unless you explicitly ask for a corner. You can't accidentally build a kink.

In a scene file, a U-shaped valley looks like this:

{ "track": { "pieces": [
  { "arc": { "radius": 2, "angle": 1.5708 } },
  { "line": 2 },
  { "arc": { "radius": 2, "angle": 1.5708 } }
] } }

Why only lines and circular arcs, and not Bézier curves or splines? Because for a line or a circle, the closest point to anything has an exact, closed-form answer: a projection for a line, a radial line for an arc. Collision detection becomes exact geometry instead of iterative root-finding. Lines and arcs can still approximate any curve you want.

Thick and two-sided

The track is a centre line thickened by half its thickness on each side. That has two nice consequences:

  1. It's solid from both faces. The same curve holds a ball inside it as a bowl and carries one over it as a hump.
  2. Collision is "distance to a curve". A ball touches the track when the distance from its centre to the centre line is less than its radius plus half the thickness.

Contact with a ball

For each segment, find the closest point to the ball's centre. Then deal with one subtlety: a point near a joint is closest to both neighbouring segments at the joint itself, and you don't want two identical contacts.

The rule: if a segment's closest point was clamped to its end, the next segment will find that same point or a nearer one, so drop it:

let keep = match along {
    Along::Interior => true,
    // A joint is kept once, by the segment after it, and only when both sides end there.
    Along::End => i == last,
    Along::Start => i == 0 || found[i - 1].1 == Along::End,
};

A ball over a joint touches once. A ball wedged in a narrow valley touches both walls, because those are two distinct places.

Contact with a box

A convex polygon meets a smooth curve in exactly two ways:

  1. A corner of the box touches the curve. This is how a box sits in a bowl: two corners on the curve.
  2. The curve touches the middle of a face. This is how a box sits on a hump. It can only happen where the curve runs parallel to the face, which on an arc is the arc's extreme point across the face: 
// The arc's point furthest across the face, if the arc reaches round to it.
TrackSegment::Arc { center, radius, .. } if s.sweeps_through((-normal).angle()) => {
    Some((k, center - normal * radius))
}

Add the track's two end caps and any sharp corners as points that can press into a face (that's how a box hangs over a ledge), and you have the complete contact set.

Testing against the textbook

Every scene in Soliton ships with a test that holds it to an exact physical fact. Curves got the same treatment:

Test Expected Result
Bead in a bowl swings like a pendulum Exact large-amplitude pendulum period Within 0.1%
Ball inside a ring, launched at 1.02 × √(5gr) Goes over the top ✅
Same ball at 0.9 × √(5gr) Leaves the ring at h = (u² − 2gr)/3g = 0.9225 m 0.9225 m
Box sliding across a valley for 10 s Energy conserved To 1 part in 10⁵
Box into a vertical wall (sharp corner) Elastic bounce, never passes the corner ✅
Box with a quarter of it over a ledge Rests perfectly still ✅

That leaving height is my favourite. It comes from two facts: energy conservation, and the normal force reaching zero where gravity's inward pull alone supplies the centripetal force. The engine computes neither. It just integrates forces and resolves contacts, and the ball still lets go exactly where the algebra says.

Bug 1: a steady push that looked like a hammer

The ring test failed at first, in a strange way. The motion was perfect: the ball stayed exactly on the circle and energy was conserved. But the recorded normal force flickered between its true value and zero, every other step.

Here's why. The solver has to decide, for each contact, whether this is a resting contact (a steady push) or an impact (a collision, which gets restitution and bounces). It decides by how fast the surfaces are approaching. If they're closing faster than the applied forces could explain within a few steps, it's an impact:

let pushed = 4.0 * accelerations[row.source].abs() * dt + 1e-6;
if row.active && pre[r] < -restitution_threshold.max(pushed) {
    // ... treat as an impact, aim for a bounce
}

On a flat floor, that works. On a curve it doesn't. A ball sliding along the inside of a ring closes the gap to the wall even with no force pressing it, because going straight would carry it into the bend. The rate is κv², the curvature times the speed squared. At 8 m/s on a 1.35 m radius, that's about 50 m/s² of "approach" that the solver couldn't explain from the forces. So it decided: impact! It applied a tiny bounce. Next step the ball had separated, so there was no force. Then it came back.

The fix: contacts now carry the curvature of the surface, and the solver counts the turning motion as part of the steady push:

// Riding along a curved surface closes the gap as surely as a force pressing in does.
let pressed = c.normal.dot(explicit(c.b) - explicit(c.a));
if c.curvature == 0.0 {
    return pressed;
}
let slide = c.normal.perp().dot(point_velocity(c.b, c.point) - point_velocity(c.a, c.point));
pressed - c.curvature * slide * slide

Every existing shape reports zero curvature, so nothing that worked before changes. After the fix, the normal force on the ball matches m(v²/r − g·h/r) to 1 part in 10,000 all the way round.

Bug 2 (not a bug): the box that knocks

A box sliding over a bump lost about 1.4% of its energy. My first instinct was to blame the joins between arcs. But a ball over the same bump lost nothing.

The box is right. Where the curve switches from bending down (the crest) to bending up (the dip), a rigid flat-bottomed box has to switch from rotating one way to rotating the other. There's no smooth way to do that, so its leading corner strikes the surface. That's a real collision, and with no bounce it really does absorb energy. The test now checks that this loss is booked as dissipated energy, not that it's zero.

The loop you can't build

One thing a flat world can't have: a loop-the-loop with a run-in and a run-out.

The ball's path has to cross itself. At the crossing, the ball passes along branch A past branch B, and later along B past A. For a two-sided track, both crossings are blocked. For a one-sided track, work out which side of each branch the ball approaches from. If d_A × d_B is the cross product of the two directions, passing B needs it negative and passing A needs it positive. You can't have both. Real roller-coaster loops escape by shifting sideways in the third dimension. A closed ring works fine, which is all the textbook problem needs.

Bonus: simple harmonic motion as a shadow

With springs getting heavier use, I added the textbook's reference circle: beside any body on a spring, a point goes round a circle at a steady rate, its shadow tied to the mass, while a displacement–time graph draws itself out of the circle.

It isn't an animation of a formula. Amplitude and phase are computed live from the mass, the stiffness and the actual motion, so if friction or a collision changes the swing, the circle changes with it.

Try it

  • Playground: solitonplay.com. Press U in the sandbox for a curved ramp.
  • Reference circle: a mass on a vertical spring
  • Scene format: writing tracks in a scene file
  • JavaScript: npm install @soliton-physics/engine
  • Python: pip install soliton-physics

If you've fought collision detection on curves yourself, I'd love to hear how you solved it in the comments.

title: All or Nothing: Testing DynamoDB Transaction Atomicity with Tables
description:
What a four-operation failure taught me about commits, cancellation reasons, and verifying that nothing was written.

A database transaction is easy to appreciate when it succeeds. The more important question is what happens when one operation fails after several other changes have been requested.

Suppose an application needs to create a record, update an existing balance, and delete an obsolete item. If a final validation check fails, none of those changes should be committed. Otherwise, the application could be left with data that describes a transaction that never actually completed.

I tested this behavior using Tables by ServerlessCreed and Amazon DynamoDB. The experiment had three parts: commit a valid transaction, deliberately fail the final condition in a second transaction, and correct the request before verifying the committed state independently with the AWS CLI.

The test used Tables v3.3.46, a disposable DynamoDB table in us-east-1, and on-demand capacity. The data below is synthetic test data.

Prerequisites

To reproduce this workflow, you need:

  1. Tables by ServerlessCreed installed, with access to Operations Studio → Transaction Builder.
  2. An approved, non-production AWS environment with an active DynamoDB connection configured in Tables.
  3. An AWS profile with the required DynamoDB read and transaction permissions.
  4. A disposable DynamoDB table for safely testing transaction operations.
  5. AWS CLI installed and configured for independent verification of the results.

For this test, I used:

Component Configuration
Tables version v3.3.46
Operating system Windows 11
AWS Region us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
AWS profile admin-profile
Test table TC_ADV_001_QA
Billing mode On-demand
Verification Tables and AWS CLI
Testing approach Successful transaction, deliberate failure, cancellation analysis, and recovery

Starting with a known state

I began with three items in an isolated table. The id attribute was the String partition key, and version was a Number used for optimistic checks.

Item Balance Version Status
ADV-001 100 1 ACTIVE
ADV-002 50 1 ACTIVE
ADV-GUARD 0 1 READY


Figure 1. Baseline records before running any transaction.

Having an explicit baseline made it possible to distinguish a committed change from a partial write or a stale result.

A valid transaction: all changes commit

I opened Operations Studio → Transaction Builder, selected TransactWrite, and configured three actions against distinct items:

  1. Update ADV-001: Change balance from 100 to 90 and version from 1 to 2, provided its existing version is 1.
  2. Put ADV-NEW: Create a new item with balance 10, version 1, and status CREATED, provided it does not already exist.
  3. ConditionCheck ADV-GUARD: Require status READY and version 1.

The update used the expression:

SET #b = :newBalance, #v = :newVersion

Here, #b and #v are aliases for the real attribute names balance and version; the : tokens refer to supplied values. This makes the intended update explicit while keeping the attribute names and values separate.

Tables showed 3/3 valid and indicated that atomic behavior was enabled. That was a local validation result: DynamoDB still had to evaluate the conditions and accept the transaction.


Figure 2. Three operations reviewed and locally validated before execution.

After execution, Tables displayed “Transaction committed successfully” and reported 6.00 capacity units. A fresh scan showed the expected data: ADV-001 now had balance 90 and version 2, ADV-NEW existed, and the other original items were unchanged.


Figure 3. Successful commit reported in Tables.


Figure 4. The item view confirms the committed changes.

A deliberate failure: what happens to the other writes?

The next request was intentionally designed to fail. I added four operations in this order:

Position Operation Requested action
1 Put Create ADV-FAIL, with balance 999 and status SHOULD_NOT_EXIST
2 Update Change ADV-002 to balance 999 and status SHOULD_NOT_APPEAR
3 Delete Delete the existing ADV-NEW item
4 ConditionCheck Require ADV-GUARD.version = 99

The guard item's real version was 1, not 99. The last condition was therefore guaranteed to fail against the recorded baseline. Despite that, the builder displayed 4/4 valid because the request's structure and expressions were valid.


Figure 5. The failure test is structurally valid, even though its final condition is false.

What the failure analyzer showed

When I executed the request, Tables opened its Transaction Failure Analyzer. The result was unambiguous: one of four operations failed, and no writes were committed.

The first three operations were shown as Rolled back. The fourth was marked ConditionalCheckFailed. The analyzer also displayed the actual item value, explaining that the record had version 1 while the request expected 99.


Figure 6. Tables maps the cancellation to the fourth operation and explains the version mismatch.

This is an important distinction: DynamoDB provides the all-or-nothing transaction guarantee and the cancellation response; Tables presents those results in an operation-by-operation diagnostic view. Tables did not perform a compensating rollback after partially committed writes. The transaction was canceled without those writes committing.

The downloaded diagnostic report also contained the failing operation's cancellation details:

{
  "index": 3,
  "code": "ConditionalCheckFailed",
  "message": "The conditional request failed"
}

The report uses a zero-based index, so index: 3 identifies the fourth operation. DynamoDB's cancellation reasons correspond to the order of actions in the submitted request, which makes this useful when investigating a longer transaction.


Figure 7. The exported diagnostic report confirms the operation index and failure reason.

I then returned to the table and ran a fresh scan. ADV-FAIL was absent, ADV-002 still had balance 50 and status ACTIVE, and ADV-NEW had not been deleted. ADV-001 and ADV-GUARD were unchanged as well.


Figure 8. The unchanged item state provides direct evidence that no partial writes committed.

Correct the condition, then verify the result

To test recovery, I changed the final condition to require the guard item's actual version, 1, and reconstructed the four-operation request.

One detail matters for interpreting the result: during this manual reconstruction, the Update action was also configured differently. Instead of attempting balance 999 and a changed status, it set ADV-002 to balance 90, version 2, leaving its ACTIVE status intact. This was a corrected and reconstructed request, not a byte-for-byte replay with only one condition changed.

The corrected transaction committed. Tables displayed a success banner reporting 8.00 capacity units, and a fresh scan reflected the submitted operations: ADV-FAIL existed, ADV-NEW was gone, and ADV-002 had balance 90 and version 2.


Figure 9. The corrected transaction commits as a single request.


Figure 10. The final Tables item state matches the reconstructed request.

I also verified the final state directly with the AWS CLI, rather than relying only on the application's table view. The command used DynamoDB's --consistent-read option:

aws dynamodb scan --table-name YOUR_TEST_TABLE --consistent-read --region us-east-1 --profile YOUR_APPROVED_PROFILE --query "Items[].{Id:id.S,Balance:balance.N,Version:version.N,Status:status.S}" --output table

The CLI returned four items:

Item Balance Version Status
ADV-FAIL 999 1 SHOULD_NOT_EXIST
ADV-001 90 2 ACTIVE
ADV-002 90 2 ACTIVE
ADV-GUARD 0 1 READY

The deliberately named SHOULD_NOT_EXIST item should exist at this stage: its creation was part of the now-successful corrected transaction. The absent ADV-NEW item confirmed the delete operation had committed.


Figure 11. Independent AWS CLI verification matches the final state shown in Tables.

Two practical considerations: capacity and safety

Transactions provide stronger coordination, but they have capacity implications. DynamoDB performs additional work to prepare and commit transactional writes. For an item up to 1 KB, a transactional write requires two write units. Capacity can also be consumed by a canceled transaction. The 6.00 and 8.00 figures above were the capacity measurements displayed by Tables, not dollar charges; actual cost depends on usage, billing mode, and AWS pricing.

TransactWriteItems supports up to 100 actions and 4 MB of data per request. All referenced tables must be within the same AWS account and Region, and two actions cannot target the same item. These are DynamoDB constraints rather than Tables-specific limits.

The takeaway

The clearest proof of transaction atomicity came from the failed request, not the successful one. The fourth condition evaluated to false, the failure was mapped to the correct operation, and none of the preceding put, update, or delete actions committed.

Tables helped make that failure understandable through its operation-level analyzer and downloadable diagnostic report. DynamoDB supplied the underlying transactional guarantee. Checking the item state after cancellation—and verifying the corrected final result through the AWS CLI—made the difference between seeing a status message and establishing what actually happened to the data.

Further reading

  • Amazon DynamoDB: Managing transactions
  • Amazon DynamoDB: TransactWriteItems API
  • Amazon DynamoDB: Read and write capacity consumption
  • Amazon DynamoDB: Transaction constraints

title: SQL Server to BigQuery: Build a CDC Pipeline That Lands in Your Own Bucket
description:
A SQL Server to BigQuery job often begins life as a nightly bcp export, a CSV file in a bucket and a bq load. That is enough for a dashboard refreshed once a day. It stops being enough when an order ships at noon, a customer moves city, and the afternoon report still shows the morning's values.

SQL Server already records those changes. With change data capture (CDC) on, the SQL Server Agent copies each insert, update and delete from the transaction log into a change table. What is left to decide is who reads those tables and where the rows land.

The usual options:

  • Datastream for SQL Server: Google's managed CDC service, near real time by Google's description. Nothing to run, and the rows land in native BigQuery datasets that only BigQuery reads.
  • Debezium, Kafka and a BigQuery sink connector: changes in seconds, but you operate Kafka, Kafka Connect, the Debezium SQL Server connector and the sink.
  • bcp to CSV, then bq load: hours to daily, and every run is a full reload, so a deleted row lingers until the next one.

This tutorial takes a fourth route. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, drains the change tables on a schedule and commits Apache Iceberg tables into BigLake, Google Cloud's Iceberg representational state transfer (REST) catalog. The Parquet files sit in a Cloud Storage bucket you own, BigQuery queries them by a four-part name, and DuckDB and Spark open the same files.

I ran each step below on 2026-10-30 with SQL Server 2022 Developer in Docker, OLake Go v1.1.0 in OLake UI and a bucket in us-central1. Every count and timing in this post comes from that run.

What the SQL Server to BigQuery pipeline is made of

  • Source: a shop database with dbo.customers and dbo.orders, both with CDC on, starting at 8 customers and 40 orders.
  • Pipeline: OLake Go in Docker Compose. The first sync records the current log sequence number (LSN) and copies each table; later syncs read the change tables from that LSN.
  • Destination: a BigLake catalog named after the bucket.

You need: Docker, SQL Server 2016 SP1 or later on Developer, Standard or Enterprise edition with the Agent running, and a Google Cloud project.

Step 1: Turn on CDC in SQL Server

Bring your own tables, or create the two the run used:

CREATE TABLE dbo.customers (
  id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  name NVARCHAR(100), email NVARCHAR(200), city NVARCHAR(100), tier NVARCHAR(20),
  created_at DATETIME2 DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME(),
  updated_at DATETIME2 DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME());

CREATE TABLE dbo.orders (
  id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT REFERENCES dbo.customers(id),
  product NVARCHAR(100), amount DECIMAL(10,2), status NVARCHAR(20),
  created_at DATETIME2 DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME(),
  updated_at DATETIME2 DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME());

Next, switch CDC on for the database and for each table, and create a login for OLake Go. The msdb grant at the bottom is the line people forget, and the source test refuses to pass without it.

USE shop;
EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_db;

EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_table @source_schema = N'dbo', @source_name = N'customers', @role_name = NULL;
EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_table @source_schema = N'dbo', @source_name = N'orders',    @role_name = NULL;

USE master;
CREATE LOGIN olake WITH PASSWORD = '<password>';
USE shop;
CREATE USER olake FOR LOGIN olake;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA :: dbo TO olake;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA :: cdc TO olake;
GRANT VIEW DATABASE STATE TO olake;

-- OLake Go reads the capture job definition in msdb before each sync
USE msdb;
CREATE USER olake FOR LOGIN olake;
GRANT SELECT ON dbo.cdc_jobs TO olake;

Confirm it took:

SELECT name, is_cdc_enabled FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'shop';   -- 1
SELECT capture_instance FROM cdc.change_tables;                        -- dbo_customers, dbo_orders
EXEC msdb.dbo.sp_help_job @job_name = N'cdc.shop_capture';             -- the Agent job exists

Two things to know on a real server:

  • The Agent is what fills the change tables. If it is stopped, nothing lands in cdc.* and SQL Server reports no error. EXEC master.dbo.xp_servicecontrol 'QueryState', 'SQLServerAgent' answers Running. when it is up.
  • On Cloud SQL the database step is EXEC msdb.dbo.gcloudsql_cdc_enable_db 'shop' instead. The table step stays the same.

Step 2: Create the bucket and service account in Google Cloud

Everything here happens in the Google Cloud console, inside the project that will hold the tables.

  1. Open APIs and services, then Enable APIs and services, and enable the BigLake API.
  2. In Cloud Storage, create a bucket in the region BigQuery will query from (us-central1 for me). The bucket name turns into the catalog name in SQL, so keep it short.
  3. In IAM and Admin (Identity and Access Management), Service Accounts, create one, for example olake-biglake. Grant it BigLake Editor on the project and Storage Object User on the bucket.
  4. On the account's Keys tab, pick Add key, Create new key, JSON. The key file downloads only once.

You do not create a catalog. BigLake makes one named after the bucket the first time OLake Go calls it, in end-user credential mode, and that is the mode to keep.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and add SQL Server as a source 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and sign in as admin with the password password. Under Sources, click Create Source, pick MSSQL and keep the OLake Go version on the latest release.

Leave Enable CDC on. Manage Capture Instance lets OLake Go create a new capture instance on its own after a schema change, but it needs db_owner, so leave it off for a read-only login. My connection: host host.docker.internal (SQL Server ran in another container), port 1433, database shop, user olake, SSL disabled.

Click Set up source. OLake Go tests the login, CDC on the database, a capture instance per table and a readable capture job before it saves anything.

Step 4: Point the Iceberg destination at BigLake

Under Destinations, click Create Destination, pick Apache Iceberg and choose BigLake as the catalog type:

Field Value
REST Catalog URI https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog
BigLake Catalog Path gs://<bucket>, the bucket root with no folder after it
Authentication Type GCP
GCP Service Account JSON the whole key file from step 2
Catalog Name olake_iceberg
GCP Auth Scopes https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform, the default
GCP Project ID your project ID
Enable Arrow Writes off

Click Create. OLake Go calls the endpoint, creates the catalog on first contact, then writes and drops a test table in the bucket. A 403 from biglake.googleapis.com points at a missing BigLake Editor grant, and one from storage.googleapis.com points at Storage Object User.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

Under Jobs, click Create Job. I named mine sql_server_to_bigquery, gave it a schedule and picked the new source and destination.

Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to Google BigQuery, Apache Spark and DuckDB. OLake Go then only offers delete formats all three read, and in my run it resolved Positional Deletes.

Click Next. On the Streams page, tick customers and orders, keep Full Refresh + CDC and Upsert, and leave systranschemas unticked (see the tips).

Click Create Job, then Sync Now from the job's menu. The first run copied 48 records (3.05 KB) in 36 seconds, container start included.

The namespace joins the job name, the source database and the schema, so it came out as sql_server_to_bigquery_shop_dbo. To use another name, edit the Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page before the first sync.

Step 6: Query the tables in BigQuery

There is nothing to register: the bucket is the catalog and the namespace is the dataset. Open the SQL editor, set the query location to the bucket's region, and use the four-part name:

SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.sql_server_to_bigquery_shop_dbo.customers`
ORDER BY id;

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.sql_server_to_bigquery_shop_dbo.orders`
GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

The account running the queries needs the BigQuery Job User role plus read access to the catalog. OLake Go adds its own columns to each table, among them _op_type, which is r on every row straight after the first sync.

Step 7: Change rows in SQL Server and sync again

The run then made 12 changes, 7 inserts and 5 updates:

INSERT INTO dbo.customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  (N'Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', N'Pune', 'silver'),
  (N'Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', N'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO dbo.orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE dbo.customers SET tier = 'gold',       updated_at = SYSUTCDATETIME() WHERE name = N'Liam Carter';
UPDATE dbo.customers SET city = N'Abu Dhabi', updated_at = SYSUTCDATETIME() WHERE name = N'Zara Ali';
UPDATE dbo.orders    SET status = 'delivered', updated_at = SYSUTCDATETIME() WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Click Sync Now again. The second sync read 12 records (855 bytes) from the change tables and finished in 33 seconds end to end.

The commit per table was small. customers received one data file with 4 rows (the 2 inserts and the new versions of the 2 updated rows) and one positional delete file that retires the 2 old versions. orders followed the same shape with 8 rows and 3 deletes.

Run the customers query again, with no refresh and no ALTER TABLE. BigQuery returns 10 rows, one per key: Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali is in Abu Dhabi, and Maya Patel and Lucas Silva are new. _op_type reads r on the 6 untouched rows, c on the 2 inserts and u on the 2 updates.

The orders query agreed with SQL Server to the cent. It returned 16 delivered orders worth 8659.68, 18 placed worth 10522.26 and 11 shipped worth 6397.25.

Read the same tables from DuckDB

DuckDB attaches the same catalog with a Google access token. For the files it needs a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) key for the same service account, from Cloud Storage, Settings, Interoperability.


INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;

-- gcloud auth print-access-token, or a token minted for the service account
CREATE SECRET biglake_catalog (
  TYPE iceberg,
  TOKEN '<access token>',
  EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS MAP {'x-goog-user-project': '<project-id>'}
);
CREATE SECRET biglake_files (TYPE gcs, KEY_ID '<hmac access id>', SECRET '<hmac secret>');

ATTACH 'gs://<bucket>' AS biglake (
  TYPE iceberg,
  ENDPOINT 'https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog',
  SECRET biglake_catalog
);

SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM biglake.sql_server_to_bigquery_shop_dbo.customers ORDER BY id;

DuckDB 1.5.5 gave back the same 10 customers and the same orders totals, and so did Spark 4.0.1 with Iceberg 1.10.0. The access token lasts an hour, so when a query fails with 401, run CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET with a new one.

Tips from the run

  • Untick systranschemas. Enabling CDC adds it to the database with no capture instance, so selecting it stops the first sync with CDC is not enabled for stream dbo.systranschemas.
  • A sync right after a write can come back empty. The capture job fills the change tables every few seconds, so the next sync picks the rows up.
  • A new column needs a new capture instance. Create one, or turn on Manage Capture Instance, and OLake Go adds the column on the next sync.
  • Decimals become doubles. decimal, numeric and money land as FLOAT64; round at query time for exact arithmetic.
  • Watch the metadata file. BigLake rejects a metadata.json above 1 MB, which a busy CDC table reaches after a few thousand syncs, so expire snapshots on a schedule.
  • Change rows are kept for three days. A job paused longer needs a fresh snapshot.

SQL Server to BigQuery options side by side

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
Datastream for SQL Server near real time, by Google's description yes native BigQuery datasets, read only by BigQuery a connection profile and a stream
Debezium, Kafka, BigQuery sink seconds yes, through the sink's upsert settings Kafka topics, then BigQuery tables Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and a sink
bcp to CSV, then bq load hours to daily no, full reloads native BigQuery tables a script, a scheduler and a staging bucket
OLake Go into BigLake (this post) CDC on a schedule, down to one minute yes, as Iceberg row-level deletes Iceberg tables in your bucket that BigQuery, Spark, DuckDB, Trino and Flink read one Docker Compose stack, open source

When native BigQuery tables are the whole goal, Datastream is the shorter path. The catalog route pays off once Spark, DuckDB or a notebook wants the same rows. Its limit is speed: every query reads Parquet from the bucket, so load the hot slice into a native table when a dashboard needs native speed.

FAQ

Does this work on SQL Server Express?

No. Express and Web editions cannot turn on change data capture, so there are no change tables for OLake Go to read. Those editions can still run Full Refresh, or Full Refresh + Incremental on an updated_at column.

Which region should the bucket live in?

In the region where BigQuery will run the queries, since a query over the catalog runs in the bucket's region. A query left on the default US multi-region fails with a "not found" message for a regional bucket.

Do deletes in SQL Server show up in BigQuery?

Yes. Later syncs replay deletes from the change tables too, written as Iceberg row-level deletes, and _op_type marks such a row d. My run only made inserts and updates, so the results above show c and u.

Does OLake Go use BigQuery compute to write the tables?

No. OLake Go runs wherever Docker runs and writes Parquet files to the bucket with the service account's credentials. BigQuery bills only the queries you run, by bytes scanned on demand or by slot time on an edition.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at your own database. On Cloud SQL for SQL Server only the database-level CDC procedure changes.
  • Add a table by running sys.sp_cdc_enable_table for it, then ticking it on the job's Streams page.
  • The full guide, with the CLI tabs, the Spark connection and the complete data type table, is on olake.io.

If a step behaves differently on your setup, say so in the comments and I'll update the post.

title: Replay every tool call twice: a CI test that catches non-idempotent agent tools
description:
Originally published on Loop & Retry — field notes on building LLM agents that survive production.

Idempotency is a property people assert and almost never test. A tool's docstring says "safe to retry", the wrapper adds a key, everyone nods. Then a timeout hits in production, the retry fires, and the customer gets two emails. The claim was never checked against the only scenario that matters: the same call, executed twice.

This is a practical post. For how to derive keys, see idempotency keys for agents. For what to do at runtime when a call times out, see the timeout that might have worked. For the budget and breaker side, fleet retry patterns. This one is about the test that tells you whether any of that actually holds for your tools, before an incident does.

The idea: count effects, not return values

A tool that returns the same answer twice isn't necessarily idempotent. send_email can return {"ok": true} both times and have sent two messages. What you assert on is the effect log of the backend, not the tool's output.

So the harness has three parts:

  1. A fake backend that records every side effect it receives.
  2. A registry of your tools with sample arguments.
  3. A runner that executes each call under three fault modes and checks the log.

The fake backend

Every effect goes through one object. It records, and it can be told to fail after recording, which is the case that bites.

# fakes.py
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

class AckLost(TimeoutError):
    """The effect happened; the caller never heard back."""

@dataclass
class Backend:
    effects: list = field(default_factory=list)
    drop_next_ack: bool = False
    seen_keys: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # only used if the API supports keys

    def apply(self, op: str, payload: dict, key: str | None = None):
        # Model a backend that honours idempotency keys, if one is sent.
        if key is not None and key in self.seen_keys:
            return self.seen_keys[key]
        self.effects.append((op, payload))
        result = {"ok": True, "n": len(self.effects)}
        if key is not None:
            self.seen_keys[key] = result
        if self.drop_next_ack:
            self.drop_next_ack = False
            raise AckLost(op)
        return result

Note the order: record, then raise. A backend that fails before recording tests nothing, because retrying that is always safe.

If a real third-party API gives you no key support, delete the key branch and the fake gets stricter: it will accept the duplicate, which is what the real one does.

Tools under test

Each tool takes the backend as a parameter, so the test can swap it. Here are two, one naive and one defended:

# tools.py
import hashlib, json

def send_email_naive(be, to, subject):
    return be.apply("email", {"to": to, "subject": subject})

def intent_key(op, payload):
    blob = json.dumps([op, payload], sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest()[:24]

def send_email_keyed(be, to, subject):
    p = {"to": to, "subject": subject}
    return be.apply("email", p, key=intent_key("email", p))

The key is derived from what the call is for, not from a timestamp or a counter. If you derive it from the moment, every replay gets a fresh key and the test, correctly, fails.

The runner: three modes 

# test_idempotency.py
import pytest
from fakes import Backend, AckLost
import tools

CASES = [
    # (tool, kwargs, expected effects after the logical call)
    (tools.send_email_naive, {"to": "a@x.io", "subject": "hi"}, 1),
    (tools.send_email_keyed, {"to": "a@x.io", "subject": "hi"}, 1),
]

def call_with_retry(fn, be, kwargs, attempts=3):
    for _ in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn(be, **kwargs)
        except TimeoutError:
            continue
    raise RuntimeError("gave up")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("fn,kwargs,expected", CASES)
def test_replay_twice(fn, kwargs, expected):
    be = Backend()
    fn(be, **kwargs)
    fn(be, **kwargs)                       # the retry that shouldn't have been needed
    assert len(be.effects) == expected

@pytest.mark.parametrize("fn,kwargs,expected", CASES)
def test_ack_lost_then_retry(fn, kwargs, expected):
    be = Backend(drop_next_ack=True)
    call_with_retry(fn, be, kwargs)        # first attempt lands, ack is lost, retry fires
    assert len(be.effects) == expected

@pytest.mark.parametrize("fn,kwargs,expected", CASES)
def test_replay_after_restart(fn, kwargs, expected):
    be = Backend()
    fn(be, **kwargs)
    # A fresh process re-derives everything from scratch: same args, same key.
    import importlib; importlib.reload(tools)
    getattr(tools, fn.__name__)(be, **kwargs)
    assert len(be.effects) == expected

Run it and the naive tool fails all three, the keyed one passes all three. That's the whole point: the failure is mechanical, not a judgment call in code review.

The three modes each catch something different:

  • replay twice catches tools with no dedup at all.
  • ack lost catches the retry-after-timeout path, and the one where your wrapper retries but your key generator isn't stable across attempts.
  • replay after restart catches keys derived from process state: an in-memory counter, uuid4() per call, time.time(). Anything that doesn't survive the agent being resumed from a checkpoint.

What this found in practice

The harness earns its keep on the tools that look fine. The usual finds:

  • A key that included a run ID. Safe within a run, a duplicate across a resumed run. Fix: key on the business intent (recipient + template + the thing that triggered it), not the execution.
  • Read-modify-write "upserts". append_note(ticket, text) is not idempotent however it's phrased, because the second call appends again. The fix is to make the operation a set, not an append: set_note(ticket, note_id, text) where note_id comes from the intent.
  • Counters. increment(balance, 5) fails the replay test by definition. Either send the target value, or send a delta with a unique operation ID the backend can dedupe.
  • A wrapper that dedups on the response. It cached the result locally, so it passed the replay-twice test inside one process and failed the restart test. A local cache is not a ledger.

When the backend gives you no key to send

Some third-party tools take no idempotency key and offer nothing to read. The test still applies; you just can't pass it by sending a key. You pass it by owning the dedup yourself, with a small ledger written before the call:

import sqlite3

class Ledger:
    def __init__(self, path="ledger.db"):
        self.db = sqlite3.connect(path)
        self.db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sent
            (k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, state TEXT)""")

    def claim(self, k) -> bool:
        try:
            self.db.execute("INSERT INTO sent VALUES (?, 'pending')", (k,))
            self.db.commit()
            return True
        except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
            return False

    def done(self, k):
        self.db.execute("UPDATE sent SET state='done' WHERE k=?", (k,))
        self.db.commit()

def send_email_ledgered(be, led, to, subject):
    p = {"to": to, "subject": subject}
    k = intent_key("email", p)
    if not led.claim(k):
        return {"ok": True, "deduped": True}
    r = be.apply("email", p)               # no key available downstream
    led.done(k)
    return r

Look at what that trades. A crash between claim and done leaves a pending row, so the next attempt is suppressed: you've chosen at-most-once over at-least-once. For an email that's usually right. For a payment you'd rather reconcile the pending rows by reading the effect, which is the verify-before-write step from the timeout post. Which one you want is a per-tool decision; the test just makes you write it down, because expected in the case table has to be a number.

The ledger version passes all three tests, but look at the ack-lost case: the retry is suppressed and returns deduped: True, so the caller learns the effect may have occurred, not that it did. Decide whether that return value is honest for your tool; the agent should be told the outcome is unconfirmed rather than success.

Wiring it into CI without it rotting

Three habits keep this from becoming a test nobody updates:

  1. Fail on unregistered tools. Iterate over your tool registry and assert every tool name has a row in CASES. A new tool with no case breaks the build. This is the single most useful line in the file.
  2. Mark read-only tools explicitly with expected = 0 effects, so a "read" that quietly writes (logging to a CRM, say) gets caught.
  3. Keep the fake honest. When a production incident shows a backend behaving differently, such as dedup windows that expire, add that behaviour to Backend and a case for it. A fake that is more forgiving than the real service gives you false confidence. 
def test_every_tool_has_a_case():
    registered = {t.__name__ for t in tools.REGISTRY}
    covered = {c[0].__name__ for c in CASES}
    assert registered <= covered, registered - covered

What it doesn't cover

It tests your side of the contract. It won't tell you that a vendor's dedup window is 24 hours and your retry queue holds work for 36, or that two different keys for the same intent were issued by two agents. The second one is a coordination problem; fleet retry patterns covers the shared-budget side of it, and what idempotent means has the vocabulary if you need to explain the failure to someone else.

What I'd actually do

Start with the registry assertion and the replay-twice test; that's twenty minutes and it will probably fail something today. Add ack-lost next, since it's the one that mirrors the production incident. Put restart last, and only if your agents resume from checkpoints, which most long-running ones eventually do.

Then, for each tool that fails, don't reach for a clever wrapper first. Ask whether the operation can be rewritten as a set instead of an append, a target instead of a delta. A tool that is idempotent by shape needs no key, no ledger, and no test you'll be tempted to skip.

title: Amazon Neptune introduces Neptune Graph Sessions, smaller graphs designed for agents that scale to zero and resume automatically
description:
Amazon Neptune now supports Neptune Graph Sessions, a compute mode designed for agents that scales memory and CPU automatically and scales to zero when idle. You can give each agent, user or task its own graph without paying for the 16 m-NCU minimum of a provisioned graph. You choose a starting size of 4 s-NCU (sessions Neptune capacity units) or 8 s-NCU of working memory when you create a graph.

Applications such as GraphRAG assistants, AI agents and per-user analytics improve accuracy when using a graph. These use cases often need a separate graph for each conversation or task, and the size of that graph is hard to predict. Each Graph Sessions graph starts at the size you choose and includes memory headroom up to twice that size for the data you load and the queries you run (a 4 s-NCU graph has up to 8 s-NCU of memory, and an 8 s-NCU graph has up to 16 s-NCU), so the starting size does not have to cover your largest graph. You are billed for the memory your graph uses, so a graph that fits in the smaller size is billed at the smaller size.

When a graph is idle, Graph Sessions scales to zero automatically after 15 minutes, and the graph resumes in seconds when the next query arrives. Your graph and its data are kept, so you do not reload data for each session and pay for the running price.

You can create a Neptune Graph Sessions graph using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs, and query it with openCypher like any other Neptune Analytics graph. For more information, see the Neptune Analytics User Guide and the Amazon Neptune pricing page.

title: 15 Best Sites to Buy Gmail Accounts: PVA & Aged for Marketing Success
description:
15 Best Sites to Buy Gmail Accounts: PVA & Aged for Marketing Success

Compare the 15 best sites to buy Gmail accounts (PVA, aged & bulk). Learn escrow safety, credential formats, Google ToS risks, and Workspace alternatives.

To buy Gmail accounts safely for testing, local setup, or multi-account work, pick peer-to-peer (P2P) sites with escrow first. Top picks in this group include socvait, and usabigstore. Direct social media marketing (SMM) shops ship fast in bulk. Even so, P2P sites hold your cash until you check the login, recovery email, and two-factor (2FA) codes.

Making dozens of Gmail accounts by hand is slow. Google sets strict phone checks, device checks, and IP limits. Because of that, marketers, QA testers, and ad buyers often look at outside sites for Phone-Verified Accounts (PVA) and aged Gmail profiles. Still, buying accounts breaks Google's Terms of Service. It brings real risks, like fast account locks, sellers taking back access, and weak cold-email inbox rates.

Understanding PVA, Aged, and Bulk Gmail Accounts

Before you pick a site, learn the three main types of accounts sold online.

What Is a PVA (Phone-Verified) Gmail Account?

A Phone-Verified Account (PVA) is a Gmail profile that passed a text or voice check on a phone line at sign-up. Google limits how many accounts can use one phone number. Because of that, PVA accounts often pass early bot checks better than unverified ones. Yet a PVA tag only means a phone check worked at sign-up. Logging in from a new place or data-center IP can still spark a new text check.

Aged vs. Fresh Gmail Accounts: How Account History Impacts Trust

• Fresh Gmail Accounts: Made days or weeks before sale. They cost less ($0.20 to $1.00 each in bulk). They fit quick app tests, sign-up checks, or short tasks.

• Aged (Old) Gmail Accounts: Made months or years ago (often from 2016 to 2024). Spam and abuse filters weigh age along with user habits. Older accounts may hit fewer early limits on outside tools if you move them with care.

Key Evaluation Criteria Before You Buy Gmail Accounts

Weak sellers often sell bot-made accounts from flagged server IPs. Check four things before you pay:

  1. IP Origin and Geo-Targeting (USA, UK, Canada, Australia): Match the account sign-up country to your proxy country. A US or UK workflow using accounts made on far-off or flagged IPs faces a higher chance of login checks.

  2. Full Recovery Control: Do not buy accounts where the seller keeps phone access or hides recovery details. Without your own recovery email, a seller can try to take the account back later.

  3. 2FA Secret Keys vs. SMS Dependence: Temp phone numbers used at sign-up can expire. Accounts with a 2FA secret key or backup codes help you log in without needing the old phone line.

  4. Clear Replacement Policy: Good sellers offer a short swap window (often 24 to 72 hours) if an account is locked before first login, as long as you follow their IP rules.
    Legal, Security, and Google Terms of Service Risks

Knowing the rules and tech limits helps keep your main work safe.

What Google’s Terms of Service Say About Buying and Selling Accounts

Buying or selling Gmail accounts is usually not a crime on its own, if the accounts are not stolen and are not used for fraud or spam.

Still, it breaks Google's Terms of Service, which bar selling, leasing, or passing on access to Google services. Because of that:

• Google can lock or close transferred accounts at any time with no appeal.

• Never link bought Gmail accounts to your main business Google Workspace, Google Ads billing, or AdSense account.

Why Free Gmail Accounts Fail at Cold Email Deliverability

Many blogs claim bought aged @gmail.com accounts can send loads of cold email and land in the inbox. In truth, free @gmail.com
accounts work poorly for cold outreach:

• Strict Daily Sending Caps: Free Gmail accounts have tight daily send caps, and fast cold sends from new logins often trigger locks.

• No Custom Authentication Control: Google's Email Sender Guidelines require SPF, DKIM, and DMARC setup, plus low spam rates (under 0.3% and ideally below 0.1%). You do not own gmail.com DNS settings, so you cannot set custom DMARC alignment or your own sending domain.

How to Secure and Warm Up Purchased Gmail Accounts Safely

If you buy PVA or aged Gmail accounts for testing or multi-profile work, do not rush into heavy tasks on your main browser.

Step 1: Isolate Browser Fingerprints and Residential Proxies

Logging into many bought Gmail accounts from one browser and home IP links them together. Use an anti-detect browser (like Multilogin, AdsPower, or Dolphin Anty) with steady residential or ISP proxies that match each account's country.

Step 2: Rotate Passwords, Recovery Emails, and 2FA Tokens

When you first log in (using any backup code or 2FA key given):

  1. Go to Google Account → Security.
  2. Open Your Devices and sign out of old sessions you do not know.
  3. Swap in your own recovery email address.
  4. Add your own authenticator app and backup codes, then set a new password. (Tip: Space out big security changes over two to three days if the account acts touchy about IP shifts.)

Step 3: Execute a 14-to-21-Day Gradual Warmup Schedule

Do not send bulk mail or run heavy tools right away. Build normal use slowly over two to three weeks:

• Days 1–4: Light browsing—log in via your set browser profile, read system notes, and use Google tools normally.

• Days 5–10: Inbound mail—sign up for three to five trusted newsletters so normal mail arrives.

• Days 11–21: Light manual replies—send a few real notes a day to test boxes and reply naturally before linking any tool.

Compliant Alternatives: When to Use Google Workspace Instead

For client outreach, sales leads, and agency work, bought personal Gmail accounts add risk. Google Workspace gives you a rule-safe setup with your own domain and admin tools.

Feature Purchased Personal Gmail (PVA / Aged) Google Workspace (Business Starter)

Terms of Service Compliance Breaks Google ToS (risk of sudden ban) Rule-safe and officially backed
Cost $0.30 – $6.00 one-time per account $7.00/user/month (annual) or $8.40 flexible
Custom Domain & DMARC No (@gmail.com only) Yes (your domain with SPF/DKIM/DMARC)
Daily Sending Limit Up to 500/day (often capped lower on new IPs) Up to 2,000 messages/day per user
Centralized Admin Control None (needs manual browser and proxy setup) Admin console, user recovery, and controls

Actionable Recommendation: For cold email or client outreach, buy extra lookalike domains, set up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, and add Google Workspace Business Starter seats. You get better inbox trust, clear ownership, and less risk of losing your work to a sudden lock.

Frequently Asked Questions About Buying Gmail Accounts

Is it legal to buy Gmail accounts?

Buying or selling Gmail accounts is generally not a crime if the accounts are not hacked or stolen and are not used for fraud or spam. Yet it breaks Google's Terms of Service, so Google can shut them down at any time.

How much do aged and PVA Gmail accounts cost?

Fresh PVA Gmail accounts often run $0.25 to $2.00 each in bulk packs of 50 to 500. Aged Gmail accounts (one to seven or more years old) with 2FA keys and US sign-up IPs often cost $1.50 to $6.00 or more each, based on age and site fees.

Why does a purchased Gmail account ask for SMS verification when I log in?

Google checks browser traits, cookies, and IP place at login. Even with a PVA tag, logging in from a new place or flagged server IP can spark a new text check. Using a steady proxy that matches the sign-up country helps lower that chance.

What is the safest way to buy Gmail accounts in bulk?

Pick a P2P site with escrow, such as socvait, usabigstore. Look for listings with 2FA backup codes and recovery email access, and test a small pack of five to ten accounts first.

Should I use bought Gmail accounts for cold email marketing?

No. Free @gmail.com accounts lack your own SPF, DKIM, and DMARC domain records and have tight send caps. For cold outreach, paid Google Workspace accounts on your own domains give much better inbox odds and protect your sender name.

title: Why Figma HTML Exports (Anima, Locofy) Break When Translated into German or Arabic
description:
Your Anima or Locofy export looks correct in English, then a German heading wraps and collides with the description underneath. In Arabic, the same card can keep its content pinned to the left instead of following the text direction. The usual culprit is a pair of export assumptions baked into CSS: fixed pixel widths and absolutely positioned text.

Problem

Figma records where layers appear on the canvas; it does not guarantee that exported text will stay the same size or occupy the same number of lines after translation. A rule such as width: 320px can be too narrow for a longer German phrase, while position: absolute prevents the heading from reserving space for the description below it.

.card {
  position: relative;
  width: 320px;
}

.card-title {
  position: absolute;
  top: 16px;
  left: 16px;
  width: 288px;
}

.card-copy {
  position: absolute;
  top: 56px;
  left: 16px;
  width: 288px;
}

Both text elements are positioned relative to the card, so the description stays at top: 56px even when the heading grows to two or three lines. Increasing that offset may hide one collision at one viewport, but it does not make the layout responsive to copy length.

The same offsets cause a separate problem in Arabic. left and right describe physical screen edges, not the start and end of the current writing direction. A rule anchored with left: 16px stays on the left in RTL. Manually swapping every left and right value is brittle: it can miss nested components, and it does nothing about the fixed width or the overlap.

Before changing the export, inspect the actual elements that collide. Check whether the text or its wrapper is absolutely positioned, and whether the next element is also out of flow. Temporarily setting the suspect text to position: static is a useful test: if the description moves down when the heading wraps, you have found a dependency on fixed positioning. The Anima and Locofy positioning walkthrough covers how to trace that relationship in an export.

Fix

Put text that must push other content down back into normal flow. Use a column flex container for the heading and description, and let the card’s inline size adapt to its parent. The logical sizing properties below work with the text direction rather than assuming that “width” and “left” always mean the same physical edges.

.card {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  inline-size: 100%;
  max-inline-size: 320px;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 12px;
  padding: 16px;
}

.card-title,
.card-copy {
  position: static;
  inline-size: auto;
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  margin: 0;
  text-align: start;
}

Apply the flex layout to the element that actually contains both pieces of text. If the export wraps them in another positioned element, changing only the heading’s positioning will not restore the relationship between the heading and description. Likewise, if cards themselves are absolutely positioned inside a list, one card still cannot push the next card down; make the list a flow container too.

For a card with an icon beside the text, keep the card’s children in a row and allow the text column to shrink. Set the direction on the component from the document’s language or an appropriate dir attribute. Use logical insets for any remaining intentional positioning:

.card-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: flex-start;
  gap: 12px;
}

.card-row__text {
  min-inline-size: 0;
}

.card-badge {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: 12px;
  inset-inline-end: 12px;
}

min-inline-size: 0 matters in flex layouts: without it, a text child can resist shrinking and overflow its card. inset-inline-end places the badge at the logical end, which changes sides in RTL. Avoid adding row-reverse just because the text is Arabic; combined with RTL direction, it can reverse the order twice.

Keep absolute positioning for deliberate overlays, not for text that must determine where the next element begins.

Test the patched component with a long German heading and an Arabic version at the same narrow viewport where the collision appeared. Confirm that the description moves when the heading wraps, that the card stays within its parent, and that icons and badges sit on the intended logical side. The related HTML translation layout notes are useful when checking the rest of a translated page, but this fix is specifically about restoring flow and direction-aware positioning in the exported component.

title: AI Code Bottleneck: Autonomous Testing in CI/CD
description:
As generative AI coding tools flood repositories with code diffs, software verification has replaced writing code as the main bottleneck in engineering organizations. Specialized AI testing agents that interactively explore applications catch significantly more bugs than generalist code models, but integrating them into CI/CD pipelines requires deliberate design choices.

The largest risk with autonomous QA is over-reliance on self-healing test recovery. If an AI agent automatically adapts to a broken UI flow or skipped security step to pass a build, critical business regressions will leak into production. Engineering leaders must keep agent-generated test specs version-controlled in Git and enforce strict assertion boundaries around core business invariants.
