title: Black Friday Reliability: Design a Load Test Around the Customer Journey
description:
November 27, 2026. AI-assisted editorial draft. Cover: AI-generated conceptual illustration, not a real GILNEX client or deployed dashboard.

Black Friday invites a useful engineering question: can a customer complete the operation they came to perform when the system is under pressure? A dashboard showing healthy servers is not enough if a customer cannot submit an inquiry or find out what happened next.

Start with a journey, not an arbitrary request count

Define one representative flow: find a service, submit an inquiry, receive a durable acknowledgement and assign the next action. Model the expected mix of reads, writes and failed requests. Use synthetic records and an isolated environment; never send test messages to real customers.

Choose load levels from measured traffic and an explicitly documented scenario, not an invented industry benchmark. Record the environment, data volume and assumptions so results can be reproduced.

Protect the bottleneck

A hypothetical scheduling system has two separate limits: computational throughput and available appointment capacity. Increasing the web server's request rate cannot create more available appointments. Enforce resource constraints in the authoritative transactional store and treat unavailable capacity as a normal business result.

Rate limits should protect shared resources without making a slow customer guess why an operation was refused. Bound queue depth and downstream concurrency. A retry policy should distinguish a transient failure from an invalid request or an ambiguous external side effect.

Exercise degraded modes

Simulate a slow dependency, a lost response after commit, a full queue and a worker restart. Check whether the system returns meaningful information, preserves valid requests and makes failures visible. If the notification provider is unavailable, the customer should not receive a false confirmation.

A successful test might reveal that the product must reduce the rate of acceptance rather than silently lose work. This is a design decision, not a failure to reach a marketing target.

Define acceptance before the test

Record end-to-end latency distributions, error categories, completed operations, duplicates and queue age. Select thresholds appropriate to the actual business and verify the customer-facing result independently. Include authorization and cross-tenant isolation checks alongside throughput tests.

A hypothetical acceptance rule: each valid synthetic operation has exactly one durable outcome; rejected operations have a clear reason; unknown external effects are reconciled; resource capacity is never exceeded. This rule is a design goal, not a reported test result.

After testing, compare the observed bottleneck with the expected one. Fix the weakest handoff, repeat the same experiment and retain evidence. Demand is not a test of advertising alone. It is a test of how accurately the system represents and delivers the business.

References: Google SRE book — Addressing Cascading Failures, PostgreSQL transaction isolation.

title: Gratitude as an Engineering Practice: Designing for the People Behind the System
description:
Thanksgiving weekend, November 27, 2026. AI-assisted editorial draft for GILNEX; cover is an AI-generated conceptual illustration, not a photograph of our team or customers.

This Thanksgiving, it is worth asking what engineering teams are actually grateful for. Not merely the tools that make development faster, but the people who notice a failure, explain a confusing interaction, maintain a system after its launch and help a customer recover when something goes wrong.

Gratitude becomes an engineering practice when it influences design choices.

Design for the person who needs help

Consider a hypothetical customer who submits an appointment request from a phone. A good interface does not assume uninterrupted connectivity, perfect eyesight, flawless typing or unlimited time. It gives each control a meaningful label, communicates validation errors clearly, and confirms the result without forcing the customer to guess whether anything happened.

The W3C forms tutorial provides a useful starting point for labels and error notifications. Meeting these examples alone does not establish conformance with an accessibility standard; accessibility must be evaluated across the complete interaction.

Treat operational handoffs as real work

An automated request that cannot finish should not disappear into a generic exception log. A recoverable workflow needs a durable state, an accountable owner and a safe next action. In a hypothetical service system, that might mean preserving an incomplete request, notifying an authorized operator and showing the customer a truthful message about the next step.

Avoid recording unnecessary personal information or exposing internal error details in the public response. A meaningful error message explains what the customer can do without revealing credentials or confidential infrastructure.

Respect the people maintaining the system

A runbook is a form of respect. Describe what failed, where evidence can be found, who can authorize a correction, and how to determine whether recovery succeeded. A clear rollback path helps the next engineer make a safe decision under pressure.

A useful test is to hand a simulated failure to a colleague who did not implement the feature. Can they identify the affected request, reproduce the failure safely, find the responsible component and verify the correction without seeing private customer data?

Measure the right outcome

Completion of an automated step is not necessarily completion of a customer's task. Define success in terms that reflect the intended outcome. A booking request received, a booking confirmed and a completed service are different states. A dashboard that merges them can hide friction rather than explain it.

This weekend, choose one small workflow and examine it from the perspective of the people relying on it. Improve the labels, clarify the handoff or test the recovery path. Then document what actually changed.

Technology moves progress forward. People give progress its purpose.

References: W3C form labels, W3C form notifications, NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

title: How I Stopped Passcode Brute-Force From Freezing Live Keystrokes in Carrel
description:
When I started building Carrel, a real-time collaborative CodeMirror 6 workspace, I thought auth was the easy part: hash room passcodes with scrypt, verify on join, done.

Then I tested what happens under brute-force traffic. scrypt is slow on purpose. Run it synchronously and it blocks Node's event loop; run dozens of async scrypt calls uncapped and they saturate libuv's threadpool. Either way, anyone hammering wrong passcodes starts stuttering live keystrokes for everyone typing in the room.

Here is how I ended up structuring the server and protocol across the 3-package TypeScript monorepo (@carrel/shared, @carrel/server, @carrel/client):

1. Bounded scrypt + single-use WS tickets

In server/src/throttle.ts, POST /api/rooms/:id/ticket runs async scrypt inside a 4-slot concurrency limiter paired with per-IP progressive lockouts (and ignores X-Forwarded-For unless TRUST_PROXY is explicitly enabled). Once verified, the client gets a short-lived, single-use nonce-bound HMAC ticket to upgrade /ws, which gets burned immediately on upgrade so replay attempts fail.

2. One WebSocket with a 1-byte frame header

Instead of pushing everything through JSON messages or opening parallel sockets, shared/src/frames.ts prefixes every binary WebSocket payload with one routing byte:

[0x00] -> raw y-protocols/sync CRDT updates (Y.Doc persisted via SQLite WAL)
[0x01] -> coalesced awareness updates (remote carets, selections, 80ms lerp)
[0x02] -> typed JSON control events (role changes, kicks, host handover)

CodeMirror 6 renders remote carets with an 80ms interpolation curve (CarrelProvider.ts) and turns interpolation off automatically when prefers-reduced-motion is set.

3. Not losing room admin on a 2-second Wi-Fi drop

If a host refreshes a tab or drops Wi-Fi briefly, promoting someone else on the exact close event creates constant role churn. In server/src/host.ts, a HOST_GRACE_MS (5000ms) timer marks the seat hostPending first. Only if that timer expires does seniority election promote the next peer by min(joinedAt) (tie-broken by min(clientId)), while SENIORITY_WINDOW_MS (30s) restores standing on quick reconnects. Multi-tab promotion and creator-key reclamation are verified in Playwright E2E specs (phase5.test.ts).

Full architecture notes and failure-mode diagrams: https://theayush.pages.dev/projects/carrel

Code on GitHub: https://github.com/theayushagarwal/carrel

title: Your First LangChain4j Chat: Connecting Java to Anthropic Claude
description:
Calling a large language model from Java used to mean writing HTTP clients, parsing JSON by hand and wiring retries yourself. LangChain4j removes most of that plumbing. In this article we build the smallest useful program: a Java 21 application that creates a Claude chat model with LangChain4j and sends a single prompt. The code is small on purpose, so every line has a clear job, and the structure is the same one you will reuse for tools, memory, retrieval and agents later.

The complete source is in github.com/josesaid/01-chatmodel-anthropic, and a project page with the diagrams is available at josesaid.github.io/01-chatmodel-anthropic.

What you will build

The application does four things:

  1. Reads the Anthropic API key from an environment variable.
  2. Builds an AnthropicChatModel with the builder pattern.
  3. Sends one question with chat(String).
  4. Prints the question and the answer.

The flow looks like this:

Your Java app  ->  AnthropicChatModel (LangChain4j)  ->  Claude API
     chat(prompt)        HTTPS request                  answer text

Nothing here is specific to one vendor. The concepts, a model object, a builder and a text in and text out call, appear in every LangChain4j integration. Once you understand them for Claude, switching providers is mostly a matter of changing the builder.

Prerequisites

  • JDK 21 (the project sets maven.compiler.release to 21).
  • Maven 3.9 or later.
  • An Anthropic API key. Create one in the Anthropic console and keep it out of your source code.

Project setup

The Maven project depends on the Anthropic module of LangChain4j:

<dependency>
    <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>langchain4j-anthropic</artifactId>
    <version>1.24.1</version>
</dependency>

The module brings in the core LangChain4j types, so you do not need to add them separately. The exec-maven-plugin lets you run the class with mvn exec:java without building a fat jar, which keeps the first experience short.

The code

Here is the whole main class:

package com.mx.development.jose.said;

import dev.langchain4j.model.anthropic.AnthropicChatModel;

/**
 * Example 01 - ChatModel.
 *
 * Creates a Claude chat model with LangChain4J and sends one prompt.
 * The API key is read from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable.
 */
public class ChatModelExample {

    // Change this constant to try another Claude model.
    static final String MODEL_NAME = "claude-haiku-5-5";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String apiKey = System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY");
        if (apiKey == null || apiKey.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable first.");
        }

        AnthropicChatModel model = AnthropicChatModel.builder()
                .apiKey(apiKey)
                .modelName(MODEL_NAME)
                .temperature(0.2)
                .maxTokens(512)
                .build();

        String question = "In two sentences, what is a ChatModel in LangChain4J?";
        String answer = model.chat(question);

        System.out.println("Question: " + question);
        System.out.println("Answer:   " + answer);
    }
}

Let us go through the important parts.

Fail fast on a missing key

The first check stops the program before any network call. A missing key would otherwise surface as an authentication error from the API, which is harder to read. A clear message at startup saves time when you run the project on a new machine.

The builder

AnthropicChatModel.builder() returns a builder whose methods mirror the settings you care about:

  • apiKey authenticates each request.
  • modelName selects the Claude model. Keeping it in a constant makes the example easy to change.
  • temperature controls randomness. A low value such as 0.2 favors consistent answers, which is what you want for a first test.
  • maxTokens caps the length of the response. It also caps cost, so set it deliberately.

build() returns an object that implements the ChatModel abstraction. Your application code can depend on that abstraction later, which makes it easier to test with a fake model.

One call, one answer

model.chat(question) sends the text and returns the answer as a String. The method hides the HTTP request, the JSON payload, the headers and the parsing of the response. For many first experiments, that single call is all you need.

Run it

Export the key in your shell and run the project from its root folder:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here
mvn -q compile exec:java

The output looks like this, with the wording varying from run to run:

Question: In two sentences, what is a ChatModel in LangChain4J?
Answer:   A ChatModel is the LangChain4J abstraction for a language model that takes messages or text and returns a response. It hides provider-specific details so the same application code can work with different models.

If you see an authentication error, check that the variable is set in the same shell where you run Maven.

Best practices from the first example

Even a tiny program benefits from a few habits that scale to real systems.

Keep secrets out of the repository. Read the key from the environment, or from a secret manager in production. Add environment files and local secrets to .gitignore before the first commit. Never paste a key into an issue, a README or a screenshot.

Name your configuration. Constants such as MODEL_NAME make the choice visible and reviewable. When you move to Spring Boot later, the same values become application.yml properties.

Choose the temperature for the task. Factual or structured tasks usually need low values. Creative drafts can use higher values. Make the choice explicit in the code rather than relying on defaults you do not remember.

Budget tokens. maxTokens is a ceiling on output, but input size matters too. Long prompts cost more and respond more slowly. Measure with real examples before you scale.

Handle failures on purpose. A production call needs timeouts, retries with backoff for transient errors, and logging that never records the key or the full user data. The example omits these to stay readable, but you should add them before any real traffic.

Test the boundary, not the vendor. Because the application depends on ChatModel, unit tests can use a stub that returns fixed text. Reserve the real API for a smaller set of integration tests that run on demand.

Mapping the code to LangChain4j concepts

It helps to name the pieces once, because the same vocabulary returns in every later example.

In the code Concept Why it matters
AnthropicChatModel Chat model integration Adapts one provider to the common LangChain4j API.
builder() and build() Builder pattern Makes optional settings explicit and readable.
modelName, temperature, maxTokens Model parameters Control which model answers, how varied the answer is, and how long it can be.
chat(String) Convenience method Sends one user message and returns the text of the reply.
MODEL_NAME constant Configuration Keeps the model choice in one place that is easy to review.

Later examples work with richer inputs. A conversation is a list of messages, the response carries metadata about tokens and the reason the generation stopped, and tools are declared with descriptions the model can read. Those are extensions of the same idea: a model object that takes input and returns output through a stable interface.

Why the example reads the key from the environment

Hard-coding a key feels faster during a demo, but it creates three problems. The key ends up in version control, where it is copied to every clone and every backup. It must be changed in code when it rotates. And it is easy to paste into a chat or a ticket by accident.

An environment variable avoids all three. The application code stays identical across machines, each developer uses a personal key, and a leaked file does not expose a secret. The same rule applies to other settings that change between environments, such as the model name when you compare two versions of Claude.

Testing without calling the API every time

Calling a paid API from every test run is slow, costs money and makes results hard to reproduce. A simple refactoring solves most of this. Put the question-and-answer logic in a method that receives the model as a parameter:

static String ask(dev.langchain4j.model.chat.ChatModel model, String question) {
    if (question == null || question.isBlank()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("The question must not be blank.");
    }
    return model.chat(question);
}

A unit test can then pass a stub that returns a fixed string, and verify that blank questions are rejected before any model call happens. The real AnthropicChatModel stays in one integration test that runs only when the key is present, which keeps the everyday build fast and offline. This is the practical benefit of depending on an interface rather than on a provider class.

Troubleshooting the first run

Most first-run problems fall into a few groups.

  • The program stops with the message about the environment variable. The variable is not visible to the process. Run echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the same terminal, and remember that a variable exported in one terminal tab is not available in another.
  • Authentication errors from the API. The key is wrong, revoked, or copied with extra spaces. Create a new key, paste it again, and avoid quotes that become part of the value.
  • The model name is rejected. Model identifiers change over time. Check the current list in the Anthropic documentation and update MODEL_NAME. Keeping the constant in one place makes this a one-line fix.
  • Maven cannot find the dependency. Confirm the version in pom.xml and that your network allows access to Maven Central. A corporate proxy may need explicit configuration.
  • The compiler uses an older Java version. The project targets Java 21. Run java -version and mvn -v, and make sure both point to a JDK 21 installation.
  • The answer is empty or truncated. The response reached maxTokens. Raise the limit for this experiment, or ask for a shorter answer in the prompt.

Cost and latency

Every call has a cost in input and output tokens, and every call takes time while the model generates text. For a classroom example, the numbers are negligible. In a real product they add up quickly, so it is worth making three habits automatic: log the token usage the API returns, keep prompts short and specific, and set a sensible limit on output length for each use case.

Latency matters as much as cost. A user waiting for a page to render will not tolerate a long blocking call on a request thread. When you move beyond this example, consider asynchronous calls, streaming responses where the user interface supports them, and a clear timeout that tells the user what happened.

Writing better prompts from the start

A single question is enough to test the connection, but the quality of the answer depends heavily on how you ask. A few habits make a large difference even in a one-line prompt.

State the audience and the format. Compare "What is a ChatModel?" with "Explain a ChatModel in two sentences for a Java developer who has not used LangChain4j." The second prompt tells the model who is reading and how long the answer should be, so there is less guessing.

Give the model the facts it needs. If the answer depends on your own data, put that data in the prompt. The model cannot see your files, your database or the code in your project unless you send it.

Ask for one thing at a time. Long prompts that mix three tasks produce answers that do only part of each. Split them into separate calls, and combine the results in your code. This also makes failures easier to diagnose.

Ask for a structure you can check. When your code needs to read the answer, ask for a fixed format, such as a numbered list or a JSON object with named fields. Later in the series you will see how LangChain4j turns that requirement into typed Java objects, which removes most of the manual parsing.

Keep the prompt in code, not in a string scattered through the project. A constant or a template file makes prompts reviewable and testable, and it lets you change wording without touching the logic around it.

Reading the response beyond the text

The chat(String) method returns only the text, which is the right choice for this first example. Under the hood, the provider also reports information that matters in production: how many input and output tokens the call used, and why the generation stopped. When you need those details, the chat model offers a method that returns a richer response object. Use it when you start tracking cost per feature, or when you need to know whether an answer was cut off at the token limit.

Treat that metadata as part of the contract of your code. Log it with a request identifier, never with the full user content, and watch it over time. A sudden rise in output tokens often points to a prompt change that you did not intend.

Moving this example toward Spring Boot

Many Java teams will not keep a main method for long. The natural next step is to expose the same call through a REST endpoint. The model object becomes a bean, the key moves to application.yml or to an environment variable mapped by Spring, and the question arrives as a request parameter. The logic inside the method does not change, which is the reason to keep it small and explicit now.

The security rules also stay the same. Validate the input length before it reaches the model, limit the rate of calls per user, and never return the raw provider error to the client, because it can reveal details about your configuration. Those are the same concerns you would have for any external service, and they apply to language models in exactly the same way.

Common questions

Do I need a paid plan to try this? You need an Anthropic account with API access and enough credit for the requests you send. Check the current pricing page before you run loops of many calls.

Can I use another model with the same code? Yes, by changing the model name, provided it is available to your account. Be aware that different models have different limits, prices and behaviors, so results will vary.

Is it safe to commit the pom.xml? Yes. The file contains dependency versions and build settings, not secrets. The key is the only value that must stay private.

Why not call the HTTP API directly? You can, and it is a good exercise once. LangChain4j is worth using because it gives you the same interface for many providers, shared types for messages and responses, and higher-level tools that you would otherwise write yourself.

Where this leads

The same structure grows naturally. Adding a system message gives the model a role. Chat memory keeps the conversation history. Tools let the model call your Java methods. Retrieval connects the model to your documents. Each step adds one concept on top of the ChatModel you have just used, so it pays to get this first example right.

LangChain4j also offers higher-level building blocks, such as AI Services, which turn an interface into an assistant. You will see them in later examples in the same series. For now, the explicit version above is the best way to understand what those abstractions do underneath.

Summary

  • A LangChain4j chat model is a small object you configure with a builder.
  • AnthropicChatModel connects that object to Claude, so the call chat(String) returns the answer.
  • The API key belongs in the environment, not in the code.
  • Model name, temperature and token limits are explicit choices, and they deserve a conscious decision.

The full project is public, and it is the starting point for the rest of the series. Clone it, set your key, run it, then change the question and watch how the answer changes.

Sources

  • Source code: github.com/josesaid/01-chatmodel-anthropic
  • Project page with diagrams: josesaid.github.io/01-chatmodel-anthropic
  • LangChain4j documentation: docs.langchain4j.dev

title: Next.js 16.4.4 Fixes PPR CSP Nonces: Verify the Backport
description:
Next.js 16.4.4 shipped a backported fix that puts the CSP nonce on the Partial Prerendering (PPR) resume bootstrap, the small inline script that wakes up the dynamic part of a prerendered page. If you run a strict, nonce based Content Security Policy on top of PPR, that script has to carry the nonce your policy expects, or the browser is supposed to block it. Here's how I'd reproduce the problem on your current version, prove the patch fixes it on yours, and wire a check into CI so it never sneaks back.

TL;DR

  • 16.4.4 is a patch release with two backports: a Turbopack startup CSS update fix and the CSP nonce fix for the PPR resume bootstrap. It is not the canary feature set, so don't upgrade expecting anything else.
  • A nonce only protects you if every script the framework emits carries it. Verify that against the raw HTML and in a real browser, not by reading the release note.
  • Put a two part check in CI: every executable script in the HTML has the response nonce, and a headless browser reports zero CSP violations on your PPR routes.

What changed and what is actually available

The Next.js 16.4.4 release notes list two backports: one for Turbopack startup CSS updates and one described as a CSP nonce fix for the PPR resume bootstrap. That's the whole verified surface. The release explicitly does not bring in everything that's on canary, so if a feature you saw in a canary changelog isn't in that note, assume it isn't in 16.4.4.

Quick refresher on why one script matters. A nonce is a random value your server generates for every request. It goes into the Content-Security-Policy header (script-src 'nonce-<value>') and onto each <script> tag, and the browser only runs scripts whose nonce matches. MDN's practical CSP implementation guide recommends exactly this, nonce based strict CSP for dynamically generated content, hashes for static content, and strict-dynamic where appropriate.

PPR adds a twist. The static shell of a route is prerendered, and the dynamic holes are filled in at request time. Something has to kick off that resume step in the browser, and that something is an inline bootstrap script. The release note calls the fix a nonce fix for that bootstrap, so the practical question for you is simple: on your current version, does that script carry your nonce, and on 16.4.4, does it?

You want a clean repro app for this, separate from your real one, so nothing else in your config muddies the result. If you're setting one up on a fresh machine, my walkthrough on installing Next.js on Windows, Mac and Linux covers the toolchain. After that, create the app and pin the exact version you run in production today.

Implementation details and limits

Here is the nonce wiring I'd use for the repro. It mints a nonce per request, sends the policy on the response, and also passes it on the request headers, because that's where Next.js reads it from when it stamps its own scripts.

// proxy.ts (Next.js 16). On apps still using middleware.ts, export the same function as `middleware`.
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server";

export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  const nonce = btoa(crypto.randomUUID());
  const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV === "development";

  const csp = [
    `default-src 'self'`,
    `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'${isDev ? " 'unsafe-eval'" : ""}`,
    `style-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}'`,
    `img-src 'self' blob: data:`,
    `object-src 'none'`,
    `base-uri 'self'`,
    `frame-ancestors 'none'`,
  ].join("; ");

  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers);
  requestHeaders.set("x-nonce", nonce);
  requestHeaders.set("Content-Security-Policy", csp);

  const response = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers: requestHeaders } });
  response.headers.set("Content-Security-Policy", csp);
  return response;
}

export const config = {
  matcher: [
    {
      source: "/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)",
      missing: [
        { type: "header", key: "next-router-prefetch" },
        { type: "header", key: "purpose", value: "prefetch" },
      ],
    },
  ],
};

Then a route that actually exercises PPR: a static heading in the shell and one component that reads cookies, so it can only render at request time.

// app/ppr-check/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from "react";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";

async function Personalized() {
  const store = await cookies();
  const theme = store.get("theme")?.value ?? "default";
  return <p data-testid="dynamic-hole">Theme from cookie: {theme}</p>;
}

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Static shell</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading the personalized part</p>}>
        <Personalized />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

Three limits worth knowing before you trust any result:

  • Test the production build. Run next build and next start. The dev server needs 'unsafe-eval' and behaves differently enough that a clean dev run proves nothing.
  • Nonces need request time HTML. A per request value can't live inside HTML that was generated once at build time. For pages that are fully static, MDN's advice is hashes, not nonces.
  • The spec is still moving. W3C's latest CSP Level 3 document is a Working Draft, not a final Recommendation, so how browsers treat strict-dynamic and friends follows what they've implemented. Test in the browsers you actually support.

Evidence and verification checklist

Don't take the release note as the test. Run the same checks on your current version and on 16.4.4 and compare.

Check 1: the raw HTML. This script fetches a route, pulls the nonce out of the response header and fails if any executable <script> tag doesn't carry it. Because res.text() waits for the whole streamed response, it also sees the scripts that arrive with the dynamic part.

// verify-nonce.mjs
// usage: node verify-nonce.mjs http://localhost:3000/ppr-check
const url = process.argv[2] ?? "http://localhost:3000/ppr-check";
const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { accept: "text/html" } });

const csp = res.headers.get("content-security-policy") ?? "";
const match = csp.match(/'nonce-([^']+)'/);
if (!match) {
  console.error("FAIL: no nonce in the Content-Security-Policy header");
  process.exit(1);
}
const nonce = match[1];

const html = await res.text();
const dataTypes = /type="application\/(ld\+)?json"/i;
const scripts = [...html.matchAll(/<script\b[^>]*>/gi)]
  .map((m) => m[0])
  .filter((tag) => !dataTypes.test(tag));

const missing = scripts.filter((tag) => {
  const found = tag.match(/\bnonce="([^"]*)"/);
  return !found || found[1] !== nonce;
});

console.log(JSON.stringify({ url, scripts: scripts.length, missing: missing.length }, null, 2));
if (missing.length > 0) {
  for (const tag of missing) console.error("MISSING NONCE:", tag.slice(0, 160));
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log("PASS: every executable script carries the response nonce");

Check 2: a real browser. The HTML check tells you what was sent. The browser tells you what was blocked. This Playwright spec listens for securitypolicyviolation events and also asserts that the dynamic hole actually rendered.

// tests/csp.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("PPR route renders with zero CSP violations", async ({ page }) => {
  const violations: string[] = [];
  page.on("console", (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === "error" && msg.text().startsWith("CSP_VIOLATION")) {
      violations.push(msg.text());
    }
  });

  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    document.addEventListener("securitypolicyviolation", (event) => {
      console.error(`CSP_VIOLATION ${event.violatedDirective} ${event.blockedURI}`);
    });
  });

  await page.goto("/ppr-check");
  await expect(page.getByTestId("dynamic-hole")).toBeVisible();
  await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

  expect(violations).toEqual([]);
});

Check 3: compare versions. Same app, two installs:

# baseline: the 16.4.x you run today
npm install next@"$CURRENT_NEXT" && npx next build && (npx next start -p 3000 &) && sleep 5
node verify-nonce.mjs http://localhost:3000/ppr-check; npx playwright test tests/csp.spec.ts
kill %1 2>/dev/null || pkill -f "next start"

# patched
npm install next@16.4.4 && npx next build && (npx next start -p 3000 &) && sleep 5
node verify-nonce.mjs http://localhost:3000/ppr-check; npx playwright test tests/csp.spec.ts

If the baseline already passes both checks, your setup wasn't hitting that path, which is good to know, and the upgrade is still a cheap patch bump. If the baseline fails and 16.4.4 passes, you've reproduced the bug and verified the backport in one go.

Where rollout or governance fails

The patch is the easy part. These are the ways I'd expect a CSP rollout to go wrong anyway:

  • One app upgraded, the rest forgotten. In a monorepo it's easy to bump the app you tested and leave three others on the old 16.4 patch. Check every lockfile, not just the one in front of you.
  • 'unsafe-inline' as a quick fix. When a script gets blocked, adding it feels like progress. It quietly undoes the reason you have a nonce. Fix the script, don't widen the policy.
  • A CDN caching nonce HTML. If a shared cache stores the HTML, every visitor gets the same nonce, and a "number used once" becomes a constant. HTML that carries a nonce shouldn't be shared cached.
  • Report only, forever. Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only is the right way to start, so you see violations without breaking pages. It is the wrong place to stay. Put a date on flipping to enforce.

My take: treat the CSP check like a type check. It's boring, it runs on every PR, and the day it fails is the day it pays for itself.

Situation Reach for Why
HTML rendered per request (SSR, PPR dynamic holes) Nonce plus strict-dynamic MDN recommends nonces for dynamically generated content
Fully static page whose inline scripts never change Hashes No per request value exists to put in the HTML
Third party script loaded by your own trusted script strict-dynamic Trust flows from the nonce'd loader to what it loads
Brand new policy on a busy site Report only first, then enforce You see violations before users do

Actionable next steps

  1. Bump to next@16.4.4 in every app that combines PPR with a nonce based CSP.
  2. Add a small /ppr-check route with one Suspense wrapped dynamic component.
  3. Run verify-nonce.mjs against a production build in CI.
  4. Add the Playwright spec so blocked scripts fail the PR, not your users.
  5. If the policy is new, ship it report only, read the reports, then enforce.

FAQ

How does Next.js 16.4.4 CSP nonce PPR work?
Your proxy generates a nonce per request and sends it in the Content-Security-Policy header. Next.js reads it from the request headers and stamps it on the scripts it renders. With PPR, the static shell is prerendered and an inline resume bootstrap fills the dynamic holes at request time. 16.4.4 backports a fix so that bootstrap gets the nonce too.

When should developers adopt Next.js 16.4.4 CSP nonce PPR?
Now, if you run PPR with a strict nonce CSP. It's a patch release, so the risk is low, but verify it with the two checks above instead of assuming it.

Does 16.4.4 include the canary features?
No. The release notes say it carries specific backports and does not include everything on canary.

Is CSP Level 3 final?
Not yet. W3C's latest CSP Level 3 publication is a Working Draft, not a Recommendation.

Related reading: Next.js rendering patterns from CSR and SSR to Partial Prerendering and Next.js security hardening with middleware, Server Actions and CSP.

If you want a deeper look at how PPR splits a page into a static shell and dynamic holes, the rendering patterns piece above goes much further than this post.

If you want a Next.js app with streaming, a strict CSP and AI features wired up end to end, that is exactly the kind of Next.js work for AI products I take on.

Drop a comment if your setup looks different. I'm curious what CSP setups people are running with PPR in production.

title: EagleDiff: visual regression testing that sets up in minutes and gives the same answer every run
description:
Visual regression testing that sets up in minutes, gives the same answer every run, handles modern animated sites with sensible defaults, and lets you add your own capture rules when a site needs them. EagleDiff screenshots your pages in a real browser, compares them with your references and shows exactly what changed. When nothing changed, it says so: no false alarms from carousels, animations or images that load late.

A one-letter typo ("supermaket") in a heading, caught on a phone-sized screenshot of a long page.

What is it?

EagleDiff is a command-line tool. You point it at a site, and it:

  1. finds pages to test (up to 25 by default) and writes a config.json;
  2. captures every page, full length, at phone, tablet and desktop sizes;
  3. compares new captures with the references, using reg-suit under the hood;
  4. opens an HTML report with each change side by side, and exits with 0 when everything passes and 1 when something changed, so it fits a CI pipeline.

Why I built it

I've used BackstopJS for years at work, on the sites we build and maintain. It's a great tool and it inspired a lot of EagleDiff. But on many of our sites it kept giving me different results on different runs of the same pages.

The obvious test for any visual regression tool is to compare a site with itself: take the references, capture the same pages again straight away, and expect everything to pass, because nothing changed. Far too often that didn't happen.

It wasn't really the screenshot technique that was at fault. The web has changed. A typical page today keeps moving after it has "loaded":

  • images load lazily as you scroll, and web fonts arrive late;
  • carousels autoplay, counters count up, testimonials rotate on a timer;
  • JavaScript libraries such as GSAP run entrance animations and endless logo marquees;
  • videos play, GIFs animate, and cookie banners slide in;
  • scripts wait for jQuery or Drupal to finish starting up before they add content.

Take a screenshot at a slightly different moment and you get a slightly different page. The tool reports a "change", someone has to look at it, and it turns out to be nothing.

I still wanted a tool that gives consistent answers on these sites. So I set out to build one that compensates for the quirks of modern pages before it takes the screenshot.

That's where the name comes from. An eagle spots the smallest movement from far away, and that's the job I wanted done: notice the one-pixel shift and the one-letter typo, and ignore everything that doesn't matter. EagleDiff: an eagle's eye for differences.

Calibration comes first

The step I care most about is the one that comes before any real test. I call it calibration: compare the site with itself and make sure the tool passes.

eaglediff reference    # save screenshots of the site as it is now
eaglediff calibrate    # capture the same site again and compare

If calibration fails, nothing has changed on the site: something on the page moves between visits, and the tool isn't handling it yet. That's when you find out which pages need attention, before those false alarms reach your pipeline.

This matters most in CI. A visual check in a pipeline is only useful if it is reliable in both directions: it passes when nothing visible changed, and it fails when something did. A check that fails now and then for no reason soon becomes a burden. Someone has to open every report to see whether the failure is real, and eventually people stop looking. A tool you can't calibrate to a clean pass isn't ready for your pipeline.

Calibrate when you set up a project, and again at the start of a testing session: the live site may have changed since you took the references.

What it does for you by default

Out of the box, before each screenshot, EagleDiff:

  • waits for lazy images (scrolling the page to trigger them), web fonts, background images, jQuery and Drupal start-up, network activity and count-up counters;
  • steadies carousels (Swiper, Slick and others), CSS and Web Animations, JavaScript animations such as GSAP timelines and marquees, timer-driven rotators, SVG animations, animated GIFs, and videos and YouTube or Vimeo embeds;
  • handles common cookie banners;
  • fails loudly when an image or font is broken, instead of comparing a page with a hole in it, while still comparing the other pages;
  • keeps responsive scripts still while it takes full-page screenshots, so menus and animations don't restart mid-capture.

Each of these is a small hook you can switch off, reorder, or replace with your own. Site-specific needs go in your config: hide a live chat widget, wait for a selector, pin a random image. If you test many sites, a team defaults file merges your agency's common settings into every project.

A first test in a minute

Let's try it on https://example.com. The commands below work exactly as they are, so you can paste them into a terminal, then swap in your own site's address when you're ready. You need Node.js 22.12 or newer and Chrome or Chromium.

npm install -g eaglediff

mkdir -p tests/eaglediff
cd tests/eaglediff

eaglediff config --ref=https://example.com   # create config.json
eaglediff reference                          # save the references
eaglediff calibrate                          # compare with itself

example.com has a single page, captured at three sizes:

[eaglediff] Wrote config.json with 1 discovered scenarios
[eaglediff] Promoted 3 screenshots from .reg/actual to .reg/reference
[eaglediff] reference completed in 4s
...
[results] current  2026/11/23 14:45:04 | run=3 | passed=3 | dur=5s | workers=10
[eaglediff] calibrate completed in 5s

Calibration passed. Now set testBaseURL in config.json to your staging or local site and run the real comparison:

eaglediff test      # exit code 1 if anything changed
eaglediff report    # review the differences
eaglediff approve   # accept the changes as the new references

Coming from BackstopJS? eaglediff import --backstop=path/to/backstop.json brings over your scenarios and supported settings.

A harder test: sites that move

example.com proves the workflow, not the tool. To test Eaglediff honestly, I built three benchmarks anyone can install and run, with any tool. Each one adds known visual bugs to a demo site, one per page, and keeps a few pages unchanged as controls. The bugs live in the site, not in EagleDiff:

  • Drupal 11 Umami: the official Drupal demo, with responsive and lazy images, web fonts, two languages and an accented URL;
  • WordPress with Elementor: carousels, counters, progress bars, entrance animations and lazy backgrounds;
  • Svelte with GSAP: an animation-heavy agency template with smooth scrolling, an endless logo marquee, scroll-triggered reveals and a rotating testimonial.

The bugs are the kind that slip through review: a 1px shift, a 2px button move, a faded colour, a one-letter typo, a missing menu item on phones only, a broken lazy image below the fold, a missing web font file, a notice bar added by JavaScript two seconds after load, a page that answers with a server error.

With EagleDff's default settings and no site-specific configuration:

Site Calibration Bugs found False alarms
Drupal Umami passed every run 26 of 27 0
WordPress with Elementor passed every run 15 of 18 0
Svelte with GSAP passed 10 of 10 runs 11 of 12 0

The misses are all changes smaller than the default thresholds allow: image corners rounded by 8px, one digit or letter changed in small text, and a button colour shifted by a few shades. That's the trade-off that keeps real sites from failing on harmless rendering noise.

These are also changes that other kinds of tests catch better. A wrong digit in a price or in opening hours is a content bug: an end-to-end test that checks the text, for example with Playwright, finds it every time. A different corner radius or a slightly different brand colour is a design detail: component-level visual tests at strict thresholds, such as snapshot tools for Storybook, are made for that. Full-page visual regression testing is strongest at catching visible breakage across whole pages: layout shifts, missing or broken elements, wrong fonts and images, typos in headings. If you need more, you can still tighten the thresholds for your own project.

The Svelte site was the most useful of the three: on its first run, the unchanged site failed calibration on almost every attempt. It led to three fixes in EagleDiff:

  • endless JavaScript animations are now held at their starting position;
  • repeating timers, which rotate testimonials and tickers, are paused;
  • full-page screenshots no longer make responsive scripts restart their animations.

Every fix became a default, so the next site like it should calibrate cleanly without any configuration.

And BackstopJS?

Because the bugs live in the sites, the same benchmarks run with any tool. Here is BackstopJS 6.3.25 with the defaults backstop init creates, on the same sites on the same day. The scripts to reproduce it are in the repository too.

Site Calibration Bugs found
Drupal Umami passed (0 of 99 screenshots flagged) 19 of 27
WordPress with Elementor failed (15 of 66 flagged) not meaningful
Svelte with GSAP failed (42 to 45 of 48 flagged) not meaningful

On Umami, Backstop is steady but misses content added after load and the smaller changes. On the two animated sites, it flags pages that didn't change, run after run, so a flagged bug page tells you nothing. That is exactly the problem I started with.

To be fair to BackstopJS: these are its defaults, without tuning. Delays, hide selectors and custom scripts can steady many of these pages, and that's what we used to do, page by page and site by site. EagleDiff's aim is to make that work unnecessary for the common cases.

Where it stands

EagleDiff has been tested extensively on the projects I work on, and there it is far more consistent than what I used before. I'll keep improving it as I meet new kinds of sites, and keep turning fixes into defaults where they make sense.

It hasn't been tested by a wider audience yet. You'll find sites where it needs refining. It's tested on Linux; macOS and Windows should work, but I haven't tried them. Not every BackstopJS feature is there either; I'll add what people ask for.

I built EagleDiff with the help of AI coding assistants, OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code.

Try it

  • GitHub: https://github.com/GiorgosK/EagleDiff
  • npm: npm install -g eaglediff
  • Benchmarks: benchmark/ in the repository; run them with your favourite tool and compare.

Try it on your own sites and start with eaglediff calibrate. If it doesn't pass, please open an issue with the page and what moved. That's exactly the feedback that makes the defaults better. Pull requests are very welcome.

I'm releasing EagleDiff in the hope that it saves other people the hours I spent opening reports that turned out to show nothing at all.

title: Black Friday A100 at $399 a Month BEATS Hourly Rental. The Math Says Buy BEFORE Nov 28 👇
description:
Black Friday A100 at $399 a Month BEATS Hourly Rental. The Math Says Buy BEFORE Nov 28 👇

GPU Mart runs its Black Friday GPU sale from November 15 to November 28, 2026. The sale ends tomorrow. Eight GPU plans carry cuts of 45 to 60 percent off list price. The headline deal is an A100 with 40GB of memory at $399.50 a month, down from $799. Prices checked November 27, 2026 on gpu-mart.com.

The catch sits in the fine print. These monthly prices assume a two-year term, paid up front. The A100 deal costs $9,588 before you run a single job. That number changes the whole decision. This guide runs the math so you can judge the deal in ten minutes.

The price table

Plan GPU memory Monthly Was Cut
GPU VPS-2GB 2GB $11.60 $29.00 60%
GPU Dedicated-P1000 4GB $33.30 $74.00 55%
GPU VPS RTX Pro 2000-16G 16GB $98.45 $179.00 45%
GPU Dedicated-3060Ti 8GB $107.55 $239.00 55%
GPU Dedicated-A4000 16GB $139.50 $279.00 50%
GPU Dedicated-A100 40GB 40GB $399.50 $799.00 50%
GPU Dedicated-2x4090 2 x 24GB $449.50 $899.00 50%
GPU Dedicated-A100 80GB 80GB $764.55 $1,699.00 55%

The table lists the provider's own page prices. The "was" column is the provider's list price. Treat it as the anchor, not a market price. Every plan renews at the same Black Friday rate for the life of the service, according to the provider's FAQ page.

The math: turn a monthly price into an hourly price

A month has about 730 hours. Divide any monthly price by 730 and you get the cost of running the box around the clock.

Effective hourly cost = monthly price / 730.

  • A100 40GB: $399.50 / 730 = $0.55 an hour.
  • Two RTX 4090s: $449.50 / 730 = $0.62 an hour.
  • RTX Pro 2000 16GB: $98.45 / 730 = $0.13 an hour.
  • A100 80GB: $764.55 / 730 = $1.05 an hour.

Now compare that with hourly rental. RunPod lists its A100 40GB Community Cloud at $1.00 an hour. Its Secure Cloud lists the same card at $1.59 an hour. Price trackers checked November 27, 2026 confirm the $1.00 community rate. The Secure rate comes from RunPod's own comparison page.

Break-even hours = monthly price / hourly rental rate.

Against the $1.00 community rate, the A100 box pays for itself at 400 hours a month. That is about 13 hours a day. Run it more than that and the flat box wins. Run it less and hourly rental wins.

Against the $1.59 Secure rate, break-even drops to 251 hours a month. That is about 8 hours a day. A weekday-only workload still clears it.

At full use, the gap is wide. The A100 box costs $399.50 a month. The same card on community rental costs $730 a month at $1.00 an hour. The flat box saves $330.50 a month, or $3,966 a year. Against Secure Cloud at $1.59 an hour, the rental bill hits $1,160.70 a month. The flat box saves $761.20 a month.

What fits in the memory

VRAM decides which models a card can run. A simple rule covers it. Full precision needs about 2 bytes per parameter. A 4-bit quantized model needs about 0.5 bytes per parameter.

An 8-billion-parameter model needs about 16GB at full precision and about 4GB quantized. A 70-billion-parameter model needs about 35GB quantized and about 140GB at full precision.

That maps to the sale table cleanly. A 16GB card runs an 8B model at full precision, or a 32B model quantized. A 40GB card runs a 70B model quantized. An 80GB card runs a 70B model at higher precision, or two smaller models side by side.

The 2GB card fits no serious local model. Weights alone would leave almost nothing for context. Skip it for LLM work. It still suits light rendering and small graphics jobs.

Three ways to use the sale

  1. Starter: RTX Pro 2000 16GB at $98.45 a month. Total for two years: $2,362.80. This is the cheapest card that runs a real local model. Use it to learn serving, test a small assistant, or run a private 8B model all day. At full-time use it costs $0.13 an hour.

  2. Serious: A100 40GB at $399.50 a month. Total for two years: $9,588. This is the pick for a 70B quantized model, long-context work, or a small team sharing one box. Break-even sits at 400 hours a month against community rental. If the box runs most days, it pays.

  3. Heavy: two RTX 4090s at $449.50 a month, or one A100 80GB at $764.55 a month. Totals for two years: $10,788 and $18,349.20. The pair gives 48GB in total, but split across two cards. One model cannot use both pools unless you set up tensor parallelism. The single 80GB card keeps memory in one pool, so it suits one big model. Pick the pair for two jobs at once. Pick the 80GB card for one big job.

What can go wrong

The two-year term is the biggest risk. You pay $9,588 up front for the A100. If the project dies in month three, the saving dies with it. Only buy the term if the workload already exists today.

The discount has strings attached. It applies to new orders only. It does not cover paid add-ons. Upgrading or downgrading to a plan outside the sale kills the discount. Stock is limited, and the provider caps purchases at three per customer.

The renewal rate is the bright spot. The provider says the Black Friday price renews at the same rate for the life of the service. That claim comes from the provider's own FAQ page. It is not a contract term I could check elsewhere. Read the order page before you pay.

The host is a small US provider, in business since 2005, not a large cloud. Support runs around the clock by ticket, with no phone support listed. Uptime and hardware replacement terms sit in its own terms page. If your workload needs a service-level agreement, ask for it in writing before you order.

Verdict

The A100 deal is real math, not a sticker trick. At $0.55 an hour of full-time use, it undercuts the cheapest hourly rental by 45 percent. The condition is use: 400 hours a month against community rental, or 251 against Secure Cloud.

First step: open your rental dashboard and count the hours your GPU ran last month. If the number tops 400, buy the A100 before November 28. If it sits under 250, stay on hourly rental and skip the sale. If it lands between, run the same break-even math on the 16GB card first.

Follow along

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ovu-lab
  • YouTube: https://youtube.com/@oVuCyber

title: My agent passed every check I wrote. The product manager said it solved the wrong problem.
description:
I built a support agent for order questions. It looked up the order number, checked the shipping status, and drafted a notification email for the customer.

My eval suite was green. The tool calls hit the right APIs with the right arguments. The emails matched the schema. Nothing made up a tracking number.

Then the product manager on the project read through a batch of conversations with me. On one of them, the agent had done everything my checks asked for. It found the order, reported the status, and drafted a clean email. The customer had written in to change the delivery address.

Every check I had written asked whether the agent did the job correctly. None of them asked whether it was doing the job the user came for.

An agent gets graded on two questions

The question I was asking is the engineering one. Is the agent solving the problem correctly? Is the reasoning sound, are the tool calls correct and secure, and does it stay efficient and stable under load?

The product manager was asking the other one. Is the agent solving the right problem? Did it understand what the user wanted, did it finish the task, and would the user trust the exchange?

Both are evaluation. They need different metrics.

The engineering list is task adherence and planning accuracy, tool-call accuracy (precision, recall and correctness of each call), hallucination and error rate, and latency, tokens and dollars per task.

The product list is intent resolution, task completion rate, user feedback and satisfaction, and one I had never scored at all: whether an answer that is not exact is still helpful.

My suite only had the first list.

Small step errors compound across a run

An agent makes a chain of decisions, so the eval has to score the whole trajectory.

If each step fails 5% of the time, a five-step run fails about 23% of the time.

That is why per-step checks matter. They catch a low-confidence output at the step where it happens, before later steps build on it.

Agree on what done means before anyone writes a check

What fixed this was a conversation before the next round of work. We answered three questions together.

Which multi-step task is the agent for? How do we measure success: task completion rate, decision accuracy, or cost per resolution? What are the guardrails: which tools can it call, and what data can it touch?

Once those answers were written down, both lists of metrics had something to point at.

Product writes the stories and engineering breaks them

Test scenarios now come from both sides. The product manager brings user stories that outline the ideal paths, drawn from what users actually ask for. I add the edge cases. What happens if the shipping API is down? What happens if the order number is wrong?

A customer who wants a new delivery address is a user story. It was never going to show up in my edge cases.

Read the logs and the strange decisions together

We also read logs side by side. I check whether the execution was right. The product manager checks whether it matched the business goal.

Agents do things nobody planned. When one of those decisions shows up, it gets reviewed by both of us.

I ask what data it used, which function it called, and why. The product manager asks whether the decision was actually wrong or just surprising, and whether it followed a business rule or found a creative workaround.

Reviewing these together sharpened the agent's logic and our eval metrics at the same time.

Every eval layer has a product half and an engineering half

Tracing. Engineering logs every step of the reasoning loop: the plan, each tool call's input, and each output. Product decides which user-journey milestones the traces must capture.

Testing. Engineering owns most of the synthetic and adversarial tests: rare edge cases, contradictory user goals, faulty API responses, prompt injection, data leakage and bad error handling. Product owns most of the real-world side: a golden dataset built from real user interactions, which becomes the regression baseline, plus human review where automation cannot judge tone, helpfulness or brand fit.

Automated scoring. Engineering writes code-based evaluators for JSON formatting, schema adherence and factual consistency against a database. Product configures the LLM-as-judge evaluators: helpfulness, summary quality and intent alignment. The results feed prompt and configuration changes, and the suite runs again. Wire it into CI so a regression fails the build.

What I would tell myself before building an agent eval suite

  • Ask both questions: solving the problem correctly and solving the right problem need separate metrics.
  • Define done together: the task, the success measure and the guardrails come before the first check.
  • Source scenarios from both sides: user stories from product, edge cases from engineering.
  • Review surprises jointly: a surprising decision is not automatically a wrong one.
  • Split every layer by owner: tracing, tests and judges each need a product half and an engineering half.

The full framework, with the three layers and how each team owns its part, is in this piece.

Who writes the success criteria for your agent evals? On my project it was only me, and that was the problem.

title: Docker developer learning Cloud: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan
description:
What carries over

Docker habit Cloud equivalent Why it still matters
Declarative container images (Dockerfile, docker build) Infrastructure as Code (IaC) – Docker images are still the unit of deployment in most cloud services (ECS, GKE, Cloud Run). The same layered image format is pushed to registries (ECR, GCR, Artifact Registry) and referenced by cloud resources.
Compose for multi‑container orchestration (docker-compose.yml) Service definitions – docker-compose maps closely to Kubernetes Pod/Deployment specs, ECS task definitions, or Docker Swarm stacks. The mental model of a single YAML describing how containers talk to each other stays intact; you just translate fields.
Port mapping & networking (-p 8080:80) Service exposure – Cloud load balancers, Ingress, or Cloud Run's automatic URL mapping replace manual -p. Understanding inbound/outbound ports, health checks, and service discovery is still required, just at a higher abstraction.
Environment variables for config (-e KEY=val) Secrets & config stores – aws ssm put-parameter, gcloud secrets create, or Kubernetes ConfigMap. The principle of externalizing config remains; the delivery mechanism changes.
Layered caching (docker build --cache-from) Build cache in CI/CD – Cloud Build, GitHub Actions, or CodeBuild cache layers between builds. Efficient builds still rely on reusing unchanged layers; the tooling differs.
Logging to stdout/stderr Centralized log services – CloudWatch Logs, Stackdriver Logging, Loki. The contract of “container writes to stdout” is unchanged; the collector is now a managed service.
Health‑check directives (HEALTHCHECK) Readiness/Liveness probes in Kubernetes or health‑check settings in load balancers. The same idea of a container reporting its health, just expressed in a different resource.
Image tagging and immutability (myapp:1.2.3) Versioned deployments – immutable tags in ECR/GCR, rollout policies. Guarantees repeatable deployments across environments.

What's new

Example task: Deploy a simple “Hello World” HTTP service

Docker (local)

# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY app.py .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

# Build & run locally
docker build -t hello .
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 hello

Cloud (AWS ECS Fargate)

# task-definition.json
{
  "family": "hello-task",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512",
  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "hello",
      "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hello:latest",
      "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 8080, "protocol": "tcp" }],
      "essential": true,
      "logConfiguration": {
        "logDriver": "awslogs",
        "options": {
          "awslogs-group": "/ecs/hello",
          "awslogs-region": "us-east-1",
          "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

# Push image to ECR
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag hello:latest 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hello:latest
docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hello:latest

# Register task definition
aws ecs register-task-definition --cli-input-json file://task-definition.json

# Create a service in a cluster (assumes VPC, subnets, SG already)
aws ecs create-service \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --service-name hello-service \
  --task-definition hello-task \
  --desired-count 1 \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-abc123],securityGroups=[sg-abc123],assignPublicIp=ENABLED}"

What changed and why

Aspect Docker Cloud (ECS) Reason
Image registry Local daemon Managed registry (ECR) Cloud services need a globally reachable, authenticated store.
Runtime Local Docker Engine Managed Fargate compute No servers to patch; you pay per vCPU/GB‑second.
Networking Host‑port mapping VPC‑aware ENI, security groups Cloud isolates workloads; you must declare subnets and SG rules.
Logging docker logs CloudWatch Logs integration Centralized, searchable logs across all tasks.
Scaling Manual docker run Desired count, auto‑scale policies Cloud can automatically adjust task count based on metrics.
Deployment docker run command Declarative task definition + service Immutable infrastructure; changes trigger new task revisions.

Common pitfalls

  1. Assuming “run locally = run in cloud.”

    Local networking (localhost) disappears behind VPCs and load balancers. Forgetting to open the right security‑group ports leads to “connection refused” errors that look like container bugs.

  2. Hard‑coding credentials

    Docker -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=… works locally but is a security nightmare in the cloud. Use IAM roles for ECS tasks, Workload Identity for GKE, or instance profiles instead.

  3. Neglecting resource limits

    In Docker you may run with default CPU/memory, but cloud services enforce limits per task/pod. Under‑provisioned limits cause throttling or OOM kills that surface as intermittent failures.

  4. Over‑relying on docker-compose up

    docker-compose does not translate 1‑to‑1 to Kubernetes or ECS. Missing fields (e.g., health‑check intervals, rollout strategies) cause deployments that never become ready. Use tools like kompose or write native manifests.

  5. Ignoring regional latency and data residency

    A container image stored in a distant registry adds pull latency; some services (e.g., S3) have region‑specific endpoints. Always pick the same region for compute, storage, and registry.

  6. Treating logs as a side‑effect

    Cloud platforms charge for log ingestion and retention. Unbounded stdout can explode costs. Configure log drivers and retention policies early.

Your 30‑day plan

Week 1 – Foundations

  • Task 1: Set up a free‑tier cloud account (AWS, GCP, or Azure). Enable the container registry service (ECR, Artifact Registry, or ACR).
  • Task 2: Push an existing Docker image to the cloud registry using the CLI (aws ecr get-login-password …). Verify it appears in the console.
  • Task 3: Deploy a single‑container task using the managed serverless compute (ECS Fargate, Cloud Run, or Azure Container Apps). Confirm you can reach it via the provided URL or load balancer DNS.
  • Mini‑project: “Hello Cloud” – a tiny Flask (or Express) app that returns the request’s IP address. Deploy it and test from your laptop.

Week 2 – Networking & Configuration

  • Task 1: Create a VPC (or use the default) with at least two subnets, a security group, and a NAT gateway if needed.
  • Task 2: Move configuration from docker run -e to a managed secret store (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault). Update the task definition to pull the secret at runtime.
  • Task 3: Set up a Cloud Load Balancer (ALB, HTTP(S) LB, or Azure Front Door) that routes traffic to your service. Add health‑check settings.
  • Mini‑project: “Config‑driven API” – expose an endpoint that reads a value from the secret store and returns it. Deploy with the load balancer and verify secure access.

Week 3 – Orchestration & CI/CD

  • Task 1: Write a Kubernetes manifest (Deployment + Service) that mirrors your docker-compose.yml. Deploy to a managed K8s service (EKS, GKE, AKS).
  • Task 2: Install a CI pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Cloud Build) that builds the image, pushes to the registry, and triggers a rolling update (kubectl rollout restart).
  • Task 3: Enable auto‑scaling: configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (or ECS Service Auto Scaling) based on CPU utilization.
  • Mini‑project: “Scalable worker” – a background job container that processes messages from a queue (SQS, Pub/Sub, or Service Bus). Verify it scales up when you artificially increase load.

Week 4 – Observability & Cost hygiene

  • Task 1: Wire the service to a centralized logging solution (CloudWatch Logs, Stackdriver Logging, or Azure Monitor). Create a query that filters error‑level logs.
  • Task 2: Add distributed tracing (AWS X‑Ray, OpenTelemetry on GKE, or Azure Application Insights) to the same service. Generate a few requests and view the trace graph.
  • Task 3: Set up budget alerts and enable log retention policies (e.g., 30 days). Review the cost dashboard for any surprises.
  • Mini‑project: “Production‑ready demo” – take the “Config‑driven API” from Week 2, run it behind the load balancer, enable logs/traces, and document the end‑to‑end request flow.

FAQ

How much of my existing Dockerfile can I reuse?

Almost all of it. The image build process is identical; you only need to push the resulting image to a cloud‑accessible registry.

Do I still need docker-compose when using Kubernetes?

Not for production. docker-compose is great for local iteration, but Kubernetes uses its own YAML manifests. Convert the compose file with kompose or rewrite manually for finer control.

What’s the simplest way to get IAM permissions for a container without embedding keys?

Assign an IAM role to the compute resource (ECS task role, GKE Workload Identity, or Azure Managed Identity). The SDKs automatically pick up temporary credentials.

Is it worth learning Terraform now, or can I stick to the cloud CLI?

For a single service you can use the native CLI, but Terraform gives you repeatable, version‑controlled infrastructure. Starting early saves time when you scale to multiple services.

Keep going
