title: Thumbnail Metadata After Upload: 10 Durable Checks for Signed Documents
description:
Thumbnail Metadata After Upload: 10 Durable Checks for Signed Documents

The important trade-off is simple: put thumbnail metadata in the same durable write as the thumbnail object when possible, then verify the stored representation before acknowledging the upload. A successful image resize proves only that bytes were produced; it does not prove that the object store received the metadata, that a later reader is using the same key, or that a deletion deadline can be enforced and audited.

Short answer: treat metadata persistence as part of the upload contract. Generate the thumbnail, build one immutable object descriptor, write the bytes and metadata, read the object back through the same interface, and record the result in an audit trail. Keep searchable business fields in a database, because object metadata is a transport and retrieval aid rather than a replacement for a ledger.

This matters in a B2B SaaS system that retains signed documents until an explicit deadline. Large source files make throughput important, but throughput cannot justify acknowledging a thumbnail whose metadata has not been observed at its destination.

How do I keep thumbnail metadata persisting in object storage after upload?

Start with the boundary, not with the resize algorithm. There are four different artifacts: the source document, the derived thumbnail bytes, the object metadata sent with those bytes, and the database record that tells the application where the thumbnail belongs. A user-visible failure can come from any mismatch among them.

Ask a narrow question: did the metadata disappear during resizing, during serialization, during the object write, or during the subsequent read? Capture the object key, content type, byte length, checksum when available, and the exact metadata map at each boundary. Do not log signed-document contents or secrets.

The common trap is a two-step implementation: upload the thumbnail first, then issue a separate metadata update. That creates a race with readers, retries, replication, and deletion jobs. A timeout after the first step also leaves an ambiguous state. The retry may create another object, or it may update the wrong key if the key was generated twice.

A better invariant is deliberately boring: one deterministic object key, one idempotency key, one upload result, and one database transition from pending to stored. If any part is uncertain, the state remains pending and a reconciler can inspect it later. The choice is deliberate: a delayed acknowledgement is easier to explain and repair than a durable record that says stored when the object cannot satisfy its contract.

Do not guess.

Why does metadata vanish when the image is correct?

Thumbnail pipelines often use a new in-memory image object and then serialize it into a fresh buffer. The bytes therefore have a new content type, length, and identity. Metadata attached to the source object is not automatically inherited by the derived object; the application must select which fields are meaningful for the thumbnail and write them explicitly.

Another failure is name normalization. Object stores commonly distinguish user metadata from system-controlled fields, and providers expose those fields through different request and response shapes. A key such as Document-ID may be normalized, rejected, or returned with a different case. Use a small, lowercase, provider-neutral vocabulary such as document-id, derivation, and delete-at, then compare normalized values after the write. The authoritative deadline should also live in the application database, where a deletion worker can query it without scanning every object.

The third failure is a successful response interpreted too broadly. A response can indicate that the write request was accepted while the application still has not verified the object it will later read. Verification does not require downloading a 500 MB source document: issue a metadata-only read, check the expected key and content type, and compare the fields that the contract requires.

Here is a deliberately generic Go shape for that contract. The storage interface leaves provider behavior outside the application core, while the record makes retry decisions explicit.

type Thumbnail struct {
\tKey         string
\tContentType string
\tSize        int64
\tMetadata    map[string]string
}

type ObjectStore interface {
\tPut(ctx context.Context, key string, body io.Reader, contentType string, metadata map[string]string) error
\tHead(ctx context.Context, key string) (Thumbnail, error)
}

func storeThumbnail(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, t Thumbnail) error {
\tif t.Key == "" || t.ContentType == "" || t.Size < 0 {
\t\treturn errors.New("invalid thumbnail descriptor")
\t}

\t// The production implementation supplies a rewindable or regenerated body.
\tif err := store.Put(ctx, t.Key, bytes.NewReader(nil), t.ContentType, t.Metadata); err != nil {
\t\treturn err
\t}

\tgot, err := store.Head(ctx, t.Key)
\tif err != nil {
\t\treturn err
\t}
\tif got.ContentType != t.ContentType || got.Metadata["derivation"] != t.Metadata["derivation"] {
\t\treturn errors.New("stored thumbnail does not satisfy contract")
\t}
\treturn nil
}

The empty reader is a contract example, not a complete uploader. In the real path, the body must contain the encoded thumbnail and the observed size must match the encoded bytes. Keeping that distinction visible prevents sample code from becoming a misleading production recipe.

Which storage boundary should the design assume?

The application should depend on capabilities, not on one provider's metadata naming. Amazon S3 documents user-defined metadata as headers supplied with an object request; Google Cloud Storage exposes custom metadata on objects; Azure Blob Storage separates metadata from HTTP headers. Those are similar enough for an adapter, but not identical enough to hide validation. Provider adapters should reject unsupported keys, normalize case, and expose the post-write values in one internal type.

Boundary Useful fact for this bug Design response
Amazon S3 User-defined metadata is sent with the object request and is associated with that object. Include the map in the idempotent write and verify it with a metadata read.
Google Cloud Storage Custom metadata is an object property and is returned as part of object metadata. Treat the derived object as a new resource; copy only an explicit allowlist.
Azure Blob Storage Blob metadata and HTTP headers are distinct concerns. Keep business metadata separate from content headers in the adapter.

These products are evidence of differing interfaces, not recommendations. A self-hosted S3-compatible service or another object store still needs the same contract tests: write, read metadata, retry, and delete at the deadline. The right choice for large-file throughput depends on sustained multipart behavior, network placement, concurrency limits, and recovery tooling; a metadata field alone does not answer that question.

The adapter boundary is also where a subtle operational distinction belongs. If a provider returns the thumbnail bytes correctly but omits a custom field from its metadata read, the adapter should report verification failure rather than silently filling the field from the database. If the provider returns the field with normalized casing, the adapter should compare canonical names and retain the provider response for the audit event. If the request times out before its result is known, the adapter should expose an indeterminate outcome so the caller can reconcile by stable key. Those three outcomes are different: a confirmed mismatch can be repaired, a normalized match can be accepted, and an unknown result must not be treated as a second write. This small vocabulary prevents storage-specific behavior from leaking into deletion workers and document APIs.

How do throughput and deletion deadlines fit together?

For large source files, stream the source and resize work through bounded queues. Do not make the thumbnail path wait for a full-document database transaction, and do not let an unbounded retry queue consume all workers. The thumbnail is usually smaller than the source, but its upload still deserves a deadline, a cancellation path, and a measurable result.
A practical record might contain document_id, thumbnail_key, source_version, delete_at, idempotency_key, status, and verified_at. The object key can include the immutable source version, so a reprocessed thumbnail cannot silently overwrite the result of a different source. The database row is the queryable control plane; the object metadata is useful context for operators and downstream readers.

Deletion is a separate state transition. At or after delete_at, a worker marks the record eligible, deletes the object, verifies absence according to the provider contract, and appends an audit event. A retryable deletion error remains visible rather than being converted into a successful status. Retention obligations and data-portability duties must be checked with the applicable legal team; GDPR Article 20, for example, describes a right to receive personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, subject to its stated conditions and limits.

That is where exactly-once thinking helps, even though distributed systems usually provide at-least-once delivery around the edges. Make the business transition idempotent, use stable keys, and make audit events deduplicable. The system can then tolerate a repeated message without claiming that an uncertain write happened exactly once.

A compact rollout and test plan

Before enabling the path for every document, test the adapter against each supported storage implementation with a matrix of metadata keys, casing, empty values, Unicode-free identifiers, retries, cancellation, and large bodies. Include a test where the byte upload succeeds but the verification read times out. The expected result is pending plus a reconciliation task, never a false stored state.

Observe four rates separately: resize failures, object-write failures, metadata-verification failures, and deletion failures. A single upload-success metric hides the failure mode this article is trying to find. Sample object keys and hashes in logs, but keep document content and sensitive metadata out of them.

Roll out with a bounded concurrency limit and a replayable queue. Reconcile records in pending for longer than the upload SLA, compare the database descriptor with the object metadata, and repair only when the source version and idempotency key still match. After that, migration is a small, defensible sequence: dual-write the descriptor, verify it, backfill missing thumbnails, then remove the old two-step path.

The decision rule is compact: if metadata changes the meaning, retention, or auditability of a thumbnail, it belongs in the same durable workflow as the bytes and must be verified before acknowledgement. If it is merely an optimization for lookup, keep the database authoritative and allow the object metadata to be rebuilt. That separation preserves throughput without weakening deletion evidence.

Sources

  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-20-gdpr/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/metadata
  • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/set-blob-metadata

title: Go User Session Containment: Choosing Revocation Scope During Classroom Abuse
description:
Targeted logout preserves a student's other devices, but it is an inadequate response when the account itself may be compromised. TL;DR: revoke one session for an isolated device or session exposure; revoke all sessions when the suspected compromise crosses devices, affects the credentials used to establish trust, or cannot be bounded. For an education platform accepting Google and GitHub social sign-in, suspend abusive activity separately: logging a bot out does not establish that it cannot sign in again.

For a production design review, I would start with this explicitly hypothetical case: a student has a classroom laptop, a home browser, and a phone, and an abuse alert implicates the classroom laptop's session. The decision is whether there is evidence of an isolated session leak or a broader account takeover. These are assumed devices, not incident measurements. Forcing all three offline buys little if the same actor can immediately authenticate again, while leaving the other two active is difficult to defend if the account's authentication authority is suspect.

Scope follows evidence.

The invariant is that invalidating existing access and controlling the creation of new access are separate responsibilities. That distinction carries the incident lesson: a successful logout response is insufficient evidence that an abuse incident has been contained.

When should one session become every session?

Use single-session revocation when the user is removing a known device, ending a session on a shared classroom computer, or responding to evidence that identifies one exposed session without implicating the account's other credentials. A session is a server-recognized login instance; a browser label is only a usability aid. Don't promise that deleting one cookie signs out every browser profile on the same laptop.

Account-wide revocation fits suspected account takeover, uncertain exposure scope, or a recovery event where previously established sessions should lose trust. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet treats reauthentication after risk events and session invalidation as security controls; the operational policy should connect those controls to explicit incident evidence rather than silently treating every routine logout as an emergency. Sensitive actions, including changes to the authentication relationship, deserve fresh authentication under the platform's risk policy.

An abuse alert also needs classification. A legitimate account can automate disruptive classroom activity without any stolen credential. Revoking all its sessions may interrupt that activity, but the account can authenticate again unless a separate authorization or abuse control prevents it. Conversely, an account-wide revocation should not require permanently suspending a student whose credentials were stolen. These decisions have different reversal criteria, different support consequences, and different owners.

Keep them separate.

The scope selector belongs on the server. A request to revoke a specific session must prove ownership or an explicitly authorized administrative role, and a request to revoke every session must be protected as a sensitive action. An opaque session identifier isn't authorization.

The callback can undo your containment

Social sign-in creates a second trust boundary: the application has its own sessions, while the external identity system has its own authentication state. Terminating an application session does not, by itself, terminate the identity provider's session or revoke an upstream grant. Document exactly which boundary the logout control covers.

For the classroom case, a callback that establishes a new application session must consult the current account policy before issuing usable access. If the account is temporarily restricted during an abuse investigation, successful external authentication is evidence about identity; the application's authorization decision still applies. The same restriction must govern existing authenticated requests, otherwise an old phone session can continue the prohibited activity.

There is a concurrency trap here. Suppose an account-wide revocation advances an account generation while a callback is still processing. If session creation reads the old generation, then commits after the revocation, the resulting session must fail subsequent authorization checks. If the intended policy also prohibits new logins, generation checks alone cannot enforce it: session issuance must atomically check the restriction against current account state. Design that transaction before arguing about logout button wording.

Make the rejection path explicit in Go

One possible server-side design stores an account generation on each session. Single-session revocation marks that session revoked; account-wide revocation atomically advances the account generation. Each protected request compares its stored session generation with the current account value, checks expiry, and applies the current account restriction. This is a proposed implementation model, not a requirement of an authentication protocol.

The following Go example isolates that authorization decision. Its caller must first validate the presented credential, load the associated session and its account from authoritative storage, and handle storage failures; the example does not implement credential parsing, persistence, or concurrency control.

package sessionpolicy

import (
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrDenied = errors.New("session denied")

type Account struct {
    ID         string
    Generation uint64
    Restricted bool
}

type Session struct {
    AccountID  string
    Generation uint64
    Revoked    bool
    ExpiresAt  time.Time
}

func Authorize(a Account, s Session, now time.Time) error {
    if a.ID == "" || s.AccountID != a.ID {
        return ErrDenied
    }
    if a.Restricted || s.Revoked || !now.Before(s.ExpiresAt) {
        return ErrDenied
    }
    if s.Generation != a.Generation {
        return ErrDenied
    }
    return nil
}

The difficult part is the read contract. If a service authorizes a self-contained access token without consulting current revocation state, changing a database row cannot make that service reject the token immediately. A renewal endpoint must also reject revoked sessions, but blocking renewal alone leaves any already-issued access usable until the receiving service's validation policy rejects it. OWASP's Session Management Cheat Sheet supports server-side invalidation; the application must make that invalidation observable wherever access is accepted.

A cache changes the promise. As an illustrative design target, a team might require rejection within 60 seconds of a committed revocation; that number is an acceptance criterion, not a benchmark or a universal security recommendation. Cache age, propagation, in-flight work, and authorization frequency must fit inside the promised bound. Long-running classroom connections need their own reauthorization or termination mechanism, because checking a session only when a connection opens leaves later messages outside the revocation check.

Buy or build the enforcement responsibility

The buying decision should turn on who owns the rejection path during an incident. Outsourcing login can reduce authentication plumbing, while the education platform still owns its classroom permissions, abuse policy, and the integration that makes session revocation effective across services. Evaluate those responsibilities through an acceptance test, without assuming a feature label proves the required behavior.

Responsibility Managed implementation: evidence to require Self-hosted implementation: work to budget
One-session containment Demonstrate rejection of that session while another remains usable Maintain session identity, ownership checks, and revocation state
Account-wide containment Demonstrate effects on existing access and concurrent issuance Implement atomic account state changes and consistent enforcement
Abuse restrictions Verify where application policy is evaluated Own policy storage, decision availability, and support tooling
Incident operations Establish observable propagation and exportable audit records Own monitoring, capacity, recovery procedures, and on-call coverage

Capacity planning should count authorization checks, not just login traffic. In a proposed workload with 10,000 active students making one protected request every 5 seconds, the authorization path receives approximately 2,000 checks per second before bursts or reconnects. Those are planning assumptions. Requiring current server state on that path increases its availability obligations; caching it reduces read pressure while extending the interval during which old state can authorize activity.

Budget for the burst.

An account-wide action during a busy lesson can produce reauthentication attempts and support requests as well as database writes. The operational cost includes those effects, integration maintenance, and on-call ownership. Portability matters too: the application needs a stable definition of session identity and revocation scope if the authentication implementation changes.

Prove containment before rollout

Test two sessions for one account and a third for another account. Revoke the first, verify its rejection, and verify both unaffected sessions still work. Then revoke all sessions for the first account and verify that both of its old sessions fail while the other account remains usable. Include expired credentials, denied renewal, unauthorized attempts to revoke another user's session, a callback racing the account update, and a long-running connection that predates revocation. For a restricted account, also verify that a new successful identity assertion cannot restore prohibited access.

Treat the interval from committed revocation to enforced rejection as a measurable containment SLO, distinct from login availability. Record the action's actor, scope, reason, commit time, and enforcement outcome, using internal identifiers rather than raw session secrets. Test propagation under load before relying on the bound, and make a storage outage's behavior explicit: failing closed protects the restricted operation but may interrupt classroom access. Different operations can justify different availability policies; any exception should be deliberate.

Deploy the authorization path before enabling the new revocation controls. Otherwise, a control plane can report successful invalidation while an older request handler continues accepting access. Rollback planning must preserve revocation enforcement, including already-advanced generations.

This generation model has a limitation: it requires access to current account state. A genuinely stateless service that accepts access until token expiry must express containment in those terms, or introduce a current-state check. An isolated-session incident may justify preserving other devices; evidence of broader compromise should expand the revocation scope. In either case, abuse resistance also requires controlling the next authorization decision. The completion criterion is observable rejection within the promised bound, with legitimate access preserved only where the evidence supports it.

References

The authentication guidance supports reauthentication after risk events; the session guidance covers invalidation and session lifecycle controls. The generation model, classroom scenario, and capacity figures above are proposed design choices and explicit planning assumptions.

Sources

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Loco 1.3 for Laravel developers: sessions, retries, unique jobs and notifications, side by side
description:
Loco is the Rust web framework that feels most like Laravel: generators, models, migrations, workers, mailers, a scheduler, all from one CLI. Version 1.3 closed the gaps a Laravel developer hits on day one. You no longer write your own browser login, retries are built in, and emails can go through notifications.

I moved a complete blog to it, and this is the map from the Laravel code you already write to the Loco 1.3 code that does the same job. All snippets come from a real app that runs in production on Postgres.

Login: Auth::login() becomes a session

Before 1.3, browser login in Loco meant a JWT in a cookie and your own extractor. Now there's the auth_session feature: sessions stored in the database, with "Remember me".

# Cargo.toml
loco-rs = { version = "1.3", features = ["auth", "auth_session", "with-db", "worker", "mailer", "notifications"] }

# config/development.yaml
auth:
  session:
    secret: <%= get_env(name="SESSION_SECRET") %>
    store: database          # rows in `loco_sessions`, so logout really ends a session
    sign_in_path: /login     # where a signed-out browser is sent
    ttl: 86400               # one idle day
    remember_for: 2592000    # 30 days with "Remember me"

The login handler, after checking the password:

// `renew()` drops the old session (session fixation), `set_user_id` is `Auth::login($user)`.
let mut session = session.renew().set_user_id(user.pid.to_string());
if form.remember.is_some() {
    session = session.remember()?;
}

Logout is session.clear(), Laravel's Auth::logout() plus session()->invalidate(). A copy of the old cookie no longer works, because the row in the database is gone. Protected handlers take CurrentUser<users::Model>, the equivalent of the auth middleware plus $request->user(). The JSON API can keep its JWT, like Laravel's api guard next to web.

$tries and $backoff 

class ProcessPost implements ShouldQueue
{
    public $tries = 4;
    public $backoff = 10;
}

impl BackgroundWorker<WorkerArgs> for Worker {
    /// Laravel's `$tries = 4`: the first run plus 3 retries.
    fn max_retries() -> u32 {
        3
    }

    /// Laravel's `$backoff`: 10 s before the first retry, then 20 s, 40 s.
    fn retry_backoff() -> Duration {
        Duration::from_secs(10)
    }
    // ...
}

Two things to know. Loco counts only the repeats, so $tries = 4 is max_retries() = 3. And the backoff doubles each time, capped at an hour, where Laravel repeats the same number unless you give it an array. The default is 0 retries, as in Laravel, so the first failure is final until you opt in.

Retries work with the persistent queue (BackgroundQueue mode on Postgres or SQLite). A job that ran out of retries stays in the queue table as failed, and cargo loco jobs retry is your php artisan queue:retry all.

ShouldBeUnique

Saving a post three times in a row should process it once:

// Laravel's `ShouldBeUnique` with `uniqueId()`. The key is free again once the job starts.
process_post::Worker::perform_later_unique(
    ctx,
    process_post::WorkerArgs { post_id: post.id },
    format!("post:{}", post.id),
)
.await?;

Notifications

The notifications feature is Laravel's Notification class: a message, channels (via()), and an email built from your own templates.

impl Notifier for NewPost {
    fn message(&self) -> Message {
        Message::new(format!("New post: {}", self.title)).url(&self.url)
    }

    /// Laravel's `via()`.
    fn channels(&self, _ctx: &AppContext) -> Vec<Channel> {
        vec![Channel::email_to(&self.email)]
    }

    fn email(&self, _message: &Message) -> Result<EmailContent> {
        EmailContent::from_template(&template, self)
    }
}

NewPost::new(...).deliver_later(&ctx).await queues one delivery per channel, and each delivery is its own job with its own retries. One bad address no longer fails the whole mailing. I stopped the mail server on purpose and watched the retries come 10, 20 and 40 seconds apart, then go through when it came back. In tests, notifications.stub: true is Notification::fake().

A cache every process can see 

cache:
  kind: Database   # CACHE_STORE=database: a `loco_cache` table, shared by web, worker and scheduler

The in-memory cache is faster. On two cores the cached home page served about 20,500 requests per second from memory and about 5,900 from the database, against about 1,500 with no cache. But the in-memory cache belongs to one process. With a separate worker, the worker clears its own cache, and the web server keeps serving the old page until the TTL runs out. For a blog, 5,900 pages a second is plenty, and correct beats fast.

The rest of the map

Laravel Loco 1.3
config/filesystems.php a storage: block in YAML (Local or Aws)
Storage::fake() drivers::mem::new() swapped in from a hook in the test environment
session()->flash() session.insert(...), removed on read
a scheduled queue:prune-failed queue.retention

title: Shareable travel filters with URLSearchParams: accents, repeated values and privacy
description:
By the Mapitt team. This educational example was prepared with AI assistance; it is fictional and does not describe Mapitt's implementation.

A travel search can become much easier to revisit when the destination and a few public filters are in its URL. There are several details worth handling deliberately: destinations can contain accents, a traveler may choose more than one interest, and a query string can be copied, logged or shared.

Build, don't concatenate

The browser's URL and URLSearchParams APIs handle query encoding. Start with raw values and let the API encode them; do not pre-encode values or interpolate them into a query string.

function createSearchLink(base, destination, interests) {
  const url = new URL(base);
  url.searchParams.set('destination', destination);
  url.searchParams.delete('interest');
  for (const interest of interests) {
    url.searchParams.append('interest', interest);
  }
  return url.href;
}

const link = createSearchLink(
  'https://example.com/search?language=es',
  'Mérida + montaña',
  ['cultura', 'naturaleza']
);
const parsed = new URL(link);
console.log(parsed.searchParams.get('destination')); // Mérida + montaña
console.log(parsed.searchParams.getAll('interest')); // ["cultura", "naturaleza"]

set replaces values for the single destination; append preserves each interest as a separate parameter. Starting with an existing URL keeps the unrelated language parameter. When reading filters, use getAll for a key that can appear multiple times. The code uses example.com deliberately; it is not a claim about a live Mapitt endpoint.

Avoid a subtle plus-sign bug

If you build new URLSearchParams('destination=' + value), a literal + in value is interpreted as a space. Passing the raw value to set or append instead preserves it during the round trip. Similarly, pre-encoding a value and then passing it to set can encode the percent signs a second time.

Validate and keep private details out

Treat URL parameters as untrusted input. Limit length and accepted values, handle missing or repeated fields, and render text as text rather than injecting it as HTML. The server must apply its own validation even if the browser checks inputs. URLs can appear in browser history, analytics, logs and shared screenshots; do not put names, contact details, booking references, tokens, exact current locations or other sensitive travel information in them. A link can preserve a broad search without exposing a traveler's private itinerary.

For a production search, also provide labeled controls, sensible defaults and a clear way to reset filters. These examples demonstrate URL handling, not a complete search system.

References: MDN: URLSearchParams and MDN: getAll().

The Mapitt team works on travel discovery in Venezuela.

title: SaaS Website Design: 10 Patterns That Convert (2026)
description:
Originally published on pzhydkykh.com.

Good SaaS website design is weirdly consistent: study the products that convert well and the same ten patterns keep appearing, regardless of industry or price point. I build SaaS marketing sites for a living, and these are the patterns I reuse on every project - plus the reasoning, so you can adapt the patterns instead of copying blindly.

Key takeaways

  • High-converting SaaS website design is pattern-driven: clarity in the hero, proof everywhere, and zero friction on the path to signup.
  • Your headline should say what the product does - cleverness is the most expensive vice in SaaS copy.
  • Show the product early: real UI beats abstract illustrations for anything self-serve.
  • Pricing transparency is a conversion feature, not a leak of competitive intel.
  • Speed and mobile behaviour quietly cap everything else; a beautiful slow site still loses.

Why SaaS website design converges on the same patterns

SaaS buyers see dozens of product sites a month, and buyers have been trained by the best of them. When your site follows the patterns buyers already know, cognitive load drops and evaluation speeds up; when the site fights those patterns, visitors leave rather than adapt. That is why the sites of high-converting products look related without looking identical. I laid out the section-by-section anatomy in my guide to SaaS landing page structure - this article zooms into the ten design decisions inside that structure that do the actual converting.

Clarity converts before beauty does. A visitor who understands you in five seconds forgives almost everything else.

The ten patterns

1. A headline that states the job, not the vibe

“Payroll for remote teams in 40 countries” beats “Work, reimagined”. The strongest SaaS heroes name the user, the job and the outcome in under a dozen words, then let a subline add nuance.

2. Real product UI above the fold

Self-serve buyers want to see the thing. A crisp screenshot or short looping product clip in the hero consistently outperforms abstract 3D shapes - the product shot answers “what am I buying” without a click.

3. One primary action, repeated

Trial or demo - pick the motion that fits your price point and repeat that single button down the page. Competing CTAs (trial AND demo AND contact AND docs) measurably split intent.

4. Logo walls with context

Logos work when they carry a number or a sentence: “Trusted by 2,400 engineering teams” above the wall converts; a silent logo strip is wallpaper. If you cannot name customers yet, use outcome statements instead.

5. Feature sections that lead with the outcome

Each feature block should open with what the user gets, then show how. Screenshot right, outcome-first heading left, three lines of copy maximum - the pattern survives because people skim.

6. Social proof next to every decision point

Testimonials pull hardest when placed beside the pricing table and the signup button, not corralled on a separate page. One specific quote with a name, face and company beats five anonymous ones.

7. Transparent, three-tier pricing

Hiding pricing behind “talk to sales” filters out the self-serve majority. Three tiers with a highlighted middle, a monthly/annual toggle and a plain-language feature list is the shape I recommend for most self-serve products.

8. An objections section disguised as FAQ

Security, data ownership, migration effort, cancellation - answer the deal-killers on the page where the decision happens. Every unanswered objection is a tab opened on a competitor.

9. Motion with a purpose

Scroll-triggered reveals and micro-interactions should direct attention to the product, not compete with the product. Animation is seasoning: the sites that feel premium use restraint, and the fastest way to feel cheap is animating everything.

10. Ruthless performance

Sub-two-second loads, stable layout, instant interaction. SaaS visitors extrapolate: a janky marketing site quietly suggests a janky product. Performance is a brand statement before performance is an SEO metric.

How to apply this without a redesign

You rarely need to rebuild from zero. Run this audit order on your current site:

  1. Rewrite the hero headline until a stranger can repeat back what you sell.
  2. Replace abstract hero art with real product UI.
  3. Collapse competing CTAs into one primary action.
  4. Move your best testimonial next to pricing.
  5. Add the objections FAQ to the pricing page.
  6. Measure load speed on a mid-range phone and fix the worst offender.

If you are starting fresh instead, my free Verius SaaS template ships with these patterns built in - outcome-first feature sections, three-tier pricing with a toggle, and trust blocks ready to fill.

Prefer video? This walkthrough of what every SaaS landing page needs covers the essentials well:

Budget and build notes

None of these patterns requires an enterprise budget - most are copy and layout decisions, not engineering. I have broken down what a full build actually costs in how much a SaaS website costs to build, and if your current site is trapped on a platform that fights you, my guide to migrating to Framer without losing SEO covers the safe path out.

Want a SaaS site that converts like the good ones?

Pavlo Zhydkykh designs and builds fast, conversion-first SaaS websites on Framer - the ten patterns above, tuned to your product and shipped with clean Core Web Vitals. If your signup graph is flatter than your product deserves, get in touch.

FAQ

What makes a SaaS website design convert?

Clarity first: a headline that states the job, real product UI early, one repeated call to action and proof beside every decision point. Design polish matters, but it multiplies clarity rather than replacing it. If visitors cannot explain what you sell after five seconds, nothing else on the page gets a chance.

Should a SaaS website show pricing?

For self-serve and mid-market products, yes - transparent three-tier pricing converts better and pre-qualifies signups. Keeping prices hidden mainly helps true enterprise sales motions with six-figure contracts. If you gate pricing, expect fewer but warmer conversations, and be honest that that is the trade.

Is a free trial or a demo the better call to action?

It follows your price and complexity: a lower-priced product with quick setup suits a free trial; a complex or high-touch product usually needs a demo. The mistake is offering both with equal weight - pick a primary motion and make the other a quiet secondary link.

How much animation is too much on a SaaS site?

If motion ever makes a visitor wait or distracts from the product UI, it is too much. Purposeful scroll reveals and hover micro-interactions add perceived quality; animating every section erodes it and hurts performance. Restraint reads as confidence.

How long should a SaaS homepage be?

Long enough to answer the evaluation questions - what it does, who uses it, proof, pricing, objections - and no longer. For most products that is six to nine sections. Depth belongs on feature and docs pages; the homepage’s job is confident orientation, not exhaustive reference.

title: Why Classic Minesweeper Fails on 50/50 Endgames — And How Subset-Deduction Proofs Fix It
description:
Why Classic Minesweeper Fails on 50/50 Endgames — And How Subset-Deduction Proofs Guarantee Solvable Boards

Every longtime Minesweeper player knows the exact moment a great run dies to bad math. You clear 95% of the board through crisp logical deduction, only to arrive at two remaining covered tiles tucked against a corner. Every adjacent clue reads 1, the mine counter reads 1, and both permutations satisfy every constraint on the board. Your skill no longer matters—the game has collapsed into a coin flip.

Standard Minesweeper implementations almost always include "first-click safety" (relocating mines away from your opening click), yet they stop there. Random mine placement guarantees nothing about downstream solvability. On Fogboard's No Guess Minesweeper, every 7x7 to 9x9 board passes an end-to-end subset-deduction proof before gameplay begins, mathematically eliminating 50/50 endgames.

The Linear Algebra Behind the 50/50 Trap

To understand why classic Minesweeper breaks, model the frontier between revealed numbers and covered tiles as a system of binary constraint equations. Let each covered frontier tile carry a variable xi∈{0,1}x_i \in {0, 1}xi​∈{0,1}, where 111 denotes a mine and 000 denotes a safe cell.

Every revealed numbered cell uuu with mum_umu​ unflagged mines remaining among its covered neighbors N(u)N(u)N(u) yields one equation:

∑i∈N(u)xi=mu\sum_{i \in N(u)} x_i = m_ui∈N(u)∑​xi​=mu​Now consider the classic two-tile border trap. Two adjacent revealed clues uuu and vvv both border the exact same pair of covered cells {a,b}{a, b}{a,b}, with no other covered neighbors:

xa+xb=1x_a + x_b = 1xa​+xb​=1Because both clues generate identical rows in the constraint matrix and neither tile touches any outside clue, the system is locally rank-deficient. Both (xa=1,xb=0)(x_a = 1, x_b = 0)(xa​=1,xb​=0) and (xa=0,xb=1)(x_a = 0, x_b = 1)(xa​=0,xb​=1) satisfy every local clue and the global mine count. No deductive algorithm—human or machine—can separate the two states.

How End-to-End Subset-Deduction Proofs Work

Avoiding 50/50 traps requires verifying that a deterministic solver can clear the entire board from the opening click to the final safe tile without guessing once. As documented on Fogboard's open solver verification page, the verifier loops over two layers of human-accessible constraint propagation:

  • Single-Cell Trivial Deduction: For every frontier clue (A,mA)(A, m_A)(A,mA​), if mA=0m_A = 0mA​=0, every tile in AAA is proven safe. If mA=∣A∣m_A = \vert{}A\vert{}mA​=∣A∣, every tile in AAA is proven to be a mine.

  • Pairwise Subset Deduction (Set Difference): Whenever two frontier constraints (A,mA)(A, m_A)(A,mA​) and (B,mB)(B, m_B)(B,mB​) satisfy A⊂BA \subset BA⊂B (every covered neighbor of AAA is also a covered neighbor of BBB), subtracting the equations yields a strict difference constraint on D=B∖AD = B \setminus AD=B∖A with remaining mine count mD=mB−mAm_D = m_B - m_AmD​=mB​−mA​:

  • If mD=0m_D = 0mD​=0, every tile in DDD is guaranteed safe.

  • If mD=∣D∣m_D = \vert{}D\vert{}mD​=∣D∣, every tile in DDD is guaranteed to be a mine.

In TypeScript, the subset-reduction step runs cleanly over bit-packed or index-sorted neighbor sets inside a fixed-point loop:

TypeScript

interface Constraint {
  cells: number[]; // sorted covered neighbor indices
  mines: number;   // remaining unflagged mines
}

function isStrictSubset(a: number[], b: number[]): boolean {
  if (a.length >= b.length) return false;
  let i = 0;
  let j = 0;
  while (i < a.length && j < b.length) {
    if (a[i] === b[j]) {
      i++;
      j++;
    } else if (a[i] > b[j]) {
      j++;
    } else {
      return false;
    }
  }
  return i === a.length;
}

function deduceSubsetMoves(constraints: Constraint[]) {
  const safe = new Set<number>();
  const mines = new Set<number>();

  for (const a of constraints) {
    for (const b of constraints) {
      if (!isStrictSubset(a.cells, b.cells)) continue;
      const diff = b.cells.filter((cell) => !a.cells.includes(cell));
      const diffMines = b.mines - a.mines;

      if (diffMines === 0) diff.forEach((c) => safe.add(c));
      if (diffMines === diff.length) diff.forEach((c) => mines.add(c));
    }
  }
  return { safe, mines };
}

During generation, the engine places mines deterministically using FNV-1a + Mulberry32 seeding (synchronized daily at 00:00 UTC across the 30-day archive), opens the starting safe zone, and runs this fixed-point loop until either every safe tile is revealed or the solver stalls. If the solver stalls with even one ambiguous tile remaining, the candidate board is discarded and regenerated until a 100% end-to-end proof succeeds.

Pure Deduction vs. Probabilistic Search Across Logic Games

Not every deduction game relies on the same mathematical foundation. Comparing three games across Fogboard's catalog illustrates how solver design adapts to information structure:

Game Grid / State Space Core Reasoning Model Role of Probability
No Guess Minesweeper 7x7 to 9x9 grids End-to-end subset-deduction proof Zero (50/50 guesses eliminated)
Mastermind 4–5 numbered pegs Information-theoretic set narrowing Minimal (deterministic clue elimination)
Battleship Online Classic / Quick / Salvo fleets Probability radar AI over legal placements Central (hidden state cannot be solved on turn 1)

In Mastermind, each feedback pair (exact position matches and color-only matches across 4–5 numbered, color-blind-friendly pegs) partitions the remaining code space deterministically, rewarding guesses that minimize the worst-case remaining bucket. By contrast, Battleship Online begins with zero public constraints. Rather than firing randomly, Fogboard's probability radar AI enumerates every legal horizontal and vertical placement of remaining unsunk ships across Classic, Quick, and Salvo modes, sums overlap frequencies per cell, and targets the highest-density coordinate until a hit triggers localized hunt logic.

Honest Engineering Trade-Offs

Guaranteeing zero-guess boards purely in client-side JavaScript introduces deliberate design boundaries:

  • Board size ceiling: Rejection-sampling full end-to-end subset proofs stays snappy in browser tabs at 7x7 to 9x9 dimensions. Scaling the same unmutated proof loop to giant 30x16 Expert grids increases rejection rates exponentially unless the generator dynamically mutates hidden mines mid-game.
  • Proof ceiling versus advanced counting: Restricting verification to single-cell and pairwise subset rules ensures every board is genuinely readable by human players without brute-force global tank-solver arithmetic, though veteran players hunting exotic mine-count edge cases will find the logic cleaner and more direct.
  • Local-only storage: In keeping with Fogboard's zero-login, zero-paywall architecture, solve histories and 30-day archive completions live strictly in local browser storage with no cross-device cloud sync.

If you have ever closed a Minesweeper tab in disgust after losing a clean board to a final corner coin flip, playing a mathematically verified grid changes how the game feels. You can test the subset-deduction engine firsthand on No Guess Minesweeper and review the underlying solver verification notes on How Solvers Work.

title: HTML Color Code Picker: HEX, RGB, HSL and CMYK Explained (Plus a Free Tool to Pick Them)
description:
Color shapes how a website feels before anyone reads a word. Behind every shade on screen sits a code that tells the browser exactly what to display. Get that code wrong by a few digits and your brand blue turns into "almost the brand blue," which is how designers and developers end up arguing about which blue was meant.

This guide covers the color formats you'll actually use in HTML and CSS, when to pick each one, and how to build a palette that is readable and accessible. At the end, I'll share a free browser tool I use to pick, convert and save colors.

The same color in every format

Here is one color, a popular blue, written five ways:

Format Value
HEX #3B82F6
RGB rgb(59, 130, 246)
HSL hsl(217, 91%, 60%)
HSV 217°, 76%, 96%
CMYK 76, 47, 0, 4

They all describe the same color. The difference is which one is easiest to work with for a given job.

HTML color code formats explained

HEX

HEX is the most common format on the web: a hash sign followed by six characters, like #FF5733. Every browser understands it, it's short, and it's easy to copy. It's ideal for solid colors.

.button {
  background-color: #3B82F6;
}

RGB and RGBA

RGB describes a color as a mix of red, green and blue light. RGBA adds an opacity value, which makes it useful for overlays, shadows and translucent panels.

.overlay {
  background-color: rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5);
}

HSL and HSLA

HSL describes color the way people think about it: which hue, how vivid, and how light or dark. That makes it the easiest format for building lighter and darker versions of one color. Change only the lightness value and you get hover states and borders that still feel related.

.button {
  background-color: hsl(217, 91%, 60%);
}
.button:hover {
  background-color: hsl(217, 91%, 50%);
}

HSV

HSV swaps lightness for brightness. Many design apps build their picker squares on it, which is why dragging across a color area feels natural.

CMYK (for print)

CMYK is the ink-based model used by printers. Browsers don't read it, so treat a CMYK value as a helpful estimate when you move a screen color into a print project.

Modern CSS color formats

Newer CSS adds OKLCH, Display P3 and the color-mix() function. These produce more even color scales and richer shades on wide-gamut screens. You can start with HEX and explore them later.

Which format should you use?

  • HEX for everyday solid colors
  • RGBA when you need transparency
  • HSL when you're building shades for buttons, borders and hover states
  • CMYK for print work only

Where HTML color codes get used

Backgrounds, text and borders. Page sections use background-color, text uses color, and frames use border-color. Always set text and background together so the result doesn't depend on a visitor's browser defaults.

Link colors. Links have four states: normal, visited, hover and active. Style them in that order (the old "LVHA" rule), or later rules will override earlier ones and your hover color may never appear.

Named colors and web-safe colors. CSS includes 148 named colors, from aliceblue to yellowgreen, plus rebeccapurple, added in tribute to a designer's daughter. Names are readable but cover a limited range. Web-safe colors, a small palette built for old 256-color monitors, no longer matter on modern screens.

Color harmonies and palette basics

Harmonies are color combinations based on positions on the color wheel:

  • Complementary: two opposite colors for strong contrast
  • Analogous: neighbors on the wheel for a calm, related look
  • Triadic: three evenly spaced colors for lively balance
  • Tetradic: four colors in two opposing pairs for rich variety
  • Split-complementary: a base color plus the two beside its opposite, with softer contrast
  • Monochrome: one hue in several lightness levels

A simple website palette needs a primary color, a dark text color, a light background and one accent. The 60-30-10 rule helps: use a dominant color for about 60% of the page, a secondary color for 30%, and the accent for 10%.

Don't skip contrast and accessibility

Readable text is not optional. The WCAG 2.2 contrast requirements set minimum ratios between text and its background, starting at 4.5:1 for normal text. Light text on a bright color is the most common failure.

Also, don't rely on color alone to carry meaning. Some people have color vision deficiency, so pair status colors (red/green) with icons or labels. Test your palette on a real page and on a phone in daylight, where weak contrast shows up fastest.

3 color mistakes to avoid

  1. Using too many colors. Three or four, reused consistently, look more professional than seven.
  2. Sampling from screenshots. Compression can shift colors slightly, so pick from the original file when possible.
  3. Skipping the live preview. A shade that looks fine in a picker can vanish against a real background.

A free tool to pick, convert and save colors

When I need a color code fast, I use the ToolNexus HTML Color Code Picker. It runs in the browser with no signup, and everything is organized into four tabs: Color Picker, Pick From Image, Color Names and Saved Colors.

What it does:

  • Interactive color picker: drag across the color area, move the hue slider, and the HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV and CMYK values update live. It works with both mouse and touch.
  • One-click copying: click any format card to copy that value in CSS-ready form, or use the Copy Color Code button for the main HEX.
  • Quick colors and random: popular starting swatches, plus a Random button when you need inspiration.
  • Built-in color harmonies: complementary, analogous, triadic, tetradic, split-complementary and monochrome schemes generated from your color. You can copy a whole scheme as a list of HEX codes in one click.
  • Shades and tints: rows of darker and lighter versions of your color, with the HEX code on hover. Handy for hover states, borders and soft backgrounds.
  • Pick from image: upload or drag and drop a JPG, PNG, WEBP or GIF, then click any pixel. A magnifier loupe shows the exact HEX under your cursor, and your picks collect in a history strip. The image is processed in your browser, so it isn't uploaded.
  • Searchable color names: search names like crimson or teal and see their codes right away.
  • Saved colors: save colors you like and come back to them later. They stay in your browser, with a counter and a Clear All button. (They don't sync between devices, and clearing browser data removes them.)
  • Download a swatch: export your selected color as a PNG labeled with its HEX code, which is a quick way to share a color with a client or teammate.

How to use it

  1. Choose a color with the color area and hue slider, or load an image and click a pixel.
  2. Check the live preview and fine-tune with shades, tints or a harmony.
  3. Click the format you need to copy it.
  4. Paste the code into your CSS, HTML or design file, and save it for later.

👉 Try it here: toolnexus.org/tools/html-color-code-picker

More free tools for web developers and designers

Once your colors are chosen, these other ToolNexus utilities help you put them to work. They also run in your browser with no signup:

  • CSS Minifier: compress your stylesheet, color codes included, for faster page loads
  • JavaScript Minifier: shrink or beautify scripts that set colors dynamically
  • SVG to PNG Converter: turn colored vector graphics into PNG files
  • Free Online Photo Editor: crop and adjust an image before picking colors from it
  • JSON Validator and Formatter: check design-token files that store your palette

Quick FAQ

Is the color picker free?
Yes. You can pick colors and copy codes as often as you like with no account.

Are my images uploaded when I pick a color from a photo?
No. The image is processed inside your browser, so it never leaves your device.

How do I get a color from a website?
Take a screenshot and load it in the Pick From Image tab, then click the color you want. You can also right-click an element, choose Inspect, and read its color value in the Styles panel.

What's the difference between a shade and a tint?
A shade is a color mixed with black, so it looks darker. A tint is a color mixed with white, so it looks lighter.

Over to you 💬

Which format do you reach for most in your projects: HEX, HSL, or the newer OKLCH? And do you keep your palette in CSS variables or design tokens? Share your setup in the comments!`
