title: IndraMQTT vs EMQX: 3.18 QoS 1 throughput in our test
description:
On November 14, we put IndraMQTT against EMQX Enterprise 6.3.0 on four cores. In our MQTT 5 point-to-point QoS 1 test, IndraMQTT delivered 79,353 messages per second; EMQX delivered 24,947. Both runs recorded zero message loss. That's a 3.18× gap in delivered rate.

We ran this benchmark ourselves. I want you to challenge it.

We've released IndraMQTT Beta 2026.11, a Rust MQTT broker for single-node evaluation. I want MQTT developers to run their own workloads, push it hard, and tell me where it wins and where it breaks.

Where we beat EMQX in this test

The point-to-point QoS 1 setup paired each publisher with one subscriber on its own topic. We used 256-byte payloads over plaintext loopback. Each broker got four pinned CPUs and an 8 GiB memory limit. We tested one broker at a time, in a fresh container for each step. EMQX Enterprise 6.3.0 used its default configuration; IndraMQTT used its native Rust MQTT listener.

These are each broker's highest passing 180-second confirmation runs. Passing meant complete delivery plus limits on publishing time, interval-average latency, memory growth, and drain time. The next QoS 1 step did not pass for either broker.

The other passing workload results point in the same direction:

MQTT 5 workload IndraMQTT delivered/s EMQX Enterprise 6.3.0 delivered/s
Point-to-point, QoS 0 184,829 79,692
Point-to-point, QoS 1 79,353 24,947
Fan-in, QoS 0 49,648 19,946
Fan-out, QoS 0 99,442 79,748

Fan-out counts deliveries to subscribers, and the two fan-out runs used different subscriber counts. QoS 0 turned into a staring contest between the broker and our load generator. The generator blinked; the broker was near full CPU too. The 184,829 deliveries/s are real, but the broker's actual ceiling is still an open question.

The memory result also got my attention

Both brokers connected all 10,000 idle clients. After 30 seconds, docker stats reported 186.3 MiB for IndraMQTT and 842.3 MiB for EMQX Enterprise 6.3.0. In this setup, ours used about 22% of EMQX's broker-container memory. That is a total-memory observation for this workload, not a universal per-client cost.

What the chart cannot tell you

I want this comparison to survive scrutiny, so here are the boundaries:

  • The beta image is a later build. The measured IndraMQTT binary came from commit 2342a432. The public beta uses a later release tree and a different build configuration. The numbers above are not a performance measurement of the beta image.
  • The rival confirmation steps ran once each. We do not have error bars. IndraMQTT ran first and EMQX second in each scenario, so run-order effects remain possible.
  • EMQX was untuned. Its default configuration may not be its best configuration. If you have a tuned EMQX setup, I would particularly like to see your numbers.
  • The test was narrow. It used plaintext loopback on one host, one 256-byte payload size, no TLS, no connection churn, and no persistence or clustering comparison. The latency values were interval averages, not p99. At the passing QoS 1 loads, EMQX's reported interval-average latency was lower than ours (5 ms versus 12 ms); those loads were different, so that is not a matched-load latency comparison.

Our public benchmark write-up gives the test conditions and result tables. The full raw logs and harness for this November run are not published there, so treat this as a founder-reported comparison until you reproduce it.

Try the beta on your workload

The image is pinned to indusstack/indramqtt:2026.11.0-beta.1. With Docker Compose v2, start the single-node example locally:

git clone https://github.com/Indus-Stack/indramqtt.git
cd indramqtt
git checkout v2026.11.0-beta.1
docker pull indusstack/indramqtt:2026.11.0-beta.1
docker compose up -d --no-build --wait
curl -fsS http://localhost:18083/healthz

The health check should print OK. If you have Mosquitto CLI tools, keep a subscriber running in one terminal:

mosquitto_sub -h localhost -p 1883 -t 'test/hello' -C 1

Then publish from another terminal:

mosquitto_pub -h localhost -p 1883 -t 'test/hello' -m 'hello from beta'

The subscriber should print hello from beta. The release notes and Compose guide cover admin login and further tests. The example permits anonymous MQTT clients and exposes the management port, so keep it on a trusted network and rotate the default admin password before broader testing.

I'd love early testers to try MQTT 5 QoS 1 with their real payload sizes, long-lived and reconnecting clients, retained messages, SQL rules, TLS, and WebSocket clients. Please tell us where IndraMQTT is slower, where it breaks, and where EMQX performs better after tuning. Include the image tag, hardware, configuration, client tool, send rate, delivered rate, and a short reproduction in a GitHub issue.

This is a single-node beta. Clustering is disabled; client sockets close on restart, and retained durable sessions resume only when clients reconnect. APIs and data formats may change before 1.0, and some operations still expose legacy licence checks. Use it for evaluation, keep backups of test data, and read the current limits.

If the EMQX gap survives your test, tell me. If it doesn't, I want that issue even more.

title: Custom Domain Exit in Go: Delete Tenant Records Within the Approved Zone
description:
A customer support console can retire a sending domain without owning the DNS zone that contains it. That ownership boundary determines the deletion scope before any API call. TL;DR: remove the sending-domain registration first, delete only records identified by the tenant's zone identifier and exact record name, and delete the zone only when your inventory proves it was created exclusively for that tenant.

Keep the evidence.

Consider a bounded production review scenario: a support administrator requests removal of help.customer.example, while another tenant still depends on records in the same platform-owned zone. This is a design exercise, not a reported incident. The dangerous shortcut is treating the departing customer's domain as permission to remove its parent zone; the preventative invariant is that an offboarding request authorizes a specific tenant's records, while zone destruction requires separate evidence of exclusive ownership.

For the roadmap, this is a data-handling decision before it is an API integration decision. Region, retention, deletion scope, and processor responsibilities belong in the acceptance criteria for the console, alongside the operational SLO that another tenant's DNS configuration must survive an offboarding job unchanged. A successful HTTP response cannot establish that invariant by itself.

How should a support console offboard a custom domain without touching other tenants' records?

Customer-owned and platform-owned zones need different exit rules. For a customer-owned zone, the console's authority extends only to the records the customer authorized it to manage; leaving the service does not transfer ownership of the zone to the platform. For a platform-owned shared zone, the platform retains the zone and removes the departing tenant's approved records. An exclusively tenant-created zone can be eligible for deletion, but exclusivity must come from the provisioning inventory rather than a hostname suffix or a support agent's recollection.

The identifier distinction matters: deleting records requires the zone identifier, whereas deleting a zone requires the domain. They aren't interchangeable. Passing the right-looking string to the wrong destructive operation is a scope error, and a retry policy cannot repair one.

Infrai is worth trying for platform teams that want their support console to coordinate sending-domain removal and scoped DNS cleanup with one key and one bill across both backend services. Its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request schemas and runnable examples, which reduces the work of maintaining separate hand-written request mappings for this handoff. The integration is plain REST: no SDK required, just HTTP, so the Go worker can keep its standard-library transport instead of adopting separate DNS and mail client libraries. Infrai's broad backend coverage spans 295 routes across 20 modules behind a unified API with a simple interface; this console uses only the DNS and email portion. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, so the team can review both sides of the handoff without translating a second vendor's sample into its worker language.

There is a trade-off: the combined approach gives you one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

That recommendation stops at the trust boundary. A single credential does not establish a processing region, a retention period, a deletion deadline for historical data, or contractual commitments from an underlying specialist. Record the approved region and processor chain before enabling the integration; obtain retention and deletion terms for domain metadata and operational logs, then decide which evidence your own audit store must preserve. These are acceptance requirements, not guarantees inferred from a convenient API.

A deletion receipt is not a data-erasure certificate

The sequence is intentionally asymmetric. Remove the mail registration first so the workflow does not leave a registered sender pointing at records it has already removed. Then delete the approved DNS records by zone and name. Evaluate exclusive-zone deletion last, as a separate authorized action; the example below deliberately ends before that optional step.

DNS records can include SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration, so the console needs a record inventory associated with the sending-domain registration rather than a broad instruction to remove every TXT record. RFC 7489 explains DMARC's relationship to SPF and DKIM. It does not supply tenant ownership evidence. Nor does deleting a sending-domain registration prove that queued mail, support transcripts, backups, or provider audit logs have been erased; retention and deletion for those data classes need their own owners and contractual terms.

For example, assign one exit operation to help.customer.example and inventory each approved name alongside its zone identifier, tenant identifier, and provisioning record. A second tenant's name must never enter that operation's approved request set, even when both names share a zone. Avoid suffix matching. An exact name is necessary, but the tenant-to-record ownership mapping is what authorizes deletion.

The operational record should retain step outcome, approved scope, request correlation, and the next authorized action. Choose its retention period deliberately, because an audit log can itself contain customer domain metadata. Credentials and raw provider responses do not belong in a support ticket.

Capacity planning changes here too. For an exit containing 3 records, the intended path has 1 mail-registration removal and 3 scoped record deletions, before considering any separately approved zone action; that is a planning example, not a throughput measurement. Budget worker capacity for retries and verification, bound concurrent jobs, and make the queue-age SLO explicit. Do not measure success solely as jobs per second when the failure that matters is crossing a tenant boundary.

Buy or build the ownership boundary

The useful comparison is who performs the mapping and who holds the authority. The following table is a buy-versus-build assessment for this console, not a claim that any vendor contract automatically meets a residency requirement.

Stack What the team buys What the console still owns
Infrai across DNS and email One key and bill; public discovery schemas for the two capabilities Tenant ownership inventory, deletion approvals, and verification of region, retention, and processor terms
Amazon Route 53 with Amazon SES Direct DNS and mail service integrations within the AWS ecosystem Service-specific permissions and request mappings, plus the workflow connecting sender removal to record cleanup
Cloudflare DNS with Resend Separate specialist DNS and email integrations Provider-specific credentials, the domain-to-zone mapping, and a durable handoff between the two services
Build the orchestrator around the customer's existing providers Control over the console's approval and execution policy Adapter maintenance, checkpoints, audit retention, and the on-call burden of partial progress

Route 53 plus SES involves 2 service integrations within an AWS account; it does not inherently require 2 company signups or 2 unrelated root credentials. Permission scopes still need deliberate separation. Cloudflare plus Resend involves 2 provider account relationships and 2 provider credential sets, plus glue that carries the approved sender identity into the DNS cleanup request. Both approaches can be sensible. Counting dashboards alone is a weak architecture review.

Choose direct specialist integrations when the customer already requires a specific DNS provider, when existing service-specific permissions fit the operating model, or when the contractual processor boundary is decisive. A unified API remains useful when consolidating credentials and integration discovery matters enough to justify the additional intermediary. It does not replace the specialist's responsibility for its processing environment, record execution, and agreed retention behavior, or your team's responsibility for deciding which records belong to the tenant.

The expensive build decision is usually the ownership ledger. Every option needs one.

Make the handoff explicit in Go

The preventative path below is a small execution core for an already approved exit plan. It removes one sending-domain registration, takes the successful removal receipt into the DNS step, and deletes one approved record using the same key and base URL. It performs no zone deletion.

The example accepts the DNS request's query string and optional JSON body as operator-supplied input because their binding must come from the current discovery schema. It deliberately invents no provider parameter names. Before execution, review that encoded request against the schema and confirm its zone identifier and exact name match the ownership ledger; this runner does not implement schema validation or your approval system. For multiple records, the production worker applies this handoff to the approved inventory and checkpoints each result.

Save the code as main.go and run it with go run main.go. Supply INFRAI_API_KEY, EXIT_DOMAIN, EXIT_OPERATION_ID, and DNS_DELETE_QUERY and/or DNS_DELETE_BODY from that reviewed request. The operation identifier must remain stable across retries. Empty DNS input is rejected before mail removal.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type mailReceipt struct {
    domain string
}

func pause(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if n, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && n >= 0 {
        if candidate := time.Duration(n) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func remove(client *http.Client, key, operation, target string, body []byte) error {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(operation + "\n" + target + "\n" + string(body)))
    id := fmt.Sprintf("%x", sum)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodDelete, target, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        if len(body) > 0 {
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 65536))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(pause(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func retireMail(client *http.Client, key, operation, domain string) (mailReceipt, error) {
    target := base + "/email/domain/delete/" + url.PathEscape(domain)
    if err := remove(client, key, operation, target, nil); err != nil {
        return mailReceipt{}, err
    }
    return mailReceipt{domain: domain}, nil
}

func retireRecord(client *http.Client, key, operation, domain string,
    receipt mailReceipt, query string, body []byte) error {
    if receipt.domain != domain || domain == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("matching mail removal receipt required")
    }
    target := base + "/dns/record/delete"
    if query != "" {
        target += "?" + query
    }
    return remove(client, key, operation, target, body)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    domain := os.Getenv("EXIT_DOMAIN")
    operation := os.Getenv("EXIT_OPERATION_ID")
    query := strings.TrimPrefix(os.Getenv("DNS_DELETE_QUERY"), "?")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("DNS_DELETE_BODY"))
    if key == "" || domain == "" || operation == "" ||
        (query == "" && len(body) == 0) {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "key, domain, operation and approved DNS request required")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if _, err := url.ParseQuery(query); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 30 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    receipt, err := retireMail(client, key, operation, domain)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "mail removal:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("mail registration removal acknowledged")
    if err := retireRecord(client, key, operation, domain, receipt, query, body); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "record removal:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("approved record removal acknowledged")
}

The receipt is local control-flow evidence: a successful mail step is required before this process calls the DNS step. It is not a provider response field, a distributed transaction, or proof that the record request is tenant-scoped. Those distinctions are deliberate. The approved request and durable ownership inventory supply the scope; the runner supplies order, bounded retry attempts, explicit methods, status checks, and error propagation.

Do not turn error output into broadly accessible logs. The caller should route provider error details to a restricted diagnostic destination, while the support console receives an operation identifier and a bounded status.

Infrai specifies a platform idempotency convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, but each capability's discovery metadata still needs checking before relying on retries. A stable key is useful; it does not authorize an operation and cannot replace durable progress after that window. Persist the mail-removal checkpoint before advancing in a production worker. On restart, reconcile the existing state and resume the approved remaining records rather than assuming that every absence response means success.

Where the exit should stop

Stop before zone deletion whenever ownership evidence is missing, the zone is shared, or the customer owns it. Stop before the initial mail removal if the DNS cleanup request has not been approved. For an exclusively tenant-created zone, authorize its deletion separately using the domain, after confirming that the remaining inventory does not belong to anyone else.

This advice also stops at retention obligations. Removing DNS and mail configuration does not finish a customer's data-erasure request, and neither an API gateway nor a DNS specialist can decide your support transcript retention policy for you. The exit record should identify who must delete each data class, the approved region and processor boundary, and what evidence closes the request. If those terms require a direct provider relationship, use that relationship.

The useful SLO is a scoped, auditable exit that preserves other tenants' records. Fast cleanup is secondary.

Sources

References for the protocol, the comparison, and the implementation boundary:

  • DMARC, SPF, and DKIM relationships
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES domain identity documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Resend domain documentation

If this ownership boundary fits your console, start with the discovery schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Frontend resume keywords belong in your bullets, not a tag cloud
description:
Most frontend resumes try to win the keyword game by dumping a giant stack list into the skills section. That looks tidy. It also quietly kills you.

The claim: keywords need context, not just a skills blob

A typical frontend posting can list 15+ specific technologies. JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js, Redux, Tailwind, Jest, Cypress, Vite, Storybook, Figma, GitHub Actions, Vercel, Datadog. Easily that many.

If your resume response to that is a single skills block like:

Skills: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js, Redux, Tailwind, Jest, Cypress, Vite, Storybook, Figma, GitHub Actions, Vercel, Datadog

you probably think you're covered. The ATS will see the words, the human will scan the section, everybody's happy.

The argument I agree with is different: those keywords should show up inside achievement bullets, not just sit in the skills list. React, TypeScript, Next.js, Redux, Vite, Storybook, Jest, Cypress all anchored to what you built and what changed.

Some people push back on that. They worry the bullets will get long, or that repeating tech names is noisy. They assume a clean skills section is enough for both ATS and humans.

I don't buy it.

What most people do and why it fails

Here's the usual pattern I see on frontend resumes:

  • A short, vague summary
  • A dense skills section with every tech in a single list
  • Experience bullets that talk about "features" and "pages" with no numbers and no stack

The skills section looks like this:

Skills: JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, React, Next.js, Redux, Tailwind CSS, Jest, Cypress, Webpack, Figma, Git, CI/CD

Then the job bullets say things like:

Built customer-facing pages and improved performance.

This fails in two ways.

First, ATS scoring. The system is not just counting words. It cares where they show up and how close they sit to other relevant terms. A bullet about "React" that also talks about "performance optimization" or "Core Web Vitals" and "LCP" is a stronger signal than a lonely "React" up in the skills section.

Second, a human reader. If I'm scanning your resume and all the tech is in one block at the top, I have to trust that you actually used those tools in real work and didn't just list whatever's hot. If your bullets say what you built with React and TypeScript and how many accounts or visitors it affected, I don't have to guess.

Here's the difference in one line:

Version Line
Skills-only keywords Skills: React, TypeScript, Next.js, Redux
Keywords in context Built a React + TypeScript dashboard serving 800+ accounts

Same words, very different signal.

What to do instead: wire tech into impact

You don't need to rewrite your whole resume. You need to move the important words into the places that carry weight.

One line in the summary, one skills line, one bullet. That's enough to change the feel of the whole document.

Fix the headline / summary

What people usually write:

Frontend developer experienced in modern JavaScript frameworks.

Nothing specific. No tech, no scope.

A better version that puts keywords in context:

Frontend engineer with 4 years of experience building production React and Next.js applications.

Same length. Now the stack is real and connected to "production applications", which is what you're actually being hired to build.

Fix one skills line

The default:

Skills: JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, SQL

This is just a bucket.

Swap it to a structured line that still hits the keywords:

Languages: JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, SQL

It's a small change, but it matches how frontend stacks are usually grouped. Languages together, frameworks somewhere else, testing tools as a separate cluster. That makes it easier for a human to see your stack at a glance, and the ATS still gets every word.

More important than the label is what happens in the bullets.

Fix one experience bullet

Typical "tech-free" bullet:

Built an analytics dashboard and reduced support tickets.

This sounds OK on the surface. It doesn't say how big, what tools, or how much.

A keyword-anchored version:

Built a React + TypeScript analytics dashboard with real-time WebSocket updates, serving 800+ enterprise accounts and reducing customer support tickets by 35%.

Now React and TypeScript live next to "real-time WebSocket updates" and "800+ enterprise accounts" and "35%". It reads like actual work, not a buzzword list.

You can do the same thing with performance work:

Instead of:

Improved page load times.

Write:

Implemented server-side rendering with Next.js for the marketing site, improving Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) from 3.8s to 1.2s and increasing organic traffic by 28%.

Same story. Next.js and LCP are not floating in the skills section. They are attached to numbers and a business effect.

You don't need numbers for everything, but you do need tech in the right place

Not every line will come with a perfect metric. The data can be thin, or you may not track everything.

You can still tie the stack to something concrete: "virtualized lists handling 50K+ SKUs", "design system components adopted by 3 product teams", "tests catching 8 critical bugs pre-production". Numbers plus React, Next.js, Redux, Jest, Cypress, Vite, Storybook. Inside the bullets.

Keep the skills section. It does work. Just stop treating it as the only place the keywords belong.

One sentence in the summary, one structured skills line, and one real bullet with tech plus impact will do more for you than a perfect-looking tag cloud.

The longer version of this is at https://writecv.ai/blog/frontend-developer-resume-example

title: Diseñar una búsqueda de destinos que funcione con teclado y lector de pantalla
description:
Por el equipo de Mapitt, plataforma venezolana de viajes. Este ejemplo es una maqueta educativa: no describe ni demuestra la interfaz real de Mapitt. Fue preparado con asistencia de inteligencia artificial.

Una búsqueda de destinos puede verse clara y aun así dejar fuera a alguien que navega con teclado o usa un lector de pantalla. El problema no se reduce a añadir ARIA: hacen falta etiquetas visibles, controles nativos, mensajes comprensibles y pruebas con personas y tecnologías de asistencia.

1. Empieza por HTML con significado

El siguiente fragmento propone una búsqueda mínima. La etiqueta permanece visible y está asociada al campo. El botón envía el formulario; los resultados se presentarán como enlaces porque llevan a otra página. Los destinos son ficticios y los enlaces de ejemplo deben reemplazarse por rutas reales.

<form id="busqueda" novalidate>
  <label for="destino">Destino en Venezuela</label>
  <p id="ayuda">Escribe una ciudad o un parque.</p>
  <input id="destino" name="destino" type="search"
         aria-describedby="ayuda error-destino">
  <p id="error-destino"></p>
  <button type="submit">Buscar destinos</button>
</form>

<p id="estado" role="status"></p>
<section aria-labelledby="titulo-resultados">
  <h2 id="titulo-resultados">Resultados</h2>
  <ul id="resultados"></ul>
</section>

La W3C explica cómo asociar etiquetas y controles. El texto de ejemplo dentro de un campo no sustituye una etiqueta permanente: desaparece al escribir y no debe ser la única instrucción.

2. Explica el error y anuncia el resultado

Esta versión no llama a un servidor: usa un conjunto ficticio para mostrar el comportamiento. Muestra un error por escrito, marca el campo como inválido y devuelve el foco cuando se envía vacío. La región de estado existe desde el HTML inicial y anuncia un resumen breve; la lista sigue disponible para navegar con teclado.

const form = document.querySelector('#busqueda');
const input = document.querySelector('#destino');
const error = document.querySelector('#error-destino');
const estado = document.querySelector('#estado');
const lista = document.querySelector('#resultados');
const destinos = [
  { nombre: 'Coro', ruta: '/destinos/coro' },
  { nombre: 'Mérida', ruta: '/destinos/merida' }
];

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const consulta = input.value.trim();
  lista.replaceChildren();

  if (!consulta) {
    error.textContent = 'Escribe un destino antes de buscar.';
    input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    estado.textContent = '';
    input.focus();
    return;
  }

  error.textContent = '';
  input.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
  const coincidencias = destinos.filter(({ nombre }) =>
    nombre.toLocaleLowerCase('es').includes(consulta.toLocaleLowerCase('es'))
  );

  for (const destino of coincidencias) {
    const item = document.createElement('li');
    const enlace = document.createElement('a');
    enlace.href = destino.ruta;
    enlace.textContent = destino.nombre;
    item.append(enlace);
    lista.append(item);
  }
  estado.textContent = coincidencias.length === 1
    ? '1 destino encontrado.'
    : coincidencias.length + ' destinos encontrados.';
});

La búsqueda es deliberadamente simple: no elimina acentos, no distingue lugares homónimos y no presenta resultados reales. En producción hay que definir cómo se consultan los datos, evitar respuestas antiguas que sobrescriban búsquedas nuevas y tratar errores de red. No interpretes «0 resultados» como un fallo de conexión.

MDN describe el rol status como una región para avisos que no necesitan interrumpir al usuario. Su comportamiento puede variar entre navegadores y lectores de pantalla: no basta con revisar que el atributo exista.

3. Prueba los estados, no solo la apariencia

  • Sin ratón: llega al campo y al botón con Tab, escribe y envía con Enter. Comprueba que el foco sea visible y siga un orden lógico.
  • Campo vacío: verifica que aparezca una explicación junto al control, que este indique el error y que la persona pueda corregirlo.
  • Cero, uno y varios resultados: revisa el anuncio de estado y que los enlaces reciban nombres claros y foco individual.
  • Cambio de consulta: comprueba que no queden errores ni resultados anteriores mezclados con los nuevos.
  • Lector de pantalla y zoom: prueba combinaciones reales de navegador y tecnología de asistencia, así como pantallas pequeñas y ampliación. Anota lo que se anuncia y cualquier pérdida de contexto.
  • Con participantes: incorpora personas con distintas necesidades en las pruebas. Un chequeo automático ayuda a detectar errores, pero no reemplaza esa experiencia.

Fuentes: etiquetas de formularios de W3C, identificación de errores de W3C y regiones vivas de MDN.

title: React Component Lifecycle & useEffect
description:
Have you ever wondered what happens when a React component is created, updated, or removed from the screen? React components go through different stages during their lifetime. These stages are known as the Component Lifecycle.

In modern React, the useEffect() hook helps us perform tasks such as fetching data, updating the document title, setting timers, and handling event listeners.

What is the Component Lifecycle in React?

The component lifecycle refers to the different stages a component goes through from the moment it appears on the screen until it is removed.

A React component generally goes through three important stages:

  • Mounting – The component is created and displayed on the screen.
  • Updating – The component re-renders when its state or props change.
  • Unmounting – The component is removed from the screen.

1. Mounting Phase

Mounting is the stage when a component is created and displayed for the first time.

For example, when we open a webpage and a React component appears on the screen, the component is in its mounting phase.

We can use useEffect() to run a function only once when the component initially mounts.

import { useEffect } from "react";

function App() {
  useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");
  }, []);

  return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;
}

export default App;

How does this code work?

  • useEffect() is a React hook used to perform side effects.
  • The function inside useEffect() runs after the component renders.
  • The empty dependency array [] tells React to run the effect when the component initially mounts.

2. Updating Phase

The updating phase occurs when a component re-renders because its state or props have changed.

We can use useEffect() to run a function whenever a particular state value changes.

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Count Updated:", count);
  }, [count]);

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Count: {count}</h1>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
        Increase
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

How does this code work?

  • useState(0) creates a state variable called count.
  • setCount() updates the count value.
  • When the count changes, the component re-renders.
  • The useEffect() runs whenever the count value changes.

3. Unmounting Phase

Unmounting is the stage when a component is removed from the screen.

Sometimes, we need to clean up tasks such as timers, event listeners, or subscriptions when a component is removed.

We can use the cleanup function inside useEffect().

import { useEffect } from "react";

function App() {
  useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");

    return () => {
      console.log("Component Unmounted");
    };
  }, []);

  return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;
}

export default App;

How does this code work?

  • The effect runs after the component renders.
  • The cleanup function is returned from the useEffect().
  • The cleanup function runs when the component is removed from the screen.

Understanding the useEffect Dependency Array
The dependency array determines when the effect runs.

Example 1: Without a dependency array

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Runs after every render");
});

This effect runs after every render, including the initial render and subsequent re-renders.

Example 2: With an empty dependency array

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Runs after initial render");
}, []);

This effect runs after the initial render. In development, React Strict Mode may run an additional setup and cleanup cycle.

Example 3: With a dependency

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Runs when count changes");
}, [count]);

This effect runs after the initial render and whenever the count value changes.

Conclusion

Understanding the React component lifecycle helps us know when components are created, updated, and removed from the screen. The useEffect() hook makes it easier to handle side effects in functional components.

By understanding the dependency array and cleanup function, you can use useEffect() more effectively in your React applications.

title: Hackers acessam plano de controle da Cloud One da Força Aérea dos EUA
description:
Invasão interrompe operações na nuvem

Hackers invadiram a Cloud One, principal plataforma de computação em nuvem da Força Aérea dos Estados Unidos. O ataque pode comprometer dados ligados a operações militares, pessoal e logística, mas ainda não se sabe qual foi o alcance do acesso nem se houve roubo de informações.

O caso foi divulgado em 27 de novembro com base em fontes do governo norte-americano ouvidas pela Reuters, segundo relato do Olhar Digital. A invasão foi descoberta cerca de um mês antes, durante trabalhos de atualização, segundo dois relatos.

Acesso ao plano de controle

As fontes disseram que os invasores exploraram uma vulnerabilidade de software ainda não identificada e acessaram o plano de controle, estrutura que administra recursos e operações da nuvem. Uma delas comparou esse nível de acesso a um “controle remoto universal”.

Em tese, o acesso poderia permitir consultar o status operacional de aeronaves militares ou acompanhar a movimentação de peças de reposição. Não está claro se os hackers fizeram isso, e a identidade dos responsáveis permanece desconhecida.

Migrações e atualizações suspensas

A descoberta levou à suspensão da migração de aplicações de retaguarda para a nuvem e bloqueou atualizações de sistemas já ativos, impedindo a aplicação de correções de segurança. Alguns usuários também tiveram seus privilégios de administrador revogados.

Investigadores acionaram o Comando Cibernético das Forças Armadas dos Estados Unidos para avaliar os danos. A Força Aérea disse à Reuters que não comenta detalhes sobre a segurança ou a situação operacional de sistemas específicos, mas afirmou que adota medidas contínuas para proteger informações, sistemas e capacidades de missão.

Plataforma sustenta sistemas militares

Criada em 2017 para centralizar as necessidades tecnológicas da Força Aérea, a Cloud One combina recursos da Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle e Alphabet. A plataforma dá suporte a dezenas de aplicações de pessoal, pagamentos, logística e manutenção.

Um dos sistemas conectados — a plataforma de Comando e Controle baseada em nuvem, que reúne dados de radares de defesa aérea e outras fontes da América do Norte — pode ter sido impactado. Outro sistema integrado à Cloud One, o Sistema Integrado de Munições de Combate, rastreia bombas e mísseis em mais de 200 instalações da Força Aérea pelo mundo.

A SAIC foi a principal contratada do projeto até 2025, quando a Leidos assumiu a função. A Cloud One está entre as maiores plataformas de nuvem das Forças Armadas norte-americanas. Em 2023, sua liderança afirmou ao FedScoop que a equipe havia repelido todas as tentativas de invasão contabilizadas até então.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/hackers-invadem-nuvem-cloud-one-forca-aerea-eua/

title: Guia Técnico PT-BR: Extração de Áudio de Vídeos, Transcrição Whisper Local e Remoção de Ruído
description:
Guia Técnico: Extração de Áudio de Vídeos, Transcrição Local Whisper e Remoção de Ruído no Navegador

Criadores de conteúdo, podcasters e redações jornalísticas no Brasil enfrentam um gargalo de infraestrutura raramente discutido em tutoriais gringos: a combinação de arquivos de vídeo 4K cada vez maiores com conexões de upload assimétricas, redes móveis 4G/5G instáveis em externas e exigências rígidas de confidencialidade sob a LGPD (Lei nº 13.709/2018). Em 2026, enviar um arquivo bruto de 6 GB para um servidor desconhecido apenas para extrair uma faixa estéreo ou gerar legendas .srt tornou-se um desperdício mensurável de tempo, banda e segurança jurídica.

A virada técnica veio da maturidade conjunta de Rust compilado para WebAssembly (WASM com extensões SIMD) e da API WebGPU. Em benchmarks de DSP de áudio, módulos Rust em WASM executam transformadas rápidas de Fourier (FFT) de 5x a 15x mais rápido do que JavaScript puro, enquanto o WebGPU acelera a inferência de modelos neurais como o Whisper entre 5x e 10x em relação ao WASM rodando apenas em CPU. Todo o processamento ocorre na RAM e na GPU da máquina local — zero upload, zero fila de servidor e zero exposição de fontes jornalísticas. OfflineTTS

1. O Custo Real do Upload na Produção Brasileira

Considere uma gravação padrão de videocast ou entrevista jornalística de 60 minutos em 4K H.264 a 20 Mbps: o contêiner .mp4 resultante pesa aproximadamente 9 GB. Em uma conexão banda larga residencial típica com taxa real de upload de 40 Mbps (5 MB/s), apenas o envio desse arquivo para um conversor na nuvem consome 30 minutos — antes mesmo de o servidor iniciar a demuxagem ou a transcrição. Em campo, roteando 4G/5G a 10 Mbps, o fluxo simplesmente inviabiliza o fechamento da matéria.

Além da latência, existe o risco de conformidade. Entrevistas em off, depoimentos jurídicos, reuniões estratégicas e materiais pré-embargo contêm dados pessoais e biométricos (voz identificável). Ao processar localmente no navegador, os bytes jamais cruzam a placa de rede externa, eliminando a necessidade de contratos de transferência internacional de dados com provedores SaaS opacos.

2. Comparativo Técnico: Arquitetura Local (WASM + WebGPU) vs. Ferramentas em Nuvem

| Critério de Engenharia | Processamento Local (Rust WASM / WebGPU) | Conversores e Transcritores em Nuvem |
| Latência de Início | Imediata (menos de 1 s após leitura do arquivo local) | Alta (depende do upload integral + fila do servidor) |
| Privacidade e LGPD | 100% local (zero upload; ideal para sigilo de fonte) | Dados trafegam e permanecem em servidores de terceiros |
| Limite de Tamanho de Arquivo | Limitado apenas à RAM/disco local (suporta múltiplos GB) | Travas artificiais comuns entre 100 MB e 2 GB no plano grátis |
| Velocidade Whisper (60 min) | ~6 a 12 min via WebGPU (varia conforme GPU integrada/dedicada) | Rápido no servidor, porém penalizado por upload + fila |
| Exportação SRT / VTT | Nativa com timestamps por segmento, pronta para edição | Frequentemente restrita a planos pagos ou com marca d'água |
| Operação Offline / Campo | Funciona após carregamento inicial do app no navegador | Impossível sem conexão estável de alta banda |

3. Demuxagem Direta e Conversão Otimizada sem Perda de Geração

Um erro recorrente na extração de áudio de vídeos é forçar a recodificação desnecessária de um fluxo já comprimido (por exemplo, decodificar AAC 192 kbps para PCM e recomprimir novamente para MP3 128 kbps), acumulando artefatos de pré-eco e perda de agudos acima de 16 kHz.

Quando o objetivo é preservar a integridade máxima para pós-produção em DAWs (Reaper, Audition, DaVinci Fairlight), a abordagem correta é a demuxagem direta ou exportação em PCM WAV 48 kHz / 24-bit usando o AIAC Extrair Áudio de Vídeo. O motor WASM lê os átomos moov e mdat do contêiner diretamente do armazenamento local, isolando a trilha de áudio em segundos, mesmo em gravações longas de câmera mirrorless ou OBS Studio.

Já para fluxos de entrega rápida — distribuição em grupos de redação, publicação em portais de rádio ou revisão móvel — a compatibilidade universal fala mais alto. Nesses cenários, converter diretamente via AIAC MP4 para MP3 utilizando codificação LAME de alta eficiência (192 kbps a 320 kbps CBR para voz e música, ou 128 kbps mono para entrevistas faladas) garante tamanho reduzido sem destruir a inteligibilidade das consoantes fricativas (4 kHz a 8 kHz).

4. Limpeza Neural de Ruído, Separação Vocal e Transcrição Local Whisper

Um pipeline profissional de áudio no navegador segue uma ordem estrita de processamento: restaurar o sinal antes de transcrever. A taxa de erro por palavra (WER) de modelos automáticos de fala cai drasticamente quando o ruído de fundo abaixo de 150 Hz e as interferências não estacionárias são removidos previamente.

Passo 1: Supressão de Ruído Ambiente em Campo

Gravações externas no Brasil convivem com motores a diesel (energia concentrada entre 60 Hz e 250 Hz), vento no diafragma, ar-condicionado split e eco de ambientes com piso frio. Passar o áudio bruto pelo AIAC Removedor de Ruído de Fundo executa inferência neural via WebAssembly SIMD diretamente no navegador, preservando os formantes da voz humana enquanto rebaixa o piso de ruído estacionário e transiente sem exigir instalação de plugins VST pesados. feyard.com

Passo 2: Isolamento Vocal Sobre Trilhas e Som Ambiente Denso

Em reportagens gravadas dentro de eventos, coletivas com música ambiente ou recortes de videocasts com trilha musical alta demais, um redutor de ruído convencional não distingue música de voz. Nesses casos, o AIAC Removedor de Voz por IA separa o espectro em stems independentes (voz limpa vs. instrumental/fundo), permitindo recuperar diálogos antes inutilizáveis ou criar versões instrumentais para vinhetas.

Passo 3: Transcrição Local em Português com Whisper WebGPU

Com o áudio limpo e reamostrado internamente para o front-end de 16 kHz mono exigido pelo espectrograma Mel do Whisper, o AIAC Transcrição MP3 para Texto utiliza aceleração WebGPU para transcrever português brasileiro com alta precisão em sotaques regionais, siglas e entrevistas aceleradas. Em notebooks modernos com GPU integrada, a inferência roda múltiplas vezes mais rápido que o tempo real, entregando texto corrido e legendas padronizadas em SRT e VTT prontas para importação direta no Adobe Premiere Pro, CapCut, DaVinci Resolve ou YouTube Studio.

Para maximizar estabilidade em sessões longas acima de 90 minutos no navegador, prefira navegadores baseados em Chromium atualizados (Chrome ou Edge com WebGPU habilitado nativamente), feche abas pesadas de vídeo para preservar VRAM compartilhada e trabalhe sempre sobre a faixa de áudio já limpa antes de disparar a transcrição final. OfflineTTS

title: Hosting platforms with an MCP server that deploys, reads logs and rolls back
description:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post. This post was written with AI assistance.

Three hosting platforms ship an official MCP server whose tools cover all three jobs: Gregale, Vercel and Dokploy. An AI agent connected to one of them can deploy, read the app's logs and roll back to an earlier release through MCP tools alone. Render, Railway, DigitalOcean App Platform, Heroku, Google Cloud Run and Netlify have MCP servers that deploy but have no rollback tool. Fly.io's hosted server manages Machines, volumes and secrets but has no deploy or app-log tool, and Cloudflare's reaches its whole API through code the agent writes rather than through named tools.

Checked against each vendor's MCP documentation and published server source on November 26, 2026. Tool names are the vendors' own.

What each platform's MCP server can do

Platform Server Deploy Read logs Roll back
Gregale Hosted at https://api.gregale.dev/mcp (preview) gregale_plan_upload_deploy or gregale_plan_source_deploy, then apply gregale_get_logs gregale_plan_rollback, then gregale_apply_rollback
Vercel Hosted at https://mcp.vercel.com create_deployment, deploy_to_vercel get_runtime_logs, get_deployment_build_logs request_rollback
Dokploy Runs beside your own Dokploy instance application-deploy application-readLogs rollback-rollback, once registry-based rollbacks are on
Render Hosted at https://mcp.render.com/mcp trigger_deploy list_logs No tool
Railway Hosted at https://mcp.railway.com redeploy, accept-deploy Through the railway-agent tool; get_logs on the local server No tool
DigitalOcean App Platform Hosted at https://apps.mcp.digitalocean.com/mcp apps-create-app-from-spec, apps-update apps-get-logs No tool
Heroku Runs locally (@heroku/mcp-server) deploy_to_heroku get_app_logs No tool
Google Cloud Run Hosted at https://run.googleapis.com/mcp deploy_service_from_image, _from_archive, _from_file_contents Google's separate Cloud Logging MCP server No tool
Netlify @netlify/mcp netlify-deploy-site Edge request analytics only No tool
Fly.io Hosted at https://mcp.fly.io No deploy tool; create_machine starts a Machine from a configuration Machine events only No tool
Cloudflare Hosted at https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp Through API code the agent writes The separate Workers Observability server Through API code the agent writes

"No tool" means the MCP server has none. Each of those platforms can still roll back from its dashboard, CLI or API, so an agent that needs to roll back falls back to the CLI, or asks you.

What else to check before you give an agent write access

Deploy, logs and rollback are the minimum. These decide what happens when the agent gets it wrong:

  • Who approves a production change. Connecting Vercel's server gives the agent the same access as your Vercel account, and Vercel's docs ask you to turn on human confirmation in your MCP client. Railway marks destructive tools so that clients which respect the hints ask first. Fly.io's server grants access per organization, app and operation, and its Claude Code plugin adds a confirmation hook. On Gregale the check is in the platform: by default, an agent's production deploy or rollback returns a review link, and it goes through only after a person approves it in a signed-in session. A client set to approve every tool call can't skip it.
  • What reaches users first. On Gregale, a deploy to an app that is already serving is staged at 0% of traffic until the agent promotes it with gregale_promote_deployment.
  • What a rollback covers. Every rollback tool above puts back an earlier release. A database migration that ran with the bad release stays; see Roll back a bad migration.
  • Everything else the agent changed. Gregale's server lists the agent's own changes, such as settings, scaling, variables and the resources it created, with what undoing each would do (gregale_plan_undo), and undoes them once you approve (gregale_apply_undo).
  • What the platform is for. Vercel's server fits frontend and Next.js projects. Dokploy suits teams that run their own servers. Gregale is built for backend APIs, workers, crons and MCP servers.

Connect Gregale's MCP server

In Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http gregale https://api.gregale.dev/mcp

ChatGPT and claude.ai add the same URL as a connector. When you connect, choose "Deploy and manage apps" so the agent can deploy, promote and roll back, or "Inspect only" to let it read apps, deployments and logs. An agent with nobody at a browser, such as one in CI, uses an agent key instead:

gregale key create ci-agent --scopes agent,deploy:write

Sources

Vercel MCP tools, Dokploy MCP tools, Dokploy rollbacks, Render MCP server, Railway MCP server, DigitalOcean MCP server, Heroku MCP server, Cloud Run remote MCP server, Netlify MCP server, Fly MCP guide, Cloudflare MCP server.

Related

  • Human approval before an AI agent changes production
  • Undo what an AI agent changed in production
  • Best cloud platform for AI coding agents in 2026
  • Reference: Connect an agent to Gregale

FAQ

Which hosting platforms have an MCP server that lets an AI agent deploy, read logs and roll back?

Gregale, Vercel and Dokploy, as of November 26, 2026. Render, Railway, DigitalOcean App Platform, Heroku, Google Cloud Run and Netlify can deploy over MCP but their servers have no rollback tool. Fly.io's hosted MCP server manages Machines, volumes and secrets but has no deploy or app-log tool.

Can an AI agent roll back a Render or Railway app over MCP?

Not with a tool: neither MCP server has one as of November 26, 2026. Both platforms can roll back from the dashboard, so the agent has to fall back to another route or ask you.

Does an agent need my approval to deploy or roll back over Gregale's MCP server?

For a production app, yes by default. The tool call returns a review link, and the change goes through only after a person approves it in a signed-in session. Reads and previews are not gated.

Can I give an agent read-only access to Gregale's MCP server?

Yes. Choose "Inspect only" when you connect, and the agent can list apps and deployments and read logs, metrics and health, but cannot deploy or roll back.

title: Northflank alternatives for AI agent sandboxes: focused sandbox APIs vs full platforms
description:
Northflank is a general cloud platform: services, jobs, databases, builds and GPUs, on Northflank's cloud or in your own cloud account. Sandboxes for untrusted code are one product on it, and they inherit the platform's strengths: per-second billing with no seat fees, bring-your-own-cloud on the major providers, and GPU workloads next to everything else.

If you want one vendor for the agent and everything around it, that is hard to beat. If you only want the sandbox, there are narrower tools. We build Sandscale, one of them. Northflank facts are from its sandboxes quickstart, sandboxes in your own cloud, product page and pricing as of November 2026.

Where Northflank stands

  • Isolation: each sandbox runs against its own kernel. On Northflank's cloud, CPU sandboxes run as microVMs on Cloud Hypervisor through Kata Containers, and GPU sandboxes use gVisor. In your cloud, you install both runtimes and pick per workload; microVM nodes need bare metal or nested virtualization.
  • Billing: per second, no seat fees. Northflank Cloud lists $0.01667 per vCPU-hour and $0.00833 per GB-hour of memory, with egress at $0.06 per GB. In your cloud, $0.02083 per managed node vCPU-hour plus your provider's bill. A free tier includes up to $20 a month of resources and one small BYOC cluster.
  • Platform: services, jobs, databases, builds, GPUs, CLI and API, with a custom SLA on Enterprise.

Why teams look elsewhere

  1. You only need the sandbox. Your agent already runs somewhere else, and a platform with projects, services and clusters is more surface than the job needs.
  2. Agent governance. Approvals for risky tool calls, policy on what the agent runs, prompt DLP and an agent-oriented audit trail are things you assemble on a general platform.
  3. Per-run lifecycle. You want a box created per agent run and gone at the end, with pause that keeps memory between turns.
  4. One runtime everywhere. On Northflank, the runtime differs between CPU and GPU sandboxes and between its cloud and yours.

Quick picks

  • Sandscale. Best for: a focused sandbox API with a Firecracker microVM per agent run and approvals, policy, DLP, Vault and audit built in.
  • E2B. Best for: a focused Firecracker SDK with BYOC on AWS, GCP or Azure for Enterprise.
  • Modal. Best for: GPUs next to sandboxes and serverless functions, without running a cluster.
  • Daytona. Best for: many sandbox shapes, including GPU, Windows and macOS, from one SDK.
  • Railway. Best for: teams already deploying on Railway who want sandboxes there. See Sandscale vs Railway sandboxes.
  • Fly Machines. Best for: a general VM API with global regions if you want to build your own sandbox layer.

Focused sandbox with controls: Sandscale

Every Sandscale sandbox is a Firecracker microVM, the same runtime on every plan. It is created per run through the API, the SDK, the CLI or an MCP tool, and goes away when stopped. Pause keeps memory and files; workspaces cover persistent machines and build hosts cover large, clean build machines on a lease.

Around the box: networking off by default with an organization egress allowlist, approvals, agent policy, DLP, Vault and a hash-chained audit log on every plan. Team adds SSO, roles and audit export; Enterprise adds SCIM, your own keys and your own AWS account.

Billing is per awake vCPU-hour with 4 GiB per vCPU included and paused time not counted. Free includes 100 awake vCPU-hours a month; Pro is $20 a month billed annually or $25 monthly with 1,500; beyond the plan, $0.05 per awake vCPU-hour if you turn it on, or a 500-hour pack for $10. See pricing.

Where Northflank is ahead: GPUs, BYOC on GCP and Azure as well as AWS, databases and services on the same bill, no plan fee, lower list rates per vCPU-hour for always-busy boxes, and a custom SLA on Enterprise. Sandscale's service levels page says there is no availability commitment yet. The side-by-side is in Sandscale vs Northflank.

Focused Firecracker with BYOC: E2B

E2B runs Firecracker microVMs from a dedicated SDK, with BYOC on AWS, GCP or Azure for Enterprise and E2B Embed for a single machine. Pro is $150 a month plus usage. See E2B alternatives.

GPUs without a cluster: Modal

Modal runs GPU sandboxes on gVisor inside a serverless platform, billed per second, with sandboxes capped at 24 hours. See Modal Sandbox alternatives.

Many shapes: Daytona

Daytona defaults to containers with VM, GPU, Windows and macOS classes, billed per second on reserved resources. See Daytona alternatives.

Comparison table

As of November 2026. "Not published" means not found on the pages we read.

Option Product shape Isolation Your cloud GPU Meter Agent approvals and audit
Northflank Full platform Kata microVM (CPU), gVisor (GPU) AWS, GCP, Azure and more Yes Per second, no seat fees Not published
Sandscale Focused sandbox service Firecracker microVM AWS on Enterprise Not published Awake vCPU-hours Every plan; export on Team+
E2B Focused sandbox SDK Firecracker microVM AWS, GCP, Azure on Enterprise No Per second, CPU and RAM Not published
Modal Serverless platform gVisor or VM runtime No Yes Per second, max(request, used) Not published
Daytona Sandbox platform Container default, VM classes Enterprise Yes Per second, reserved Audit logs on Enterprise
Fly Machines General VM API VM No Not checked Per second while running You build it

When Northflank is still the right pick

  • You want sandboxes, services, databases and GPUs from one vendor.
  • You need sandboxes in your own GCP or Azure account.
  • You prefer per-second resource billing with no plan fee.
  • You need a custom SLA.

FAQ

What is the best Northflank alternative for AI agent sandboxes?

If you only need the sandbox, Sandscale (Firecracker microVM per run with approvals, policy, DLP and audit built in) or E2B (focused Firecracker SDK with BYOC). For GPUs without running a cluster, Modal.

What isolation does Northflank use for sandboxes?

As of November 2026, CPU sandboxes on Northflank's cloud run as microVMs on Cloud Hypervisor through Kata Containers, and GPU sandboxes use gVisor. In your own cloud you can install both and choose per workload.

Is there a Northflank alternative that runs in my own cloud?

E2B offers BYOC on AWS, GCP and Azure for Enterprise. Sandscale runs in your own AWS account on Enterprise, with self-hosted installs on request. PandaStack and Temps are self-hosted options.

Is Northflank cheaper than Sandscale?

For boxes that are busy all the time, Northflank's per-vCPU-hour list rate is lower. Sandscale includes 4 GiB of memory per vCPU and does not count paused time, which matters for agents that wait. Model your own workload.

Does Sandscale offer GPUs like Northflank?

GPU support is not published for Sandscale. For GPU sandboxes, look at Northflank, Modal, Beam or Daytona.

Related

  • Sandscale vs Northflank
  • The best AI agent sandboxes in 2026
  • Modal Sandbox alternatives, E2B alternatives
  • Self-hosted gVisor vs a hosted microVM sandbox

Sources

Read in November 2026:

  • Northflank: https://northflank.com/docs/v1/application/sandboxes/quickstart, https://northflank.com/docs/v1/application/sandboxes/sandboxes-in-your-own-cloud, https://northflank.com/product/sandboxes, https://northflank.com/pricing, https://northflank.com/docs/v1/api/use-the-cli
  • E2B: https://e2b.dev/pricing, https://docs.e2b.dev/byoc
  • Modal: https://modal.com/docs/guide/sandboxes
  • Daytona: https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/sandboxes
  • Fly.io: https://fly.io/docs/machines/overview/

Originally published on the Sandscale blog.

title: Freestyle alternatives: VMs for AI agents, compared by plan, persistence and controls
description:
Freestyle makes a clear argument: once an agent product grows past a code interpreter, you are choosing a computer, not a command runner. Its VMs are full Linux machines for tasks that run for hours, days or weeks, with memory-preserving pause, live cloning, default-deny networking, preview domains, nested virtualization and a Git product alongside. Runloop even published a migration guide pointing its customers to Freestyle.

That argument is right for many teams. This page is for the ones it does not fit. We build Sandscale, one of the options below. Freestyle facts are from its home page, pricing and VM docs as of November 2026.

Where Freestyle stands

  • Isolation: hardware-virtualized Linux VMs with a full kernel (FUSE, eBPF, nested virtualization). The hypervisor is not named on the pages we read.
  • Lifecycle: running, paused, stopped, snapshot, deleted. Pause saves memory; stopping a persistent VM keeps disk and drops memory; idle timeout can be disabled.
  • Plans: Free at $0 (10 concurrent VMs, 4 vCPU and 8 GiB per VM, no persistent VMs or persistent snapshots), Hobby at $50 a month (40 concurrent, 8 vCPU), Pro at $500 a month (400 concurrent, 32 vCPU and 64 GiB). The monthly fee covers usage dollar for dollar.
  • Usage: $0.04032 per vCPU-hour and $0.0129 per GiB-hour after 200 vCPU-hours and 400 GiB-hours included each month.
  • Enterprise: SAML SSO and SCIM, audit logs and a 99.99% SLA.

Why teams look elsewhere

  1. Persistence starts at $50 a month. Persistent VMs and persistent snapshots are not on Free.
  2. Audit logs and SSO are Enterprise. If you need to show who did what, that is a sales conversation.
  3. You want a fresh box per run. Evals, untrusted submissions and PR test runs want disposable machines with nothing carried over.
  4. You want approvals and policy on what the agent runs, not just network rules.
  5. GPUs or your own hardware. Not offered; Freestyle connects to your private cloud rather than running in it.

Quick picks

  • Sandscale. Best for: approvals, policy, DLP, Vault and a hash-chained audit log on every plan, a Firecracker microVM per run, and workspaces when the agent needs a persistent computer.
  • Fly.io Sprites. Best for: persistent agent computers with automatic checkpoints, compute billed on actual use.
  • E2B. Best for: hosted Firecracker sandboxes with memory-preserving pause and snapshots that keep memory.
  • Morph Cloud. Best for: branching running VMs for RL or search.
  • Daytona. Best for: many machine shapes, including GPU, Windows and macOS.
  • PandaStack or Temps. Best for: running VMs on your own hardware.

Governance on every plan: Sandscale

Sandscale's sandboxes are Firecracker microVMs, one per agent run, disposable by default. Workspaces are the persistent cloud computer for a coding agent. Pause keeps memory and files on every plan, Free included.

The difference from Freestyle is where the controls live. On every Sandscale plan: approvals with a named approver and self-approval refused, agent policy with Claude Code hooks and reporting from Codex and Gemini CLI, DLP on prompts and MCP tool calls, a Vault, and a hash-chained audit log. Exporting the log, SSO and roles come with Team ($40 per member a month billed annually, $48 monthly). SCIM is Enterprise.

Billing is per awake vCPU-hour with 4 GiB per vCPU included and paused time not counted. Free includes 100 awake vCPU-hours a month with up to 2 vCPU and 3 boxes at once; Pro is $20 a month billed annually or $25 monthly with 1,500 hours, 30 boxes and up to 16 vCPU. Networking is off by default with an organization egress allowlist. Agents connect through the CLI, REST API, TypeScript SDK, or MCP at https://mcp.sandscale.dev/mcp.

Where Freestyle is ahead: live cloning of running VMs, nested virtualization, larger VMs and concurrency on Pro, a published SLA on Enterprise, and a Git product built for agents. Sandscale's service levels page says there is no availability commitment yet, and it runs in one US region today.

Persistent and checkpointed: Fly.io Sprites

Sprites are persistent, hardware-isolated VMs that checkpoint themselves and bill CPU and memory on actual use, with warm and cold Sprites not billed for compute (sprites.dev). See Sprites alternatives.

Hosted Firecracker: E2B

E2B pause and resume keep memory and files, snapshots capture memory and filesystem, and sessions run 1 hour on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro. Freestyle's own E2B comparison is fair about where E2B fits: interpreter-shaped products. See E2B alternatives.

Branching: Morph Cloud

If cloning is why you chose Freestyle, Morph Cloud branches instances from snapshots and bills in compute units at $0.05 (pricing). See Morph Cloud alternatives.

Comparison table

As of November 2026. "Not published" means not found on the pages we read.

Option Isolation Persistence on the free tier Pause keeps Entry paid plan Audit log Clone or branch
Freestyle Hardware-virtualized VM No (paid plans) Memory and processes $50 a month Enterprise Live clone
Sandscale Firecracker microVM Pause on every plan; workspaces Memory and files $20 a month annually, $25 monthly Every plan; export on Team+ Start many from a snapshot
Fly.io Sprites Hardware-isolated microVM See Sprites plans Filesystem, checkpoints Plans with allowances Not published Restore checkpoints
E2B Firecracker microVM Pause on Hobby Memory and files $150 a month plus usage Not published Snapshots with memory
Morph Cloud VM instances Buy MCUs Pause and resume $40 a month Not published Branch
Daytona Container default, VM classes Persist until stopped Memory on VM classes Pay as you go Enterprise Not checked

When Freestyle is still the right pick

  • Your agent runs for days in one machine and users SSH in or watch a terminal.
  • You need nested virtualization, Docker inside, FUSE or eBPF.
  • Live cloning of a running VM is part of your product.
  • You want a Git service built for agents from the same vendor.

FAQ

What is the best Freestyle alternative?

For governance on every plan with a Firecracker microVM per run, Sandscale. For persistent checkpointed agent computers, Fly.io Sprites. For hosted Firecracker with memory-preserving pause, E2B. For branching VMs, Morph Cloud.

Is there a cheaper Freestyle alternative for persistent agent machines?

Freestyle's persistent VMs start with Hobby at $50 a month. Sandscale Pro is $20 a month billed annually or $25 monthly, with workspaces for persistent machines and pause on every plan. Sprites bill on actual CPU and memory use. Compare on your own workload.

Which Freestyle alternatives include an audit log without Enterprise?

Sandscale includes a hash-chained audit log on every plan, Free included, and export on Team and Enterprise. Freestyle lists audit logs on Enterprise.

Does Freestyle use Firecracker?

Freestyle describes its VMs as hardware-virtualized with a full Linux kernel; the hypervisor is not named on the pages we read. Sandscale, E2B and Vercel Sandbox use Firecracker.

Can I run Docker inside these sandboxes?

Freestyle supports nested virtualization and Docker inside. Modal's VM runtime and Beam's VMs support Docker as well. Check each provider for your exact need.

  • Audit log for AI coding agents

title: Building Market Chart From Scratch: An Open-Source Financial Charting Engine
description:
Building Market Chart From Scratch: An Open-Source Financial Charting Engine

What does it take to build a financial charting library from scratch?

Not just rendering candlesticks.

A serious market charting engine needs to handle rendering performance, large datasets, real-time updates, technical indicators, interactive drawing tools, multiple chart types, persistence, and much more.

I wanted to explore these engineering challenges by building an independent charting engine rather than relying entirely on an existing charting solution.

That's how Market Chart started.

Today, I'm working on developing it into a modular financial charting ecosystem built with TypeScript, Canvas 2D, and React integration.

GitHub: https://github.com/SinaMohammadi/market-chart

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@market-chart/core

Documentation and demos: https://sinamohammadi.github.io/market-chart/

Why build another charting library?

There are already excellent charting solutions available.

So why start from zero?

My motivation wasn't simply to create another candlestick component.

I wanted to understand the engineering behind a complete financial charting system and have control over its architecture.

Some of the challenges I wanted to explore included:

  • Efficient rendering of large financial datasets.
  • Real-time market data updates.
  • Extensible technical indicators.
  • Interactive drawing tools.
  • Multiple chart types.
  • Independent rendering and framework integration.
  • Server-side rendering.
  • Workspace persistence.

One architectural principle became particularly important:

The charting engine should not depend on the UI framework that consumes it.

This decision shaped the entire project.

1. Architecture: Separating the Engine from React

Market Chart uses a modular architecture.

The core rendering engine is implemented independently of React, using TypeScript and Canvas 2D.

React integration is provided through a separate package.

The architecture looks roughly like this:

Market Chart
│
├── Core Engine
│   ├── Canvas Renderer
│   ├── Chart Management
│   ├── Scales
│   ├── Events
│   ├── Interaction System
│   └── Plugin System
│
├── React Integration
│   ├── Components
│   ├── Hooks
│   └── Lifecycle Management
│
├── Indicators
├── Drawing Tools
├── Datafeed
├── Persistence
├── Internationalization
├── UI
└── Trading Integrations

Why separate the engine from React?

Because rendering financial data and managing application UI are different responsibilities.

For example, receiving a new market price shouldn't require unnecessarily re-rendering an entire React component tree.

The rendering engine should manage its own updates, while React handles application integration and lifecycle management.

This separation also makes the core engine more reusable.

2. A Modular TypeScript Ecosystem

I didn't want every feature to live inside one enormous package.

Instead, Market Chart is organized into independent packages.

Package Responsibility
@market-chart/core Core rendering engine
@market-chart/react React integration
@market-chart/indicators Technical indicators
@market-chart/drawing-tools Interactive drawing tools
@market-chart/charts Advanced chart types
@market-chart/datafeed Market data integrations
@market-chart/persistence Storage and workspace management
@market-chart/i18n Internationalization
@market-chart/ui Optional chart interface
@market-chart/trading Trading-related visual overlays
@market-chart/testing Testing utilities

The advantage is that developers can use the capabilities they actually need.

A project that only requires a basic chart shouldn't necessarily need the complete charting interface.

3. Canvas 2D Rendering

One of the most interesting parts of this project is the rendering architecture.

Instead of representing every candle as an individual React element, the core engine uses Canvas 2D.

This provides a different rendering model, particularly useful when dealing with large financial datasets and frequent updates.

The engine also provides column-based data access using typed arrays.

For example:

const { times, fields } = series.columns();

other.setColumns({
  times,
  fields: {
    value: fields.close!,
  },
});

Working with columnar data can reduce object allocation overhead and make certain data-processing operations more efficient.

Performance is an ongoing area of development, especially as the project grows.

4. Multiple Financial Chart Types

Candlestick charts are only one part of financial visualization.

Market Chart includes support for several chart representations:

  • Candlestick
  • Line
  • Area
  • Histogram
  • Heikin-Ashi
  • Renko
  • Kagi
  • Point and Figure
  • Line Break
  • Footprint
  • Heatmap
  • Volume Profile
  • Market Profile

Different chart types provide different perspectives on market behavior.

The goal is to make these visualization capabilities available through a consistent charting architecture.

5. Technical Indicators

Technical indicators are another major part of the project.

Market Chart includes 44 technical indicators.

The indicator architecture is designed around incremental calculations and integration with the chart engine.

Why is incremental calculation important?

Imagine receiving a new candle every few seconds.

Recalculating every historical indicator value after every update can introduce unnecessary work.

An incremental calculation model allows the indicator to maintain its previous state and process new data as it arrives.

This is especially useful for applications displaying continuously updating financial information.

6. Interactive Drawing Tools

Drawing tools are essential for technical analysis.

Traders use them to identify support and resistance levels, visualize trends, and annotate market structures.

Market Chart includes 35 drawing tools.

The drawing system also supports:

  • Object selection.
  • Magnet mode.
  • Undo and redo.
  • Clipboard operations.
  • Serialization.
  • React integration.

A drawing shouldn't just be a collection of pixels on a canvas.

It should be an independent object with its own state, configuration, and lifecycle.

This makes it possible to edit, serialize, restore, and manage drawings separately from the rendering process.

7. Datafeed Architecture

A charting engine shouldn't force developers to use one specific market data provider.

Different exchanges and financial platforms have different APIs and data structures.

Market Chart provides a datafeed abstraction with support for:

  • Static data.
  • REST adapters.
  • WebSocket adapters.
  • Server-Sent Events.
  • Synthetic data.
  • CSV and JSON imports.
  • Historical data pagination.
  • Real-time updates.

This allows developers to connect their own market data infrastructure.

For example, a cryptocurrency exchange could connect its backend WebSocket service to the chart without coupling the rendering engine to that exchange.

The separation is intentional:

Market Chart handles visualization. Your application controls the market data source.

8. Persistence and Workspace Management

A useful charting application should allow users to save their configurations.

Think about a trader who has configured multiple indicators, created drawing objects, and customized several chart layouts.

That configuration should be recoverable.

The persistence package provides different storage adapters:

  • Memory storage.
  • Web Storage.
  • IndexedDB.
  • REST storage.

It also includes functionality for autosave, versioned schemas, conflict handling, and cross-tab synchronization.

The objective is to keep persistence independent of the core rendering engine.

9. React and Next.js Integration

Modern financial applications often use React and Next.js.

However, integrating browser-based rendering engines into server-rendered applications introduces some interesting challenges.

The chart engine must not assume that browser APIs are available during server-side execution.

Market Chart includes a dedicated SSR entry point:

import { StaticChart } from '@market-chart/react/ssr';

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <StaticChart
      type="area"
      data={history}
      height={180}
      title="Price, last 90 days"
    />
  );
}

The project supports static SVG chart rendering on the server.

It also provides a progressive approach to chart rendering, allowing an initial representation to be delivered before the interactive chart engine is activated.

This is particularly useful when building financial dashboards where initial rendering and interactive functionality both matter.

10. Internationalization and RTL

Internationalization is another feature I wanted to include from the beginning.

Market Chart includes support for:

  • English.
  • Persian.
  • Arabic.
  • Custom language registration.
  • Right-to-left layouts.
  • Locale-aware formatting.
  • Translation fallbacks.

RTL support is especially important for financial applications targeting Persian- and Arabic-speaking users.

Internationalization shouldn't be an afterthought added when the interface is already complete.

It needs to be considered throughout the architecture.

11. Optional Full Chart Interface

Some developers want complete control over their chart UI.

Others want a ready-made interface.

Market Chart includes an optional UI package with functionality such as:

  • Chart headers.
  • Drawing sidebars.
  • Context menus.
  • Settings dialogs.
  • Keyboard shortcuts.
  • Symbol search.
  • Saved preferences.
  • Price actions.

The interface also supports extensibility through an action registry.

Developers can register custom actions and adapt the interface to their applications.

The important part is that the UI remains optional.

You can use the underlying engine without adopting the complete interface.

12. Trading Integrations

Financial charting and trade execution are separate responsibilities.

A chart can display open orders, positions, alerts, stop-loss levels, and take-profit levels.

But the actual execution logic belongs to the integrating application.

Market Chart includes a trading package for visual trading-related overlays and interaction callbacks.

It doesn't act as a broker or execute trades.

This keeps the charting infrastructure separate from sensitive financial operations.

13. What's Next?

Market Chart is still evolving and currently in its pre-1.0 development stage.

There is plenty of work ahead.

Some areas I'm continuing to focus on include:

  • Performance improvements.
  • API stability.
  • Testing and visual regression coverage.
  • Documentation.
  • More integration examples.
  • Architecture improvements.
  • Developer experience.

I also want to hear from developers who are building financial applications and have real-world charting requirements.

Feedback is extremely valuable at this stage.

Try Market Chart

If you're building a cryptocurrency exchange, trading platform, fintech dashboard, or financial analytics application, I'd love you to explore the project.

GitHub repository:

https://github.com/SinaMohammadi/market-chart

npm:

https://www.npmjs.com/package/@market-chart/core

Documentation and demos:

https://sinamohammadi.github.io/market-chart/

You can explore the source code, try the examples, report issues, and contribute ideas.

Issues and contributions are welcome.

Final Thoughts

Market Chart started as an engineering challenge.

I wanted to build an independent financial charting engine and explore the architecture behind a complete charting ecosystem.

It has grown into a modular project covering rendering, indicators, drawing tools, datafeeds, persistence, internationalization, and React integration.

It's still a work in progress, and that's part of the journey.

If you're interested in TypeScript, Canvas rendering, financial software, or open-source development, I'd love to hear your thoughts.

What do you think is the most challenging part of building a financial charting engine?
