title: Java4Shell: 65 Characters That Turned a Base64 Decoder Into a Shell
description:
Java4Shell: 65 Characters That Turned a Base64 Decoder Into a Shell

Last Tuesday, a string 65 characters long could take over a Jenkins server. No login. No password guessing. Just 64 letter A's and an equals sign, sent to the right endpoint, and the Java process on the other end would start doing what the sender wanted.

I read the disclosure twice because the first time I thought I had misread it. The bug was not in Jenkins. It was not in Jira, or Keycloak, or any of the other products the researchers broke into. It was in Java itself, in the part that decodes Base64, which is about as basic as a function gets. If you have ever written a login flow, you have leaned on Base64. Your auth headers are Base64. Your tokens are Base64. Your file uploads often are. The researchers at Calif found a way to make that decoder write past the end of its own buffer, and then they turned that small overflow into code execution on six products at once, all with default settings, all without logging in.

The flaw is CVE-2026-114938. Calif calls it Java4Shell. Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes on November 17, the same day the details went public, a little earlier than planned, because the details had leaked.

What actually broke

Modern Java does not decode Base64 with a plain loop. On x86-64 machines with AVX-512 VBMI instructions, HotSpot uses a hand-written, vectorized fast path. It is the kind of code that exists because somebody measured it and found it meaningfully faster, and it is the kind of code where a small arithmetic mistake hides for years because the fast path only runs on specific hardware and the tests pass everywhere else.

The mistake is in how the decoder calculates the output length when the input ends with an unexpected number of padding characters. Feed it a malformed string, something like 64 A's followed by a single =, and the length calculation underflows to a negative number. The decoder then writes 62 or 63 bytes past the end of the output array. Java does reject the input. It just rejects it after the write has already happened.

That ordering is the whole bug. The check exists. It runs too late.

Calif's Quang Luong found it. Oracle's patch notes also credit Albert Yang. The researchers demonstrated full pre-authentication takeovers on default installations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. With a login, the list grows: Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker, Apache Tomcat, and custom Spring Boot apps. They are holding back the attack code for the six products. Other labs have reproduced crashes and a memory leak so far, not the code execution, which tells you something honest about this bug: the crash is easy, the takeover is work.

Why this one is not Log4Shell, and why it still matters

Every writeup reaches for the Log4Shell comparison, and it is only half right. The reach is similar. Java runs a huge share of business software, and the vulnerable code is on by default. But Log4Shell needed one string pasted into one log line. Java4Shell needs three things to line up at once: the right processor, the right Java version, and an exploit built for each individual product, because every application arranges its heap differently and handles Base64 in its own way.

The researchers get past the corrupted bytes by arranging the server's memory so the overflow stretches a neighboring array, then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read memory back. They call the reading part JavaBleed, and it is the Heartbleed-shaped half of the story: a leak that can spill private keys and tokens out of a running server. One researcher, samczsun, showed the scarier direction: any Java program that reaches out to a hostile server over TLS becomes open to takeover, even when it exposes no services of its own. Your server does not have to be listening. It only has to talk to the wrong peer.

The hardware filter is what keeps this from being a fire for everyone. The vulnerable path only runs on Intel Xeon chips from Ice Lake onward, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and AMD processors from Zen 4 and newer. ARM64 machines are immune. If your servers are ARM, or old Intel, or running Java older than 17.0.6, this particular bug cannot touch you. That is genuinely good news, and it is also the reason the scoring is split: Calif rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, Red Hat rates it 9.8, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, calling it hard to exploit but requiring no login. All three can be true at once. The severity depends on where you stand.

The part that should bother builders

I build a messenger. My server is Node, my Android app is Kotlin, my phone is ARM. This bug did not touch my code directly, and I checked that before I wrote a word of this, because the worst thing a security writer can do is cry wolf about his own stack. But I still spent an evening on it, because the lesson is not about Java. The lesson is about the layer underneath your code that you never think about.

Nobody audits the Base64 decoder. It is too boring. It has been in the runtime since forever, it has tests, and it is the kind of function you would bet your reputation on without a second thought. The bug lived in OpenJDK from 17.0.6, released in January 2023, until last week. Almost four years. The fast path was the vulnerability, and the fast path was the point: somebody optimized a boring function, the optimization had a bug, and the bug sat in every Java distribution built from OpenJDK. Oracle Java SE, Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Microsoft's build. All of them.

That is the shape of modern supply chain risk. It is not always a compromised package or a typosquatted library. Sometimes it is a three-year-old arithmetic error in a function so fundamental that nobody thinks to question it, sitting under the login page of half the enterprise.

And the fix is not dramatic. Update to 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, depending on your line. If you cannot patch yet, the JVM flags -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or -XX:UseAVX=2 turn the fast path off. Restart the service after patching. Then do the unglamorous part that actually matters: find every Java runtime you run, including the ones bundled inside other products. The Jenkins you forgot about in a corner. The Keycloak that came with something else. The build server that has not been touched in a year. Those are the ones that stay vulnerable, because nobody owns them.

Scanning started within a day of disclosure, and at least two security firms say they hold working exploits. The window between "researchers published" and "somebody weaponizes it" is not a grace period anymore. It is a race, and the people running it do not sleep.

What I would do this weekend

If you run Java anywhere, check three things in order. First, what Java version is actually running, on every box, including the ones you did not set up yourself. Second, what CPU it runs on, because AVX-512 VBMI is the gate. Third, whether anything internet-facing decodes untrusted Base64 before authentication, which is nearly everything with a login page, an upload form, or a token endpoint.

Then patch, restart, and move on. This is not a week-long project. It is an afternoon. The bug is fixed upstream, the workaround is one flag, and the only way to lose is to not look.

What stays with me is simpler than any of that. The most dangerous code in your stack is the code you trust the most. Not the dependency you vetted suspiciously. Not the new library with twelve stars. The Base64 decoder. The function you would never think to read. Somebody finally read it, and it had been wrong for almost four years.

Check yours.

Sources: Calif's Java4Shell writeup; Oracle and OpenJDK security advisories, November 17, 2026; The Hacker News; Wiz; VulnCheck's reproduction notes.

title: Aprendendo sobre filas 1 - Conceitos básicos e prática com RabbitMQ + SpringBoot
description:
Eu sei que você entrou nessa postagem achando que eu seria direto e prático logo de cara, mas eu gosto de escrever, dar exemplos, entender os fundamentos, e explicar o que está por trás de cada parte da tecnologia. De certa forma, ainda serei direto e prático, não entrarei em todos os detalhes possíveis, mas tentarei explicar quase todos com simplicidade. Se precisar entender e aplicar no seu contexto, leia a documentação da sua ferramenta lembrando do que leu aqui.

Qual problema resolve?

Considere que você tem um negócio de carimbos que é muito solicitado, e possui uma demanda tão grande, que em determinados momentos do dia você não dá conta de receber as solicitações e modelar/imprimir todos carimbos que chegaram. Pensando em como resolver esse problema, você introduz uma latência na criação dos carimbos, com a promessa de que mesmo que demore um pouco, todos serão feitos. A proposta foi a seguinte: "vocês me entregam a solicitação seguindo os padrões que defini, eu coloco a solicitação na minha esteira (em ordem de chegada), e quando eu criar o seu, eu te aviso!" .

Figura 1 - Representação do enfileiramento de solicitações de trabalho

Você pode não ter percebido, mas resolveu diversos problemas de uma só vez:

  • Nunca mais "deixa de ouvir" uma solicitação feita em conversa direta;
  • Faz os carimbos no seu tempo, respeitando suas limitações;
  • Se falhar, consegue refazer com base na especificação, não mais com base na conversa que teve;
  • Não tem mais o cliente no seu cangote (mas se quiser...);

A fila é praaaticamente isso, com detalhes, mas quase isso. É um sistema intermediário de comunicação que permite sistema A produzir mensagens para um sistema B. Pra além disso, conta com mecanismos onde o consumidor da fila (nosso personagem esforçado) pode avisar o broker (inteligência por trás da entrega da mensagem... no nosso cenário, seria algo como esteira/rampinha da fila) que determinada mensagem foi processada corretamente ou avisar que não deu pra processar corretamente, e que a mensagem precisa voltar pra fila.

A base

É importante entender o que está por trás das filas. O Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP) é o protocolo principal adotado por diversas "filas"/message brokers para garantir que o funcionamento comum (interoperabilidade) de um sistema de filas não seja específico entre "vendors"/implementações diferentes. Na prática, é um protocolo de comunicação open source que estabelece como deve ser realizada a interação entre producers, message brokers e consumidores em um sistema de filas. Garante a recepção, armazenamento e entrega confiável das mensagens (desde que configurado para isso), além disso, também cuida do enfileiramento correto das mensagens, roteamento (inteligência que direciona uma mensagem para a fila correta), segurança (autenticação, autorização e criptografia) e controle de fluxo das mensagens (com backpressure).

O AMQP oferece comportamento transacional sobre a entrega de mensagens, onde algum consumidor que não pode "falhar e perder a mensagem" pode (se configurado) "reenfileirar" a mensagem até que seja processada corretamente ou seja colocada em uma *Dead Letter Queue* (DLQ), fila onde as mensagens que não foram processadas vão parar.

Ademais, também suporta diferentes estratégias de comportamento entre publicação x consumo das filas: pub/sub, point-to-point e outros, suportando diversos casos de uso diferentes.

Em resumo o AMQP estabelece que é necessário: entrega garantida de mensagens, persistência das mensagens até que sejam processadas, reconhecimento de processamento correto das mensagens (ack), roteamento simples ou complexo das mensagens e segurança.

Figura 2 - Representação simples de uma implementação AMQP

Fonte: https://fidelissauro.dev/mensageria-eventos-streaming/

"Ok, o desenho me parece coerente, mas o que é cada coisa nessa imagem?"

  • Publisher: produtor das mensagens enviadas a exchange do broker. Normalmente é um serviço que recebeu determinada solicitação;
  • Broker: conjunto de mecanismos que fica entre o produtor e consumidor da mensagem. Gerencia recepção, tratamento, armazenamento e direcionamento das mensagens para as filas. É dentro do broker que fica outros mecanismos como exchanges, routes e queues;
  • Exchanges: componente do broker responsável por receber as mensagens dos producers e entregá-las corretamente para fila(s) observando as regras (bindings) de roteamento. Cada exchange tem um tipo:
    • Direct: É o tipo padrão de exchange. Considerando que não criamos uma exchange, e estamos usando uma "default", já provisionada pelo broker, toda fila criada é associada a uma 'routing key', que possui o mesmo nome da fila (veja, se fosse outra exchange que não a default, poderíamos criar as routing keys). No geral, no tipo 'direct', a exchange encaminha a mensagem para a fila baseado na routing key da mensagem. Se múltiplas filas estiverem ligadas a uma mesma routing key, a exchange roteará a mensagem para todas elas.

Figura 3 - Funcionamento de direct exchange->routing->queue

Fonte: https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts#exchange-direct

  • Fanout: roteia mensagens para todas as filas linkadas a essa exchange, ignorando a routing key. É ideal para casos onde todas as filas precisam receber determinada mensagem. Algumas pessoas podem lembrar do tópico/evento, e aqui, a diferença é que você não consegue filtrar apenas um subconjunto de mensagens/eventos.

Figura 4 - Funcionamento de fanout exchange->queue

Fonte: https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts#exchange-fanout

  • Topic: roteia mensagens para uma ou várias filas baseado no pattern matching entre a routing key e o pattern usado para vincular determinada fila a uma exchange. Funciona como pub/sub. Exemplos de uso: distribuição de dados para localização específica, tarefas de background sendo processadas por múltiplos workers, atualização no preço de ações ou dados financeiros, atualização de notícias que envolver categorização ou classificação, arquiteturas distribuídas etc;
  • Headers: é modelado para rotear de acordo com vários atributos que são melhores descritos/identificados por cabeçalhos (headers) em vez de uma routing key, além disso, ignora a routing key. É basicamente uma 'direct exchange' roteada de acordo com headers.
    • Queues: filas recebem mensagens das exchanges e armazenam de maneira "enfileirada" de forma que as mensagens possam ser consumidas. No geral, compartilham algumas características com as exchanges, mas possuem suas próprias, como: nome, durabilidade, exclusividade de conexão, auto-deleção após o desvínculo do consumidor, argumentos como ttl, queue length limit etc. Precisa ser criada antes de ser usada. Se os argumentos declarados por alguma das partes sobre a fila forem diferentes dos argumentos da criação, a fila retornará um 'PRECONDITION_FAILED';
    • Bindings: São regras que as exchanges usam para rotear mensagens para as filas. No geral, para que a exchange entregue mensagens para a fila, elas precisam estar "conectadas/vinculadas", esse vínculo se dá por meio do 'binding' (se o binding não existir, a mensagem pode voltar para o produtor), que possuem (opcionalmente) uma routing key. Algumas exchanges usam essa routing key para selecionar mensagens marcadas com aquela routing key, e encaminhá-las para as filas vinculadas as routing keys. Segundo a doc., a fila é como o destino, a exchange é o aeroporto, e a binding é como se fosse a rota entre o aeroporto e o destino. Dependendo das configurações do publicador da mensagem, caso um binding não exista, a mensagem pode voltar ao publicador.
    • Consumer: são sistemas que processam/recebem as mensagens armazenadas nas filas. Existem duas formas de consumidores: inscritos, que aguardam as mensagens chegarem para eles, e polling, que fica perguntando para a fila se existem mensagens a serem consumidas. Este último é ineficiente e deve ser evitado. É possível determinar mais de um consumidor por fila, mas também é possível ter exclusividade sobre o consumo de uma fila.Cada consumidor possui uma tag e podem se 'desinscrever' de uma fila.

A práxis

Existem alguns detalhes importantes dentro de queues e consumers. E vou abordá-los em breve, mas antes, eu gostaria de fazer um switch para a parte prática, afinal, você já pegou uma visão geral do funcionamento de um message broker só por absorver os conceitos do AMQP. Para esta parte, vai ser o feijão com arroz: RabbitMQ, Java e Spring Boot. A ideia é fazer uma implementação com direct exchange, mas você pode customizar e experimentar diversas outras coisas com as abordagens exibidas aqui: https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials

Neste site:

Crie um projeto Java adicionando a dependência 'Spring for RabbitMQ':

Figura 5 - Site do spring initializr para criar projetos

Basta nomear o artefato, escolher suas especificidades (maven ou gradle, versão do spring, nome do artefato, etc) e clicar em 'Generate'. Extraia o projeto para uma pasta que sua IDE possa trabalhar e abra o projeto.

A única dependência presente no projeto deverá ser essa:

Figura 6 - pom.xml do projeto recém criado

Agora, execute o seguinte comando docker (estou considerando que você já tem na sua máquina, com setup feito e tudo certinho):

docker run -it --name rabbitmq -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:4-management

Esse comando subirá o rabbitmq e o "painel de controle" criado para a ferramenta. Enquanto o message broker fica na porta 5672, o painel ficará na porta 15672.

Depois de subir o nosso message broker, podemos criar a fila na UI disponibilizada pelo rabbitmq management acessando http://localhost:15672/ com a credencial guest (a senha também é guest):

Figura 7 - Página inicial do rabbitmq manager ui

Clique em "Queues and streams" e em "add a new queue". Preencha o name com o nome que quiser... eu colocarei "my_first_queue":

Figura 8 - Página de filas e streams do rabbitmq manager ui

Depois disso, basta clicar em "Add queue".

Agora, no projeto, crie uma classe "MyFirstQueueConsumer" e faça a seguinte implementação (importante mencionar que o rabbitmq já resolve o routing key na default exchange automáticamente na criação desta fila):

Figura 9 - Implementação de um consumer ultra-mega-simples

Crie também uma classe de configuração:

Figura 10 - Implementação para instanciar os nossos beans necessários

Rode a aplicação:

Figura 11 - Aplicação rodando após configurar consumer e beans

Volte no "Queues and Streams", clique na fila, e desça até "Publish message", faça as configurações indicadas e publique uma mensagem:

Figura 12 - Configuração e publicação de message simples na fila recém criada

E pronto, sua aplicação já está recebendo mensagens da fila (importante observar que neste modelo, a aplicação está em auto ack, ou seja, recebe a mensagem da fila, tenta processar, e decide "sozinha" se a mensagem foi processada corretamente e sai da fila ou volta pra fila para ser reprocessada. Isso será abordado em breve):

Figura 13 - Aplicação recebendo mensagem publicada na fila

Isso é legal e tudo mais, mas lembra que comentei sobre detalhes importantes? Então... Existem coisas como: TTL para determinar quanto tempo uma mensagem pode existir na fila, quantidade de retentativas possíveis, envio de mensagens que não foram processadas corretamente para uma outra fila DLQ, notificação para o publisher que determinada mensagem não foi processada e coisas nesse sentido. Entretanto, a coisa imprescindível a ser configurada para todas as filas, é a maneira de consumo das mensagens:

  • Peek-lock: onde recebemos a mensagem da fila, tentamos processar, e se der certo, sinalizamos para o broker que ele já pode remover da fila. Se não der certo, a mensagem deve ser "reenfileirada". Se for inválida, podemos pedir para não enfileirar novamente; e
  • "Fire-and-forget" ou "Receive and delete": recebemos a mensagem da fila, e antes mesmo de saber se foi corretamente processada, o broker é liberado para remover a mensagem da fila (para entrar nesse modo, seria necessário configurar o ack mode como 'none', mas não será abordado aqui).

Da forma que fizemos, se algo acontecer durante o processamento de alguma mensagem, a mensagem voltará pra fila e continuará sendo entregue infinitamente (auto ack comentado anteriormente):

Figura 14 - Inclusão de exception caso a mensagem seja "abc"

Figura 15 - Publicação de mensagem abc

Figura 16 - Resultado da aplicação tentando processar a mensagem infinitamente

Para tratar isso, nós precisamos alterar a configuração que fizemos para o consumer, indicando que queremos realizar o ack manualmente, e isso nos possibilitará dizer:

  1. Quando a mensagem foi processada e pode ser removida da fila (ack);
  2. Quando a mensagem foi recebida, mas o conteúdo é inválido e deve ser removido da fila (reject, mas também daria pra fazer com o nack + requeue false);
  3. Quando a mensagem foi recebida, mas não foi possível processar no momento e precisará ser reprocessada (nack com requeue true, ou seja, acontecerá porque eu pedirei o redelivery); Para além disso, também é possível configurar quando a mensagem deve ir para uma DLQ para auditoria ou depurar algum problema, e/ou várias outras alternativas que possibilitam interagir de forma muito mais rica com AMQP->message broker. Mas para nosso cenário, cobrindo os 3 pontos mencionados, ficamos assim no listener: 
package com.example.mfqS;

import com.rabbitmq.client.Channel;
import org.springframework.amqp.rabbit.annotation.RabbitListener;
import org.springframework.amqp.support.AmqpHeaders;
import org.springframework.messaging.handler.annotation.Header;
import org.springframework.messaging.handler.annotation.Payload;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.io.IOException;

@Component // lembre-se de apagar o @Bean na config se for usar este código;
public class MyFirstQueueConsumer {

    @RabbitListener(queues = "my_first_queue", ackMode = "MANUAL")
    public void consume(
            @Payload String text,
            Channel channel,
            @Header(AmqpHeaders.DELIVERY_TAG) long deliveryTag,
            @Header(AmqpHeaders.REDELIVERED) boolean redelivered) throws IOException {
        try {
            System.out.printf("%n----- start %d -----%n", deliveryTag);
            System.out.printf("text=%s redelivered=%s%n", text, redelivered);
            process(text, redelivered);
            channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false); // reconheça a entrega dessa msg
        } catch (InvalidMessageException ime) {
            channel.basicReject(deliveryTag, false); // encerre a entrega dessa msg, e não permita um novo enfileiramento dela
        } catch (IllegalStateException ise) {
            channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, true); // sinalize que essa mensagem deve ser entregue novamente por conta do requeue true
        } finally {
            System.out.println("----- finish -----");
        }
    }

    private static void process(String text, boolean redelivered) {
        if ("abc".equals(text))
            throw new InvalidMessageException(text);
        if ("work_more".equals(text) && !redelivered) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("processing failed");
        }
        System.out.printf("Received and deleted: %s%n", text);
    }

    static class InvalidMessageException extends RuntimeException {
        public InvalidMessageException(String message) {
            super(message);
            System.out.printf("""
                    Invalid message received and deleted: %s
                    """, message);
        }
    }
}

Figura 17 - Publicando mensagem na nova impl.

Ao publicar uma mensagem convencional, comprovamos o funcionamento do ponto 1, processar e remover da fila:

Figura 18 - Recebendo e processando mensagem

Agora, caindo no cenário de "mensagem inválida" que criamos, publicamos "abc", que cai no ponto 2, onde a mensagem é inválida e deve ser removida da fila:

Figura 19 - Recebendo e invalidando mensagem

Por fim, para comprovar o "redelivery" do ponto 3, publicamos a mensagem "work_more":

Figura 20 - Recebendo, reenfileirando a mensagem, e processando corretamente

Essa implementação nos proporciona um cenário onde acatamos mensagens corretas, dispensamos mensagens incorretas, e retentamos cenários específicos (normalmente de indisponibilidade). Embora você precise fazer adaptações e tratar suas especificidades em seu código, esta implementação provê ideias sobre o funcionamento dos conceitos apresentados, e pode ser usado como base para estudos e aplicações práticas.

Nas próximas aulas, abordaremos os detalhes de cada exchange, como funcionam, configurações adicionais, tráfego de payloads reais e paralelismo nos consumidores.

Bibliografia

https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts
https://fidelissauro.dev/mensageria-eventos-streaming/

Repositório

https://github.com/Zodh/queue-studies

title: React Interview Questions and Answers (2026)
description:
Originally published on nostrobeai.com.

React interviews concentrate on a predictable core: the virtual DOM and reconciliation, state versus props, the hook rules and why they exist, why lists need stable keys, and how to avoid unnecessary re-renders. Most questions are testing whether you understand the mental model rather than whether you have memorised an API — an interviewer asking about keys wants to hear about reconciliation, not about avoiding a console warning. Be ready to explain why a rule exists, not just what it says, and to name the trade-off in any performance optimisation you propose, since useMemo and useCallback both cost something.

Below are the common questions, with concise answers you can adapt in your own words.

Core concepts

What is the virtual DOM and why does React use it?

The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and applies the minimal set of real DOM updates. This avoids expensive, manual DOM manipulation and lets you write declarative UI as a function of state.

What is the difference between state and props?

Props are inputs passed into a component by its parent — read-only from the component's perspective. State is data a component owns and can update over time with a setter (such as the one returned by useState). Props flow down; state is local. When state changes, the component re-renders.

What are keys and why do they matter in lists?

Keys give React a stable identity for each item in a list so it can match elements between renders. Without stable keys (or when using array indices for dynamic lists), React can misattribute state and produce subtle bugs when items are reordered, inserted, or removed. Use a stable, unique id from your data.

What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?

A controlled component derives its value from React state and updates it via onChange — React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled component keeps its own internal state in the DOM, which you read with a ref when needed. Controlled inputs are easier to validate and keep in sync; uncontrolled inputs are lighter for simple cases.

Hooks

What rules govern hooks?

Call hooks only at the top level of a component or another hook — never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions — so the call order is stable between renders. And call them only from React functions (components or custom hooks). These rules let React associate hook state with the right call.

When does useEffect run, and what does its dependency array control?

useEffect runs after the render is committed to the screen. The dependency array controls when it re-runs: an empty array runs it once on mount; a populated array re-runs it whenever any listed value changes; omitting the array runs it after every render. Return a cleanup function to undo subscriptions or timers before the next run and on unmount.

What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?

useMemo memoizes a computed value; useCallback memoizes a function reference. Both recompute only when their dependencies change. Use them to avoid expensive recalculations or to keep stable references for dependency arrays and memoized children — but don't reach for them by default, since memoization has its own cost.

What problem does useRef solve?

useRef gives you a mutable container whose .current persists across renders without triggering a re-render when it changes. Common uses: referencing a DOM node, storing a previous value, or holding a mutable value (like a timer id) that shouldn't cause renders.

Performance

How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders?

Identify what actually changed. Tools include React.memo to skip re-rendering a component when its props are shallow-equal, stable references via useCallback/useMemo, splitting components so state lives close to where it's used, and lifting expensive work out of render. Always measure first with the Profiler rather than guessing.

What is reconciliation?

Reconciliation is React's process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one to determine the minimal DOM updates. It assumes elements of different types produce different trees and uses keys to match children efficiently. Understanding it explains why keys and component identity matter.

Mental model

What does "React is declarative" mean in practice?

You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React figures out how to update the DOM to match. You don't imperatively add and remove nodes; you change state and let React reconcile. This makes UIs easier to reason about because the render output is a pure function of props and state.

How would you explain when to lift state up?

When two or more components need to share or stay in sync with the same data, move that state to their closest common ancestor and pass it down as props (with callbacks to update it). This keeps a single source of truth and avoids duplicated, drifting state.

The best way to make these answers stick is to explain each one out loud, in your own words, as if to an interviewer. After that, review JavaScript fundamentals: closures, the event loop and this are the language underneath React.

title: Mail Authentication: How to Stage DNS Automation Beyond the Manual Console
description:
Faster DNS writes help only if they shorten customer onboarding without making mail activation premature. For a developer tool publishing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, keep a documented manual console process while the records are static; build a provisioning pipeline once customers repeatedly need their own domain setup. Separate propagation from the decision to start sending.

Short answer: DNS automation is worth building when domain setup becomes part of customer onboarding, especially when different people repeatedly create the same records. Start with a read-only inventory. Automate writes once that inventory exposes a recurring queue, and keep activation dependent on evidence. A handful of stable records for one company website can stay in the console.

The useful cost question is how much coordination each additional customer requires. Counting API calls misses the person waiting for access, the reviewer comparing record values, and the customer asking whether they can start sending. These are responsibilities to design for, not measured savings to assume. The design below treats mail activation as the unit of progress: a record-submission worker can finish while the customer's onboarding remains open.

1. When is DNS automation worth building for customer mail onboarding?

Begin with the repeated work. List what happens when a customer wants to send authenticated mail from their own domain through the developer tool. Someone gathers the intended SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration, identifies who controls DNS, checks existing records, submits changes, and records the evidence used to permit sending. Automation becomes attractive when those responsibilities repeat across customers and operators. The tipping point is the customer-facing queue, rather than a particular record count.

Keep the console.

That's a reasonable decision for one company's stable setup. A pipeline brings credentials, ownership checks, review rules, and recovery decisions to maintain. If a documented procedure handles occasional changes without turning onboarding into a queue, those moving parts need a concrete justification. There isn't a universal customer-count threshold here. Frequency and handoffs matter together.

Make the assessment reproducible with a local exercise. These inputs are illustrative planning choices, not production measurements; replace them with observations from your onboarding process. Run this Python program to produce a starting recommendation.

case = {
    "customer_domain_onboarding": True,
    "records_repeat": True,
    "multiple_operators": True,
}

if case["customer_domain_onboarding"] and case["records_repeat"]:
    recommendation = "Inventory first; plan reviewed provisioning."
elif case["records_repeat"] and case["multiple_operators"]:
    recommendation = "Inventory first; investigate repeated handoffs."
else:
    recommendation = "Keep a documented manual console procedure."

print(recommendation)

The output is a planning prompt, not authorization to change DNS.

If it recommends provisioning but nobody can identify repeated customer work, revisit the inputs. A rule that always recommends a pipeline has stopped being useful.

2. Read before adding a write worker

An inventory is useful long before automated writes. Connect each customer domain to its responsible operator, expected mail-authentication configuration, and next required observation. A flat list of values leaves support guessing which customer is waiting and who can act. Keep the initial implementation narrow: retrieve the inventory, inspect the actual response, and decide what the application needs to retain before adding mutations.

For a team evaluating a common REST interface, this minimal Python example reads the domain inventory. Set INFRAI_API_KEY through your environment and set DNS_API_BASE to the service's documented API base, including its version prefix. No credential belongs in source control. The program prints the returned JSON without inventing response fields; mapping that response into your customer inventory is a separate implementation step.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

base = os.environ["DNS_API_BASE"].rstrip("/")
if not base.startswith("https://"):
    raise ValueError("DNS_API_BASE must use HTTPS")
key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
request = Request(
    base + "/dns/domain/list",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + key},
    method="GET",
)

for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError("Unexpected status: " + str(response.status))
            print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2))
        break
    except HTTPError as error:
        body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
        delay = float(2 ** attempt)
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        if retry_after:
            try:
                delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
            except ValueError:
                deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                delay = max(delay, (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
        time.sleep(delay)

The explicit GET makes this a read-only starting point.

It checks status and retries rate limits with bounded attempts, exponential backoff, and Retry-After support. The numbers 5 and 30 are example retry and timeout settings, not service guarantees. Reads don't need a write-deduplication strategy; introducing mutations does.

Now inspect the handoff. If the customer controls the zone, an inventory response from your own account doesn't prove that you can publish their records. Identify the authorized operator and obtain the intended values from the sending service and the approved domain configuration. A compliance-aware onboarding flow needs that ownership boundary even when record creation is automated.

Mail authentication needs its own review, too. DMARC describes policy and alignment in relation to SPF and DKIM. A checklist containing all three names doesn't certify the configuration or guarantee delivery. Keep the distinction visible to the support team, which otherwise inherits an ambiguous green status.

3. Gate activation on the configuration actually reviewed

The provisioning side should own submitting approved changes and retaining the result. The activation side should own deciding whether the customer can begin using the sending domain. Putting both behind one successful write response is convenient, but hides the propagation-versus-cutover trade-off the system has to manage.

Wait for evidence.

Define that evidence with the team responsible for mail: intended records, required observations, and approval for activation. Don't invent a fixed propagation duration to make the workflow appear deterministic. Record what was observed, who reviewed it, and which configuration the review covered. Evidence attached to yesterday's intended values must not silently approve today's change. Consider the specific review failure represented below: an operator approves one configuration, the intended configuration changes, and a worker sees an approval flag that still says true. Without tying the observation to a revision, the worker cannot tell that the approval is stale. This runnable local gate makes the distinction explicit. Its fields belong to the example application, not a DNS provider's request schema; it neither queries DNS nor sends mail.

def activation_decision(change):
    if not change["authorized"]:
        return "hold: authorization required"
    if not change["submitted"]:
        return "hold: submission required"
    if change["observed_revision"] != change["desired_revision"]:
        return "hold: collect evidence for the current revision"
    if not change["mail_review_approved"]:
        return "hold: mail review required"
    return "eligible for activation"

example = {
    "authorized": True,
    "submitted": True,
    "desired_revision": "mail-config-2",
    "observed_revision": "mail-config-1",
    "mail_review_approved": True,
}
print(activation_decision(example))
example["observed_revision"] = "mail-config-2"
print(activation_decision(example))

The first result holds activation despite completed submission and review.

The second becomes eligible because the evidence now covers the intended revision. This is worth catching before adding write throughput: a faster queue would otherwise accelerate the wrong transition.

Use the same boundary for console edits. An operator can submit records manually and attach evidence to the customer workflow. That gives the team one definition of readiness while introducing automation gradually. Customers who retain DNS control can still participate through instructions and review.

4. Choose the control surface after defining readiness

Compare products against the work you intend to automate. Cloudflare DNS, Amazon Route 53, and Google Cloud DNS are real alternatives for managing DNS; start by evaluating whichever already holds the relevant zone. Moving a zone is a separate decision that repeated mail-record creation alone doesn't settle. These are selection criteria, not measured performance rankings.

Option Where to evaluate it Boundary for this workflow
Cloudflare DNS Its console for occasional edits and its API for recurring work when the zone is managed there. Existing zone control doesn't establish mail-activation readiness.
Amazon Route 53 Teams already managing the relevant zone and permissions through AWS. Provisioning permission and customer activation approval remain separate responsibilities.
Google Cloud DNS Teams already operating the zone within Google Cloud. The existing cloud environment doesn't remove the need to collect activation evidence.
Infrai A unified REST API where switching the vendor behind a capability keeps the calling contract unchanged; public, self-describing discovery supports integration planning. Inspect the DNS capability's declared schema and vendor readiness; a stable interface isn't a propagation guarantee.

For a stable domain, a documented console procedure in the existing service can be the best answer. For repeated customer onboarding, compare how provisioning fits the team's current permissions and review process. A common interface earns its place when vendor substitution matters to the application. A direct integration earns its place when the team wants the DNS service's own operational surface. Neither choice demonstrates faster delivery.

Customer-controlled zones deserve special attention. Your application can automate instructions, inventory, and evidence collection while the customer still publishes records. Define exactly which responsibility the pipeline owns before describing the whole onboarding process as automated.

5. Roll out one transition at a time

Start by recording the manual process and its owners. Add the read-only inventory, then use recurring customer tasks to choose a narrow write workflow. Require approval for the intended configuration, retain the submission result, collect evidence for that revision, and activate after mail review. These are proposed rollout stages, not claims about a provider's internal behavior.

For an initial trial, keep the customer's currently approved sending configuration in service until the replacement passes review. Record what would need restoring if the change is rejected. Restoration is another reviewed change with its own observations; calling a procedure rollback doesn't eliminate propagation.

The acceptance criterion is concrete: can the operator tell which customer is waiting, who owns the next action, and why sending remains on hold? If that's clear and recurring console work remains a queue, automate the next transition. If the records are static and the manual procedure is enough, stop there.

References

  • DMARC specification, RFC 7489: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/Welcome.html
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation: https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/overview

Sources

The references above identify the authentication standard and the primary DNS product documentation. The code's planning inputs and activation states are illustrative application design choices, not production observations or provider response fields.

title: Implementing 2nd-Generation Eurocodes (EN 1997-3:2025, EN 1992-1-1:2023 & EN 1998-5:2024) in Rust/WASM: What Changed from 1st-Gen
description:
The first-generation Eurocodes are scheduled for withdrawal on 30 March 2028. For European civil and geotechnical practices, the biggest bottleneck ahead of that date isn't the large finite-element packages—it is auditing and migrating thousands of bespoke first-generation Excel and Mathcad templates built over the past fifteen years.

Engineers need a straightforward way to check how a design's utilization changes between the 2004 rules and the new second-generation framework without rewriting formulas by hand or uploading proprietary project geometry to external servers.

Inside HyGeoWorks, our single Rust calculation engine (compiled both into HyGeoWorks Desktop and into a bare wasm32-unknown-unknown browser module running 100% locally with zero server upload) now runs 1st-generation and 2nd-generation Eurocode checks side by side. Using the browser workbench's Pin as baseline control, engineers can change only the design code selector and compare both generations on the exact same geometry and soil profile.

Here is a look at the three major second-generation modules we just shipped—EN 1997-3:2025, EN 1992-1-1:2023, and EN 1998-5:2024—and how we structured the Rust code to enforce explicit engineering guardrails.

1. EN 1997-3:2025 Table 7.2 (Retaining Walls: MFA vs. RFA)

First-generation EN 1997-1:2004 relies on Design Approaches (DA1, DA2, DA3). Second-generation EN 1997-3:2025 restructures geotechnical verification into explicit Verification Cases (VC1–VC4) paired with Material sets (M1, M2) under two primary philosophies in Table 7.2:

  1. Material Factor Approach (MFA) — Verifies two parallel combinations:
    • (a) VC4 + M1: Structural/action effects are multiplied by γE = 1.35 · kF while soil shear parameters remain unfactored (M1).
    • (b) VC3 + M2: Soil parameters tan(φ') and c' are factored by M2 (scaled by kM).
    • Crucially, per EN 1997-1:2024 §4.4.1.1(6), a single verification applies only one of the consequence factors (kF, kM, or kR)—so our Rust solver applies kF to VC4/VC1 and kM to VC3+M2, rather than double-counting both in the same check.
  2. Resistance Factor Approach (RFA) — Verifies combination (d) VC1 with unfactored soil parameters and explicit resistance partial factors: bearing γRN = 1.4, sliding γRT = 1.1, and earth resistance γRe = 1.4.

In our online default example (a 5.0 m inverted-T RC cantilever wall, surcharge q = 10.0 kPa, base width B = 3.50 m, Consequence Class CC2), switching between the two 2nd-generation approaches yields:

  • MFA (VC4 + M1 & VC3 + M2): VC4+M1 sliding utilization factor of safety ratio 1.291 >= 1.000 and bearing ratio 1.834 >= 1.000; VC3+M2 sliding ratio 1.087 >= 1.000 and bearing ratio 1.015 >= 1.000.
  • RFA (VC1): sliding ratio 1.174 >= 1.000 and bearing ratio 1.310 >= 1.000.

For transparency, geometric eccentricity is reported as an advisory precautionary check per §5.6.3(6), and overturning on soil foundations is subsumed into bearing capacity per §5.6.3(1) NOTE (Not judged separately) rather than inventing a separate pass/fail threshold.

Inside crates/hy-regs/src/intl.rs, the partial factor sets map cleanly without magic runtime tables:

pub fn ec7_gen2_retaining_factors(approach: Ec7Gen2Approach) -> Vec<Ec7Gen2Set> {
    // ...
    let r_unit = Ec7RetainingResistance { bearing: 1.0, sliding: 1.0, earth: 1.0 };
    let r_rfa = Ec7RetainingResistance { bearing: 1.4, sliding: 1.1, earth: 1.4 };
    match approach {
        Ec7Gen2Approach::Mfa => vec![
            mk("EN 1997-3 Tab. 7.2 MFA (a): VC4 + M1", Ec7Gen2Vc::Vc4, Ec7MaterialSet::M1, r_unit, None),
            mk("EN 1997-3 Tab. 7.2 MFA (b): VC3 + M2", Ec7Gen2Vc::Vc3, Ec7MaterialSet::M2, r_unit, Some(1.0)),
        ],
        Ec7Gen2Approach::Rfa => vec![mk(
            "EN 1997-3 Tab. 7.2 RFA (d): VC1 + γR",
            Ec7Gen2Vc::Vc1,
            Ec7MaterialSet::M1,
            r_rfa,
            None,
        )],
    }
}

2. EN 1992-1-1:2023 §9.2.3 & Annex H (Crack Width & Tightness Class 1)

In liquid-retaining concrete structures (detention tanks and U-channels), second-generation Eurocode 2 overhauls both material relations and crack-width mechanics:

  • Unified Mean Tensile Strength & Modulus: Table 5.1 unifies fctm = 1.1 · fck^(1/3) across grades up to C100 (replacing the piecewise logarithmic curve above C50 in 2004), and §5.1.4(2) Eq. (5.1) sets Ecm = kE · fcm^(1/3) (with kE = 9,500 for quartzite aggregates).
  • Updated Crack-Width Formulation (§9.2.3): We implement Eq. (9.8)–(9.20) computing wk,cal = kw · k1/r · sr,m,cal · (εsm − εcm) with kw = 1.7 and:
    • sr,m,cal = 1.5·c + (kfl · kb / 7.2) · (φ / ρp,eff) <= (1.3 / kw)·(h − x)
  • Tightness Class 1 (Annex H §H.4.2(2)): The hydrostatic head-to-wall-thickness interpolation (hD / h <= 5 -> 0.20 mm, hD / h >= 35 -> 0.05 mm) now formally judges flexural faces.

Strict Mechanical Guardrail: For faces under net axial tension (such as the base slab inside a submerged tank), a pure-flexure cracked-section steel stress model underestimates σs. Rather than returning an optimistic pass, the engine explicitly locks axial-tension faces as Not judged with the exact mechanical reason displayed.

3. EN 1998-5:2024 Annex B (SPT Liquefaction)

For seismic liquefaction triggering under the second-generation seismic geotechnical code, the SPT borehole solver implements EN 1998-5:2024 Annex B (CN overburden iteration, fines-content adjustment, CRR7.5, magnitude scaling factor, Kσ, stress reduction rd, and CSR).

Following §6.5(2) and §7.3.5(2), cyclic undrained shear resistance is factored by the EN recommended material partial factor γτ,cy,u = 1.25, evaluating the design condition (CRR / 1.25) / CSR >= 1.0. Where Atterberg limits and soil column profiles are supplied, it also evaluates §B.4 susceptibility screening (IP < 10) and §B.7 severity indices (LPI < 5, LSN < 15).

4. Explicit "Not Judged" Guardrails & Per-Metre Reference Embodied Carbon

Engineering software often fails users in one of two ways: silently falling back to unverified numbers when a National Annex clause isn't available, or forcing engineers to copy concrete and rebar quantities into a separate spreadsheet just to estimate embodied carbon.

We enforce two rules in our shared Rust core:

  1. Zero Silent Guessing: When an engineer selects a 1st-generation National Annex preset whose pile or uplift (UPL) clauses have not been obtained from primary standards, hy-workflow and hy-tools explicitly tag those checks as Not judged (reference values only) while still computing unverified numbers transparently.
  2. Same-Section Embodied Carbon Reference: Across four structural calculators (retaining-wall, counterfort-wall, box-culvert-rebar, and water-tank-rebar), the solver reuses the exact concrete volume and reinforcement mass per metre from the structural check to output a material-stage reference embodied carbon figure (kgCO2e/m), using UK DESNZ 2026 (OGL v3.0) factors for the international market (285.1 kgCO2e/m³ for concrete and 3,821.9 kgCO2e/t for primary steel). It is clearly scoped as a material-stage reference aid—not a full-lifecycle PAS 2080 audit—and saves manual hand-copying during preliminary sizing.

Try the Live WASM Calculators & Inspect the Benchmarks

Every tool runs locally in your browser with no login or parameter upload:

  • Cantilever Retaining Wall (1st-gen EC7 DA1 vs. 2nd-gen EN 1997-3:2025 MFA/RFA): https://hygeoworks.com/en/tools/retaining-wall/
  • Liquid-Retaining RC (EN 1992-1-1:2023 §9.2.3 & Annex H Tightness Class 1): https://hygeoworks.com/en/tools/water-tank-rebar/
  • Liquefaction Triggering (SPT): https://hygeoworks.com/en/tools/soil-liquefaction/
  • 69 Verification Benchmarks Whitepaper: https://hygeoworks.com/en/benchmarks/
  • Open Benchmark Repository (CC BY 4.0): https://github.com/hygeoworks/hygeoworks-benchmarks
  • Zenodo Permanent Concept DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24458320

title: Tackling LLM Prompt Bloat: Building a Just-In-Time Context Router in Rust (Part 8)
description:
As autonomous agent frameworks grow in complexity, developers continually add rules, domain doctrines, coding style guides, and edge-case remediations.

The easiest path—and the most common anti-pattern—is simply appending every new rule to the global system prompt. Within a few months, the base prompt balloons from 500 tokens to 8,000+ tokens.

This phenomenon, known as Fatal Prompt Bloat, has severe consequences:

  1. Context Window Saturation: Drastically reduces available token space for real codebase context, compiler logs, and deep conversation history.
  2. Inference Latency & Cost: Every single turn incurs the quadratic attention overhead of parsing thousands of irrelevant static tokens.
  3. Reasoning Degradation (Attention Diffusion): When a model is bombarded with 50 disparate rules (e.g. Docker rules, Blender instructions, React best practices, and Git protocols simultaneously), its attention mechanism diffuses, leading to subtle instruction non-compliance.

When architecting the cognitive subsystem for Flowork OS, we outlawed always-on static prompts in favor of a Formula 5-3-3 Just-In-Time Sliding Window Router written in Rust.

The Zero-Bloat Mandate: 100% Conditional Directives

Under the Flowork OS system prompt architecture, the base prompt remains locked to a minimal anchor (~400 tokens covering identity and approval boundaries).

Every other domain instruction exists as a Passive Trigger (/opt/floworkos/system/system_promp/promps/triggers/) or a native compiled Rust rule checker (rules/.bin/*).

Directives are injected dynamically only when their environmental conditions match:

  • Not modifying an ISO build script? $ ightarrow$ The ISO build directive is completely absent from context.
  • Not working with Android APKs or Scrcpy? $ ightarrow$ The Android subsystem prompt is not loaded.
  • Not configuring Glass HUD compositing? $ ightarrow$ The HUD styling rules never enter the prompt envelope.

Sub-Millisecond Native Rule Evaluation

To ensure dynamic context injection introduces zero noticeable user latency, rule evaluation is executed natively in Rust (mrflow-rs/src/cognitive/mod.rs):

// Fast-path landmark and structural inspection (<50ms timeout)
let structural_checks = vec![
    (
        is_build_intent && (has_tool("compile_code") || has_tool("run_command")),
        "triggers/code_engineering.md",
    ),
    (
        is_search_intent && (has_tool("grep_search") || has_tool("glob")),
        "triggers/search_efficiency.md",
    ),
    (
        cwd.join("FLOWORK.md").exists() || cwd.join(".flowork/MEMORY.md").exists(),
        "triggers/memory_routing.md",
    ),
];

By keeping individual trigger directives dense and strictly under 250 words, the agent retains razor-sharp focus on the task at hand without suffering cognitive drift.

Explore the Codebase

The entire prompt router, native cognitive loop, and Landlock security sandbox are open-source.

  • Read the architecture documentation on GitHub: flowork-os/flowork-os

title: Should you sync your customer data to your notification platform?
description:
Introduction

Sending notifications is a vast subject. Many questions and architecture decisions that have a huge impact on your product. Sending too many notifications, the wrong type, to the wrong people can shatter your company's reputation.

One crucial process about notifications is data. What to do when an event triggering a notification doesn't contain all the data necessary to prepare the message? How do I retrieve the extra information? Where does that information live? There are two approaches to this problem.

In this article, we'll look at the pros and cons of syncing your customer data to your notification platform or keeping your data on your side to access it on demand.

Approach A: Synchronize your data

This approach means that the notification platform holds a copy of your customer data on their side. The notification platform usually doesn't need to make extra external calls to retrieve data, and you can create segments easier on their side. On the other end, it means that your customer data is duplicated elsewhere and you have to implement processes to guarantee data integrity and the data could be obsolete compared to the real data.

Pros

  • Availability: Your app fails, the data could still be available on the notification platform if they are synchronized.

  • Segmentation: Easier to create segments on the stored profiles.

  • Performance: No external calls, we read the data from the local attributes.

Cons

  • Privacy: You have to duplicate your customer data in an external provider, creating another point of failure for that data to be stolen.

  • Data Freshness: Data could be out of sync between the copy and the real data.

  • Integration: You need to implement mechanisms to keep your data in sync or update it.

  • Maintenance: You need to maintain data integrity.

Approach B: Retrieve it on demand

This approach means that you keep your data in one place: your own systems. It means that there is only one source of truth and you don't need to worry about being in sync with other providers. However, performance might be a bit slower because the notification platform will need to make external calls to retrieve the data. It's also your responsibility to provide the endpoints necessary to retrieve the data and create the segments.

Pros

  • Data Freshness: You get the freshest data from the one source of truth used, depending of availability and cache strategies.

  • Privacy: Possibility to limit the data exposed to the external service providers

  • Segmentation: Depends, could be more difficult to implement but you have complete control of your filters and criteria.

Cons

  • Availability: Depends on the availability of your API to retrieve business data

  • Integration: Need to implement endpoints and/or enrichment functions.

  • Performance: More latency to call external services.

  • Maintenance: Need to maintain API contracts, their performances and their errors.

A concrete example

To revisit what I talked about in this article, we'll talk about invoice creation.

I create an invoice and I want to notify my customer that a new invoice is available for him. I trigger an event invoice.created that contains the invoice's id and an organisation's id.

Notifications must be sent to that organisation's billing managers and include the amount, due date and name of the organisation.

Approach A — Synchronisation

The platform already possesses the necessary attributes to identify the billing managers and personalize the message.

Question: Has this information been correctly synchronized?

Approach B — Fetch on demand

The system calls the application to get the recipients and fetch the missing data.

Question : What happens if the API is slow, unavailable or throws an error?

What we chose at Notifizz

At Notifizz, we went straight to approach B. We believe that your data should stay on your side and avoid duplication. We feel like it's better to limit the amount of data stored by a third party.

This approach allows our clients to define their endpoints on their API and their enrichment functions as they wish. Doesn't matter how complex their business logic might be, if they can implement it in their code and expose it, we can use it. We believe it allows for lot of possibilities when it comes to retrieve data or creating segments.

To tackle certain performance issues, we allow clients to use a cache for their enrichers data. That way, you choose if you want Notifizz to keep in cache data that you know won't change too much and avoid unnecessary calls or call your API every time to make sure you get the freshest data. The choice is yours.

How does your team handle notifications? Are you closer to approach A or B?


We built Notifizz using Approach B to retrieve customer data on demand and avoid data duplication. Check it out if you're looking for an event-driven notification architecture!
Explore Notifizz
