title: Feature Flag API Decisions: 2 Signal Boundaries for Fintech Notification Delivery
description:
Keep release permission separate from delivery evidence. TL;DR: use an authenticated GET to check whether the notification feature flag is enabled, but page on notification delivery failures under an independently owned policy; a successful lookup proves neither that a notification was attempted nor that it reached its recipient.

The operational question is what page fired. A dashboard showing fewer failures proves little if a disabled sender also stopped producing observations, and a green configuration request cannot close a delivery incident. Start the postmortem with the outcome and work backward to the release decision.

This runbook uses a fintech notification service as a design example. Its two boundaries are release eligibility and recipient delivery. The numbers below are local configuration choices, not incident measurements; the objective is signal quality, so repeated configuration reads must not manufacture repeated delivery failures.

How should an API check whether a feature flag is enabled?

For a Node.js API checking a feature flag, the request contract is straightforward: authenticate a GET with the flag key as its path parameter, then interpret the returned enabled state using the documented response schema. The executable probe below uses Go, but the same HTTP contract applies to the Node.js backend. Keep the credential on the server.

Preserve three outcomes.

An enabled result permits the candidate sender under your release policy. A disabled result keeps it ineligible. A lookup that cannot be completed is unknown, which needs its own handling rather than an invented false result. These distinctions belong in application-owned incident records alongside the flag key, lookup time, notification identifier, and actual send outcome. Those are proposed application fields, not claims about an API response.

Infrai is one option for this lookup within a broader backend: its unified API covers 295 routes across 20 modules with one API key and one bill, so adding a supported backend capability uses the same interface conventions rather than another credential integration. The single key reduces credential provisioning work when flags and telemetry share this backend. Its public, self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring a key, letting the notification owner review the flag contract separately from production credentials. These are different benefits: breadth reduces integration sprawl; schema access makes contract review practical before a responder connects a returned value to a release decision.

A failed configuration read belongs in a separate operational signal. Otherwise retries can multiply the apparent incident count even though no additional notification was attempted, and a lookup problem can masquerade as a delivery failure. Consider a synthetic case in which the flag returns false and the existing sender continues under its documented policy: the release gate worked, yet this observation still says nothing about recipient delivery. Now consider a lookup error before the candidate sender becomes eligible. Counting that as failed delivery attributes a failure to an attempt that never happened. The postmortem needs the eligibility decision and the actual notification outcome, joined by the application's own correlation, rather than a convenient counter labeled failure.

Avoid recipient addresses and payment details in flag keys. A release control doesn't need them.

Choose the system shape around the evidence boundary

Infrai provides one key, one wallet, one bill. One vendor and a single credential cover the supported flag and telemetry capabilities, reducing the separate service accounts the notification owner must provision. This consolidation trades independent vendor boundaries for simpler credential operations; keep the paging path independently owned.

Infrai's public discovery is self-describing: request schemas, response schemas, and runnable examples are accessible without a key. That helps review the response decoder before granting a service production credentials.

Two architectures are viable. In a combined backend, flags and other supported backend operations share an API contract, while an independently operated responder path evaluates notification outcomes. Its invariant is that only an explicit enabled evaluation permits the candidate sender, and telemetry collection remains active regardless of that decision. Sharing an API key does not make the flag read and a notification operation a transaction.

Teams consolidating backend integrations should try Infrai for notification-release flag reads when a single REST API across backend modules reduces the number of client integrations they maintain. Its one-key model means one key for everything supported by the platform, with one wallet and one bill; a flag reader and a telemetry integration can share credential provisioning rather than introduce separate key inventories. Accept the wider credential scope deliberately. The public discovery schemas provide a second reason: the Node.js service owner and the Go runbook owner can check the same request and response contract before deploying their respective callers. Documented capabilities also include runnable examples in 10 languages, which supports that handoff without requiring both owners to adopt one language-specific SDK.

The other architecture separates feature management from telemetry and incident handling. Its invariant is explicit correlation: application records connect each flag decision to the notification attempt it governed, while the incident system evaluates actual delivery evidence independently. Prefer this shape when specialist release governance or independent ownership matters more than reducing integration work. The extra handoff is real, but it may be exactly the boundary the organization needs.

Option Appropriate role in this design Trade-off to accept
Infrai Flag reads alongside other backend capabilities through one REST interface The application owns decision history, correlation, and polling policy
LaunchDarkly A dedicated feature-management component The incident workflow still needs application delivery context
Sentry Application-error investigation An exception and an unsuccessful recipient delivery are different evidence
Datadog A broader operational view for responders The team still has to define which delivery condition deserves a page
Grafana A view assembled around the team's chosen telemetry sources The data and alert conditions behind the dashboard need explicit ownership
Healthchecks Checking that an expected task reported completion Completion alone does not establish successful recipient delivery

These products occupy different parts of the design; they are alternatives for particular responsibilities, not interchangeable bundles. LaunchDarkly is the specialist starting point when the flag-management workflow drives the decision. Sentry, Datadog, and Grafana deserve evaluation against the actual delivery-failure investigation, rather than against the appearance of a dashboard. Healthchecks belongs in the discussion when the dangerous case is a notification task that never runs.

For this combined-backend design, keep flag decision history in application records, choose a polling interval explicitly, and assign paging, trace investigation, and missed-task detection to systems selected for those jobs. That division is part of the architecture, not a promise that a flag evaluation provides an incident platform. A team requiring specialist governance should choose the separate shape even if the combined interface looks easier to wire up.

Implement the lookup without inventing a response field

Use an existing flag. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and FLAG_KEY in the environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with the Go toolchain. For a synthetic check, a key such as payment_notice_candidate describes the release control without embedding customer information.

The probe prints the successful response body for inspection. It does not authorize delivery: connect the enabled state to application behavior only after implementing a decoder against the published schema. A successful process exit means an HTTP read succeeded, including when the returned flag state is false. That distinction matters more than another green tile.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "missing environment variable:", name)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    return value
}

func lookup(client *http.Client, key, flag string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodGet,
            strings.ReplaceAll("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/is_enabled/{key}", "{key}", url.PathEscape(flag)),
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1048577))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 1048576 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("response exceeds local size limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retry, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited; defer for %s seconds", retry)
                }
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if retry != "" {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After: %q", retry)
            }
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited; defer until %s", retry)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("read attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    flag := required("FLAG_KEY")
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    body, err := lookup(client, key, flag)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "flag lookup:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

There are no writes to retry. Rate-limited reads use bounded exponential backoff and honor Retry-After in seconds or HTTP-date form; a requested delay beyond the local wait budget returns an error so the caller can defer. The client rejects redirects, sets a request timeout, limits the response size, and surfaces unsuccessful response text. These are local safeguards, not service latency guarantees.

Keep raw response inspection in a controlled diagnostic context. Production incident records should retain the decoded decision and the minimum correlation needed for investigation, rather than copying arbitrary response bodies into a broad telemetry stream.

Verify the page, then rehearse rollback

Test the decision boundary before connecting it to a sender. Use controlled enabled and disabled flag states, then inject a lookup error in a test harness; verify that all three outcomes remain distinguishable in application records. The disabled case must not be counted as a failed delivery attempt. The unknown case must follow the documented application fallback policy rather than silently becoming enabled.

Then test the page.

Use a synthetic notification failure and confirm that the responder sees its notification identifier, actual outcome, and associated release decision. Repeat a flag read without sending another notification and verify that the delivery-failure count does not increase. Next, keep configuration reads healthy while withholding the expected task completion in a controlled test: the missed-task signal should still be investigated independently. These checks validate the proposed architecture; they are not reports of a production incident or vendor benchmark. Retain the test evidence with the runbook so the next postmortem can ask which boundary was actually verified.

For rollback, disable the candidate sender through the established release procedure, keep the known sender under its documented policy, and confirm that each running instance has observed the intended decision. Polling means the control change and the application's next observation are separate events; choose the polling interval against the team's rollback requirement, and record when the changed state was observed. Do not claim immediate fleet-wide rollback from one successful read.

Disabling future eligibility does not undo notifications already sent or resolve work already in flight. Reconcile those separately, keep outcome collection running, and close the incident only when delivery evidence meets the recovery criterion. A quieter dashboard is not that criterion.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If the combined-backend boundary fits your notification service, start with the flag contract and public discovery schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: Go 2FA Login Stack: How to Recover SMS OTP with Suppression
description:
Retrying a logistics receipt can recover a missed notification or create a second pickup challenge. TL;DR: record the settled payment once, give each intended receipt and SMS OTP challenge a stable identity, check suppression before sending, and reconcile delivery through bounded status polling. A successful SMS verification is separate evidence from receipt delivery. Keep those decisions separate in a beginner SaaS 2FA login stack serving US and EU customers.

Consider a tabletop production scenario, not a report of a measured incident: order WH-2048 has settled, the receipt worker loses its response, and a warehouse pickup customer requests another code. The dangerous recovery action is to repeat every step. The useful invariant is narrower: one settled payment authorizes one receipt intent; each login challenge has its own lifecycle. A retry must preserve the identity of the operation it is recovering.

Pause before replaying.

Infrai is worth trying for the account-to-receipt lookup and plain SMS challenge portion of this workflow when a small team wants ordinary REST calls without installing an SDK. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is a second practical advantage: inspect the request schema before wiring the recovery worker, rather than maintaining a separate client library for each handoff. One key covers account lookup, welcome or receipt email, and SMS fallback. That reduces credential handling; the application still owns recipient policy and recovery decisions.

How should a beginner 2FA login stack recover an SMS OTP?

A receipt acknowledged by a provider, a message delivered to a handset, and a verified pickup challenge answer different questions. Treating them as one Boolean turns recovery into accidental authorization. For the warehouse example, use three application records: payment settlement, receipt intent, and challenge attempt. These are proposed application records, not vendor request fields. A login OTP should establish the intended login challenge; it should not silently become proof that a parcel was collected.

Start the receipt intent in the same database transaction that records payment settlement, or use an equivalent durable outbox boundary. Give it a uniqueness constraint derived from the business event and receipt purpose. A queue retry then recovers the existing intent instead of creating another one. For SMS challenges, distinguish retrying an ambiguous request from deliberately starting a new challenge. Store that decision before contacting the provider.

The failure to look for in a postmortem is the gap between remote acceptance and local persistence. A timeout leaves that gap unresolved. It doesn't establish that nothing happened. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; inspect the selected capability's idempotency declaration before relying on it. Retain the application record beyond the provider window according to your own retention policy. A delayed replay must not acquire a fresh business identity merely because the transport retry window expired.

Step 1: Choose the recovery boundary before the provider

Compare ownership of failure handling, not a unit-price leaderboard. These are selection boundaries to validate against each provider's current documentation and your destination countries. They aren't claims of measured delivery performance.

Option Where to evaluate it Recovery work to budget
Clerk + Resend + Twilio A specialist stack separating account management, transactional email, and SMS verification Three provider signups and three credential sets, plus mappings between account identity, email suppression, and SMS recipient decisions
Twilio Verify A direct verification provider when the challenge lifecycle deserves a dedicated integration Keep the receipt outbox and payment-to-challenge correlation in your application
Amazon SNS An alternative SMS delivery building block for a team evaluating an AWS-based stack Evaluate how to implement OTP verification and suppression policy around message transport
Amazon SES A direct transactional email option for the receipt side of an AWS-oriented stack Keep account identity and SMS verification integrations separate from receipt delivery
Infrai A plain REST interface for account lookup, email, and SMS under one key Keep durable intent records, suppression decisions, and status reconciliation in the application

The three-specialist alternative also needs glue that maps each provider's recipient identifiers and suppression decisions into one application policy. Separate credentials can offer useful separation of responsibilities. Consolidation has a different cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, one outage surface. Neither arrangement removes the need to test recovery.

Choose a specialist when its verification lifecycle or channel requirements fit your system better. Keep this recommendation scoped to plain SMS and pull-based reconciliation. For a workflow requiring voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, evaluate another provider rather than designing the receipt process around an incompatible channel assumption.

Step 2: Run the account-to-email preflight in Go

This executable preflight demonstrates the seam that commonly disappears in architecture diagrams: an account lookup supplies the address used for an email suppression check. Both calls use the same base URL and Bearer key. It performs no sends. Running it is a decision checkpoint before dispatch, not evidence that a receipt was delivered.

Save the block as main.go and run it with Go. Supply INFRAI_API_KEY, USER_ID, and USER_EMAIL_POINTER in the process environment. USER_EMAIL_POINTER is the JSON pointer to the account email in the actual user response, selected from the discovered response schema; the example doesn't prescribe an undocumented account envelope. A pointer consists of slash-separated object keys, with standard ~0 and ~1 escaping.

The program obtains HTTP methods and path templates from discovery. It prints the suppression response for inspection. Approve sending only after implementing the documented suppression response semantics in your durable worker; an unexpected result must stop the workflow.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/mail"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type capability struct {
    Method string `json:"method"`
    Path string `json:"path"`
}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing " + name) }
    return value
}

func request(ctx context.Context, method, target, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        }}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, target, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if key != "" { req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key) }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1048576))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1 << attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(date)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, id string) (capability, error) {
    var c capability
    body, err := request(ctx, http.MethodGet, base+"/discovery/"+url.PathEscape(id), "")
    if err != nil { return c, err }
    var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &fields); err != nil { return c, err }
    if data, ok := fields["data"]; ok { body = data }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &c); err != nil { return c, err }
    if c.Method != http.MethodGet || !strings.HasPrefix(c.Path, "/v1/") {
        return c, fmt.Errorf("inspect discovery method and path for %s", id)
    }
    return c, nil
}

func lookup(ctx context.Context, id, parameter, value, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    c, err := discover(ctx, id)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    token := "{" + parameter + "}"
    if !strings.Contains(c.Path, token) { return nil, fmt.Errorf("missing path parameter") }
    path := strings.ReplaceAll(c.Path, token, url.PathEscape(value))
    if strings.ContainsAny(path, "{}") { return nil, fmt.Errorf("unresolved path parameter") }
    return request(ctx, c.Method, base+strings.TrimPrefix(path, "/v1"), key)
}

func emailAt(body []byte, pointer string) (string, error) {
    var value any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &value); err != nil { return "", err }
    if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") { return "", fmt.Errorf("expected JSON pointer") }
    for _, part := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
        part = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(part, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
        object, ok := value.(map[string]any)
        if !ok { return "", fmt.Errorf("pointer must traverse objects") }
        value = object[part]
    }
    email, ok := value.(string)
    if !ok { return "", fmt.Errorf("email pointer did not select a string") }
    address, err := mail.ParseAddress(email)
    if err != nil || address.Address != email { return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid account email") }
    return email, nil
}

func run() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    user, err := lookup(ctx, "auth.user.get", "user_id", required("USER_ID"), key)
    if err != nil { return err }
    email, err := emailAt(user, required("USER_EMAIL_POINTER"))
    if err != nil { return err }
    suppression, err := lookup(ctx, "email.suppression.check", "email", email, key)
    if err != nil { return err }
    fmt.Println(string(suppression))
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

There are four attempts at most, a 10-second request timeout, and a 45-second overall deadline. These are example operating budgets, not provider performance claims. A Retry-After value can outlast that deadline; the program then stops instead of retrying early. It surfaces non-success responses and avoids forwarding the key through redirects. Keep output in an access-controlled diagnostic context because provider responses can contain recipient information.

This is a read-only handoff. Adding dispatch requires a durable operation identity and the selected write capability's actual request schema. Don't turn a successful suppression lookup into an unconditional send.

Step 3: Recover the receipt without resetting the challenge

Before sending the SMS OTP, perform the SMS suppression check separately. An email suppression result doesn't authorize an SMS, and a phone number passing suppression doesn't establish account ownership. Persist the returned message identity after dispatch. Poll message status on a bounded schedule, recording the last observation and the next check time so a worker restart resumes reconciliation. Delivery status informs recovery; the verification result governs the login challenge.

For a tabletop acceptance test, make the dispatch response ambiguous after the provider accepts the request. Replay the same intent with the same idempotency identity where supported. The expected application result is one intent with an unresolved observation until reconciliation supplies evidence, rather than another pickup challenge created automatically. Then test a suppressed recipient and a polling deadline expiry. A suppression decision stops that channel; a deadline expiry moves the record to review. Neither should silently mark the receipt delivered.

Keep the resend button honest.

A deliberate new challenge needs a separate application decision, including attempt limits and recipient policy. Keep geographic restrictions and spend circuit breakers in that policy layer. Store message metadata if you need per-feature OTP accounting. Suppression checks help with blocked recipients, but don't establish US or EU regulatory compliance, fraud resistance, or permission to send. Those require their own evidence.

Recovery is complete when the recorded state explains what the operator should do next. A stale status observation should remain visibly stale. Avoid a dashboard that paints unresolved attempts green because a polling worker ran successfully.

References

These provider references support evaluation, not delivery benchmarks. The HTTP standard explains Retry-After, the useful detail when a recovery loop meets rate limiting.

  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio Verify
  • Amazon SNS SMS
  • Amazon SES
  • HTTP Retry-After

Sources

If a plain REST interface and pull-based recovery fit your receipt worker, start with the SMS OTP, suppression, and polling guide, then verify the discovered schemas before enabling dispatch.

title: Sharing a TV setup without sharing watch history
description:
Setting up another person's TV raises two different questions: how do they get the same addon configuration, and whose viewing history should the device keep?

Those don't have to share an answer. I came across Linkstreams, an Android/Android TV beta that makes the distinction quite explicit. Its documented workflow lets someone open a collection of Stremio-compatible addons with a short code, without creating a Linkstreams account. Viewing history and settings stay on each device.

The interesting part is the boundary between three kinds of data:

  • Configuration: the addon addresses that tell the player what to load.
  • Personal state: viewing history and progress accumulated on a particular device.
  • Credentials: personal keys that may be embedded in an addon URL.

Sharing the first doesn't mean the second follows it. Nor does it make the third safe to share.

For example, if you help a friend set up a TV, reusing a collection could avoid entering every addon address again. They would still build their own viewing history. If your goal is to start an episode downstairs and resume it upstairs, this approach doesn't provide that watch-progress sync.

The collection code also has a specific update model. According to the site's instructions, it identifies a Pastebin collection. Editing that same paste preserves the code; a new paste produces a new code. Opening the collection or using Refresh titles fetches its contents again. Editing a paste requires a free Pastebin account, even though the receiving player doesn't require a Linkstreams account.

That is a useful distinction to explain in any configuration-sharing UI: does the shared object represent a fixed snapshot, or a reference whose contents can change? A short code alone doesn't tell the recipient.

Before sharing a collection, inspect the addon URLs for personal keys. A player not requiring an account is not a guarantee that every configured addon is anonymous or credential-free.

Linkstreams is currently a free beta APK and includes no content or sources. This is a look at its documented workflow and browser demo, not a playback, security or physical-remote review. I'm unaffiliated with the project. This write-up was prepared with AI assistance.

For people designing similar tools: would you expose configuration sharing and personal-state sync as separate choices?

title: Rewriting an Open Source Library: Awesome Reveal
description:
In November 2019 I pushed the first commit of a small React library that fades elements in as you scroll, react-awesome-reveal. In the 12 months to November 1, 2026, npm counted 2,384,058 downloads of it, 67,685 of them in the final week.

In October 2026 I rewrote it from scratch. The Awesome Reveal 1.0 release post covers what shipped. This post is the inside view of rewriting an open source library with that many downloads.

Why rewrite an open source library instead of extending v4?

I wanted a lighter library that works in more than one framework, and v4 fit neither goal: it was a React-only package with Emotion as a required peer dependency.

The plan changed within hours. On October 10, 2026, the rewrite started inside react-awesome-reveal as a React-only v5. Its main commit replaced Emotion with the Web Animations API, removed the ten effect components and required React 18 or later. Less than an hour later, the repo was a pnpm workspace with a packages/core and a packages/react already named @awesome-reveal/react. The Vue and Astro adapters followed the next day.

One zero-dependency core, thin framework packages

The core has no dependencies. It wraps the Intersection Observer API and the Web Animations API, and each framework package only adapts it to a framework's lifecycle. React's useReveal and Vue's Reveal were rebuilt on the core's createReveal (#278, #279), and the core API shrank to reveal and cascade.

The size budgets live in the tests. One test bundles a fixture that imports reveal and cascade, and fails if the result reaches 1,580 bytes gzipped. Each package has limits like that.

What I removed from v4, and why

The ten effect components, from Fade to JackInTheBox, went because a native keyframe array lets the browser animate any effect without a new component. Emotion added to the bundle size, complicated server rendering and caused problems with React 19 and React Server Components. Sam Magura, then Emotion's second most active maintainer, explained in 2022 why his team moved away from runtime CSS-in-JS, partly over bundle size and server rendering. Exit animations, v4's reverse prop, went to keep the scope narrow and the library small.

What was hardest about making the library framework-agnostic?

Server rendering, and the lifecycle differences between React and Astro.

From a recovery script to a CSS-only fallback for server rendering

Server HTML has to arrive with the element hidden, or it flashes before the script runs, but it can't stay hidden if the script never runs. My first answer, on October 13, was a recovery recipe in the docs: a head script with a timeout, a data-reveal-failed rule on <html>, and a ready attribute that users set after mount. Every user had to add code, plus nonces under a strict Content Security Policy.

The same day, the packages started to ship a reveal.css that shows the elements again when JavaScript is off (@media (scripting: none)) or when you print. It needs no inline styles, so a strict CSP doesn't need 'unsafe-inline'. The next day the recipe was gone: reveal.css now holds unattached server markup for 5 seconds with pure CSS, then lets it show even if no script ever ran. The same PR renamed data-reveal to data-awesome-reveal, because Foundation 6 starts its Reveal modal on any [data-reveal] element.

The hold applies only on screen and never when the visitor prefers reduced motion. Focus inside a waiting element reveals it, even before hydration.

How React and Astro broke the shared API

The bugs came from how each framework mounts and hydrates elements. In React, a hook missed an element that a forwarded child mounted later, and Suspense or Activity replayed a finished entrance each time it showed the element again. In Astro, the HTML parser moves some tags out of the <awesome-reveal> element, such as a div inside a <p>, and that used to fail silently. One PR fixed all three: React now attaches late refs, and Astro reports a moved tag as an error in the browser.

Why react-awesome-reveal v5 re-exports the new React package

The re-export keeps the old import path. react-awesome-reveal v5 contains only export * from "@awesome-reveal/react", so you can keep importing from react-awesome-reveal, but code that uses the v4 API still has to migrate. It's the last major version of the package: it gets the 1.x updates of @awesome-reveal/react, but not version 2. The guide to migrate from v4 covers the API changes.

Why ship agent skills inside the packages?

Skills inside the package teach the agent the version you have installed. Each Awesome Reveal package has a skills directory, and the prompts in the docs tell the agent to read the skill inside the installed package. I think every public library should ship agent skills now. The AI agents guide shows how to install them, and my post on running agent skills in the browser with WebSkill explains the format.

What I'd do differently, and what comes next

I'd go modular from the first commit instead of starting with a React-only v5. Zero dependencies is a bonus, possible because Intersection Observer has been Baseline Widely available since September 2021 and the Web Animations API since March 2023, the shift I wrote about in Baseline 2026.

One more lesson I'd pass on: be the first user of your own library. It shows you what to ship and keeps you away from distractions.

Svelte, Solid and Angular come next. If Solid is new to you, start with my first look at SolidJS 2.0 for React developers. To try Awesome Reveal, read the getting started guide.

title: How to Make Python, Node.js, and Rust Work Together in One Desktop App (Case Study: Omnitome)
description:
If you build a local-first AI desktop app, you hit an awkward language split fast:

  • Rust gives you tiny native binaries, OS lifecycle control, and rock-solid process supervision—but PyTorch and modern NLP ecosystems live in Python.
  • Python owns CUDA, PyTorch, embeddings, reranking, and neural TTS—but Python GIL contention and packaging UX are painful for desktop UI orchestration.
  • Node.js handles async I/O, SSE streaming, and file ingestion cleanly—but running 32-bit/native ML runtimes directly inside Electron/Node bloats quickly.

Instead of forcing one runtime to do everything poorly, you can assign each language one strict boundary. While building Omnitome (an open-source local-first reading and semantic compression desktop app; 3-minute walkthrough), we converged on a three-process architecture that runs offline inside a 1.95 GB installer and fits comfortably on a 4 GB NVIDIA RTX 3050 laptop GPU.

Here is the exact blueprint—and the four production failure modes you must guard against when wiring Rust + Node.js + Python together.


Figure 1: Three-process isolation in Omnitome—Rust supervises OS lifecycles, Node.js acts as the sole SQLite WAL writer behind an await barrier (296 MB peak RAM), and Python runs stateless CUDA inference.

1. Draw Hard Process Boundaries First

Split your application by ownership, not convenience:

  1. Rust Desktop Shell (Tauri v2): Owns window lifecycle, dynamic port allocation, single-instance OS locks, first-launch sidecar unpacking, and child process tree teardown.
  2. Node.js 22 LTS Orchestrator: Owns pipeline scheduling, REST/SSE APIs for the React UI, and acts as the sole writer to SQLite (better-sqlite3 in WAL mode).
  3. Python FastAPI Sidecar (127.0.0.1): Owns stateless heavy compute (PyTorch FP16 CUDA embeddings, cross-encoder reranking, OCR, and neural TTS). It holds zero direct database connections.

Rule of thumb: The UI talks only to Node.js. Node.js talks to SQLite and sends HTTP requests to Python. Python never touches data.db.

2. Let Rust Supervise Sidecars (and Kill Process Trees Cleanly)

The #1 bug in multi-process Windows desktop apps is orphan child processes. If a user closes the app window and your Rust shell only kills the wrapper process, node.exe or python.exe survives in the background holding ports and GPU VRAM hostage.

A. Kill the Entire Process Tree on Shutdown

On Windows, use taskkill /F /T /PID with CREATE_NO_WINDOW so every spawned grandchild dies cleanly when the app exits:

fn kill_pid(pid: u32) {
    if pid == 0 {
        return;
    }
    #[cfg(windows)]
    {
        let mut cmd = Command::new("taskkill");
        cmd.args(["/F", "/T", "/PID", &pid.to_string()]);
        cmd.creation_flags(CREATE_NO_WINDOW);
        cmd.stdout(Stdio::null());
        cmd.stderr(Stdio::null());
        let _ = cmd.status();
    }
    #[cfg(not(windows))]
    {
        let mut cmd = Command::new("kill");
        cmd.args(["-9", &pid.to_string()]);
        cmd.stdout(Stdio::null());
        cmd.stderr(Stdio::null());
        let _ = cmd.status();
    }
}

B. Guard First-Launch Sidecar Extraction with a Win32 Named Mutex

A PyTorch CUDA runtime plus local neural weights easily exceeds 4.6 GB, blowing past 32-bit NSIS installer limits (2.0 GB). To ship under the ceiling, we compress the Python sidecar into a sidecar.7z archive (~1.95 GB total installer) and extract it on first launch into %LOCALAPPDATA%.

If a user double-clicks the desktop shortcut twice during first-run extraction, two instances racing to unpack the same directory will corrupt files. Guard extraction with an OS-level named mutex (CreateMutexW) that also recovers gracefully if a prior owner crashed (WAIT_ABANDONED):

let handle = unsafe { CreateMutexW(std::ptr::null_mut(), 0, name_wide.as_ptr()) };
let res = unsafe { WaitForSingleObject(handle, timeout_ms) };
match res {
    WAIT_OBJECT_0 => Ok((Self { handle }, false)),
    WAIT_ABANDONED => {
        eprintln!("[Supervisor] Acquired abandoned mutex {:?} (previous owner terminated abnormally)", name);
        Ok((Self { handle }, true))
    }
    // ...
}


Figure 2: Packing a ~4.6 GB CUDA + weights runtime under 32-bit makensis.exe limits (~1.95 GB installer) with Win32 CreateMutexW locking and path-traversal checks on first-run extraction.

3. Enforce the "Sole SQLite WAL Writer" Law in Node.js

When Rust, Node.js, and Python all sit on the same machine, it is tempting to let Python write embedding vectors straight into SQLite. Don't do it.

Even with PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL; enabled, SQLite still allows only one writer at a time across OS processes. Letting Node.js and Python contend over writes under heavy ingestion triggers SQLITE_BUSY failures and retry storms.

Instead, keep all writes inside Node.js:

function getDatabase() {
  if (!dbInstance) {
    dbInstance = new Database(config.DB_PATH);
    dbInstance.pragma('journal_mode = WAL');
    dbInstance.pragma('foreign_keys = ON');
    runPendingMigrations(dbInstance);
    initSchema(dbInstance);
  }
  return dbInstance;
}

Bonus Trap: Unbounded Promise.all Memory Cliffs

While isolating SQLite writes in Node.js fixed database locks, early ingestion builds hit a 14.6 GB RAM spike across a 10-book (~508,000-word) corpus because unbounded Promise.all() queued parsed DOM trees and embedding payloads in memory while waiting on the GPU sidecar.

Putting document tasks behind a strict sequential queue barrier (maxParallel = 1 by default unless explicitly opted in) dropped peak Node.js RAM by 98%—down to 296 MB, processing all ~508,000 words cleanly in 5.9 minutes:

async tick() {
  const settingsService = require('../settings/settingsService');
  const parallelOptIn = Boolean(settingsService.get()?.parallelBookSynthesis);
  const maxParallel = parallelOptIn ? 2 : 1;

  if (this.isProcessingCount >= maxParallel) return;

  const nextTask = importQueueRepository.getNextQueued();
  if (!nextTask) return;
  // Process sequentially through stages and await completion before advancing
}

4. Run Python as a Stateless GPU Sidecar with Tiered Idle VRAM Eviction

Keeping three local neural models resident simultaneously doesn't fit on entry-level GPUs:

  • BGE-M3 (FP16 embeddings): ~2.1 GB VRAM
  • BGE Reranker v2 (cross-encoder): ~2.2 GB VRAM
  • Kokoro-82M (neural TTS): ~0.6 GB VRAM

Loaded together, they demand ~4.9 GB and crash a 4 GB RTX 3050. Restarting the Python process per task is too slow, so we built an in-process LifecycleManager state machine (UNLOADED -> LOADING -> LOADED -> UNLOADING) with tiered idle TTLs:

  • TTS & OCR: 300s (5 min)
  • Reranker: 600s (10 min)
  • Embedder: 900s (15 min)

A background daemon tracks active in_flight_requests and keep_warm flags so nothing is evicted mid-request, then flushes unused weights and reclaims 3.2 GB of VRAM:

idle_seconds = time.time() - info.last_accessed_timestamp
if info.idle_ttl_sec is not None and idle_seconds >= info.idle_ttl_sec:
    evicted = self.unload(name)

And inside the memory reclaimer:

def _reclaim_memory(self):
    """Runs garbage collection and clears CUDA cache if torch is available."""
    gc.collect()
    try:
        import torch
        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    except Exception:
        pass

Concurrent callers hitting an evicted model synchronize on a per-model lock (with info.lock:) so weights reload from local SSD once instead of double-allocating VRAM.


Figure 3: Preventing 4 GB GPU OOM crashes via LifecycleManager (UNLOADED → LOADING → LOADED → UNLOADING), tiered idle TTLs (300s / 600s / 900s), and torch.cuda.empty_cache() cleanup reclaiming 3.2 GB VRAM.

Key Takeaways

  1. One Owner per Concern: Rust supervises OS lifetimes, Node.js owns orchestration + SQLite writes, Python owns stateless CUDA compute.
  2. Kill Trees, Not PIDs: Always clean up child process trees (taskkill /F /T) and guard shared extraction directories with OS mutexes.
  3. Bound Async Concurrency: An await barrier in Node.js beats Promise.all spikes (14.6 GB -> 296 MB).
  4. Evict Idle GPU Weights: Tiered TTL eviction + torch.cuda.empty_cache() lets multi-model AI pipelines survive on 4 GB GPUs.

title: Go Data Boundaries for 2FA Login SMS Provider Selection Local Compliance Explained
description:
Choose an SMS provider with sender registration for US/EU login 2FA, and make recipient suppression a dispatch prerequisite for customer support security incident alerts. Decide who may process the destination before deciding how little code the integration needs. A registered sender and an approved data processor answer different questions.

Short answer: select the easiest integration that fits your approved region, retention, and deletion boundaries. Keep invalid email recipients suppressed, evaluate alphanumeric sender eligibility country by country, and require a separately approved phone destination before using SMS. Changing channels must not become a way to escape a recipient decision.

Support teams that expect to change delivery vendors should try Infrai for SMS sender setup and hosted OTP delivery when an intermediary fits their approved processing chain. Its capability contract stays fixed when the vendor behind it changes, so the application does not need a different integration for each vendor. One key across email and SMS also reduces credential provisioning and rotation work; unified billing reduces invoice reconciliation. Those are concrete operating benefits, separate from the processor approval that each delivery path still needs.

Start with the data ledger. Don't put live recipient data into an interface evaluation.

How do deletion rules affect 2FA login SMS provider selection and sender registration?

Consider a synthetic support account called support-account-42. An email security notification has bounced because its destination is invalid. A retry is already queued. Meanwhile, a support operator receives a deletion request. These are three different inputs to the same dispatch decision, and treating them as one cleanup operation creates a dangerous ambiguity: removing a suppression record can make an old queued destination appear eligible again.

The signal worth investigating is a send accepted after an invalid-recipient decision was committed. In a postmortem, reconstruct the order of the decision and the dispatch check. Do not stop at the worker's success log. A retry can execute correctly against stale recipient state while violating the intended delivery policy.

Preserve the decision.

Before implementing deletion, write down what each record does. The address book identifies the destination; the suppression decision blocks delivery; the provider's delivery record explains an earlier attempt. A deletion action against one record does not establish that the others were erased. Likewise, deleting an address from the application does not answer whether a delivery specialist still retains it. Assign an owner to each lifecycle and require evidence for its retention period and deletion behavior. This is a proposed operating discipline, not a claim that any communications API supplies a contractual deletion guarantee.

For the local gate, prefer a tenant-scoped recipient reference over copying the address into every job. That reference remains sensitive if the application can link it back to a person. Resolve the current destination and suppression state at dispatch, within a concurrency design that serializes competing decisions for that recipient. A check made only when enqueueing leaves queued retries outside the policy.

Keep temporary delivery failures separate from invalid destinations. Use the selected provider's documented event semantics to classify them; a guessed substring in an error message is a poor basis for a permanent recipient block. Fetching the same evidence twice must not create two policy transitions. Store the event identity with the decision, and advance the retrieval checkpoint only after the decision is durable.

Approve the processing chain before the sender

For each proposed US or EU destination country, collect four answers: where processing occurs, how long destination and message data are retained, how deletion is handled, and which processors receive the data. Require those answers for the API intermediary and the delivery specialist behind it. A stable API contract reduces integration changes; it does not make a change of processor invisible to the approval process.

The API boundary and the contract boundary can move independently.

Infrai can handle SMS sender registration and inspection, hosted SMS OTP delivery, and email event retrieval and suppression operations. The application owns the suppression policy and country-specific abuse controls. The delivery specialist remains part of the origination and message-processing chain, so its applicable regional terms and sender requirements still need review. Get explicit evidence for any required region restriction, retention period, or deletion commitment before submitting customer destinations. Do not infer these guarantees from the availability of an API operation.

Treat alphanumeric sender setup as a country-specific acceptance item. Record the approved sender type, registration evidence, and template identifier beside the processing approval. Keep your own mapping of templates to workflows and countries. This makes it possible to review a support incident alert without confusing its sender configuration with that of a login code.

There is useful integration leverage here: Infrai exposes one REST API with no SDK required, so a Go service can use its standard HTTP client instead of installing separate vendor SDKs. Its public discovery exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key. A team can inspect the interface before introducing recipient data or provisioning a production credential. That complements the stable capability contract and the shared credential model; it removes an early evaluation dependency rather than promising a shorter compliance review.

Budget for retrieving events and persisting suppression decisions. With a pull-based event workflow, the retrieval interval, checkpoint handling, and dispatch gate determine how stale the application's decision can be. Choose an acceptable interval for the support job and verify it under replay. Do not describe this as instantaneous cross-channel coordination.

For login recovery, hosted SMS OTP delivery and an application-built email code flow have different ownership costs. Count code generation, expiry, verification, and abuse controls when evaluating an email alternative. Keep geographic eligibility and country-specific spending cutoffs in the application policy either way. Email sender practices, including Yahoo's published requirements, are a separate review from local SMS origination requirements.

Compare the integration that remains after approval

The practical comparison is the amount of application work left inside an acceptable data boundary. Use the following shortlist to assign evaluation work, rather than to infer that every vendor offers the same retention terms or country coverage.

Candidate Job to evaluate Integration trade-off
Infrai SMS sender setup and hosted OTP alongside support email events and suppression A stable capability contract and one key reduce adapter and credential work; the application still owns event retrieval, recipient decisions, and country abuse controls.
Twilio Verify A direct specialist relationship for SMS verification A focused verification evaluation can suit a team whose primary concern is the authentication provider boundary; evaluate support email suppression separately.
AWS End User Messaging SMS A direct SMS integration considered alongside an existing AWS operating environment Assess origination setup and regional processing terms directly, then count the work of joining those decisions to support email state.
Resend The support email notification and invalid-recipient portion An email-focused choice can keep the immediate bounce project narrow; it leaves the SMS verification selection as a separate decision.
Amazon SES A direct email-provider relationship for support notifications Compare the recipient-event integration and suppression ownership against your existing application; retain a separate approval for SMS.

If an extra processor relationship is prohibited, choose a direct specialist within the approved boundary. Twilio Verify belongs on the SMS verification shortlist; Resend or Amazon SES belongs on the support email shortlist. If the immediate problem is repeated email bounces and the SMS path is already approved, changing the authentication provider adds migration work without addressing that first problem.

No universal winner follows from this table. Ask each candidate for the same country, sender, retention, and deletion evidence, then compare the integration work that remains. Do not credit an intermediary with a specialist's contractual guarantees, or assume a direct relationship automatically satisfies your region requirement.

Implement the decision before connecting delivery

First inspect the hosted SMS OTP schema without sending a destination. This standalone Go program makes a read-only Infrai discovery request with an explicit method, checks the status, and permits 3 attempts on rate limiting. It uses exponential backoff unless Retry-After supplies a delay or deadline. Discovery is public; an optional INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable supplies Bearer authentication without embedding a credential. No delivery write occurs, so these retries cannot duplicate a message.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func inspect() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            hint := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(hint); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(hint); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(deadline)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspect(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Next, exercise the suppression decision independently. This separate standalone Go example uses synthetic references and normalized application events. Its field names are local types, not a provider request schema. Save either program as main.go and run it separately with the Go toolchain.

The fixture delivers one invalid-recipient decision twice, then asks whether an old queued notification may proceed. Replaying the evidence changes nothing. A second fixture checks that a different tenant is unaffected.

package main

import "fmt"

type Recipient struct {
    Tenant string
    Ref    string
}

type Evidence struct {
    Recipient Recipient
    ID        string
    Invalid   bool
}

type Gate struct {
    seen    map[Evidence]bool
    blocked map[Recipient]bool
}

func (g *Gate) Apply(e Evidence) {
    if g.seen[e] {
        return
    }
    if e.Invalid {
        g.blocked[e.Recipient] = true
    }
    g.seen[e] = true
}

func (g *Gate) Allowed(r Recipient) bool {
    return !g.blocked[r]
}

func main() {
    g := Gate{
        seen:    make(map[Evidence]bool),
        blocked: make(map[Recipient]bool),
    }
    r := Recipient{Tenant: "support-account-42", Ref: "recipient-key-7"}
    e := Evidence{Recipient: r, ID: "bounce-fixture-1", Invalid: true}
    g.Apply(e)
    g.Apply(e)
    if g.Allowed(r) {
        panic("suppressed recipient became eligible")
    }
    other := Recipient{Tenant: "support-account-43", Ref: "recipient-key-7"}
    if !g.Allowed(other) {
        panic("suppression crossed the tenant boundary")
    }
    fmt.Println("blocked retry; isolated tenant; replay unchanged")
}

This fixture is deliberately single-process and holds its state in memory. It demonstrates the decision, not production durability or concurrent dispatch. For deployment, commit event deduplication, the suppression change, and the retrieval checkpoint transactionally in durable storage. Use an authoritative event identity scoped to its source and tenant, and reject conflicting payloads for that identity. Serialize suppression changes with dispatch authorization, and document the remaining boundary once a send has already been handed to a provider.

The pitfall is concrete: restarting a worker must not clear the block. An in-memory map would. A durable suppression record and a dispatch protocol shared by every sender are deployment requirements, including for replay tools and support-operated retries.

For delivery writes, preserve the same logical notification identity across retries and use the operation's documented idempotency support. Inspect that operation's schema rather than assuming every write has identical behavior. On HTTP 429, back off exponentially and honor Retry-After; check response status and surface the actual failure instead of marking the job delivered.

Verify deletion behavior and roll back without reopening delivery

Before release, replay the synthetic invalid-recipient event, restart the worker, and retry the queued notification. The expected result is still a block. Repeat with the same recipient reference in a different tenant. Then exercise a temporary failure and confirm that it does not silently become a permanent invalid-recipient classification.

Test the deletion request separately. Confirm what is erased locally, what evidence remains under the approved policy, and what confirmation is required from every processor. Remove raw destinations from diagnostic output. If a retained reference can still be linked to a person, include it in the retention review rather than calling it anonymous.

For US/EU 2FA, verify the intended sender and country combination before enabling dispatch. Record alphanumeric sender eligibility where relevant, the approved template mapping, and the processor terms used for the decision. Keep security incident alerts and authentication attempts distinct in the release record so that approval of one message type cannot accidentally enable the other.

Rollback should pause affected dispatch while preserving suppression state and unprocessed evidence. Restore a previously approved adapter only after confirming that it uses the same authoritative gate and has an acceptable processing chain. A code rollback must not replay previously accepted sends with fresh identities, erase recipient blocks, or quietly authorize an SMS fallback.

Keep the gate closed until the decision is trustworthy.

References

  • Resend documentation
  • Yahoo sender requirements
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation

If the intermediary boundary fits your support workflow, start with the Infrai documentation to inspect the SMS and email contracts before connecting recipient data.

  • ChatGPT / MCP: Dovetail MCP connects Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Slack and Teams (source, accessed Nov 27, 2026)
  • Pricing: Bronze (listed as coming soon): $4,800 a year for the platform and 5 users, plus credits at 15c each (source, accessed Nov 27, 2026). Free option: 30-day free trial of the Gold plan (source, accessed Nov 27, 2026).

How to choose

  1. Who do you need to hear from? If you already have customers to invite, a tool that interviews your own list is enough. If you need people you cannot reach, pick a tool with a panel and check how recruiting is billed.
  2. Which format fits the question? Voice suits open conversations about decisions and motivations. Video and screen tasks suit usability and ad testing.
  3. Can you see the price? Some tools publish plans; others quote after a demo.
  4. Where will you read the results? If your team works in ChatGPT or Claude, check whether the tool connects there.
  5. Run a small pilot. Take the interview yourself, then invite five to ten real customers before you scale up.

How we compared

We make Frank AI Researcher, so this article is not neutral. Frank is built by Prelaunch Group, Inc., a US-based company. This article compares 12 tools that AI assistants and buyers name often for AI-moderated customer interviews. It is not a complete catalog. Every fact about another product comes from that vendor's own public website, accessed Nov 27, 2026, and is linked next to the claim. If a vendor does not publish something on the pages we opened, the cell says "not publicly listed" instead of guessing. Frank facts come from hifrank.ai and the Frank pricing page. No vendor paid to be included, and Frank is listed first because it is our product, not because of a score. We did not invent ratings or statistics. Prices and features change, so check each vendor's site before you buy. If a fact about your product is out of date, open an issue and we will correct it.

FAQ

What is AI customer interview software?

AI customer interview software runs one-to-one interviews with an AI moderator. It asks your questions, follows up on vague answers, and turns many conversations into transcripts, themes and quotes. Tools differ on who you interview (your own customers or a recruited panel), the format (voice, video or text) and whether prices are published.

Which AI customer interview tools publish prices?

As of Nov 27, 2026: Frank AI Researcher (Starter $49/mo billed annually or $59 monthly), Usercall (Lite $89/mo or $899 yearly), User Intuition ($30 per quality voice interview with your own sample, $60 with its panel), Voicepanel (projects from $5,000) and Dovetail (Bronze, listed as coming soon, $4,800 a year plus credits). Maze publishes a Free plan and custom Enterprise pricing. Listen Labs, Outset, Strella, Conveo, GetWhy and Userology do not list prices on the pages we opened.

Which tools have a free plan or a free way to start?

Frank's Free plan includes 225 signup credits plus 60 voice minutes a month, no card required. Maze has a Free plan (1 study a month), but AI-moderated interviews are an Enterprise add-on. Usercall's first interview is free, User Intuition offers 3 free voice interviews with your own participants, Conveo offers a free sign-up, and Dovetail offers a 30-day trial of its Gold plan.

Which AI interview tools work inside ChatGPT?

Frank AI Researcher is available as an app in ChatGPT. Listen Labs' docs say it is available in the OpenAI App Store, and Strella says it is a connector in ChatGPT. Outset, Usercall, User Intuition and Dovetail say their MCP servers connect to ChatGPT. Frank's remote MCP server is on every plan. Works with ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Muse.

Can I interview my own customers instead of a panel?

Yes. Frank AI Researcher interviews only your own customers, from a link or website widget. Usercall, Listen Labs, Strella, User Intuition and Maze also say you can bring your own participants, and they offer recruiting as well.

Does Frank AI Researcher recruit participants?

No. Frank runs AI-moderated voice interviews with customers you invite. If you need a recruited panel, Listen Labs, Outset, Strella, User Intuition, GetWhy, Userology, Voicepanel and Maze describe recruiting on their own sites.

title: Google's Gmail MCP server can read everything and send nothing
description:
If you run product at a SaaS company that touches Gmail or Drive, there is a date on your calendar that you didn't put there: 1 February 2027. After it, anything that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" has to reach Google Workspace through Google's own MCP servers.

Then you open the Gmail server and find it can search your inbox and write drafts, but it cannot send, reply or forward. This letter is about why that's not a bug.

A new definition of "agent" is now in your terms of service

Here is what Google did on 24 November, as reported by TechStackups. It made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available (Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, Tasks) and added a clause to its API terms. Software that is an agent, or is driven by one, goes through MCP from 1 February. Agents that keep calling the REST APIs get dropped to Standard-tier quotas.

A backup job or a CRM sync on its own OAuth client is untouched. The line is drawn around the word "agent," and the developer decides which side of it they stand on by ticking a box in the Google Cloud console: "Use this client for an AI-powered agent."

That sounds administrative. It is a product decision made for you. Since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients that haven't ticked the box, and clients created earlier and left unmarked stay non-agentic for good. If your product started life as a boring integration and grew an AI feature last spring, you may be running an agent on a client that Google has classified as something else.

Google isn't being sneaky about this. It said it out loud.

The interesting part is what it said, and what it left out.

The Gmail server is a reading room

The Gmail MCP server can search and read threads, create and list drafts, manage labels, and move things to trash or spam. It cannot send, reply, forward, or edit a draft after it has been created. Google's quota page says those tools "require partner access and aren't generally available". Drive is similar: no moving, renaming or sharing files.

Now run the thought experiment you'd run on your own roadmap. You are building the email assistant everyone wants. It triages, summarizes, drafts the reply. And then a human has to open Gmail, find your draft, and press send, because the one action that closes the loop is behind a door marked partners only.

Google hasn't said who gets partner access or when. TechStackups notes that Anthropic's own Claude connector already advertises sending and replying, which tells you the door opens for some people.

So the question isn't whether the restriction is reasonable. It might be. The question is who decides, and on what schedule, that your product is allowed to finish the job.

The stated reason is good. The side effects are also good, for Google

Google's case, per the Cloud blog post it cites, is that OAuth was built for human-paced apps and "a valid token is no longer enough" for something autonomous. A single gateway means admins get one place for policy, approval, auditing and data-loss prevention. Prompt injection is the nightmare scenario for an inbox agent, and a send button is exactly where it hurts. I'll concede all of that.

Here's the part the safety story doesn't cover. The same terms say Workspace data can only be used for active, user-authorized tasks and must be deleted when the user disconnects. Google can cap how long you keep embeddings, memory indexes and user profiles at 30 days. Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, and so is building a competing Workspace product with it.

Read that list again as a roadmap for a startup. Memory that persists across sessions is the feature that makes an assistant feel like it knows you. A 30-day cap on the index behind it is a design constraint you didn't choose. Then, from 1 April 2027, TechStackups says paid MCP usage starts billing from the first request, while REST keeps big free daily allowances. A Gmail search_threads call counts as ten of your 5,000 daily requests, so a project gets about 500 searches a day before it pays.

None of those lines is outrageous alone.

Together they say that the company that owns the inbox also owns the speed limit, the memory limit and the price of an assistant that lives in it. Safety can be true and also convenient.

The last platform to try this ended up with a marketplace

Slack ran the earlier cut. In May 2025 it moved conversations.history for commercially distributed apps outside its Marketplace from Tier 3 to Tier 1: one request a minute, 15 messages per request. Marketplace apps kept their old limits. The pitch was protecting workspace data from unvetted apps, and the practical effect was that every serious vendor applied to the Marketplace.

Slack drew its line by distribution channel. Google is drawing it by what the software is. That is a harder line to game, and a harder one to appeal, because "is this an agent?" is a question that gets blurrier every quarter. Is a feature that auto-suggests a reply an agent? Is a rules engine with a language model inside it?

A product that sits on Gmail should stop assuming the answer will go its way. Ask Google in writing which side your client is on, while there are still ten weeks of runway.

Signal is fighting the same fight from the other end

The other side of this is the operating system, and it showed up the same week. On 20 November Meredith Whittaker published Signal's response to AI assistants built into phones: on iOS 27 the app blocks screenshots and adds a "Block Siri AI" setting, and on Android it detects an assistant trying to read the screen and switches on its screen-security mode by itself. Signal admits the fix is partial and doesn't cover the filesystem, and it asks Apple, Google and Microsoft for a documented way to opt an app out of AI access.

Put the two stories next to each other. Google tells apps that agents may only come through the front door it built. Signal tells Google and Apple that agents shouldn't get through the front door at all unless the app agrees. Both are right about their own data.

Both are arguing about who holds the key.

Your product is on the receiving end of one of those arguments, probably both. You are somebody's app, so an OS agent can read your screen. You are also somebody's agent, so a platform can decide what you may touch.

Design the product that survives a closed door

I'd build for the world where the send button stays locked longer than you want. That doesn't mean giving up. It means treating the human handoff as the product instead of the apology.

A draft that opens in one tap with the right thread, the right recipient and a diff of what changed beats a draft you have to go hunting for. A queue of five ready replies that takes ten seconds to clear is a real workflow, even when a person presses the final key. I'd also keep your own record of what the assistant knows, outside anything Google may make you delete in 30 days, and be honest in your UI about what gets forgotten and why.

And I'd decide now, as a product call and not an engineering afterthought, whether your assistant is an agent by Google's definition. Marking it as one buys you a supported path and a quota clock. Leaving it off buys you a clean conscience until a reviewer disagrees.

My bet is that by summer the question every Workspace-adjacent roadmap meeting asks isn't "what can the model do?" but "what is the platform going to let it finish?" If your Q1 plan has no answer to that, it's a plan for someone else's product.

Originally published on kireev.us.
