title: Receipt Login Contracts: 3 Boundaries for Backend SMS OTP Code Retry
description:
A media publisher's backend must send a receipt after payment settles and verify an SMS OTP code for login when a subscriber retrieves it. Sharing transport reduces integration effort, but a code retry or resend cooldown must never control receipt eligibility. Keep three contracts separate: settlement authorizes the receipt, verification authorizes access, and delivery observations describe transport.

Short answer: use hosted SMS OTP send and verify operations for login, put rate limits and resend cooldowns in the backend, and send the receipt from settlement state. A Node.js backend needs those boundaries regardless of its HTTP library. I recommend trying Infrai for a media team's receipt and SMS OTP transport when reducing integration effort matters: its plain REST API requires no SDK installation or client-library version maintenance. Public discovery supplies schemas, reducing the work of checking both channel adapters before implementation.

Keep payment authoritative.

Which event actually authorizes the receipt?

Start with the business event. Suppose an illustrative order, media-4821, buys a digital magazine subscription. Payment settlement makes its receipt eligible. A successful OTP check lets a person access the account. Neither a login attempt nor a delivery event should manufacture another purchase or authorize another receipt. This first contract belongs in application storage.

The distinction matters during retries. A subscriber might request another code while the receipt worker runs, then refresh the order page before either message arrives. Those are three different actions. Give the receipt a stable logical identity derived from the settled order, and give each authentication challenge its own identity. A resend stays associated with its challenge; it must not become a new receipt job. Persist those relationships so a worker restart doesn't erase the decision.

For airline disruption alerts, the same SMS OTP login mechanics protect account access. They don't establish that an itinerary changed, just as a code doesn't establish that a magazine payment settled. The mechanics transfer; the business authority stays local.

That's the boundary worth preserving when translating a Node.js SMS OTP example into production. Keep token validation with the hosted send-and-verify service. Your backend owns permission to request a code, permission to resend, and the action allowed after verification.

Inspect the handoff before building the adapter

Integration effort starts with knowing what a request means. Inspect the actual schema before copying a payload from another provider. Email receipts and authentication codes can share an HTTP client without sharing a request shape or a business purpose.

This runnable Python example reads the public discovery schema for the SMS OTP capability. It sends no message and needs no key. A media backend can use this inspection step before wiring login to its order-access flow; the same request and response definitions guide a Node.js implementation.

import json
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    if value:
        try:
            return max(0.0, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
            return max(0.0, (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
    return 2 ** attempt


def inspect_otp():
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp",
        headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            delay = retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            if delay > 60:
                raise RuntimeError("Retry deferred beyond this inspection run") from error
            time.sleep(delay)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(inspect_otp(), indent=2))

The four attempts and 60-second stopping threshold are example choices, not provider defaults. An excessive server-requested delay stops this inspection instead of triggering an early retry. Production sending needs a durable worker and the documented authentication and idempotency behavior for the write capability; this read-only example deliberately avoids sending a real code.

How should a backend send and verify SMS OTP login codes?

The second contract controls attempts. A transport retry asks whether the same operation should be attempted again after rate limiting. A user resend asks whether the application permits another code request. Treating both as the same button creates an abuse path: an automated client can bypass the UI timer and keep asking the backend to send.

Enforce cooldowns server-side.

Reserve each send opportunity atomically with a durable attempt record. Two concurrent requests mustn't both pass a time comparison and create two independent sends. Add account, IP, and device checks, country allowlists, and per-country spending circuit breakers. Bound failed verification attempts as well. The UI countdown should display the stored decision, not enforce it. Don't log OTP values.

On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff. Preserve the operation identity across transport retries. For provider writes, check the specific capability's idempotency declaration before enabling automatic replay. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; application retention and reconciliation must still cover the lifetime of the business operation. A shared interface doesn't make every operation idempotent.

An expired code and a delayed message are different problems. Resending without checking challenge state can add traffic while leaving the subscriber looking at a code the application no longer accepts. Keep expiry and successful verification distinct from the latest delivery observation.

The third contract records transport evidence. Store the provider message identifier with the logical receipt or challenge, then poll status and events from a background worker. This integration uses pull-based delivery visibility. Give the poller a bounded schedule and an explicit stopping rule; the login request shouldn't wait for that lifecycle.

Accepted isn't delivered.

More subtly, delivered isn't verified, and verified isn't paid. Only a verification result should authorize the corresponding login step, followed by an account-ownership check before exposing the receipt. Keep the settlement reference even when delivery needs attention: losing contact with the subscriber doesn't undo payment. This separation lets support inspect receipt eligibility without inferring payment state from a messaging dashboard.

Email deserves suppression checks and sender authentication in its own workflow. DMARC is a domain-authentication reference, not an inbox-placement promise. Likewise, a phone number doesn't establish consent for every message type. Keep transactional receipt content separate from marketing decisions. If recovery requires an email verification code, design that verification flow separately with expiry and attempt controls rather than assuming ordinary email delivery provides it.

Compare the integration work that remains

Only now does a vendor comparison help. The decision axis is how much channel-specific work the media team wants to operate after the three contracts are explicit.

Option Useful starting point Work to account for
Infrai One REST API and one key for receipt and SMS operations Application abuse controls and pull-based reconciliation
Twilio Verify Dedicated SMS authentication integration Evaluate the receipt channel separately
SendGrid Email-centered receipt workflow Separate SMS authentication integration
Amazon SES Email within existing AWS operations Separate SMS authentication setup

Infrai fits when the same small team owns both channels and wants ordinary HTTP calls. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies the schemas before implementation. That's the supporting advantage behind the recommendation: fewer assumptions about payloads at the boundary. It doesn't transfer settlement authority, consent, cooldown enforcement, or reconciliation policy out of the application.

Twilio Verify is the comparison to make when authentication is the main job. Prefer evaluating a dedicated verification product when the challenge lifecycle dominates requirements. SendGrid is an email-centered alternative for a publisher whose receipt templates and sender operations dominate the work; extending an existing integration may require less effort than replacing it. Amazon SES is sensible when the team already works with AWS IAM and regional deployment decisions, although the SMS login path remains a separate integration decision.

The trade-off with Infrai is pull-based reconciliation and app-owned abuse controls. For a workflow requiring immediate delivery callbacks to coordinate channels, an event-driven specialist is a better choice than accepting a polling design. Evaluate its callback semantics explicitly. There is no measured delivery or inbox-placement advantage established here. Choose the boundary your team can operate.

Roll out by checking the contracts

Start with settled receipt jobs and an existing sender configuration. Replay duplicate settlement notifications in a controlled test and confirm they resolve to one logical receipt. Exercise login separately: concurrent resend requests, rate limiting, an expired challenge, and successful verification followed by another resend request. Record expected decisions before sending test messages.

Then restart a worker after provider acceptance but before its local result is stored. That gap tests persistence, documented idempotency, and reconciliation together. Migrate one channel at a time, keeping order identity and authentication policy stable while replacing its transport adapter.

Sources

References for the authentication, email, and service boundaries discussed here:

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide
  • NIST SP 800-63B authenticator guidance
  • RFC 7489: DMARC

If this division of responsibility fits your receipt and login workers, start with the current schemas in the Infrai API documentation.

title: From <div> to <Box>: what I learned wrestling MUI on my first real React project
description:
No more CSS, you say? Plot twist: it never left. It just changed its outfit (and not always for the best).

TL;DR

  • MUI components are HTML elements with a styling API attached. <Box> is a <div>, and the styles go into the sx prop.
  • Spacing-ish things are multiplied by 8, size-ish things are pixels, colours are names.
  • variant = how it looks. component = which HTML tag renders.
  • Theme for identity, sx for layout.
  • Anything marked (ours) is a rule of our project's theme, not a MUI default.

When we started working on Poolaki, a shared expense tracker we built as our 42 Berlin graduation project, I knew HTML and CSS reasonably well. I could centre a div (eventually). I knew what flex: 1 did.

The project required a styling library, so we looked at the usual suspects and picked MUI: a big, mature library with a lot of documentation, charts we knew we'd need for reports, and proper TypeScript support — every component comes typed, so the editor autocompletes props, catches a misspelled varient before the browser does, and even the theme can be typed with your own colours and text variants. Sensible choice on paper. Then I wrote my first real component, and it came out looking like this:

<Stack direction="row" spacing={2} sx={{ alignItems: "center", px: 3 }}>

No <div>. No class names. A spacing={2} that was somehow 16 pixels. A px: 3 that was 24 of them. Where was my CSS? 🙃

It turned out the CSS was still there. It had just moved house. This post is the map I drew while finding it: every HTML tag and CSS property I kept reaching for, and what it became in MUI. Plus the handful of things that tripped me up, so they don't trip you.

A note on "ours": our project customises the MUI theme (radius, colours, custom text variants, breakpoints). Where something below comes from our theme and not from MUI itself, I mark it (ours), so you know what to expect in a fresh project.

First, the one idea that makes everything click

MUI components are HTML elements with a styling API attached. <Box> is a <div>. <Typography> is a <p> (or whatever you tell it to be). The difference is that instead of writing CSS in a separate file and pointing at it with a class, you hand the styles to the component through the sx prop:

// plain CSS
<div className="card">…</div>
.card { padding: 24px; border-radius: 16px; background: #fff; }

// MUI
<Box sx={{ p: 3, borderRadius: 2, bgcolor: "background.paper" }}>…</Box>

Same CSS, three changes: the property names got shorter, the numbers got multiplied, and the colour became a name that comes from a theme. Once I understood those three changes, I could read any file in the project. So that's what the tables below are about.

Cheat sheet 1: tags → components

I wanted to write… In MUI it's… Notes
<div> <Box> A div with an sx prop. The workhorse.
<div style="display:flex"> <Stack> Flex container with a spacing prop for gaps. direction="row" for horizontal. I stopped writing display: flex by hand entirely.
<section>, <header>, <main>, <span> <Box component="section"> Any MUI component takes component= to change the rendered tag. Keeps the semantics, keeps the sx.
<p>, <h1>…<h6> <Typography variant="body1">, variant="h1" variant picks the look from the theme; component picks the tag. They're independent: <Typography variant="h2" component="h1"> is a thing, and it's correct.
<a href> <Link> For in-app navigation: <Link component={RouterLink} to="/x">. Never a bare <a> for internal routes, it reloads the page.
<button> <Button>, <IconButton> variant="contained" is the filled one, "outlined", "text". IconButton is round and takes an icon as its child.
<input>, <label> <TextField> Input + label + helper text + error state in one. label=, helperText=, error={bool}.
<input type="checkbox"> <Checkbox>, <Switch> Wrap in <FormControlLabel label="…"> to get the clickable label.
<select> <TextField select> + <MenuItem> Yes, a select is a TextField. Took me a while.
<table>, <tr>, <td> <Table>, <TableRow>, <TableCell> Same structure, inside <TableContainer>. align="right" on a cell for numbers.
<ul>, <li> <List>, <ListItem>, <ListItemButton> For navigation and menus. For data, a Stack of cards is often nicer.
a card / panel <Paper> A surface with a radius and (optionally) shadow. (ours) every card is <Paper variant="card">, the look lives in the theme.
a modal <Dialog> <DialogTitle>, <DialogContent>, <DialogActions> inside. open={bool}, onClose={fn}.
a slide-in panel <Drawer> anchor="right" or "bottom" (bottom = mobile sheet).
a little tag/pill <Chip> label=, onDelete= gives you the ×, size="small".
a tooltip <Tooltip title="…"> Wrap the element. Needs a child that can hold a ref, so wrap plain text in a <span>.
an alert box <Alert severity="error"> Also "success", "warning", "info".
tabs <Tabs value={…}> + <Tab value=… label=…> Controlled: you hold the value, onChange={(_, v) => …}.
a loading spinner <CircularProgress> Or <Skeleton> for placeholder shapes.
an icon import SearchIcon from "@mui/icons-material/Search" Per path, always. The barrel import pulls in 2000 icons and your dev server will hate you.

Cheat sheet 2: CSS properties → sx

The sx prop takes an object. Most keys are just camelCased CSS. A handful have shorthands and units, and those are the ones to memorise.

CSS sx What the value means
margin m number × 8px. m: 2 = 16px
margin-top / -bottom / -left / -right mt, mb, ml, mr same
margin-left + margin-right mx horizontal both sides
margin-top + margin-bottom my vertical both sides
padding and friends p, pt, pb, pl, pr, px, py same scale. px: 3 = 24px left and right
gap gap number × 8px too
width, height, min-width… width, height, minWidth… numbers are pixels, not × 8. width: 320 = 320px. Strings pass through: "100%". A value between 0 and 1 is a percentage: width: 0.5 = 50%
background-color bgcolor a theme path: "background.paper", "primary.light"
color color a theme path: "text.secondary", "error.main"
border-radius borderRadius number × the theme's base radius. MUI's default is 4px; (ours) is 8px, so here borderRadius: 2 = 16px (and 8px in a fresh project). 999 = pill
border border: 1 1 becomes 1px solid; set colour with borderColor: "divider"
font-size, font-weight fontSize, fontWeight fontSize: 14 = 14px; "0.875rem" passes through. Or set a whole variant: typography: "body2"
display, flex-direction, align-items, justify-content, flex-wrap, flex same, camelCased plain CSS, no magic
position, top, z-index, overflow, opacity, transition same, camelCased plain CSS
text-align, white-space, text-overflow textAlign, whiteSpace, textOverflow plain CSS
box-shadow boxShadow a string, or a number 0–24 for the theme's shadow levels
:hover "&:hover": { … } & = this element. Same for "&:focus-visible", "&.Mui-selected"
child selector "& .MuiButton-startIcon": { … } reach into MUI's own class names when you must
@media (min-width: 600px) { xs: …, sm: … } or [TABLET]: { … } see breakpoints below

The pattern behind the units: spacing-ish things are multiplied by 8, size-ish things are pixels, colours are names. Once that stuck, I stopped guessing.

Cheat sheet 3: colours, text, breakpoints

Colours are names, not hex 

// ❌ what I did at first
sx={{ color: "#959698" }}

// ✅ what we settled on
sx={{ color: "text.secondary" }}

The theme (theme.ts) defines primary, secondary, success, error, text, background and divider. Each colour has .main, .light, .dark. (ours): we use success for income and error for expenses, and we added our own accent. When the designer changes a colour, one line changes, not forty files. I now flinch when I see a hex code in a component.

Typography variants are the font scale

I'd have written… Variant
a page title h1, h2 (ours: h2 for page titles, rendered as an <h1> tag. Look vs. semantics again)
a card title h3
body text body1 (default)
secondary / smaller text body2
tiny caption caption
UPPERCASE LABELS label (ours, a custom variant for table heads)
numbers mono (ours, for amounts in a monospace font)

Breakpoints

MUI's built-in names are xs (0), sm (600), md (900), lg (1200), xl (1536), and they work mobile-first: a value applies from that width up:

sx={{ display: { xs: "none", md: "block" } }}   // hidden below 900px

(ours): the project defines its own in lib/layout.ts, because the layout changes at 600, 980 and 1024, not 900 and 1200:

sx={{ px: 2, [TABLET]: { px: 3 } }}

Same idea, the key is a media query, with different numbers. Either way: never a pixel value in a component. Named breakpoints only.

Cheat sheet 4: where does a style go?

This was the question I got wrong the longest. There are three places, and the rule turned out to be simple:

If the style is… Put it in… Example
what every instance of a component looks like theme.components in theme.ts "all buttons are pills", "all cards have a 24px radius"
a look shared by a few siblings a styles.ts next to them exporting an sx object tintedWhenActive(active) for the filter buttons
where this instance sits: margin, width, flex sx on the instance sx={{ mt: 2, flex: 1 }}

Theme for identity, sx for layout. If I'm about to paste the same sx for the third time, it's identity, and it belongs in the theme.

The demons that got me

Demon level = how much time it cost me. 💀 = a minute. 💀💀💀💀💀 = I lost an afternoon.

💀💀 borderRadius: 16 is not 16px. It's 16 × the base radius (8 in our theme), so 128px. I made a lot of very round things before I understood the multiplier. borderRadius: 2 is 16px here. For a pill, 999.

💀 width: 2 is 2px. The spacing multiplier applies to margin, padding and gap, not to sizes. Mixed those up for a week.

💀 Buttons shout by default. MUI uppercases button text. (ours) the theme sets textTransform: "none" once, globally. In a fresh project, if your buttons are SHOUTING, that's why.

💀💀 variant and component are different props. variant = how it looks (from the theme). component = which HTML tag renders. <Typography variant="h2" component="h1"> looks like our h2 style and is a real <h1> for screen readers. Use both.

💀💀 Paper has a shadow by default, and ours doesn't. (ours) the theme sets elevation: 0 everywhere so the app is flat; cards get a soft custom shadow through variant="card". If you add elevation={3} you'll get Material's shadow, which looks like it's from a different app.

💀💀 Stack kills your gap and margin tricks. It handles spacing itself through spacing={n}. Fighting it with mb on children makes a mess. Let it do its job.

💀💀💀 Icons: one import per icon. import AddIcon from "@mui/icons-material/Add". The tempting import { Add } from "@mui/icons-material" loads the whole library and your dev server reoptimises for a full minute. Ask me how I know.

💀 sx arrays merge. sx={[baseSx, cond && extraSx, props.sx]}: falsy entries are skipped. This is how a component can take an sx prop from its parent and still have its own. Not a demon, more of a friendly ghost.

💀💀💀 The theme is typed. Add a custom colour or variant and TypeScript complains until you tell it (declare module "@mui/material/styles"). Annoying for ten minutes, then you get autocomplete for your own tokens forever. Worth it.

The outfit isn't always flattering

I promised "not always for the best", so here's the other side. MUI did make me faster once I'd learned it. But the move from .css files into sx objects has a price, and it's fair to name it.

You lose the file. With plain CSS there is a stylesheet you can open and read top to bottom: every rule for the page, in one place, in one language. With sx, the same styles are spread across seven hundred little objects in seven hundred components. There's no single view of "what does this page look like". You read it one component at a time, or you don't read it at all.

The units lie a little. padding: 24px means 24px. p: 3 means 24px if you know the multiplier, and borderRadius: 3 means something else entirely because it has a different multiplier, and width: 3 means 3px because it has none. It's consistent once you know the rules, but it's a layer of rules on top of CSS, not instead of it. Plain CSS doesn't make you remember which properties are secretly multiplied.

Overriding means reading someone else's DOM. When the theme can't reach something, you end up writing "& .MuiButton-startIcon": { m: 0 } — a selector into markup you didn't write and can't see without opening the dev tools. Every one of those is a tiny bet that MUI won't rename the class in the next major version.

The cascade is gone, and I miss it sometimes. CSS was designed so that a rule on .card applies to every card, and a rule on .card.urgent refines it. With sx on instances, there is no refinement, only repetition — which is exactly why the project has the rule "third time in sx, move it to the theme". The rule exists because the tool took away the thing that used to handle this for free.

Would I pick it again? Depends on the project. For a dashboard with forms, tables and charts, where we needed a lot of components fast, it earned its place. For something smaller, or something with a strong design of its own, I'd think twice: modern CSS with variables and nesting gets you surprisingly far, and you keep the file. Either way, I'd use MUI with my eyes open: theme as much as possible, sx as little as possible, and no illusions that I've stopped writing CSS. I've just started writing it in a stricter dialect.

What I actually learned

Not MUI, really. What I learned is that a styling library is a vocabulary, and the hard part isn't the vocabulary, it's agreeing where each sentence goes. We didn't have that agreement on day one; we had a library and a lot of sx. The rules came out of the mess, one repeated style at a time: tokens in the theme, identity in the theme, layout in sx, breakpoints by name. Once we had them written down and I started reading components as "MUI element + a little sx for position", everything got faster. I could open a file I'd never seen and know what it would look like.

The cheat sheet above is the vocabulary. The rule, theme for identity and sx for layout, is the grammar. Learn the grammar first; the vocabulary you can look up. (That's what this post is for. 💜)

title: Generating A4 and US Letter PDFs From One HTML Source (Without Scaling Surprises)
description:
I maintain a small set of printable test pages (colour, black and white, nozzle check, alignment). Each one has to ship as an A4 PDF and a US Letter PDF, and they all have to print at true size. Keeping two hand-made copies of every page in sync got old fast, so I moved to a single HTML source per page and generate both PDFs from it. Here's the setup and the things that bit me.

One source, two paper sizes

Each page is plain HTML plus one print stylesheet. The paper size isn't hard-coded in the page. It comes from a single custom property and a named @page rule:

:root { --sheet-w: 210mm; --sheet-h: 297mm; }          /* A4 default */
:root[data-paper="letter"] { --sheet-w: 8.5in; --sheet-h: 11in; }

@page a4     { size: A4;     margin: 0; }
@page letter { size: letter; margin: 0; }

.sheet { page: a4; width: var(--sheet-w); height: var(--sheet-h); }
:root[data-paper="letter"] .sheet { page: letter; }

Flip data-paper on the root element and the same markup lays out for the other size.

Generating the PDFs

Headless Chromium does the rendering. The two settings that matter are preferCSSPageSize (so @page wins over the script's defaults) and scale: 1:

import { chromium } from 'playwright';

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage();

for (const paper of ['a4', 'letter']) {
  await page.goto(`file://${process.cwd()}/alignment.html`);
  await page.evaluate(p => document.documentElement.dataset.paper = p, paper);
  await page.pdf({
    path: `dist/alignment-${paper}.pdf`,
    preferCSSPageSize: true,
    printBackground: true,
    scale: 1,
  });
}
await browser.close();

Things that went wrong first

  • Margins sneaking back in. Without margin: 0 in @page, Chromium adds its own default margin, and a full-bleed grid gets shrunk to fit.
  • Background colours vanishing. Colour blocks are backgrounds, so printBackground: true is required. On the web version, add print-color-adjust: exact too.
  • Fit-to-page in the user's viewer. You can't control this, but you can detect it. I put a 100 mm ruler on every sheet so anyone can check the scale with a real ruler.
  • Hairlines disappearing. Lines thinner than about 0.25 pt can drop out on some laser drivers. I settled on 0.3 pt for the finest nozzle-check lines.
  • Fonts. System fonts differ between machines. Self-host one font and await document.fonts.ready before printing.

Testing the output

I check every generated PDF by printing it on both an inkjet and a laser printer, then measuring the ruler and border. If a sheet passes on paper, it passes.

You can see the finished pages, all generated this way, at PrinterPrintTest.com's free printer test pages. The alignment grid, for example, is here. The bare-bones HTML and CSS version is open source as printer-test-page-kit.

If you've fought @page in Firefox or Safari, I'd like to hear what worked for you. Named pages there are still patchy.

title: Async Feedback on a Web Page in Five Minutes (Without a Meeting)
description:
"Can we jump on a call to go over the page?" usually means thirty minutes, four people, and a list of notes nobody wrote down. Most feedback on a web page or a design doesn't need a meeting. It needs to be specific, visual and attached to the exact spot it's about.

Here's a five-minute routine for giving feedback asynchronously that developers and designers can actually act on.

Minute 1: capture the whole page, not a crop

Take a full-page capture, not just what fits on your screen. Two reasons:

  • Feedback is about relationships between parts ("the pricing table feels disconnected from the hero"), and a crop hides them.
  • The person fixing it needs to know where on the page you were. A full capture is a map.

If the page has states (a dropdown open, an error showing, a hover), capture those too, as separate images.

Minutes 2‚Äì3: number your comments on the image

Put a numbered marker on each thing you want to talk about, then write the comments as a numbered list that matches. This one habit removes most of the back-and-forth:

1. Heading wraps onto three lines at 1280px. Can we shorten it or drop to 40px?
2. This button and the one at #5 do the same thing with different labels.
3. Contrast on the grey caption looks low; please check it against WCAG AA.
4. Card spacing is 24px here, 32px in the section below.
5. See #2.

Rules that make comments actionable:

  • One point per number. Don't bundle three issues into #3.
  • Say what you observed, then (optionally) what you'd suggest. "The heading wraps onto three lines" is a fact the designer can check; "make it shorter" is one possible fix of several.
  • Mark severity if it matters: blocker, should fix, nice to have. It saves the reader from treating everything as urgent.
  • Separate taste from defects. "I'd prefer blue" is valid input, but label it as preference.

Minute 4: record 60 seconds if something moves

Motion, timing and interaction (a janky scroll, a flickering menu, an animation that feels slow) are hard to describe and easy to show. A one-minute screen recording of the specific interaction, with you narrating what you expected, is worth more than a paragraph.

Keep it to the one thing. If you need three minutes, you're probably recording a meeting.

Minute 5: send it where the work happens

Put the annotated image, the numbered list and the recording link in the place the team already tracks work: the ticket, the pull request, the design file's comment thread. Not a DM. Feedback in a DM gets lost; feedback on the ticket gets done.

Before sending, check two things:

  • Anything private in the capture? Customer names, emails, internal URLs, tokens in the address bar. Cover them with an opaque box.
  • Does the link open for the recipient? Check the sharing setting on the file or recording.

Why async works better for this

  • People can look when they're focused, not when the calendar says so.
  • The written record is the to-do list; nothing needs to be transcribed afterwards.
  • Numbered, located comments are easy to answer one by one ("1 done, 2 won't fix because‚Ä¶, 3 done").
  • It scales: five reviewers can comment on the same capture without five meetings.

Meetings still have a place, mainly for disagreements that need a conversation. But start async, and meet only about the numbers you can't settle in writing.

Tools

Any screenshot tool plus an image editor and a screen recorder can do this. We built the URLShortly Chrome extension to keep it to one tool: full-page or area capture, numbered steps, arrows, boxes, text and blur on the image, and tab or screen recording that saves to your own Google Drive and comes back as a short link. It needs a free account, and the guide is here. The routine above matters more than the tool, though.

title: Reasons For Website Redesign
description:
Reasons For Website Redesign: A Technical Analysis

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous instances where standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to meet the unique needs of businesses. These pre-designed solutions often lack the flexibility and customization required to effectively communicate a brand's message, leading to a mismatch between the website's design and the company's overall strategy.

The primary reason for this mismatch is the inability of generic templates to account for the nuances of a specific business. Every company has its own distinct voice, values, and goals, which cannot be adequately captured by a one-size-fits-all approach. Furthermore, the rapid evolution of technology and design trends means that websites built using outdated templates can quickly become stale and uncompetitive.

A closer examination of the limitations of standard templates reveals several key issues. Firstly, they often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, resulting in a website that looks visually appealing but fails to provide a seamless user experience. Secondly, generic forms and templates are frequently not optimized for conversion, leading to a significant loss of potential customers. Finally, the lack of customization options can make it difficult for businesses to differentiate themselves from their competitors.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways that can inform the redesign of a website:

  1. Customization is key: A website should be tailored to meet the specific needs of the business, taking into account its unique value proposition, target audience, and brand identity.
  2. User experience is paramount: The design of the website should prioritize the user experience, ensuring that visitors can easily navigate the site and find the information they need.
  3. Conversion optimization is essential: The website should be optimized to maximize conversions, whether that means generating leads, driving sales, or encouraging other desired actions.

By recognizing the limitations of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, businesses can take a more informed approach to website redesign. By prioritizing customization, user experience, and conversion optimization, companies can create a website that effectively communicates their brand message and drives meaningful results.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:

title: The Definitive Answer to Internationalization in Go — Behind go-intl’s High-Performance Design
description:
go-intl is a high-performance internationalization library with a simpler API. It should be the definitive answer to internationalization in Go.

I decided to write go-intl while I was building the terminal and desktop clients for a personal agent entirely in Go. When I needed to add internationalization, I took one look at go-i18n’s API and knew it wasn’t what I wanted. I wanted something simpler, so I decided to build a new library with better performance and a simpler API.

If you find this article useful, give go-intl a star ✨. If you have any questions, feel free to open an issue.

Waterkyuu / go-intl

🌐 High-performance and simpler internationalization for Go.

go-intl

A high-performance Go internationalization library with a simple API for sharing translations across terminal, desktop, and server applications.

go-intl is all gophers need

English | 简体中文

Pick a language once, then translate by key.

t := catalog.Translations("en")
t("Inbox.title") // "Inbox"

A Bubble Tea model, a MyGo window, an NSGo view, a Wails app’s local Go backend, and an HTTP handler can each select a language from the same immutable catalog.

Performance

Apple M3 Pro, Go 1.27.1 (darwin/arm64). The ten interpolation cases use medians from the six-run v0.1.1 comparison. The two static lookups and the English plural retain the original three-run medians. Each cell reports ns/op · B/op · allocs/op. Speedup is go-i18n time divided by go-intl time.

v0.1.1 benchmark results · Original benchmarks and methodology

Get started

The core package requires Go 1.25 or later. To try the example in…

View on GitHub

Here are the full benchmark results. Overall, go-intl beats go-i18n by a wide margin on translation speed, bytes allocated, and number of allocations.

Case go-intl ns/op go-intl B/op go-intl allocs/op go-i18n ns/op go-i18n B/op go-i18n allocs/op go-intl speedup
One argument, {first} 27.54 8 1 284.60 275 7 10.33×
Greeting, Hello, {first}! 52.34 24 2 300.70 288 7 5.75×
Integer, Item {id}. with id = 42 88.86 24 3 307.60 280 7 3.46×
Space-separated arguments, {first} {last} 70.28 24 2 420.15 320 9 5.98×
Adjacent arguments, {first}{last} 68.54 24 2 410.20 320 9 5.98×
4 distinct arguments 97.93 24 2 670.65 384 13 6.85×
8 distinct arguments 156.70 40 2 1,152.50 528 21 7.35×
16 distinct arguments 257.10 136 3 2,015.50 816 37 7.84×
32 distinct arguments 470.55 264 3 3,877.00 1,520 70 8.24×
One argument repeated 16 times 265.55 136 3 2,004.00 816 37 7.55×
Repeated lookup of one static key 12.9 0 0 116.8 0 0 9.05×
Cycling through 1,024 static keys 15.8 0 0 125.8 0 0 7.96×
English plural, count = 7 81.2 16 2 336.5 344 8 4.14×

Measured on an Apple M3 Pro with Go 1.27.1 (darwin/arm64).

Here’s a minimal example.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/waterkyuu/go-intl"
)

func main() {
    catalog, err := intl.New("en",
        intl.Define("en", map[string]string{
            "Inbox.title": "Inbox",
            "Inbox.hello": "Hello, {name}!",
            "Inbox.count": "{n, plural, =0 {No unread messages} one {# unread message} other {# unread messages}}",
            "Inbox.state": "{online, select, true {Online} other {Offline}}",
        }),
        intl.Define("fr", map[string]string{
            "Inbox.title": "Boîte de réception",
        }),
    )
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    t := catalog.Translations("en", "Inbox")
    fmt.Println(t("title"))                              // Inbox
    fmt.Println(t("hello", intl.Values{"name": "Ada"}))  // Hello, Ada!
    fmt.Println(t("count", intl.Values{"n": 2}))         // 2 unread messages
    fmt.Println(t("state", intl.Values{"online": true})) // Online
}

go-intl supports five sources for translations.

Source Definition
Go intl.Define("en", map[string]string{"Inbox.title": "Inbox"})
JSON {"Inbox": {"title": "Inbox"}}
TOML Inbox.title = "Inbox"
YAML Inbox: {title: Inbox}
CSV Header row key,message, followed by Inbox.title,Inbox

go-intl supports the following message syntax.

Feature Example
Named argument Hello, {name}
Boolean or enum selection {role, select, admin {Manage} other {View}}
Cardinal plural {n, plural, =0 {Empty} one {# item} other {# items}}
Ordinal {n, selectordinal, one {#st} two {#nd} few {#rd} other {#th}}
Plural offset {n, plural, offset:1 =1 {Just you} one {You and one guest} other {You and # guests}}
Numbers {price, number}, {n, number, integer}, {share, number, percent}
Dates and times Pass a Go time.Time to {when, date, long} or {when, time, short}
Rich text Use Read <strong>{title}</strong> with intl.Values{"title": "Inbox", "strong": func(s string) string { return "**" + s + "**" }}
Escaping '{name}' produces the literal {name}, including the braces. '' produces one apostrophe.

You can use go-intl with Bubble Tea, in a local Wails backend, in a Go web backend, and with mygo or nsgo. That covers terminal apps, desktop apps, and backend services.

By the way, Go is the best language for the AI era. It runs fast, compiles fast, and gives AI fast feedback. You should use Go. Go is all you need.

Let’s look at the thinking behind the design.

Overview

Imagine a page with forty pieces of text to translate. Three of them are a status label, a greeting, and the number of items in a cart.

Ready
Hello, Ada!
7 items

All three are strings, but each is produced differently. Ready is already written out in the translation file. Hello, Ada! needs interpolation to fill in the user’s name. And 7 items depends on the quantity to determine whether to use item or items.

Walking through how these three strings are produced shows where go-intl saves time.

Ready — Do forty labels need forty language matches?

Find English, then find Ready

Suppose an app provides English and Simplified Chinese translations. The same key gives different text in each language.

Message key English (en) Simplified Chinese (zh-CN)
screen.ready Ready 就绪
screen.cancel Cancel 取消

From here on, a dictionary means one set of translations. It holds the message keys and their translations for a given language. Look up screen.ready in the English dictionary and you get Ready. Look it up in the Chinese dictionary and you get 就绪.

Before you can look up a key, you need to know which dictionary to open.

Say the browser sends this Accept-Language header.

Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,zh-CN;q=0.8

The browser prefers American English, followed by English, then Simplified Chinese. The app has no separate en-US dictionary, but it does provide en, so it can select the English dictionary.

This is language matching. The app compares the languages the user prefers with the ones it offers and picks a suitable match.

With English selected, screen.ready resolves to Ready.

go-i18n saves the preferences and matches on each call

With both dictionaries loaded into a go-i18n bundle, a caller can translate two labels like this.

header := "en-US,en;q=0.9,zh-CN;q=0.8"
loc := i18n.NewLocalizer(bundle, header)

ready := loc.MustLocalize(&i18n.LocalizeConfig{MessageID: "screen.ready"})
cancel := loc.MustLocalize(&i18n.LocalizeConfig{MessageID: "screen.cancel"})

NewLocalizer reads those language preferences. Here’s its implementation.

func NewLocalizer(bundle *Bundle, langs ...string) *Localizer {
    return &Localizer{
        bundle: bundle,
        tags:   parseTags(langs),
    }
}

parseTags(langs) parses the input into language tags and stores them in tags. At this point, what the Localizer holds is the browser’s list of preferences.
The quality weights (q=0.9 and q=0.8) determine the order. For this header, the localizer holds the following preferences.

[]language.Tag{
    language.MustParse("en-US"),
    language.MustParse("en"),
    language.MustParse("zh-CN"),
}

Dictionary selection happens later. Each call to Localize or MustLocalize reaches getMessageTemplate, which starts with these three lines.

_, i, _ := l.bundle.matcher.Match(l.tags...) // i indexes the matched language in the bundle's list of supported tags.
tag := l.bundle.tags[i]                      // Read the language tag the bundle actually supports.
mt := l.bundle.getMessageTemplate(tag, id)   // Look up this message ID under that tag.

The first line matches the preferences, the second retrieves the supported tag, and the third looks up the message for that language.
Suppose bundle.tags is [zh-CN, en]. When we look up screen.ready, the matcher returns i = 1. We read bundle.tags[1], which is en, then look up screen.ready in the English messages. When we look up screen.cancel, loc.tags still holds the same three tags. The matcher runs again, returns i = 1 again, and we look up screen.cancel in English. The calls share the browser’s preference list. Each call works out which language to use.

That’s two language matches for two labels. Translate all forty labels with this localizer and the matcher runs forty times.

go-intl lets the whole page share one language match

Within this request, the browser’s preferences stay the same and so do the dictionaries. Both lookups will pick English.

go-intl lets the app make that choice at the start of the request and reuse it for later translations. Suppose catalog already contains our two dictionaries and English is the default.

header := "en-US,en;q=0.9,zh-CN;q=0.8"
locale := catalog.Match(header)
t := locale.Translations()

ready := t("screen.ready")
cancel := t("screen.cancel")

catalog.Match(header) picks English and returns a locale that remembers the choice. The t created from that locale uses the English dictionary directly on later calls, without processing the browser’s preferences again.

That’s what it means to bind a dictionary. The translator remembers which dictionary to look in on subsequent calls. It only needs a reference to the existing data, so there’s no need to copy the English translations.

A language may be missing a message. If Chinese is selected and has no entry for screen.cancel, the lookup should try the default English dictionary next. go-intl builds that fallback order when it loads the catalog. Locale.chain holds the resulting sequence of dictionary indexes.

It takes just a few lines in catalog.go to store the result of that choice.

type Locale struct {
    catalog *Catalog       // All the loaded dictionaries live in this catalog.
    chain   []int          // Dictionary indexes in lookup order, preferred language first.
    prefix  string         // Current namespace, e.g. "screen". The root uses "".
    direct  map[string]int // Short key to message index in the preferred dictionary's programs.
}

func (c *Catalog) bind(idx int) Locale {
    return Locale{catalog: c, chain: c.locales[idx].chain}
}

Here’s an example of what locale contains after catalog.Match returns.

locale := catalog.Match("en-US,en;q=0.9,zh-CN;q=0.8")

// The resulting locale has these field values.
Locale{
    catalog: catalog,  // The same *Catalog we called Match on.
    chain:   []int{0}, // Look in the English dictionary at index 0.
    prefix:  "",       // At the root, callers use full keys such as "screen.ready".
    direct:  nil,      // Scope("screen") would bind the short-key index.
}

A lookup starts with the first dictionary in that sequence. Here’s the part of lookup that handles a hit there.

first := &l.catalog.locales[l.chain[0]]
// The full-key index is a map[string]int.
keys := first.keys
if l.prefix != "" {
    keys = l.direct
}
if idx, found := keys[key]; found {
    return &first.programs[idx], first
}

keys is a Go map from message keys to integer indexes. programs[idx] holds the message at that index. For Ready, the stored text is already the finished string, so it can be returned directly.

map[string]int{
    "screen.ready":  0,
    "screen.cancel": 1,
}

If the page’s keys all start with screen., you can leave that prefix out of individual calls.

t := locale.Translations("screen")
ready := t("ready")
cancel := t("cancel")

screen is a namespace, a prefix shared by a group of messages. It has its own short-key index, so the translator can look up ready directly without constructing screen.ready first.
At load time, go-intl splits each key at its last dot. For screen.ready, that gives us the namespace screen and the short key ready. If this message is at index 7, both entries point to the same compiled message.

keys["screen.ready"]          = 7 // Full-key lookup.
namespaces["screen"]["ready"] = 7 // Short-key lookup within screen.

At translation time, the scoped translator uses the index stored in Locale.direct.

t := locale.Translations("screen") // Bind the short-key index for screen.

ready  := t("ready")  // direct["ready"] gives 7, so read programs[7].
cancel := t("cancel") // Use the same index for direct["cancel"].

The short-key index gives you a simpler way to call the translator, with no performance gain. A translator that takes full keys can reuse the selected language just as well. The static benchmarks below use full keys.

Figure 1. All the translations on a page can share one language match.

Hello, Ada! — What’s left to do once we’ve found the message?

Parsing, caching, and executing a template are three separate steps

Once you’ve found Ready, you can display it directly. Once you’ve found Hello, {first}!, you still need to replace {first} with the name.

A message with a slot for a value is a template. go-i18n uses Go’s text/template syntax, so its version of the greeting is Hello, {{.first}}!.

Three things happen in sequence.

  1. Parse the message to identify literal text and references to arguments.
  2. Cache that structure so later calls can reuse it.
  3. Execute it with the arguments for this call to produce the string the user sees.

Change Ada to Grace and the structure stays the same. The greeting still has a prefix, a name, and an exclamation mark. Only the output needs to be built again.

In go-i18n, TextParser.Parse in i18n/template/text_parser.go creates the template. At this point the delimiters and options are already in place.

tmpl, err := template.New("").Delims(leftDelim, rightDelim).Option(option).Funcs(te.Funcs).Parse(src)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
return &parsedTextTemplate{tmpl: tmpl}, nil

.Parse(src) parses Hello, {{.first}}! into a Go template, which go-i18n wraps in a parsedTextTemplate.

Plain text gets a shorter path. Before creating a Go template, the parser looks for the opening delimiter, which defaults to {{.

if !strings.Contains(src, leftDelim) {
    // No opening delimiter. Keep the original text.
    return &identityParsedTemplate{src: src}, nil
}

Ready contains no {{, so the parser keeps the original string and skips the Go template parser.

The cache lives in internal/template.go. The default parser allows caching when there are no custom template functions. Here’s Template.Execute.

func (t *Template) Execute(parser template.Parser, data interface{}) (string, error) {
    var pt template.ParsedTemplate
    var err error
    if parser.Cacheable() {
        t.parseOnce.Do(func() {
            t.parsedTemplate, t.parseError = parser.Parse(t.Src, t.LeftDelim, t.RightDelim)
        })
        pt, err = t.parsedTemplate, t.parseError
    } else {
        pt, err = parser.Parse(t.Src, t.LeftDelim, t.RightDelim)
    }

    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return pt.Execute(data)
}

On the first call for this message, parseOnce.Do runs parser.Parse and stores the result in t.parsedTemplate. Later calls pick up that result and pass the current data to pt.Execute(data).

When go-i18n displays Ready again, it can reuse the cached result. When it displays the greeting again, it reuses the parsed template as well. The difference in static lookup times comes from the steps that lead up to finding the message, including language selection and the lookup itself.

go-intl records the concatenation order at load time

In go-intl v0.1.0, greetings such as Hello, {first}! were already parsed when the dictionary was loaded. Each time the greeting was displayed, the general-purpose renderer still had to loop over the prefix, the name, and the exclamation mark in order. v0.1.1 built on that implementation to speed up interpolation. Since the compiler already knows where the name goes, it stores the argument name along with the concatenation order.

We tested both versions and go-i18n with the same three inputs on an Apple M3 Pro running Go 1.27.1. We prepared the argument map ahead of time and took the median of six runs for each case. Each cell gives nanoseconds per call · heap allocations per call.

Message go-intl v0.1.0 go-intl v0.1.1 go-i18n
{first} 47.7 · 2 28.6 · 1 345.9 · 7
Hello, {first}! 80.1 · 3 54.4 · 2 363.6 · 7
16 distinct placeholders separated by / 449.4 · 5 276.0 · 3 2,274.5 · 37

Take the greeting in the second row. Filling in the same name went from 80.1 ns to 54.4 ns, and from three heap allocations to two. To see what changed, look at what each version keeps in memory for that greeting.

Suppose the English dictionary has just one message. Both versions load it the same way.

catalog, err := intl.New("en", intl.Define("en", map[string]string{
    "screen.hello": "Hello, {first}!",
}))
if err != nil {
    return err
}

At load time, compileMessage parses "Hello, {first}!". It’s the only message, so keys["screen.hello"] is 0 and the compiled result goes in programs[0]. We already know the argument is called first. We’ll get the actual name when someone calls the translator.

After loading in v0.1.0, programs[0] holds three instructions

An instruction is a Go struct. Its kind tells the renderer how to interpret text. With opText, it writes the text as given. With opValue, it uses the text as an argument name.

type instruction struct {
    text string    // Literal text or argument name.
    end  int       // End of a branch or block. Unused in this greeting.
    kind messageOp // Operation for the renderer to execute.
}

// Contents of programs[0] after loading.
compiledMessage{
    raw: "Hello, {first}!",
    code: []instruction{
        {kind: opText,  text: "Hello, ", end: 0},
        {kind: opValue, text: "first",   end: 0},
        {kind: opText,  text: "!",       end: 0},
    },
}

Now bind t := catalog.Translations("en") and call t("screen.hello", intl.Values{"first": "Ada"}). The first instruction writes "Hello, " to a strings.Builder. The second looks up "first" and writes "Ada" to the same builder. The third writes "!". Pass a different name and the renderer walks the same three instructions again.

If we spell out the successful path through (*messageRender).body in message_render.go, it amounts to this.

var b strings.Builder
b.WriteString("Hello, ")                // First instruction, opText.
value := values["first"]                // Second instruction, opValue. The lookup gives us "Ada".
b.WriteString(messageString(value))     // Write "Ada" to the same builder.
b.WriteString("!")                      // Third instruction, opText.
return b.String(), nil                  // "Hello, Ada!"

After loading in v0.1.1, programs[0] has just one argument to fill in

The parser starts with the same three instructions. The compiler sees only literal text and ordinary placeholders, so it pairs each argument with the literal text immediately before it. Two structs hold the result.

type interpolationArg struct {
    prefix string // Literal text immediately before this argument.
    key    string // Argument name to look up when translating.
}

type interpolation struct {
    args   []interpolationArg // One entry per placeholder, in order of appearance.
    suffix string             // Literal text after the last argument.
}

// Contents of the same programs[0] after loading.
compiledMessage{
    raw:  "Hello, {first}!",
    code: nil,
    plain: &interpolation{
        args: []interpolationArg{
            {prefix: "Hello, ", key: "first"},
        },
        suffix: "!",
    },
}

The "Hello, " from the first instruction and the "first" from the second now share an entry. The "!" from the third goes in suffix. Pass in "Ada" again and the renderer only has to read args[0], look up its key in the argument map, and concatenate the prefix, name, and suffix. Both versions look up values["first"] exactly once. v0.1.1 saves the work of interpreting two literal-text instructions and writing the pieces to a builder on every call.

compileInterpolation in message.go builds the plain field at load time.

func compileInterpolation(code []instruction, count int) *interpolation {
    args := make([]interpolationArg, 0, count)
    start := 0
    for i, op := range code {
        if op.kind != opValue {
            continue
        }
        args = append(args, interpolationArg{prefix: literalText(code[start:i]), key: op.text})
        start = i + 1
    }
    return &interpolation{args: args, suffix: literalText(code[start:])}
}

Each opValue marks a placeholder. literalText collects the text since the previous placeholder, and that becomes the new argument’s prefix. Whatever follows the last argument becomes the suffix.

Here, “compiling” means putting the message into a form that’s easy to use later. To produce the greeting, the renderer just looks up the value by its argument name and joins the pieces.

If the value is already a string, messageString returns it directly. Otherwise, it converts the value to a string and returns that.

func messageString(value any) string {
    if s, ok := value.(string); ok {
        return s
    }
    return fmt.Sprint(value)
}

A message with one argument reaches these lines at the end of interpolation.render.

if arg.prefix == "" && p.suffix == "" {
    return text, nil
}
return arg.prefix + text + p.suffix, nil

For the greeting, the result is "Hello, " + "Ada" + "!". For a message that consists entirely of {first}, both surrounding strings are empty. The renderer can return "Ada" itself.

go-i18n hands the greeting to the Go template executor. Here’s the execution code in i18n/template/text_parser.go.

func (t *parsedTextTemplate) Execute(data any) (string, error) {
    var buf bytes.Buffer
    if err := t.tmpl.Execute(&buf, data); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return buf.String(), nil
}

These benchmarks pass the same map[string]any{"first": "Ada"} to both libraries. go-i18n also accepts a struct as TemplateData. Even with the template cached, Go’s text/template has to decide how to read {{.first}} each time it executes. It first looks for a method with that name, then uses reflection to distinguish a struct from a map. Here the input is a map, so the executor uses MapIndex to read "first" and writes "Ada" to the buffer along with the surrounding text. Field evaluation in Go’s template executor

go-intl defines named arguments as type Values map[string]any. At load time it records "first" in arg.key. At execution time values[arg.key] reads the map directly, so the renderer can skip checking the container type and looking up the value through reflection. The value itself is still any, so messageString checks whether it’s a string. Here it gets "Ada", which can go straight into the concatenation.

go-i18n’s default template uses text/template.(*state).evalField. Here receiver is the object being read, and fieldName is "first". The excerpt shows the struct and map branches after the method lookup. Comments mark the omitted code. Go standard library source

switch receiver.Kind() {
case reflect.Struct:
    tField, ok := receiver.Type().FieldByName(fieldName)
    if ok {
        field, err := receiver.FieldByIndexErr(tField.Index)
        // … check field visibility, access errors, and call arguments
        return field
    }
case reflect.Map:
    nameVal := reflect.ValueOf(fieldName)
    if nameVal.Type().AssignableTo(receiver.Type().Key()) {
        // … check call arguments
        result := receiver.MapIndex(nameVal)
        // … handle a missing key
        return result
    }
// … other cases
}

For ordinary interpolation, go-intl uses (*interpolation).render. The same name is already stored in arg.key. Inside the loop over the placeholders, these lines look up the value and turn it into text.

value := values[arg.key]
if value == nil {
    return "", fmt.Errorf("missing value for %q", arg.key)
}
text := messageString(value)

Figure 2. Caching avoids parsing the template again. When the message is simple enough, its execution can be shortened as well.

From one name to sixteen fields

Now consider a message with sixteen placeholders.

{k00}/{k01}/{k02}/…/{k15}

The keys run from v00 through v15. If we kept doing result = result + next, each concatenation could copy everything accumulated so far. The longer the message, the more often we’d copy its opening bytes.

For ordinary placeholders, go-intl starts with a local [128]byte array. It appends literals and argument values in order, then builds the final string. Here’s the full implementation in message_render.go.

func (p *interpolation) render(values Values) (string, error) {
    var local [128]byte
    out := local[:0]
    for i, arg := range p.args {
        value := values[arg.key]
        if value == nil {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("missing value for %q", arg.key)
        }
        text := messageString(value)
        if i+1 < len(p.args) {
            out = append(out, arg.prefix...)
            out = append(out, text...)
            continue
        }
        // The last argument goes straight into the final concatenation.
        if len(out) > 0 {
            return string(out) + arg.prefix + text + p.suffix, nil
        }
        if arg.prefix == "" && p.suffix == "" {
            return text, nil
        }
        return arg.prefix + text + p.suffix, nil
    }
    return p.suffix, nil
}

The first fifteen values go into the buffer. The sixteenth goes straight into the final concatenation, saving a trip through the buffer.

Each value here is three bytes. The first fifteen values and the fourteen slashes between them occupy 15 × 3 + 14 = 59 bytes. They all fit in the same local array.

Through the public API, this case took three heap allocations per call in go-intl and 37 in go-i18n. The final string still needs storage. Longer arguments can also push append past the capacity of the local array and force it to grow the buffer.

If the same argument appears sixteen times, go-intl still reads it sixteen times in order. An argument can implement String(), and successive calls can produce different results, so each occurrence is evaluated separately. The occurrences share the space used to hold intermediate text.

Another interpolation experiment — Joining multiple variables with strings.Join

While working on general-purpose interpolation, I also tried filling a string slice with the pieces and then calling strings.Join(parts, "") to produce the translation. For {first}/{last}/{id}, the filled slice is []string{"", "Ada", "/", "Lovelace", "/", "42", ""}. Three values and four literals take up seven slots. The empty strings at the beginning and end each take a slot, too.

Scale that up to sixteen placeholders separated by slashes. There are fifteen slashes between the values, and the slice still keeps an empty string before the first value and after the last.

Figure 2a. Sixteen values have fifteen separators between them. With the two empty pieces at the ends, that makes 33 slots.

I ran this experiment on an Apple M3 Pro (darwin/arm64) with Go 1.27.1. Each argument value was three ASCII bytes, with slashes between placeholders. I bound the translation function and prepared the arguments before starting the timer. Each timed call produced one translation. The table gives the median of six runs with -cpu=1 and 250 ms per case per run.

Interpolation case Slots needed ns/op B/op allocs/op
4 distinct arguments 9 140.90 24 2
8 distinct arguments 17 243.10 40 2
16 distinct arguments 33 624.40 648 3
32 distinct arguments 65 1,196.50 1,288 3
One argument repeated 16 times 33 639.45 648 3

Repeating one argument sixteen times also takes 33 slots. Each occurrence still contributes its own value to the slice. Both sixteen-placeholder cases used 648 bytes across three heap allocations per translation.

7 items — First choose the wording, then decide how to write the number

A cart label needs more than a number in a fixed sentence. In English, a cart with one item reads 1 item. A cart with seven reads 7 items.

Figure 2b. For an English cart count, 1 selects one. Every other nonnegative integer selects other.

Here’s the cart message in go-intl.

{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}

count is the number of items in the cart. one and other are English plural categories. Inside either branch, # stands for the count to display.

How the two branches are stored at load time

At load time, compileMessage parses the cart message into its code slice. The body of one occupies indexes 2 and 3. The body of other occupies indexes 5 and 6. We can already say what each branch will write. Which one runs depends on the count supplied at translation time.

compiledMessage{
    raw: "{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}",
    code: []instruction{
        {kind: opPlural, text: "count", end: 7}, // 0: the whole plural block
        {kind: opCase,   text: "one",   end: 4}, // 1: label for the one branch
        {kind: opPound},                         // 2: write the count
        {kind: opText,   text: " item"},         // 3: write the literal text
        {kind: opCase,   text: "other", end: 7}, // 4: label for the other branch
        {kind: opPound},                         // 5: write the count
        {kind: opText,   text: " items"},        // 6: write the literal text
    },
}

When the parser reaches the closing brace of one, the slice has four instructions. It sets code[1].end to 4, the first position past that branch. Here that position happens to be the label for other. By the time the parser closes other, the slice has seven instructions. Index 7 is also the end of the whole plural block.

compileMessage turns the input string into a sequence of steps the renderer can follow. If you’ve studied compilers, two familiar ideas can help here. One is a grammar, a set of rules describing how sentences in a language can be formed. The other is nesting.

At translation time, the renderer uses those indexes to run the chosen branch.

case opSelect, opPlural, opOrdinal:
    branch, adjusted, err := r.choose(i, op, value)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("argument %q: %w", op.text, err)
    }
    if err := r.body(b, branch+1, r.code[branch].end, adjusted); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    i = op.end

Follow a call with count = 7. The outer loop has read opPlural at index 0 and advanced i to 1. r.choose(1, op, 7) starts checking labels there. English puts 7 in other, whose label is at index 4, so branch is 4. This message has no plural offset, so adjusted, the value for #, is still 7.

The recursive call is now r.body(b, 5, 7, 7). The first two numbers describe the half-open instruction range [5, 7). The last is the quantity. Instruction 5 writes "7" into b. Instruction 6 appends " items". The result is "7 items".

With a count of 1, it’s easier to see what the last line, i = op.end, does. The body of one occupies indexes 2 and 3. After writing "1 item", the outer loop jumps straight to index 7, skipping the other branch.

If the author adds =7 {Exactly seven}, a count of exactly 7 takes that branch ahead of other. The renderer still checks candidate labels, but the recorded boundaries let it skip their bodies.

In English, 7 can be converted straight to a string

After selecting # items, we still need text for #.

For the integer 7 in English, strconv.Itoa(7) gives us exactly "7". With 12345, English normally calls for a grouping separator, as in 12,345. Other languages may also use different digit shapes.

localizedNumber uses strconv.Itoa only when the two forms are known to agree.

if kind == opNumber && (locale.tag == language.English || locale.tag == language.AmericanEnglish) {
    if n, ok := value.(int); ok && n > -1000 && n < 1000 {
        return strconv.Itoa(n)
    }
}

The conditions are narrow. The format must be an ordinary number, the dictionary language must be en or en-US, and the value must be a Go int between −999 and 999 inclusive.

The 7 in 7 items qualifies. Other cases go through the locale-aware number printer. Each dictionary gets its printer when the catalog is built and reuses it across calls.

How go-i18n turns its Other template into 7 items

The go-i18n benchmark uses the same message ID, screen.items. In its English dictionary, One holds {{.PluralCount}} item and Other holds {{.PluralCount}} items. Here’s the call.

cfg := &i18n.LocalizeConfig{
    MessageID:    "screen.items",
    PluralCount:  7,                              // Used by the plural rule to select One or Other.
    TemplateData: map[string]any{"PluralCount": 7}, // Used by the template to evaluate .PluralCount.
}
text := loc.MustLocalize(cfg) // "7 items"

The two occurrences of 7 are used in different places. go-i18n first reads cfg.PluralCount to prepare the value its plural rule needs. As before, the Localizer calls l.bundle.matcher.Match(l.tags...) to select the English dictionary, then looks up "screen.items". The English rule puts the first 7 in Other, so it selects {{.PluralCount}} items. At this point, all it has done is choose the template. The template still has to run, as we saw in the interpolation section. That’s one reason go-i18n is slower here.

In go-intl, English was bound before the call. Once other is selected, the renderer already has the integer 7 for that branch. opPound writes "7", then opText appends " items".

Figure 3. Choosing the wording and formatting the number are two separate steps, each with its own input and output.

How much time do these changes save?

Now we can return to the benchmarks and connect each row to the steps we’ve just walked through.

Case go-intl ns/op go-intl allocs/op go-i18n ns/op go-i18n allocs/op go-intl speedup
One argument, {first} 27.54 1 284.60 7 10.33×
Hello, {first}! 52.34 2 300.70 7 5.75×
Item {id}. with id = 42 88.86 3 307.60 7 3.46×
{first} {last} 70.28 2 420.15 9 5.98×
{first}{last} 68.54 2 410.20 9 5.98×
4 distinct arguments 97.93 2 670.65 13 6.85×
8 distinct arguments 156.70 2 1,152.50 21 7.35×
16 distinct arguments 257.10 3 2,015.50 37 7.84×
32 distinct arguments 470.55 3 3,877.00 70 8.24×
One argument repeated 16 times 265.55 3 2,004.00 37 7.55×
Repeated lookup of one static key 12.9 0 116.8 0 9.05×
Cycling through 1,024 static keys 15.8 0 125.8 0 7.96×
English plural, count = 7 81.2 2 336.5 8 4.14×

ns/op is the time per operation in nanoseconds. Allocations are also counted per operation. Speedup is the go-i18n time divided by the go-intl time.

The static cases use full keys and a translator bound with locale.Translations(). The 12.9 ns result uses no screen namespace or short-key index. Both libraries recorded zero heap allocations, so the timing difference lies in the work they do to find and return the same text.

In a CPU profile of go-i18n repeatedly looking up one key, language matching accounted for 64% of the samples, the largest single cost. Even removing it entirely, with everything else held constant, would give a theoretical speedup of about 1 / (1 − 0.64) ≈ 2.8×. The roughly ninefold difference in the table reflects the two lookup paths as a whole.

The greeting uses direct concatenation for ordinary placeholders. The sixteen-field case shows the benefit of sharing a temporary buffer. The English plural case includes both branch selection and small-integer formatting. These inputs take different paths, which is why their timings and allocation counts differ.

Record what you know as soon as you know it

A message index has one job. Given a string key, it returns the message index. I wanted to know whether a sorted slice was worth using when the keys were short and the dictionary had only a dozen or so entries. With a larger dictionary, how much lookup time could a hash table built specifically for these keys save? I tested three implementations on the same keys, using a sorted slice, a custom hash table with linear probing, and a Go map. At 16, 1,024, and 16,384 keys, Go’s map was the fastest on successful lookups, both when looking up one key repeatedly and when cycling through different keys. That’s why go-intl kept map[string]int.

Say a dictionary contains four messages and "screen.ready" is at index 2. With a Go map, index["screen.ready"] gives us that 2 directly.

A sorted slice keeps the keys in lexical order. In this example the messages sit in the same order, so a key’s position in the slice is also its message index.

keys := []string{"screen.cancel", "screen.copy", "screen.ready", "screen.save"}
i, ok := slices.BinarySearch(keys, "screen.ready") // i == 2, ok == true

Binary search compares the middle key and uses that ordering to narrow the range. For instance, "screen.copy" sorts before "screen.ready", so we can discard it and everything to its left. The first key equal to the target is keys[2].

Figure 4. slices.BinarySearch finds the first key greater than or equal to the target, then checks for equality. The diagram omits the shared prefix screen..

For the custom hash table, I used FNV-1a hashing and linear probing. With the same four keys, the experiment builds a table with eight slots. A key’s hash determines its starting slot. Each occupied slot stores the message index plus one, leaving 0 to mark an empty slot. Both "screen.copy" and "screen.ready" start at slot 4. We insert "screen.copy" first, so "screen.ready" takes the next slot, 5. Here’s the lookup for "screen.ready".

Slot examined Stored value Recover the index and check the key
4 2 keys[2-1] is "screen.copy". Try the next slot.
5 3 keys[3-1] is "screen.ready". Return message index 2.

Stepping through successive slots after a collision is called linear probing. Reaching an empty slot before finding the key tells us the key is absent.

Figure 5. Linear probing takes us from slot 4 to slot 5. The stored value there is 3, so the message index is 3 − 1 = 2.

The table shows how long it took to find the integer index for a message key, in nanoseconds per lookup (ns/op). Lower values are faster. Every lookup was a hit. The figures are medians from three runs on an Apple M3 Pro with Go 1.27.1.

Keys in dictionary Lookup pattern Go map Sorted slice Linear probing
16 Repeated key 7.2 18.4 10.0
16 Cycling through keys 7.2 19.4 12.2
1,024 Repeated key 7.3 34.1 9.9
1,024 Cycling through keys 8.0 38.3 19.8
16,384 Repeated key 7.4 40.9 10.0
16,384 Cycling through keys 12.3 126.0 29.8

Most of the changes described above happen before the map lookup or after the message has been retrieved.

As soon as the translation file is loaded, we know which text is literal, where the arguments go, and where each branch ends. We can keep all of that. Once a request has a language, the forty strings on the page can share it, too.

What has to wait until display time is the user’s name, how many items are in the cart, and how the number should appear.

That leaves each message with just the steps it needs at display time. For Ready, return the stored text. For Hello, Ada!, look up the name and concatenate the pieces. For 7 items, choose the wording based on the quantity, then write the number.

The code versions are go-intl v0.1.1 and go-i18n v2.7.0. The implementation details in this article come from those two versions. Each excerpt identifies the function it comes from, and the examples use the respective library’s template syntax.

title: This Week In React #307 : Security, React Router, Next.js, TanStack Query, RTL, RTK | Reanimated, Worklets, Expo, Skia | TC39, Node.js, Parcel
description:
Hi everyone, Seb and Jan here 👋!

This week, Ricky Hanlon leaves Meta after 8 years on React. React Router fixed 7 vulnerabilities, and an automated React2STEAL campaign is leaking secrets from unpatched React and Next.js servers. TanStack Query shared its v6 roadmap. Next.js is experimenting with a Go server.

On mobile, Reanimated 4.8 makes Shared Element Transitions stable. An RFC proposes a platform-agnostic React Native core, to make out-of-tree platforms easier to maintain. Skia and WebGPU now download their prebuilt binaries at build time, which makes the npm packages much lighter.

Elsewhere, next week's TC39 meeting could move Import Text to stage 4. Firefox 161 unlocks CSS random() in all browsers. Parcel 3 can now build static sites on its own. Node.js is preparing to enable pointer compression by default.

Let's dive in!

💡 Subscribe to the official newsletter to receive an email every week!

💸 Sponsor

Fewer findings. Only real risks.

AI-generated code can introduce vulnerabilities that are easy to miss in a pull request. CodeRabbit Security continuously reviews your codebase for complex bugs and security risks, using full-codebase context to follow data flows, dependencies, and patterns beyond the latest diff.

Run CodeRabbit Security on your own repositories today.

⚛️ React

  • 💸 Nexity - Next.js + Sanity with AI workflows built in. 16 skills, 9 agents, project-specific rules and read-only code reviewers. MIT.
  • 🐦 Ricky Hanlon leaves Meta after 8 years on React - Most of the React core team has already left Meta. He will keep working on React at a new company.
  • 🔐 React Router vulnerabilities - 4 high and 3 moderate advisories, upgrade to 7.18.6 or 8.5.2
  • 🔐 React2STEAL - Automated campaign exploits unpatched React and Next.js servers from hijacked GitHub accounts - At least 1,281 servers still vulnerable to React2Shell (React 19.0–19.2) or to the Next.js middleware bypass were hit, and their env vars, .env files and API keys were committed to public GitHub repos. If you're still on a vulnerable version, upgrade and rotate your secrets.
  • 👀 Next.js PR - Switchyard, an experimental Go server in front of next start - For now, it only forwards requests to Node. Routing could move to it over time, and requests to the experimental Go Route Handlers would skip Node entirely.
  • 💬 TanStack Query v6 roadmap - Planning a small major with few breaking changes. ESM-only, React 19 minimum to use use() for Suspense, scheduler using microtasks, deprecated APIs removed, stable streamedQuery. Considering the removal of enabled in favor of skipToken.
  • 📜 React Testing Library is faster when it's part of the DOM - What if a DOM implementation had built-in Testing Library queries? @ctrl/dom replaces jsdom for component tests and runs existing RTL test suites 32–54% faster. Node 26+ and React 19 only.
  • 📜 Your Tools are Hiding npm Audits from You - A fresh Next.js app reports 0 vulnerabilities. But its 139 dependencies bundled in next/dist/compiled have 3 critical and 19 high ones, which npm audit can't see.
  • 📜 React Forms Beyond onSubmit - Compares onSubmit, onSubmit with useTransition, and the action prop on a newsletter subscription form, with a summary table.
  • 📜 On Drawing Icons - The Figma-to-React pipeline behind Pierre icons.
  • 💸 The Joy of React - Build an intuition for how React really works through an interactive learning experience. On sale for Black Friday!
  • 📦 Pierre Words - Streaming Markdown renderer written in WebAssembly, with a React renderer - Built for streamed AI replies. Its own benchmark against Streamdown highlights 6x less streaming work, 20x less memory, and a 65% smaller React renderer.
  • 📦 Talata 0.4 - Drop-in faster replacement for remark - Now parses MDX - It claims to parse MDX 4x faster than remark-mdx.
