title: Conditional Statements in Java
description:
Conditional Statements in Java

Conditional statements are one of the fundamental concepts in Java programming. They allow a program to make decisions and execute different blocks of code based on specific conditions.

Normally, a program executes statements sequentially. However, in real-world applications, we often need to perform different actions depending on the situation. For example, checking whether a student has passed an exam, verifying login credentials, calculating grades, or determining whether a person is eligible to vote.

Java provides conditional statements to handle these decision-making scenarios.

Types of Conditional Statements

Java supports the following conditional statements:

  • if
  • if-else
  • if-else-if ladder
  • Nested if
  • switch

1. if Statement

The if statement executes a block of code only when the given condition is true. If the condition is false, the block is skipped.

Syntax:

if (condition) {
    // Code executes if condition is true
}

Example:

int age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
    System.out.println("Eligible to vote");
}

Output:

Eligible to vote

Here, Java checks whether the age is greater than or equal to 18. Since the condition is true, the statement inside the if block executes.

2. if-else Statement

The if-else statement is used when we need to execute one block of code if the condition is true and another block if it is false.

Syntax:

if (condition) {
    // Executes if true
} else {
    // Executes if false
}

Example:

int number = 7;

if (number % 2 == 0) {
    System.out.println("Even number");
} else {
    System.out.println("Odd number");
}

Output:

Odd number

The modulus operator (%) returns the remainder. If the remainder is zero, the number is even; otherwise, it is odd.

3. if-else-if Ladder

The if-else-if ladder is used to check multiple conditions sequentially. When a condition becomes true, its corresponding block executes, and the remaining conditions are skipped.

Example:

int mark = 85;

if (mark >= 90) {
    System.out.println("Grade A");
} else if (mark >= 80) {
    System.out.println("Grade B");
} else if (mark >= 70) {
    System.out.println("Grade C");
} else if (mark >= 50) {
    System.out.println("Grade D");
} else {
    System.out.println("Fail");
}

Output:

Grade B

Since the mark is 85, the second condition is true. Therefore, Grade B is printed.

The order of conditions is important. Conditions should be arranged carefully to avoid incorrect results.

4. Nested if Statement

A nested if means placing one if statement inside another if statement. It is useful when one condition must be satisfied before checking another condition.

Example:

String username = "admin";
String password = "1234";

if (username.equals("admin")) {
    if (password.equals("1234")) {
        System.out.println("Login successful");
    } else {
        System.out.println("Incorrect password");
    }
} else {
    System.out.println("Incorrect username");
}

Output:

Login successful

First, the username is checked. If it is correct, Java checks the password. If both conditions are satisfied, the login is successful.

5. switch Statement

The switch statement is used to execute different blocks of code based on the value of an expression. It is useful when comparing a variable against multiple fixed values.

Example:

int day = 3;

switch (day) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("Monday");
        break;

    case 2:
        System.out.println("Tuesday");
        break;

    case 3:
        System.out.println("Wednesday");
        break;

    case 4:
        System.out.println("Thursday");
        break;

    default:
        System.out.println("Invalid day");
}

Output:

Wednesday

Important Keywords

  • case – Defines a possible matching value.
  • break – Terminates the switch block and prevents fall-through.
  • default – Executes when no case matches.

Without break, Java may continue executing the following cases. This behavior is called fall-through.

title: What a Token Picker Should Show When You Search for “Pepe”
description:
Type pepe into a wallet's search box and you might see PEPE, PEPECOIN, and PEP. Putting the network next to each result helps with one of them. PEP runs on Pepecoin Network. The other two are both ERC-20 tokens on Ethereum, so the network label leaves you with two plausible matches.

The names have a history. PEPECOIN traces back to a project from 2016, PEPE launched as a separate Ethereum token in 2023, and PEP arrived in 2024 as the native coin of a network built from Dogecoin's code. That history explains the search results. The wallet still needs a way to carry one exact choice through to the confirmation screen. The ChangeNOW guide compares the three projects and their networks.

Give the search results enough room

Search result Network Detail shown in the row
PEPE Ethereum ERC-20 · 0x6982…1933
PEPECOIN Ethereum ERC-20 · 0xa9e8…489a
PEP Pepecoin Network Native coin

Use the symbol for search and display. For an ERC-20 entry, store the chain ID and full contract address so the app can find the same record again. The ERC-20 standard makes both name() and symbol() optional, and the Uniswap Token Lists schema stores chainId and address alongside the display fields. A short address fits in a row. Give the user the full one in the asset details so they can compare it with a source they trust. ERC-20 specification · Uniswap Token Lists schema

Carry the selection forward

Here's the smallest version of the state I'd use for this example. The search result passes its asset record into the transfer draft. Once the user enters a destination, the app puts it in a separate field on that same draft.

type Asset =
  | { kind: "erc20"; chainId: number; contract: `0x${string}` }
  | { kind: "native"; network: "pepecoin-mainnet" };

type TransferDraft = {
  asset: Asset;
  recipient: string;
};

function startTransfer(asset: Asset): TransferDraft {
  return { asset, recipient: "" };
}

const draft = startTransfer({
  kind: "erc20",
  chainId: 1,
  contract: "0xa9e8acf069c58aec8825542845fd754e41a9489a",
});

pepecoin-mainnet is a local label for this demo. PEP runs on its own chain and has no ERC-20 contract to fill in. In an Ethereum-only wallet, the PEP result can say Pepecoin Network transfers unavailable before the user gets to the address field. A wallet that supports the chain can route the selection into its own address validation and transfer flow. Pepecoin Core · Pepecoin FAQ

Show the same asset at confirmation

Field What the confirmation screen shows
Asset PEPECOIN
Network Ethereum mainnet
Token contract 0xa9e8acf069c58aec8825542845fd754e41a9489a
Recipient The destination entered by the user

For a direct ERC-20 transfer, the wallet calls transfer on the selected token contract and passes the recipient as the _to argument. Both addresses begin with 0x, so the labels do real work here. Someone checking the token should be able to find its contract without wondering whether they're looking at the address that'll receive the funds. ERC-20 transfer method

One test I'd run before shipping is to select PEPECOIN from the results, change the search query, then continue to confirmation. The same contract should still be there. I'd also add a test record that shares a symbol with an existing entry but has a different contract. Picking either row should produce its own draft, and neither selection should overwrite the other.

title: Memcached for Beginners: Speed Up Your App With Simple In-Memory Caching
description:
Memcached is a free, open-source caching system that stores data in memory so your app does not have to hit the database for the same thing twice. It is one of the oldest and simplest caching tools in existence: a key-value store, running as a single daemon, that answers in microseconds. When your app is slow because the database is doing the same query a thousand times a minute, Memcached is often the fix.

How it works: your app checks the cache before the database. On a cache miss, it queries the database, stores the result in Memcached with an expiry time, and returns it. On the next identical request, the result comes straight from memory. Keys expire automatically, and when memory fills up, the least-recently-used items are evicted — so the cache never needs manual cleanup.

Memcached is a good fit for beginners because the API is tiny: set, get, and delete cover almost everything. There is no query language, no schema, and no clustering to configure for a first project. You can add it to an existing app in an afternoon and measure the difference immediately.

A quick example — caching a user profile in Python:

from pymemcache.client import base

cache = base.Client(("localhost", 11211))

def get_user(user_id):
    user = cache.get(f"user:{user_id}")
    if user is None:
        user = db.query_user(user_id)      # slow database call
        cache.set(f"user:{user_id}", user, expire=300)  # cache for 5 minutes
    return user

The first call hits the database; every call in the next five minutes hits memory instead.

Who is it for? Developers whose apps repeat the same database queries; teams caching sessions, rendered pages, or API responses; students learning what caching is before they need Redis.

Limits to know: Memcached stores only strings and simple values — no data structures like Redis has. It is a cache, not a database: data can vanish at any time, so your app must always work when the cache is empty. And it has no built-in persistence, so a restart means a cold cache.

To start today: run the Memcached daemon, store one value with a 60-second expiry, read it back, and watch it disappear after a minute.

title: Celery for Beginners: Run Background Jobs in Python Without Blocking Requests
description:
Celery is the standard way to run background jobs in Python. Some work should not happen inside a web request: sending an email, resizing an image, generating a report. Celery lets your web app hand that work to a queue and answer the user immediately, while worker processes pick the jobs up and run them in the background.

How it works: your app creates a task — a Python function decorated with @app.task — and calls it with .delay() instead of calling it directly. The call goes to a message broker (usually Redis or RabbitMQ) as a message. A Celery worker, a separate process, reads the message, runs the function, and stores the result. Your web request never waits for the slow work to finish.

Celery is a good fit for beginners because the core idea is one decorator and one method call. You can run the broker, the worker, and your app all on your laptop while learning, and the same code scales to separate servers later. The result backend lets you check on a job's status, so "is my report ready yet?" is a simple query.

A quick example — sending a welcome email in the background:

from celery import Celery

app = Celery("tasks", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0")

@app.task
def send_welcome_email(user_id):
    user = get_user(user_id)
    send_email(user.email, "Welcome aboard!")

# In your web request — returns instantly, email sends in the background
send_welcome_email.delay(new_user.id)

The user sees "account created" in milliseconds; the email goes out a moment later, from a worker.

Who is it for? Python developers whose web apps do slow work; teams adding email, reports, or image processing to a Django or FastAPI project; students learning how background processing actually works.

Limits to know: Celery adds moving parts — a broker, workers, and a result store — so debugging gets harder when a job fails silently. Tasks must be idempotent (safe to run twice), because retries happen. And for very simple needs, a lighter queue or even a cron job may be enough.

To start today: install Celery with Redis, write one task that sleeps for five seconds, call it with .delay(), and watch the worker pick it up while your script continues.

title: Refilling custom dropdowns from a Chrome content script: MUI, Ant Design, Radix, react-select
description:
I made FormEcho to save answers from a web form and put them back when I needed the same form again. The ordinary text inputs were the straightforward part. A dropdown that looked ordinary could have a button, a search input, a hidden input, and a list of options mounted somewhere else in the document.

The useful distinction was between the element that displays an answer and the interaction that makes the application accept it. A native input can often be restored with a setter and events. A custom dropdown usually has to be opened, searched or navigated, and selected. You also need to check that it actually selected the answer you wanted.

Start with the native setter, but know where it stops

A plain assignment can make a text box look right without updating the state a React form uses. In particular, an assignment can go through the setter the framework is tracking. Dispatching an event afterward might then leave React seeing no change. The content script calls the platform setter from the appropriate prototype, rather than starting with the instance setter. This is the actual helper from the extension:

  function setNativeValue(el, value) {
    const proto = el.tagName === 'TEXTAREA' ? HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype : el.tagName === 'SELECT' ? HTMLSelectElement.prototype : HTMLInputElement.prototype;
    const desc = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(proto, 'value');
    if (desc && desc.set) desc.set.call(el, value);
    else el.value = value;
  }

The ordinary input path then dispatches bubbling input and change events. In a custom dropdown the same native setter can help type a search string, but it does not choose an item. A search box displaying “Ontario” and a widget actually having “Ontario” selected are two different states. For a combo, the script saves the selected labels and later looks for a matching option, rather than treating whatever was in the search input as the answer.

Material UI: ignore the hidden twin

A Material UI select can expose a visible control and also keep a native input around for form submission. Writing .value on the hidden input can change what you see in the inspector without updating the component. Saving both nodes is worse: the capture sees two fields where the person using the form sees one. On refill, one can be reported missing even when the visible answer was set correctly.

This is the filter from the field scan. It keeps the hidden twin out of the list before the script reads answers:

      if (el.tagName === 'INPUT' && el.getAttribute('aria-hidden') === 'true' && el.tabIndex === -1) continue;

The visible control still needs the dropdown interaction. Open it, look through the visible options and pick the saved label. For related widgets such as an autocomplete, the actionable input can be smaller than the visible box around it, so the scan also considers whether the enclosing combo is visible. A rule that excludes every small input would miss some of the controls it was supposed to restore.

Ant Design: distinguish the search handle from a password field

The search handle in an Ant Design select can carry autocomplete="new-password" to keep browser suggestions out of the widget. I originally treated that attribute as reason enough to skip the input. That made a working privacy filter look like a dropdown compatibility problem. It also meant a plain .value assignment was the wrong repair: even if I reached the input, I would only be putting text into the filter box.

The capture code makes the autocomplete exception only after the element has been classified as a combo, and still checks its identifying attributes for sensitive names:

    if (SENSITIVE_AUTOCOMPLETE.test(ac) && kindOf(el) !== 'combo') return true;
    const hay = [el.getAttribute('name'), el.id, el.getAttribute('placeholder'), el.getAttribute('aria-label')].filter(Boolean).join(' ');
    return SENSITIVE_NAME.test(hay);

The combo path opens the menu, types into an editable handle when there is one, and looks for the saved label. Ant Design option elements can be found through their option class as well as the standard option role. The separate selected-item display gives the script a better way to check the outcome than reading the search text back.

Radix: send the pointer sequence, including the release

A Radix select trigger can be a button. Assigning .value does not tell that trigger to open, and calling click() does not produce a pointer-down event. In the demos I tested, opening the list and then choosing an option required more than a lone click.

The shared helper dispatches pointer-down, mouse-down, pointer-up, mouse-up and click. The selection path also sends a separate release on the document before pressing the option. That release gives the opening guard a chance to clear so the first option press is not swallowed. Here is the order in the current code:

      hit.scrollIntoView?.({ block: 'nearest' });
      // Some libraries swallow the first pointer release after opening (a guard against accidental picks).
      el.ownerDocument.dispatchEvent(new PointerEvent('pointerup', { bubbles: true, pointerId: 1, pointerType: 'mouse' }));
      press(hit);
      await sleep(160);

The script checks the displayed value after the press. If it did not change and the option is still connected, it tries focusing the option and pressing Enter. The check matters more than whether the script managed to dispatch all the events. Dispatch is something the extension controls; accepting the choice is something the page controls.

react-select: look for a choice, not just an input

In react-select, the input you can type into is a handle for the menu. .value = savedAnswer can put a string into that handle without committing a selection. The script recognizes the familiar react-select input ID pattern as one signal that a combobox is a genuine select handle:

    if (el.getAttribute('role') !== 'combobox') return false;
    if (/^react-select-.+-input$/.test(el.id)) return true;

That pattern helps classify a control, but it does not make the exact ID a durable record key. To find options the script first checks the list referred to by aria-controls or aria-owns. Otherwise it looks for visible options in the same document. That fallback matters when the menu is mounted apart from the control. Once the menu is open, the script searches where it can type, picks the option by displayed text, and checks the selected labels in the widget. It avoids toggling an option that is already selected during a multi-select refill.

The field you found can disappear

A form that shows state or province choices after a country change can replace the control while you work. The plain fields are written first, with the combos handled afterward. When a queued combo node is detached by the time its turn comes, the script searches the current DOM for the control again before trying to open it.

The stored description includes the kind of field, its name, label, placeholder, ARIA label, autocomplete token and position. A generated ID gets less weight than a stable one. A position-only fallback is allowed if the form still has the same field count and the candidate at that position is of the same kind. That narrows the fallback, but it cannot tell two truly indistinguishable controls apart after a reorder. This is a practical reason to report misses rather than say every refill worked.

For my own test cases, I treat a dropdown refill as successful only when the control reports the selected label after the menu closes. Seeing the search text appear or getting an option to highlight is not enough. A dependent control is another useful check: change the parent selection, let the new options render, then confirm the child control took the intended answer too.

On the public demo pages for Material UI, Ant Design, Radix and react-select, the script restored 12 of 12 dropdowns. On 20 ordinary public form pages it restored 128 of 129 fields. Those are results for those pages, not a compatibility guarantee. Headless UI listboxes are not detected, and I have not tried very long virtualized lists. If an option never appears in the DOM after opening or filtering the menu, the current lookup cannot pick it.

title: How I Built a Real-Time Collaborative Code Editor with Spring Boot, WebSockets, and React
description:
Sharing code quickly during technical interviews, remote pair programming, or mentoring sessions shouldn't require heavy IDE setups or mandatory sign-ups. Most existing tools either lock basic features behind paywalls or feel bloated for quick collaboration.

To solve this, I built Codeshares.in — a fast, zero-setup, real-time collaborative code editor that works directly in the browser.

👉 Try the Live App: https://www.codeshares.in/

🏗️ System Architecture & Tech Stack

For a collaborative editor to feel instantaneous, low-latency communication and reliable state persistence are critical. Here is the architecture powering the platform:

  • Backend: Java & Spring Boot
  • Real-Time Communication: WebSockets (STOMP / SockJS) for instant bi-directional code synchronization
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite for a responsive, snappy UI
  • Database: TiDB Cloud (distributed SQL) for scalable session persistence
  • Deployment & DevOps: Containerized with Docker, backend hosted on Render, and frontend served via Netlify/Vercel

⚡ Key Features

  1. Zero-Setup Instant Rooms: Open the site, get a unique room URL, and share it. No login or account creation required.
  2. Real-Time Multi-User Sync: Changes appear instantaneously across all connected browsers as participants type.
  3. 50+ Language Support: Automatic syntax highlighting and clean formatting for Java, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C++, Rust, SQL, and more.
  4. Built for Interviews & Teaching: Clean distraction-free dark interface tailored for live coding assessments and debugging sessions.

Explore the full list of capabilities on the Codeshares Features Page.

🧠 Key Engineering Challenges Solved

1. Low-Latency State Synchronization

Handling concurrent edits over WebSockets requires careful session and room management. Using Spring Boot's WebSocket messaging broker, each room acts as an isolated topic where code state updates are broadcast only to active subscribers in that specific session.

2. Session Persistence Without Friction

Users expect their shared code snippet to remain accessible if they refresh the browser or revisit the link later. Integrating TiDB Cloud allowed me to persist room states asynchronously without blocking the real-time WebSocket message loop.

3. Technical SEO for a Single-Page Application (SPA)

React SPAs often struggle with search engine indexing. To make the platform discoverable, I implemented dynamic route metadata, semantic below-the-fold documentation, structured JSON-LD schema (WebApplication), and clean multi-page routing (/features, /about, /faq).

🚀 What's Next?

I'm continuously improving the editor based on developer feedback. Upcoming additions on my roadmap include:

  • In-browser code execution sandbox for popular languages
  • Custom room expiration controls and read-only view modes
  • Voice/text chat integration for seamless remote interviews

🤝 Feedback & Contributions

If you're preparing for technical interviews, mentoring students, or just need a quick way to share a code snippet without sending screenshots, give Codeshares.in a try!

I'd love to hear your thoughts, feature requests, or architectural feedback in the comments below. 👇

title: Kinetic Typography in the Browser: Graphemes, Staggered Timelines, and Frame-Accurate Export
description:
Almost every "animated text" effect you see in a video is the same three-stage pipeline: split a string into animatable units, give each unit a time offset, then scrub the resulting timeline deterministically when it's time to export. The visual variety — typewriter, blur, stretch, 3D spatial — is mostly just different keyframes on top of that skeleton.

Here's how to build the skeleton with plain browser APIs.

1. Split text into graphemes, not characters

The tempting one-liner is [...text]. It splits by Unicode code point, which quietly breaks emoji with skin tones, ZWJ sequences like 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦, flags, and combining accents. Intl.Segmenter gives you what a reader actually perceives as one character:

function splitGraphemes(text) {
  const seg = new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: 'grapheme' });
  return [...seg.segment(text)].map(s => s.segment);
}

function render(text, container) {
  return splitGraphemes(text).map((g, i) => {
    const span = document.createElement('span');
    span.className = 'glyph';
    span.style.setProperty('--i', i);
    span.textContent = g === ' ' ? '\u00A0' : g; // don't let spaces collapse
    container.append(span);
    return span;
  });
}

Two details that save debugging time: use a non-breaking space for whitespace so inline-block glyphs keep their width, and await document.fonts.ready before measuring anything — a late-loading webfont shifts every glyph box.

2. A timeline is just offset + duration + easing

Once every glyph has an index, the whole animation is one CSS rule:

.glyph {
  display: inline-block;
  animation: reveal 600ms cubic-bezier(.2, .7, .2, 1) both;
  animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 45ms);
}

@keyframes reveal {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(0.4em) rotateX(-70deg); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

both holds the start state during the delay, so glyphs don't flash before their turn. Total runtime is (n - 1) * stagger + duration — useful when you need to size an export.

Stick to transform and opacity. They stay on the compositor; animating width, top, or font-size triggers layout on every frame and will drop frames on a long headline.

3. Four effects from the same primitives

Once you have staggered glyphs, most preset effects are just a different pair of keyframes:

  • Typewriter: reveal by clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0) with steps() timing, rather than animating width.
  • Blur-in: filter: blur(8px) → blur(0) plus opacity. Looks great, but filter is expensive — keep it to short clips.
  • Stretch: scaleY() with a slight skewX(), released with a spring-ish cubic-bezier(.2, 1.4, .4, 1).
  • Spatial / 3D: keep the per-glyph stagger but put perspective and rotateX/translateZ on the container so the whole line moves as one plane. 
.typewriter .glyph {
  animation: wipe 300ms steps(1, end) both;
  animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 90ms);
}
@keyframes wipe {
  from { clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0); }
  to   { clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0); }
}

Different keyframes, identical timing model. That's why a template system can expose a dozen "effects" without a dozen implementations.

The image links to a browser tool that packages these presets — useful when you want the effect, not the plumbing.

4. Scrubbing is what makes export possible

CSS animations are fine for playback but awkward to control frame by frame. The Web Animations API gives every glyph a seekable object:

const glyphs = render(text, container);
const anims = glyphs.map((el, i) =>
  el.animate(
    [
      { opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(0.4em)' },
      { opacity: 1, transform: 'none' }
    ],
    {
      duration: 600,
      delay: i * 45,
      easing: 'cubic-bezier(.2, .7, .2, 1)',
      fill: 'both'
    }
  )
);

function seek(t) {
  for (const a of anims) {
    a.pause();
    a.currentTime = t;
  }
}

Now seek(1200) produces the exact same frame every time, on any machine. That determinism is the difference between a preview that plays and a video you can actually render.

5. Render frames at a fixed rate

Don't record a live tab and hope for 30fps. Compute each frame's timestamp, seek to it, capture, repeat:

const fps = 30, seconds = 3;

for (let f = 0; f < fps * seconds; f++) {
  seek((f / fps) * 1000);          // deterministic time
  await new Promise(requestAnimationFrame);
  // draw to canvas, then hand the frame to an encoder
}

From there: MediaRecorder on a canvas.captureStream() is the quick path but runs in real time; VideoEncoder (WebCodecs) or a server-side ffmpeg pass gives you frame-accurate output with a guaranteed fps. Use canvas.toBlob() / createImageBitmap for frames — toDataURL() is a serialization bottleneck at 90 frames.

If you animate SVG text instead of DOM nodes, serializing the SVG into an image per frame is another clean route, and it keeps the type vector-sharp at any resolution.

6. Things that will bite you

  • Fonts: measure only after document.fonts.ready, or kerning changes mid-render.
  • Compositor pressure: will-change on several hundred glyphs creates hundreds of layers. Add it for the animation, remove it after.
  • Filter + shadow: both defeat cheap compositing; prefer opacity/transform.
  • Reduced motion: honor @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) and skip the stagger in the browser, even if the exported video still has it.
  • CJK and RTL: Intl.Segmenter handles segmentation, but you still need correct dir and line-breaking rules. Grapheme-aware is not the same as layout-aware.

When you want the effect, not the pipeline

Building this once is a fun weekend. Building the templates, presets, font handling, and export UX around it is a different project. TypeMotion.Art is a browser tool for kinetic typography — typewriter, blur, stretch, and spatial text presets with instant preview and video-ready output.

The useful takeaway is the shape of the pipeline: segment → stagger → seek → encode. Once those four stages are separate, adding a new effect is just writing two keyframes.

Disclosure: I work on TypeMotion.Art. Everything above is plain browser API code and works without the tool.

title: Kafka without the confusion: one Rust implementation, three artifacts (grpc-over-datachannels 0.49)
description:
The Kafka side of grpc-over-datachannels had a naming
problem. We shipped kafka-native, kafka-grpc, and
kafka-proxy, and even we had to stop and think about
which one a given user needed. 0.48 and 0.49 are the
cleanup: one Kafka implementation, three artifacts with
sharp boundaries, and generated wrappers for every
language we support.

The model.

  • kafka-native — the direct Kafka protocol client library. Embed it in your process (Rust, C, Python; crates.io + PyPI). No gRPC, no proxy.
  • kafka-grpc — generated client stubs for the grpcdc.kafka.v1 gRPC service, per language ecosystem. This is how browsers (and any language that prefers a service) reach Kafka.
  • kafka-proxy — the runnable gateway that serves kafka-grpc clients and speaks the native Kafka protocol to Apache Kafka or Redpanda.

Browsers never use kafka-native: a browser cannot open
a raw TCP connection to a broker, and Kafka does not
speak WebRTC. Browser Kafka is kafka-grpc through
kafka-proxy, full stop. KAFKA.md now opens with a
"Which Kafka package do I need?" decision guide, and
every Kafka README states what it is and what it is not
in its first screen.

The split (0.48). Under the hood there is exactly
one Kafka implementation, in Rust. It used to live in a
single crate that exported both the direct client and
the gRPC service layer, which is how the confusion
started. It is now three components:

  • kafka-native — the protocol + Broker client.
  • kafka-service — KafkaService, StreamsService, and the C ABI (libkafka_native), new on crates.io in this release.
  • apps/kafka-proxy — the gateway binary.

The generated public repos match: kafka-native ships
only its two crates, kafka-proxy ships only the proxy
crate, and releasegen now fails the build if a
boundary is violated (a proxy binary in the native
export, client sources in the proxy, and so on).

Native everywhere (0.49). Every language wrapper is
a thin generated FFI shim over libkafka_native —
method name plus protobuf bytes in, protobuf bytes out.
0.49 adds the four that were missing:

  • Kotlin and Scala, through the same JNI shim as Java;
  • Zig, through the C ABI directly;
  • Lua, through a small new C bridge module.

Each has a TestKafkaNative roundtrip in the
make test-kafka gate (create topic, produce three
records, consume them back, verify offsets): 14 native
legs, all green against a real broker.

Packaging. Node finally has a first-class native
package: @browser-grpc/kafka-native on npm, with
per-platform prebuilt libraries (linux-x64, linux-arm64,
darwin-arm64) so npm install just works. For the other
wrappers, per-platform libkafka_native tarballs are
attached to every kafka-native GitHub release, and
KAFKA.md documents exactly how each language loads it.

The Kafka implementation did not change. What changed
is that a human landing on any of these packages can now
tell — in the first screen — whether they are holding a
library, a client stub, or a gateway, and which one they
actually need.

title: How to autoplay an embedded video (and why it has to be muted)
description:
A video that starts by itself can bring a landing page to life: a product in motion, a short loop in the header, a demo that runs while people read. But if you have ever tried it, you know browsers often refuse to start the video. Here is why, and how to get it right.

Why browsers block autoplay

Nobody likes a website that suddenly starts talking. That is why Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge all limit autoplay:

  • Muted videos may start on their own. This is allowed in all major browsers.
  • Videos with sound usually may not. They only autoplay in some cases, for example when the visitor has already interacted with the page or the site, and the rules differ between browsers.

So if you want autoplay to work reliably for everyone, the video has to start muted. Visitors can still turn on the sound with one click.

Autoplay with Vidlify

Take the embed code of your video (see How to embed a video on your website) and add two parameters to the address:

https://vidlify.to/e/VIDEO-ID?autoplay=1&muted=1
  • autoplay=1 tells the player to start right away.
  • muted=1 starts it without sound, which is what browsers require.

The embed code from Vidlify already contains allow="autoplay" in the iframe, which is the permission the browser needs to let an embedded player start. If you write your own iframe, keep that attribute.

You can combine it with a start time, for example ?autoplay=1&muted=1&t=15 starts at second 15.

When autoplay is a good idea

  • Short, silent clips that work without sound, like product shots, background visuals or screen recordings.
  • A page that is about the video, where the visitor came to watch anyway.

When it isn't

  • Long videos with speech. Muted, nobody understands them. Let people press play.
  • Several videos on one page. Autoplaying all of them costs your visitors data and makes the page slow.
  • Mobile visitors on data. A video that starts on its own uses their data allowance. The player only loads a quality that fits the screen, but it still downloads video.

Tips

  • Put the key message in the picture, not in the sound. Muted autoplay should make sense without audio.
  • Use subtitles burned into the video if speech matters, so the message comes across muted.
  • Test on a phone. Mobile browsers are the strictest about autoplay and data.

Originally published on the Vidlify blog.

title: Hotjar and Clarity are trackers too: wiring session replay into consent
description:
Someone on the product or design side asks for "a quick Hotjar snippet so we can see where people get stuck". It gets pasted into the theme header, it works, and everyone moves on. Months later someone configures the cookie banner, and that snippet is never mentioned, because whoever set up the banner was thinking about marketing pixels, not UX research.

That gap is how session replay and heatmap tools such as Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity and FullStory end up running before consent. From a consent point of view they are trackers like a Facebook Pixel. They just usually come from a different team.

Check it first: four tests

1. Is it loading before consent? Open a private window, then DevTools → Network, and load the site without touching the banner. Filter for the tool's domain:

hotjar.com   clarity.ms   fullstory.com

Any request here was sent before the visitor made a choice. You can also check whether the tool's global object (under its default name) exists yet:

({ hotjar: typeof window.hj, clarity: typeof window.clarity, fullstory: typeof window.FS })

Before consent you want "undefined" for every tool you use.

2. Does it stop after Reject? Clear the log, click "Reject", and keep moving around the page and opening other pages. The banner closing tells you nothing. What matters is whether recording requests keep going out. This is the same Reject check that applies to every other tracker (see our piece on Reject buttons that don't actually reject).

3. How was it installed? Find where the snippet lives. If it is pasted directly into a template, it bypasses the banner entirely, which is a common shortcut during initial setup. It should go through your consent platform's script-blocking mechanism instead.

4. What do your forms leak? Open a recording of a session that used a form and look at what the tool captured. This is the step most often skipped, and it gets its own section below.

What these tools actually collect

"Session replay" sounds lighter than it is:

  • Mouse movement, clicks and scrolling for the whole session, not just aggregate numbers.
  • Form interaction, and depending on configuration, sometimes the values typed. Most tools mask password fields by default, but not necessarily every sensitive field (an email field, a name field, a search box) unless configured to.
  • A visual recording of the page, in effect a screen recording of what the visitor saw and did.
  • Device, browser and often approximate location, as with most analytics tools.

Behavioural input combined with a visual recording makes these tools considerably more data-heavy than a standard analytics pageview.

Masking is a per-site job

Every major session replay tool masks some fields automatically. The defaults differ a lot between tools, though, and what the default treats as "sensitive" is often narrower than what a particular site actually collects.

The usual weak spot is free text. A support form with a "describe your issue" box isn't masked by most defaults, and visitors do paste sensitive things into fields like that: an account number, a health detail, a password typed in the wrong place. Each tool has its own setting for marking extra elements as masked. Go through every free-text field on the site and decide one by one, rather than assuming the defaults cover them.

Yes, it needs consent

Session replay tools use cookies or similar storage to keep track of a session, and they collect far more than is strictly necessary for the site to work. That puts them under the same ePrivacy/GDPR consent requirement as analytics and advertising trackers. In practice few people dispute this. The usual failure is organisational: the team that installs the tool and the team that manages the banner never compare notes, so the tool runs unconditionally before consent, like any other forgotten script.

A note for whoever owns the site

These tools solve a real problem, and the people installing them are right to care about where visitors struggle. That doesn't replace a compliance check. Put session replay on the same list as every other tracker in your audit, and give it the same tests: nothing before consent, nothing after Reject, and forms masked for the fields your site actually has.

This article first appeared on the Bannerproof blog. Bannerproof checks whether tools like these fire before, or after, a visitor's consent choice: you can scan a site for free at bannerproof.app.

Written with AI assistance.

title: A/B testing tools for the Next.js App Router, compared (2026)
description:
We make one of the tools on this list, so read it with that in mind. We stuck to what each vendor documents, linked a source for every claim and left out any number we couldn't confirm on the vendor's own site. Everything was last checked on November 7, 2026; if something has changed, tell us and we'll fix it.

For a Next.js app, the feature list matters less than where the variant gets decided. Decide it in the browser after the page loads and you either flash the original before the variant appears or hide the page until a script runs (we wrote about what that does to LCP). Decide it on the server before rendering and neither happens. Our guide to A/B testing in the App Router walks through the server-side setup step by step, including a version you can build without any vendor.

The short table

Tool Where the variant is decided Where event data lives Stats Public price
GrowthBook SDKs, incl. a Vercel Flags SDK provider Your warehouse (or their managed one) Bayesian or frequentist; sequential and CUPED on Pro Free (3 users); Pro $40/seat/month
Croct Next.js SDK, server-side Croct's cloud Bayesian Free to 10K MAU; Growth from $100/month (annual)
Vercel Flags Flags SDK, precompute in the proxy Vercel None built in; pair with an analytics partner Usage-based
PostHog SDK; server bootstrap avoids flicker PostHog's cloud Bayesian or frequentist First 1M flag requests/month free
Optimizely Head snippet (Web); server SDKs (Feature Exp.) Optimizely's cloud Sequential (mSPRT) with false discovery rate control Not public
VWO (Wingify) SmartCode script VWO's cloud Bayesian with sequential correction Not listed
Kameleoon Client engine after hydration, with anti-flicker CSS Kameleoon's cloud Not checked Not public
AB Tasty Script, or Flagship server SDK AB Tasty's cloud Not checked Sales-led
evolveAB Next.js proxy, from a local signed bundle Your Postgres; we get aggregates only Bayesian; Thompson-sampling bandits 30-day free trial; Pro $149/site/month

Built for developers

GrowthBook is open source and warehouse-native: it runs experiment analysis as SQL against your own data warehouse, which suits teams that already have one. Every plan gets Bayesian and frequentist engines, Pro and up add sequential testing and CUPED (pricing), and there's a provider for Vercel's Flags SDK (GrowthBook blog). It's strongest on feature flags and statistical depth, and with a warehouse and a data team behind you it's a serious choice. We go through it point by point in evolveAB vs GrowthBook.

Croct is the one to look at for personalization. It has an official Next.js SDK with an npx croct@latest init setup and a Vercel integration, and it pairs content personalization with testing. Its pricing is public, which we appreciate: free up to 10,000 monthly active users, then Growth from $100/month billed annually (pricing).

Vercel Flags went generally available on April 16, 2026 (Vercel community). The Flags SDK's precompute pattern serves static variants from the proxy. That's the right serving model (our static mode works the same way), but Flags has no stats engine: you assign with Flags and analyze somewhere else (evolveAB vs Vercel Flags has the detail).

PostHog builds experiments on its feature flags and analyzes them with Bayesian or frequentist methods (docs). You can bootstrap flags from the server so the first render already has the right variant. If PostHog is your product analytics already, it's the obvious place to start; evolveAB vs PostHog covers where the two differ.

The visual-editor suites

Optimizely, VWO (now part of Wingify, after the merger with AB Tasty announced in January 2026), Kameleoon and AB Tasty grew up around a script on the page and an editor for marketers, with the data in the vendor's cloud. Several now document a server-side path as well. Optimizely has server SDKs and Performance Edge, and AB Tasty has a guide to avoiding flicker with Next.js SSR through its Flagship SDK (AB Tasty docs).

Their App Router docs show where the default path still lands, though. Optimizely's React SSR guide says to run experiment code after hydration and warns that flicker may occur (Optimizely docs); Kameleoon's Next.js guide does the same and adds anti-flicker CSS (Kameleoon docs). These are mature products, and Optimizely's Stats Engine is especially well documented. None of the four publishes prices.

Where evolveAB fits

We built evolveAB for a Next.js App Router site that wants server-rendered tests, a results page a marketer can read and an AI that keeps writing new challengers. The proxy decides the variant without a network call. Raw events stay in your Postgres, and our cloud receives four sums per variant, never a visitor row. Results are Bayesian, bandits use Thompson sampling, and every AI suggestion passes five checks before a person sees it.

What we don't do yet:

  • Pages Router. We're App Router only (Next.js 15.5+, 16 recommended).
  • Running without Postgres. You need a database, though your app's existing one works.
  • Feature flags. We test UI regions, not code paths.
  • Warehouse-native analysis. SQL goals against BigQuery or Snowflake aren't built.
  • A track record. Sign-up opened in November 2026, so there are no large customers or case studies yet.

If you need flags across a large codebase and already have a warehouse, look at GrowthBook first. If you want personalization driven by a headless CMS, look at Croct. And if you're on Vercel Flags and only need the statistics, that's a gap we fill; the quickstart takes about 30 minutes.

title: React, deeply · 4. Data fetching: Suspense, transitions and cache boundaries
description:
React, deeply · Chapter 4 of 12 · Web · new chapter every Monday night

By the end of this chapter: Fetch data without the loading-flash and waterfall problems.

The problem

Marcus is a senior engineer at a fintech startup. He is responsible for the "Portfolio Overview" dashboard, a complex screen that aggregates data from four different microservices: user profile, asset balances, historical performance, and real-time market alerts.

When the dashboard was first built, the team used the standard useEffect pattern: each component fetched its own data on mount. In local development, it looked fine. In production, users on 4G connections see a "popcorn UI." First, the header appears. Then, 200ms later, the sidebar flashes. 500ms after that, the balance card appears, pushing the performance graph down the page. Finally, the market alerts pop in, causing the entire layout to shift again.

The metric that moved was the Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), which spiked to 0.45 (well into the "poor" category). More importantly, the Time to Interactive (TTI) was delayed because the browser was stuck in a "waterfall": Component A had to render to trigger the fetch for Component B, which had to render to trigger Component C. This cost the team a 15% drop in mobile engagement, as users perceived the app as "broken" or "slow" before they could even click a button.

Before you start

To follow this chapter, you need a React 18 or 19 environment. We will use a mock API to simulate network latency reliably.

  1. Ensure you have Node.js 18+ installed.
  2. Create a new project: npm create vite@latest suspense-demo -- --template react
  3. Install the only external dependency we will use for cache management: npm install @tanstack/react-query@5.59.0
  4. Verify your setup by running npm run dev. If the Vite splash screen appears, you are ready.

Why does the "loading spinner" pattern fail?

In Chapter 1, we looked at how React reconciles changes. When you use the useEffect fetch pattern, you are essentially telling React: "Render what you can now, and I'll give you more data later."

The problem is that React cannot "see" into your useEffect. To React, the component is finished rendering as soon as it returns a loading spinner. Only after the browser paints that spinner does the effect run, the fetch start, and—eventually—a state update trigger a second render cycle.

This creates three production failures:

  1. The Waterfall: If <Parent> fetches data and only then renders <Child>, and <Child> then fetches its own data, the user waits for Latency A + Latency B.
  2. The Loading Flash: If a fetch takes 50ms, the user sees a spinner flicker for one frame. This is more jarring than seeing nothing at all.
  3. Race Conditions: If a user clicks "User A" then quickly clicks "User B", the response for "User A" might arrive after "User B", overwriting the state with the wrong data.

Suspense changes the contract. Instead of rendering a "hole" (the spinner) and filling it later, a component "suspends." It tells React: "I am not ready to render yet; here is a Promise. Wake me up when it settles."

How do Transitions prevent the "loading flash"?

The biggest mistake engineers make with Suspense is thinking it is just a new way to show spinners. The real power of Suspense lies in useTransition.

When you trigger a state change inside startTransition, React does something counter-intuitive: it keeps the old UI on screen while it renders the new UI in the background. If the new UI hits a Suspense boundary (because it needs data), React waits.

It does not show the fallback spinner immediately. It stays on the current screen, keeping it interactive, until either the data is ready or a timeout is reached. This is the difference between a "cheap" feeling app that flickers and a "pro" app that feels like a native OS.

Where does the cache live?

Suspense is not a data-fetching library; it is a communication mechanism. It requires a cache that lives outside the component tree.

When a component renders, it asks the cache for data.

  • If the data is there: The component renders immediately.
  • If the data is missing: The cache initiates a fetch and throws the Promise.
  • If the fetch is in progress: The cache throws the existing Promise.

This "throwing a promise" is the part most developers find embarrassing because it breaks standard JavaScript expectations. But it allows React to catch the promise at the Suspense boundary and manage the scheduling of the render.

Build it

We will build a profile viewer that switches between users without showing a loading spinner for every click, and without layout shift.

1. Set up the Mock API and Query Client

Create a file src/api.js. We use a manual delay to simulate a slow 3G connection.

// src/api.js
export const fetchUserData = async (id) => {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
  return {
    id,
    name: id === 1 ? "Marcus" : "Emma",
    joined: "2023-10-01",
  };
};

Update src/main.jsx to provide the Query Client. We must set suspense: true (in v5, this is done via the useSuspenseQuery hook).

// src/main.jsx
import React from 'react';
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import App from './App';

const queryClient = new QueryClient();

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </React.StrictMode>
);

2. Create the Suspenseful Component

Create src/UserProfile.jsx. This component does not handle its own loading state.

// src/UserProfile.jsx
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { fetchUserData } from './api';

export function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  // This hook throws a promise if data is missing.
  // The component logic stops here until the promise resolves.
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['user', userId],
    queryFn: () => fetchUserData(userId),
  });

  return (
    <div style={{ border: '1px solid #ccc', padding: '1rem', marginTop: '1rem' }}>
      <h2>{data.name}</h2>
      <p>Member since: {data.joined}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

3. Implement the Transition logic

In src/App.jsx, we will use useTransition to switch users.

// src/App.jsx
import { useState, useTransition, Suspense } from 'react';
import { UserProfile } from './UserProfile';

export default function App() {
  const [userId, setUserId] = useState(1);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  const handleUserChange = (newId) => {
    // startTransition tells React: "Don't show the Suspense fallback yet."
    // Keep the current UI responsive while the next user's data loads.
    startTransition(() => {
      setUserId(newId);
    });
  };

  return (
    <main style={{ padding: '2rem', opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <h1>Dashboard</h1>
      <button onClick={() => handleUserChange(1)} disabled={userId === 1}>
        User 1
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => handleUserChange(2)} disabled={userId === 2}>
        User 2
      </button>

      {isPending && <span> Loading next profile...</span>}

      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading initial profile...</p>}>
        <UserProfile userId={userId} />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

How to confirm it worked:

  1. Refresh the page. You should see "Loading initial profile..." for 1 second. This is the initial Suspense fallback.
  2. Click "User 2".
  3. The Result: The "User 1" profile stays on screen. The UI does not disappear. The "Loading next profile..." text appears (because of isPending), and the opacity drops.
  4. After 1 second, the UI updates instantly to "User 2".
  5. There was no layout shift and no "popcorn" effect.

When this breaks

1. The "Infinite Loop" fetch

Symptom: The network tab shows hundreds of requests per second, and the browser tab eventually crashes.
Cause: You are calling a fetch function inside the render body that is not wrapped in a cache (like TanStack Query or React's cache function in Next.js).
Fix: Ensure your data fetching logic is stable. The function passed to useSuspenseQuery must not create a new promise on every render unless the queryKey changes.

2. The "Nested Waterfall"

Symptom: You have three Suspense boundaries, and they still load one after another.
Cause: You placed a <Suspense> boundary around every single component.
Fix: Move the Suspense boundary higher. One boundary around a group of components allows React to coordinate them. If you want them to load in parallel, they must be siblings under the same boundary, and their data fetching must start as soon as they begin rendering.

3. "Transition ignored"

Symptom: You wrapped setUserId in startTransition, but the UI still jumped to the loading spinner.
Cause: You likely have a useEffect inside UserProfile that is triggering a secondary state update, or you are using a library that doesn't fully support React 18's concurrent features.
Fix: Remove useEffect for data fetching. Use useSuspenseQuery or the use hook (in React 19).

What it costs

Complexity of State: You can no longer rely on if (loading) return <Spinner /> inside your component. This logic is moved to the parent or the boundary. This makes components cleaner but the architecture harder to trace for juniors.

Memory Overhead: Caching data "outside" the tree means you must manage cache invalidation. If you never clear the cache, your app's memory usage will grow linearly with every "page" the user visits.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR) Requirements: Suspense requires a streaming-capable server (like Node.js or Edge functions) to be truly effective. If you are using a static "Single Page App" (SPA) on a basic CDN, you still get the UX benefits, but you don't get the SEO/First Contentful Paint benefits of streaming.

In the interview

The Question: "How do you handle data fetching in a large-scale React app to avoid waterfalls?"

A Weak Answer: "I use useEffect and show a loading spinner. If it's slow, I use Promise.all in the parent." This is weak because it doesn't address layout shift or the fact that Promise.all requires the parent to know exactly what every child needs, breaking encapsulation.

A Strong Answer: "I use Suspense boundaries combined with Concurrent Transitions. This allows the UI to stay interactive on the current state while the next state is prepared in memory. I use a cache-integrated fetcher (like TanStack Query) to ensure that multiple components requesting the same data don't trigger redundant network calls. For performance, I lift the fetch as high as possible—or use prefetching in event handlers—to ensure the network request starts the moment the user intends to navigate, not after the component mounts."

The Senior/Staff Follow-up: "How do you handle a scenario where one data source is fast (50ms) and another is slow (2s) on the same screen?"
A senior engineer will discuss Selective Hydration or Nested Suspense Boundaries. They might suggest wrapping the "slow" component in its own <Suspense> boundary so the rest of the page can become interactive immediately, while the slow part shows a skeleton state. This is a trade-off between "loading everything at once" and "getting the user to the first interaction as fast as possible."

Your tasks

  1. The "Slow Component" trap: Add a second component, MarketAlerts, that takes 3 seconds to load. Place it inside the same <Suspense> boundary as UserProfile. Observe how the entire profile is now delayed by 3 seconds.
  2. The "Independent Boundary" fix: Move MarketAlerts into its own <Suspense> boundary with its own fallback. Confirm that the UserProfile now appears after 1 second, while the alerts continue to load.
  3. The "Prefetch" challenge: Add an onMouseEnter handler to the buttons in App.jsx. Use the queryClient.prefetchQuery method to start fetching the user data when the user hovers over the button. Use the Network tab to prove the fetch starts before the click.
  4. The "Broken Cache" simulation: Create a component that fetches data using a raw fetch inside the render body (throwing the promise manually) but without a cache. Observe the infinite loop in the Network tab and explain why it happens.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

title: How to Compare SaaS SMS Alerts API — Replay Marketplace Bounces
description:
Choose the provider whose receipt handling survives a replay before letting it influence marketplace contact policy. TL;DR: For US/EU SaaS SMS alerts, compare Twilio, Vonage, Plivo, and Infrai against a repeatable suppression drill: a permanent-invalid finding must stay effective when an older delivery record arrives later, and an email bounce must leave a separately authorized phone destination alone. Keep the evidence that explains both decisions.

Order matters here.

Marketplace teams with application-owned recipient policy should try Infrai for basic outbound SMS alerts because its plain REST API works through an ordinary HTTP client, without a messaging SDK to install or version to maintain. Its public, keyless discovery supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, reducing the work of establishing the contract an evidence collector must preserve. Those are concrete integration benefits; neither proves that a seller's contact is eligible.

The trade-off with Infrai is polling: delivery and event collection add an observation interval, making it unsuitable for workflows that require immediate callback-driven orchestration. Choose Twilio or Vonage for that requirement; choose a specialist with the required channels when a voice, WhatsApp, or RCS escalation is essential. The experiment below treats provider selection as one leg of an application recovery exercise, with no assumed winner and no reported benchmark results.

Infrai's one key, one wallet, one bill model covers 295 routes across 20 modules. For the marketplace team connecting email suppression and SMS dispatch, that shared boundary reduces separate credential provisioning and invoice reconciliation, although it doesn't replace access controls around recipient evidence.

1. What page fired before the seller was contacted again?

Start with a proposed page: the marketplace authorized another seller notice after committing a permanent-invalid finding for that destination. The postmortem question is whether replay changed eligibility, not whether a dashboard still displayed a reassuring delivery total. A receipt for an earlier message can be useful historical evidence without becoming permission to send another one, and an email bounce says nothing by itself about permission to contact the seller's phone.

Keep channels separate.

In the drill, contain the affected dispatch partition while collectors keep recording evidence. Capture the application authorization decision, the original provider record reference, the channel and destination token, and the mapping-rule version. Preserve provider occurrence time separately from application observation time: sorting only by arrival time can turn a late observation into a misleading description of what happened first. These are proposed application records, not promises about any vendor's response fields or a claim of legal compliance.

The rollback hazard deserves attention before implementation. Restoring an older application snapshot may remove a suppression learned after that snapshot, so resuming dispatch immediately after a restore can reauthorize the very destination the incident review is trying to protect. A delivery console cannot answer that question. The recovery procedure needs an evidence log that survives the snapshot boundary and a check that newly learned invalid destinations remain blocked before workers restart.

How should SaaS teams compare an SMS alerts API?

Use the same seller fixture and the same acceptance criteria for every candidate. This comparison distinguishes documented collection behavior from questions the trial must answer; a shortlist position is not a declaration that a provider owns your suppression policy.

Candidate Relevant fit Boundary to test before selection
Twilio Callback-style delivery updates suit an application that reacts to incoming status changes. Replay callbacks through the application's mapping rules; a callback must not automatically reverse an invalid-recipient decision.
Vonage Callback-style updates are another fit for delivery-driven workflows. Evaluate its receipt contract independently rather than assuming status meanings match Twilio's.
Plivo Include it as a direct SMS alternative in the same authorized-destination trial. Require documented permanent-outcome mapping and recoverable receipt evidence; this guide makes no measured delivery or compliance ranking for it.
Infrai Plain HTTP single-send or batch-send flows suit straightforward outbound alerts; discovery helps establish the adapter contract. Measure the polling-to-durable-decision interval and confirm that the application's recovery procedure preserves suppression.

Review the Twilio callback contract, Vonage delivery receipt guide, and Plivo SMS documentation independently. For Plivo, checking the receipt documentation is part of qualification rather than permission to infer equivalence from another provider. For all four, keep raw evidence restricted and export destination tokens to reviewers. Account configuration, destination requirements, and legal obligations need their own review; selecting an API does not certify US or EU compliance.

Before any live trial, set a collection budget, such as 60 seconds from the application's first observation of an actionable outcome to its durable suppression decision. That is a proposed test budget, not a delivery guarantee or legal deadline. Evaluate transport-to-observation delay separately, because a perfectly fast reducer cannot repair a collector that has stopped advancing. For SMS dispatch, also apply application geo-fencing, per-country spending limits, and alert throttling; receipt correctness does not stop abusive sends.

3. Replay an older delivery record after the bounce

Save this standard-library-only program as replay.go and run go run replay.go. It exercises two recovery orders and a repeated receipt using synthetic marketplace data. No messages are sent, and the event names, times, record IDs, and destination tokens belong to this local model rather than a provider schema. To inspect the live suppression contract first, set INFRAI_API_KEY and run go run replay.go contract; that mode prints the discovery response, not recipient data or a suppression mutation. Compare its request and response schemas with the adapter before collecting test evidence.

The reducer deliberately has no automatic reopening operation. A normalized permanent-invalid finding creates a suppression; a later-arriving delivery record is retained as history and cannot remove it. Reusing a receipt ID with different contents is rejected, because silently accepting that conflict would make a postmortem depend on whichever copy arrived first.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func contract() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.suppression.add", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == 429 && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1 << attempt)
            value := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(when); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

type Contact struct {
    Seller, Channel, Token string
}

type Event struct {
    ID, Kind, Rule string
    Contact Contact
    Occurred int
}

type State struct {
    Seen map[string]Event
    Blocked map[Contact]map[string]bool
}

func newState() *State {
    return &State{
        Seen: make(map[string]Event),
        Blocked: make(map[Contact]map[string]bool),
    }
}

func (s *State) apply(e Event) error {
    if e.ID == "" || e.Rule == "" || e.Contact.Seller == "" ||
        e.Contact.Channel == "" || e.Contact.Token == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("incomplete evidence identity")
    }
    if e.Kind != "delivered" && e.Kind != "permanent-invalid" {
        return fmt.Errorf("unmapped outcome: %s", e.Kind)
    }
    if old, found := s.Seen[e.ID]; found {
        if old != e {
            return fmt.Errorf("conflicting receipt: %s", e.ID)
        }
        return nil
    }
    s.Seen[e.ID] = e
    if e.Kind == "permanent-invalid" {
        if s.Blocked[e.Contact] == nil {
            s.Blocked[e.Contact] = make(map[string]bool)
        }
        s.Blocked[e.Contact][e.ID] = true
    }
    return nil
}

func drill() error {
    email := Contact{"seller-73", "email", "address-token-9"}
    phone := Contact{"seller-73", "sms", "phone-token-6"}
    delivered := Event{"receipt-1", "delivered", "mapping-v1", email, 10}
    invalid := Event{"receipt-2", "permanent-invalid", "mapping-v1", email, 20}
    orders := [][]Event{
        {delivered, invalid, invalid},
        {invalid, delivered, invalid},
    }
    for index, events := range orders {
        s := newState()
        for _, e := range events {
            if err := s.apply(e); err != nil {
                return err
            }
        }
        if len(s.Seen) != 2 || !s.Blocked[email][invalid.ID] ||
            len(s.Blocked[email]) != 1 || len(s.Blocked[phone]) != 0 {
            return fmt.Errorf("replay %d changed the contact boundary", index)
        }
        conflict := invalid
        conflict.Kind = "delivered"
        if s.apply(conflict) == nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("replay %d accepted conflicting evidence", index)
        }
        fmt.Printf("replay %d: email blocked; phone unchanged; conflict rejected\n", index)
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) > 1 {
        if os.Args[1] != "contract" {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "expected contract or no argument")
            os.Exit(2)
        }
        if err := contract(); err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        return
    }
    if err := drill(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Pass means both orders retain exactly two distinct receipts, the email suppression still cites the invalid finding, the phone has no inherited email block, and a conflicting repeat is rejected. Phone unchanged does not mean phone authorized: SMS permission still needs its own policy decision. The program states expected assertions; the printed lines are local checks, not measured provider results.

There is a cost to this conservative rule. It cannot restore a corrected address or interpret temporary bounces, and it should not try. Put ambiguous outcomes into review, define permanent classifications against each provider's contract, and treat a verified replacement destination or an approved reopening as a separate audited transition. Blindly converting every failure into permanent invalidity would produce a tidy suppression list by excluding people who could still receive valid notices.

This is a reducer, not a production sender.

Production adapters must namespace receipt identities by provider and account, preserve the original records, and commit evidence and suppression durably before acknowledging collection progress. An in-memory map disappears on restart. The dispatch authorization boundary must also serialize against suppression updates; checking eligibility and then sending independently leaves a race that no later audit entry can undo. Keep an explicit record of already handed-off messages so the incident review can distinguish them from future intents still under application control.

4. Verify recovery before releasing the held notices

Run the fixture first, then collect records for authorized test destinations through each candidate's documented interface. For the Infrai leg, compare the discovered response contract with the adapter, record polling observations, and replay the normalized evidence after rebuilding the application state. Capture collection timing during that trial rather than inferring it from a dashboard. A provider passes only when its adapter satisfies the same evidence checks and the team's predeclared collection budget; if immediate event-driven escalation is required, prefer a callback-oriented candidate even when the local reducer passes.

Next, test a restore from a snapshot taken before the invalid finding. Keep sending paused, replay the retained evidence through the selected rule version, and compare suppression identities with the pre-restore record. A missing invalid finding, conflicting receipt, or unauthorized dispatch is a failed recovery drill. Preserve the failure for analysis rather than changing the acceptance threshold after seeing it.

Rollback preserves suppression.

If a new mapping rule fails verification, retain the dispatch hold and return to the last approved mapping only after checking that every previously accepted invalid finding remains accounted for. Quarantine disputed outcomes for review. Do not empty a suppression list, reclassify a late delivery as permission, or automatically drain old notices merely to make the recovery graph turn green. Recheck authorization and notice relevance before release; evidence that a recipient is reachable does not establish that an old marketplace notification should still be sent.

Choose on the recovery result and the operating boundary, with delivery-driven specialists favored where the required response cannot tolerate collection by polling. That is a narrower recommendation than a universal provider ranking, and a more useful one during a postmortem.

If that boundary fits your marketplace, use the email-versus-SMS workflow guide to start checking the delivery design against your application's suppression policy.

References

  • Twilio message status callbacks.
  • Vonage SMS delivery receipts.
  • Plivo SMS documentation for independent receipt-contract review.
  • DMARC specification, for the separate email-authentication boundary rather than proof of recipient eligibility.
