title: Why My Kids are Learning to Program - The New Baseline
description:
Type one paragraph into Claude Code or Codex and an agent builds a Codename One app, taps through every screen, draws the icon, signs it, and submits it to TestFlight and Google Play. This week we wired our build cloud straight into that loop, so the whole trip from prompt to store is one conversation. You approve screenshots. You never see a line of Java. You don't need a Mac.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

I'm teaching my kids to program anyway. Java, specifically.

Agents moved the baseline so far up that the people who understand what's under it just became the most valuable people in the room.

TL;DR

  • Your first app is now a complete app. An Uber clone used to be the final exam. Now it's what one prompt hands you before lunch.
  • An agent can take it all the way to the App Store. It builds in our cloud, reads the log, fixes the error and submits. You tick three boxes.
  • I'm still teaching my kids Java. An agent is brilliant at sounding right. Only someone who reads code can tell when it isn't.
  • Apps are about to be a thousand times bigger. Billions of lines, and the people who understand them run the show.
  • Don't own code you didn't need to write. We maintain 4.5 million lines and paid $21,512.95 last month to test them on every platform. That bill stays ours.
  • Your enterprise features, behind your firewall. Corporate Server is back.
  • A spreadsheet engine, PDFs, flowcharts, a SaaS backend and a game studio. All in this week's release, all free.

Coming This Week

  • Saturday, November 21: A Million Rows and Live Excel Formulas, Inside Your Own App. DataGrid, and spreadsheets with XLSX files and 402 live functions.
  • Sunday, November 22: Build a Multi-Tenant SaaS Backend That Can't Leak One Customer Into Another. Tenant isolation, GraphQL, SAML and LDAP, object storage on four clouds, MongoDB, DynamoDB and search.
  • Monday, November 23: Invoices, Tickets and Reports: Generate, View and Print PDFs From One Java Codebase. On the phone and on the server.
  • Tuesday, November 24: Fieldline: Launch Your Own Field Service App, With a Scheduler That Plans the Week. Dispatch, routes, signatures and a heuristic optimizer.
  • Wednesday, November 25: Flowcharts, Node Editors and Kanban Boards Are Now Standard Components.
  • Thursday, November 26: Brickyard: Launch Your Own Game Platform, With the Studio Inside the App. Plus portable shaders and 3D audio.

Live formulas.
Fieldline dispatch.
Flowcharts.
Brickyard's studio.

Hello world is now a complete app

For forty years the first program anyone wrote printed one line. Then it was a screen with a button. Then a to-do list.

Today the first program an agent writes for you is a complete app. It has sign-in, a database, push notifications, dark mode, and builds for iOS, Android, the desktop and the web. That's what one prompt produces today, and it gets bigger every quarter.

When the floor rises, everything above it rises too. A few years ago "build an Uber clone" was the hardest assignment in a mobile course. We made one you can generate in a minute. Cloning Uber is now where a modern app starts, not where it ends.

So what does the ceiling look like? Embedded systems on a factory floor talking to the cloud and to the phone in a technician's pocket. Every spreadsheet in a company pulled into one app, with each formula wired to live data. Business processes as diagrams that people edit and the server executes. Games where players build the games. Each of those used to need a department. Now it needs three people and an agent.

An agent can ship your app

We spent the last few weeks making sure agents can drive all of Codename One, not only write code for it. The front door is codenameone.com/agents. Point any agent at our llms.txt with a prompt like this:

Use Codename One (read https://www.codenameone.com/llms.txt) to build me an
iPhone and Android app that tracks daily habits with streaks and reminders.
Show me screenshots before you submit it to TestFlight and Google Play testing.

The agent installs our skill, interviews you once, and creates the project with a script that downloads its own JDK. It runs the app, taps through it and screenshots every screen, then makes the icon. Before anything ships, it reviews the app against the App Store and Google Play rules that get apps rejected.

Then it talks to our build cloud directly. Every new project carries the Codename One cloud MCP server in its .mcp.json, so the agent can start builds, read the build log, fix what broke and build again. You sign in once in the browser and choose what it's allowed to do. Three checkboxes grant Apple signing, push setup and store submission. Anything outside them, like revoking a certificate or touching billing, stops and sends you a link to approve that one request. You decide what the agent may touch.

Somebody who has never heard of Java can now publish a real app, and plenty of good ones will come from people who know their problem better than any programmer.

So why am I teaching my kids Java?

For the same reason the best Java developers know assembly language and what the CPU does with their code.

Almost none of us write assembly. But knowing what a cache line is, why a branch costs something, what the JIT is doing with your loop, makes you write better Java. Fundamentals are what let you work one level up without being a passenger.

I learned that from the other direction. I'm a terrible graphic artist. Out of necessity I learned GIMP, Photoshop and Sketch well enough to get by. I never became good at it. What I got instead was a much better sense of style, and something I value more: I can talk to people who actually have talent. I understand what they do, so I can give feedback they take seriously instead of "make it pop."

Working with a coding agent is the same relationship. It explains what it did. If you can't read the code, you can't judge the explanation, and you can't steer it to where you need to go. An agent is very good at sounding right. Its answers are often not right, and the only way to tell is to look at the code. Java is a good language to learn that in: it's explicit, it's typed, and what it does is what it says.

A couple of weeks ago I wrote that you should rewrite everything in Java, not Rust. Same idea from the other side. A developer who knows the language can push an agent much further, because they catch the confident wrong answer on the second line instead of in production. That's how you build software that's both more sophisticated and more reliable than what came before, instead of more of the same, faster.

From millions of lines to billions

Will you read every line an agent writes? No. Nobody reads every line now either.

But understanding is what keeps a system in check as it grows. It's how you know whether your tests cover the code or only run it. It's how you notice that the agent's fix for one bug added a second code path that nothing tests. It's how you see complexity piling up layer by layer before it falls over.

We used to call a million lines a big system. Agents write code faster than any team that ever wrote one of those, they never get bored, and they never say no to a feature. The apps of the next decade will reach billions of lines. A codebase that size isn't navigated by prompting harder. It's navigated by engineers who understand architecture, testing and failure modes, and can tell an agent precisely what to do. That's the job my kids are training for.

A framework should take you past the OS

This is what this week's release is about.

An agent can write a spreadsheet engine for you, on top of any framework. It can write a PDF renderer, a diagramming library, tenant filtering for your ORM, a heuristic scheduler. Each one will look fine in the first demo. Then it's yours. It's more code in your repository, more context the agent has to hold, more tests in your CI, more platforms to verify, forever. Code is cheap to generate and expensive to own, and the complexity binds you. A homegrown PDF renderer is a tax you pay every release.

So a framework's job is no longer to wrap what the operating system offers. Agents do that easily. The job is to take you far beyond it. Neither iOS nor Android ships a spreadsheet with live formulas, a flowchart editor, a Gantt chart or a multi-tenant backend. A complete spreadsheet is now the starting point. A flowchart of a business process is the bare minimum for a business app.

Codename One is 4.5 million lines of code you don't have to write. We test it on every commit across iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, with screenshot comparisons on each one. That costs us about $20,000 a month in CI ($21,512.95 last month, to be exact). Generate the same coverage yourself and that bill is yours.

Enterprises have to move like startups

Large companies are now expected to ship at the speed a three-person startup ships with agents. But they can't take the risks an indie developer takes. Their source code, signing keys and user data can't leave the network, and no compliance team will approve a build pipeline they don't control.

Codename One itself is free and open source, and that includes building offline on your own machine. Every developer, in every company, can build for every platform without sending a byte to anyone. That never changes.

What a large company wants on top of that are our commercial, enterprise grade services, and until now those lived in our cloud. So we're bringing back Corporate Server. It's an optional product that runs those services on premises at your site, or in a dedicated private cloud isolated from every other customer:

  • The build cloud, so developers keep sending a build and getting a signed app back, without a Mac on every desk.
  • The push server for your backend.
  • App Shield attestation, so your API serves only genuine, untampered copies of your app.
  • App Hardening, obfuscation at the level of DexGuard: renamed classes, encrypted strings and scrambled control flow, on every port.
  • Crash Protection, with symbolicated crashes filed into your own issue tracker.
  • Analytics and the rest of the enterprise services.

All of it inside your network, under your compliance rules.

More This Week

A million rows, and spreadsheets with live formulas

DataGrid doesn't replace Table. It's the extreme version, in the spirit of SwingX's JXTable and JXTreeTable: a painted grid that scrolls a million rows, with frozen columns, grouping with aggregates, in-place editing and a lazy tree mode. On top of it, Workbook reads and writes XLSX, ODS and CSV and evaluates 402 Excel functions live, with completion and syntax highlighting while you type a formula.

Sheet sheet = new Workbook().addSheet("Orders");
sheet.addRow("Item", "Units", "Price", "Total");
sheet.addRow("Bolt", 40.0, 0.25);
sheet.setCellFormula("D2", "=B2*C2");
DataGrid grid = new DataGrid(sheet);

A million rows.
Grouping and aggregates.
Formulas that feel like Excel.

My high school finishing exams included a test in Lotus 1-2-3. Lotus didn't invent the spreadsheet, VisiCalc did. Lotus put charts next to the numbers, and two great ideas combined made one of the first iconic software startups. That's my theme for this week: here are the components, remix them into something wonderful. Saturday's article has the details.

A backend that can't leak one customer into another

@TenantId on an entity filters every ORM query, count and bulk update by the current tenant. Native SQL in a multi-tenant session is blocked by default, because the forgotten WHERE tenant_id = ? in a hand-written query is the most common data leak in SaaS. You opt in explicitly, and allowNativeSql becomes the one thing a security review has to search for.

@Entity
public class Invoice {
    @Id @GeneratedValue long id;
    @TenantId String tenant;
    String customer;
}

The backend also gained a Spring-style GraphQL server, SAML 2.0 single sign-on, LDAP and Active Directory, object storage on S3, R2, Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob with no SDKs, and MongoDB, DynamoDB and Elasticsearch through the same entity classes. Sunday's backend article covers all of it.

PDFs on the client and the server

com.codename1.pdf writes documents with a canvas or a flowing layout of paragraphs and tables, and the same classes run in the app and on the backend. PdfViewer renders in pure Java, so a file looks identical on every platform. It opens encrypted documents and prints them.

Monday's PDF article walks through invoices, tickets, and printing.

Fieldline, a field service company in a template

One of my first jobs was at a scheduling company, writing heuristic scheduling algorithms that planners watched as Gantt charts full of constraints. It's a hard field. Fieldline makes it a template: technicians follow their day as a route on a map, fill checklists, photograph problems for an AI diagnosis and collect signatures. Dispatchers drag work on a Gantt chart, ask the assistant to re-plan in plain words, and let a solver plan the week around skills, hours, and travel. Maps, location, an AI expert on call and heuristic optimization, connected in one app.

Download the Fieldline video.

Tuesday's Fieldline article opens up the optimizer.

Diagrams, node editors and Kanban boards

NodeGraph draws diagrams with automatic layered, tree, radial and force layouts, flowchart shapes and swim lanes, and doubles as a port-based node editor. KanbanBoard adds draggable cards, swim lanes and WIP limits. In most frameworks these are commercial add-ons. The baseline for a business app moved, so they're in the core.

DefaultGraphModel model = new DefaultGraphModel();
model.addNode(new GraphNode("web", "Web app"));
model.addNode(new GraphNode("api", "API gateway"));
model.addEdge("web", "api");
NodeGraph graph = new NodeGraph(model);
graph.arrange(new LayeredArrangement(), false);

Flowcharts with swim lanes.
Node editors.
Kanban with WIP limits.

Wednesday's article shows flowcharts, editors, and boards.

Brickyard, shaders and 3D audio

Brickyard is a real game development studio, and it ships as a template. Games are Luau scripts in a 3D world of parts, and the interpreter runs the full Luau language with its standard libraries. Bring a Roblox place file, .rbxlx or binary .rbxl, and it opens and runs, with a compatibility report listing any API the engine doesn't cover yet. Export it back out when you're done.

The studio has an explorer, a properties panel, a Luau editor with syntax checking and completion, lighting, models, undo, play test with several players, and publish, on a phone, a tablet or a desktop. Multiplayer runs on an authoritative server. An AI agent can drive the whole studio through MCP and play test its own game to see what broke.

Luau, with completion and syntax checks.
The studio on the desktop.
Play test before you publish.

Download the Brickyard video.

Under it, the GPU package gained portable shader nodes that compile to Metal, Direct3D, GLSL and WebGL from one Java definition, a library of water, terrain, surface and effect shaders, image-based lighting, GPU skinning, instancing and a full post-processing stack. The new audio graph, modeled on Web Audio, adds spatial sound with HRTF for headphones. Thursday's article covers all three.

Foldable skins you can record

The simulator now draws foldable skins in 3D and animates them between flat, half open and closed, moving your app to the cover display when the device closes. Posture events fire at the same angles Android uses, so your fold handling runs in the simulator exactly as it will on the device. Simulate, Record Device Tour records the device folding and rotating to an MP4 at a smooth 60 frames per second, staged and ready for your store listing. Here's a raw recording, straight out of the simulator:

Download the foldable tour video.

The skin designer has a new Fold tab for building your own foldables, and agents can fold the device too, through the sim_fold MCP tool.

Xcode 27.1, Gradle 9 and goodbye to Mac Catalyst

With next week's update, iOS builds move to Xcode 27.1 by default and the iOS 27 styling becomes the default theme. Liquid Glass stays your choice, on your schedule. The same update turns on Gradle 9 by default for Android builds, part of keeping the Android toolchain current. Try it today with the android.gradleVersion=9 build hint, so next week is a non-event for you.

We're dropping Mac Catalyst support. The native Mac port is better in every way: a real AppKit app with real menus and windows, not an iPad app on a Mac. Keeping Catalyst in CI was eating resources that serve you better elsewhere. If you still build for Catalyst, switch to the native Mac target.

Everything, for everyone

Look at the size of this one week. A spreadsheet engine with 402 functions. A PDF writer and viewer. A diagram editor and a Kanban board. Tenant isolation, GraphQL, SAML and four object stores for the server. A field service product with an optimizer. A game studio that runs Roblox places. Shaders, spatial audio, foldables. Any one of those is a product somebody sells on its own.

That's the scope I mean when I call Codename One a universal platform. Instead of coding to an operating system, you code to Codename One, and it runs your app on iOS, Android, the desktop, the web and the watch, with your backend in the same language. Bring Java, Kotlin, Swing, JavaFX, Android or Flutter code. Build a bank, a game, a SaaS product or a homework app. It's free and open source, for a solo developer and for a company with ten thousand of them.

Every week it grows, and it has to. When an agent can generate the boring parts of any app in a minute, the framework underneath has to cover everything else: every platform, every component a business expects, every service a company has to run. The bar moved for everyone, so the platform has to give everything to everyone.

That's also why I'm comfortable teaching my kids Java. They won't spend their careers wrapping an OS or rebuilding a PDF renderer. They'll start where all of this ends, and the ones who can read the code will take it further than we can picture today.

Start with Saturday's spreadsheets, or point your agent at llms.txt and see what it ships.

title: Dependabot Is a Contributor, and Other Things My Scripts Got Wrong
description:
For a while now I have been finding open source issues to fix with three small Python scripts. Together they were about sixty lines. One counted how many pull requests from outsiders a repository merged in the last 30 days and how long they waited. One listed open issues with a "good first issue" style label that nobody had linked a pull request to. The third looked for recent bug reports from users rather than maintainers.

They worked. They are how I found my two most recent Apache CloudStack fixes, both reproducible bugs that nobody had picked up. But they were the kind of scripts you only trust because you wrote them yesterday. So I rebuilt them as a proper tool in Java, with tests, and called it merge-radar.

Rebuilding them properly meant checking every assumption the scripts made. Several were wrong.

What the tool answers

Two questions, both from the GitHub API:

  • Does this project merge pull requests from people like me, and how fast?
  • Which of its open issues is nobody already working on?

Here is the first one, run against a handful of Java projects:

$ merge-radar health --repos-file examples/java-repos.txt
REPO                            SCORE  MERGED  PEOPLE  MEDIAN  ACCEPT
hiero-ledger/hiero-sdk-java        99      13      10     22h     93%
OpenAPITools/openapi-generator     98     129      59    2.5d     88%
keycloak/keycloak                  97    161+      44    3.1d     84%
apache/dolphinscheduler            97      18       9     26h     78%
spring-projects/spring-boot        95      71      32     29h     65%
checkstyle/checkstyle              95    179+      37     27h     67%
apache/cloudstack                  72      42      26   56.6d     82%

"Outsider" means anyone who is not an owner, organisation member or collaborator, and is not a bot. The score adds four capped parts: how many outsider pull requests were merged, how many different people that was, the median time to merge, and the share of decided outsider pull requests that were merged rather than closed.

The CloudStack row is the one I recognise from experience. It merges plenty of outside work, 42 pull requests from 26 people in a month, and accepts 82% of what it decides on. But the median pull request waits almost two months. My domain-limits fix was opened in October and approved in late November. That is not a reason to avoid the project. It is a reason to plan for a long review, and to have something else going in parallel.

Dependabot is a contributor

The first test I wrote used two pull requests recorded from the real CloudStack API: one of my merged ones, and one from Dependabot. This is what GitHub says about the Dependabot one:

"user": { "login": "dependabot[bot]", "type": "Bot" },
"author_association": "CONTRIBUTOR"

According to author_association, Dependabot is a contributor, exactly like me. Count by association alone and every busy repository with dependency updates looks wonderfully welcoming. My old script got away with it because it also checked for a login ending in [bot], almost by accident. merge-radar checks the user type as well, and the recorded Dependabot pull request is now a permanent test case.

Private members look like outsiders

Look at Keycloak in the table: 161 outsider pull requests merged in a month, from 44 people. I had already learned the hard way that this number is too good. When I looked at a Keycloak issue earlier this month, the code it touched was being changed by two core developers at the same time. A newcomer's pull request there would have collided with theirs.

The reason is that organisation membership on GitHub can be private. When it is, the API reports that person as CONTRIBUTOR, not MEMBER. In company-backed projects, many employees keep their membership private, so they count as outsiders. There is no way to tell from the public API.

I could not fix this, so the README says it plainly: in company-backed projects, read the score as an upper bound. A tool that is honest about where it is wrong is more useful than one that pretends to be precise.

"since" does not mean what it says

The issues endpoint takes a since parameter, and I assumed it meant "issues created since". It means "issues updated since". Ask for issues since last week and you get two-year-old issues that someone commented on yesterday. merge-radar passes since to keep the response small, then filters on the creation date itself.

Deciding whether an issue is taken

This is the part that saves the most time. An issue counts as claimed if an open pull request references it, if someone is assigned, or if someone asked to work on it in the last 30 days. If a merged pull request references it, it is probably already fixed.

Requests to work on an issue are where it gets interesting. Most of them are a single comment, "can I take this?", and the person never comes back. So a request older than 30 days is reported as a stale claim but does not hide the issue. Pull requests that were closed without merging do not hide it either; they are shown as earlier attempts, which are usually worth reading before you start.

The phrases are matched narrowly on purpose. "Can I work on this?" is a claim. "Is anyone working on this?" is not, and neither is "I can reproduce this on 4.22". Quoted lines are ignored, so someone replying to an old claim does not count as claiming it. When the matching is unsure, it errs towards showing the issue. Wrongly hiding a good issue costs you the issue. Wrongly showing a taken one costs you ten seconds reading the thread.

Against the real timeline of a CloudStack issue I worked on, the tool gets it right:

CLAIMED: open pull request #14722

That pull request is mine.

Running it for free

Without a token, GitHub allows 60 API requests an hour. Checking one issue costs a request for its timeline, so a run over a few repositories can use a few hundred. I wanted it cheap enough to run every week without thinking about it.

The answer was conditional requests. merge-radar stores every response with its ETag in a small SQLite file. On the next run it sends If-None-Match, and when nothing changed GitHub replies 304 Not Modified, which does not count against the rate limit. After one run over seven repositories, a second run used none of the hourly quota.

When the quota does run out, the client waits for the reset and retries, but only for up to two minutes by default. Past that it stops with a message saying when the limit resets. I would rather get an error than a tool that silently hangs for 58 minutes.

Each repository and each issue timeline is fetched on its own Java virtual thread, with a semaphore capping how many requests are in flight. GitHub's secondary rate limits punish bursts, not totals, so a hundred threads firing at once would be a good way to get blocked.

A weekly digest

The tool also runs as a GitHub Action. Point it at the projects you care about and every Monday it writes a Markdown digest to the job summary, or opens it as an issue. Keep the cache with actions/cache and the weekly run costs almost nothing.

One small trap while building it: a Docker-based action receives its inputs as environment variables named INPUT_<NAME>. I had named an input repos-file, which becomes INPUT_REPOS-FILE. That is a valid environment variable, but bash cannot read a variable with a hyphen in its name. The inputs use underscores now.

What it does not do yet

  • It cannot tell which contributors are really maintainers when GitHub labels them CONTRIBUTOR, as it does for Apache committers.
  • Pull requests linked to an issue only through GitHub's "Development" sidebar appear in the timeline without their number, so the tool misses them unless they also mention the issue. Most do, with "Fixes #123".
  • The claim phrases are English only.

Try it

The code, the scoring rules and the limits are in the repository. It needs Java 21 and borrows your token from the GitHub CLI if you have it logged in:

mvn package -DskipTests
java -jar cli/target/merge-radar.jar issues apache/cloudstack --recent 30d --outsider-reports

If you have been staring at "good first issue" labels wondering why they never lead anywhere, this is the method I use instead, written down as code. And if you find a case where it gets the verdict wrong, open an issue. Nobody has claimed it yet.

This article was written with the help of AI. It first appeared on my blog.

title: A forced PHP2Shell upgrade is the cheapest time to choose PHP 8.4 or Java 21
description:
On 16 November 2026, AWS published a guide on moving legacy PHP onto a patched runtime after PHP2Shell. The useful part is the decision it forces on anyone still running PHP 8.1 or older.

A forced security upgrade is the cheapest moment to decide where the application goes next: stay on PHP, or move to Java 21 / Spring Boot. Upgrading PHP is a valid answer for many teams. Skipping the decision is the expensive one.

What PHP2Shell actually is

PHP2Shell is the name used for two critical bugs in the PHP engine, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. AWS gives both a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, because either one can let an unauthenticated caller run code on a server that handles PHP requests. CISA uses the same name and CVE IDs, and on 26 October 2026 it added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The PHP project fixed the bugs on 21 October 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. The PHP Foundation and php.net confirm those CVE IDs and releases. If you already run a supported 8.2 to 8.5 branch, the immediate work is a point-release update and a worker restart. That is a patch, not a rewrite.

Where an in-place patch stops

AWS is direct on older runtimes: if you run PHP 8.1 or older, you cannot patch PHP2Shell in place, because no official PHP release fixes those branches. The same AWS article, and php.net, add a caveat. Some Linux distributions and LTS vendors ship backported fixes, and the PHP security team published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 as a stopgap for people who build from source. Those are holding measures, not a supported PHP branch.

For the official upgrade path, AWS recommends moving the application to PHP 8.4 or 8.5, based on remaining support dates. That is often harder than a point release, because legacy code can break on a newer PHP runtime. AWS itself says the code upgrade is the real blocker.

Two valid next steps

Once you have to change the application to leave 8.1, you have two honest options.

The first is to upgrade PHP, to 8.4 or 8.5 as AWS recommends, or to another supported branch if that is what your team can run. For many products this is the right call. The team already knows PHP, and the business may have no reason to leave it. A planned PHP upgrade is a complete answer to PHP2Shell.

The second is to use the same forced change as the moment to move off PHP, if Java 21 / Spring Boot was already on the roadmap, or if the hiring, integration or long-term support case for Java is already made. The security incident does not create that case by itself. It only makes the cost of waiting more obvious, because you are already paying to touch the code.

Neither option should be a panic rewrite with no proof that the new system matches the old one on real user journeys. A PHP major-version jump and a language change can both alter responses, database writes or outgoing calls.

If the destination is Java 21

MigrateForge converts plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3 to Java 21 / Spring Boot. Laravel is not supported. It runs locally. It replays recorded journeys and compares HTTP responses, database writes and outgoing calls. Cutover stays blocked until replay reaches 99.5% or better. Each wave is at most 150 units or 8,000 lines.

On two benchmarks, WA Blast Pro and InvoicePlane, not client projects, 858 fixtures reached 100% parity. That is a benchmark result. It is not a claim of 100% behavioural parity in production, and it is not a claim of zero risk.

A free report on one module is ₹0 at migrateforge.com.

The AWS article is here: PHP2Shell: Using AWS Transform to move legacy PHP onto a patched runtime. CISA's alert and the php.net advisory of 21 October 2026 independently confirm the CVE IDs, the fixed releases, and the position on PHP 8.1 and older.

CTOs and engineering leaders: if a security fix already forces you off PHP 8.1, will you upgrade PHP, move to Java, or postpone the choice until the next CVE?

title: No Password, No Extension: A Developer's Walkthrough of the BKC Nex Email Wallet (Plus the EVM Chain Underneath)
description:
If you've ever built a dApp, you know the drop-off. A visitor lands on your page, sees "connect wallet," realizes they don't have one, and leaves. The BKC team just published a short sign-up guide video for BKC Nex, the BKC Network app for social, maps and shopping. It shows a flow that sidesteps that problem. Below is a written version of the video, along with notes on how the pieces fit together and what the chain looks like from a builder's point of view.

The flow in four steps

If you only have thirty seconds, here's the whole thing:

  1. Pick "Email wallet." On the BKC Nex sign-in screen, choose the option labeled "Sign in with a code sent by email." The page describes it as "Nothing to install, works on your phone."
  2. Enter your email. A BKC Wallet window opens with a single "Email" field.
  3. Hit "Send code." The window explains: "We will email you a 6-digit code. No password, nothing to install."
  4. Type the 6-digit code. That's it. You're signed in with a BKC Wallet. You never create a password, and there's no extension to set up.

The video runs through exactly these steps on screen, so it's handy to send to a non-technical friend or teammate.

Why this matters for onboarding

There are two ways into BKC Nex, and that design choice is interesting:

  • Email wallet: code-by-email, aimed at people who don't already run a wallet, including mobile users.
  • Extension wallet: "Sign quickly right in your browser," for people who have the BKC Wallet extension from the Chrome Web Store. If it's missing, the app says so and offers an "Install BKC Wallet" button, then asks you to reload.

So the low-friction path is the default for newcomers, and the power-user path is still there. If you're designing your own onboarding, that split is worth borrowing: don't make an extension a prerequisite for a first visit.

What the sign-in actually does

From the public pages, here's what happens in order.

When you choose Email wallet, the Nex tab shows "Waiting for the wallet…" and the actual sign-in happens in a separate pop-up at wallet.bkc.network/signin. The app warns: "If you see no window, unlock the wallet or allow pop-ups, then try again." If a user reports that "nothing happened," a blocked pop-up is the first thing to check.

The wallet and the app are kept separate. The sign-in page footer states: "The wallet signs only when you confirm. Your secret keys never leave the wallet." The app requests a signature, and the wallet window is where the user approves it.

The wallet window also carries a "post-quantum" label. That matches the BKC docs. Every account and every validator on BKC signs with ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, security category 3). BKC accounts have no ECDSA key, and the chain rejects secp256k1 and ed25519 signers. It's not a hybrid scheme. Addresses are derived from the public key and can be shown as bkc1... (bech32) or 0x... (hex).

A few account rules worth knowing up front

These are documented in BKC Nex's security settings. Users should hear them before signing up, not after:

  • The linked wallet is the only way in. It can't be removed or swapped for another wallet. If you lose the wallet, you lose access to the account.
  • Sessions are revocable. You can see active sessions, sign one out (it's revoked on the server at once), or use "Sign out of all devices." Removing a device revokes every session tied to it.
  • Activity history lists your own sign-in and session events, newest first. It never shows passwords or tokens.
  • Deleting an account needs a signature in BKC Wallet. It's a soft delete with a 30-day grace period, and signing in again during that window restores the account.

The chain from a builder's angle

BKC runs as a Layer-1, and right now it's a testnet (Chain ID 262144). The BKC Nex terms describe the site as a demo using test wallets, with no real money involved. Here's what the explorer at explorer.bkc.network exposes for developers:

  • EVM JSON-RPC: https://rpc.bkc.network. The explorer's own hint is "Point MetaMask, ethers, viem or Hardhat here."
  • EVM WebSocket: wss://ws.bkc.network
  • Cosmos side: REST (LCD) https://api.bkc.network, CometBFT RPC https://comet-rpc.bkc.network, gRPC grpc.bkc.network:443

Why are both stacks listed? Per the explorer: "EVM calls are wrapped in Cosmos transactions, so both stacks are listed." Validators run on forks of CometBFT and the Cosmos SDK with ML-DSA-65 consensus keys.

The explorer is built on Blockscout. It supports contract verification (filters for Solidity, Vyper, Yul and Geas) and indexes ERC-20, ERC-721 and ERC-1155 tokens. It also documents REST, ETH RPC, core and Stats APIs. Staking, Governance, Swap and Bridge are marked "Soon," so don't plan around them yet.

title: feature-flags: a small self-hosted feature-flag server with a Go SDK
description:
Feature flags separate two things that are usually tied together: deploying code and turning it on. With a flag, the new checkout can be merged and deployed while it is still off, enabled for the team first, then for 10% of users, then for everyone, and switched off in seconds if something goes wrong.

The idea is simple, but a flag system that works needs more than an if and a config file. The same user must get the same answer on every request and on every server. A rollout that grows from 10% to 20% must keep the first 10%. Changes must reach running instances without a redeploy. And checking a flag must not add a network call to every request.

feature-flags is a small self-hosted server that does this, with a Go SDK. The README describes who it is for: teams that want trunk-based development and gradual rollouts without a SaaS bill. It is a single binary and a JSON file, which the README says is enough for dozens of flags and many app instances.

What it does

Flags with variants. A flag is not only on or off. Its variants can be booleans, strings, numbers or any JSON value.

Environments. Development, production and any others you create. Each environment has its own SDK key and its own configuration for every flag.

Targeting rules. Rules match on context attributes with these operators: eq, in, not_in, contains, starts_with, ends_with, matches, and gt/gte/lt/lte. A list attribute matches if any of its elements does.

Percentage rollouts with consistent hashing. A user keeps their variant, and widening 10% to 20% keeps the first 10%.

Live updates. A REST API for management, Server-Sent Events that push every change to SDKs, and an htmx admin UI embedded in the binary, with no build step.

A Go SDK that evaluates locally. The SDK keeps the configuration in a cache and evaluates flags in process. There is no network call per check, and it keeps working on the last known config if the server goes down.

How to use it

Install the flagd server with Go, and add the SDK to your module:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/feature-flags/cmd/flagd@latest
go get github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/feature-flags/sdk@latest

Or build from a checkout and start the server:

go build -o flagd ./cmd/flagd
FLAGS_ADMIN_TOKEN=change-me ./flagd -addr :8080 -data flags.json
# prints one SDK key per environment
open http://localhost:8080/admin          # Basic auth: any user, the admin token as password

Create a flag through the API. This one turns the new checkout on for the pro and team plans, and for 10% of everyone else:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer change-me" localhost:8080/api/flags -d '{
  "key": "new-checkout",
  "variants": {"on": true, "off": false},
  "environments": {
    "production": {
      "enabled": true,
      "off_variant": "off",
      "rules": [
        {"clauses": [{"attribute": "plan", "op": "in", "values": ["pro", "team"]}], "serve": {"variant": "on"}}
      ],
      "default": {"rollout": [{"variant": "on", "weight": 1000}, {"variant": "off", "weight": 9000}]}
    }
  }
}'

Weights are in basis points, so 1000 is 10%. Then use the flag from Go:

c := sdk.New("http://localhost:8080", os.Getenv("FLAGS_SDK_KEY"))
go c.Start(ctx)
c.WaitReady(ctx)
if c.Bool("new-checkout", flag.Context{"key": user.ID, "plan": user.Plan}, false) {
    // new code path
}

The last argument of c.Bool is the fallback value. The context is a map of attributes: key identifies the user for rollouts, and the other attributes feed the targeting rules.

The API also has a kill switch at POST /api/flags/{key}/environments/{env}/toggle, an admin POST /api/evaluate that returns the result with its reason, and three SDK endpoints: GET /sdk/flags for the full config of the key's environment, GET /sdk/stream for SSE, and POST /sdk/evaluate for server-side evaluation by clients that are not written in Go. SDK keys go in Authorization: Bearer …, or in ?sdk_key= for the browser's EventSource, which cannot set headers.

How it works

Evaluation lives in the package flag and is shared by the server and the SDK, so both give the same answer. If the flag is disabled, the result is off_variant. Otherwise the rules are tried in order, and the first rule whose clauses all match serves its variant or rollout. Everyone else gets default. Each result carries a reason: OFF, RULE_MATCH with the rule index, DEFAULT or ERROR, and whether a rollout picked the variant.

One detail is worth knowing before you write rules. A clause on a missing attribute never matches, not even neq or not_in. A rule therefore cannot accidentally target users you know nothing about.

Rollouts use this formula: bucket = sha256(flagKey + "." + salt + "." + id) mod 10000. Variants take consecutive bucket ranges in the order listed, so increasing the first variant's weight only adds users. The salt is random per flag, which means different flags bucket users independently: being in the 10% of one flag says nothing about another. bucket_by can split by another attribute, such as org, so a whole organisation gets the same variant.

The server holds its state (version, environments, flags) in memory and writes it to one JSON file atomically on every change. The version counter increases on every change. SSE subscribers get a coalescing signal and re-send the full payload, so a slow client cannot make the server queue stale diffs.

The SDK holds one SSE connection with a watchdog. If nothing arrives for 60 seconds, not even a ping, it reconnects. When streaming fails, which happens behind proxies that buffer or block SSE, it polls /sdk/flags between reconnect attempts with exponential backoff, so updates still arrive. Payloads with an older version are ignored.

The admin UI is server-rendered html/template plus htmx 1.9.12, embedded in the binary. Toggles swap a single table row. The config editor is a JSON textarea with server-side validation, and a "try it" box evaluates any context. Writes require htmx's HX-Request header. A cross-site form cannot send custom headers, so this blocks CSRF even though Basic-auth credentials are sent automatically.

Things to know

  • Storage is a single JSON file. The README says that is fine for one server instance and hundreds of flags. It does not support multiple replicas, which would need shared storage and fan-out of changes.
  • No audit log, no accounts, no schedules. There are no per-user accounts or roles, and no scheduled changes.
  • No segments. There are no reusable user lists, and no semver or date operators.
  • The SDK fetches the whole environment. That is fine for server-side use. Do not ship an environment's full rules to browsers if they contain sensitive targeting data.
  • Only a Go SDK. Other languages can call /sdk/evaluate, or reimplement the evaluation rules described above.
  • What was tested. go test -race ./... covers three packages. For flag: off and default, every operator, number types (Go int versus JSON float64), list attributes, missing attributes, a 20% rollout over 20k users within ±1.5%, stickiness when widening to 50%, independence across flags, bucket_by, validation messages and a JSON round trip. For server: CRUD and validation, toggle, evaluate, reload from disk, admin and SDK auth, the SSE stream, and the htmx endpoints including the CSRF guard. For sdk, against a real server in-process: readiness, local evaluation, an update pushed after a toggle, the cache surviving server shutdown, falling back to polling behind a proxy that rejects SSE, and a bad SDK key.

Why I built it

The README states the need in one line: trunk-based development and gradual rollouts without a SaaS bill. A team that merges small changes to the main branch every day needs a way to keep unfinished work switched off in production, and a way to release it to a few users first. Hosted flag services do this well, but they are one more subscription and one more external dependency in the request path.

For a team with dozens of flags, the core is small enough to own. What I wanted to get right were the parts that are easy to get subtly wrong: bucketing that stays sticky when a rollout widens, flags that bucket independently, a rule engine that does not match users with missing data, and an SDK that keeps answering from its cache when the flag server is down. A flag check that can fail or block defeats the point, so the server being unavailable has to be a non-event for the application.

Sharing one evaluation package between the server and the SDK follows from that. The "try it" box in the admin UI and the code running in the application cannot disagree, because they run the same function.

Get the code

The server, the SDK, the admin UI and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/feature-flags. It is MIT licensed. The embedded htmx is © Big Sky Software, under the 0BSD license. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

title: cert-monitor: TLS certificate alerts on Telegram and email, once per stage
description:
An expired TLS certificate is an outage with a date on it. Everyone knows months ahead when it will happen, and it still happens: the renewal job failed quietly, a certificate was installed by hand on one server and forgotten, or the mail server on port 993 was never part of the automation.

Expiry is also not the only way a certificate breaks. A server can be configured without its intermediate certificate and work in some clients while failing in others. A certificate can be valid but issued for a different hostname. An old endpoint can still negotiate TLS 1.0. From the outside, each of these looks like the same vague "handshake failed".

cert-monitor watches the TLS certificates of your hosts and tells you, once per stage, before something breaks. It is a single Go binary with a status page and alerts on Telegram and by email. The README describes the audience as small teams and self-hosters with a handful to a few hundred endpoints, such as web servers, mail servers on 993/465 or internal APIs, who want a heads-up rather than a full observability stack.

What it does

It runs four kinds of checks on every target.

Expiry. It alerts at 30, 14, 7 and 1 days left, and again when the certificate has expired. The thresholds are configurable. Each alert is sent once per threshold per certificate. Renewing the certificate gives it a new fingerprint, and the sequence starts over.

Chain of trust. An unknown issuer, a self-signed certificate, a missing intermediate, or an expired intermediate.

Hostname. The certificate must cover the name you connect with (SNI).

Weak crypto. SHA-1 or MD5 signatures on the leaf or the intermediates, RSA keys under 2048 bits, ECDSA keys under 256 bits, and servers that negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1.

Flexible targets. A target is host, host:port or sni@host:port. The last form connects to one address while asking for another name, as in api.example.com@10.0.0.5:8443, which is useful for checking one backend behind a load balancer.

Detailed diagnosis. The tool dials with InsecureSkipVerify and then verifies by hand with x509.Verify, VerifyHostname and its own algorithm checks. That is why a broken certificate is reported in detail, such as "missing intermediate" or the list of names the certificate does cover, instead of failing with one handshake error. Eight hosts are checked in parallel.

Alerts that do not repeat. The state per target is the leaf fingerprint, the most urgent threshold already alerted, the set of non-expiry problems, and a streak of connection errors. An expiry alert fires when the days left reach a stage that has not been alerted for that certificate. Problems alert when their set changes, and a "resolved" message follows when it empties. Connection errors must happen twice in a row before you hear about them.

Alerts that are not lost. State only advances when at least one notifier delivered the message. A Telegram outage therefore means a retry on the next round, not a lost alert. The state file is saved atomically, with a temp file and a rename.

Status page. A server-rendered table sorted by urgency, plus JSON at /api/status, a POST /api/check endpoint, and /healthz.

How to use it

Install the binary with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/cert-monitor/cmd/cert-monitor@latest

Or build it from a checkout and run a one-off check:

go build -o cert-monitor ./cmd/cert-monitor

# One-off check (exit code 0 ok, 1 warning, 2 critical):
./cert-monitor -check example.com mail.example.com:993 api.example.com@10.0.0.5:8443

The exit code makes the one-off mode usable from a script or a cron job. The README shows this example output:

TARGET                        STATUS    DAYS   EXPIRES     DETAILS
github.com                    ok        43     2026-11-29
expired.badssl.com            critical  -4206  2015-04-12  certificate expired on 2015-04-12; chain: …
wrong.host.badssl.com         critical  72     2026-12-28  hostname: certificate is not valid for wrong.host.badssl.com (it covers *.badssl.com, badssl.com)
sha1-intermediate.badssl.com  critical  -2331  2020-05-30  …; weak signature: intermediate COMODO SSL CA is signed with SHA1-RSA

To run it continuously, copy the example config and start it:

cp config.example.json config.json   # edit targets and notifiers
TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=… TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID=… SMTP_PASSWORD=… ./cert-monitor -config config.json
open http://localhost:8090/

The config is one JSON file:

{
  "listen": ":8090",
  "interval": "6h",
  "timeout": "10s",
  "state_file": "state.json",
  "thresholds": [30, 14, 7, 1],
  "targets": [
    "example.com",
    "mail.example.com:993",
    "api.example.com@203.0.113.10:8443"
  ],
  "telegram": {"bot_token": "${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}", "chat_id": "${TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID}"},
  "smtp": {
    "addr": "smtp.example.com:587",
    "username": "alerts@example.com",
    "password": "${SMTP_PASSWORD}",
    "from": "alerts@example.com",
    "to": ["ops@example.com"]
  }
}

${VAR} references are expanded from the environment, so secrets stay out of the file. interval is the time between check rounds (6 hours by default), and timeout is the per-host dial and handshake timeout. Without state_file, the dedupe state lives in memory only, so set it if you do not want alerts to repeat after a restart. SMTP uses STARTTLS when the server offers it.

Things to know

  • No revocation checks. There are no OCSP or CRL checks, no Certificate Transparency lookups and no CAA checks.
  • Implicit TLS only. STARTTLS protocols, such as SMTP on 25/587 or IMAP on 143, are not supported as targets. Only implicit TLS ports (443, 465, 993, 8443 and so on) are.
  • No routing. Alerts go to every configured notifier. There is no per-target routing and there are no quiet hours.
  • The status page has no authentication. Bind it to localhost or put it behind a proxy if your host list is sensitive.
  • Weak-crypto checks have a scope. They cover signatures, key sizes and the protocol version, not individual cipher suites.
  • What was tested. go test -race ./... generates its own PKI at runtime, with a root, intermediates and leaves, and serves it with httptest TLS servers. The check tests cover a healthy certificate, warning and critical expiry, an expired certificate, a hostname mismatch, SNI picking the right certificate among several, self-signed and missing-intermediate chains, a 1024-bit RSA key, a SHA-1-signed leaf, a server capped at TLS 1.1, and a connection failure. The alert tests cover the full threshold sequence including renewal, problem sets and resolution, the two-strikes rule for errors, state persistence, the Telegram Bot API against a fake server, and SMTP against a minimal in-process SMTP server. The monitor tests cover one alert per stage across runs, retry after a failed delivery, and the status page and JSON.

Why I built it

For a small team, certificate monitoring usually goes wrong in one of two ways. Either nothing checks, and the first alert is a user saying the site shows a warning. Or a script checks every day and sends "expires in 12 days" every morning, until the message becomes background noise and nobody reads it on the day it matters.

The design answers the second problem as much as the first. One alert per stage per certificate means a message is rare enough to be read. Requiring two connection errors in a row avoids waking someone up for one dropped packet. Advancing state only after a successful delivery means a notifier outage does not swallow the one alert you needed.

The detailed diagnosis exists for the same reason. An alert that says "missing intermediate" or lists the names the certificate covers tells you what to fix. An alert that says "handshake failed" only tells you to start investigating.

And it is one binary with a JSON file, because the people it is for do not want to run a monitoring platform to watch a few dozen certificates.

Get the code

The source, the example config and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/cert-monitor. It is MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

title: Designing Construction Takeoff Software for Trade Users: Lessons From a Button Refresh
description:
Most software design writing assumes users who live in software. Construction takeoff tools serve a different crowd: subcontractors and small trade teams who would rather be on site, and who open their estimating software because a tender is due, not because they enjoy it. That changes how you think about something as small as a button.

The prompt for this post is a modest update. In ContractorCounter, a browser-based construction takeoff and estimating workspace, buttons across the product now have a cleaner, rounder look. Nothing more dramatic than that. But it's a useful example for anyone building vertical software for people whose real job is somewhere else.

The change itself

Buttons throughout ContractorCounter were restyled to look cleaner and rounder. The update applies across the product, so the controls share one look rather than varying from screen to screen.

That's the factual scope. The rest of this post is about why that kind of change deserves design and engineering time in a trade tool.

Trade users face different UI pressure

A few things are true of most people doing estimating for a trade business:

  • They use the tool in bursts. A small team might price several jobs in a week and then not touch the estimating screen for days. Every return trip is a small re-orientation.
  • The content is already dense. Construction drawings are full of linework, symbols, dimensions and notes. Anything the interface adds on top competes with information the user actually needs.
  • Mistakes cost money directly. A missed item in a takeoff isn't a bug report, it's margin gone from a job.
  • The tool is a means to an end. Nobody in a trade business opens estimating software to admire it. They open it to get a quote out.

Under those conditions, visual noise is not just cosmetic. If the chrome around a drawing is busy, it pulls the eye away from the drawing. A calmer set of controls hands attention back to the content.

Buttons are the connective tissue of a workflow

ContractorCounter puts the whole estimating path in one workspace: take off construction drawings, review AI-generated counts, add rates and build quotes. Each stage puts different content on screen, but buttons are the common element running through all of them. They're how the user moves the job forward.

When a workflow spans several stages, consistent controls do a quiet job. They signal that this is one tool, not four bolted together. Rounder, cleaner buttons applied product-wide are a small contribution to that sense of continuity.

Consistency beats novelty

If you build vertical SaaS, it's tempting to spend design time on new, visible features. Shared components like buttons are less glamorous, but they are the parts every user touches on every visit. Improving them across the product reaches more of the experience than polishing one new screen.

There's also a maintenance angle developers will recognise: a component that looks the same everywhere is easier to reason about than one with a dozen local variants. That's a general principle, not a description of anyone's codebase, but it's a good reason to treat visual consistency as more than decoration.

Scope your changelog honestly

One more lesson that's easy to forget: describe small changes as small. People in the trades are rightly suspicious of marketing language. Saying plainly that buttons now look cleaner and rounder, rather than dressing it up as a reinvention, respects the reader's time. It also builds credibility for the days when an update really is big.

Takeaways for builders of trade software

  1. Treat interface calm as a functional requirement when the content is dense.
  2. Invest in shared components, because they show up in every session.
  3. Keep visual language consistent across a multi-stage workflow.
  4. Write update notes in plain words and match the claim to the change.
  5. Give users somewhere to go when things look different. ContractorCounter, for example, offers a help centre and guides for contractors.

Wrapping up

A button refresh won't trend on anyone's timeline. In construction takeoff software, though, where the user is a subcontractor trying to get a price out before the deadline, it's the kind of detail that makes a tool feel lighter to come back to. If you're designing for trade users, it's worth asking which of your shared components deserve the same attention.

You can see the refreshed interface at ContractorCounter.

title: Written feedback or a screen recording? What $3.99 and $5.99 per tester actually get you
description:
If you pay strangers to test your app, the first choice is the format. Do you want them to write down what they thought, or record their screen and talk while they use it? The written report is cheaper and quicker to read. The recording is slower to watch and costs more.

I run a testing marketplace that sells both, at $3.99 and $5.99 per tester, so I have a stake in this. I also have the numbers from about 1,600 sessions, and they say something more specific than "video is better".

What you get from each

Written report Screen recording
Price per tester (TestFi) $3.99 $5.99
Sessions since March 2026 774 825
Median time the tester spent 5.8 minutes 13.8 minutes
Written answers to your questions Yes, median 73 words Yes, median 77 words
Reports the developer rejected 15% of those reviewed 7% of those reviewed
Shows where they hesitated No Yes, with timestamps

Three things in that table matter more than the price.

A recording includes the written report

Testers in recorded sessions answer the same questions afterwards, and their answers are about as long. So the choice isn't really "written or video". It's "written, or written plus a recording".

Testers spend more than twice as long

The median recorded session ran 13.8 minutes, against 5.8 for written. I don't think recorded testers are more diligent people. Talking out loud slows everyone down, and knowing the screen is being recorded keeps people on task. Either way, you get more of the app covered.

Developers rejected written reports twice as often

Developers turned down 15% of the written reports they reviewed and 7% of the recordings. A written report can look thorough and still come from someone who barely opened the app. A recording can't hide that. You either see the app being used or you don't.

That's also the main reason I'd pay the extra $2: not the video itself, but knowing the session happened.

When written is the better buy

  • Checking a specific fix. "Does the export work now?" doesn't need a recording.
  • Copy and first impressions. "What do you think this app does after reading the store listing?" is a writing question.
  • Breadth. If you want 20 opinions on a feature idea, 20 written reports cost $79.80. Twenty recordings would take you an afternoon to watch.
  • Ratings and yes/no questions you'll compare across testers.

When the recording is worth it

  • The first time anyone outside your team uses a flow. Onboarding, sign-up, checkout, a paywall.
  • Bugs you can't reproduce. The recording shows the device, the order of taps and what was on screen.
  • Anything where "it was a bit confusing" won't tell you where. A recording shows the exact screen and the exact pause. In a count of 5,583 pauses across our recordings, most testers stalled for the first time within a minute. Nobody remembers a two-second pause well enough to write it down afterwards.

Mixing them

You don't have to pick one per test. A setup I'd use for a new flow: five recordings to see where people stall, then ten written reports a week later to check the fixes. That's $29.95 plus $39.90, so $69.85 in total.

Disclosure

The numbers are from TestFi, which I run, and the prices are ours. Both formats are on this page. There's an older, longer comparison on our blog.

If you've paid for either kind and one surprised you, I'd like to hear which and why.

title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Practice: Thinking Tier Routing, Native Semantic Sensor, and DORA Telemetry in Pure Go
description:
When a multi-agent workflow grows from two or three ad-hoc prompts into 16 specialized skills — spanning triage and data modeling through TDD, code review, security auditing, and PR creation — a quiet engineering bottleneck emerges: the cost and latency of Single-Model Orchestration.

Using the same heavyweight frontier model at maximum reasoning effort to update a delivery index in docs-ai/deliveries/INDEX.md or open a PR in git-delivery, while also using it to audit security surfaces in security-review or architectural invariants in architecture-guardrails, wastes quota, inflates pipeline Lead Time, and adds zero quality to mechanical steps.

In this 6th technical article on the architecture of Pipeline-AI — covering the capabilities introduced in release v0.12.0 (DEL-039) and their end-to-end integration in DEL-043 (D-44) —, I show how Gemini 4 Hydrogen plays two complementary roles in the pipeline while keeping 100% adherence to the Go 1.24 standard library (zero external dependencies in go.mod).

1. The Single-Model Problem in Multi-Agent Pipelines

In deterministic AI-assisted pipelines, not every stage requires the same cognitive budget:

  • Mechanical and formatted stages: updating delivery reports, synchronizing indexes, and running Git commands have rigid scopes and low ambiguity. Deep reasoning here only adds latency.
  • Implementation and triage stages: turning requirements into tests (TDD), writing scoped code, and validating the test suite require a balance between speed and accuracy.
  • Critical architecture and security stages: setting implementation boundaries before coding, reviewing diffs for subtle flaws, and auditing queries, DDL migrations, and security surfaces demand maximum analytical depth.

Without explicit capability routing, an orchestrator falls into one of two traps: either over-provisioning everything (paying maximum quota and latency for trivial tasks) or under-provisioning everything (degrading architectural and security reviews).

2. Two Roles for Gemini 4 Hydrogen in pipeline-ai

To resolve this trade-off deterministically and auditably, pipeline-ai uses Gemini 4 Hydrogen across two integrated layers:

flowchart LR
    subgraph R1["1. Thinking Tier Matrix (internal/config)"]
        CFG[".pipeline-ai.json<br/>model_routing"] --> RES["DefaultModelRouting() &<br/>ResolveSkillModel(skill)"]
        RES --> LOW["gemini-4-hydrogen-low<br/>docs-update, git-delivery, context-loader"]
        RES --> MED["gemini-4-hydrogen-medium<br/>pm-triage, test-writer, dev-implementation,<br/>qa-validation, release-ops"]
        RES --> HIGH["gemini-4-hydrogen-high<br/>architecture-guardrails, code-reviewer,<br/>security-review, supply-chain-review,<br/>migration-reviewer, query-performance,<br/>data-model, agent-auditor"]
    end

    subgraph R2["2. Native Semantic Sensor (internal/sensor/semantic)"]
        EVAL["pipeline-ai eval -provider gemini<br/>or Runner -semantic-gate"] --> HTTP["Pure Go net/http POST<br/>:generateContent + x-goog-api-key"]
        HTTP --> GEM["generationConfig:<br/>thinkingLevel + responseSchema"]
    end

    RES -. "exposed as JSON" .-> MCP["MCP: pipeline://catalog<br/>& pipeline://routing"]
    GEM -. "records telemetry" .-> DORA["internal/metrics<br/>ByProvider & ByModel"]

2.1. Role 1: Thinking Tier Matrix (model_routing in internal/config/config.go)

In internal/config/config.go, the model_routing matrix deterministically maps every skill in the ecosystem to its recommended Gemini 4 Hydrogen tier via DefaultModelRouting() and (*Config).ResolveSkillModel(skill string) string:

Tier Model Default Assigned Skills Execution Profile
Low gemini-4-hydrogen-low docs-update, git-delivery, context-loader High speed, low cost, mechanical & documentation tasks
Medium gemini-4-hydrogen-medium pm-triage, test-writer, dev-implementation, qa-validation, release-ops (and default fallback) Balanced reasoning and latency for triage, TDD, and coding
High gemini-4-hydrogen-high architecture-guardrails, code-reviewer, security-review, supply-chain-review, migration-reviewer, query-performance, data-model, agent-auditor Maximum analytical depth for guardrails, reviews, and security

Any project can override individual mappings in .pipeline-ai.json via model_routing. When a skill has no local override, ResolveSkillModel falls back to DefaultModelRouting(), and for unknown skills it defaults safely to gemini-4-hydrogen-medium.

To let orchestrators and subagents inspect this matrix at runtime without parsing prose documentation, the MCP server exposes two structured resources:

  • pipeline://catalog (D-41): full catalog of native skills, available modules, and model_routing.
  • pipeline://routing (D-44): dedicated JSON resource returning the resolved Thinking Tier Matrix directly.

2.2. Role 2: Native Semantic Sensor (internal/sensor/semantic)

Beyond orchestrating subagents, pipeline-ai implements a native client for the "gemini" provider (ProviderGemini = "gemini", DefaultGeminiModel = "gemini-4-hydrogen-low", DefaultGeminiThinkingLevel = "low") inside internal/sensor/semantic/client.go.

Instead of adding an external SDK to go.mod, calls to the generateContent endpoint (https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/<model>:generateContent) are implemented in pure Go (net/http), leveraging two native Gemini 4 Hydrogen capabilities:

  1. thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel: explicitly controls the reasoning budget (low, medium, or high) per semantic evaluation.
  2. responseMimeType: "application/json" + responseSchema: enforces strict structured output matching the evaluation mode (noul boolean, choice multiple-choice with an options probability map, or continuous score).

Security Safeguards (SEC-01, SEC-02, and SEC-03)

Because the semantic sensor handles code diffs and communicates with an authenticated external API, three defense layers are built in:

  • SEC-01 (Header Authentication & Anti-Hallucination): GEMINI_API_KEY is sent exclusively via the x-goog-api-key HTTP header — never as a ?key= URL query parameter, preventing accidental leakage in net/url error messages or logs. In choice mode, the returned selection is validated against allowed choices (ErrInvalidChoice).
  • SEC-02 (Score Bounds & Normalization): In score mode, values outside [0, max_score] trigger ErrInvalidScore.
  • SEC-03 (Secret Redaction, Payload Caps, and Timeouts): Network or unexpected HTTP status errors pass through sanitizeErr (replacing the API key with [REDACTED]), response bodies are capped via io.LimitReader (default 10 MB MaxBodyBytes, returning ErrResponseTooLarge), and all requests enforce context.WithTimeout.

Furthermore, the Gemini response parser is continuously fuzz-tested via FuzzParseGeminiResponse (internal/sensor/semantic/fuzz_test.go), with over 638,000 executions and zero panics.

Usage from the CLI and MCP is straightforward:

export GEMINI_API_KEY="AIzaSy..."

# Binary evaluation (noul) with Thinking Tier low
pipeline-ai eval -provider gemini -model gemini-4-hydrogen-low -thinking-level low \
  -state "func foo() {}" -question "is the code complete?" -threshold 0.8

# Multiple-choice routing (choice)
pipeline-ai eval -provider gemini -mode choice \
  -state "SQL syntax error" -question "which skill should run?" \
  -choices "data-model,migration-reviewer,dev-implementation"

3. End-to-End Runner Integration and DORA Telemetry (DEL-043)

With delivery DEL-043 (D-44), Gemini 4 Hydrogen moved beyond standalone eval calls to close the loop inside the Pipeline Runner and DORA Telemetry:

3.1. Optional 4th Advisory Stage in the Runner (-semantic-gate)

pipeline-ai run (and the MCP tool pipeline_run_pipeline with semantic_gate: true) now accepts the -semantic-gate flag, appending an optional 4th stage to the deterministic cascade:

doctor → sensor → validate → semantic_gate (advisory)

Per architectural decision D-44, semantic_gate operates strictly in advisory mode:

  • Without configured credentials (GEMINI_API_KEY or JEV_ENDPOINT), it returns StatusSkip without interrupting the pipeline.
  • With credentials configured, it evaluates using the yagni preset, returning StatusPass or StatusWarn while applying redactSecrets to any error output.
  • External API outages never flip a local deterministic pass (gofmt, go vet, go test) into StatusFail.

3.2. DORA Telemetry by Provider and Model (internal/metrics)

To provide real visibility into cost, adoption, and latency across providers and tiers, internal/metrics/metrics.go added:

  • RecordSemanticEvalWithProvider(rootDir, deliveryID, mode, provider, model, duration, success, confidence): records the provider (gemini or jev) and exact model (gemini-4-hydrogen-low, etc.) on every semantic event.
  • SemanticSummary.ByProvider and SemanticSummary.ByModel: aggregations in the DORA summary (pipeline-ai metrics summary -json) tagged with json:"...,omitempty" for full backward compatibility with existing .pipeline-state/metrics.json files.

4. The 100% Go Stdlib Invariant (Zero External Dependencies)

A core engineering invariant of pipeline-ai is keeping go.mod completely free of external runtime dependencies:

module github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai

go 1.24

tool (
    github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai/cmd/pipeline-hook
    github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai/cmd/pipeline-validate
)

There is no require block. The entire Gemini 4 Hydrogen integration — from the net/http client with responseSchema and thinkingConfig to tier routing, the JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP server, the Runner, and DORA telemetry — runs on pure Go 1.24 stdlib, ensuring static CGO_ENABLED=0 binaries, fast builds, and minimal supply-chain surface.

Conclusion

Separating where to think fast and cheap (Hydrogen Low) from where to think deeply (Hydrogen High), while coupling a Native Semantic Sensor with responseSchema, thinkingLevel, an advisory Runner gate, and ByProvider/ByModel DORA telemetry, turns multi-agent orchestration into predictable software engineering.

The full source code is available under the MIT license at:

  • Repository: github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai
  • Architectural Decisions: docs-ai/DECISOES.md (D-41 and D-44)

Case Room (사건방) — Unsolved & missing cases, forensic/investigative methods, and a Bookshelf curating related books and documentaries

Missing Persons Garden (실종자들의 정원) — An interactive waiting space featuring real missing person records from Korea and the FBI, designed to help visitors remember them rather than scroll past

Briefing Room (브리핑룸) — Domestic & international crime/case news along with data charts

What Cases Changed (사건이 바꾼 것들) — Laws and everyday safety standards born from major incidents

I'd love honest, blunt feedback on the whole site (even via browser translate or just judging the UI/UX flow):

UI & first impression: Does the layout or visual design feel awkward or unclear?

Features & usefulness: Do the features (including the Bookshelf & forensic methods in the Case Room, the news & charts in the Briefing Room, and the Missing Persons Garden) actually make sense and work smoothly?

What's missing overall? Anything that feels broken, confusing on mobile, or holds this project back from growing.

I know it still has a lot of rough edges, so any honest critique means a lot. Thank you!
