title: core.hooksPath outside the checkout: a finding, not a refusal
description:
A repository that shows up as plain files brings its own git configuration along, and that configuration decides which programs a git run starts. Before anyone types a command, an inspector has to answer one narrow question: which directory would git take its hooks from, and what is sitting in it. The interesting case is the one where that directory lies outside the checkout, and the answer there cannot be the answer the inspector gives to a .git file pointing out of the tree.

Two rules in the same tree

I wrote repo.Resolve in gitdisarm to read a checkout's pointer files as data: .git as a directory, as a symlink, or as a file carrying a gitdir: line taken relative to the directory holding it; the commondir pointer a linked worktree leaves in its git directory; the gitdir pointer that leads back to that worktree's own .git file. Every one of those paths has to stay inside the checkout. One that leaves it refuses the repository outright:

type EscapeError struct {
    // Pointer is the file that named the path.
    Pointer string
    // Field is what it stood for: "gitdir", "commondir" or "worktree".
    Field string
    Path  string
    Root  string
}

func (e *EscapeError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s %s %s at %s", e.Pointer, e.Field, e.Path, ErrEscapesCheckout, e.Root)
}

func (e *EscapeError) Unwrap() error { return ErrEscapesCheckout }

The question gets asked twice: lexically, so a path that never existed is refused all the same, and then again after filepath.EvalSymlinks has followed as much of the path as exists, so a .git symlinked out of the tree is refused just like a gitdir: ../elsewhere line. Nothing is followed once it fails. For a pointer file that is the right behaviour, because a pointer file leaving the checkout is not a configuration choice anybody makes on purpose in a tree you were handed: it is the tree reaching for something you did not receive.

Extending that rule to core.hooksPath would be consistent. It would also be wrong.

Why the same rule cannot apply to the configuration

Git reads core.hooksPath as a path to a hooks directory, and it accepts that path pointing anywhere. A shared hooks directory kept outside the repository is an ordinary, supported setup. So a hooks path that leads out of the checkout is not a malformed repository, it is a configured one, and git will run what it finds there whatever an inspector thinks about the location.

Refuse at that point and the person running the tool gets an error where they needed a list. The directory, the entry that chose it, and the executables in it are exactly what a reviewer came to the tree to learn. Refusing would hide the thing the tool exists to show.

I have spent most of the last several years on payment and crypto systems, where refusing early is almost always the correct instinct: an unexpected value in a settlement path should stop the transaction, not get reasoned about. Carry that instinct into an inspector and you get a tool that is safe and useless. A gate refuses. A report does not get to refuse the parts it finds alarming, those are the findings.

So in gitdisarm, Layout.Hooks returns no error for a hooks directory outside the checkout. It records the fact and lists the directory anyway.

The effective directory is a computation, not a lookup

There is no single place to read the hooks path from. Git applies configuration in order, a later declaration of the same key overrides an earlier one, and included files are spliced in where their directive stood. gitconfig.Load hands back entries in that order, each one keeping the file and line it came from, so the effective value is whatever the last matching entry says, not the first one found.

That shapes the loop: it does not break.

func (l *Layout) Hooks(entries []gitconfig.Entry) (*Hooks, error) {
    h := &Hooks{Dir: filepath.Join(l.CommonDir, "hooks")}
    for i := range entries {
        e := &entries[i]
        if e.Section != "core" || e.Subsection != "" || e.Key != "hookspath" || e.Value == "" {
            continue
        }
        h.Dir = against(l.Worktree, e.Value)
        h.FromConfig = e
    }
    // ...
}

Four details are doing work there.

The section and key are compared lowercased because the parser reports them that way (git's section and key names are case-insensitive), and the subsection has to be empty, so nothing inside a [core "something"] block gets mistaken for the real key.

An empty value changes nothing. It is skipped instead of being treated as a request to use the empty path, so a stray hooksPath = cannot quietly point the effective directory at the work tree root.

The path is taken relative to the top of the work tree, not to the git directory and not to the process's working directory. against keeps an absolute path as it is and joins a relative one onto l.Worktree, which, for a linked worktree, is the directory holding its .git file rather than the checkout root.

And the fallback is CommonDir, not GitDir. Hooks are shared from the common directory, so a linked worktree with no core.hooksPath resolves to the same hooks its main checkout would run.

Given this configuration, the second declaration wins and the first one is not a finding at all:

[core]
    hooksPath = .githooks

[core]
    hooksPath = /opt/shared-hooks

Reporting the first line would describe a git run that is not going to happen. Reporting only that "a hooks path is set" would describe nothing. The entry that actually chose the directory is kept in FromConfig, so the report can name the file and the line responsible.

Outside is a field, not an error 

type Hooks struct {
    Dir string
    // FromConfig is the core.hooksPath entry that chose the directory, nil
    // when git would take its default.
    FromConfig *gitconfig.Entry
    // Outside reports that Dir lies outside the checkout, which the
    // configuration may ask for where a pointer file may not.
    Outside bool
    Executables []string
}

The outside test reuses the same two-stage question Resolve asks, and ends in a boolean instead of an *EscapeError: the directory is compared against Root lexically, then again after the symlinks of the longest part of the path that exists have been followed. A path that does not exist yet still gets an answer, and a hooks directory that is a symlink out of the tree is answered the same way as one spelled ../../hooks. Only an unexpected filesystem error on the way is passed up as an error.

That asymmetry (identical reasoning, different outcome) is the whole design. The checkout boundary is a hard constraint on structure and a reportable fact about intent.

A missing directory runs nothing

With the directory decided, what is left is the question of what git would actually start from it:

func executables(dir string) ([]string, error) {
    info, err := os.Stat(dir)
    if errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) {
        return nil, nil
    } else if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if !info.IsDir() {
        return nil, nil
    }
    ents, err := os.ReadDir(dir)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    var names []string
    for _, ent := range ents {
        st, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, ent.Name()))
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        if m := st.Mode(); m.IsRegular() && m.Perm()&0o111 != 0 {
            names = append(names, ent.Name())
        }
    }
    return names, nil
}

A directory that is absent, or that is no directory at all, runs nothing, and "runs nothing" is an empty list rather than an error. A core.hooksPath pointing at a path that does not exist on this machine is a real and common state; treating it as a failure would turn a finding worth one line into a stack of noise, and would stop the rest of the report from being produced.

Every entry is stat'ed again instead of trusting the type os.ReadDir already returned. That extra call is the point: DirEntry reports a symlink as a symlink, and a symlink to an executable file is one more program git would start. Following it costs one syscall per entry, and it is the difference between listing pre-commit and missing it. An entry that cannot be stat'ed is skipped rather than guessed at, and a name is kept only when the target is a regular file with any bit of 0o111 set, because git does not care which bit, so neither does this.

What I would do differently

Two things.

Executables carries names, in the order the directory lists them, and nothing else. A reviewer who reads pre-commit in the output does not learn from it that the name is a symlink, or where it leads. The stat already follows the link, so the resolved target is free information that currently gets thrown away, and I would carry it.

The second one is about how the finding is framed rather than how it is computed. The catalog row for core.hooksPath classifies it as executing and carries its own override, -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null, so the report can print the invocation that neutralizes the setting next to the finding. Alongside it, NotCovered has to be printed too: it names what can still end in a program being run and has no verdict, including the executables already sitting in .git/hooks. A short list of findings must not read as a clean repository, and that is probably easier to get wrong in the presentation layer than in the resolution logic.

The rule

Refuse what the format does not permit. Report what the format permits and a reviewer would want to know. Pointer files are structure, and a structure that leaves the checkout is broken. Configuration is intent, and intent that leaves the checkout is the finding itself.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: The Most Ignored Screen in Your Product: Designing Empty States
description:
Every product has a screen that nobody on the team looks at very often: the one with nothing on it.

An empty dashboard. An inbox with no messages. A project list before the first project exists. When you build a product, you work with data in it, test accounts, seeded records, demo content. So the empty version rarely gets opened. Yet it's exactly what every new user sees first, at the moment they're deciding whether the product is for them.

An empty state is not an error and not a blank. It's the most honest moment in your onboarding, and it deserves to be designed.

Why this screen matters more than it looks

A new user arrives with a small amount of patience and a goal. They've signed up, maybe confirmed an email, and now they land inside. If the first thing they see is an empty table with column headers and a faint "No data", they have to guess what to do and what the product is even for.

Compare that with a screen that says what belongs here, why it's useful, and offers one clear button to add the first item. Same product, same data, very different first minute.

It also matters later. Empty states reappear: after a filter returns nothing, after someone clears their inbox, after a search finds no results. The same craft applies each time.

Not all empty states are the same

The most common mistake is treating "nothing here" as a single case. There are at least four, and each needs different copy and a different action.

1. First use

The user hasn't created anything yet. This is the one that needs the most care. Explain what this area is for in a sentence, and make the first action obvious.

2. Cleared or completed

The user did the work: inbox zero, no pending tasks. This is a small moment of success. A calm, short message is enough. Don't push them to "add more" right away.

3. No results

A search or filter found nothing. The user doesn't need a lecture; they need a way out. Say what was searched, and offer to clear filters, change the query, or see everything.

4. Not available yet or no permission

The content exists in principle but this user can't see it, or the data hasn't arrived (an integration is still syncing, say). Say which, and say what will change it. "Nothing here" is misleading when the truth is "still loading" or "ask an admin".

If you build one generic component for all four, the result usually fits none of them.

What a good empty state contains

For the first-use case, a useful structure is short:

  • A plain headline that says what this place is. "Your projects will appear here" beats a clever pun.
  • One line of support on why it's worth filling, ideally in terms of the user's outcome rather than the feature.
  • One primary action that creates the first item. Not three equal buttons.
  • An optional secondary path such as importing existing data, or opening a short guide.
  • Visual structure that hints at the finished screen, so the user can picture what it will look like.

An illustration is optional. If you use one, it should support the message rather than fill the space. A decorative drawing with no action beneath it is still an empty screen.

Show the shape of the finished product

One of the most effective techniques is to make the empty state look a little like the full one. A greyed-out chart outline, a sample row in a table, a preview card. People understand a product faster by seeing its shape than by reading about it.

If you offer sample data, label it clearly as sample data and make it easy to remove. Nothing is worse than a user who can't tell which numbers are theirs.

Write the copy like a person

Empty-state copy is often written last, in a hurry. A few habits help:

  • Say what the user can do, not what's missing. "Add your first customer" over "No customers found".
  • Avoid blame. "You haven't created anything yet" can sound like a telling-off. "Nothing here yet" or a plain statement of purpose is gentler.
  • Keep the button label specific. "Create project" is better than "Get started".
  • Don't use humour as a substitute for guidance. A joke is fine as seasoning, not as the meal.

Don't forget the in-between states

Between "empty" and "full" there's "almost empty." A dashboard with one data point can look broken: a line chart with one dot, an average based on a single entry. Think about what the screen shows at one item, two items, and ten. Often a small tweak, like showing a list instead of a chart until there's enough data, is enough.

Also consider the loading state. A blank white panel that later fills in looks identical to an empty state for a moment. Use a skeleton or a progress hint so people don't read "loading" as "nothing".

A fast review you can do this week

You don't need a redesign to improve this. Try:

  1. Create a brand new account with no data and walk through every main screen.
  2. Write down what each screen asks the user to do. If the answer is "nothing", that's a gap.
  3. Trigger every "no results" path: search for nonsense, apply a filter that matches nothing.
  4. Check what one item looks like in lists and charts.
  5. Check the screens on mobile too. Empty states often break in strange ways on narrow widths.

Fix the first-use screens first. They're seen by every single user.

For the developers on the team

A few small engineering habits make this easier:

  • Keep a "fresh account" seed or script, so anyone can reproduce the empty experience in a minute.
  • Build empty states as part of each feature's definition of done, not as a later polish task.
  • Distinguish loading, empty, error and no-permission as separate states in code. Mixing them is how "nothing here" ends up shown for a failed request.

The short version

  • Empty states are the first thing new users see, so design them deliberately.
  • There are several kinds: first use, cleared, no results, and unavailable. Each needs its own message and action.
  • A good first-use state has a plain headline, a reason, and one clear action.
  • Show the shape of the finished screen, and handle the "one item" case too.
  • Test with a brand new account, regularly.

What does a brand new user see on your product's busiest screen?

title: How I use AI as a solo designer
description:
Things that work well, and things that kind of failed.

I’ve been part of a growing 30+ strong design team for 6 years — a great team with a wide skill set, within a large organization. When AI became popular, Figma Make was the natural thing to try, as it lived within Figma, with a few specks of usage in Gemini and assisted user interviews (Maze), resulting in tiny glimpses of impact. Things changed quite a lot in January, as I’ve decided to take on a new challenge in a B2B e-comm scale-up as a solo UXer.

Suddenly, I faced a wall of work: support features in flight, drive discovery work, improve processes, user research, prototype, set up guidelines…the amount of split focus was scary in the beginning. I did however, see that design had the opportunity to contribute with clarity; to drive a future experience that solves user problems in a more focused way. For that to happen, though, I needed to be able to focus myself. All of this combined with the intriguing launch of Claude Code to Figma, reignited my curiosity about AI.

Prototyping with Claude Code

This works well, dangerously well | Using it almost daily.

To say that anything killed Figma is kind of lazy and silly. It’s not that I care too much about Figma, it’s more about the creative freedom to move an element from A to B in any way I want, directly on a canvas, with no intermediary interaction. Why would I give up drawing digitally with superpowers, or force myself to learn any other tool for this? However, I do think tools like Figma provided underwhelming prototyping capabilities, for far too long. Specialised software came in e.g. Axure, Protopie and excelled within their niche, but led to multi-tool management, had their own constraints and still felt slow at times. This is where AI filled in a gap, for me, especially useful being on my own.

I’ve only built maybe one or two Figma click through prototypes since February. Prototyping with Claude Code enables me to express rich, complex interactions, much much faster. Practically, I often sketch ideas and tons of alternatives on paper, then materialise some of those layouts in Figma, fleshing out multiple states too. For longer, more complex journeys, I rely on FigJam diagrams too. Then I bring it all to life in Claude Code with prompts, focusing on interactions, motion and flows, resulting in a local working prototype, usually as a single .html file. It’s not always in this order, sometimes I skip steps, but it’s always a loop. The .html file is then published online, in a private prototype hub using Figma Make. The truth is always in the live web version. Technically, I can get from one end to another in only a few minutes…which allows me to iterate a lot, in many directions. The number of big or small loops until I get to a good design though… no idea, I always lose count. (Since I’ve started writing this Claude Code just released Artifacts, which I’ll test as a way to publish prototypes).

Overall, it’s been easier for me, devs, PMs, users, pretty much everyone involved in the process of building something, to interact and feel flows instead of imagining how static Figma frames move. Interpretation of how flows connect and behave often led to divergent implementation in the past, so this helped with consistency as well. What I miss in prototyping with AI is tracking relevant variety, as I explore and test. This can happen across an entire flow, on a page layout, or within a tiny component. I need something that enables me to save variation on any level, based on context and hypothesis. To deal with this, I often hide little settings panels to switch variations, but now I’m exploring a lab-like setup to visualise prototype variety on a flow and element level.

There’s a downside to speed, though. In the beginning, I had the tendency to either jump into AI too quickly, or prompt a few too many times focusing on unnecessary details within a single direction, just because I could. Rookie mistake; associating a polished interaction and flow with a good experience. That’s something I noticed happening among the team too, with devs, PMs, others using AI to prototype, but we’ve started keeping each other accountable by going back to goals, research, testing, stepping away from the tool. Overall, given the right control and focus, this is a part of AI that helps me tremendously to build a better product and gives me back extra time to either collect feedback earlier and iterate, or explore alternatives instead of spending it on tooling.

Usability testing

This works well | Using it a lot

A critical point of usability testing is to give people a scenario and a clear task to be completed, then step away and shut up; let them voice their thoughts and observe what they do. The more you interrupt with “sorry, this doesn’t work; it’s just a prototype…oh…that doesn’t work either”, the less likely you are to capture a full end-to-end experience. For me, turning concepts into fully working prototypes enabled exactly this: back up and observe. Being a B2B back-end ecommerce tool, UIs and flows can get quite complex, especially when tables are at the core. Having the possibility to express a lot of depth lets participants try different pathways to achieve their goal, which in turn enabled me and the team to learn more about their mental models. There are still dead ends and not all states are covered, but prototyping with AI has given me the chance to be intentional in this aspect too. Questions as “what did you expect to happen” are now focused on parts of the experience that I truly wish to learn about, not a consequence of tooling constraints.

Adjusting context for each session and carrying data across a flow become way easier too. We’re working with different kinds of companies selling all sorts of things, from electronics to fashion. Now, as late as 15 min before a session starts, I just tell Claude “change products in this prototype to be about electronics” and it’s done. This level of nuance and detail brings a natural feeling into the research session. When it comes to carrying data over, since flows are complex, it’s important to reflect real values, sometimes created by the user, e.g., setting a product’s price, selecting a certain number of products to publish, etc. When these values don’t match across the flow, it tends to distract some participants, once again interrupting their experience.

User research synthesis

This works well | Using it biweekly

I had the chance to study different ways of coding user research, mostly within academia; it was pure research done without chasing economic impact for a product; quite refreshing to do once in a while. In a nutshell, coding is analyzing your research by going back through documentation such as recordings, notes, diaries, etc., and highlighting findings to eventually extract common themes. Handling all this data requires a lot of mental effort, but leads to a deep connection and understanding of users, while reflecting on the quality of your own method. However, realistically, I can’t spend a week analyzing interviews or testing sessions, creating video clips, documenting, and presenting it all as well…as much as I love doing this detective kind of work.

Therefore, I’ve been experimenting with different degrees of AI usage when synthesizing data and I’ve noticed something. Let’s say I conduct a series of 8 user interviews and discover a bunch of problems with a feature across all sessions. Since everything is recorded in Google Meet, I then ask Gemini to merge all sessions and extract common themes, quotes, and action points. This is lightning fast. However, a couple of weeks in, I recall very few of these findings, having to constantly go back to double-check what they meant. On top of that, a lot of nuance is getting lost in AI’s own interpretation and writing style. It all becomes a bit too generic or even worse, insights get skewed with words and expressions participants never used(often even when guided not to do this). The less I handle the insights myself, the less they get embedded into my design mind. I feel less confident in early design decisions, diminishing my ability to advocate for them among stakeholders.

It would be foolish to just ignore the huge advantage of speed. Currently, I use Gemini to summarise individual interviews, but also write down timestamps during the session to know which parts to rewatch, turn into clips to be shared with the team, and extract genuine quotes. Having another person join to take notes and observe helps too. I then take all the summaries and run them through AI just like before, but don’t use the outcome directly. I treat AI as a super text editor, mostly useful to validate occurrences of words and expressions, within large amounts of input. Now, I rely on those key timeframes, myself and the note taker to really form common themes and capture nuance instead. Usually, a couple of weeks later, I also force myself to go through a couple of sessions to get reconnected to participants. For now this feels like a good balance of speed and quality. It gives me back time that I use to phrase and share insights, or to run more research.

New visual directions

This was meh.. | Tried a couple of times only

Part of improving the current experience is a refreshed interface. The product’s functionality has grown over the years, but the UI hasn’t always kept this pace, so it was time to present all that power and data more clearly. It’s an interesting exercise, trying to capture enough of the product scope to understand core user problems without being trapped in too many edge cases and constraints. My instinct said that we needed something clear, bear bones that lets the content shine, while leveraging a few playful elements used in external materials. Nevertheless, it’s the kind of activity that requires a lot of mental space; and something that I’ve never done without a design team around. Comparing perspectives born from a similar affinity of solving other people’s problems has always been a really fun part of the process for me. That’s how I hoped to use AI too; to fill in this gap, and to have a fellow (junior?) designer next to me.

I was also hoping there was a big enough pool of training data to make AI work well for these types of elements our product mostly consists of (data dashboards, graphs, complex tables, and product cards). I was mostly looking for diversity in visual expression both in interfaces and interactions in core steps of the product. I’ve never expected end-to-end flows and perfectly tweaked screens to just pick up. Practically, I’ve tried Figma Make, Claude Code in Figma, Claude Design, and Google Stitch and I’ve been feeding them different kinds of contexts, data and prompts to get diversity in outcome.

The interesting takes, mostly from Claude Design and Google Stitch were getting a bit far from the brief, but in a fun way, sparking a few thoughts. Some of these turned into ideas for functionality that might or might not lead to anything, or made me wonder about details as typography scales, spacing, and elevation. Many results simply validated directions I didn’t want to take, being impractical or way too expressive, which is valuable in a way. Sadly, nothing was solid enough to inspire me to chase an entirely new direction and AI didn’t come close to being a sparring partner; it lacked the depth I was looking for, and overall like it went literally out of the box without a real purpose; the kind of quick and dirty exploration you’d do in between meetings, or Friday afternoon, that you look back at later “hmm… what was I thinking…”

To be fair, I do think that if one spends more time to iterate on guiding the AI, perhaps feeding it a more precise combination of inputs and skills, you could probably get better results. I’m saying this as things are evolving fast, and also after seeing skills like this take one, an attempt at applying Nothing’s visual style to dashboard UIs.

UX feedback skill

This works well | In trial for adoption

User research in the B2B space is quite different from research for B2C products, where I used to have quick access to a large panel of users within tools, agencies, or by simply walking outside... Even with the help of customer facing teams, reaching specific users takes time and effort — making it challenging to plan research around sprints for multiple initiatives. What if, while I empower others to run research, we use AI as a first round of user feedback? Felt so wrong to even consider this…since I’ve been trained to do the exact opposite — spend less time behind the laptop and expose the company to our users’ emotions and stories. After talking to a few other designers, and reading about companies as Synthetic users, I’ve started experimenting.

My goal was to create a UX feedback AI based skill that we can all use, to improve our work. The skill had to be aware of our business, be knowledgeable of our UX guidelines and be aware of users’ core goals and pain points. After trying a few overly complex set ups, among which was inevitably creating my own new shiny SaaS… I ended up with a skill in our repo. There were two things I’ve tweaked the most:

  • getting the skill to ask the right questions upfront to force people to reflect on the problem they’re solving.
  • providing the user perspective without extra interpretation.

The user perspective is already surprisingly good. It analyses the context of the prompt, then replies with how different users might react to the given solution, idea, etc. It does a good job of raising pain points and whether they are addressed across different kinds of interests people have. It’s not as good at providing specific usability feedback, besides the obvious stuff. AI reduces these user portraits to lines of text, ignoring all the other context they’ve built by using this and other software. This leads to some of the suggestions being overzealous, trying to explain every element through text and icons.

Product owners were the first to try out this part of the skill, to either help with setting a direction for tricky flows, or get more perspectives on a solution they’ve had in mind. In most cases, they brought the outcome of their session back to me and we continued the discussion. I was mostly surprised to see how often they also asked the skill to visualise its output, for them.

The skill also checks UI pattern usage against our guidelines and components. I underestimated this initially, but then noticed how front-end engineers got excited while demo-ing it. As our goal is to become much more consistent in the interface, the skill easily catches unnecessary deviations and provides recommendations pointing to relevant guidelines and elements. Front-end engineers could get immediate feedback on their work, instead of only manually checking guidelines. We didn’t try the full loop yet, as I’m tweaking the guidelines and the skill, but I think there’s something here that will lead to increased efficiency.

Ultimately, it’s not about replacing user research because it’s not as easy to get to people; we’re doing that anyway; it’s about catching critical misjudgments early on in the process.

Gathering context

There are quite a few people within the organisation playing around with different AIs, to become more efficient. One of these is centralising context, starting with documentation across our tooling, using Atlassian’s Rovo agents. These have been quite useful for me, as a newcomer to a very technical company, as I must prioritise impact on users’ experience.

Instead of digging through dozens of pages and boards, while throwing tons of basic questions at a team, I first ask different Rovo agents to collect context. A few prompts and some reading later, I have a basic understanding of a concept and when things get too technical, I ask them to simplify it using metaphors and analogies. In the end, this enables me to get in and out of topics much more efficiently, leaving more time to discuss what the real issues are to be solved, and what should be improved next. Lately, as these tools have been connected with other parts of the organisation, as support, we can tap into a great deal of evidence when collecting context and help steer the conversation better. I’d love to create some kind of mega shared context that eventually combines multiple data systems and our own skills or agents, working together. When someone wants to jump right into prompting solutions, or tends to have a single path to solving a problem, this shared context (tool?) would know which core issues to raise, with clear evidence, and push them to understand the problem first.

Conclusion

Useful overall, definitely not an extra designer, at least not yet.

It took me around 3 months to get comfortable with the shocking speed of AI, trying out new tools and new ways of working. When it comes to what’s being said nowadays about roles becoming more fluid within the design, engineering and product trio, I have mixed feelings. The best teams I’ve been in, had people who were always curious to understand how the others work, while trusting each other’s expertise. I must admit that using a shared tool does bring us a little closer. Can we really pour our expertise into these tools, so that others can genuinely step into our roles? Not sure yet. As a solo designer, AI hasn’t necessarily given me extra hands, but it has given me a lot of time back: time to test earlier, explore more alternatives, and frame problems better, together with the team.

Inspiration and further reading

I spent two months building an AI workflow for my design team. Here’s what I actually learned.

AI design isn’t ugly. It’s fluent — and that’s the problem.

Are synthetic users (really) the future of UX research?

Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents: Same Conclusion, Less Variation

Humans + machine: responsible AI workflows for UX research

Vibe prototyping is a double edged sword

The design engineer symptom: what a rising job title reveals

The User Experience Team of One (book)

How I use AI as a solo designer was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: October 27, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

  • The ai.extract function lets you extract structured data from unstructured text directly within your database queries without needing external extraction pipelines. For more information, see Extract structured data.

  • The ai.classify function lets you categorize unstructured text into predefined labels directly within your database queries. For more information, see Classify text.

  • Parameter names and signatures for AI query engine functions (ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, and ai.agg_summarize) are updated. For more information, see Model endpoint reference.

    • The prompt and prompts parameters are renamed to input and inputs in scalar and batch functions respectively.

    • An optional additional_instructions parameter is added to ai.summarize and ai.agg_summarize to provide custom instructions to guide summary formatting, length, and tone.

    • In cursor-based versions of ai.analyze_sentiment and ai.summarize, the prompt parameter is removed.

    • ai.agg_summarize supports multiple positional signatures, including passing optional additional instructions and specifying model IDs.

Apigee X

Feature

The Apigee API Health & Availability dashboard is now generally available in Cloud Monitoring to help you monitor the health, performance, and availability of your Apigee API proxies in real time:

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Apache Avro schema bundles to query individual fields within Avro records stored as serialized bytes in Bigtable. You can query your Avro data using GoogleSQL for Bigtable, continuous materialized views, and logical views. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Regular expression URL rewrites (regexRewrite) for route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA) for Application Load Balancers. You can use regular expression pattern rewrite actions to rewrite URL paths by substituting or removing URL path components before forwarding requests to your backends.

This feature is available in:

  • Global external Application Load Balancers

  • Regional external Application Load Balancers

  • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers

  • Regional internal Application Load Balancers

For more information, see Regular expression URL rewrites for route rules.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports configuring direct access ports on workstation clusters in Preview. Direct access ports let you connect directly to a workstation port using the standard https://WORKSTATION_NAME.CLUSTER_ID.cloudworkstations.dev:PORT URL format instead of encoding the port as a prefix in the URL.

To set direct access ports, use the --direct-access-ports flag with the gcloud beta workstations clusters create and gcloud beta workstations clusters update commands—for example, --direct-access-ports=80,8080.

Config Connector

Announcement

Config Connector version 1.160.0 is now available.

Feature

New Alpha Resources (Direct Reconciler):

  • CCInsightsAnalysisRule

    • Manage Customer Experience Insights analysis rules to define rules for analyzing conversational data.

  • ConfigDeploymentGroup

    • Manage Infrastructure Manager deployment groups to orchestrate and manage deployments collectively.

  • DataLineageProcess

    • Manage Knowledge Catalog data lineage processes to track data origin and movement.

  • DataplexDataProduct

    • Manage Knowledge Catalog data products to package and share data assets across an enterprise.

  • DialogflowKnowledgeBase

    • Manage Dialogflow ES knowledge bases to provide FAQs and articles for agent answers.

  • DiscoveryEngineSchema

    • Manage Agent Search schemas to define document structures and schemas for data stores.

  • DiscoveryEngineSession

    • Manage Agent Search sessions to maintain conversation context and history for search and recommendations.

  • DiscoveryEngineSitemap

    • Manage Agent Search sitemaps to crawl web pages for search data stores.

  • ManagedKafkaConnectCluster

    • Manage Managed Service for Apache Kafka Connect clusters to run connectors that integrate Apache Kafka with Google Cloud and external systems.

  • MigrationCenterPreferenceSet

    • Manage Migration Center preference sets to specify migration preferences and target cloud architecture assumptions.

  • MigrationCenterSource

    • Manage Migration Center sources to configure data sources for importing asset data.

  • NetAppActiveDirectory

    • Manage NetApp Volumes Active Directory configurations to enable SMB and NFS domain-joined authentication.

  • NetAppHostGroup

    • Manage NetApp Volumes host groups to group client hosts for volume access.

  • NetworkConnectivityTransport

    • Manage Network Connectivity transports for connecting network endpoints.

  • NetworkSecurityMirroringEndpointGroupAssociation

    • Manage Network Security Integration mirroring endpoint group associations to associate packet mirroring endpoint groups with Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.

  • NetworkServicesLBEdgeExtension

    • Manage Service Extensions load balancing edge extensions to customize Cloud CDN and edge proxy traffic processing.

  • NetworkServicesLBTrafficExtension

    • Manage Service Extensions load balancing traffic extensions to customize request and response processing in Application Load Balancers.

  • NetworkServicesServiceLBPolicy

    • Manage Cloud Service Mesh service load balancing policies to configure fine-grained traffic distribution across backend services.

  • SaaSServiceMgmtUnit

    • Manage App Lifecycle Manager units to manage SaaS deployment units.

  • StorageInsightsReportConfig

    • Manage Storage Insights report configurations to generate inventory and audit reports for Cloud Storage buckets.

  • WorkloadManagerEvaluation

    • Manage Workload Manager evaluations to scan and evaluate workloads against best-practice rules.

Feature

New Fields:

  • BigtableTable

    • Added support for spec.columnFamily[].type.

  • MemorystoreInstance

    • Added support for spec.gcsSource.

  • MonitoringDashboard

    • Added support for timeSeriesQuery.opsAnalyticsQuery in dashboard widgets.

Feature

New Features:

  • Added support for a configurable maximum exponential backoff delay ceiling and retry halting for direct controllers by using the cnrm.cloud.google.com/backoff-max-delay-in-seconds annotation.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: VPC connectivity and static IP egress for custom MCP servers

You can configure Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity for custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) server data stores by routing outbound tool traffic through Agent Gateway (supported in us-central1 and europe-west1). You can host private MCP servers inside your VPC network by using Private Service Connect (PSC) network attachments and agent connectivity templates. You can also route traffic to public MCP servers through Cloud NAT with static external IP addresses for strict IP allowlists.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see:

  • Prerequisites to set up a custom MCP server data store with VPC connectivity
  • Set up your custom MCP server data store

Cloud Armor supports advanced match conditions to include attributes for inspecting request body content and parameters. Google Cloud VMware Engine

Feature

VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available (GA). VMware solution lets you deploy, configure, and manage VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated bare-metal Compute Engine instances within your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network under a Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model.

Key features include the following:

  • Provision dedicated bare-metal ESXi nodes (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal) directly in your project with deletion protection and Local SSD storage for vSAN.
  • Automate node preparation, Secret Manager credential storage, vSwitch and Dynamic NIC networking, Cloud DNS zone and record synchronization, vSAN storage initialization, and VCF installer appliance deployment by using Terraform and the VMware solution toolkit.
  • Distribute nodes across isolated availability domains by using spread placement policies to align with vSAN fault domains for high availability.
  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.

  • 1.34.300-gke.59
  • 1.35.0-gke.525

  • 1.35.300-gke.87 and later 1.35 patch versions

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

API Gateway

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

Streaming gateways can now call Google Cloud APIs such as aiplatform.googleapis.com. A gateway with an effectiveStreamingMode of EFFECTIVE_STREAMING_MODE_ENABLED authenticates to backends whose host ends in .googleapis.com or .vertexai.goog with an access token for the gateway's service account. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. New ApigeeValkey custom resource

Apigee hybrid v1.15.10 adds the ApigeeValkey custom resource definition (CRD), the apigee-valkey Helm chart, and the valkey configuration properties. ApigeeValkey is the replacement for the ApigeeRedis resource.

In version 1.15.10, the runtime continues to use ApigeeRedis. When you upgrade, install the new CRD with the other CRDs. Leave the new ao.args.valkeyBackend property set to its default value, false. You don't need to install the apigee-valkey chart or change your configuration.

For the supported upgrade sequence, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid. For more information about the resource, see Kubernetes resources.

  • 15.18 is upgraded to 15.19.

  • 16.14 is upgraded to 16.15.

  • 17.10 is upgraded to 17.11.

  • 18.4 is upgraded to 18.6. This version includes a backported fix for PostgreSQL bug #19616 that prevents logical decoding from emitting STREAM_ABORT messages for unstreamed transactions when an aborted transaction with a subtransaction is truncated during memory eviction.

This release also exposes the wait_for_pods_ready configuration for Kueue in the kubectl-apply module and sets the recovery_timeout field to 0s by default for Pathways workloads.

Gemini Enterprise: End of Gemini Code Assist entitlement for existing subscriptions

Bundled Gemini Code Assist entitlements for existing Gemini Enterprise Standard and Gemini Enterprise Plus subscriptions will end on March 31, 2027. Gemini Notebook Enterprise: Updated web addresses

The URL path for the Gemini Notebook Enterprise web app is changing in two ways. In both cases, existing links redirect automatically.

"go/" added: Starting immediately, go/ is being added to the URL path:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/
    changes to
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/.

  • For Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise,
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/global/
    changes to
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/go/global/.

The dates for this go/ path change are as follows:

Region Rollout date
global and us Live
eu Rolling out
All other locations Starting November 9, 2026

"lm" removed: Starting November 16, 2026, lm is being removed from the hostname:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Google Identity,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.com.

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Workforce Identity Federation,
    notebooklm.cloud.google
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.

Action is required: if your organization uses a firewall, proxy, or secure web gateway that allows access to Gemini Notebook by a specific URL path. If this applies to you, Google recommends that you add the following URLs to your allowlist:

  1. Allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google.com/* and notebook.cloud.google.com/*

  2. If you use Workforce Identity Federation, allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google/* and notebook.cloud.google/*

  3. If you use Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise, allowlist vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/*.

Google recommends allowing entire domains (/*) so that future path changes don't require additional updates.

If you don't allow /*, you must allow both /REGION and /go/REGION, where REGION is your location value: global, us, eu, asia-northeast1, au, ca, de, europe-west2, in, kr, or sg. For example, notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/ and notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/

Temporary workaround: If your firewall blocks users before you update your allowlist, users themselves can access the original URLs by removing /go from the URL and adding version=legacy. For example: notebooklm.cloud.google.com/eu/?project=1234567&version=legacy. This fix will fail when Google sunsets the legacy version.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where abandoned queue records incorrectly calculated wait times from the call's initial queue entry rather than the time the caller entered the specific queue they abandoned from.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter header title on SmartActions and virtual task assistant screens was truncated with an ellipsis, preventing users from viewing the full text.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter froze on Calling and didn't dial the customer during recovery calls following an unanswered in-app call.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls became unroutable and remained stuck in the queue until abandoned if an agent's browser delivered a delayed connection request after a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue in the CCaaS portal where active Spanish IVR queues were incorrectly displayed as Setup is required and grayed out when switching languages from English to Spanish.

  • Fixed an issue where transient network errors during platform validation incorrectly marked virtual agent credentials as invalid.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS and WhatsApp virtual agent chats became unresponsive and didn't escalate to a human agent when encountering a custom payload validation error.

  • Fixed an issue where campaigns didn't resume after being paused, resulting in repeated call session failures and missing participant information.

  • Fixed an issue where call-related actions such as disconnecting or updating status took up to 72 seconds to complete.

  • Fixed an issue where a Not Found banner incorrectly appeared in the call adapter when a phone number couldn't be matched in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where the In-email status bar in the agent desktop appeared white.

  • Fixed an issue where agents in the In-email status couldn't change their status directly from the status bar.

  • Fixed an issue where the first letter of uppercase acronym field names was incorrectly lowercased in virtual task assistant input placeholders.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly set to an Unresponsive status instead of receiving a missed call when a new deltacast offer arrived while the call adapter was already ringing.

  • Fixed an issue where agents became stuck in a projected state and stopped receiving calls after a caller abandoned the call at the moment of routing.

  • Fixed an issue where transient carrier timeouts during outbound callbacks were incorrectly classified as invalid numbers.

  • Fixed an issue where forced virtual agent callbacks booked through the Apps API were incorrectly routed to the original call's queue instead of the requested destination.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback capacity was under-calculated due to a mathematical rounding error.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls were prematurely disconnected if the initial connection request timed out and was retried.

  • Fixed an issue where valid Canadian phone numbers using newer area codes were rejected by the Callback call API.

  • Fixed an issue where certain agents were missing from the directory during outbound calls, preventing other agents from transferring calls or adding them to a call.

  • Fixed an issue where dynamic queues incorrectly offered a minimum of one slot even when WFM staffing was zero or resulted in less than one available slot.

  • Fixed an issue where Dynamic Agent Availability queues were saved without a required custom queue identifier, causing workforce management synchronization to fail silently.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce cases and contacts were incorrectly created for voice calls handled entirely by a virtual agent, even when the Create CRM records for calls attended by Virtual Agents setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where voice transfers addressed to a specific agent were never offered to the target and didn't expire, leaving callers on hold indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where NICE WFM session data exports didn't generate for instances with subdomains exceeding 20 characters.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual callbacks routed through external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) were missing captured virtual agent custom parameters, causing routing engines to lose the caller's intent.

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist transcriptions permanently stopped following transient network or quota errors.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound phone number restriction rules weren't applied to agents with the Allow unrestricted international calling setting enabled.

title: November 09, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now support function calling

The SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now handle LLM function calling (tool use) flows. Two new optional XML elements extract function calling content for Model Armor sanitization:

  • <FunctionResponseSource> in SanitizeUserPrompt: extracts function/tool response data from user turns. Used as a fallback when <UserPromptSource> returns empty on function calling turns.
  • <FunctionCallSource> in SanitizeModelResponse: extracts function call arguments from model responses. Used as a fallback when <LLMResponseSource> returns empty.

Default templates target the Gemini format and require no additional configuration. For OpenAI and Anthropic formats, configure custom JSONPath templates. For more information, see FunctionResponseSource and FunctionCallSource.

575563262 Updated the Google Cloud client library stack to match Apigee hybrid 1.17 (protobuf 4.x, gRPC 1.82, GAX 2.83, Guava 33.5). With this update: (1) a malformed inbound gRPC request frame is now reported to the client as grpc-status INTERNAL (13) and recorded in analytics as x-apigee.grpc.status=13, instead of an Apigee ServiceUnavailable fault (UNAVAILABLE, 14) with no x-apigee.grpc.status; (2) an ExternalCallout policy whose Google service account does not exist now fails with gRPC UNAUTHENTICATED (16) instead of UNAVAILABLE (14); and (3) Gson parse-error messages, such as in proxy validation errors, now end with a link to Gson's troubleshooting guide.
572875915 Fixed an issue where the apigee-env Helm chart and Apigee operator ignored the synchronizer pollInterval configuration (synchronizer.pollInterval, envs[].pollInterval, and envs[].components.synchronizer.pollInterval); configured values now take effect, and values below 60 seconds are raised to 60.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Carbon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-carbon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

Feature

Govern agents on any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster with Agent Gateway for cross-cloud (Limited Preview)

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available in Limited Preview. It extends Agent Platform governance to agents that run on Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes clusters outside of Google Cloud, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Red Hat OpenShift, and bare-metal clusters. Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

For more information, see Set up Agent Gateway for cross-cloud.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.
