Together, these capabilities can make AI-assisted engineering more structured.

But they're not a substitute for engineering judgment.

A bad requirement can still produce a bad implementation.

An incorrect architectural assumption can still cause problems.

Tests can still miss important cases.

And an AI-generated fix can still introduce regressions.

That's why I increasingly believe the developer's job is not just to tell AI what to build, but to design the conditions under which its work can be trusted.

Don't Measure AI Development Only by Speed

Imagine two developers using Claude.

Developer A generates a feature in 10 minutes.

Developer B takes 30 minutes to clarify the requirement, review the architecture, implement the feature, and run verification.

Who is more productive?

We can't answer that from the time taken alone.

What if Developer A's feature introduces a production bug?

What if Developer B's implementation is easier to maintain?

What if both implementations are equally good?

We need to measure the outcomes, not simply the speed of code generation.

This is a principle I also emphasize in my work at ReThynk AI: AI evaluation should consider the quality, reliability, and value of the complete workflow, not merely whether the underlying model produced an output.

For teams looking beyond individual coding tricks, our AI Evaluation Framework: 7 Critical Metrics for AI Success explores how to think more systematically about assessing AI performance.

Because the goal isn't to make developers type fewer characters.

The goal is to help them build better software.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • What's the difference between Claude and Claude Code?

Claude is Anthropic's AI assistant, which can help with programming questions, code explanations, and other tasks through a conversational interface.

Claude Code is designed for development workflows and can interact with project files, execute supported commands, and use development tools with configured permissions.

Several techniques in this article, such as CLAUDE.md, Plan Mode, and hooks, specifically refer to Claude Code.

  • Which Claude trick should a beginner try first?

I would start with Plan Mode.

Before asking Claude to build something, ask it to examine your requirements, identify assumptions, and propose a simple implementation plan.

Then add a clear way to verify the result.

You don't need complicated agent architectures to benefit from structured AI-assisted development.

  • Can Claude Code replace human code review?

I wouldn't treat it as a complete replacement.

Claude can help identify suspicious logic, missing tests, and potential maintainability issues.

But it may misunderstand requirements, overlook vulnerabilities, or recommend unnecessary changes.

Human review and appropriate automated testing remain essential, especially for security-sensitive and high-impact systems.

Final Thoughts

I think we're entering an interesting stage of software development.

Knowing how to ask AI to write a function is becoming commonplace.

The bigger opportunity is learning how to make AI useful across the entire engineering workflow.

Not by adding as many tools and agents as possible.

But by creating better context, clearer boundaries, stronger verification, and simpler processes.

The best Claude trick isn't a secret command.

It's knowing how to turn AI assistance into a reliable engineering practice.

And that's a skill worth developing.

title: How I built my own OS
description:
I run my own operating system now. Not a fork with a new wallpaper and a different logo in the about screen. A whole desktop, with its own settings app, its own CLI, its own theme engine, its own bar plugins, its own boot animation, its own project manager and its own editor. It's called CLOUDWERX OS, I use it all day every day, and it's the most fun I've had with a computer since I was a kid.

This is how I got here. It's a long one, so grab a coffee. Or something stronger, it's your life.

It started with a BBS

I was 12 when I ran my own BBS in DOS. It was called Burning in Hell BBS, because I was 12 and that was the most metal name I could think of. It ran on Oblivion/2 (OBV/2 if you're cool), and yes, people actually dialed in. A phone line, a modem screaming at another modem, and some kid's cursed ANSI art. That was my first taste of running something that other people used, and I was hooked immediately.

After DOS came Windows 3.1, and I stayed on Windows basically forever. I got into computers right away and I've been obsessed ever since. I started working professionally at 19 as a bench tech, and then I worked my way through pretty much every corner of the industry. Refresh and imaging, support as an IT Analyst, field services, cloud migrations for a large financial firm, O365 support, and a pile of smaller, weirder roles that don't fit on a resume without a footnote.

Somewhere in there I tried Linux. Many, many times. I'd learn a little bash here, a little something there, get excited, and then hit the wall. Hardware wouldn't work, wifi wouldn't connect, some driver wanted a ritual sacrifice. Eventually I'd pull my hair out and run straight back to the sweet, sickly embrace of Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer.

The funny part is I always knew I was in a prison of my own choosing. A pretty limited one. I just had no idea how free the people on the other side actually were.

Three years ago, something changed

About 3 years ago I realized I could use ChatGPT to get through the growing pains. That was the missing piece. All the stuff that used to make me quit (the 2am "why is there a black screen" problems) suddenly had a patient teacher sitting next to me.

Here's the part I don't talk about much. I have severe ADD, and it did me no favors when it came to learning Linux. Or coding. Coding always felt like it was on another planet, because I could never get through a damn book. I'd read the same page four times and nothing would stick. I bought the books, I really did. They made nice shelf decorations.

What changed was having something I could just talk to. I could ask the dumb question, ask it again in a different way, get an answer that fit the exact thing I was staring at, and keep moving. That's how I learn, it turns out. In the last 3 years I've learned more than in the 20 before it, and I'm not exaggerating even a little.

The moment I knew it was working was when I updated my kernel and then couldn't log into my computer. Old me would've reinstalled Windows by sunrise. New me got dropped into a tty with ChatGPT in my ear and fixed the whole thing. I didn't quit. I never went back after that.

I landed on Linux Mint and loved it for the first few years. Then Claude Code came out and something clicked that I'm still thinking about. I could run agents in my terminal.

The terminal is really the key to this whole story, so let me explain why. You can do everything from it. Want to move your mouse cursor? Done. Edit a file? sed. Compare and combine files? Easy. Shell scripting, cron jobs, systemd timers? Now you're cooking with gas. It came slowly, and then one day it was just there: I'm free to tear things apart and rebuild them. The source is open and sitting out in the world. I can mix and match, redesign, and make things exactly how I want them.

Niri broke my brain (in a good way)

A few months ago I installed CachyOS and gave Niri a shot. Niri BLEW MY MIND. If you haven't seen it, it's a scrolling tiling Wayland compositor, and it was like someone read my mind about everything I hated in floating window managers and fixed all of it. Windows live on an infinite strip. You scroll. That's it. I've never wanted to go back.

Then I tried Quickshell, which lets you build your whole shell (bars, panels, launchers, lock screens) in QML, and boom. This was what I'd been looking for my whole life without knowing it.

Omarchy had just come out around then, and after poking at it for a bit I had the same thought I think DHH must've had. I can build my own desktop environment, exactly how I want it.

So I did.

What CLOUDWERX OS actually is

It's a keyboard first desktop on CachyOS, niri and Quickshell. I used the best models I could get to help me write the code, and I brought my own design and UX instincts, and it came together faster than I believed it could. I've shipped countless projects over the years and none of them has been as much fun as this one.

It's smart, it's sexy, it's capable, and most of all it's free.

Here's the tour.

The CLI is the heart

There's a Rust binary called cloudwerx and it's the stable API for the whole machine. Everything goes through it. Themes, wallpapers, volume, snapshots, tailscale, tasks, the project manager, the editor, the radio. Fifty something commands and every one of them has --json, so scripts and agents can drive the desktop the same way I do.

cloudwerx theme set tokyo-night
cloudwerx wallpaper next
cloudwerx fx set koi-pond
cloudwerx doctor

That last one checks the entire install and tells you how to fix whatever it finds. I built it because I knew I'd break things at 1am. I was right.

The settings app covers everything

Holy shit, does this cover everything. It's a native GTK4 app with a left rail that groups every page into ten categories, and there's a page for basically every part of the machine. Lock screen, login screen, boot logo, desktop FX, keyboard shortcuts, app rules, startup apps, Tailscale, firewall, SSH and file sharing, disks, power, updates, and on and on. Search works with normal words, so typing "wifi" or "dark mode" lands you on the right page.

All of my servers sit behind Tailscale and get managed from here. My security camera, Noteism, the snipping tool, TaskPass, Hangar, a Herdr app that's been customized into something freakish. They all have a home in this one window.

Here's a few more pages, because I'm proud of them.

Themes, and the part that still makes me grin

I have 69 themes. They don't just change the colors of my windows. One command re-renders dozens of apps at the same time: niri's focus ring, the terminal, GTK, Qt, the editor, the browsers, btop, fzf, the shell, all of it. Then the shell cross fades and a transition shader plays over the whole screen while it happens. You can pick Ink bloom, Melt, Shatter, Scanline, Prism, whatever, or let it roll the dice. It can even start the effect from wherever you clicked.

Here's the theme switcher running through a few of them. This is a real recording of my real desktop, with a terminal and the settings app open so you can watch everything change at once.

Most of the GIFs in this post are a lot slower then reality, just a warning.

And it can build a theme out of a wallpaper. It grabs the prominent colors from the image, makes a full palette, and applies it everywhere right after the transition. It works on video wallpapers too. It takes the first frame, pulls the colors from that, and builds the whole theme around it. I thought that was genius when I came up with it and I still do.

Wallpapers get the same treatment

Same shader engine, same transitions, a switcher panel along the bottom of the screen. Wave, drop, curtain, bloom and a lot more. Here it is cycling through a few.

Desktop FX, aka the part I should've been doing something productive instead of building

I have shaders playing on my desktop, between the wallpaper and my windows. There are 34 of them. Aurora, koi pond, meteor showers, rain on glass, a synthwave horizon. They stop drawing completely when a window covers the screen, so they don't cook the battery. Some of them react to music. Oh yeah and they double as screensavers too.

And then there's Littlewick.

I made an entire pixel art village simulation that runs on my desktop. It's a little town called Applebrook with a clock tower, a bakery, a school, a clinic, an inn, 36 folks wandering around, and a Christmas tree in the middle of the square (it is Nov 27th afterall!). It's synced to my computer's time and date and to my weather widget, so when it rains here, it rains there. Today was Thanksgiving and the whole town was celebrating with a feast.

I realize I built a tiny town to live behind my terminal. I'm fine with it. Don't @ me.

There are also audio reactive effects. Spectrograms and skylines that dance to whatever's playing, and what's playing is usually the Radio panel, my own internet radio player. It searches hundreds of thousands of stations, and you can sort them, search them and like them.

The boot logo

Even the boot screen is mine. It's a Plymouth theme, built from a page in Settings, with a comet of light that runs around the ring, goes behind the cloud and comes out the other side, plus a breathing halo and a shimmer. When startup finishes there's a finale flare. These are the actual frames the system plays on boot.

The login screen and the lock screen are customized too.

And if you type a wrong password, my camera takes a picture of whoever did it so I can look at their face later. It's off by default, because I'm not a monster, but I turned it on. I keep the photos. For science.

Bar plugins are one of my favorite things

I took what Omarchy did and ran with it. The bar is built out of plugins, and so is basically everything else. Each island, each panel, each picker, each background service. I've made dozens of my own now, and they connect everything together. There's a launcher that searches apps, files, the words inside files and even files by meaning. There's a clipboard history, a time panel, a planner with a Pomodoro, a tray, a sysmon, and a couple of islands I'm not totally sure I'll ever explain to anyone.

Omarchy plugins run on it too, unmodified.

Sixteen bar styles

The bar isn't one look. It has sixteen styles and you flip between them live with Super+Alt+Shift+B or cloudwerx bar style next. Floating islands, one floating panel, a full width edge, a molded edge where the screen corners curve in under it, corner pods, hanging tabs, a liquid band that swells into each group of islands, a screen frame, powerline segments, minimal, capsules, a hanging bar, scrim, zone pills, a compact pill like a dynamic island, and an outline. Here's the whole lineup, and the recording cycles through them.

Panels that earn their spot

Every island on the bar can open a panel, and I went a little overboard on a few of them.

The clock is a good example. Click it and you get a big readout, a month calendar with your events and reminders, timers with presets and progress rings, alarms with repeat days and a stopwatch with laps. The rings keep running and still go off with Snooze and Stop buttons even when the panel is closed. Tasks from the planner show up in there too, so the calendar is the one place I look to see what the rest of my week wants from me.

The control center holds the volume, mic and brightness sliders, the toggles (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, focus, night light, power profile, caffeine, tablet mode, recording, Tailscale and exit nodes), the weather card with an hourly strip, and the notifications at the bottom. Notifications are my own daemon, so there's no second one fighting it, and there's a Do Not Disturb you can flip from the bell with a right click.

I blurred my face, my Wi-Fi name, my Tailscale IP and my city in this one. The notifications are test ones I fired off with notify-send, because I'm not putting my real messages in a blog post.

Thirty five ways to open a panel

Panels don't just appear. Every panel in the shell (clock, control center, launcher, agents, radio, all of it) opens with the same animation engine, and there are 35 presets to choose from. Smooth glide is the original and my default. Then there's spring, liquid pour where the panel stretches out of the island you clicked, flap, drop and bounce, jelly, cinematic, a bunch of Material 3 ones, and some I borrowed ideas for from other Quickshell shells I was reading through. Super+Alt+Shift+M cycles them live, and Settings › Panels & Motion has a gallery where every card plays on hover so you can see the real motion before you pick it. There's an editor for your own too, with curve plots (expo, cubic, back, elastic, bounce).

Here are ten of them opening the clock panel, one after another.

Window shaders in niri

This one makes me laugh every time. niri lets you write a GLSL shader for how a window opens and closes, so I bundled a whole shelf of them. There's the niri shader collection (fades, slides, scales, ribbons, masks, noise, burn, honeycomb) and 13 Window FX shaders: ember, dissolve, pixel, shatter, melt, glitch, tube off, snow, scan, code rain, swirl, squares and blinds. Pick them in Settings › Niri Compositor › Individual animations, separately for open and close. If a shader fails to compile, niri falls back to the default and tells you in the journal, so you can't brick your windows.

Mine is code rain. Here are a few of the others opening and closing a terminal.

Search, and why I'm a little obsessed with it

This is the feature I'd miss most if you took it away. You hit Super+Space, start typing, and it finds a file anywhere on the computer in a few milliseconds. By name, by the words inside it, or by what it's about even if you can't remember a single word from it.

Right now my machine has 13,973,978 items in the name index, 40,762 documents with their text indexed, and 477,799 passages from 36,818 files turned into vectors for meaning search. The screenshot below shows it answering a name search for /changelog in 11 ms.

You switch modes with a prefix, or with the tabs under the search box.

Type this You get
invoice apps and commands first, then the best file matches
/invoice every file and folder named like it, ranked
/~/Code/ browse a folder, or complete names inside it
#tax deduction documents, notes, PDFs and code containing those words
~notes about moving house documents about it, even with totally different words

There's a filter syntax too, and it stacks with everything. ext:pdf size:>10mb mod:week in:~/Documents does exactly what you think it does. Name matching is fuzzy, so rtrn finds return-2025.pdf.

How it actually works

There's a Rust daemon called cloudwerx-searchd running as a user service. No root, no background cron job. It keeps three separate indexes, and the launcher, the CLI and the settings page all talk to it over a unix socket with JSON lines.

launcher / cloudwerx search / settings page
                  |
         cloudwerx-search.sock (0600)
                  |
          cloudwerx-searchd (Rust)
        /         |            \
  names (RAM)   text (tantivy)   meaning (vectors)
        \         |            /
              inotify watches

Names live in a compact in-memory table, 24 bytes plus the name for every file and folder on the machine. It's the same idea as Everything on Windows. A full walk of the disk runs in parallel at idle priority. Each search scores every entry with nucleo (the fuzzy matcher from the Helix editor) across all cores, after a 64 bit character set test throws out most names in a single instruction. That's how you get single digit milliseconds across millions of entries. My home folder updates live through inotify, and the rest rescans on a schedule. I deliberately didn't use fanotify, because it would watch the whole disk but needs root, and I'm not putting a root daemon on my search box.

Words inside files go through tantivy, which is Lucene style BM25. It reads text, Markdown, HTML, CSV, source code, PDFs (through pdftotext) and Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument and EPUB files by cracking open their zipped XML. I build the queries by hand so typing feels instant. Every word also matches the common indexed words it starts, so keybind finds keybinds, phrases match exactly, a hit in the file name counts double, and the snippets highlight what matched.

Meaning is my favorite. Documents get split into passages of about 700 characters, and each passage is embedded with Model2Vec static embeddings (potion-retrieval-32M, the best static retrieval model I could find). A static model turns each token into a vector with a table lookup and averages them. That's hundreds of times faster than running a transformer, with no GPU and no model server, so a whole home folder gets embedded in about a minute. The vectors are stored as 8 bit integers and searched exhaustively in parallel, which is exact and takes around 5 ms. Junk like hashes, base64 and minified code gets skipped before it ever gets embedded.

The # search mixes the text and meaning rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. A document that matches your words and your intent floats to the top, and a meaning match can surface a file that uses none of your words at all. Meaning matches only join in when they're strong (similarity of at least 0.45 and close to the best hit), because static embeddings will always hand you some nearest neighbor, even when the honest answer is "nothing".

That second one is me typing "how do I make the desktop look different", and getting results from files that don't contain those words. The footer says it found it by meaning. (The first word search in the screenshot above it shows 447 ms because it was cold. Warm it's usually somewhere between 3 and 15 ms.)

Indexing never gets in the way of work. The threads run at nice 15 with the idle I/O class, the first content index does the newest files first and commits every 20 seconds, and a manifest of modification times means a restart only re-reads what changed. Everything stays local. Nothing leaves the machine.

And once you find the file, it's not a dead end. Enter opens it, Ctrl+Enter shows it in the file manager, Alt+Enter opens it in Noteism, Ctrl+T drops you into a terminal in its folder, and Ctrl+K opens every other action. Files you open from here rank higher next time.

My apps all grow up here

This is the part that's changed how I work. CLOUDWERX OS is now my breeding ground. Every new project, app or idea I have gets grown inside it, with its own plugin on the bar and its own page in settings, hooked up to everything else.

Noteism is the code and text editor I've been building for a year and a half. Picture VS Code and Obsidian having a very good time together. It's fast, it's pretty, it's agentic, and it renders markdown in a way where you can type straight into code blocks, like Typora does.

That screenshot is Noteism with nothing open, so you can see the default screen. It's version 1.8.3 right now, and we've been updating the hell out of it lately. I wrote this whole post in it, by the way. Every word, in live preview, with the images dropped in as I went.

The big new thing is a complete AI panel. It's off until you turn it on, and when it's off there's no panel, no menu, no status item and no network calls. When it's on, Ctrl+Shift+A opens a chat beside your notes that can actually do things. It reads and searches your notes and files, looks at the note you're in and your selection, edits and rewrites, creates notes, opens files, checks and draws Mermaid diagrams, looks at pictures and loads skills. Every change it makes shows up as a line diff you accept or reject first (Ctrl+Enter to accept), and Ctrl+Z undoes it either way. You add context with @ for notes, files, folders and the selection, / for quick prompts and skills, and chats are saved, named, searchable and come back when you restart.

Then there's Tab completion, and yes, I mean the Cursor kind. Grey text suggests the rest of what you're writing, and a marked change suggests the next edit nearby, like a rename you started or a typo a few lines down. Tab takes it, Ctrl+Right takes one word, Esc dismisses it.

It's all bring your own accounts. Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini keys, any OpenAI compatible server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, OpenRouter), your Claude Code sign in, and your ChatGPT sign in through Codex. Keys live in the system keyring, encrypted, and never reach the window or a chat. Encrypted notes are never sent to AI at all. A few other things I love: it counts tokens live in the status bar, it can make 18 kinds of Mermaid diagram from a selection, and it has a "changed on disk" bar so a Git pull or a sync tool never silently stomps your text.

It also ships as an AppImage now, so it runs on almost any Linux, not just mine. It is coming soon at noteism.app.

Herdr is where all my agents live. I run all my agents and sub-agents in there, and with my own handoff skills I can drop a TASK.md on an agent and it'll go assign sub-agents to knock out every task, orchestrating the whole thing, picking the engine, the model and the thinking level either perfectly or exactly how I pre-set it. I've got a library of 125 skills that agents load on demand, so they stop making things up about APIs.

Some details, because I'm a nerd about it. Herdr has two halves. hc (herdr-core) is a small server that runs terminals and agents and keeps them alive when the window closes. herdr-app is the desktop window. It's drawn with GPUI, the GPU toolkit from the Zed editor, so there's no web view and no Electron, and mods are JavaScript written against gpui-kit. Agents report whether they're working, blocked, idle or done with an escape sequence (OSC 7501), and the app turns that into badges and toasts in the sidebar. Everything is files in ~/.config/herdr-app. Save one and the window reloads it in about a second.

My layout on top of it is called cloudwerx-herdr. It started life as someone else's layout (Bettr, by dissimulate) and I've taken it a long way. It has usage cards for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode with a meter for each limit window and the time left until it resets, CPU, GPU and RAM, an agent activity panel with running sub-agents, a context and cache breakdown, and a Tasks panel that renders the TASK.md of whatever project you're in and updates live while an agent edits it. The theme gets rewritten from my desktop theme every time I change it, so Herdr follows along. And the bar has an island for it, with jumps straight to a pane. I am a HUGE fan of the new herdr-app, it's kind of genius. Get it at http://herdr.dev

Being able to see every agent, what it's doing, and how much of its limit it has left, all in one window, changed how I work. I love this thing.

I also wrote TaskPass for it, a small native editor (Rust and GPUI) for one job: writing long careful TASK.md files, where every task gets worked by a brand new agent session with its own engine, model, autonomy and effort.

Hangar is where all my projects get managed. It's a CLI, a web UI and a desktop app that all sync together, and I mean deliciously. Projects go in there, tasks get made with a quick capture box, agents can add their own, and it can dump a TASK.md out to hand to an agent. Rust and PostgreSQL underneath.

Task Manager is a new one I wrote in Rust with GPUI. Not a port, not a wrapper. It's got per core CPU graphs, GPU, disks, services, startup items and a flight recorder.

Snip is my screenshot and annotation tool, and it's easily one of the most useful things on the machine. Hit Print and the screen freezes. The freeze happens before the overlay opens, so menus, tooltips and hover states end up in the picture, and the overlay itself can never be in the shot. Drag a rectangle, or click a window to snap to it. There's a magnifier with the pixel colors while you aim, a size label in real pixels, and an action bar with Copy, Save, Edit, Pin and Text.

It has a mode for everything. Region, window, this screen, all screens in one wide picture, repeat the last region, a timer (3, 5 or 10 seconds with a countdown ring, so you can open a menu first), a color picker that copies #rrggbb, and a "copy text from the screen" mode that runs OCR with tesseract over whatever you drag across. It also refuses to capture anything while the session is locked, which is the kind of thing you only think about once.

Then there's the editor, and this is where it gets ridiculous. Pen, highlighter, lines, arrows (filled, open, double, dashed), rectangles, ellipses, text, numbered step badges with a Renumber button, blur, pixelate, spotlight, crop with aspect locks, an eraser and a color picker. The highlighter multiplies on light pages and screens on dark ones so text stays readable. Blur and pixelate actually redact what's under the box, which is handy when you're about to post a screenshot of the control center and your Wi-Fi name is sitting right there.

Here's one I made in about ten seconds. That arrow, the label, the two step numbers and the box are all separate objects.

A few more things I like. Beautify wraps the picture in a frame with padding, rounded corners and a soft shadow, using your theme colors. Pin floats a screenshot over everything in a borderless window, and you can scroll to resize it. When you save a picture that has annotations, it also stores the untouched original and every annotation as an object, so you can open the file later and move an arrow that you got wrong. The whole thing is scriptable too:

cloudwerx snip region --action edit
cloudwerx snip window --focused
cloudwerx snip ocr-file receipt.png --copy

Every mode has a hotkey, a bar island, a menu and a page in Settings.

Voice dictation is the one that makes people stop and stare. I hit Super+Alt+Space, talk, hit it again, and the words get typed wherever my cursor is. It runs on Voxtype, which is Whisper running on my own machine. No cloud, no account, nothing leaves the laptop.

The part I'm proud of is the bar. While it's recording, an island shows up in the middle of the bottom bar with a mic that breathes with your voice, a live waveform of what the microphone is actually hearing, and a timer. The waveform is drawn from Voxtype's own audio stream, colored with my theme's accents, and it goes red if you clip. When you stop, it turns amber and ripples while the words get transcribed. There's a bars style and a ribbon style, and everything about it is configurable.

Here's a real take. I'm talking into the mic, the waveform is moving on the bar, and the text shows up in a terminal when I'm done. That's 10 seconds of talking, and you can watch the words get typed out right after the mic stops. It transcribes on the CPU with the small base.en model, so it takes a few seconds to finish.

It's more than a toggle, too. It supports Whisper, Parakeet, Moonshine, SenseVoice and a few other engines, with model downloads from Settings. There's spoken punctuation, filler word removal, word replacements for the stuff it always gets wrong, and a "submit" command that presses Enter for you. It pauses my music while I talk, and it has a meeting mode with speakers and past meetings. I even had to fix the volume OSD, because a Bluetooth headset flips into headset mode when you record and the volume jumped around like a toddler on a trampoline.

cloudwerx voice toggle
cloudwerx voice replace set "cloud works" "CLOUDWERX"
cloudwerx voice meeting start

The updater and the rest work the same way. Tiny focused things that all talk to each other.

The tools I built so agents can work on my machine

A funny thing happened while I was building all of this. I kept running into the same three problems whenever an agent worked on the desktop, so I fixed each one properly and put them out in the open. They're all CLOUDWERX LAB projects, they're all small Rust binaries, and all three are public.

Ghosthand: a real hand on a real pointer

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/Ghosthand

I got tired of agents that could write an entire UI but couldn't right click a menu on it. A screenshot tells you what's there. It can't tell you what happens when you hover or drag. So Ghosthand gives an agent my actual mouse and keyboard. Click, double click, right click, drag, scroll, hover, type text, press shortcuts, then take a screenshot and see what happened.

How it works is simple. It creates a virtual absolute pointer through /dev/uinput, so the display server just sees a normal mouse. That means it isn't tied to one compositor. No portals, no plugins. It reads my real keyboard layout so it types what it should, and focus tells the agent which window will get the keys before it types.

The part I care about most is the gate. Before anything moves or types, a card shows up on my screen saying who's asking, why, and exactly what it's about to type. Nothing happens until I click Allow. No answer counts as a no. While an agent is driving, a little "Agent Control" tag and a ring follow the cursor, so I always know it isn't me. One key takes the pointer back at any time, and it refuses to run while the session is locked. For a long testing job I approve one session instead of a card per click.

It's one small Rust binary, with a background daemon keeping the virtual devices alive so a run starts in milliseconds. I've tested it daily on niri. The README is honest that Hyprland, sway, X11, KDE and GNOME are parser tested but not driven live by me, so bug reports are welcome.

Here's the prompt. This is what I see before an agent touches anything. It says who's asking, why, how long I've got to answer, and exactly what it's about to type, word for word. Then Deny, Allow for 10 minutes, or Allow. If I don't answer, it counts as a no.

And this is a real recording of it working. The card pops up, I click Allow for 10 minutes, and from there every click, scroll and keystroke is the agent. It jumps around Settings pages, types into the search box, and opens the launcher to search for a file. I didn't touch anything after clicking Allow.

While an agent is driving, you can't mistake it for yourself. There's a ring around the pointer and an Agent Control tag that follow the cursor everywhere. Here's a close up, with it gliding across the desktop and clicking.

agent-sudo: root without a password, with a seatbelt

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/agent-sudo

Regular sudo wants a password from a terminal. A script or an agent can't type one, so it hangs forever, or you do the dangerous thing and put NOPASSWD: ALL in your sudoers file and now one bad command takes the whole machine with it. An empty variable in rm -rf "$DIR/"* is all it takes.

agent-sudo (or asudo for short) sits in the middle. It runs the command as root with no prompt, but first it reads the command against ten named guardrails that refuse the catastrophic stuff: rm -rf /, mkfs on a disk, dd onto /dev/sda, editing /etc/shadow, fork bombs. It reads the command, it doesn't just regex a string, so env, nice, timeout, sh -c "...", $(...), redirections, .. and symlinks don't hide anything. Every run goes into an audit log at /var/log/agent-sudo.log with when, who, where and how it ended, and I get a desktop notification each time.

agent-sudo pacman -S --noconfirm ripgrep
agent-sudo --explain dd if=x of=/dev/sda    # which rule fires, and why
agent-sudo --logs 10                        # what ran lately

I want to be straight about what it is. It's a seatbelt, not a security boundary. It stops mistakes and careless commands. It can't stop something that's actively trying to get around it, because anything running as root can do anything, and the README says so in a big warning box. The installer checks the sudoers rule with visudo before it touches anything, and it's only two dependencies.

skills-cli: stop paying for skills you aren't using

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/skills-cli

Skills are great, but the usual way of using them doesn't scale. Put a hundred of them where your agent looks and every single conversation starts by paying for the name and description of all hundred, whether you need them or not. The agent also gets worse at picking the right one, and one careless read of a big skill can dump a couple hundred thousand tokens of docs into the context.

So I flipped it around. The library lives on disk, and the agent gets one tiny instruction. From there it searches, loads and fetches only what it needs.

skills search "pdf merge"
skills load pdf-tools
skills ref get pdf-tools merge        # one reference page, not the whole folder
skills run pdf-tools split.py in.pdf  # only the output comes back

My own library is 130 skills in 3,377 files, about 14.8 million tokens. The instructions alone are around 400 thousand. Listing every one of them takes about 4 ms. And the agent only ever sees what it asked for, with a 30,000 token guard so a slip can't flood the context. It also makes new skills (skills new), installs them from git, validates them, and can pin one as a slash command. skills skill prints a guide built into the binary, so an agent can learn the whole tool with one command.

My laptop is also a security camera

I can watch my laptop's camera and listen to its microphone from my phone, from anywhere, and nothing is exposed to the internet. It works over Tailscale only. There's nothing to forward on the router, and the server listens only on the machine's Tailscale addresses and refuses anything outside the tailnet.

You turn it on in Settings › Security Camera, open the address on your phone, and add it to the home screen for a full screen app. The camera only opens when the first viewer arrives and closes about ten seconds after the last one leaves, so it's off while nobody's watching. Up to eight phones at once. By default only devices signed in to my own Tailscale account are allowed, checked with tailscale whois, so someone else on a shared tailnet gets refused and logged. And the camera's activity light is always on while it streams. It's never hidden or faked, which I think is the right call.

Tailscale shows up everywhere else too. Settings › Tailscale handles devices, exit nodes, SSH and file sharing, and in Files you can right click a file and choose Send over Tailscale to Taildrop it to any of my devices.

Keeping it all alive

You should see the size of the CHANGELOG for cloudwerx-os. It's pushing 3,000 lines, and it's come a REAL long way. I work on it every day.

From any of my many connected devices I can push a new PR and sync it onto any of my hardware with a single click. I wrote an updater for the whole OS that handles the AUR packages, the kernel and everything else, and it takes a snapshot before it touches anything, so I can roll back when (not if) I mess something up.

I also have a Telegram bot, and a Tasks page that's basically cron with a user interface. I can set up a job that makes Claude Code go hunt for the coolest open source GitHub projects from the last week, formats a nice rich message and sends it to me on Telegram. Every week, completely automated. I wake up on Monday to a newsletter that my computer wrote for me.

I have a similar system on my NAS called JONAS (Joint Operations NAS Admin System). That's a story for another day. Let's just say Synology wishes it had this many features.

Things I've built in the last three years

CLOUDWERX OS isn't the only thing that came out of the last 3 years. My portfolio at cloudwerxlab.com is a descent through a mycelium network with 15 projects in it, and a lot of them run on my NAS behind Cloudflare tunnels. A few I'm especially fond of:

  • X-Tracks (x-tracks.app) is a self-hosted music archive. Paste a Spotify or YouTube Music link and it archives the tracks as MP3, FLAC, Opus or M4A with real metadata and artwork. No Spotify login or developer key. It has 29 visualizers, 20 of them audio reactive (way nicer than Winamp ever was), and you can write your own GLSL shaders in a Visualization Studio. It also has DJ X, an AI agent. Give it one prompt and it researches the web, searches YouTube Music and Spotify, downloads the music, builds you a playlist with generated artwork and starts playing it. It can even write new visualizers. It's still in development.
  • Terminaut (terminaut.app) is mission control for every server you run. Start and stop them in batches, watch their output stream live, and drop into a real interactive shell.
  • Pretty Hooker (Docker Hub) turns webhooks into desktop notifications for your homelab. Point Uptime Kuma, Grafana, GitHub, Sonarr, Home Assistant or a plain curl at it.
  • R2Up (r2up.cloudwerxlab.com) uploads past Cloudflare's 300 MB dashboard limit by chunking files into S3 multipart uploads, all in your browser.
  • CapGen (capgen.cloudwerxlab.com) builds, cleans and captions image datasets for LoRA training.
  • SugarStem separates stems locally, so your audio never leaves your computer. Cinnaroll is a theme browser for Linux Mint. TaskPunk is a markdown first task manager. And there's a whole desktop that runs in a browser tab, with a tiny AI unicorn who can redecorate it.

I run a pile of self hosted goodies on the homelab too, Immich among them, plus the NAS agent I keep teasing.

So, why do this?

Because I could. That's the real answer, and it's the answer that would've made 12-year old me, running a BBS on a phone line, lose his mind. I spent decades inside systems somebody else decided were good enough. Then it turned out I could just... build the thing. The tools got good enough, and so did I.

My OS is everything I've ever wanted from a computer. It does what I say, it looks how I want, it tells me when it's broken, and it never once asked me to sign into a Microsoft account to look at a calculator.

Stories for another day

I've got a lot more where this came from, and I plan to write them all up here. A few teasers, in no particular order:

  • How I run ablated open weights models on a custom VPS for the times I want to do things the frontier labs won't let me. (Shh.)
  • How I got a root shell on my DJI drone, which let me fly it literally inside the clouds, and very nearly visit outer space.
  • My custom astrophotography rig, built around a hacked DSLR.
  • The MAME cabinet I built from a classic Mortal Kombat II arcade machine, with custom vinyl side art, a custom desktop living inside it running a custom frontend, and a totally customized control panel.
  • JONAS, the admin agent that runs my NAS. Synology wishes.
  • What I got up to in AOL chatrooms in the early 2000s, with classic remote access tools disguised as images, and the very bad people it was aimed at. Maybe I'll tell that one with a drink in my hand.

My wife, Sizzlebop, builds a ton of her own projects too, and I get to live next to all of it. Go follow her on GitHub and on dev.to. You won't regret it.

I'll write more of these. There's plenty left to tell, like how the theme engine works, how the plugin system works and how I run a small army of agents without losing my mind. If any of this sounds like your kind of fun, say hi. I'm genuinely curious what you'd build.

Ty
CLOUDWERX LAB, Digital Food for the Analog Soul
cloudwerxlab.com · github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV

title: How long should an AI video ad be?
description:
What is the right length for a first ad?

Fifteen seconds is the length I would use for a first ad. It fits one product, one message and about four scenes. It is the length I publish a price for, and it is the length the plans are counted in: Creator makes about 7 videos of 15 seconds a month, and Pro about 19.

I do not have a study on the ideal length for ads, so I will not tell you a duration wins. What I can say is that a short ad leaves less room for error and for confusion.

What are the limits of the studio?

One generation runs up to 30 seconds, and a project can grow to 10 minutes by joining scenes. Most product clips are far shorter than that.

The limits are about what the studio can make. What your ad should be is a separate question, and the answer comes from the placement and the message.

Does length change the cost?

Yes. The credit cost depends on the length and the quality. A 15 second video at 720p is 515 credits, which is $5.15, and that is the only figure I publish. Longer costs more, and so do 1080p and 4K.

For any other length, read the credit cost in the studio before you generate. Do not scale my number by guesswork. More on credits is in how AI video credits work.

Does the placement set the length?

Often it does, and the platform has the final say. Platforms set limits on length and file size, and they change, so check the current rules of the one you use. A vertical slot for short video suits a short ad. A product page or a site banner can take a longer, calmer clip.

The ratio choice goes with it, which I cover in which video ratio to use for each ad placement.

How many scenes fit in 15 seconds?

About four, if each does one job. A simple structure is an opening on the product or the payoff, one detail, one use and a closing frame with the offer.

  1. Open on the product or its result.
  2. Show the detail a shopper should notice.
  3. Show the product in use.
  4. Close on the product with the offer line.

If you find yourself adding a fifth or sixth scene, ask whether the ad has two messages. Two messages usually make two ads.

When does a longer ad make sense?

  • A product page video where a visitor is already interested.
  • A small brand commercial with a short story, where one idea needs room.
  • A video for a website or YouTube, where the viewer chose to watch.
  • A real estate piece that moves through the rooms of a property.

Even then, build it from short checked scenes. Every extra scene is another chance for the product to drift, and each one needs a look against the real item.

How do I test length?

Make a short version and a longer one with the same opening, message and offer, and run both with the same budget. Change only the length. The hook test method in how to test ad hooks with AI video applies here too.

Your ad account will tell you which one works. The studio does not.

How do I cut a longer idea down to 15 seconds?

Pick the one thing a viewer must remember and delete everything else. Write the message in one sentence, then keep only the scenes that carry that sentence. If a scene could be removed without the sentence changing, remove it.

It helps to read the scene list as a storyboard before you generate anything. The scene list shows each moment in order, so a wasted scene is only a wasted line at that point and not a wasted generation.

How does length affect retakes?

Longer videos have more scenes, and each scene is another place where fine detail can drift. A scene that completes and misses the brief still spends credits, so a longer ad usually costs more in retakes as well as in generation.

You can regenerate a single scene and keep the rest, which keeps the cost of a fix small. Still, a short ad checked carefully is better than a long one checked in a hurry.

What should I check before I pick a length?

Open the current spec for the platform and the placement, and write down the maximum length, the file size and the ratio. Then pick the length that fits the message, not the maximum the slot allows.

If you are unsure, export the short version first. You can always build a longer one from the same scenes, and a short ad is quicker to review.

I do not quote platform limits here, because they change and I cannot promise they are right when you read this.

Where do I start?

Make one 15 second ad on Creator, $39 a month, which includes the commercial license for ads. Starter, $9 a month, is for a personal test. The page for brands shows the flow.

Originally published at hubcontent.ai.

HubContent turns product photos into AI-made short videos and ads. hubcontent.ai

title: Best robot dog for oil and gas site inspection: B2, X30, A2 or Spot
description:
Short answer: For oil and gas rounds outside classified hazardous zones, the Unitree B2 (40 kg rated payload) or DEEP Robotics X30 (20 kg, IP67 per its maker) is usually the practical choice for a full thermal, gas and acoustic payload; the Unitree A2 suits lighter payloads at lower cost, and Spot (14 kg) suits teams that value its software ecosystem. Do not assume any standard version is certified for explosive atmospheres.

Start with the area classification, not the robot

The first question on any oil and gas site is where the robot will walk. Tank farms, compressor stations, wellpads and process units are often split into classified zones (for example Zone 1 and Zone 2 under IECEx or ATEX). A robot that enters a classified zone needs an explosion-protection certificate for that zone, and so does every sensor on its back. Ask the robot maker for the certificate covering the exact model and zone; do not rely on an IP rating, which only covers dust and water.

Many operators start with routes that stay in unclassified areas or are run under a work permit with gas monitoring, and use the robot for the repetitive parts: walking the same route every shift, logging gauge values, taking thermal images of pumps and motors and sniffing for leaks. That is the job the four robots below are compared for.

The four robots side by side

Robot Own weight Rated payload Built-in perception Maker's protection rating Best fit on an oil and gas site
Unitree B2 60 kg 40 kg 3D LiDAR, front and rear depth cameras IP67 Heavy multi-sensor payloads, long outdoor routes
DEEP Robotics X30 56 kg 20 kg Front and rear LiDAR, depth and wide-angle cameras IP67 Industrial routes in rain, dust and at night
Unitree A2 37 kg 25 kg Front and rear LiDAR, HD camera Check with the maker Medium payloads where cost and handling weight matter
Boston Dynamics Spot 32.7 kg 14 kg 5 stereo camera pairs Check with the maker Teams that value its existing software and integrations

Weights and payloads are the manufacturers' published figures. The rated payload is an upper limit; real routes with stairs, grating and slopes go better well below it.


Unitree B2 carrying a YUANZHI ROBOTICS sensor payload (3D render)

What an oil and gas inspection payload actually weighs

The robot choice usually follows from the payload. A typical oil and gas round combines four jobs: thermal checks on rotating equipment, gas detection, acoustic leak finding and reading analog gauges. Some real component figures:

  • Dual-spectrum PTZ (Hikvision DS-2TD5566T-15/V2): about 4.5 kg and 18 W. Zoom for gauges and radiometric thermal for bearings and motors in one unit.
  • Acoustic imager (CRYSOUND CRY8124): about 1.4 kg; the Fluke SV600 is lighter at about 0.85 kg. Acoustic imaging finds compressed-gas and steam leaks that a thermal camera cannot see.
  • Multi-gas module (Winsen ZCE04B, four gases including CO and H2S): about 50 g and 0.5 W. Light and cheap, but it only measures the air that reaches it, so mounting position and airflow matter.
  • Navigation LiDAR (Livox Mid-360): 265 g and 6.5 W, if the robot's own sensors are not enough for your mapping needs.
  • Onboard compute (Jetson Orin NX 16GB class): budget up to around 40 W at peak for gauge-reading and detection models.

Add brackets, an enclosure, cabling and a 5G or mesh radio, and a full thermal, acoustic, gas and PTZ payload can reach 8 to 10 kg. On a B2 that is a comfortable fraction of the rating. On an X30 or A2 it fits, but you trade some runtime. On Spot you are close to the limit and will usually swap the large PTZ for a lighter camera. Our weight and power budget guide shows how to add this up for your own list.


Optical gas imaging view of a leak plume during a robot dog patrol (scene from the YUANZHI ROBOTICS product film)

Gas detection: point sensors, acoustic or optical gas imaging

Point gas sensors confirm a concentration where the robot is standing; they do not show where the leak is. Acoustic imagers locate pressurized leaks by sound, even in noisy plants, but say nothing about which gas it is. Optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras make hydrocarbon plumes visible and are the most direct way to find methane and VOC leaks, but cooled OGI cameras are heavy, power-hungry and expensive, which pushes you towards the B2. Many sites combine a point sensor for alarms with an acoustic imager for localisation. Our thermal vs optical gas imaging guide explains what each camera can and cannot detect.

Terrain, weather and the route

  • Grating and stairs: process units are full of open-mesh grating and steep steel stairs. All four robots can climb stairs, but check foot slip on wet grating during your trial and keep the payload's centre of mass low and central.
  • Rain, dust and heat: the B2 and X30 carry IP67 ratings from their makers, but the payload enclosure, connectors and camera windows must be sealed to match. A rated robot with an unsealed payload is only as good as the payload.
  • GNSS and localization: open sites suit RTK GNSS; dense pipe racks block satellites and need LiDAR localization. Most real routes need both.
  • Night rounds: thermal works in the dark, but gauge reading needs light. Plan an illuminator and test reading accuracy at night, not just during the day.


Robot dog gimbal reading analog pressure gauges at an inspection point

How to choose

  • Map the route and mark every classified zone. If the robot must enter Zone 1 or Zone 2, start by asking each maker which certified variant exists.
  • List the payload you really need and total its weight and power before you pick the robot.
  • If the total is above roughly 10 kg or includes a cooled OGI camera, shortlist the B2. Between about 5 and 10 kg, the X30 and A2 are both reasonable. Below that, Spot also works.
  • Run a pilot on your worst stretch of route (wet grating, stairs, pipe racks) before committing to a fleet. Our pilot project guide covers what to measure.

Next steps

You can assemble an oil and gas payload on any of these robots in our online payload configurator and see the total weight and power live. Platform notes are on the Unitree B2, DEEP Robotics X30, Unitree A2 and Boston Dynamics Spot pages. For a full build, see our robot payload integration and inspection robot services, or autonomy software if you need custom routes, gauge reading or alarm logic.

Written by the engineering team at YUANZHI ROBOTICS. Original article: Best robot dog for oil and gas site inspection: B2, X30, A2 or Spot

title: How do I automate functional software testing?
description:
Short answer: decide which behaviors matter most, check each one at the lowest layer where it actually lives, give your tests predictable data and fake versions of outside services, then make your CI pipeline run them on every change.

That's the whole loop of automated functional testing. The rest of this post walks through it with a small, concrete example, because "automate your tests" is easy advice to give and surprisingly hard to act on when you're staring at an empty test folder.

The example is a basic online store with a cart and discount coupons. Swap in your own product as you read. The steps don't change much.

Start with a list, not a tool

Most people open a browser tab and start comparing frameworks. That's backwards. The tool matters a lot less than knowing what you're going to test.

Grab a doc and write down three things:

  • The flows that make or lose money, like signup, login, adding to cart, checkout and refunds
  • The last ten or so bugs that reached production
  • Anything you or your QA folks re-check by hand before every release

For our store, the list might start like this: a customer can log in, add items, apply a valid coupon, get a clear error for an expired coupon, and pay with a saved card. Five items. That's plenty for a first pass.

Write the expected behavior in plain words

Before any code, write each item as a short scenario. A simple format works well:

Given a cart with two mugs at 50.00 each
When the customer applies coupon SAVE10
Then the total is 90.00

Given a coupon that expired yesterday
When the customer applies it
Then they get an "expired coupon" error and the total doesn't change

This feels like busywork. It isn't. Half the arguments about whether a test is "right" turn out to be arguments about what the feature should do, and it's much cheaper to settle those in a sentence than in a pull request.

Decide where each check belongs

Now ask where each behavior actually lives in your system.

The discount math happens on the server. So test it by calling the API directly. You don't need a browser to confirm that 100 minus 10% is 90, and a browser test for it will break whenever someone renames a button.

The fact that a customer can get from the product page to a paid order is a journey that crosses the UI, the API and the payment step. That one deserves a browser test.

For our store, the split ends up like this:

Scenario Layer Why
Valid coupon applies the right discount API Pure business logic, fast to check
Expired coupon is rejected API Error handling lives in the backend
Login with wrong password fails API Same reason
Customer checks out with a saved card UI The full journey is what matters

Three API tests and one UI test. That ratio holds up well as suites grow.

A worked example at the API layer

Here's what the coupon tests might look like in Python with pytest and requests. Any language and HTTP client will do the same job.

import uuid
import requests

BASE = "http://localhost:8000"


def new_customer():
    email = f"qa-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.test"
    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/users", json={"email": email, "password": "Passw0rd!"})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {r.json()['token']}"}


def test_save10_takes_ten_percent_off():
    headers = new_customer()
    requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/items", json={"sku": "MUG-01", "qty": 2}, headers=headers)

    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/coupon", json={"code": "SAVE10"}, headers=headers)

    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.json()["total"] == "90.00"


def test_expired_coupon_is_rejected():
    headers = new_customer()
    requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/items", json={"sku": "MUG-01", "qty": 2}, headers=headers)

    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/cart/coupon", json={"code": "OLD5"}, headers=headers)

    assert r.status_code == 422
    assert r.json()["error"] == "coupon_expired"
    assert r.json()["total"] == "100.00"

A few things worth pointing out, because they're where beginners usually slip:

  • Every test creates its own customer with a random email. No test depends on another one having run first.
  • Each test checks one behavior and says exactly what "correct" means. "Status is 200" alone would pass even if the discount were wrong.
  • The expired coupon test also checks that the total didn't change. Bugs love to hide in the "nothing should happen" cases.

Handling the database and outside services

Those tests assume two things exist: a product called MUG-01 priced at 50.00, and a coupon called OLD5 that has already expired. Don't create those by hand in a shared staging database and hope nobody touches them. Someone will.

Put them in a seed script that runs before the suite, against a database that exists only for testing. A throwaway container started in CI is the usual approach. Fresh data every run means a failure points at your code, not at whatever a colleague did on staging last Thursday.

Outside services need the same treatment. If checkout calls a payment provider, your test suite shouldn't depend on that provider's sandbox being up. Replace it with a mock that returns realistic responses, including the unpleasant ones like a declined card or a timeout. Then keep a handful of separate checks that hit the real sandbox on a schedule, so you still find out if their API changes.

If writing mocks by hand sounds tedious, it is. Some teams record real traffic between their service and its dependencies and replay it as mocks, which saves a lot of typing and keeps the mocks closer to reality.

Adding a few UI tests

Once the API layer is covered, add browser tests for the journeys a customer can't live without. Here's the checkout one in Playwright:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('customer can check out with a saved card', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('saved-card@example.test');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('Passw0rd!');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();

  await page.goto('/products/mug-01');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});

Notice it finds elements by their label and role, not by CSS classes. Designers change class names all the time. They rarely change a button that says "Pay now" without also changing what it does.

Keep this layer small. Ten to twenty UI tests covering real journeys will tell you more than a hundred that click every button on every page.

Getting it into CI

Tests that only run on someone's laptop stop running. Put them in your pipeline so they run without anyone having to remember. A minimal GitHub Actions setup looks like this:

name: functional-tests
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  api-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker compose up -d db app
      - run: python scripts/seed_test_data.py
      - run: pip install -r requirements-test.txt
      - run: pytest tests/api -q

Start there. Once that's stable, add the UI tests on merge to your main branch, the full regression set before releases, and a nightly run against staging. Keep the pull request stage under about ten minutes, or people will merge before it finishes and the whole thing loses its point.

Keeping the suite alive

Writing the first tests is the fun part. Keeping them useful is the actual job.

When a test turns flaky, fix it or delete it that week. A retry button teaches the team that red builds don't mean anything, and that lesson is very hard to unlearn.

When a production bug slips through, write the test that would have caught it before you write the fix. Your suite slowly becomes a record of everything that has ever gone wrong, which is exactly what you want it to be.

And review test code in pull requests the same way you review everything else. A test nobody understands is a test nobody will fix when it breaks.

FAQs

What's the first functional test I should automate?

Pick the flow that would hurt most if it broke tomorrow. For most products that's login or checkout. Automate the happy path and one or two common failures, get it running in CI, then move on to the next one.

Do I need to know how to code to automate functional testing?

It helps a lot. Low-code and record-and-playback tools exist and can get you started, but suites written in code are easier to review, version and maintain once they grow past a few dozen tests.

Which framework should I use?

Use whatever fits your stack. For APIs, your language's standard test runner plus an HTTP client is enough. For browsers, Playwright and Cypress are both solid choices. The habits in this post matter far more than the framework.

How long does it take to automate functional testing?

A first useful set, say ten API tests and two UI tests running in CI, is usually a few days of focused work. Getting to a suite the whole team trusts takes months, mostly because of data, flakiness and ownership rather than writing tests.

Wrapping up

Automating functional testing comes down to a short loop: choose what matters, test it where it lives, control the data, and let CI run it every time. Start with five tests, not five hundred. Get them green, keep them green, and add more each time something breaks. That's slower than it sounds on paper, and it works.

title: Go AI Agent Framework With Retries, Budgets and Human Approval
description:
One of my team's main projects has an AI-heavy backend written in Go. I work mostly in Python, where agent frameworks are mature, so I know what the Go side was missing: an agent that's a normal value inside the service, not a Python process reached over a queue. The loop itself takes an afternoon. Deciding what happens at each place it can break is what became Golem, an open-source Go AI agent framework.

This post is about that second part: bad tool calls, provider errors, loops, cost and human sign-off, and where each one lands in a run. It also covers how Golem compares with the other Go options and when you should pick something else. It describes v1.2.0, released on 16 November 2026.

What breaks once the agent loop is running?

The loop is short. The model reads a conversation, asks for a tool, you run it, you feed the result back and repeat until the model answers. Each step then fails in its own way:

  • The provider returns a 429 or a 503 halfway through a run.
  • The model calls a tool with arguments that don't match your schema.
  • The model returns JSON that is almost the shape you asked for.
  • The model asks for the same tool call again and again.
  • A tool needs a person to approve it before anything irreversible happens.
  • A run dies on turn six and you lose the first five turns.

Python has good answers to several of these. Pydantic AI showed that an agent can have typed dependencies and validated output, and I used it as a reference. But copying Python mechanisms into Go would have given me something un-Go-like: decorators are awkward, runtime validation hides what the compiler could check, and exceptions as control flow don't suit a language that returns errors. So the question I started from was what an agent should look like if you begin with Go's strengths.

What is Golem?

Golem is an open-source Go library for building agents. The repository started on 16 August 2026, and v1.0.0 on 25 October 2026 froze the API under a rule written down in ADR 0041: semantic versioning, additive changes only below v2, checked by an API diff against the previous tag.

The short version:

  • Agents are generic: Agent[Deps, Output]. Dependencies and the final output are real types.
  • The module has no dependencies outside the standard library, and needs Go 1.26 or newer.
  • Adapters cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama or LM Studio.
  • An MCP client works over stdio and streamable HTTP, and an MCP server exposes one agent as a tool.
  • Retries, fallback models, self-correction, usage limits, loop detection, streaming and run events are built in.
  • A deterministic fake model lets you test agents offline.
  • It ships with 39 guides, every example runs offline, and statement coverage is 81.6%. 
go get github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

The layering is plain. Your service owns the dependencies, the core owns the run, and everything that touches the outside world sits behind a small interface.

Why build agents in Go at all?

Agent work is mostly waiting on a network, so it's fair to ask whether the language matters. I think it does once the agent leaves the notebook. An agent service holds many conversations at once, calls tools concurrently, streams tokens to clients and has to shut down cleanly. Goroutines, context.Context and a single static binary fit that shape. A deployed agent can be one small container image with no interpreter, no virtualenv and no dependency tree to audit.

The compiler is the second reason. When a tool depends on a database handle and a tenant ID, I want the compiler to tell me if I pass the wrong one. In Golem that's a type parameter, not a convention.

What does a first agent look like?

This is the smallest working agent, from the README:

client, err := openai.New(openai.Config{
    APIKey: os.Getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
    Model:  "gpt-4o-mini",
})
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

agent, err := golem.New[struct{}, string](client,
    golem.DecodeFunc[string](func(_ context.Context, r model.Response) (string, error) {
        return r.Message.Content, nil
    }),
)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "Why is Go ideal for AI agents?")
fmt.Println(result.Output)
fmt.Printf("Tokens: %d input, %d output\n", result.Usage.InputTokens, result.Usage.OutputTokens)

You build the agent once with golem.New and run it many times. It needs a model and an output decoder, and the decoder is the line where untrusted model text becomes a value your program is willing to use. Everything else is an option function. The result carries the typed output, the full normalized conversation and cumulative token usage.

How do typed tools and dependencies work?

Most agent bugs I've seen live in tools. A tool needs a database, an HTTP client or a user identity, and frameworks often solve that with globals or closures, which makes tools hard to test. In Golem a tool is a typed value, and its Exec function receives the run's dependency value directly:

type Database struct {
    Users map[int]string
}

getUser := tool.MustNew(tool.Tool[Database]{
    Name:        "get_user",
    Description: "Look up a user name by their ID.",
    Schema: json.RawMessage(`{
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}},
        "required": ["id"]
    }`),
    Exec: func(ctx context.Context, db Database, args json.RawMessage) (tool.Result, error) {
        var input struct {
            ID int `json:"id"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(args, &input); err != nil {
            return tool.Result{}, err
        }
        name, ok := db.Users[input.ID]
        if !ok {
            return tool.Text("User not found"), nil
        }
        return tool.Text(name), nil
    },
})

agent, err := golem.New[Database, string](client, decoder,
    golem.WithTools[Database, string](getUser),
)

result, err := agent.Run(ctx, golem.RunContext[Database]{Deps: Database{Users: map[int]string{42: "Alice"}}}, "Who is user 42?")

The schema is written by hand and the arguments arrive as raw JSON. That's deliberate. Arguments are untrusted model output, and I'd rather you see the validation than have reflection do it somewhere you can't read. It costs a few more lines per tool, and in return a tool's behavior is visible in the file where it's defined.

What happens when a run goes wrong?

A Golem run is a transparent loop, and each failure has a named place to land.

How does an agent correct bad output?

When the model returns bad output or bad tool arguments, the cheapest fix is often to say what was wrong and ask again. A decoder or tool does that by returning an error that wraps *model.ModelRetry:

if input.N <= 0 {
    return "", &model.ModelRetry{Err: fmt.Errorf("n must be positive, got %d", input.N)}
}

The run feeds that message back to the model. Self-correction is opt-in, with separate budgets from WithOutputRetries and WithToolRetries, so a model can't argue with your validator forever. With no budget, the same error fails the run at a named stage with its cause intact. A failure the model should simply see, like a missing file, is &tool.Failed{Reason}: the model gets the reason as a tool result and no retry budget is spent.

How do you survive provider errors?

Transient provider errors (408, 429, 5xx and transport faults) are retried with WithMaxAttempts. The default is one attempt, so retries are opt-in. Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles and caps at 30 seconds unless you supply your own. Tool and decode failures are never retried by this mechanism, since they aren't transport problems.

When retrying isn't enough, model.NewFallback(primary, backup) tries models in order. For streams there's one rule: a fallback only happens before the first fragment is forwarded, because after the caller has seen output, switching models would replay it.

How do you stop a runaway agent?

Two limits cover it. golem.UsageLimit bounds input, output and total tokens, model requests and tool calls, and a dollar cost if you supply a price table with WithPrice. Token counts come from the provider's reported usage, so a token limit only trips when the provider reports usage, while requests and tool calls are counted by the run itself. Pricing is yours to supply, because I don't want to ship a table that goes stale between releases, and the library says plainly that the cost estimate is only as good as your rates and isn't a billing guarantee.

The second limit is loop detection, added in v1.2.0 (ADR 0051). WithLoopDetection(maxRepeats) counts calls to the same tool with canonically equal arguments across the whole run, and fails the run before the offending call executes. That ordering is the point: a model that polls a tool can't repeat a side effect while you wait for the check. WithLoopPolicy adds checks for repeated results, alternating A-B calls and repeated final text, with a choice between stopping the run and nudging the model.

Oversized tool output is the quieter cost. WithToolOutputLimit caps a tool result before it enters the conversation, keeps the head and tail, and appends a marker with the original size (ADR 0050).

What do you keep when a run fails?

When a run fails on turn six, you still want turns one to five. Golem attaches them to the error as RunError.Partial: the conversation through the last completed turn, the usage so far and the counts of requests and tool executions. Pass Partial.Messages to RunWithHistory to resume instead of starting over, which matters when the run has already spent real money.

How does an agent wait for a person?

Some tools shouldn't run without sign-off: deleting files, moving money, sending email. A tool defers by returning an error wrapping *tool.Deferred, of kind tool.DeferApproval or tool.DeferExternal. The other tool calls in that batch execute, and Run returns successfully with Result.Pending listing what's waiting. No further model call happens.

You resume with RunWithDeferredResults, passing the paused conversation and a decision for each pending call. Approved calls run, denied calls tell the model it was denied, and external results are inserted as given. Because a pause is a returned value, you can store it, show it in a UI and resume it hours later from another process. The reasoning behind that boundary is in the case for keeping meaningful actions with people.

Can a Go agent use MCP?

The Model Context Protocol is now the usual way to expose tools to agents, so Golem includes a client. mcp.NewStdio starts a server as a subprocess, mcp.NewHTTP connects to a remote endpoint, and mcp.AsTools turns the server's tool list into ordinary tool.Tool values with the server's own schema. A server error flagged as isError comes back as a correctable ModelRetry, and protocol or transport failures fail the run instead of being quietly corrected.

The guide says one thing I agree with: don't reach for MCP when a typed Go tool is one function away. A subprocess speaking JSON-RPC has more moving parts than a function call.

How do you test an agent without a model?

Agent tests are usually flaky (a real provider) or meaningless (mocked HTTP). Golem ships testmodel, a scripted in-memory model that plays back the responses you queue and records the exact request the agent sent:

client := testmodel.New().Respond(
    model.Response{Message: model.Message{Role: model.RoleAssistant, Content: "pong"}},
)
agent, _ := golem.New[struct{}, string](client, decoder)
result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "ping")

You can assert on the normalized request, the ordered messages in Result.Messages and which stage failed, with no network, keys or sleeps. The repository's CI runs its suite with the race detector, plus a fuzz target on the message JSON format.

How does it compare with other Go agent frameworks?

I compared Golem with the three other Go options I'd look at: langchaingo, Eino and Genkit for Go. I read each repository's source tree and go.mod on 27 November 2026. Dependency counts are the non-indirect lines in the require block, so they're approximate, and frameworks move fast, so check upstream before you depend on a detail.

Golem langchaingo Eino Genkit (Go)
Direct dependencies 0 About 60 About 10 About 40
License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0
MCP client In the core module Not in the repository Separate eino-ext module Plugin in the repository, client and server
Pause for human approval tool.Deferred, resumable Not found Interrupt and resume in adk Tool approval middleware
Retry and model fallback Built into the run Not found Retry and failover in adk Retry and fallback middleware
Design centre One explicit agent loop with typed dependencies LangChain-style chains and agents Graph and workflow composition Flows with OpenTelemetry tracing

Two things stand out. Golem is the only one with no dependencies outside the standard library, and the only one where a tool receives a typed dependency value for the run. I haven't found an equivalent of RunContext[Deps] in the others, but I haven't audited every API, so read that as what I found, not a proof.

The other half is that Golem is not alone on the guardrails. Genkit's Go module ships MCP, retry, fallback and tool approval as plugins and middleware, and Eino's adk package has retry, failover and interrupt-and-resume. Only langchaingo lacks them in the repositories I read. The Golem README understated Genkit on this.

The others are ahead in other places. Eino's graph model is more expressive than Golem's linear loop for branching, parallel and multi-agent pipelines, and it has more community components. langchaingo covers more providers and vector stores. Genkit has first-party Google tooling and tight Gemini integration. What Golem offers is a smaller surface: one runtime for a single agent inside a service, with the controls in the core module instead of in add-on packages.

When should you pick something else?

Pick Golem if you want agents inside a Go service, typed dependencies, a module with nothing else to audit and tests that run offline. Pick something else if your agent is mostly prompt experimentation, if you need a graph engine for complicated multi-agent pipelines, or if you need a large catalog of prebuilt integrations today. Python is still ahead on that last one, and I won't pretend otherwise. Golem also has no evaluation harness and no durable workflow engine, and v1.0.0 lists both as non-goals.

Herbie, a self-hosted chat and workflow app I built, runs its Go backend on Golem. I don't have production numbers to publish yet, so everything above is design reasoning plus what the repository's tests and examples show.

The documentation site has a guide for each feature, and examples/ has runnable programs for nearly all of them, several with no API key.

  • Project page: the Golem overview and capability matrix
  • Repository: github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem
  • Docs: abubakarsiddik31.github.io/golem
  • API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you try it and something feels un-Go-like, I want to hear about it.

Frequently asked questions

What is Golem?
Golem is an open-source AI agent framework for Go. It provides typed agents, tools with dependency injection, structured output, MCP support, and controls like retries, usage limits, loop detection and human approval.

Does Golem have external dependencies?
No. It uses only the Go standard library.

Which LLM providers does it support?
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Can I test agents without calling an API?
Yes. The testmodel package gives you a deterministic fake model, and the examples run offline.

Does it support MCP?
Yes. The mcp package is a client for stdio and streamable HTTP servers, and mcpserver exposes an agent as an MCP tool.

Originally published at abubakar-siddik.com.
