title: Your Grant Auditor Can Ask About Your AI Agent Years From Now. Can You Answer?
description:
A how-to for compliance-heavy European organisations that run on public money: universities, research institutes, public hospitals, municipalities, agencies, NGOs and companies in EU-funded consortia.

If your organisation depends on government or EU funding, you already live with a particular kind of accountability. Every euro has conditions. Every claim needs evidence. Auditors can arrive long after the work is done, and what they find can be extended to other grants and recovered with money you may have already spent.

Now add AI agents. They draft cost statements, classify expenses, answer citizens, triage applications, prepare reports and pull data from systems of record. Each of those tasks touches an obligation. And a year or three later, an auditor, a funder, a regulator or a citizen asks the same simple question: how was this decided, and can you show us?

This guide explains why publicly funded organisations face that question earlier and harder than most, how to map agent work to the obligations it touches, and how to build the record that lets you answer. It closes with a 30 day plan.

A note on scope. This is general information, not legal or audit advice. Funding rules differ by programme and member state, so check your grant agreement, national rules and your own legal and audit advisers. The case is an illustrative composite with invented names. Parameter names in code are illustrative. ZizkaDB records events and shows whether the record has been altered. It does not decide eligibility, make a system compliant or replace your audit function.

Why funded organisations are different

Four features set publicly funded bodies apart.

  1. Your costs are conditional. Funding is paid against rules on what counts as an eligible cost. If a cost is later found ineligible, it can be recovered. Under the Horizon Europe model grant agreement, beneficiaries must keep records and supporting documents to confirm proper use of funds and the costs claimed, and a published guide summarising the rules says records must be kept for five years after the final payment for grants over 60,000 euros, or three years for grants of 60,000 euros or less. A national contact point for Horizon Europe adds that the period can be longer in case of ongoing audits or national requirements. Other EU programmes and national funders have their own conditions, so check yours.

  2. Many bodies can audit you, and findings can travel. The model grant agreement includes provisions for checks, reviews and audits, including by OLAF, the European Public Prosecutor's Office and the European Court of Auditors, and a clause on the consequences of audits that deals with extension of findings. In plain terms, a weakness found in one project can prompt questions about others that used the same process. An agent that applied the same classification rule across thirty grants is one finding multiplied by thirty.

  3. Public-law rules on AI apply to you directly. The EU AI Act asks deployers of certain high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before use, and to notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Deployers of high-risk systems must also keep the logs the system generates, where under their control, for at least six months. The Digital Omnibus moved the application date for Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, so check the final text and your timeline. Which of your systems count as high-risk depends on what they do, and that includes systems used to assess eligibility for public benefits and services.

  4. Cyber and incident rules are stricter for public bodies. Under NIS2, public administration entities of central governments are essential entities, regional ones are covered on a risk basis, and member states may extend coverage to local governments. A significant incident triggers an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. If an agent is involved in an incident, you need to reconstruct what it did quickly.

Add to this the usual public-sector layer: data protection law, public procurement rules, freedom of information duties in many countries, and the expectation that public money is spent transparently. The result is an organisation that is asked to prove its decisions more often than almost any other.

The case: the research office and the cost classification agent

This is a composite, with invented names. A university research office, call it Northfield University, uses an AI agent to prepare the cost statements for dozens of EU and national grants. The agent reads time records, invoices and payroll extracts, classifies each item against the cost categories in each grant agreement, and drafts the periodic financial report. A research accountant reviews a sample before submission.

Year one. The agent classifies a recurring item, a shared equipment service contract, as a direct eligible cost for twelve projects. A prompt update in month five changes how it reads certain invoice descriptions. Staff turnover follows. The accountant who set up the review sample leaves.

Year three. After final payment, a funder audit selects one of the projects. The auditor asks about the service contract cost: why was it classified as direct eligible, which version of the grant rules was applied, what evidence supported it, who verified it, and was the same treatment applied elsewhere?

What Northfield has. The final report, the invoices and some application logs. The logs show the output, not the reasoning inputs. The prompt version in force that month is unclear. The reviewer has left. The agent's classification of the same item in other projects cannot be listed without re-running the whole year.

What the auditor does. Finds the cost ineligible in this project, and asks whether the treatment applies to other grants. The university spends weeks reconstructing, and the answers are partly guesses. Recovery is demanded on the one project, and the finding is extended to the others.

None of this requires fraud. It requires only that nobody could show how the decision was made.

What an auditor, funder or regulator will ask
What source documents did the agent use for this item?
Which version of the grant rules and which cost category definitions applied?
Why was it classified this way?
Who verified it, what did they see and when?
Which model, prompt and configuration were in force?
How many other items and projects were treated the same way?
Has the record been altered since?
Can you produce it for the full retention period?
Why ordinary logs fail the funded organisation
They rotate long before the retention period ends, which can be five years or more after final payment.
They record outputs, not the sources, rules and versions behind them.
They cannot list everything affected by one faulty rule.
They do not show who reviewed what.
They can be edited, and an auditor's first question about any record is whether it is original.
They sit in vendor systems you may no longer have access to when the audit arrives.
Step 1: map agent work to obligations

Start with a register, not with technology. List every task an agent performs, and for each one record which obligation it touches.

Agent task Obligation touched Evidence needed later
Classify costs against grant categories Eligibility of costs, record keeping, audit Source docs, rule version, classification, reviewer
Draft periodic technical or financial reports Reporting accuracy Inputs, draft, edits, approver
Answer citizen or applicant questions Duty of care, transparency Question, sources used, answer, handoff
Triage applications or benefits Fundamental rights, non-discrimination, explanation Inputs, criteria, outcome, human review
Draft procurement documents Procurement rules Sources, changes, approver
Handle incidents or alerts NIS2 reporting, security Timeline, actions, evidence

For every row, name an owner. A task without an owner will not have evidence.

Step 2: record decisions as linked chains tied to the funding context

Each decision should be linked to the grant, work package or programme it affects, so that an audit by grant, by rule or by period is a query and not a project.

python
src = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="source_item",
data={"grant": "HE-101012345", "wp": "WP3", "item_ref": "INV-77421",
"doc_sha256": "", "period": "RP2"})

rule = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rules_applied",
data={"grant_rules": "HE-MGA v1.2 Art 6", "national_rules": "UNI-POLICY-2026-04",
"category_table_v": "9", "prompt_v": "v18", "model": "provider-model-2026-03"},
parent_id=src.id)

cls = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="classification",
data={"category": "direct_equipment_service", "eligible": True,
"basis": ["service contract used only for project equipment"],
"confidence": "medium"},
parent_id=rule.id)

Store references and digests of documents, not full copies, and apply redaction before storage for personal data.

Step 3: separate agent judgment from verified decisions

Where money or rights depend on a decision, record the human step with what the person saw.

python
rev = await db.log(agent="research-accounts", event="human_review",
data={"reviewer": "u-acct-12", "saw": ["invoice", "contract", "classification_basis"],
"action": "confirmed", "sample_type": "risk_based"},
parent_id=cls.id)

Do not log only that someone clicked approve. Log what they were shown, what they changed and why. An auditor will weigh a review more heavily when it shows engagement with evidence.

Step 4: add rules outside the model for the costly mistakes

Put deterministic checks around the decisions that matter most. Examples for a research office: a cost above a threshold needs human review, a cost type flagged as ineligible by the programme's rules cannot be marked eligible by the agent, and an item that matches a known risky pattern, such as shared equipment or overheads, must be flagged.

python
await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rule_check",
data={"rule": "shared_equipment_needs_review", "result": "flag", "blocking": True},
parent_id=cls.id)

A flagged item is held for review. The audit record explains afterwards. The rule prevents.

Step 5: use impact queries to answer extension of findings

When an auditor, or your own review, finds a faulty rule, prompt version or classification pattern, you need to know every item that used it, across every grant.

python
affected = await db.impact(rule.id)

Use it before the funder asks. List the items, correct or document each, and approach the funder with a complete picture. Voluntarily scoping and correcting a problem is a stronger position than having it extended to you.

Step 6: align retention with the funding clock

Set retention from the longest obligation that applies, not from your IT default.

Funding. At least the period in the grant agreement, such as five years after final payment for larger Horizon Europe grants, and longer if an audit is open or national rules require.
Legal hold. When an audit, investigation or dispute starts, suspend deletion for the relevant records.
Data protection. Keep personal data only as long as needed, and decide in advance how erasure requests interact with an integrity-protected record. ZizkaDB supports redaction before storage and forget with tombstones, and your data protection officer should approve the approach.
Exportability. Export and archive before systems are retired, and test that archives can be re-imported and verified.
python
export = await db.export_events(agent="grants-cost-agent", since="2026-01-01", until="2026-06-30")
Step 7: make the record tamper evident, with custody you can defend

Every event in ZizkaDB carries a SHA-256 checksum chained to the previous one for that agent. Any edit, deletion or reordering breaks the chain. Verify on a schedule and store the chain head somewhere your own system administrators cannot edit, such as your records management system or your internal audit function.

python
check = await db.verify_chain(agent="grants-cost-agent")

store check.head with internal audit, and log the verification date

When an auditor asks whether the record is original, you can show a verification result and the independently held head. That proves the record has not changed since the head was stored. It does not prove the record was complete.

Step 8: prepare for the incident clock

If an agent is involved in a security or data incident, NIS2-type reporting starts at awareness: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month. Prepare in advance. Make sure you can freeze and export the relevant chain, list every action the agent took in the window, scope affected records through the impact query, and show who did what during the response. Our incident response how-to covers the 72 hour runbook in more detail.

Step 9: give auditors a clean, safe way in

Create an audit access procedure before you need it.

Use read-only, expiring keys scoped to the grant, period or decision set requested.
Provide a standard export with the chain verification result.
Keep a log of who accessed what.
Run a dry audit once a year with someone outside the team.
python
await db.log(agent="audit-desk", event="auditor_access_granted",
data={"auditor_org": "funder-audit-unit", "scope": "grant HE-101012345",
"expires": "2026-12-31", "approved_by": "u-compliance-3"})
Step 10: choose infrastructure that fits public-sector constraints

Publicly funded bodies often face procurement rules, data residency expectations, sovereignty concerns and vendor exit requirements. Design for them.

Self host inside your own environment or an EU-based environment you control, so the evidence stays in your custody.
Avoid lock-in. Choose tools that are open source, so your team and your auditors can inspect the code, and that are model, LLM and cloud agnostic, so you can change providers without losing history.
Keep it small. A single container on Postgres is easier to secure, accredit and operate than a sprawling platform.
Plan exit. Test exporting and re-importing your records.

ZizkaDB's core is AGPL-3.0, runs self hosted in a single Docker container, and can be placed inside the environment you choose. Whether it meets your security and procurement requirements is for your own teams to decide.

Business objectives and how to measure them
Objective Measure
Protect funding from recovery Share of audited items with a complete evidence chain; ineligible cost found per audit
Cut audit preparation time Hours to answer an auditor request, before and after
Contain a finding early Time from discovering a faulty rule to listing all affected items
Support AI governance duties Share of agent decisions with a full record; FRIA evidence ready
Strengthen future bids and procurement positions Evidence packs provided to funders and partners on request
Reduce reputational risk Citizen complaints resolved with a verifiable account
An illustrative exposure example

This is invented, to show the logic. A university manages 40 EU and national grants worth 20 million euros over the reporting period. If a systematic classification weakness caused 2 percent of the claimed costs to be later found ineligible, the exposure would be 400,000 euros, before the cost of the audit itself and the staff time to rebuild evidence. Even a modest reduction in that risk, or in the time to scope it, can justify the effort of recording decisions properly. Use your own figures.

Common mistakes
Treating AI as an IT matter. The obligations belong to finance, research administration, legal and service owners, not only to the technology team.
Keeping logs for 30 days and grants for 5 years. The shortest retention in the chain sets your real position.
Letting an agent decide eligibility alone. Put rules and human review around money and rights.
Recording output only. An auditor needs sources, rules and versions.
Forgetting the review step. Show what the reviewer saw.
One copy, one custodian. Store the chain head elsewhere.
Assuming the vendor holds the evidence. If the contract ends, so can your access.
Ignoring erasure. Decide the approach before the first request.
A 30 day plan

Days 1 to 5: build the obligation register. List agent tasks, the obligation each touches, the retention period that applies and an owner.
Days 6 to 10: choose one high-value workflow, such as cost classification, and define its event model with research administration, legal and your data protection officer.
Days 11 to 15: instrument the workflow with source, rules, classification and review events, and add the blocking rules for the highest risk items.
Days 16 to 20: set retention and legal hold, test export and re-import, and verify the hash chain with the head held by internal audit.
Days 21 to 25: run an impact query on a seeded faulty rule and measure how fast you can list affected items across grants.
Days 26 to 30: run a mock audit with someone outside the team using the eight questions above. Record the gaps, assign owners and agree the next workflow.

Where ZizkaDB fits, and its limits

ZizkaDB is an open source causal audit database for AI agents. It records each decision as a linked event, answers why() for any outcome, lists everything downstream of a faulty input through the impact route, supports replay and drift baselines, and shows whether stored history has been altered through a SHA-256 hash chain. It is model, LLM and cloud agnostic, and it runs self hosted in a single Docker container, with a managed Cloud edition at db.zizka.ai for multi-agent setups.

It does not decide whether a cost is eligible, assess fundamental rights impacts, report incidents or make a body compliant with any rule. It records what your system captures, so the rules and reviews you add are what prevent errors. The open source edition records one agent per install, so fleets and agent to agent flows use the Cloud edition or separate instances. Take advice from your legal, audit and data protection teams on retention, erasure and what the funder requires.

If you rely on public money and use AI agents, choose one funded workflow this week and trace one claimed cost from the source document to the final report. If you can do it in minutes and show the record is original, you are ready for the audit. If you cannot, you have found the gap before the auditor did.

Corrections: if you represent a party mentioned here and believe a statement is inaccurate, contact us and we will review it promptly.

Sources: Horizon Europe Model Grant Agreement, Articles 20 and 25 (European Commission, EU Funding and Tenders Portal, version 1.2, June 2026), with guidance summaries from the Canadian ISED Horizon Europe guide and the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG); EU AI Act Article 27 and Recital 96 (AI Act Service Desk and artificialintelligenceact.eu) and Article 26 (AI Act Service Desk); Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) commentary; NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 with Irish NCSC, Finnish NCSC and Morrison Foerster guidance; ZizkaDB documentation.

title: Premiere Pro MCP servers compared (November 2026)
description:
If you want an AI to work in Premiere Pro today, without waiting for Adobe's own MCP beta in 2027, there are already five open-source MCP servers on GitHub. We read the README of each on 27 November 2026 and put what they say side by side. We haven't installed and benchmarked all five, so this is a reading of their docs, not a test.

One disclosure first: we make Concierge LLM, a paid desktop agent that also works in Premiere, so we have a stake in this. It's covered at the end, apart from the open-source projects.

The five servers

Project Stars Last update Bridge into Premiere Premiere versions Tools
hetpatel-11/Adobe_Premiere_Pro_MCP 947 19 Nov 2026 CEP panel (UXP experimental) 2020 and later 283, reached through search_tools and invoke_tool
leancoderkavy/premiere-pro-mcp 591 27 Nov 2026 CEP/ExtendScript, plus UXP see its site 453 core, plus 98 when UXP is connected
ayushozha/AdobePremiereProMCP 152 5 Oct 2026 CEP panel 2020 to 2026 74 in the default profile, more behind other profiles
antipaster/Adobe-Premiere-Pro-MCP 53 29 Oct 2026 CEP panel over WebSocket 2023 and later 170+
morim3/mcp_adobe_premiere 5 Apr 2025 UXP plugin not stated a small set

All five are MIT licensed. Star counts are from the GitHub API on 27 November.

What they have in common

They're bridges. Each one runs a small server on your computer and a panel inside Premiere, and the AI on the other end is whatever MCP client you connect: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor are the ones their READMEs name. So the thinking, and the bill for it, comes from that client. If you use a cloud model, every step of an edit is a paid request.

Four of the five use a CEP panel, and the installers of hetpatel-11, leancoderkavy and antipaster switch on Adobe's CEP debug mode (PlayerDebugMode) so Premiere will load an unsigned extension. That's normal for CEP development, but it's a machine-wide setting, and leancoderkavy's uninstaller deliberately leaves it on so other extensions don't break. Worth knowing before you install on a work machine.

How they differ

Tool count isn't the thing to compare. The bigger servers hide most of their tools behind a search step or a profile, because hundreds of tool schemas in one prompt crowd the model's context. ayushozha's default profile shows 74 tools and hides the risky ones (file I/O, external editors) unless you pick an "unsafe" profile, which we think is the right default.

Maintenance varies a lot. hetpatel-11 and leancoderkavy were both updated this month. morim3 hasn't changed since April 2025.

Telemetry. hetpatel-11 sends anonymous usage telemetry by default. Its README shows how to turn it off with PREMIERE_MCP_TELEMETRY=0.

Seeing the footage

None of them ships a model, so how well shots get chosen depends on what your client can see. leancoderkavy goes furthest: its README lists scene detection, still capture and transcription (which asks for consent first), so a client that reads images can look at frames. With the others, the model mostly works from clip names, markers and metadata.

Where Concierge LLM fits

Concierge LLM is a desktop app, not an MCP server you plug into Claude. It brings its own open model, which runs on your graphics card, and drives Premiere, After Effects and Photoshop itself. It looks at the footage before it picks a shot. Our longest timed job: one request became a 35-shot music edit, cut to the beat on a new sequence, in 11 minutes 46 seconds on one RTX 3090. It's $100 once ($50 right now with code LAUNCH50), and it needs a strong PC: a 24 GB graphics card is what we'd want. https://conciergellm.com/?s=devto&c=premiere-mcp

If you already pay for Claude or Codex and want to script Premiere yourself, one of the five above is the cheaper start. hetpatel-11 and leancoderkavy are the most active.

title: How Should Singapore Enterprises Assess AI Delivery Capacity
description:
Singapore enterprises should assess AI delivery capacity by determining whether existing infrastructure, internal expertise, and governance controls can support production AI at a sustainable cost. The assessment should guide a critical investment decision: scale existing initiatives, address capability gaps internally, or engage an AI implementation partner based on verified delivery readiness.

A successful AI pilot does not necessarily mean an enterprise is ready for full-scale deployment. Legacy system dependencies, fragmented data, unpredictable infrastructure costs, and evolving regulatory requirements can turn promising AI initiatives into expensive operational challenges. 

The key consideration is no longer simply whether AI can work, but whether existing capabilities can deliver measurable business value at scale and whether scaling, strengthening internal capabilities, or engaging external expertise offers the most sustainable path forward.

In this guide, Kyanon Digital examines how Singapore enterprises can evaluate AI delivery capacity, identify critical readiness gaps, and make informed decisions about scaling AI initiatives, strengthening internal capabilities, or engaging a specialized implementation partner.

Key takeaways

  • Validate production readiness: A successful AI pilot is not enough. Evaluate whether enterprise data, infrastructure, and engineering teams can sustain real-world workloads.
  • Prioritize measurable business value: Compare expected operational improvements against total implementation and operating costs before expanding AI investment.
  • Balance flexibility with delivery speed: Assess cloud dependencies, vendor lock-in, and switching costs without overengineering infrastructure unnecessarily.
  • Treat governance as a deployment requirement: Address applicable PDPA obligations, AI security risks, and human oversight before introducing AI into business-critical workflows.
  • Close critical capability gaps first: Kyanon Digital recommends validating an end-to-end production workflow before scaling, then deciding whether internal improvements or specialist integration support are needed.

Further reading:

  • How Do You Bridge Data and AI Consulting with Execution? 
  • LLM Integration Services for Enterprise Systems 
  • What Is the True Cost of AI in Manufacturing in Singapore?

Why do enterprise AI pilots fail to scale in Singapore?

Enterprise AI pilots often fail to scale because production environments expose infrastructure limitations, integration complexity, unpredictable costs, and governance gaps. While AI models may perform well in controlled tests, sustainable deployment requires reliable enterprise data, operational ownership, and measurable business value. These gaps can determine whether further AI investment is justified.

According to Gartner (2026), at least 50% of generative AI projects globally were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, largely due to data quality, cost, risk controls, and unclear business value. In Singapore, the Ministry of Manpower's 2026 research found that larger firms identified integration complexity (56.1%) and data security concerns (55.4%) as major barriers to AI adoption.

Key bottlenecks preventing enterprise AI from scaling

  • Fragmented data and legacy infrastructure: Inconsistent data and complex ERP/CRM integrations may require targeted modernization before AI can scale.
  • Unpredictable infrastructure costs: Rising inference, cloud, and maintenance expenses make total cost of ownership (TCO) critical to investment decisions.
  • Security and AI governance risks: Sensitive data exposure and unauthorized AI actions require stronger governance before production deployment.
  • Limited execution capacity: Gaps in AI engineering, MLOps, and operational ownership may justify internal capability development or external expertise.
  • Unclear ROI and business value: Without measurable operational improvements, enterprises risk expanding AI initiatives that cannot justify their costs.

[caption id="attachment_121806" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Overcoming five critical bottlenecks, infrastructure gaps, rising costs, compliance, execution limits, and unclear ROI - is vital for Singapore enterprises to successfully scale AI beyond pilots.[/caption]

Are you risking vendor lock-in with your current AI architecture?

AI vendor lock-in becomes a risk when critical workflows depend heavily on proprietary models, APIs, or cloud infrastructure. For Singapore enterprises, the concern is not using a single provider, but whether future migration, pricing changes, or service disruptions could create unacceptable costs and operational risks.

Key AI vendor lock-in risks to assess

Warning sign Business risk

What to ask your AI vendor

Model and workflow dependency

 Proprietary APIs, RAG pipelines, and agent frameworks increase redevelopment costs. Can critical workflows support alternative AI models?
Cloud and pricing dependency Provider outages, pricing changes, and migration complexity threaten operational continuity.

What are the switching costs and fallback options?

Limited data and IP portability

 Restricted access to business logic, data, or configurations complicates migration and governance.

Who owns these assets, and can they be transferred?

How should enterprises reduce AI vendor lock-in?

Before selecting an AI implementation partner, prioritize three architectural safeguards:

  • Model-agnostic design: Separate business logic, orchestration, and model access to reduce provider-specific dependencies.
  • Open interfaces and portability: Use standardized APIs and modular components where future migration justifies the investment.
  • Tested switching capabilities: Require evidence that an alternative model can support critical workflows with acceptable performance, security, and migration effort.

However, avoiding vendor lock-in should not come at the expense of delivery speed. Managed AI services may be the better starting point when they accelerate deployment without creating unacceptable switching risks.

[caption id="attachment_121808" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] A model-agnostic architecture reduces AI vendor lock-in through modular integration, open APIs, and tested model switching.[/caption]

The key decision: Choose a single-provider architecture when its cost and operational benefits outweigh manageable dependencies. Prioritize greater portability when business-critical AI workflows require long-term flexibility and resilience.

How should enterprises evaluate their AI delivery capacity?

Enterprise AI delivery capacity should be evaluated across business value, data readiness, technical execution, workforce capabilities, and governance. The assessment should test these capabilities against a real business workflow to determine whether the organization can scale AI internally, needs targeted improvements, or requires external implementation expertise.

5 critical areas to assess before scaling enterprise AI

Enterprises should evaluate both internal capabilities and external AI implementation partners across five dimensions before committing to large-scale deployment.

[caption id="attachment_121809" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Evaluating business value, data infrastructure, MLOps, workforce capability, and governance ensures enterprise AI scales reliably and securely.[/caption]

Business value and ROI

  • Baseline performance: Identify existing operational KPIs, such as processing time, error rates, labor costs, and transaction volume.
  • Financial viability: Compare expected business improvements against development, infrastructure, licensing, and maintenance costs.
  • Decision point: Prioritize use cases with measurable business value and clear ownership rather than investing in AI without a validated business case.

Data and technology foundations

  • Data readiness: Check data quality, accessibility, ownership, and compatibility with AI models and RAG pipelines.
  • Infrastructure scalability: Evaluate compute capacity, inference latency, cloud costs, and integration with existing ERP and CRM systems.
  • Decision point: Address critical data and infrastructure gaps before expanding AI workloads.

Technical execution and MLOps maturity

  • Production deployment: Verify experience moving AI solutions from proof of concept into live enterprise workflows.
  • Continuous evaluation: Assess model monitoring, RAG performance, version control, regression testing, and rollback procedures.
  • Agentic workflow testing: For AI agents, evaluate tool usage, execution traces, permission boundaries, and human approval checkpoints.
  • Decision Point: Require production evidence and ongoing maintenance capabilities, not just model demonstrations.

People and operational ownership

  • Technical expertise: Identify gaps across AI engineering, data engineering, cloud, DevOps, and MLOps.
  • Domain knowledge: Ensure business teams can validate AI outputs and manage exceptions in critical workflows.
  • Operating model: Establish clear ownership for deployment, monitoring, incident response, and continuous improvement.
  • Decision point: Determine whether to develop internal expertise, engage external specialists, or adopt a hybrid delivery model.

Governance, security, and compliance

  • Data protection: Review data access, retention, privacy controls, and third-party processing arrangements.
  • AI risk management: Test hallucinations, bias, unauthorized access, and potential information leakage.
  • Auditability: Verify logging, traceability, human oversight, and accountability for AI-generated decisions and actions.
  • Decision point: Resolve material security and governance gaps before deploying AI in business-critical operations.

For Singapore enterprises, AI Singapore's AI Readiness Index (AIRI) provides a broader organizational benchmark, while IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI offers additional guidance for organizations adopting autonomous AI workflows.

How should enterprises turn assessment findings into investment decisions?

The objective is to identify which capabilities are ready, which require improvement, and which need external support.

  • Scale internally: When business value is demonstrated and internal teams can manage production delivery and ongoing operations.
  • Strengthen existing capabilities: When specific data, infrastructure, or engineering gaps can be resolved without replacing the entire technology stack.
  • Engage an AI implementation partner: When complex integrations, specialist engineering, or insufficient delivery capacity prevent internal teams from moving into production.
  • Defer investment: When business value remains unclear or critical security and governance risks are unresolved.

A practical perspective from Kyanon Digital: In its guide to bridging data and AI consulting with execution, Kyanon Digital emphasizes starting with a measurable business decision, prioritizing the first production data path, and establishing accountability beyond deployment.

For example, when evaluating an AI invoice-processing solution, enterprises should test more than document extraction accuracy. They should verify ERP integration, exception handling, approval workflows, processing costs, and the reduction in manual review effort.

The key decision: Invest in the capabilities that make a priority business workflow production-ready. Expand AI deployment only when operational performance, business impact, and ongoing ownership can be demonstrated.

How do you assess the operational risks of undocumented shadow AI?

Shadow AI creates governance gaps when employees use unapproved AI services with enterprise information. An assessment should identify active tools, business purposes, data classifications, access permissions, and approved alternatives. Prioritize sensitive workflows before introducing restrictions or replacing existing tools.

For enterprises needing governed internal AI access, Kyanon Digital's WisdomMind AI platform offers enterprise knowledge retrieval, RAG, access controls, and AI orchestration capabilities.

[caption id="attachment_121812" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] WisdomMind AI by Kyanon Digital enables governed enterprise knowledge access, RAG-powered retrieval, and AI orchestration to help manage shadow AI risks.[/caption]

However, deployment architecture, data residency, provider access, retention, and contractual safeguards must still be verified for each implementation.

How Kyanon Digital scaled AI-powered supply chain automation for a Singapore retailer

Kyanon Digital's Singapore retail supply chain automation project illustrates how enterprise integration and workflow readiness contribute to operational AI delivery.

[caption id="attachment_119807" align="aligncenter" width="960"] AI-powered supply chain automation for a Singapore retailer, integrating supplier document processing, SAP reconciliation, and inventory synchronization into existing enterprise workflows.[/caption]

Challenges

  • Thousands of supplier documents required manual processing.
  • Disconnected SAP, inventory, and financial workflows created reconciliation bottlenecks.
  • Inconsistent inventory information affected omnichannel operations.

Solution from Kyanon Digital

  • Implemented AI-powered supplier document extraction.
  • Integrated automated reconciliation with existing SAP systems.
  • Established event-driven inventory synchronization and exception handling.

Results and impact

[caption id="attachment_115704" align="aligncenter" width="1000"] Kyanon Digital helped the retailer automate supply chain operations, improve inventory accuracy, and scale finance workflows without adding headcount.[/caption]

  • 90% reduction in manual data entry time.
  • Supplier invoice processing reduced from days to under 30 minutes.
  • Over 80% reduction in omnichannel inventory discrepancy incidents.

The project demonstrates the value of connecting AI capabilities to existing enterprise systems and controlled workflows. These outcomes are project-specific and do not establish equivalent results for other implementations.

Explore the full case study Scaling Singapore Retail Operations with Intelligent Supply Chain Automation.

Conclusion

Assessing AI delivery capacity helps enterprises determine whether to scale existing initiatives, strengthen internal capabilities, or engage external expertise. Before expanding AI investment, prioritize production readiness, measurable business value, and manageable operational risks. Address critical capability gaps before committing to large-scale deployment.

Considering your next AI investment? Discuss your AI delivery readiness with Kyanon Digital to identify critical capability gaps and determine whether to scale internally or engage specialist support.

References

  • Why 50% of GenAI Projects Fail — And How to Beat the Odds — Gartner, 2026.
  • Inaugural Release of Report on Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Among Firms — Ministry of Manpower, Singapore, 2026.
  • Guidance by Topic — Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore, 2026.
  • AI Readiness Index (AIRI) — AI Singapore; current framework v3.1 maintained by AIRI Foundation.
  • Updated Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI — Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), 2026.
  • How Do You Bridge Data and AI Consulting with Execution? — Kyanon Digital, 2026.
  • WisdomMind for Transforming Enterprise Knowledge into Strategic AI Assets — Kyanon Digital, 2026.
  • Scaling Singapore Retail Operations with Intelligent Supply Chain Automation — Kyanon Digital.
  • Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions — Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), 2026.

title: Testing Stored Procedures in Postgres — Why PL/pgSQL Only Fails at Call Time, and What a Test Has to Build First
description:
A click on "Duplicate" in the project list, a red notice "The project could not be duplicated", nothing else. The server log has the reason: a procedure reads a column that has not existed for five months. During those five months, the deploy ran green on four environments, production included. The convention check had nothing to complain about, and more than a thousand unit tests were green. None of these nets had ever called the procedure. PL/pgSQL resolves the column names in a body only at call time, and in an empty throwaway database nothing calls the procedure.

This article shows why there is no cheap test layer for the behavior of stored procedures in Postgres, and how to test Postgres stored procedures without installing a tool for it. The means are probes, integration tests against the real database in testing vocabulary: small SQL scripts that build an initial state from synthetic data in the gate's throwaway database, call the real procedure, and check each requirement individually.

The key points up front:

  • Three nets, one gap: A convention check checks the form, the deploy checks that everything can be created, and unit tests stop before the database. None of them checks the behavior of a procedure.
  • A probe is a SQL script that creates test data, calls the real procedure, and writes every result to a table. The checking happens outside SQL, and when it goes red, the stored state comes first, not a guess.
  • The test consists mostly of setup: In the DI² project, 85 percent of the probe code is the SQL files that create test data and call the procedure, 7,266 lines across 22 probes. The checks for them take 1,328 lines of shell script.
  • A probe counts only once it has gone red against the broken state. Performance requirements need volume via generate_series, and a time gate in CI is still a bad idea.
  • Transparency: The project's script, fixtures, and checks come from Claude Code sessions. The maintainer reported the bugs or requested the checks, verified the negative probes, and made the decisions this article is about.

Prerequisite: Postgres and psql, a CI run with a throwaway database as described in GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys, and basic knowledge of PL/pgSQL. All code blocks were executed against PostgreSQL 17.11 in a throwaway Docker container, including the negative probe and the measurement. The examples use a small domain of their own made of customers and orders, and the figures from the DI² project are as of November 5, 2026.

Three Nets, One Gap

In the DI² project, three automated nets stand in front of every merge. A convention check reads every SQL file line by line and checks the form: banners, naming rules, forbidden constructs. What it can and cannot do is in Why sqlfluff Can't Lint Our SQL Conventions. The deploy smoke applies the complete schema to a fresh throwaway database, and it does so twice, so that the second run on an existing state is proven as well. That gate is described in GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys. The application's unit tests check TypeScript, and by an explicit rule only code without database access.

Each of these nets has a job. But no net checks the behavior of a procedure. How big the gap is was measured by a Claude Code session in September 2026, by deliberately removing a working safeguard and then checking whether any net would fire. First it removed from a procedure the block that truncates an overlong text to the column width before the insert, and ran all gates. That block was one half of a fix, the other half lived in the TypeScript. There, a function writes a batch of messages in one transaction. Since the fix, each insert step sits in its own savepoint, so that a failed message rolls back only itself and not the whole batch. The session deliberately removed those savepoints too, ran all gates again, and restored both files afterwards. The question was not whether the safeguard should go, but whether anyone would notice it was gone.

Intervention Convention check Deploy smoke Unit tests
Truncation block removed from the procedure 0 findings green not in scope
Savepoint isolation removed from the TypeScript not in scope not in scope 1,101 of 1,101 green

For the SQL half, the reason is easy to name. The convention check sees form, not behavior. The deploy smoke at the time ran against an empty database, and in an empty database an overlong text never occurs. Both nets were green although the safeguard was gone. For the TypeScript half, it is shorter still: the function accesses the database, and such functions have no unit test by rule. There was nothing that could have gone red.

The case of the vanished column sits one level deeper still, because there not even a call with the right data would have been needed. Any call would have done. The example below reproduces it in the small domain. A procedure copies a customer along with their orders and takes a column legacy_state with it. Three days after this procedure, a schema script removes the column. The next deploy creates the procedure again:

CREATE TABLE shop.customer
(
    id              bigint          GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
   ,name            varchar(100)    NOT NULL
   ,legacy_state    varchar(20)         NULL
);

CREATE TABLE shop.sales_order
(
    id              bigint          GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
   ,customer_id     bigint          NOT NULL REFERENCES shop.customer (id)
   ,amount          numeric(12, 2)  NOT NULL
   ,approved_on     timestamptz         NULL
);

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE shop.sp_dup_customer
(
    IN    p_customer_id        bigint
   ,INOUT p_new_customer_id    bigint
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $procedure$
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO shop.customer (name, legacy_state)
   SELECT
       name || ' (copy)'
      ,legacy_state
   FROM
      shop.customer
   WHERE
      id = p_customer_id
   RETURNING id INTO p_new_customer_id;

   INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount)
   SELECT
       p_new_customer_id
      ,amount
   FROM
      shop.sales_order
   WHERE
      customer_id = p_customer_id;
END;
$procedure$;

-- Three days later, a schema script removes the column.
ALTER TABLE shop.customer DROP COLUMN legacy_state;

-- The next deploy creates the same procedure again, unchanged (abridged here,
-- it is lines 16 to 43 once more). Postgres answers as it did the first time:
-- CREATE PROCEDURE

-- Only the call resolves the body, even with empty tables.
CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(1, NULL);
-- ERROR:  column "legacy_state" of relation "customer" does not exist
-- CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function shop.sp_dup_customer(bigint,bigint) line 3 at SQL statement

Lines 48 to 50 are the point. The repeated CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE goes through although the body reads a column that no longer exists. When creating a PL/pgSQL routine, Postgres checks the syntax and the declarations. The identifiers in the body's SQL statements are resolved only when the statement is executed for the first time, in the example at the first call. A statement in a branch that only a later call passes through is resolved only then. That is how the Postgres documentation describes it in the chapter PL/pgSQL under the Hood, and that is what the context of the error message in line 55 shows: line 3 at SQL statement, not CREATE PROCEDURE. With check_function_bodies switched off, even this check at creation time is skipped, and syntax and declarations are then also checked only at the first call: a body with a typo in the SELECT or an unknown type in DECLARE can be created, and only the CALL reports the error. For the same reason, the schema script in line 46 was allowed to remove the column at all: for the tables and columns that the SQL statements of a PL/pgSQL body use, Postgres registers no dependency, so DROP COLUMN finds no object hanging on the column. A SQL function with a BEGIN ATOMIC body does register them, and there the DROP COLUMN already fails with a hint to the dependent function.

For a CI gate, this means: a deploy that creates a procedure proves that it can be created. What it does, and whether it runs at all, it does not prove.

What Requirement a Probe Checks, and Where It Is Written

A requirement here is a sentence about behavior that the code has to satisfy. "The copy takes over the customer and all orders, but no approval." "An overlong text is truncated to the column width before the insert, without two different texts becoming identical in the process." "No path via the parent table deletes the foreign key of an approved child table." Two of these sentences speak of an approval, a business state of the data. In the DI² project, the owner approves a fully configured table. From that moment on, its configuration is locked: columns can no longer be deselected, the table can no longer be deactivated, and the procedures that try reject the call. In the small domain of this article, an order is approved once the customer has inspected and released the delivery. In the schema, the timestamp approved_on stands for that. A copy starts without approval: what was released was the original, not the copy.

Each probe in the project checks one or a few such requirements, and they are written verbatim in the header of the fixture file, before the first line of SQL. Fixture is the testing term for the prepared initial state a test needs before it can check anything. In this article it means the SQL file of a probe. It creates the test data, calls the real procedure, and writes every result to the result table.

The rule for this is short and came out of the measurement above: SQL behavior belongs in a probe of the deploy smoke. A check is cheap there, because the throwaway database is up anyway and the schema has just been applied. The rule has a counterpart that is just as important. Not every requirement gets a probe. The savepoint half from above, for example, lives in a TypeScript function with database access, and such functions are exempt from unit tests in the project by rule. For every requirement that deliberately stays without a net in this way, the project keeps a row in an inventory table. Its four columns record which requirement it is, why no net checks it, what a refactoring would silently break, and which planned change will close the gap later. Without this entry, a deliberately unchecked requirement would look exactly like one that simply nobody thought of. In both cases there is no test that could go red, and CI is green.

The Initial State Before the Test

What data a single requirement needs is shown by the third one above. "No path via the parent table deletes the foreign key of an approved child table" is one sentence. The probe for it needs two parent tables and two child tables, two foreign keys, a column snapshot of the first parent table, an approval on exactly one child table, and after that seven named cases: deactivating the parent is rejected, deselecting a parent column is rejected, deselecting a different column goes through, the second parent without an approved child may be deactivated, plus three diagnostic rows that record the state afterwards. That is 183 lines of SQL for one sentence.

That is not an outlier, it is the rule. The project's 22 probes consist of 7,266 lines of fixture SQL, and the checks for them of 1,328 lines of shell script. So 85 percent of the probe code is in the SQL files, and in those files only around 15 percent of the lines belong to calling the procedures and recording the results. The rest build the initial state. The three largest probes have 1,030, 944, and 923 lines, and most of that is setup: accounts, projects, memberships, connections, tables, columns, rules, foreign keys, approvals, in the right order and with the right roles.

This is the real complexity of testing database behavior, and it does not lie in the check. The check, in the end, is a counter or a comparison. The work lies in producing a state in which the requirement has any meaning at all. A procedure that protects a foreign key needs a foreign key, an approval, and a caller with the matching role, otherwise there is nothing to protect. And because the probe is supposed to check the behavior against the real database, each of these building blocks has to be real. A stand-in would replace exactly the part that matters. That is where a probe differs from a UI test, which may replace its server with a stand-in that returns a prepared response: a UI test consists of a lot of checking and little setup. A probe consists of a lot of setup and little checking.

The Probe Pattern

The pattern can be shown in full on the small domain. First the corrected procedure, with the requirement in the comment:

-- 155002: The corrected procedure. The requirement on it: the copy takes over the
-- customer and all orders, but no approval.
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Parameter
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
--    p_customer_id        bigint
--       Customer to be copied
--    p_new_customer_id    bigint
--       Id of the copy (returned)
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE shop.sp_dup_customer
(
    IN    p_customer_id        bigint
   ,INOUT p_new_customer_id    bigint
)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $procedure$
BEGIN
   INSERT INTO shop.customer (name)
   SELECT
      name || ' (copy)'
   FROM
      shop.customer
   WHERE
      id = p_customer_id
   RETURNING id INTO p_new_customer_id;

   -- Copy the orders, deliberately not the approvals (approved_on stays NULL).
   INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount)
   SELECT
       p_new_customer_id
      ,amount
   FROM
      shop.sales_order
   WHERE
      customer_id = p_customer_id;
END;
$procedure$;

Then the probe. It consists of four parts: a result table, the initial state, the cases, and a check that runs outside SQL.

-- 155003: The probe. Builds an initial state, calls the real procedure
-- and writes every result to a table. The checking happens outside SQL.
-- For throwaway databases only.
SET client_min_messages = warning;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS shop._probe_dup_customer;
CREATE TABLE shop._probe_dup_customer
(
    label       varchar(40)     PRIMARY KEY
   ,sqlstate    varchar(5)          NULL
   ,message     text                NULL
   ,value       text                NULL
);

BEGIN;

-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Initial state: one customer, two orders, one of them approved
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSERT INTO shop.customer (name) VALUES ('_probe_customer');

INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount, approved_on)
SELECT
    T01.id
   ,T02.amount
   ,T02.approved_on
FROM
   shop.customer T01
   CROSS JOIN (VALUES (100.00, NULL::timestamptz), (250.00, now())) AS T02 (amount, approved_on)
WHERE
   T01.name = '_probe_customer';

-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Cases: an error is caught and recorded, not passed through
-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DO $do$
DECLARE
   l_source      bigint;
   l_copy        bigint;
   l_count       int;
   l_approved    int;
BEGIN
   SELECT id INTO l_source FROM shop.customer WHERE name = '_probe_customer';

   -- Fixture self-test: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise abort.
   SELECT count(*), count(approved_on) INTO l_count, l_approved
   FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source;
   IF l_count <> 2 OR l_approved <> 1 THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'Fixture incomplete: % orders, % approved', l_count, l_approved;
   END IF;

   -- Case 1: The procedure runs through (expected: sqlstate empty).
   BEGIN
      CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(l_source, l_copy);
      INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
      VALUES ('call_ok', l_copy::text);
   EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
      INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, sqlstate, message)
      VALUES ('call_ok', SQLSTATE, SQLERRM);
   END;

   -- Case 2: Both orders are copied (expected: 2).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('order_count', l_count::text);

   -- Case 3: No approval travels along (expected: 0).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count
   FROM shop.sales_order
   WHERE customer_id = l_copy AND approved_on IS NOT NULL;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('approved_copied', l_count::text);

   -- Case 4: The copy's amounts match the original (expected: 0).
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_count
   FROM
   (
      (SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source
       EXCEPT ALL
       SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy)
      UNION ALL
      (SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_copy
       EXCEPT ALL
       SELECT amount FROM shop.sales_order WHERE customer_id = l_source)
   ) T01;
   INSERT INTO shop._probe_dup_customer (label, value)
   VALUES ('amount_diff', l_count::text);
END;
$do$;

COMMIT;

The result table in lines 7 to 13 is the core of the pattern. Each case writes one row with a descriptive label, plus either a value or, if an error occurred, SQLSTATE and message. The label is the primary key, so a probe that writes the same label twice aborts on its own. The probe decides nothing, it records. There are two reasons for that. A RAISE EXCEPTION at the first finding would hide the remaining cases, and an error message that guesses the cause would regularly be wrong, because several requirements can be violated at the same time.

The initial state in lines 17 to 31 is as small as possible and as large as necessary: one customer, two orders, one of them approved. Whether it came out that way is checked by the self-test in lines 45 to 50 before the first case runs: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise the probe aborts.

The cases in lines 36 to 89 call the real procedure. The call in line 54 sits in its own BEGIN block with an EXCEPTION branch. An error is caught and recorded with its SQLSTATE, it does not tear down the probe. This frame assumes that the procedure can run inside the probe's transaction. A procedure that itself executes COMMIT or ROLLBACK needs a different call, more on that in the section on the limits of the pattern. Which error can be caught in the call is shown by the first block: with the old procedure, 42703 would appear here, because the body reads the column legacy_state that no longer exists, and the message would only come at the CALL. A second example sits in the copy itself: the name gets the suffix "(copy)", and for an original with more than 93 characters it no longer fits into varchar(100), error code 22001. Without the EXCEPTION branch, each of these errors would abort the DO block, cases 2 and 3 would never run, and the check would find an empty table with no hint at the cause. If the probe aborts anyway, the error does not come from the call, because that is caught. Then something is wrong with the probe itself, such as a wrong table name in the setup or a typo in a counting query. Such an abort says something about the probe, not about the procedure. The two counters after it check the two halves of the requirement separately: line 63 counts the copied orders, line 68 counts the approvals on the copy. If the requirement is violated, the label shows which half it is. The counter in line 63 checks only the number of orders, not their content, and a procedure that creates two orders with wrong amounts would stay green with it. That is why case 4, from line 74 on, compares the amounts themselves: EXCEPT ALL in both directions returns every order that occurs on only one side, duplicates included, and the target is zero deviations.

The check reads the table from outside:

#!/bin/bash
# 155004: The check. Reads the probe's result table, shows the stored
# rows first when red, and then aborts.
set -u
PSQL=(psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -tA -d "${PGDATABASE:-probe}")

fail() {
  echo "--- Probe red. Stored rows (label | sqlstate | message | value): ---" >&2
  "${PSQL[@]}" -c "SELECT label || ' | ' || coalesce(sqlstate, '') || ' | ' || coalesce(message, '') || ' | ' || coalesce(value, '') FROM shop._probe_dup_customer ORDER BY label;" >&2
  echo "ERROR: $1" >&2
  exit 1
}

# expect <label> <expected> <message>: exactly one row with this label, without SQLSTATE,
# with value = expected. The expected value "*" requires only the row without SQLSTATE.
# If psql cannot read the table, that is red as well.
expect() {
  local row
  row="$("${PSQL[@]}" -c "SELECT count(*) || '|' || coalesce(max(sqlstate), '') || '|' || coalesce(max(value), '') FROM shop._probe_dup_customer WHERE label = '$1';")" \
    || fail "psql could not read the result table."
  [[ "$row" == "1||"$2 ]] || fail "$3"
}

expect call_ok         "*" "The call aborted or left no row behind."
expect order_count     "2" "Expected 2 copied orders."
expect approved_copied "0" "An approval was copied along."
expect amount_diff     "0" "The copy's amounts differ from the original."

echo "Probe green: 4 of 4 checks passed."

It runs in the shell, because the gate is a shell script anyway and needs an exit code. The function fail in lines 7 to 12 prints the stored rows first when red and only then aborts. Whoever reads the run in the CI log sees the actual state and does not have to reconstruct it from a message. The function expect in lines 17 to 22 requires exactly one row without SQLSTATE for each label and compares the value with the expected one. A missing row is thus red and not green, and so is a psql that cannot read the table. The four lines 24 to 27 are the requirement, broken down into four checks.

The values of a probe are chosen so that each violated requirement stands out individually. The probe for the customer therefore creates two orders instead of one, so that "copies all orders" can be told apart from "copies one". One of the two is approved, the other is not. A procedure that copies approvals along thus shows up in case 3, one that skips approved orders in case 2, and one that changes an amount while copying in case 4. None of these defects hides behind another, because the label says which check is red.

The brief for such a probe is short, because the pattern is in place. The following prompt is reconstructed from the bug report and the fixture file, not quoted verbatim from the session:

The procedure for duplicating a project ran green through the deploy for
five months and was broken all the same, because nothing called it.
Write a probe for the deploy smoke following the pattern of the existing
probes: its own fixture file, a result table with label, sqlstate and
message, checks in the script. The requirement it checks: duplicating
takes over everything that makes up the working state, but no approvals.
The original must contain at least one record from every area.
Acceptance criterion: against the state before the fix the probe goes red,
afterwards green, and the CI run stays green.

From this came the project's largest probe with 1,030 lines, and almost all of them build the original, which contains at least one record from every area. The checks at the end are counters.

When a Probe Counts: Negative Probe and Fixture Self-Test

The last sentence of the prompt is the most important one, and it is the one most often left out. A probe that is green has not proven anything yet. It can be green because the requirement is met, or because it never produces the case that would violate the requirement. Without the approved order in the initial state, case 3 would always be 0, with any procedure. Only the negative probe shows the difference: the probe runs against the broken state and has to go red. In the small domain, that means the procedure copies approved_on along by mistake. The probe then reports:

--- Probe red. Stored rows (label | sqlstate | message | value): ---
amount_diff |  |  | 0
approved_copied |  |  | 1
call_ok |  |  | 2
order_count |  |  | 2
ERROR: An approval was copied along.

Three of the four checks pass, the one on the approval does not, and the dump says with which value. The negative probe thus proves that the probe reacts to this one defect. That it would find every other defect of the procedure, it does not prove. Whoever wants to know that introduces further defects one after another, the way mutation tests do systematically. In the project, this probe is part of the deal before a new probe counts. More than forty bug reports record that the new probe went red against the state before the fix, before the fix counted as done. That is the same principle as the counter-check for automated tests in The Green Test That Proves Nothing: a test that does not react to the code does not check it.

For the initial state there is a second trap that the negative probe does not see. A fixture can become ineffective without anything going red. If the approved order in the customer probe were created without approved_on through a typo, case 3 would stay green forever, and nobody would notice. That is why a fixture checks for itself, before the call, whether it has produced the state it is supposed to produce. In the probe above, those are lines 45 to 50: two orders, exactly one of them approved, otherwise the block aborts with an error message, and the check finds no row call_ok. In the project, the fixtures that are applied between the two deploy runs include such a fixture self-test, and all of them answer the same question: does this test still check anything?

Volume Instead of a Minimal State

A minimal initial state proves behavior. For a performance requirement it is worthless, because a customer with two orders is copied quickly in any implementation. The requirement in the project was that a project of a certain size is duplicated in at most ten seconds. For that, the probe needs a project of that size, and it generates one with generate_series: two connections, 200 tables, 10,000 columns, 500 rules, and 300 foreign keys. In the small domain, the same setup looks like this:

-- 155005: Volume fixture and measurement run. 200 customers with 50 orders each,
-- every customer is copied once. Completeness is checked, the duration is printed.
-- For throwaway databases only.
INSERT INTO shop.customer (name)
SELECT
   'perf_' || lpad(n::text, 3, '0')
FROM
   generate_series(1, 200) n;

INSERT INTO shop.sales_order (customer_id, amount, approved_on)
SELECT
    T01.id
   ,(n * 1.5)::numeric(12, 2)
   ,CASE WHEN n % 10 = 0 THEN now() END
FROM
   shop.customer T01
   CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 50) n
WHERE
   T01.name LIKE 'perf\_%';

DO $do$
DECLARE
   l_started     timestamptz;
   l_source      record;
   l_copy        bigint;
   l_expected    bigint;
   l_actual      bigint := 0;
BEGIN
   SELECT count(*) INTO l_expected
   FROM
      shop.sales_order T01
      INNER JOIN shop.customer T02
      ON
        T02.id = T01.customer_id
   WHERE
      T02.name LIKE 'perf\_%';

   -- The clock starts only before the loop: measured is the duration of all 200 calls together.
   l_started := clock_timestamp();
   FOR l_source IN
      SELECT id FROM shop.customer WHERE name LIKE 'perf\_%' ORDER BY id
   LOOP
      CALL shop.sp_dup_customer(l_source.id, l_copy);
      SELECT l_actual + count(*) INTO l_actual
      FROM shop.sales_order
      WHERE customer_id = l_copy;
   END LOOP;

   RAISE NOTICE 'Copied: % of % orders in % ms'
      ,l_actual
      ,l_expected
      ,round(extract(epoch FROM clock_timestamp() - l_started) * 1000);

   -- The gate is completeness, not time.
   IF l_actual <> l_expected THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'Copy incomplete: % of % orders', l_actual, l_expected;
   END IF;
END;
$do$;
-- NOTICE:  Copied: 10000 of 10000 orders in 174 ms

Lines 4 to 19 create 200 customers with 50 orders each, every tenth one approved. The measurement run from line 21 on first determines the expected number, starts the clock in line 39, and then copies every customer once. It records two things: the duration of the whole loop, that is 200 calls including the count after each, and the number of copied orders. Line 55 is the actual check, and it checks completeness, not time. It does not check the content of the copies either, the probe above did that with its minimal initial state. In the container, three runs with the small domain on one day took between 2.2 and 2.9 seconds, ten more on the following days on the same machine between 0.2 and 1.0 seconds. The probe prints this duration but does not decide on it.

That time is not a gate was a deliberate decision in the project, with two reasons. The first is the CI runner, which fluctuates. Before an optimization, the copy under the application role took eleven and twenty-three times the reference, afterwards still seven times, and none of these values works as a threshold. The second reason is more important: the time was a symptom, the cause was the shape of the execution plan. The gate has sat on that plan shape ever since, the duration is only printed, and the ten seconds are measured during the manual check on the development environment.

The most important finding of this probe, however, only came with the third measurement. The first version measured as superuser, because that is how the smoke runs. In operation, the procedure runs under the application role, with row-level permissions and an actor. The actor is the logged-in user that the application passes to the database session, and the row-level permissions refer to them. Only the measurement under this role showed 144 seconds, in one case almost five minutes. As superuser, none of that was visible, because the row-level permissions cost the superuser nothing. Since then, the probe measures three times and requires completeness for each of the three copies. The brief for that, reconstructed:

The performance probe measures the duplication as superuser. That is not
how the procedure runs in the application: there, the application role
with row-level permissions and an actor apply. Please measure the copy
three times, as superuser for reference, under the application role with
an actor and without one, and print all three times. No hard time gate,
the CI runner fluctuates. The only check is that each of the three copies
is complete.

The lesson from this applies to every volume probe: the role is part of the initial state. A measurement under the wrong role measures a different system.

Fixtures Between the Deploy Runs: Backfill and Drift

GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys explains why the gate applies the schema twice: the second run proves that every file is repeatable on an existing state. It proves this, however, only for the state the first run left behind, and that is an empty database with a fresh schema. Two error classes it therefore does not see, and the project closes both with fixtures that are applied between the two runs.

A backfill is a deploy script that brings the existing data up to date after a schema change. In the project, it loops over all active tables and calls, for each one, a procedure that derives new check rules. In the empty throwaway database there is no active table. The loop runs zero times, the call never happens, and the deploy is green. The call runs under the role of the schema owner, and that role once lacked a privilege. On the first environment with data, the deploy would have been red, and in the gate nobody saw it. The backfill fixture therefore creates three records before the second run: a project, a connection, an active table. With that, the loop runs at least once, the call happens, and a missing privilege turns the second run red. How such scripts run exactly once is in Tracking Schema Changes Without a Framework.

The drift fixture simulates an existing database that lags behind the repository: it sets eight check constraints to an old state and creates a row that is valid only under the old constraint. The second run has to bring every definition back to the target state and migrate the row. Without the fixture, there would never be an old constraint for the run to work against.

This is the answer to the open point that "GitHub Actions for Postgres Deploys" ends on. There it says that data-dependent effects stay invisible in the gate, and that the common complement is a nightly run against an anonymized production dump. For requirements on behavior, the synthetic initial state in the same gate is the better answer: it runs on every pull request, it is versioned, it contains exactly the constellation that matters, and it needs no real data. The dump keeps its place where it is about data distribution, lock durations, and runtimes on real volumes. Those are different questions, and they do not belong in the PR gate.

pgTAP, plpgsql_check, and the Limits of the Pattern

Anyone who tests Postgres routines knows pgTAP: an extension that provides assertion functions such as ok(), is(), and results_eq() in SQL, outputs results in TAP format, and fits into any test runner via pg_prove. In the DI² project, pgTAP was never evaluated. The probes grew out of the existing deploy smoke, bug by bug, and there was no tool decision. The difference therefore lies in the packaging, not in the idea. A pgTAP file builds the same initial state and checks the same requirements, only the check is written in SQL instead of the shell. For that it needs an extension in the database and a second runner. The shell variant needs only psql and runs in the same run as the deploy. Whoever starts from scratch and plans many probes anyway should look at pgTAP. Whoever has a deploy gate gets by with the pattern here without a new dependency.

For the error class of the vanished column there is, in addition, a cheaper net than any probe. The extension plpgsql_check checks the body of a routine statically, resolving the identifiers as it goes, and reports the removed column without anyone calling the procedure. Against the broken procedure from the first example, version 2.10 in the container returns:

SELECT * FROM plpgsql_check_function('shop.sp_dup_customer(bigint, bigint)');

error:42703:3:SQL statement:column "legacy_state" of relation "customer" does not exist
Query: INSERT INTO shop.customer (name, legacy_state)
--                                      ^

After the fix, the same query returns zero rows. A call of plpgsql_check_function over all routines of a schema therefore belongs at the end of every deploy run as an additional net, in the gate too. It catches orphaned columns and tables at deploy time, in seconds, without test data. What it cannot see is SQL whose text depends on parameters or data only at runtime and runs via EXECUTE. An EXECUTE string that it can assemble from constants in the body, including via format() or a variable, it does check. Conversely, it reports a temporary table that the body itself creates as missing, although the call goes through. Every finding of the check therefore needs a look into the body before it counts as an error. And what it fundamentally does not catch is everything this article is about: whether the copy takes the approval along, whether the truncation keeps two different texts apart, whether the foreign key survives the detour via the parent table. Those are requirements on behavior, and behavior needs a call with data.

The pattern has limits. Three of them are already visible in the project, a fourth is set by Postgres itself. Probes couple themselves to details: the probe for the text truncation knows the width of the column, and whoever widens the column has to touch two files. The runtime of the gate grows with every probe, and 22 probes today run one after another in a single run. And a probe checks only what someone has written down as a requirement. What nobody has written down is either in the inventory or is left to the manual click. The fourth limit concerns procedures that control their own transaction. Postgres allows COMMIT and ROLLBACK in a procedure only if the CALL sits at the top level in autocommit mode. The call in the probe, by contrast, sits between BEGIN and COMMIT, that is in an explicitly opened transaction block, and additionally in a block with an EXCEPTION branch, which internally opens a subtransaction. Either of the two is enough for the error 2D000, and the probe reports red although the procedure runs flawlessly in the application. For such a procedure, the call needs its own psql invocation without a BEGIN before it, and the check then reads its exit code and the state of the tables afterwards.

Summary

  • Creating a PL/pgSQL routine checks syntax and declarations. The columns and tables in the body are resolved by Postgres only at the first call. A deploy gate therefore proves that a procedure can be created, not that it runs.
  • A probe builds an initial state from synthetic data, calls the real procedure, catches errors, and writes every result to a table. The check runs outside SQL and, when red, shows the state first.
  • The test consists mostly of setup. In the DI² project, 85 percent of the probe code is in the SQL files, and in them only around 15 percent of the lines belong to call and recording. The initial state also includes the role under which the procedure runs in the application.
  • A probe counts only after the negative probe, a fixture only after its self-test.
  • For performance requirements, generate_series generates the volume. The gate is completeness, the time is printed.

For practice, as a decision aid:

Starting point Recommended route
A routine reads columns or tables that may change plpgsql_check over all routines at the end of the deploy run
A requirement on behavior: copies X but not Y, rejects Z Probe with a minimal initial state in the gate, validated by a negative probe
A performance requirement Volume fixture via generate_series, completeness as gate, duration as output, measurement under the application role
A deploy script depends on existing data Fixture between the two deploy runs, with self-test
Data distribution, lock durations, runtimes on real volumes Run against an anonymized dump, outside the PR gate

FAQ

How do you test a stored procedure in Postgres without pgTAP?

With a SQL script that creates the necessary tables and rows in a throwaway database, calls the procedure, and writes every result with a label to a table. Errors are caught in a BEGIN block with an EXCEPTION branch and recorded with their SQLSTATE. A shell script reads the table via psql -tAc, compares the values with the expected ones, and exits with a non-zero exit code on any deviation. In CI, the script runs right after the deploy against the same throwaway database.

Why is the double deploy from the CI gate not enough?

The second deploy run proves that every object file is repeatable on an existing state. But it calls no procedure and works against a database without data. A procedure that reads a removed column can be created any number of times, because Postgres resolves the column names in the body only at call time. And a procedure that copies something wrong only does so once there is something to copy. The first needs any call, the second a call with suitable data. A probe delivers both, and a static check with plpgsql_check delivers the first as well.

Can Postgres check a stored procedure for errors without executing it?

Partly, with the extension plpgsql_check. It analyzes the body of a routine statically, resolves table and column names as it goes, and reports, for example, a column that no longer exists, without anyone calling the procedure. It does not check behavior: whether the procedure copies, rejects, or truncates the right thing only shows in a call with data, that is, in a probe.

How do you know that a probe really checks something?

Through the negative probe. The probe runs once against the broken state, that is against the procedure before the fix or against a version from which the checked line was deliberately removed, and has to go red in the process. If it stays green, it does not reach the requirement. For fixtures, a self-test is added that proves the fixture really produced the state, for example through a counter on the created rows.
