The first run reports everything that matches and records it. "1 paid requests" is not a typo: @golang and @NASA came from the cache of the previous search (same URL, under 30 minutes old), and only @github was fetched. @github had no post over 1,000 likes in its window. The 👀-only post from @golang has the language code art. Posts without real words get codes like that: I saw art and zxx (just a link) in these runs, and X also uses und and qme. lang:en drops all of them.

A later run, after the cache expired:

fetched 51 posts (51 unique), 13 match, 3 paid requests; coverage warnings: public_api:latest_window_limited, public_api:module_entries_omitted
0 new since last run
CREATED (UTC)  AUTHOR  LANG  LIKES  RTS  REPLIES  VIEWS  TEXT

That run was at 04:45 UTC, 34 minutes after the first, with three fresh requests (3 credits). Nobody had posted anything over 1,000 likes in between, so nothing was reported and nothing was appended. That's the normal case for a watcher, and it's why the state file matters: without it, every run would report the same 13 posts again. The state file only tracks IDs, though. A post that crosses min_faves:1000 later is reported on the first run where it qualifies. A post that was already reported is never reported again, even if its likes triple. If you want that, store counts per run instead.

A crontab line that checks every two hours and logs new matches:

0 */2 * * * cd /opt/xsearch && ./xsearch watch -state data/state.json -out data/matches.jsonl 'from:golang OR from:github OR from:NASA -filter:retweets min_faves:1000' >> data/watch.log 2>&1

Each line in matches.jsonl is one post with a seen_at time. Here is the first one, pretty-printed and with the text shortened:

{
  "seen_at": "2026-11-27T04:11:30Z",
  "id": "2125318351341994436",
  "author": "NASA",
  "created": "2026-11-24T19:59:16Z",
  "faves": 37785,
  "retweets": 3322,
  "replies": 2162,
  "views": 14042369,
  "url": "https://x.com/NASA/status/2125318351341994436",
  "text": "As part of a coordinated, whole-of-government effort, NASA has rapidly mobilized..."
}

Twelve runs a day over three accounts is 36 credits a day. The account window (about 20 posts) is the real limit on the interval: for an account that posts 30 times a day, every two hours is too slow, and posts drop out of the window before you see them.

Pitfalls, in one place

  • Logged-out search is gone. x.com/search redirects to login, the API needs a token, the syndication timeline returns 429. Don't build on any of them, and don't automate a logged-in session.
  • Search-by-keyword is discovery, not a firehose. The web index gives about 10-20 relevant posts per keyword, in relevance order, across months. Treat the results as a sample and say so in anything you report.
  • Operators sent to the search endpoint don't work. from:golang since:2026-11-01 returned nothing. Send words, filter locally.
  • Timelines are a window, not an archive. About 20 latest posts. since/until filter inside that window and return nothing outside it (latest_window_limited).
  • Retweet shells have 0 likes and truncated text. Read the original from retweeted_status_result, or exclude retweets.
  • Use note_tweet for long posts. full_text stops near 280 characters, and some long posts have no note at all.
  • Whole-word matching is strict. api doesn't match "APIs". Write the variants with OR.
  • Counts move between runs. The same post had 6,605 likes in one response and 6,606 in the next. Store snapshots with a time if you want trends. Don't compare across runs as if they were exact.
  • Language codes include art, zxx, und and qme. lang:en silently drops emoji-only and link-only posts. A two-word English post can also come back as da (one @golang post did).
  • Credits add up with OR. Every alternative in the first OR group is a separate search, and every page is 2 credits. Run explain first.
  • The official X API doesn't support min_faves. If you move this tool to the official API later, keep the local filter: engagement floors stay client-side there too.

Wrapping up

  • Advanced search can be split in two: fetch candidates, then filter with operators you implement yourself. In Go that's a ~290-line parser plus a table of tests.
  • from: queries are precise; keyword queries are a sample. Print the coverage warnings next to every result, so nobody reads "14 matches" as "14 posts exist".
  • explain before search saves credits and surprises, and watch with a state file turns the whole thing into a cron job.
  • X's terms ban scraping. Read them, prefer the official API where it fits, keep volumes small, and keep individual people's handles out of anything you publish.

*I build it.

title: How I Built a 93 KB Client-Side GIF89a & WebCodecs Studio Without COOP/COEP Headers
description:
Most browser-based GIF editors take one of two trade-offs: they either upload every frame to a remote processing server, or they ship a ~30 MB WebAssembly FFmpeg bundle that requires strict Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy headers.

While building Offline GIF Editor, I wanted a zero-upload studio that opens instantly under a strict 95 KB raw core JS budget, runs 100% locally in the browser with zero COOP/COEP headers, and still handles real-world edge cases like animated transparency disposal, chat file-size caps, and multi-format video exports.

Here are the four engineering decisions that made the biggest difference:

1. Keep an Immutable baseDelay Per Frame to Eliminate Speed Drift

GIF frame delays are quantized to centiseconds (10 ms ticks). If you multiply frame delays in place when a user clicks 2x and then 1x, rounding error accumulates quickly—and custom loop repeat counts often get silently overwritten.

Instead, store each frame's original baseDelay separately and recompute active delays from that baseline whenever the user toggles 0.5x, 2x, 3x, or 1x. In the GIF Speed Changer, that keeps 2x -> 3x -> 1x bit-exact and preserves custom loop counts.

2. Edge-Connected Flood-Fill Transparency Instead of Global Chroma Key

Global color replacement ruins stickers and UI captures: removing white backgrounds also punches holes through eyes, highlights, or text labels.

Seeding a breadth-first flood fill strictly from the border pixels (plus optional click seeds) with a real-time canvas preview and auto-detected 5-color frame swatches solves this cleanly. You can test the live cutout behavior on the GIF Background Remover, where interior white pixels remain 100% opaque while border regions export clean GIF89a alpha.

3. Lazy-Load gifsicle-wasm Only When Compression Is Requested

Discord animated emojis cap at 256 KB and Slack animated emojis cap at 128 KiB. Shipping a WASM optimizer on initial page load hurts Core Web Vitals, so the core workbench boots with lightweight JS decoding/encoding (gifuct-js + gifenc) and only lazy-imports gifsicle-wasm-browser when the user opens the GIF Compressor or clicks an Auto-Fit preset.

4. Pure-JS Animated WebP/APNG Frame Compositing + WebCodecs MP4

Safari/WebKit still handles multi-frame transparent WebP and APNG inconsistently when drawn straight to a canvas. Extracting frame chunks in pure JS, decoding via createImageBitmap, and compositing disposal rectangles manually keeps 100% alpha parity across Chrome and WebKit in WebP to GIF, while WebCodecs handles hardware-accelerated H.264 exports in GIF to MP4.

Everything runs completely on-device with zero uploads and zero login at offlinegifeditor.com. Feedback from anyone else working with binary image codecs in the browser is very welcome!

title: Cloudflare MoQ CDN: Scale Sub-Second Live Streams in 10 Minutes
description:
You have MoQ running on Ant Media Server, and now you need to serve more viewers than one server can handle. Right now every viewer connects to the relay on your server, and that relay is limited by the server’s network bandwidth. A Cloudflare MoQ CDN takes that load off your server.

HLS solved the same problem years ago with a CDN. One origin server produces the stream, and the CDN caches it near the viewers and serves it from there. MoQ follows the same pattern, so a Media over QUIC CDN is a network of relays instead of caches. Cloudflare runs MoQ relays all around the world, and the Ant Media Server MoQ plugin can push to them with one setting change.

By the end of this post you will have your stream playing through Cloudflare’s relays, and you will know why that scales where a single relay does not. The setup takes about 10 minutes on a server that already has the plugin. If you do not have it yet, start with the MoQ announcement post or the MoQ on AWS walkthrough.

Table of contents

  1. Why does one MoQ relay run out?
  2. How does the Cloudflare MoQ CDN fan out?
  3. Set up the Cloudflare MoQ CDN in 10 minutes
  4. Test it: watch your stream come out of Cloudflare
  5. What’s next once your stream plays from the Cloudflare MoQ CDN?
  6. Before you build production on it
  7. Frequently Asked Questions

Why does one MoQ relay run out?

It runs out of network bandwidth long before it runs out of CPU. Every viewer gets their own QUIC connection, their own encrypted copy of every frame, and their own retransmissions when their Wi-Fi drops a packet. Nothing in that list gets cheaper as the audience grows. The thousandth viewer costs the relay as much as the first one did.

A 1 Gbps port can feed about 330 viewers of a 1080p stream at 3 Mbps, and a 10 Gbps port about 3,300. Adding a 720p rendition does not change that. The server then encodes and sends two streams, and every viewer still uses their own share of the bandwidth. A bigger instance does not move that ceiling by much.

The second limit is distance. Say a viewer sits 150 ms away from your server. Every lost packet takes a 150 ms round trip to recover, and the player’s jitter buffer grows to cover that. A relay 10 ms from the same viewer recovers the same loss in 10 ms, so the buffer can stay at the player’s default of 250 ms.

How does the Cloudflare MoQ CDN fan out?

The CDN keeps one connection per track to your Ant Media Server, no matter how many viewers it serves. Your server publishes each stream to the Cloudflare relay nearest to it. A viewer lands on the relay nearest to them, wherever they are, and that relay pulls the stream across Cloudflare’s network once for all of its viewers. Relays pass the media through without decoding it, so your encoder settings reach the viewer unchanged.

MoQ through a relay CDN gets you WebRTC’s delay and HLS’s way of scaling. A WebRTC edge holds a session for every viewer, so a bigger audience means more edge nodes. An HLS CDN carries the audience for you, but it caches segments, so viewers watch seconds behind. A MoQ relay holds one subscription per track and passes each frame on as it arrives, so it has neither problem. It is still in beta, so run the embedded relay until the server’s bandwidth is the limit, then add the CDN URL.

What does the plugin do with a CDN URL?

It publishes every stream twice. Setting moqCdnUrl adds a second destination, it does not replace the embedded relay. For every stream, and every ABR rendition of it, the plugin starts one extra moq process that sends the already encoded frames to the CDN. Nothing is re-encoded, and the broadcast names are the same on both ends: live/studio1/source, live/studio1/720p.

Everything else is untouched: ingest, playback from your own server, recording, HLS and WebRTC. If the connection to Cloudflare stalls, only the CDN copy drops frames. Viewers on your own relay never notice.

Publish to your server, never to Cloudflare. The CDN only delivers streams to viewers. The browser publisher, OBS and every other source still connect to your Ant Media Server, and the plugin forwards the stream to Cloudflare.

The plugin verifies Cloudflare’s TLS certificate. Only the local connection to your embedded relay, which uses a self-signed certificate, skips that check.

Set up the Cloudflare MoQ CDN in 10 minutes

You need Ant Media Server 3.0.0 or later with the 3.1.0 release of the MoQ plugin installed, and HTTPS on. On a new AWS instance, the MoQ on AWS post gets you there in four steps. On a server you already run, follow the MoQ docs page. You also need a Cloudflare account. Cloudflare’s MoQ docs cover the relay side in more detail than this post does.

  1. Create a relay in Cloudflare In the Cloudflare dashboard go to Media > Realtime > MoQ Relay, select Create relay, give it a name and confirm. You get two tokens, a publish token for your server and a subscribe token for your viewers. They are shown once and Cloudflare does not store them, so copy both now.

You can also create relays through Cloudflare’s API.

The publish token is the whole URL the server will use.

  1. Give the publish token to the plugin Open your application in the web panel, go to Settings > Advanced, and add the key inside customSettings: 
{
  "customSettings": {
    "plugin.moq": {
      "moqCdnUrl": "https://draft-16.cloudflare.mediaoverquic.com/<PUBLISH_TOKEN>"
    }
  }
}

Save, then restart the application so the plugin picks up the new setting. The host has to be draft-16. A draft-14 host is the trap: it accepts the publish and the logs look healthy, but no viewer can ever find the stream. The next stream that starts writes this line to /usr/local/antmedia/log/ant-media-server.log:

MoQ: 2 muxer(s) publishing for stream studio1, with CDN: true

A stream without ABR renditions gets two muxers, one for your relay and one for Cloudflare.

Ant Media Server Settings Advanced with the plugin.moq custom setting and moqCdnUrl.

One key under customSettings is the whole Cloudflare MoQ CDN configuration.

Test it: watch your stream come out of Cloudflare

Now the fun part. Start a stream on your server the way you already do. The plugin’s browser publisher at https://your-domain:5443/live/moq/publish.html is the quickest, and OBS, SRT, WHIP or an IP camera work just as well. Call it studio1.

Use Chrome for this test. Chrome, Edge and Safari 26.4 or later play MoQ, but Firefox is still unstable for it. Open the plugin’s player with your subscribe token as the url parameter:

https://your-domain:5443/live/moq/play.html?url=https://draft-16.cloudflare.mediaoverquic.com/&name=live/studio1/source

Done. The page loads from your server, but the media now comes from the Cloudflare relay nearest to you. Send the link to a friend on another continent. Their copy comes from a relay near them, and your server still sends Cloudflare just one copy.

The quality buttons stay empty on Cloudflare hosts, because the player turns off stream discovery there. To watch a rendition, change name in the URL, for example to live/studio1/720p.

The debug panel under the video shows frame rate and buffer. Set the player beside the source going in, and the two timecodes stay within a fraction of a second of each other. That small gap is what Cloudflare’s path adds for your viewers.

Ant Media Server MoQ player playing a stream from a Cloudflare relay next to the live source.
The same stream playing back from a Cloudflare relay, next to the live source.
What’s next once your stream plays from the Cloudflare MoQ CDN?
Your server now sends each track out once, and Cloudflare carries it to every viewer, wherever they are. The 330-viewer ceiling of a 1 Gbps port no longer caps your audience, and in the side-by-side test the Cloudflare copy stays within a fraction of a second of the source.

If your origin is still a test box, the AWS deployment guide gets a fresh MoQ origin running in four steps, and the same moqCdnUrl setting works there unchanged.

To prove the whole path on your own stream before you commit, from ingest through the embedded relay to the Cloudflare relays nearest your viewers, install the plugin on a MoQ test server under the 14-day Ant Media Server Enterprise Edition trial. No credit card is required, and you can watch your server’s outbound bandwidth stay flat while viewers join through Cloudflare.

Ant Media Server Free Trial – On-Premise or AWS (14 Days)

Choose your Ant Media Server free trial: 14-day on-premise (full control) or 7-day AWS Marketplace (instant launch).

antmedia.io

Contact Us - Ant Media

Contact us and let our experts find the right live streaming solution for you. Reach out today and we'll get back to you shortly.

antmedia.io

Before you build production on it

Check these five limits before you send real viewers through Cloudflare:

  • Cloudflare’s relays are in beta, with no SLA published, and Cloudflare says the API may change.
  • Only the draft-16 host works with the plugin today. Cloudflare already recommends draft-18 for new deployments and keeps draft-16 open for existing clients. MoQ is still an IETF draft, so expect version bumps on every side, including a new Cloudflare hostname.
  • One subscribe token serves all viewers. Per-viewer playback auth through Ant Media Server play tokens is designed but not shipped yet.
  • A viewer who joins late starts at the live edge, because Cloudflare’s relays do not offer rewind yet.
  • Viewers need Chrome, Edge, Brave or Safari 26.4 or later. Firefox has WebTransport, but the plugin docs list it as unstable for MoQ playback.

title: From Monitoring Alerts to IT Actions: A Practical Guide to Closing the Loop
description:
A monitoring alert is only useful if it changes what someone does next.

A dashboard can show a full fleet's CPU, disk, and security events and still leave an operator with the same question: "What should I do about this?" The gap isn't a lack of data. It's the missing path from signal to decision.

We think monitoring should be designed around that path. In this article, we'll turn a few common signals into practical, testable actions - and show how to avoid building an alert system that creates more work than it removes.

Start with the decision, not the metric

A metric is not actionable just because it crosses a threshold. "Disk usage is 85%" is a fact. It doesn't say whether the disk is filling steadily, whether a temporary job caused the spike, or who should respond.

Before adding a monitor, write down the decision it should support:

  • What condition is the monitor detecting?
  • What user or service impact could follow?
  • Who owns the response?
  • What is the first safe action?
  • When should the issue be escalated?

If the team can't answer those questions, keep collecting the metric, but don't page on it yet. An unowned alert is a notification with nowhere to go.

Turn a threshold into context

Thresholds are useful for catching immediate risk. Trends are what help distinguish an incident from normal variation.

For example, 85% disk use can mean very different things:

  • A stable volume has been at 85% for months and has enough headroom.
  • A volume has moved from 70% to 85% in a week.
  • A volume grew 2% in the last hour and is still climbing.

The same point-in-time value calls for different responses. Add rate of change, a comparison window, or a known operating baseline where it changes the decision.

A simple rule can estimate time to exhaustion from recent measurements. This Python example assumes the readings are evenly spaced and expressed as percentages:

from collections import deque
from statistics import mean

# (minutes since start, disk usage percent)
readings = deque([
    (0, 72.0),
    (60, 73.0),
    (120, 75.0),
    (180, 78.0),
], maxlen=12)

def estimate_minutes_to_full(samples, limit=95.0):
    if len(samples) < 2:
        return None

    elapsed = samples[-1][0] - samples[0][0]
    if elapsed <= 0:
        return None

    # Percentage points per minute, averaged across the window.
    rate = (samples[-1][1] - samples[0][1]) / elapsed
    if rate <= 0:
        return None

    remaining = limit - samples[-1][1]
    return max(0, round(remaining / rate))

minutes = estimate_minutes_to_full(readings)
if minutes is not None and minutes < 24 * 60:
    print(f"Investigate disk growth: estimated {minutes} minutes to 95%")

This is a starting point, not a forecasting system. A short window can overreact to a backup or deployment, while a long window can hide a sudden change. In production, calculate on a rolling window, account for missing samples, and make the threshold depend on the volume's role.

Give every alert an owner and a first move

An alert should carry enough information to begin triage without a second round of detective work. At minimum, include the affected host or service, the observed value, the time window, severity, owner, and a runbook or first check.

For instance, this configuration describes a monitor in terms of response, not just measurement:

name: disk-growth-risk
scope: customer-host
condition:
  metric: disk.used_percent
  above: 80
  duration: 15m
  trend:
    minimum_growth_percent_per_hour: 1.5
severity: warning
owner: platform-operations
summary: "Disk usage is high and growing on {{ host }}"
first_action: "Check largest directories and recent scheduled jobs"
runbook: "https://docs.example.net/runbooks/disk-growth"
maintenance_silence: true

The exact schema depends on your monitoring stack. The important part is that an operator shouldn't have to infer whether this is urgent, who owns it, or where to start.

Severity should reflect response urgency and impact, not how dramatic a metric looks. A warning that can wait until the next shift is different from a condition that risks taking a customer-facing service offline in minutes.

Use fleet data to find patterns, then scope the response

A fleet-level view is good for spotting patterns: many endpoints reporting the same failure, a patch-related change affecting one OS version, or one customer's machines drifting from their usual baseline. But remediation must stay scoped to the right account and host.

That distinction matters especially in multi-tenant operations. A query that aggregates fleet health can help identify a shared issue, but the action that follows should target only the authorized customer's devices. We built LynxTrac's monitoring and security views around customer-scoped access for this reason: operators need cross-device context without crossing customer boundaries.

A safe workflow looks like this:

  1. Detect a pattern across the authorized fleet or customer scope.
  2. Confirm whether the affected hosts share a relevant property, such as OS version or recent change.
  3. Choose a limited set of hosts for investigation or remediation.
  4. Record the operator, target, timestamp, and outcome.
  5. Verify that the signal changed after the action.

For security findings, keep the evidence attached to the response. File changes, configuration assessment results, and alerts mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics can help an operator understand whether an event is isolated or part of a broader pattern. A flat event list is harder to turn into a defensible decision.

Measure whether monitoring is helping

The number of monitors says very little about operational quality. We'd rather track a small set of measures that reveal whether signals lead to useful work:

  • Alert-to-incident ratio: How many alerts become real incidents rather than being dismissed?
  • MTTA and MTTR: Are the right people acknowledging and resolving issues promptly?
  • Owner coverage: What share of alerts has a named responder?
  • Agent coverage: What share of the managed fleet is reporting current data?
  • Remediation outcome: Did the action resolve the condition, or did it recur?

These measures need context. A falling alert count could mean better signal quality, or it could mean monitoring stopped reporting. Pair operational metrics with coverage and review them over time, not as a single weekly score.

A practical cadence is a short weekly review. Look at the alerts that were dismissed, repeated, or lacked an owner. Remove rules that don't lead to a decision, and improve the ones that produce avoidable investigation. Don't add a new dashboard panel until you know which operational question it answers.

Monitoring is a feedback loop

The useful loop is straightforward: observe a signal, interpret it in context, take a bounded action, and verify the result. If the action doesn't change the condition, or if the alert keeps recurring, the monitoring design needs another look.

That's why we see monitoring as more than a live graph or notification. It should connect infrastructure health, endpoint inventory, security context, access controls, and an auditable record of what happened. The tools can vary; the operational test is whether the next step is clear and safe.

A good starting point is to choose three alerts your team sees every week and ask: who owns each one, what decision does it support, and how do we know the response worked? Which signal in your environment still produces more investigation than action?

title: NFS2ROOT on CentOS 7: the stock kernel is affected and gets no fix
description:
NFS2ROOT (CVE-2026-99362) is a pre-authentication heap overflow in the Linux kernel's NFS server. A client that can reach TCP 2049 shrinks its NFSv4.1 session reply cache to zero bytes, pads a SEQUENCE request, and nfsd copies the whole reply into the empty slot buffer. No account or export access is needed. The kernel.org CNA rates it CVSS 9.8, Red Hat rates it Critical.

On CentOS 7 it reaches every NFS server running the defaults:

  • Stock 3.10: affected, per Red Hat, and the CentOS 7 source carries the same unbounded copy. nfsd serves +4.1 +4.2 out of the box, and having no exports does not help: the overflow happens during session setup. CentOS 7 gets no kernel updates.
  • ELRepo kernel-lt 5.4.278 and kernel-ml 6.9.7: inside the affected range (3.16 and later), and both lines ended without a fix.
  • CentOS 8: RHEL 8 got the fix on 2026-11-26 (4.18.0-553.190.1.el8_10), CentOS 8 did not. AlmaLinux 8, Rocky 8 and Oracle Linux 8 already ship that kernel, so converting in place is the free way out.

The fix

Disclosure: I maintain this package. GetPageSpeed's kernel-lt has carried the fix since 6.18.62-1, published on 2026-11-07, twelve days before the CVE went public. It uses the same package name as ELRepo, installs beside your current kernel, and is free for any use:

yum -y install https://extras.getpagespeed.com/release-latest.rpm
yum -y install yum-utils
yum-config-manager --enable getpagespeed-extras-corecare
yum -y install kernel-lt
grub2-set-default 0
grubby --default-kernel
reboot

Already on our 6.18 kernel but older than 6.18.62? yum -y update 'kernel-lt*', then check grubby --default-kernel before you reboot: builds before 6.18.62-2 did not move the GRUB default on update. uname -r after the reboot is the check that counts, not rpm -q.

The exposure checks, Red Hat's stopgap (stop nfs-server or firewall 2049) and the rollback are in the full write-up.

title: Mapping free street parking from open data with PostGIS and MapKit
description:
This post covers why OpenStreetMap gives kerb-level parking in only some
cities, how I turn a council's paid streets into "likely free" kerbs with
PostGIS, how that guess stays apart from real facts, and how SwiftUI's Map
draws a city's kerbs without stuttering. The app is Easy Find Parking, a free
iPhone and iPad map of free street parking in Berlin, Madrid, Barcelona,
València and Kraków,
on the App Store;
the user's side is in a separate post.

Server: Flask, PostGIS and a self-hosted ParkAPI. Phone: SwiftUI on iOS 17.

OpenStreetMap street parking is mostly a German dataset

My first plan was OpenStreetMap everywhere. Kerbside parking is tagged on the
street itself, with keys like parking:left=lane and parking:right:fee=no
(see Street parking on
the OSM wiki). When I measured in September 2026, this was the share of
drivable streets carrying any parking:* tag:

City Streets with parking:* tags
Berlin 99.9%
Hamburg 54%
Warsaw 26%
Lyon 22%
Milan 11%
Paris 10%
València 7%
Barcelona 4%
Lisbon 0.9%

Fee sub-tags were on about a tenth of those. Berlin works: 64,229 kerb sides and
48,567 car parks from one Geofabrik extract. Elsewhere a tag-driven layer would
be mostly blank, which reads as "no parking here". So outside Germany the
street layer comes from municipal open data, which the city actually enforces.

Reading the tags has traps. The wiki deprecated the older parking:lane=* and
parking:condition=* keys in December 2022 and asks for existing ones to be
converted, so the normaliser reads both. parking:left=no is a value, not an
absence: 43% of Berlin's tagged sides. And without closed_ways_are_polygons
in its config, GDAL put closed amenity=parking ways in the lines layer, where
my highway filter dropped them: Berlin had 42 car-park polygons instead of
63,294.

Deriving "likely free" from what a city charges for

Councils publish what they charge for, because that's what they enforce.
Barcelona's
surface parking dataset
lists its blue, green and goods-delivery segments; Kraków publishes 23 paid-zone
polygons and no kerbs. The complement is the free map: every drivable street
inside the city boundary with nothing regulated near it.

CREATE TEMP TABLE regulated AS
SELECT geom FROM efp.street_parking
WHERE city_id = :'city' AND fee_source IN ('municipal_paid', 'municipal_free')
UNION ALL
SELECT geom::geography FROM efp.paid_zone WHERE city_id = :'city';  -- Kraków's polygons

-- ...
FROM osm_stage.streets_REGIONTAG s
CROSS JOIN (VALUES ('left'), ('right')) AS sides(side)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM city_boundary b WHERE ST_Within(s.geom, b.geom))
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM regulated r
      WHERE ST_DWithin(efp.kerb_offset(s.geom, sides.side)::geography, r.geom, :clearance))
  AND s.highway IN ('residential', 'living_street', 'unclassified', 'tertiary', 'tertiary_link')
  AND lower(coalesce(s.access, '')) NOT IN ('private', 'no', 'customers')

Three of these are there because a looser version published something wrong.

Metres, not degrees. The first version buffered by 0.00025°. At
Barcelona's latitude that's 27.8 m north–south but 20.8 m east–west, and 407
streets 21–25 m from a paid kerb went out as free. Casting to geography makes
ST_DWithin measure in metres; :clearance is 25.

Test the kerb, not the centreline. efp.kerb_offset shifts the street 3 m
to one side, working in EPSG:3857 and dividing the distance by cos(latitude) to
undo Mercator's stretch. That line can sit closer to a paid kerb than the
centreline, so it's the one tested.

Leave out roads with no parking. The first run turned 17,275 regulated
segments into 10,842 free kerb sides, and the map showed dashed "likely free"
lines down Avinguda Diagonal. Arterials have no regulated segments because
nobody parks on them, so "outside every paid zone" came out true. Limiting the
rule to residential, unclassified and tertiary roads dropped 3,156 sides, 29%
of the layer. Service roads stay out: they're car-park aisles and driveways as
often as public kerb.

Kraków's polygons feed the same rule: 21,255 free kerb sides, none within 25 m
of a zone. A test samples 2,000 derived kerbs per city to assert
it. Checking every row took over 150 seconds at 29,000 derived against
105,000 regulated, and a check nobody waits for is a check nobody runs.

Free and likely free are different values

The schema never stores a bare "free". Every row has a fee_state (FREE,
PAID, CONDITIONAL, UNKNOWN) and a fee_source saying where it came from:
municipal_free, osm_tag, operator_feed, municipal_paid_complement and
municipal_outside_zone.

The last one came from Madrid, whose SER map service publishes 87,614 kerb
bands. 53,158 are grey, a colour missing from the service's own legend.
Sampling 300 bands of each colour against the SER boundary settled it: every
blue and green band tested fell inside, no grey one did. So grey bands are
published kerbs outside the paid zone: stronger than an inference from nothing,
weaker than the council saying "free". I first stored them as
municipal_paid_complement, and the overlap test failed, correctly: grey bands
sit next to blue ones on the same street, which for a derived street would be a
bug.

One function turns the pair into a claim, ordered by trust: a current count, a
published fact, a schedule, an inference, an admitted gap.

switch (feeState, feeSource) {
case (.free, .municipalFree), (.free, .operatorFeed):
    return .cityFree
case (.free, .osmTag):
    return .signpostedFree
case (.free, .municipalOutsideZone), (.free, .municipalPaidComplement):
    // This is the inference, and it must never borrow a stronger phrasing.
    return .likelyFree
case (.free, _):
    // A free claim with no provenance is not one we will repeat.
    return .unknown
default:
    break
}

Charging hours the parser can't read resolve to "charged right now": wrong
that way costs a walk, the other way a fine.

On the first build the inferred layer was mint and read as the same free as
the confirmed green. Now it's teal and dashed, which says "not solid" before
anyone reads the legend:

ForEach(model.streets) { street in
    MapPolyline(coordinates: street.coordinates)
        .stroke(street.claim.tint.opacity(0.85),
                style: street.claim.isInferred ? .inferredKerb : .kerb)
}

private extension StrokeStyle {
    static let kerb = StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 4, lineCap: .round, lineJoin: .round)
    /// Dashed: derived from an absence of regulation, not from a sign.
    static let inferredKerb = StrokeStyle(
        lineWidth: 4, lineCap: .butt, lineJoin: .round, dash: [3, 7])
}

Both hedged kinds draw the same dashed teal; the data keeps them apart.

Drawing kerbs with SwiftUI's Map

That ForEach is the whole renderer, and its cost is the count: a city-wide
Barcelona viewport holds around 660 kerbs. The obvious fix is one
MKMultiPolyline per style, about four overlays, but MapPolyline has no
initialiser that takes one. So I rewrote the map as MKMapView in a
UIViewRepresentable. It worked in the simulator and drew no tiles on a real
device. I couldn't reproduce it, and a blank map is worse than a slow one, so I
went back to SwiftUI's Map. What keeps it smooth:

  • Measure first. The database answered in 7.6 ms and the endpoint in under half a second, so the stutter was on the phone.
  • Fetch a ring, draw the screen. The app fetches 30% of the span beyond each edge, skips the request while the viewport stays inside it, and waits 250 ms for the camera to settle. Drawing is clipped to the viewport, about 60% fewer lines, and the array is reassigned only when visible IDs change: an identical array still makes SwiftUI diff every overlay.
  • Slim payload. Street name, zone, capacity and source were 65% of the bytes and none is drawn, so the layer gets four fields per kerb and coordinates rounded to six decimals, about 10 cm. A city-wide response went from 575 KB to 359 KB.
  • Nearest first. The query orders by sp.geom <-> centre with a limit of 1,500, so truncation eats the ring, not the middle of the screen.

One feature from the live API:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": {
    "type": "LineString",
    "coordinates": [[2.174812, 41.403032], [2.174847, 41.403005], [2.174876, 41.402983]]
  },
  "properties": {
    "source_id": "complement-es-barcelona-885702924-left",
    "fee_state": "FREE",
    "fee_source": "municipal_paid_complement",
    "opening_hours": null
  }
}

A cap of 400 drawn kerbs left the edges of a Barcelona screen bare, and a
driver can't tell a capped edge from a street with no parking, so it went.

València publishes individual spaces, 315,303 averaging 2.6 m, so 1,500
features covered a few blocks. ST_ClusterDBSCAN, partitioned by street, fee
state and a grid of about 300 m, now merges adjacent bays into segments with a
bay count: the same view went from 1,500 features and 453 KB to 582 and 135 KB.
Without the grid, nameless paid bays chained into lines 25 km long. A polyline
threaded through the bays zig-zagged across the street, since bays sit on both
sides, so each cluster is drawn as the longest line across its convex hull.

Zoomed out past 0.02° of span, the kerb layer switches off and the gateway
counts kerbs in roughly an 8×8 grid over the viewport, drawn as circles.
These aren't MapKit annotation clusters: the phone never downloads the kerbs at
that zoom. Circle size is logarithmic, because counts span four orders of
magnitude and linear sizing pinned nearly every circle to the maximum.

Live counts go stale after 15 minutes

The old app read api.parkendd.de, which had stopped updating. Now I run my
own ParkAPI v3 (MIT), pulling
realtime data every 300 seconds into the same Postgres as my schema, so the
gateway joins its parking_site table directly. The gateway decides freshness,
so phone and server can't disagree:

STALE_AFTER = timedelta(minutes=15)

def freshness(updated_at: datetime | None) -> str:
    if updated_at is None:
        return 'none'
    age = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - updated_at
    return 'live' if age <= STALE_AFTER else 'stale'

for row in rows:
    row['freshness'] = freshness(row.get('realtime_updated_at'))
    # Keep the number, drop the claim that it is current.
    row['realtime_is_current'] = row['freshness'] == 'live'

ParkAPI's own public API drops realtime fields once they're too old. I keep the
number and label it: a stale count shows grey as "N free when last seen", with
its age. On 9 November 2026, 15 car parks within 2 km of central Basel had a
current count.

Indigo's feed reported zero occupancy for all 558 French car parks, which naive
arithmetic shows as empty, so realtime is off for it. And 28% of upstream
ParkAPI converters were already dead when I set it up, so each source's last
success and error live in a table.

Licences and gaps

OpenStreetMap data is ODbL (© OpenStreetMap contributors). Barcelona and
València publish under CC BY 4.0, Madrid and Kraków under their own open-data
terms, the French national base and Indigo under ODbL. Derived layers credit
both the council and OSM, and the app shows these credits behind its info
button.

Missing: an offline cache, address search, and Warsaw. Its city API timed out
when I checked, and OSM had fee information on 0% of its central streets. Kerb
lines show rules, not empty spaces.

What the app does for the people who use it: Free parking app for Europe: Easy Find Parking for iPhone.

FAQ

How complete is OpenStreetMap parking data in European cities?

Very uneven. When I measured in September 2026, the share of drivable streets
with any parking:* tag was 99.9% in Berlin, 10% in Paris, 4% in Barcelona
and 0.9% in Lisbon, and about a tenth of tagged streets had fee
information. Outside Germany, municipal open data is usually the better source.

How do you find free street parking from a city's paid parking data?

Take the OpenStreetMap road network inside the city boundary and drop any
street side within a clearance (25 m in Easy Find Parking) of a published paid
segment or zone polygon. Limit it to residential, unclassified and tertiary
roads, or arterials come out free, and label the result "likely free".

Should I buffer in degrees or metres in PostGIS?

Metres. On EPSG:4326 geometry, distances are in degrees, and a degree of
longitude shrinks with latitude: 0.00025° is 27.8 m north–south but 20.8 m
east–west in Barcelona. Cast to geography and ST_DWithin takes metres.

How do I draw thousands of polylines in a SwiftUI Map without lag?

SwiftUI's Map needs one MapPolyline per line and can't take an
MKMultiPolyline, so the line count is the cost. Fetch a padded area, skip
requests while the viewport stays inside it, debounce camera changes by about
250 ms, draw only what's visible and send only the fields you draw. Zoomed out,
show area counts instead.

How do you know if a live car park count is still current?

Compare its timestamp with the server's clock. Easy Find Parking treats a count
older than 15 minutes as stale: it keeps the number but shows it as "free when
last seen" with its age, never as spaces available now.

title: Running LibRaw, WebGL2 Color Grading, and Memory-Bounded Video Reversal in a Browser Tab (Zero Uploads)
description:
Every "free online RAW converter" or "online video cutter" follows the same playbook: upload your 40 MB Sony .ARW or 4 GB action-camera .MP4 to a remote bucket, wait in a server queue, and hope the output doesn't come back with a watermark or heavy recompression.

When you come back from a shoot with hundreds of camera RAWs and multi-gigabyte 4K clips, uploading gigabytes of personal footage just to cull keepers, grade colors, or trim a few clean subclips makes no sense. Modern browsers already ship WebAssembly SIMD, WebGL2 3D textures, WebCodecs, and Worker threads.

So I built CutCull — a free, watermark-free, zero-upload RAW photo developer and multi-subclip video trimmer that runs entirely inside a browser tab (as the instant-access web companion to our upcoming native macOS/Windows desktop culling app). Your original files never leave your device.

Here are the three core engineering problems we solved to make real sensor-level RAW development, real-time WebGL2 color grading, and multi-gigabyte video processing fast and stable inside browser memory limits.

1. Real Sensor Demosaicing for 20 Camera RAW Formats (Not Embedded JPEG Extraction)

Most lightweight browser "RAW viewers" cheat: they scan the file header for the embedded preview JPEG that cameras write for their rear LCD screen, extract that 1600px 8-bit preview, and call it a conversion. The moment you push shadows or recover bright sunset highlights, 8-bit banding falls apart.

To do genuine sensor-level RAW development in the browser, we compiled LibRaw plus the GoPro GPR SDK (for VC-5 compressed .GPR RAWs) to WebAssembly:

  • 20 camera-tested RAW extensions: Sony .ARW, Canon .CR3 / .CR2 / .CRW, Nikon .NEF / .NRW, Fujifilm .RAF (X-Trans & Bayer), DNG .DNG (DJI, Leica, Ricoh, phones), OM System / Olympus .ORF / .ORI, Panasonic .RW2, Leica .RWL, Hasselblad .3FR / .FFF, Phase One .IIQ, Pentax .PEF, Samsung .SRW, Minolta .MRW, GoPro .GPR, and Sigma .X3F (plus batch .HEIC conversion).
  • Worker isolation: Demosaicing a 45–60 MP Bayer or X-Trans sensor buffer takes hundreds of milliseconds of CPU work. Running the WASM decoder inside a dedicated Web Worker keeps UI scrubbing, filmstrip navigation, and slider drags responsive at 60 fps.
  • Batch export without opening every file: If you drop 20 .CR3 or .ARW files into the workspace, grade three hero shots, and hit batch export, unedited RAWs automatically decode and export at full sensor resolution (JPG quality 90 or lossless PNG) alongside your graded picks.

2. Shared Rust Color Math & a Single-Pass WebGL2 Grading Shader

Once demosaiced wide-gamut pixels arrive from WASM, running pixel math on the CPU in JavaScript is far too slow for interactive sliders. At the same time, chaining half a dozen separate WebGL passes wastes memory bandwidth on high-megapixel photos and 4K HDR frames.

We defined a single color math specification in Rust (cutcull-core) mirrored by a single-pass WebGL2 fragment shader in the browser (and matching export pipelines), so interactive preview and final export stay consistent across photos and video:

  1. As-Shot Anchored Kelvin White Balance: Camera white balance coefficients from the RAW metadata anchor an intuitive Temperature (Kelvin) and Tint control alongside one-click Auto grade.
  2. Highlight-Safe Tone & Presence Controls: Interactive Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks, Dehaze, Vibrance, and Saturation math evaluated in linear/perceptual space within a single fragment pass, paired with non-destructive spatial aspect-ratio crop (Original, Free, 16:9, and social presets).
  3. Hardware sampler3D .cube 3D LUTs: Built-in creative looks (Warm, Cool, Black & white, Teal + orange) plus custom user .cube 3D LUT files uploaded into a WebGL2 3D texture for single-fetch hardware trilinear interpolation.
  4. Consumer HDR Pipeline & Strict Local Privacy: Preserves consumer HDR (HLG / PQ 10-bit video and gain-map photos) end to end — while zero media bytes, filenames, custom LUTs, or edit parameters ever touch a network socket.

3. Multi-Subclip Stream-Copy Cutting & Windowed Video Reversal Without OOM

Standard ffmpeg.wasm demos usually read an entire video into in-memory MEMFS, transcode it from start to finish, and crash the tab as soon as the input crosses a few hundred megabytes.

For action-camera, drone, and vlog footage, we built two specialized local execution paths:

Instant Multi-Subclip Cutting (-c:v copy)

Instead of a heavy multi-track NLE timeline, CutCull gives you J / K / L shuttle keys and I / O markers to tag multiple independent keeper ranges on a single long source video, then exports every range as its own clean file via lossless stream copy — no re-encoding, zero generation loss, and near-instant output.

Memory-Bounded Video Reversal

Reversing a video (vf=reverse,af=areverse) normally requires decoding every frame of the entire clip into uncompressed RAM at once — a 3-minute 1080p clip easily exceeds the 2–4 GB Wasm32 heap ceiling.

To make longer 1080p clips reverse reliably in a browser tab, CutCull splits the job into 2-second keyframe-aligned sliding windows:

  1. Decode only one short keyframe-bounded window into raw frames inside worker memory.
  2. Reverse video frames and audio samples for that window, encode the reversed segment, and immediately free the raw buffers.
  3. Concatenate the reversed segments seamlessly into a single MP4 download.

Peak memory stays flat whether your clip is 10 seconds or several minutes long. We pair this with pitch-preserving 0.1x–10x speed control and instant one-click audio track muting without video re-encoding.

Try It in Your Browser (No Sign-Up, No Watermark)

You can drop a camera RAW photo (.ARW, .CR3, .CR2, .NEF, .RAF, .DNG, .ORF, .RW2, .GPR, …), an iPhone .HEIC, or an .MP4 / .MOV clip directly into https://cutcull.com — no account required, no watermarks, and zero uploads.

We are also building the native macOS & Windows desktop edition of CutCull for high-volume SD-card culling (hundreds to thousands of clips per shoot, Lightroom/Bridge-compatible .xmp sidecars, and one-click FCPXML / Premiere XML / EDL handoff to DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, and Final Cut Pro).

If you work with WebAssembly media pipelines, WebGL2 color shaders, or camera RAW formats, I'd love to hear your feedback and edge cases!

title: The LXD OIDC Patch Plan: 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2
description:
The LXD OIDC Patch Plan: 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2

CVE-2026-135384 has a clear fixed-release boundary, but the repair also requires configuration checks. Canonical lists LXD 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2 as patched versions for an improper authentication flaw in OIDC bearer-token verification. Administrators should plan the upgrade around the deployed release line and verify the identity path after the service restarts.

The CVE record identifies CWE-287 and assigns CVSS 4.0 score 9.2 Critical. The GitHub advisory entry displays 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The difference should be documented in the change record, but it does not change the affected versions, the authentication impact, or the fixed release list.

What the patch addresses

The advisory says LXD checked an OIDC token's issuer, signature, and expiry. Unless oidc.audience was set, the server did not bind the token to LXD. A token from the same provider for another application could therefore be accepted. The advisory also describes a token without a user name being authenticated with an empty name, an ID token being accepted in place of an access token, and unverified email claims being used for the user name when oidc.claim was unset.

The fixed releases are intended to remove these accepting paths. The rest of the security work is to ensure the deployment uses the intended provider, audience, claim, and authorization model after the binary changes.

Identify the release line first

Use the LXD version and packaging records to place each server in the 5.0, 5.21, or 6.10 line. Confirm whether the package, snap, or source build is within an affected range. A version displayed by a client can differ from the server's running version, so collect the server value through an authenticated management path.

For systems outside these lines, consult Canonical support and the CVE record rather than applying another branch's patch by assumption. For a supported branch, the target is the fixed release listed by the vendor. The fixed release should be installed through the normal package or snap channel and followed by a service restart if the deployment requires one.

Build the upgrade order

Prioritize internet-reachable management interfaces and servers with broad OIDC authorization first. The advisory says an authenticated OIDC client has full control in the default configuration where clients are not routed through OpenFGA or a scriptlet. A delegated setup may reduce the blast radius, but an affected authentication path still needs remediation.

Group servers by evidence available: version confirmed, OIDC enabled, provider shared with other applications, email-based identities, and management exposure. This produces a defensible order without claiming that every product match is exploitable. Include cluster members and recovery nodes, since a repaired primary with an older peer can leave another management path available.

Apply temporary controls if needed

The advisory recommends setting oidc.audience to a value that the provider places only in LXD access tokens. It also recommends setting oidc.claim to a value users cannot edit, such as sub, or configuring the provider to release only verified email addresses.

These controls should be documented as temporary risk reduction. Test them with the same provider and client flow that production uses. A value copied from a different application's configuration is not sufficient unless the provider actually places it in LXD access tokens. An ID token flow must be tested separately from the normal access-token flow.

Administrators should also review access paths. If external management is not required, remove the exposure. If it is required, restrict it to trusted networks and preserve access for authorized administrators. Firewall changes are compensating controls and do not replace the fixed release.

Validate after the patch

After the upgrade, query the running server version and confirm the expected build. Test a normal OIDC login with an account that has the correct LXD permissions. Test a token with the wrong audience and verify that it is rejected. Test an ID token where an access token is expected and verify rejection. Test an unverified email identity against a non-production account to confirm the configured claim mapping behaves as intended.

Preserve the test evidence with the release and configuration snapshot. If the server uses multiple applications at one provider, test a token from a neighboring client. The purpose is to confirm the boundary that the advisory says was missing while also checking that the new package starts.

Review authorization after upgrade

Authentication repair does not automatically correct every mapping decision. Review OpenFGA or scriptlet rules, group claims, identity-provider groups, and user records created from email addresses. If the deployment relies on email, make sure the provider releases only verified addresses. If it uses a subject claim, confirm the subject is stable across provider accounts.

The advisory describes the issue as copied from an Incus advisory while listing LXD software and patched versions. That wording should not be used to broaden the product scope. Treat the LXD advisory, LXD documentation, and CVE record as the product-specific basis for the change.

Monitoring and rollback

Monitor authentication failures and successes around the deployment window. A burst of failures can indicate an audience or claim mismatch after the change. A successful login from an unexpected application suggests the configuration still needs review.

Keep a rollback plan that restores the previous service state only under an approved incident process. Rolling back to an affected release reopens the authentication weakness. If an upgrade fails, the safer immediate state is usually a restricted management interface plus the documented compensating controls, not an indefinite return to the vulnerable version.

Exposure context

The frozen ZoomEye observation recorded 12,271 matches for app="LXD" and zero for vul.cve="CVE-2026-135384". The product count is useful for finding inventory and validating change coverage. It does not confirm that a host uses OIDC or that it is running a vulnerable version.

References

[1] Canonical LXD security advisory GHSA-v3m9-p36m-qjqc

[2] CVE Program record for CVE-2026-135384

[3] LXD 6.10.2 release notes

[4] LXD server configuration reference

title: Claude Code /ship command and Claude Ship costs
description:
On 23 November 2026 Anthropic announced Claude Ship, agents that review and fix GitHub pull requests and can approve the ones a team's policy allows. Alongside it, Claude Code got a command of its own called /ship, which does a similar job from your terminal. On 26 November we gave /ship low to a fresh Claude Code 2.1.330 session as its starting prompt, in a scratch repo where we had planted a bug. It refused: "Nothing started. /ship starts only from a line that you type, not from claude -p or a program." The /code-review command, which /ship uses for its review step, started fine the same way and found the bug in about 11 seconds.

So /ship only starts when a person types it, and Anthropic's troubleshooting page lists that exact message with the fix "Type the command yourself at the Claude Code prompt." After that, per the docs, it can commit, push, open the pull request and then keep looking after it, which the docs call a watch. You can't put it in a scheduled job or hand it to another agent. /steward, its sibling, works the same way. The docs give no reason. My guess is that Anthropic wants a person to ask for something that pushes commits with that person's credentials for up to seven days, and I think that's the right call.

This post covers what the product and the command are, what /ship does once typed (from the docs, since our run stopped at the first line), what our review run showed, what Claude Ship costs, and what people have already reported.

What our run and the docs showed

  1. /ship and /steward both refused to start from a session's opening prompt on Claude Code 2.1.330. Nothing was committed, pushed or opened.
  2. /code-review low did start that way. It read the branch with a single shell command (two git diff runs), flagged the off-by-one at textkit.py:11 as "important", gave the right fix, and posted nothing to GitHub.
  3. At low effort the review skips test files ("test-file changes are not reviewed at this level", its own instructions say). /ship reviews at high by default.
  4. Claude Ship (the organisation product) and /ship (the command) are billed differently. Claude Ship's promotional credits, $10,000 to $50,000 for eligible Enterprise organisations, don't pay for /ship or for any of the commands you run in your own session.
  5. The public Claude Code changelog has no line about /ship in 2.1.330, 2.1.331 or 2.1.332. The version requirement comes only from the docs.

What is Claude Ship, and how it differs from the /ship command

Claude Ship is the organisation product. Per the Claude Ship docs it is three agents on your GitHub repositories. Code Review leaves inline comments ranked by severity. PR Steward picks up failing checks and review comments and pushes commits to fix them. Claude Approvals is a check that reports who still has to approve, based on a policy file you write in YAML (a plain settings format), .claude/approvals.yml. Code Review is generally available, and the other two are in public beta. It is for Claude Team and Enterprise plans on GitHub. Some organisations can't use it at all: those with Zero Data Retention, customer-managed encryption keys or the configuration for HIPAA (the US health-data privacy law). A person with the Owner role in the Claude organisation (its top admin role) turns Code Review and PR Steward on under Organization settings > Claude Ship. Approvals starts when someone commits a policy file to the repository.

/ship is a command in the Claude Code CLI (the terminal program) and runs in your own session, in your local clone. The ship-command page says "Cloud sessions don't have them", meaning /ship and /steward. No admin has to switch it on. It can still be missing, though. Managed settings can turn it off, and so can settings that stop feature-flag fetching (for example DISABLE_TELEMETRY). On a third-party provider such as Bedrock it needs 2.1.331. It counts against your own Claude Code usage. A commenter in the Hacker News launch thread (89 points, 36 comments when we read it) asked whether it needs Claude Code on the web and API billing. For the command, it needs neither.

What /ship does after you type it, according to the docs

Our run never got past the first line, so this section comes from the docs. /ship has four steps:

  1. Pull request. If the branch has no pull request yet, it can commit your uncommitted changes, push the branch and open the pull request as you. On the default branch it commits on a new branch and switches your checkout to it.
  2. Review. It runs /code-review on the change.
  3. Watch. It keeps checking the pull request from your session, works on whatever breaks or gets commented on (its own review findings included) and pushes fixes as it goes.
  4. Merge. You do that yourself.

/steward skips the first two steps. It starts a watch on your own open pull request, or restarts one that ended.

There is no confirmation prompt. Before the commit and again before the push, a line ending Esc to cancel says what is about to happen, and "If you do nothing, /ship continues after a few seconds." A commit made before you cancel stays (git reset HEAD~1 undoes it). I'd have liked a real yes/no here. A prompt would stall the unattended part, though.

You need Claude Code 2.1.330, GitHub CLI (gh) 2.63 signed in with gh auth login, and git 2.38 at least. With an older gh no watch starts. We had 2.1.330, gh 2.100.0 and git 2.54.0, so nothing needed an upgrade.

In a public repository it doesn't commit your uncommitted changes at all, and I'm glad, because half-finished work pushed to a public repo is the worst way for this to go wrong. In a private one, an uncommitted file whose name suggests a secret, such as .env, stops it from committing or pushing anything. It checks names only, so the docs tell you to look inside your files yourself. And if someone else has a pull request open for the branch, it commits nothing and starts no watch.

The permission mode (how much Claude Code may do without asking you) matters too. Auto mode is the one for unattended work. In Manual or acceptEdits mode it waits at every prompt, and in bypassPermissions no watch starts. From 2.1.331 it won't start in plan mode. If I were trying it for the first time, I'd do it on a branch nobody else pushes to.

Arguments go after the command. The first sets how hard the review tries, from low to max (default high); a number or URL picks the pull request, and +botname makes it read that bot's comments as well. The docs' own example is /ship low 41 +my-lint-bot.

/ship refused our script: "Nothing started. /ship starts only from a line that you type"

We set up a private scratch repo holding a small Python module, textkit.py. A GitHub Actions check (CI, the tests GitHub runs on every pull request) runs python -m unittest. Then we added a function, truncate_words, that keeps one word too few (words[: limit - 1]), plus a test that expects truncate_words("one two three four", 2) to return "one two...". Locally the test failed, which was the point.

Our fleet starts Claude Code sessions in visible terminal tabs from a script, with the first prompt passed in. We passed /ship low. The transcript held one reply, the refusal, and git status still showed the two modified files with no new branch or commit. Thirteen minutes later, after we had opened the pull request by hand, /steward gave the same answer.

The troubleshooting page lists this message, and next to it a separate one for a session that another session started. Either way you can't build /ship into a nightly job, a CI step or an agent pipeline. The ship-command page lists the alternatives: Auto-fix (/autofix-pr) for fixes from a cloud session, and Claude Ship for whole repositories, billed to the organisation. PR Steward, its fixing agent, is started per repository or with an @claude steward comment.

Claude Code's /code-review command found the planted bug in 11 seconds

/code-review is the review /ship runs, and it has no such rule. We opened the pull request ourselves (git push, then gh pr create) and the check failed, as planned.

Then we started a new session with /code-review low. It ran as a background agent on claude-opus-5-5 at low effort, made one tool call (a shell command, git diff main...HEAD; git diff HEAD) and answered 11 seconds after the prompt.

It was right. It also caught a case our test didn't cover: with limit=0 the slice becomes words[:-1] and keeps every word except the last (in Python, "a b c".split()[:-1] gives ['a', 'b']). It suggested words[:limit], then asked "Want me to apply the fix and run the tests?" It changed no file and wrote nothing on the pull request.

It read the local branch with git diff and never called gh, although the pull request was open. Version 2.1.329 changed /code-review <pr number> to read the pull request with gh pr diff, so pass the number if your checkout and the remote branch might differ. It also left test_textkit.py out, which is the low-effort rule. Here the bug sat in the code, so that cost nothing, but at low a wrong assertion in a test goes through unread.

It was cheap. The main session wrote 375 output tokens and the review agent 276, with the rest of the context cached. I can't turn that into a dollar figure, because a subscription seat doesn't show a price per command.

What a /ship watch can do with your GitHub sign-in

I'd read this part twice before typing /ship in a repo other people push to. The watch uses your gh and git sign-ins. In auto mode it pushes commits and resolves review threads without asking. While Claude acts on its own, Claude Code blocks any gh or git command that would merge, approve or force-push, and /ship terms prints the full list of limits.

Those limits cover Claude's own commands only. The docs still warn that the watch "could merge a pull request that your repository's branch rules let you merge without another person's approval". If auto-merge is on for the pull request, for example, a fix the watch pushes can end up merged once the checks pass. And if you type a message while Claude is idle, the limits are off while it answers you. The docs add: "Run a watch only where you trust everyone who can merge to the base branch or push to your branch. Any of them can run programs on your computer with your credentials." I wouldn't run one on a repo that takes pull requests from outside contributors.

Your git hooks get skipped too. The docs say the watch pushes with git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null push, so your repo's hooks don't run on those pushes. A deny rule on Bash(git push *) makes /ship leave the steps to you. An ask rule on that pattern doesn't match the hooks-off form, so you need one on Bash(git *).

To stop it, type /ship stop (what Claude pushes in the current turn still lands) or press Esc once. A watch also ends after seven days, on merge or close, or when you switch branches. An organisation can switch the command off for everyone with the managed setting skillOverrides set to "ship-local": "off" and "steward": "off". Some teams already had a /ship skill of their own, and the built-in now hides it (a commenter in the Hacker News thread and issue #111946 both raise this). The troubleshooting page's fix is to remove any "off" entry for your command under skillOverrides, then set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHIP=1 (2.1.331 or later). That turns off both built-ins and lets yours load.

What Claude Ship and its Code Review agent cost

There's no flat price per review, which I find annoying when you're trying to budget a team. The Code Review costs page says each review is billed on tokens through the organisation's usage credits, separate from plan usage, and that the cost depends on the review level, the size of the change and the code around it. To estimate, the docs suggest a pilot. Read the average cost per review for one repo, then multiply by your pull requests a month (and by pushes per pull request if reviews run on every push).

PR Steward "has no spend limit of its own until you set one." Turning off usage credits doesn't stop an agent that is on either; it keeps running and billing. Claude Approvals has no base charge, but a policy that names claude/code_review in a condition can start billed reviews on every push, and observe mode (where the policy reports but doesn't block) is billed too. The docs' turn-off order is Approvals, then PR Steward, then Code Review. If I ran the organisation, PR Steward's spend limit is the first thing I'd set.

Eligible paid Enterprise organisations can claim $10,000 to $50,000 in promo credits, set by active Claude Code seats, until 23:59 UTC on 15 January 2027, to be used within 30 days. They don't pay for /ship, /steward or the /code-review command.

For a rough comparison, GitHub's Copilot code review docs estimate $0.25, $1.50 and $10 per review across its three levels, and by default its reviews don't count toward required approvals. If you're comparing vendors, we wrote up how Atlassian is moving its Rovo code reviewer to Rovo credits from 3 December.

Where people are already tripping over it

Four issues about /ship were open in the anthropics/claude-code tracker when we looked on 26 November:

  • #111946, the built-in /ship hiding a user's own skill called ship.
  • #112018, /steward refusing a pull request when the git remote is an https:// URL with a user name in it.
  • #112183, /ship falling back to review-only on a branch name with Korean characters.
  • #112154, a request for Code Review on self-managed GitLab.

I'd expect more of these in the first month. Three days in, these are mostly about setups people already had.

Press coverage went another way. ITPro put Anthropic's own warning in its headline: Claude Ship "may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues" (the docs carry the same line). Decrypt worried about one model reviewing code written by a similar model, and The Register quoted an engineer calling it "a glorification of what I already use Claude on". TechCrunch describes the approval policies as natural language. The policy file itself is YAML with fixed keys, where only purpose is free text; plain English comes in through custom classifiers, a model asked a question in plain English whose answer a rule can test.

Anthropic's own numbers are the strongest case for it. On the claude.dev blog the Claude Code team says the share of its internal pull requests with substantive review comments went from 16% to 54% when the review launched, and that from June to September the share of merged pull requests later reverted fell by more than 40%. Those are self-reported and I can't check them. I'd still like to see them from a team outside Anthropic.

Use /code-review now, and type /ship only behind branch protection

I'd start using /code-review now. It took 11 seconds, it can be started from a script, and it found the bug plus an edge case our test missed without touching GitHub. Pass it the pull request number, and use a higher effort than low if your tests matter.

/ship is a person's command that turns your terminal into an agent acting as you for up to a week, and a program can't start it. Before typing it in a shared repo, make sure branch protection requires another person's approval and auto-merge is off. If you want the same work done with nobody at a keyboard, the options are Auto-fix from a cloud session or PR Steward, which is the organisation's call and the organisation's bill.

If you've had a watch run overnight on a real repo, I'd like to know what it pushed. And if you're wiring Claude Code into tools that act on your behalf, our post on a Claude Code agent hitting a Jira workflow validator covers the same question from the Jira side.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: Replacing LocalStack with Floci 2.4.0: pin the image, and set the hostname for other containers
description:
This is a third-party deployment note, not official Floci documentation. It follows release 2.4.0 (published 2026-10-31, checked on 2026-11-05, Asia/Shanghai). Official docs start at https://floci.io/floci/ and the LocalStack migration page is at https://floci.io/floci/getting-started/migrate-from-localstack/. Pin floci/floci:2.4.0 in production or CI; latest is only a convenience tag. If init scripts need a container-local AWS CLI or boto3, use the 2.4.0-compat image instead. The older third-party name hectorvent/floci is unmaintained; switch to floci/floci.

Floci is a local AWS emulator. It uses port 4566 and the same documented placeholder credentials as common LocalStack examples, so many SDK and CLI clients only need a new endpoint. It is not a public multi-tenant stand-in for AWS. Do not publish 4566 to the internet. For a drop-in Compose swap, changing the image and the data volume is usually enough: keep port 4566, keep the placeholder credentials, keep init files on the old LocalStack-compatible path if you already have them, and mount data at /app/data instead of /var/lib/localstack. A LocalStack-style PERSISTENCE=1 setting can be translated automatically, but only if that volume path is correct. Explicit FLOCI_* variables win over the compatibility translation.

The most common breakage is multi-container networking. Generated URLs often contain localhost. An application in another container that calls localhost:4566 is calling itself, not Floci. Set FLOCI_HOSTNAME to the Compose service name, and point the application at http://<service-name>:4566. That affects queue URLs, callback URLs, and other derived endpoints. For S3 clients, prefer path-style addressing. This note does not invent performance comparisons with LocalStack. A full Chinese step-by-step guide (Compose, persistence, LocalStack swap, and CI pitfalls) is here: https://9012938178391.gumroad.com/l/zkttzt

title: 좋은 AI 프롬프트 작성법: 원하는 답변을 얻는 10가지 방법
description:
좋은 AI 프롬프트 작성법은 특별한 주문을 외우는 일이 아니라, 해야 할 일과 판단 기준을 모델이 오해하지 않도록 적는 일입니다. 같은 프롬프트도 모델·버전·대화 맥락에 따라 결과가 달라질 수 있으므로, 한 번의 답변을 성능 보장처럼 받아들이기보다 결과를 확인하고 수정하는 과정이 필요합니다.

아래 10가지는 OpenAI·Google·Anthropic의 현재 공식 프롬프팅 안내에서 공통으로 확인되는 원칙을 실무 순서에 맞게 정리한 것입니다. 특정 모델이 언제나 더 정확해진다고 단정하지 않으며, 예시는 사용자가 자신의 과제에 맞춰 바꾸는 입력 조각입니다.

원하는 답변을 얻는 AI 프롬프트 작성법 10가지

1. 해야 할 일을 동사로 명확하게 적기

먼저 요약, 비교, 분류, 교정처럼 모델이 수행할 작업을 한 문장으로 적습니다. “알아서 잘 써줘”보다 대상, 목적, 강조할 부분을 함께 주면 무엇을 완료해야 하는지 확인하기 쉽습니다.

# 나쁜 예시
이 보고서 요약해줘.

# 좋은 예시
이 보고서의 핵심 내용 3가지를 5문장 이내로 요약해줘. 특히 시장 동향과 미래 전망에 초점을 맞춰줘.

2. 독자와 사용 목적을 알려주기

같은 내용도 초보자 안내문, 내부 검토 메모, 고객 답변은 필요한 설명 수준과 용어가 다릅니다. “이 답변은 처음 접하는 독자가 의사결정에 사용한다”처럼 누가 어디에 쓸 결과인지 적습니다. 독자 수준을 모르면 모델이 가정한 수준도 답변 첫머리에 밝히게 할 수 있습니다.

3. 필요한 관점이나 역할을 구체적으로 제한하기

역할은 말투와 검토 관점을 정하는 데 쓸 수 있습니다. 다만 “전문가 역할”이 사실의 정확성을 보장하지는 않으므로, 역할과 함께 실제 과제·독자·검토 기준을 적고 중요한 사실은 별도로 확인해야 합니다.

# 나쁜 예시
이 제품에 대한 글을 써줘.

# 좋은 예시
당신은 스타트업의 마케팅 전문가입니다. 이 새로운 SaaS(Software as a Service) 제품의 주요 기능을 소개하고, 잠재 고객의 이점을 강조하는 소셜 미디어 게시물 초안을 작성해주세요.

4. 배경 정보와 참고 자료의 경계를 표시하기

모델이 답변에 사용해야 할 전제, 원문, 데이터와 사용하지 말아야 할 추측을 구분합니다. 긴 자료를 붙일 때는 “아래 <자료> 안의 내용만 근거로 답하고, 자료에 없으면 없다고 표시”처럼 경계를 지정합니다. 자료가 서로 충돌하면 어느 쪽을 우선할지도 함께 적는 것이 좋습니다.

자료 안에 들어 있는 지시문까지 신뢰할 수 있는 것은 아닙니다. 외부 문서의 “이전 지시를 무시하라” 같은 문장도 참고 자료의 내용으로 다루고, 도구 실행이나 외부 전송 전에 별도 검증을 해야 합니다. 태그로 경계를 표시하는 것만으로 이런 위험이 완전히 사라지는 것은 아닙니다.

5. 원하는 결과의 예시를 보여주기

형식이나 분류 기준을 말로만 설명하기 어렵다면 입력과 출력 예시를 제공합니다. Google과 Anthropic의 안내도 일관되고 관련성 높은 예시를 권하며, 예시에 섞인 패턴을 모델이 따라갈 수 있으므로 잘못된 예시나 예외 없는 단일 사례는 주의해야 합니다.

# 예시
다음과 같은 형식으로 단어를 번역해줘.
입력: 사과 -> 출력: Apple
입력: 바나나 -> 출력: Banana
입력: 한국 -> 출력:

6. 출력 형식과 필수 필드를 지정하기

표, 목록, 마크다운, JSON처럼 결과를 사용할 형태를 적고 필수 항목과 순서를 정합니다. 자동 처리에 쓸 데이터라면 허용할 키, 값의 형식, 누락값 처리법까지 명시하고, 실제 시스템에 넣기 전에는 문법과 내용을 검증해야 합니다.

# 예시
다음 정보를 바탕으로 각 항목을 JSON 형식으로 정리해줘. 각 항목은 '이름'과 '설명' 필드를 포함해야 해.
[데이터 목록]
- AI 자동화: 반복적인 작업을 AI가 처리
- Docker: 애플리케이션을 격리된 환경에서 실행

7. 제약 조건과 완료 기준을 함께 쓰기

길이, 포함할 항목, 제외할 범위, 언어, 날짜 기준을 나열한 뒤 무엇이면 완료인지 적습니다. 예를 들어 “장점과 한계를 각각 두 가지 제시하고, 근거가 없는 수치는 만들지 않으며, 마지막에 확인이 필요한 항목을 분리”처럼 결과를 점검할 수 있는 기준을 사용합니다.

8. 복잡한 작업은 확인 가능한 단계로 나누기

자료 정리, 비교, 초안 작성, 최종 검토를 한 요청에 뒤섞기보다 중간 산출물이 보이도록 나눕니다. 먼저 요구사항과 누락 정보를 확인하고, 다음에 개요를 만든 뒤, 승인된 개요로 본문을 작성하는 방식입니다. 모델의 숨은 사고 과정을 요구하기보다 사용자가 검토할 수 있는 결과와 근거를 요청하는 편이 안전합니다.

9. 불확실성과 근거를 구분해 표시하게 하기

최신 정보나 중요한 판단이 포함되면 확인한 사실, 추정, 확인하지 못한 항목을 구분해 달라고 요청합니다. 링크가 필요하면 공식 출처를 우선하도록 하고, 모델이 제시한 링크·날짜·수치는 원문에서 다시 확인합니다. 역할 부여나 상세한 문장이 검증을 대신하지는 않습니다.

10. 작은 평가 기준으로 반복 개선하기

첫 답변을 보고 막연히 “더 좋게”라고 요청하기보다 빠진 항목, 불필요한 부분, 잘못된 형식을 구체적으로 되돌려 줍니다. 반복 작업이라면 정확성, 완결성, 형식 준수처럼 짧은 체크리스트로 여러 예시를 시험합니다. OpenAI의 공식 안내도 모든 작업에 통하는 단일 프롬프트는 없다고 설명하며, 실제 입력으로 평가하고 반복해서 다듬을 것을 권합니다.

바로 써보는 프롬프트 조립 순서

다음 순서는 고정 공식이 아니라 빠뜨린 요소를 찾기 위한 선택 기준입니다.

  1. 작업: 무엇을 해달라는 요청인지 적습니다.
  2. 맥락: 독자, 목적, 참고 자료와 기준 시점을 붙입니다.
  3. 기준: 포함·제외 조건과 완료 조건을 적습니다.
  4. 형식: 결과 구조와 필수 필드를 지정합니다.
  5. 검토: 불확실한 부분과 확인할 근거를 따로 표시하게 합니다.

간단한 질문에는 필요한 항목만 쓰면 됩니다. 반대로 중요한 의사결정이나 외부 공개물은 답변 자체를 사실로 간주하지 말고 출처와 원자료를 확인해야 합니다. 이 글의 예시는 실행 결과나 성능 실측값이 아니며, 실제 과제의 성공 여부는 사용한 모델과 입력 자료로 별도 평가해야 합니다.

공식 근거와 확인 범위

2026년 9월 14일에 다음 공식 안내의 현재 내용을 확인했습니다.

  • OpenAI 모델별 프롬프팅 가이드: 명확한 지시, 맥락과 예시, 출력 구조, 평가와 반복 개선
  • Google Gemini 프롬프팅 전략: 구체적인 지시, 제약과 응답 형식, few-shot 예시, 맥락, 작업 분해와 반복
  • Anthropic Claude 프롬프팅 모범 사례: 명확하고 직접적인 지시, 맥락, 예시, 구조와 출력 형식, 결과 확인

제품과 모델의 권장 방식은 바뀔 수 있으므로 이후에는 각 공식 문서의 최신 내용을 재확인해야 합니다.

관련 글

  • AI 챗봇 비교: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, 당신에게 맞는 선택은?
  • 생성형 AI란 무엇인가? ChatGPT부터 시작하는 AI 입문

이 글의 원문은 좋은 AI 프롬프트 작성법: 원하는 답변을 얻는 10가지 방법 에 있습니다. (Originally published on Briefold)
