金融服務業的雲端遷移不僅是一項技術專案，更是業務、風險、資料與營運模式的轉型。 來源文件將資料安全與合規、資料主權、效能與延遲、成本管理、停機時間，以及與傳統系統的整合列為主要考量。 這些考量是相互關聯的。 如果一項設計提升了敏捷性，卻失去了資料血緣 (data lineage)、增加了延遲、削弱了復原能力、破壞了授權機制，或造成了無法控制的成本結構，這就不是一次成功的金融業 (FSI) 遷移。

來源中最實用的遷移模式是漸進式現代化。 探索現有資產、選擇一個小型的非關鍵試點、逐步導入雲端功能、監控兩個環境、驗證結果，並透過受控且可復原的切換過程來轉移流量。 這種模式縮小了變更的影響範圍，但並不能免除依賴性分析、資料核對、安全測試、業務批准、營運就緒度，以及經過測試的復原計畫等需求。

來源中的 AWS 服務清單最好被理解為潛在功能的型錄。 Application Discovery Service 可支援依賴性探索，EC2 可支援虛擬機工作負載，Lambda 和 API Gateway 可支援特定的事件驅動介面，RDS 可提供受管的關聯式資料庫，DMS 可支援資料庫遷移，Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 可託管應用程式，Elastic Load Balancing 可分配流量，而 CloudWatch 可支援監控與日誌記錄。 正確的選擇取決於工作負載在資料、延遲、韌性、法規、營運及相容性方面的需求。

金融業遷移驅動因素與決策背景

資料安全與合規性被列為首要考量，並舉出 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS 為例。 這些規範的適用範圍和義務並不相同，其適用性取決於機構、客戶、產品、司法管轄區、資料以及處理活動。 雲端遷移應從法人實體和資料處理盤點開始，而不是假設雲端供應商的一般安全態勢即可證明合規。

資料主權意味著將資料或特定處理活動保留在規定的地理邊界內。 選擇區域 (Region) 只是該決策的一部分。 機構必須確認主要資料、複本、備份、日誌、快照、支援存取、開發副本、災難復原環境，以及下游分析可以存放在哪裡。 跨境傳輸、分包商、營運存取、保留、刪除、法定保存以及市場資料授權，都會影響允許的設計。

效能與延遲必須以業務術語來定義。 量化研究作業、投資組合風險計算、市場資料消費者、訂單管理功能和即時執行路徑，都有不同的延遲與確定性要求。 遷移應針對吞吐量、回應時間、百分位數延遲、並發性、佇列、復原行為和依賴呼叫，建立基準與目標測量值。 籠統地聲稱雲端服務具備可擴展性，並不能證明特定的金融業工作負載能達到其所需的效能。

成本管理是一項明確的考量，因為雲端消耗會隨著工作負載量、儲存增長、資料傳輸、平行處理、日誌記錄、複製和復原副本而變化。 有效的商業案例必須將雲端營運的總成本與現有資產的總成本進行比較，包括遷移期間的雙軌並行、資料來源授權、支援、安全工具、連線、測試、人員編制和合規證據。 預算和成本報告是控制機制，不能取代量化的總成本模型。

停機時間與傳統系統整合，對於持續運作或有嚴格業務日曆的金融系統尤為重要。 遷移設計應確立切換視窗、上游與下游依賴關係、外部交易對手、市場休假日、核對期間、批次截止時間，以及可接受的最大中斷時間。 傳統系統可能還需要專有協定、固定網路位置、共用檔案、大型主機介面，或無法由通用雲端端點取代的緊密耦合資料庫行為。

目標金融業工作負載邊界

頁面標題將遷移主題與避險基金活動、Alpha 因子庫 (alpha-factor zoo)、另類回測策略、量化投資研究、投資組合風險管理以及交易法規合規性關聯在一起。 這些主題暗示了潛在的工作負載，例如歷史市場資料處理、研究資料管理、因子計算、回測、投資組合分析、風險報告和合規支援。

來源並未確認目標是即時訂單管理系統、交易所閘道器、市場資料廠 (market-data plant)、撮合引擎或執行平台。 它沒有提供經紀商連線、交易所連線、訂單路由邏輯、交易監控實作或正式環境投資組合帳本。 除非有其他證據表明對延遲敏感或受監管的執行功能包含在範圍內，否則該頁面應僅用於討論研究與支援系統的遷移模式。

工作負載分類應區分核心紀錄系統 (systems of record) 與分析副本、即時服務與批次服務、有狀態應用程式與無狀態服務，以及受監管的處理與實驗性環境。 它還應記錄業務關鍵性、資料敏感度、市場時間、延遲預算、吞吐量、復原目標、授權限制，以及當責的業務擁有者。 這些屬性決定了一個工作負載應該被重新託管 (rehosted)、重新建構平台 (replatformed)、重構 (refactored)、替換 (replaced)、保留 (retained) 還是退場 (retired)。

絞殺榕遷移模式 (Strangler Fig Pattern)

來源將其營運流程稱為絞殺榕模式，並描述了五個階段：評估、試點、重構、監控與切換。 評估階段會審視現有應用程式，並找出適合遷移的元件。 試點階段會將一個小型的非關鍵元件移至雲端。 重構階段則是以雲端託管的微服務逐步取代單體架構 (monolith) 的各個部分。 監控貫穿整個過渡期。 最後，切換階段會將流量轉移至新的實作。

這個模式非常實用，因為它避免將遷移視為單一且不可逆的事件。 它允許組織在轉移更關鍵的功能之前，先了解連線、安全、效能、營運和成本。 儘管如此，試點仍必須使用明確的標準來選擇。 「非關鍵」應該意味著該元件的故障、資料外洩、延遲或錯誤結果，對業務和法規的影響是受限的，而不僅僅是因為它的使用者很少。

絞殺榕遷移並不代表在所有情況下都需要使用微服務。 機構可以逐步以受管服務、模組化應用程式、批次管道，或保留在受控介面後方的傳統元件來取代特定功能。 微服務可能會引入分散式交易、營運開銷、版本控制挑戰以及新的故障模式。 現代化的選擇應遵循領域邊界和控制需求，而不是將微服務視為理所當然的目的地。

評估與探索

第一個實際活動是對應用程式、介面、資料儲存、批次作業、身分識別、基礎架構、外部供應商、使用者、授權和營運程序進行結構化盤點。 來源點名 AWS Application Discovery Service 作為了解應用程式依賴關係和效能指標的工具。 其輸出結果應與訪談、架構紀錄、網路證據、日誌、業務流程圖以及法規清單結合，因為自動化探索本身無法識別每一個業務或控制依賴。

評估應記錄每個依賴關係的呼叫方向、協定、頻率、有效載荷、身分驗證、資料分類、故障行為、逾時、重試、順序和擁有權。 它應識別資料庫、檔案共用、佇列、排程作業、參考資料、市場資料摘要、報告目的地、下游消費者以及外部交易對手。 對於交易或風險環境，分析還應記錄市場日曆、截止時間、時區、事件時間語意、修正行為，以及處理延遲或遺失資料的方式。

每個候選的遷移階段都應有明確的範圍、業務目標、風險評級、來源和目標擁有者、驗收標準、依賴關係、復原方法和證據計畫。 評估應區分技術可行性與法規許可。 一個應用程式在技術上可能很容易搬遷，但仍可能因為資料落地 (data residency)、授權、營運韌性、紀錄保存、委外或模型治理義務而不適合遷移。

目標架構與 AWS 服務角色

來源提議將 EC2、Lambda、API Gateway 和 RDS 作為雲端原生架構的建構模塊。 EC2 適用於需要作業系統控制權、需與現有軟體相容，或採取漸進式直接搬遷 (lift-and-shift) 路徑的工作負載。 Lambda 適合具有相容執行、逾時、狀態和打包特性的受限事件驅動功能。 API Gateway 可提供受管的介面邊界，但需符合身分驗證、授權、節流、結構描述 (schema)、版本控制和可用性要求。 RDS 可以減少資料庫管理工作，但必須明確選擇目標引擎、版本、交易行為、擴充功能、連線模型、備份策略和相容性。

Elastic Beanstalk 和 ECS 被列為應用程式部署選項。 它們代表不同的營運模型，不應被視為可互換的標籤。 選擇取決於組織是否需要應用程式平台抽象化、容器編排、部署控制、服務探索、擴展行為、網路整合以及營運責任。 目標架構還應定義如何管理機密、配置、映像檔、修補程式、日誌、指標、追蹤和復原版本。

Elastic Load Balancing 用於流量分配。 確切的負載平衡器類型和路由設計必須符合協定、連線生命週期、TLS 終止、用戶端身分、健康檢查、路徑路由、WebSocket 或串流行為、來源 IP 要求和延遲目標。 單靠流量分配無法提供應用程式的正確性。 健康檢查必須代表實質的業務就緒狀態，且容錯移轉 (failover) 絕不能將請求路由至雖可連線但無法處理權威資料的服務。

CloudWatch 被點名用於效能監控和日誌記錄。 監控應超越基礎架構使用率，涵蓋業務與控制指標，例如交易完整性、佇列時間 (queue age)、核對狀態、錯誤分類、依賴關係健康狀態、資料新鮮度、身分驗證失敗、權限變更、延遲百分位數、成本異常以及復原訊號。 日誌應具備定義好的保留期限、存取控制、時間同步、遮罩 (redaction)、完整性保護，並有途徑作為事件回應與稽核證據。

使用 AWS DMS 進行資料庫與資料遷移

來源點名 AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) 用於資料庫遷移，並形容資料傳輸為「無縫」(seamless)。 「無縫」應被視為一種期望而非保證。 受控的資料庫遷移必須指定來源和目標引擎、結構描述 (schema) 相容性、全量載入行為、異動資料擷取 (CDC) 行為、交易排序、主鍵和序列處理、型別轉換、字元編碼、時區、大型物件、預存程序、權限、索引以及下游依賴。

遷移計畫必須定義在共存期間哪一個環境具有權威性。 如果傳統和雲端資料庫都接受寫入，組織就需要衝突解決和核對模型。 如果只有一方接受寫入，則必須明確規定複製方向、延遲容忍度、中斷行為和切換程序。 該計畫應能偵測重複、遺失、順序錯誤、截斷或轉換的紀錄，並應保留目標資料完整且正確的證據。

金融服務資料遷移需要時間點正確性 (point-in-time correctness)。 歷史分析、風險、估值和監控可能依賴於事件發生時存在的參考資料和市場狀態。 遷移應保留來源時間戳記、營業日、生效日期、修正歷史、血緣，以及原始資料與重編資料之間的區別。 備份、複本、快照、測試環境和匯出檔案必須繼承適當的分類和保留控制。

資料品質關卡應比對紀錄數量、餘額、部位、總計、校驗和 (checksums)、金鑰分佈、空值率 (null rates)、參照完整性、事件序列和業務核對結果。 異常狀況應被保留並指派給擁有者，而不是被回報技術成功的匯入過程所掩蓋。 不能僅因資料複製已趕上進度就宣布目標環境就緒；業務單位必須確認產生的資料能支援預期的計算、報告、控制和下游介面。

應用程式現代化與傳統系統整合

來源建議逐步以雲端託管的微服務取代單體架構的元件。 安全的現代化計畫首先要識別受限的業務能力及其資料所有權。 每個新元件都需要合約、版本控制策略、身分驗證模型、冪等性 (idempotency) 行為、逾時和重試規則、可觀測性、部署流程以及定義好的真相來源 (source of truth)。 分散式服務還需要明確處理部分故障、重複訊息、排序、最終一致性和跨服務交易。

傳統系統整合應被設計為一級邊界。 來源提到新的雲端系統應該與地端 (on-premises) 系統互動，但並未定義網路連線、路由、DNS、身分聯合、私有服務存取、加密、防火牆所有權、延遲預算或故障行為。 遷移必須確定傳統系統如何發現雲端服務、雲端工作負載如何連線到保留的系統、如何管理憑證，以及當任一方無法使用時由哪個團隊負責回應。

共存期通常比最終架構更為複雜。 介面可能需要轉譯，資料可能暫時重複，使用者可能需要跨系統的一致視圖，而營運團隊可能需要支援兩種部署和事件模型。 過渡期設計應指定共存的時間長短、每個資料領域的權威系統、讓舊元件退役的條件，以及傳統基礎架構除役前所需的證據。

遷移服務與部署選擇

來源列出了用於資料庫遷移的 AWS Database Migration Service、用於伺服器遷移的 AWS Server Migration Service、用於傳輸大量資料的 Snowball，以及用於某些應用程式或資料保留在地端的混合場景的 AWS Outposts。 這些名稱應被視為來源參考，在納入遷移計畫之前，需要檢查目前的產品狀態、區域可用性和功能。 特別是，任何使用特別點名的 AWS Server Migration Service 的計畫，都應驗證目前受支援的服務和替代路徑。

Snowball 或其他大量傳輸設備可能會減少初始大型資料傳輸的時間或網路負載。 但它本身並不能解決監管鏈、加密、來源與目的地核對、增量變更、傳輸重試、授權或最終切換等問題。 遷移團隊必須定義如何驗證初始副本，以及如何同步在設備匯出後所做的變更。

當機構需要將特定的 AWS 基礎架構或服務建置在客戶地點作為混合設計的一部分時，Outposts 就會派上用場。 這並非解決資料主權、災難復原或法規遵從的自動解答。 設計必須考量支援的服務、硬體容量、連線、修補、本地營運、故障替換、依賴行為、實體安全、資料位置，以及地端 AWS 環境無法使用時的復原路徑。

安全性、隱私與合規

來源指出 IAM、VPC 以及靜態與傳輸中的加密為核心的 AWS 安全功能。 這些是重要的基礎，但並不構成完整的金融業控制環境。 IAM 應包括聯合身分、最低權限角色、工作負載身分、特權存取控制、緊急存取 (break-glass) 程序、職責分離、存取權限重新認證、服務帳戶治理，以及變更與審查的證據。

VPC 設計應定義帳戶和環境邊界、子網路配置、路由、安全群組、網路存取控制清單 (NACL)、私有端點、檢查機制、進入與離開 (ingress/egress) 策略、DNS、日誌記錄，以及與地端系統和外部供應商的連線。 對外公開應深思熟慮並最小化。 服務應互相驗證身分、驗證輸入、使用適當的網路路徑，並產生由負責團隊監控的安全遙測數據。

加密不僅僅是勾選一個選項。 機構必須定義金鑰所有權、金鑰分離、建立與輪換、存取策略、復原、撤銷、稽核日誌記錄，以及加密備份和複本的處理方式。 敏感資料可能還需要權杖化 (tokenization)、遮罩、欄位層級保護或受限制的分析副本。 日誌和監控資料可能包含受監管的資訊，必須進行分類，不能假設為安全的。

頁面提到了 GDPR、CCPA 和 PCI DSS，但沒有提供適用性分析或控制對應。 它沒有識別持卡人資料環境、個人資料盤點、跨境傳輸依據、保留規則、市場行為義務、交易紀錄要求或委外評估。 遷移應將實際的法律與法規義務對應到系統、資料、流程、供應商、證據和控制擁有者。 雲端服務可以支援合規，但若無機構特定的設計和持續營運，則無法保證合規。

韌性、高可用性與業務連續性

來源點出資料遺失、初期效能下降、安全漏洞、意外的雲端成本和切換停機時間等為遷移風險。 它提出安全控制、成本工具、Auto Scaling、多可用區 (Multi-AZ) 部署、沙盒測試和專家指導作為降低這些風險的方法。 這些功能有助於提升韌性，但它們不會自動防止風險發生，也不能證明端到端 (end-to-end) 的可用性。

Auto Scaling 有助於回應特定的容量模式，而 Multi-AZ 部署可減少區域內特定基礎架構故障的影響。 兩者皆無法確立應用程式的復原時間、復原點、交易完整性、依賴可用性，或在故障情況下的效能。 韌性設計應定義服務層級目標 (SLO)、RTO、RPO、依賴假設、備份與還原目標、跨區域復原、網路分區行為、降級模式營運，以及來自受控測試的證據。

來源建議透過 AWS Backup 進行自動備份，使用 Outposts 或其他 AWS 災難復原解決方案的災難復原計畫，CloudWatch 警報，遷移失敗時復原回地端，以及在雲端平台驗證完成前維持地端系統的冗餘。 這些是實用的主題，但實作時必須指定備份範圍、保留期、不可變性、加密、跨帳戶或跨區域副本、還原授權、還原測試、警報擁有權以及支援的復原架構。 「AWS 災難復原解決方案」本身並不是一個足夠精確的設計描述。

冗餘必須包含資料、運算、身分、網路、可觀測性、外部供應商和營運程序。 一個應用程式可以有多個執行個體，但如果它依賴一個資料庫寫入節點、一條身分路徑、一條網路路由、一個市場資料供應商，或一本未經測試的執行手冊，它依然會故障。 連續性演練應根據工作負載的風險設定，測試執行個體、可用區、區域、連線路徑、供應商、資料庫副本、憑證路徑和關鍵依賴項遺失的情況。

切換與還原原則

來源中絞殺榕模式的最後一步是將所有流量切換至雲端實作。 正式環境切換應該是分階段且可復原的，而不是單一次的切換。 團隊應定義流量路由控制、平行驗證、寫入權限、資料核對、觀察視窗、批准權限、還原閾值，以及結案的條件。

在兩個環境都處理了不同的寫入操作後，有狀態系統的還原會變得困難。 在結構描述變更、識別碼變更、外部確認、下游發布或不可逆的副作用發生後，還原也可能變得不安全。 有效的復原計畫必須明確定義權威副本、複製方向、最大還原視窗、處理傳輸中交易的方式、核對流程、使用者與對手方的溝通，以及復原的業務批准。

地端系統應根據風險評估的需求維持可用狀態，但單純保留硬體並不能使還原成為可能。 傳統路徑必須進行維護、同步、保護、監控和測試。 遷移應在最終切換前進行至少一次實際的還原或復原演練，並應記錄證據、限制與補救措施。

成本治理與 FinOps

AWS Budgets 和 Cost Explorer 在來源中被點名為管理和預測成本的工具。 它們能提供可視性與閾值警報，但並不會建立當責或防止每一次的成本超支。 遷移應定義帳戶和環境邊界、標籤 (tagging)、成本分攤、業務擁有權、預算閾值、預測審查、新服務的批准，以及異常消耗的升級呈報流程。

成本模型應涵蓋運算、資料庫、儲存、擷取、快照、備份、複製、跨區域與網際網路傳輸、日誌記錄、監控、安全服務、遷移工具、網路連線、授權、支援、設備、混合基礎架構、測試、雙軌並行、人員配置及專業服務。 它應區分固定與變動成本、正式與非正式環境成本，以及正常營運與韌性/遷移成本。

成本最佳化絕不能妥協資料保留、市場資料權限、可復原性、效能或證據保存。 生命週期策略、排程、規格調整 (rightsizing)、承諾使用量決策和資料刪除，均應根據業務與法規要求獲得批准。 單位成本指標（例如：每次投資組合估值的成本、每次回測的成本、每筆遷移紀錄的成本，或每次監控事件的成本）能讓商業案例比一份加總的雲端帳單更具意義。

監控與營運就緒度

來源提議使用 CloudWatch 進行效能監控與日誌記錄，並提議使用 CloudWatch 警報作為遷移警示。 一個具備營運就緒度的平台應該監控技術、業務、安全、資料和成本訊號。 技術訊號包括可用性、延遲百分位數、錯誤、飽和度、佇列時間、連線健康狀態與依賴狀態。 業務訊號包括交易數量、餘額、部位、資料新鮮度、核對、損益 (PnL)、報告完成度以及異常佇列。

監控必須具備閾值、基準線、通知途徑、升級呈報規則、服務擁有者、執行手冊和證據保留機制。 不會引發當責回應的警報不是有效的控制措施。 日誌應做到時間同步、存取控制、防止未經授權的修改、必要時進行遮罩，並能跨傳統與雲端環境進行關聯，以便在跨越遷移邊界時重建事件脈絡。

在每一次遷移計畫展開之前，都應審查營運就緒度。 審查應確認支援覆蓋範圍、on-call (待命) 責任、部署與還原程序、存取批准、儀表板、警報、容量、備份、復原測試、事件分類、廠商聯絡人、使用者溝通和培訓。 只有當團隊能夠在正常和降級的情況下營運新元件時，試點才算成功，而不僅僅是因為該元件能在沙盒中運行。

治理與遷移營運模型

來源建議尋求 AWS 專業服務 (Professional Services) 和 AWS 解決方案架構師的專家指導，並使用沙盒環境進行測試。 這些可以提供有用的技術支援和安全的學習環境，但無法取代機構對架構、風險承擔、安全、合規、資料治理或正式營運的當責。

企業級遷移需要高階主管贊助、遷移決策機構、業務和應用程式擁有者、雲端平台團隊、安全與隱私擁有者、資料擁有者、網路與身分擁有者，以及營運、財務、合規、法務、供應商管理，還有適當的獨立控制或模型審查團隊。 對於批准範圍、接受殘餘風險、授權切換、宣布還原，以及結案遷移發現，應有明確的職責劃分。

營運模型應包括受管的登陸區域 (landing zone)、帳戶與區域策略、策略執行、集中式日誌記錄、身分生命週期、資產盤點、漏洞與修補程式管理、基礎架構即程式碼 (IaC)、發布控制、證據保留、例外管理、第三方監督，以及定期的韌性演練。 來源並未描述這些機制，因此它們是必須進行的設計工作，而非所列 AWS 服務隱含的功能。

遷移驗收關卡

不應僅因為應用程式已在 AWS 啟動就驗收該遷移階段。 安全驗收應展示已獲批准的身分、網路路徑、加密、金鑰控制、漏洞狀態、日誌記錄和事件回應。 資料驗收應展示完整性、核對、血緣、時間點行為、保留以及異常狀況的正確處理。

效能驗收應將目標與商定的基準在具代表性與壓力工作負載下進行比較，包括依賴呼叫、並發性、延遲百分位數、吞吐量和故障行為。 韌性驗收應展示備份與還原、復原目標、依賴故障處理、監控、營運手冊，以及經過測試的還原或復原路徑。 成本驗收應證明用量、預測、所有權和單位經濟效益皆已被理解。

業務和合規驗收應確認使用者能夠完成所需的流程，報告和計算核對無誤，受監管的紀錄保持可用，資料落地和授權要求得到滿足，且控制擁有者已審查了證據。 每個關卡都應有指定的批准人與記錄在案的例外流程。 只有當殘餘風險被理解、受限、記錄在案並獲得正式接受時，遷移才能帶著殘餘風險繼續進行。

Capital One 案例研究聲明

來源引用 Capital One 作為組織遷移到 AWS 並實現敏捷性、可擴展性和成本節約的真實範例。 它連結到 AWS 案例研究頁面 https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/capital-one。 來源沒有提供遷移範圍、日期、工作負載盤點、基準線、實測節省金額、架構、監管邊界，也沒有說明哪些成果可轉移至其他機構。

這個例子可作為進一步研究的提示，但並不能作為其他金融環境也會產生相同結果的證據。 任何重複此聲明的內部簡報，都應使用目前官方的案例研究，指出其中描述的特定工作負載和成果，區分客戶報告的結果與 AWS 一般能力，並避免將公開的案例研究視為機構特定的商業案例。

來源聲明與驗證邊界

該頁面提出了幾個需要加以限定的廣泛聲明。 它將 AWS DMS 描述為提供無縫資料傳輸、將 Auto Scaling 和 Multi-AZ 描述為確保高可用性、建議 Outposts 或未指定的 AWS 災難復原解決方案作為災難復原計畫，並得出遵循這些步驟即可確保法規遵從的結論。 這些陳述是實用的起點，但都不足以作為實作或保證聲明。

來源沒有包含資料量、交易率、延遲、可用性、成本、節省、遷移持續時間、人員配置、RTO 或 RPO 的量化數據。 除了連結之外，它沒有包含 Capital One 成果的證據、沒有 AWS 帳戶或部署的證據、沒有目標架構、沒有目前產品狀態的驗證，也沒有法規控制對應。 頁面的三張圖片僅作為簡報素材，未增加任何清晰的技術、數值或架構內容。

服務名稱和描述在使用前應與最新的 AWS 文件進行核對。 特別是，所點名的 AWS Server Migration Service 可能是過時的產品參考，應確認目前支援的遷移路徑。 確切的 Elastic Load Balancing 選項、資料庫引擎、DMS 模式、部署平台、備份設計、混合服務和災難復原架構，都必須根據現有功能和機構的需求進行選擇。

內部學習總結

長遠的教訓是：業務能力、資料與控制措施必須同時遷移。 從探索和關鍵性評估開始，選擇一個受限的試點，維持清晰的真相來源，驗證資料和效能，在共存期間審慎營運雙邊系統，並只有在安全、韌性、成本、合規和業務驗收證據皆齊全時才進行切換。

AWS 服務可提供探索、運算、資料庫、應用程式託管、流量管理、資料傳輸、監控、備份、成本可視性和混合部署的建構模塊。 但它們並不能免除架構、治理、測試、營運當責或法規判斷的需求。 對金融業而言，遷移品質的衡量標準不在於將流量轉移到雲端有多快，而在於遷移完成後，機構是否能繼續保護資料、服務客戶、履行義務、從故障中復原、解釋其紀錄，以及控制其成本。

title: Black Friday hosting deals: the renewal column is the whole decision
description:
Every Black Friday the same thing happens. A hosting plan shows ₹69/mo, someone takes it, and fourteen months later they are paying ₹289/mo for the same box.

The sale price is not a price. It is a one-time entry fee for a fixed term. The number that decides your actual cost is the renewal rate, and it is almost never on the landing page.

Here is what the India storefront showed when I checked it on 16 November 2026 (pre-GST):

Plan Sale Renews at Jump
Single ₹69 ₹289 +319%
Premium ₹139 ₹449 +223%
Unlimited ₹199 ₹649 +226%
Cloud Startup ₹599 ₹1,599 +167%

Now the VPS ladder, same storefront, same day:

Plan Sale Renews at Jump
KVM 1 ₹599 ₹999 +67%
KVM 2 ₹779 ₹1,199 +54%
KVM 4 ₹1,099 ₹2,399 +118%
KVM 8 ₹2,199 ₹4,399 +100%

Notice the pattern. Shared hosting discounts hard and renews brutally. VPS discounts less and renews gently. KVM 2 is the flattest curve on the whole list — +54%.

So the math for a project you expect to still exist in three years:

Shared Premium: ₹139 × 48 months, then ₹449 forever.
KVM 2 VPS: ₹779 × 24 months, then ₹1,199 forever.

If the site is a brochure that gets 200 visitors a month, shared is correct and the renewal jump is still cheap in absolute rupees. If it is anything with a database doing real work, the VPS renewal is the one you will be glad you read.

The one rule: take the longest term you are confident about, because the sale price only applies to that first term. A 48-month commitment at ₹139 locks four years before the ₹449 starts. A 12-month commitment at a slightly lower monthly locks one.

I keep both columns side by side with the date each figure was checked, because these numbers drift every few weeks: https://mohitkoli.in/blog/hostinger-black-friday-2026

title: Pairing a desktop agent with RFC 8628, and the confirm-step attack the RFC warns about
description:
Some of the people using our apps keep their files in a folder or on a Windows share in their office, while the app runs in the cloud. To get the files across we wrote a small agent in Go, the satellite. It runs next to the share and only makes outbound HTTPS calls, so nobody has to open a port or set up a VPN. It has to be paired with one tenant of the app once, by someone who is an admin there.

That is the problem OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) solves for TVs and CLIs: the device shows a short code, a person types it into a browser where they are already logged in, and the device collects a token. We used it as written. The part that took a second look was section 5.4, remote phishing, and the step in our own UI that the first version got wrong.

The flow

The satellite posts its client_id to /connectors/v1/device_authorization. The server answers with a long device_code, a short user_code like 7KQ2-M9XD, a verification_uri, expires_in: 600 and interval: 5. The satellite shows the code in its setup window and polls /connectors/v1/token with the device code every five seconds.

On the server side we store only hashes of both codes. The user code is 8 characters from Crockford's base32 alphabet (32 symbols, no I, L, O or U), so one random byte modulo 32 picks a symbol without bias. When a person types it, case, dashes and spaces don't matter, and I, L and O are read as 1, 1 and 0.

In the app, a TenantAdmin opens the pairing screen, types the code and clicks Check. If the code belongs to an open request, the screen shows when and from which IP address the request came, so the admin can see whether it was their own machine. Then they give the device a name and confirm. Confirming creates a connector in the admin's tenant and marks the request approved. The next poll returns a token ksat_…, which the server stores as a SHA-256 hash and which the admin can revoke per device.

The satellite's side of this is about 150 lines of Go in internal/pairing/pairing.go. The poll loop handles authorization_pending, slow_down (add five seconds to the interval), expired_token and access_denied, and gives up when expires_in runs out.

What section 5.4 says

The device flow has a built-in weakness: the device that asks for access doesn't have to be the one in front of the person who approves it. An attacker starts a pairing on their own machine, gets a valid user code, and sends it to an admin with a message like "please enter this code to finish the setup". If the admin types it in and confirms, the attacker's machine gets a token for the admin's tenant.

RFC 8628 says to tell the user they are authorizing a device and to confirm it is in their possession. It is stricter about verification_uri_complete, the optional link that already carries the code: since the user no longer types the code, the server should show it and ask the user to check that it matches what their device displays.

For us the attack has teeth. A paired satellite can upload files into the tenant's inbox, and an inbox is where people open attachments.

Version one

Our pairing screen had two steps from the start: Check, then name and confirm. Check showed time and IP of the request. That looked like the mitigation the RFC asks for.

It was a step in the UI only. The check handler read the request and changed nothing. The confirm handler took a user code and a name and claimed any pending request with that code. If an admin's browser landed on the confirm step with a code already filled in, for example through a link someone sent them, they skipped the part where a human looks at the time and the address. The safeguard lived in the order of the screens, and nothing on the server knew about it.

The fix went into the same pull request eight minutes after the first commit, on 19 November, before anything was merged.

The fix

The check now writes. It records on the pending request which admin checked the code and when:

const marked = await updateMany(
  ctx.db,
  deviceAuthorizationTable,
  { checkedByUserId: event.payload.userId, checkedAt: now },
  {
    userCodeHash: event.payload.userCodeHash,
    status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.pending,
    expiresAt: { gt: now },
  },
);

The confirm is one conditional update from pending to approved. It only matches when the same admin checked this code in the last 300 seconds:

const claimed = await updateMany(
  ctx.db,
  deviceAuthorizationTable,
  { status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.approved, ...claim },
  {
    userCodeHash,
    status: DEVICE_AUTHORIZATION_STATUS.pending,
    expiresAt: { gt: ctx.tz.now() },
    checkedByUserId: claim.approvedByUserId,
    checkedAt: { gt: ctx.tz.now().subtract({ seconds: CODE_CHECK_VALID_SECONDS }) },
  },
);

If nothing matches, the handler returns the same "invalid code" error as for an unknown or expired code, and the connector it just created rolls back with the transaction. Because it is a single update, a code confirmed twice at once produces one connector and one winner. There's a test for that race, and one that walks through the cases: no check, a check by another admin, a check that is 301 seconds old, and finally a fresh check by the confirming admin, where only the last one pairs.

With that in place we could add verification_uri_complete later the same day. The satellite shows a link that opens the pairing screen with the code filled in. The admin still has to click Check, look at the time and address, and confirm. A link sent by an attacker gets them to the same screen, where the request shows up with a stranger's IP.

The rest of the hardening

The client_id of the satellite is public; it's in an open source binary. So anyone can start pairings, and the start endpoint is the one that needed limits:

  • at most 3 open requests per address, 1000 in total, and 10 starts per minute per address. Above that the endpoint answers 429 slow_down and stores nothing.
  • IPv6 addresses count per /64. A per-address limit on a full IPv6 address is easy to get around with a fresh address per request.
  • codes expire after 600 seconds. A redeemed request is deleted, together with its address.
  • checking and confirming codes is rate limited to 20 tries per 5 minutes per admin.
  • there is no reject button. Before it is confirmed a request belongs to no tenant, so nobody has anything to reject, and it disappears after ten minutes.

What we took from it

A two-step screen is not a security control by itself. The server has to be able to tell that the first step happened, for this user and this code, and recently. Writing it as a condition in the same update that does the claim kept it to two columns and one where clause.

The satellite is open source at github.com/CosmicDriftGameStudio/kumiko-satellite, and the server side is the connectors feature in kumiko-framework. If you run a device flow with verification_uri_complete, I'd be curious how you bind the approval to the person who looked at the code.

title: How to Build a Voice AI Agent in 2026-2027: Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi (Step-by-Step)
description:
Your voice agent works in the demo. Then a real customer calls from an open-plan office.

The agent hears the caller. It also hears the colleague two desks away. It answers both, stops mid-sentence, and the call goes sideways.

If you're:

  • building your first voice agent and picking a framework,
  • moving a prototype from your laptop to real phone calls,
  • or choosing between Pipecat, LiveKit and Vapi,

this guide walks you through all three with the same agent, so you can compare them on code you can actually run.

Short answer: pick Pipecat if you want full control in open-source Python, LiveKit Agents if you want open-source code plus managed WebRTC and telephony, and Vapi if you want a hosted agent you configure instead of code. Whichever you pick, put Krisp voice isolation in front of the agent's ears. All three have a ready-made Krisp integration (on Pipecat, through Pipecat Cloud), and any other pipeline can call Krisp's standalone Voice Isolation API. In my LiveKit test recordings, it cut the words the agent picked up from a background voice from 224 to 35.

How a voice AI agent works

Every voice agent is the same pipeline, whatever framework you use:

  1. Transport brings the caller's audio in (WebRTC, a phone line, a browser).
  2. Voice isolation keeps the caller's voice and removes background voices and noise.
  3. VAD and turn detection decide when the caller is speaking and when they've finished.
  4. Speech-to-text (STT) turns the audio into words.
  5. The LLM decides what to say.
  6. Text-to-speech (TTS) speaks the answer back.

Some agents replace steps 4 to 6 with a single speech-to-speech model, which may also handle step 3. Others merge only part of the pipeline: Deepgram Flux, for example, builds turn detection into speech-to-text. Voice isolation can sit in front of either setup.

It's also the easiest step to leave out.

That's the step that decides whether the rest of the pipeline is working with the caller's words or with everyone in the room.

Speech-to-text handles noise well now. It still transcribes a second person talking near the mic, and the LLM answers it. In Krisp's test for its Voice Isolation 2.5 release, 10 speech-to-text systems averaged 2.10% word error rate on clean single-speaker audio and 35.92% with a second person talking. With Voice Isolation 2.5 in front, that 35.92% fell to 10.90% (release post).

Pipecat vs LiveKit vs Vapi: which one to pick

The three tools sit at different levels of control:

Pipecat LiveKit Agents Vapi
What it is Open-source Python framework for voice and multimodal pipelines Open-source agent framework on top of LiveKit's WebRTC platform Hosted voice agent platform
You write The whole pipeline, frame by frame An agent class and a session config A JSON assistant config
Hosting Anywhere, or Pipecat Cloud LiveKit Cloud or self-hosted Vapi
STT / LLM / TTS Bring your own providers Your own keys, or LiveKit Inference (no provider keys) Picked in the config, billed through Vapi
Krisp voice isolation KrispVivaFilter on Pipecat Cloud; Krisp's Voice Isolation API (or a licensed SDK) for local pipelines krisp.voice_isolation() plugin Smart Denoising, one config field
Best for Teams that want full control over every frame Teams that want code plus managed real-time infrastructure Teams that want an agent live without running servers

I built the same agent on each one: Ava, a support agent for an online store that answers order-status questions in one or two sentences.

1. Build a voice agent with Pipecat

Pipecat is the most hands-on option. You assemble a pipeline of processors and Pipecat moves audio and text frames through it.

I used pipecat-ai 1.16.0 and OpenAI for all three AI services, so the only key needed is OPENAI_API_KEY.

pip install "pipecat-ai[openai,silero,webrtc,runner]" python-dotenv

import os
from pipecat.audio.vad.silero import SileroVADAnalyzer
from pipecat.frames.frames import LLMRunFrame
from pipecat.pipeline.pipeline import Pipeline
from pipecat.pipeline.runner import PipelineRunner
from pipecat.pipeline.task import PipelineParams, PipelineTask
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_context import LLMContext
from pipecat.processors.aggregators.llm_response_universal import LLMContextAggregatorPair, LLMUserAggregatorParams
from pipecat.runner.types import RunnerArguments
from pipecat.runner.utils import create_transport
from pipecat.services.openai.llm import OpenAILLMService
from pipecat.services.openai.stt import OpenAISTTService
from pipecat.services.openai.tts import OpenAITTSService
from pipecat.transports.base_transport import TransportParams

# Krisp VIVA ships preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud; locally the import fails and the bot runs without it
try:
    from pipecat.audio.filters.krisp_viva_filter import KrispVivaFilter
    krisp_filter = KrispVivaFilter()
except Exception:
    krisp_filter = None

INSTRUCTIONS = ("You are Ava, a support agent for an online store. Keep answers short: one or two sentences, "
                "spoken style. If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today.")

async def run_bot(transport, runner_args):
    key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
    stt = OpenAISTTService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4o-transcribe")
    llm = OpenAILLMService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4.1-mini",
                           settings=OpenAILLMService.Settings(system_instruction=INSTRUCTIONS))
    tts = OpenAITTSService(api_key=key, model="gpt-4o-mini-tts", voice="alloy")

    context = LLMContext()
    user_agg, assistant_agg = LLMContextAggregatorPair(
        context, user_params=LLMUserAggregatorParams(vad_analyzer=SileroVADAnalyzer()))

    pipeline = Pipeline([transport.input(), stt, user_agg, llm, tts, transport.output(), assistant_agg])
    task = PipelineTask(pipeline, params=PipelineParams(enable_metrics=True))

    @transport.event_handler("on_client_connected")
    async def on_connected(transport, client):
        context.add_message({"role": "developer", "content": "Greet the caller and ask how you can help."})
        await task.queue_frames([LLMRunFrame()])

    await PipelineRunner(handle_sigint=runner_args.handle_sigint).run(task)

async def bot(runner_args: RunnerArguments):
    params = lambda: TransportParams(audio_in_enabled=True, audio_out_enabled=True, audio_in_filter=krisp_filter)
    transport = await create_transport(runner_args, {"daily": params, "webrtc": params})
    await run_bot(transport, runner_args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pipecat.runner.run import main
    main()

Run python bot.py and open http://localhost:7860/client. Pipecat serves a small playground where you connect and talk to the bot over WebRTC, with no account needed. Mine greeted me, and when I sent "Hi, my order number is 4471. Where is it?" it answered "Your order 4471 is out for delivery today."

Adding Krisp. The KrispVivaFilter goes in audio_in_filter, so it cleans the caller's audio before VAD and STT ever see it. Its dependencies come preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud (base image 0.1.8 or later), and you turn it on when you deploy:

pipecat cloud deploy --krisp-viva-audio-filter tel

Pick tel (models up to 16 kHz, suited to phone audio) or pro (up to 32 kHz). According to Pipecat's docs, the first 10,000 Krisp minutes per month are free, then $0.0015 per minute.

Running KrispVivaFilter outside Pipecat Cloud needs a commercial VIVA SDK license. For local development there's a simpler route: Krisp's self-serve Voice Isolation API. Any pipeline that can open a WebSocket can call it, so you send the caller's audio and feed the cleaned audio into VAD and STT. New accounts start with $30 in free credits. It's a separate integration, not the KrispVivaFilter above. I didn't deploy to Pipecat Cloud for this guide, so my measured Krisp results come from LiveKit below.

Pros

  • Full control over every processor in the pipeline.
  • Open source, runs anywhere Python runs.
  • Krisp VIVA preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud, one deploy flag to enable.

Cons

  • More code to own than the other two.
  • The built-in KrispVivaFilter needs Pipecat Cloud; locally you call Krisp's Voice Isolation API instead (or use a licensed SDK).

Best for: teams that want to own the pipeline end to end.

2. Build a voice agent with LiveKit Agents

LiveKit Agents gives you an open-source agent framework on top of LiveKit's real-time platform. Your agent joins a "room" like any other participant, and LiveKit handles WebRTC and telephony.

I used livekit-agents 1.8.13 with LiveKit Inference, so the only credentials are the LiveKit Cloud project URL, key and secret. STT, LLM and TTS are billed through LiveKit, with no provider keys.

pip install "livekit-agents[silero,turn-detector]" livekit-plugins-krisp python-dotenv

from livekit import agents
from livekit.agents import Agent, AgentSession, inference, room_io
from livekit.plugins import krisp, silero

INSTRUCTIONS = """You are Ava, a support agent for an online store.
Keep answers short: one or two sentences, spoken style.
If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today."""

class SupportAgent(Agent):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(instructions=INSTRUCTIONS)

async def entrypoint(ctx: agents.JobContext) -> None:
    session = AgentSession(
        stt="deepgram/nova-3",          # LiveKit Inference model IDs
        llm="openai/gpt-4.1-mini",
        tts="cartesia/sonic-3",
        vad=silero.VAD.load(),
        turn_detection=inference.TurnDetector(),
    )
    await session.start(
        room=ctx.room,
        agent=SupportAgent(),
        room_options=room_io.RoomOptions(
            audio_input=room_io.AudioInputOptions(
                # Krisp voice isolation before VAD, turn detection and STT
                noise_cancellation=krisp.voice_isolation(noise_suppression_level=100),
            ),
        ),
    )
    await session.generate_reply(instructions="Greet the caller and ask how you can help.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    agents.cli.run_app(agents.WorkerOptions(entrypoint_fnc=entrypoint))

python agent.py download-files   # once: VAD and turn-detector weights
python agent.py dev              # registers the agent with LiveKit Cloud

The Krisp plugin needs no Krisp account and no model files: it authenticates through your LiveKit Cloud project. LiveKit's free Build plan includes 100 voice-isolation minutes, then $0.0012 per minute on paid plans (pricing). For SIP phone calls, use krisp.voice_isolation_telephony() instead.

One setting matters more than it looks. LiveKit's plugin defaults to noise_suppression_level=75. That's LiveKit's default, not Krisp's: Krisp's own default is full strength (100). In my four test recordings below, going from LiveKit's default to 100 roughly halved the word error rate again.

Pros

  • Open-source code with managed WebRTC and telephony.
  • LiveKit Inference: one account instead of three provider keys.
  • Krisp plugin works out of the box with a LiveKit Cloud project.

Cons

  • The Krisp plugin needs LiveKit Cloud for real-time transport, unless you hold your own Krisp license.
  • On Windows, dev mode didn't reload my code changes; I had to restart the worker.

Best for: teams that want to write the agent in code but not run real-time media servers.

3. Build a voice agent with Vapi

Vapi is the no-servers option. An agent is a JSON "assistant" config, and Vapi runs the whole pipeline.

import os
import requests

assistant = {
    "name": "Ava - store support",
    "firstMessage": "Hi, this is Ava from the store. How can I help you today?",
    "transcriber": {"provider": "deepgram", "model": "nova-3", "language": "en"},
    "model": {
        "provider": "openai",
        "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
        "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are Ava, a support agent for an online store. "
                      "Keep answers short. If the caller gives an order number, say it is out for delivery today."}],
    },
    "voice": {"provider": "vapi", "voiceId": "Elliot"},
    # Smart Denoising uses Krisp to remove background voices and noise
    "backgroundSpeechDenoisingPlan": {"smartDenoisingPlan": {"enabled": True}},
}

r = requests.post("https://api.vapi.ai/assistant",
                  headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['VAPI_API_KEY']}"},
                  json=assistant, timeout=30)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["id"])

Vapi answered 201 with the new assistant ID, and the response echoed "smartDenoisingPlan": {"enabled": true}. To call it from a web page, Vapi provides the @vapi-ai/web SDK, which uses your public key.

Vapi's docs describe Smart Denoising as Krisp's technology for removing background voices and noise in real time (docs). It replaces the older backgroundDenoisingEnabled flag.

Pros

  • No servers: an agent is one API call.
  • Krisp voice isolation is one config field.
  • Transcriber, model and voice configured in the same request.

Cons

  • Less control over the pipeline than code-first frameworks.
  • Model, voice and transcriber usage is billed through Vapi by default.

Best for: teams that want a hosted agent without running infrastructure.

Test your agent like a real call

A voice agent that works on your laptop mic proves very little. Real calls have other people in them.

So I tested the LiveKit agent the way a real call would hit it. A small script joins the room as the caller and plays a real recording into the agent at real-time pace: four recordings from Krisp's open Voice Isolation Benchmark Dataset, two from working call centers and two from home and office settings, each with a second person talking. Then I captured what the agent's speech-to-text actually heard and compared it with the dataset's hand-written transcripts.

Agent input Word error rate Extra words in the transcript
No voice isolation 58.2% 224
Krisp at LiveKit's default (75) 41.6% 139
Krisp, level 100 21.8% 35

Same LiveKit agent, same four recordings, Deepgram nova-3 through LiveKit Inference. "Extra words" are insertions against the main speaker's transcript, mostly from the background voice. One run per setting, so treat small differences between files as noise.

Without voice isolation, the agent's transcript picked up 224 words the caller never said. With Krisp at level 100, 35. On one office recording, the extra words went from 43 to zero.

That's the gap between an agent that answers the caller and one that answers the room.

Krisp's open voice isolation benchmark points the same way at a bigger scale: across 265 recordings and 11 speech-to-text configurations, word error rate fell from 23.24% to 6.24% with Voice Isolation 2.5.

My relative drop (58.2% to 21.8%, about 63% fewer errors) is almost the same as Deepgram Nova-3 streaming in Krisp's benchmark (20.4% to 8.0%, 61% fewer). My absolute numbers are higher, likely from the scoring and the small sample, but the two results agree.

Going multilingual with Krisp's Voice Translation API

Once the agent hears the right person, the next wall is language. Krisp's voice translation API does real-time speech-to-speech translation across 61 languages, with background voice cancellation built in. Each session translates one direction (I tested English to Spanish); for a two-way call you run one session per direction.

It's a WebSocket: you get a short-lived session key with your Krisp API key, send one config message, then stream 16 kHz PCM.

import asyncio, json, os, requests, websockets

def session_key():
    r = requests.post("https://api.developers.krisp.ai/v2/sdk/tokens/session",
                      headers={"Authorization": f"api-key {os.environ['KRISP_API_KEY']}"},
                      json={"usage_type": "vt", "expiration_ttl": 30})
    return r.json()["data"]["session_key"]

async def translate(pcm_chunks):
    url = "wss://streaming.krisp.ai/vt?authorization=" + requests.utils.quote(f"Api-Key {session_key()}")
    async with websockets.connect(url, max_size=None) as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"config": {
            "audio": {"format": "pcm_s16le", "sample_rate": 16000, "channels": 1},
            "source_language": "en-US", "target_language": "es-ES", "voice": "female",
            "transcript": {"interim": False, "final": True, "translate": True},
            "features": {"background_voice_cancellation": True},
        }}))
        # stream 20 ms chunks with ws.send(chunk); translated audio comes back as binary frames,
        # transcripts and translations as JSON events

I streamed 30 seconds of a real call-center recording through it. It sent back 29.3 seconds of Spanish speech plus both transcripts, for example:

"Thank you, Lilith. Your account 4471-B reflects usage of 512 kW per hour this cycle."
"Gracias, Lilith. Su cuenta 4471-B refleja un consumo de 512 kW por hora en este ciclo."

One gotcha: URL-encode the authorization value. The space in Api-Key <key> made my first handshake fail with HTTP 400.

Production checklist

Before your agent takes real calls:

  • Isolate the caller's voice at the start of the pipeline, and check the level: in my four test recordings, noise_suppression_level=100 cut errors sharply compared with LiveKit's default (75). Krisp's own default is full strength (100). Measure it on your own audio.
  • Use the telephony model for phone calls: voice_isolation_telephony() on LiveKit, tel on Pipecat Cloud.
  • Budget for latency. Krisp voice isolation adds no more than 20 ms, 15 ms of it algorithmic latency; through the SDK, plan for about 25 ms. If you call the WebSocket API, add network time on top.
  • Test with real recordings from calls, homes and offices, not your own mic in a quiet room. A second voice is the case that breaks agents.
  • Watch turn-taking and interruptions. Krisp also ships Turn-Taking and Interrupt Prediction models in its VIVA SDK for teams that run their own pipeline.
  • Load secrets explicitly. An old OPENAI_API_KEY in my Windows environment silently overrode my .env and returned 401s until I used load_dotenv(override=True).

FAQ

How do I build a voice AI agent?

Pick a framework (Pipecat, LiveKit Agents or Vapi), connect a transport, add voice isolation, VAD and turn detection, then speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. All three frameworks in this guide get a basic agent running in under 100 lines of code or one API call.

Pipecat vs LiveKit: which is better?

Neither is better in general. Pipecat gives you full control of the pipeline in open-source Python. LiveKit Agents gives you open-source agent code plus managed WebRTC and telephony. Pick Pipecat for control, LiveKit for infrastructure you don't want to run.

LiveKit vs Vapi: what's the difference?

LiveKit Agents is code: you write the agent and LiveKit runs the real-time transport. Vapi is a hosted platform: you send a JSON config and Vapi runs everything. Vapi is faster to start; LiveKit gives you more control.

Do Pipecat, LiveKit and Vapi support Krisp?

Yes. Pipecat has KrispVivaFilter, preinstalled on Pipecat Cloud; for local development, call Krisp's Voice Isolation API over a WebSocket. LiveKit has the livekit-plugins-krisp plugin with krisp.voice_isolation(). Vapi's Smart Denoising uses Krisp, enabled with backgroundSpeechDenoisingPlan.smartDenoisingPlan.enabled.

Why does my voice agent stop mid-sentence or answer things the caller didn't say?

Usually because it hears more than the caller: a colleague, a TV, another agent on a call-center floor. The agent takes that voice for the caller cutting in and stops mid-sentence, and speech-to-text transcribes its words too. Voice isolation before VAD and STT removes it; in my tests it cut the extra words in the transcript from 224 to 35.

Can a voice agent handle callers in other languages?

Yes. Krisp's voice translation API translates speech to speech in real time across 61 languages. Each session handles one direction, so a two-way call uses two sessions.

The takeaway

Getting a basic voice agent running is the easy part on any of these three frameworks.

Making it hear the right person on a real call is the part that's easy to skip. It's a ready-made integration on all three, and one API call for any other pipeline.

title: Calculating percentiles at scale
description:
Some times ago, We designed an analytics dashboard with lots of analytical aggregated information, most of which we didn't know why was needed there.

We had a bunch of Third Party APIs, and based on the requests, their responses and timings used to differ. It was decided that all the requests will be logged in our database for analytics purpose, along with their latencies, the dashboard will have a dedicated section to show the p50, p95, and p99 latencies. Any unusual spikes in latency would be noticed and alerted accordingly.

Before moving forward, let me tell you the tech stack:

  • MSSQL for database
  • Node.js for backend

That's all we need to know.

The mistake

Initially, we tried to calculate the percentiles directly from the raw request logs stored in the database, expecting that simple queries and basic indexing would be enough.

Then came the api integrations, some of these APIs had either extremely high latencies like going upto 40 seconds, some of them required us to poll repeatedly until a certain condition was met. Irrespective of all these, we continued to log them directly in the database. we had a timeout threshold of 60 seconds which means no request will go beyond this point in time.

Our dashboard had filters - date range with minute level granularity, endpoint selection, query params selection, response status, and other important values, and by default, we were showing the latency over the week, with none of the other filters applied.

It didn't take longer to realize that querying raw logs for percentiles was becoming increasingly inefficient and slow, especially as the volume of data grew and the variability in request latencies widened. In the test environment, with limited data, the dashboard APIs started taking more than 26s to return with the default filters.

Trying the fix

We had to launch it, so we didn't had enough time to properly look at the problem. Still we went through couple of iterations:

  • First, we were calculating percentiles after fetching all the records in node. we moved it to calculating percentiles directly in the database using SQL queries.
  • for filters, we created individual indexes and composite indexes on the columns that were frequently used together.
  • In the final iteration, asking claude, we found that our SQL query was calculating p50, p95 and p99 separately, it suggested changes that helped us calculate all in a single pass, bringing down the query execution time significantly.

Finally, the dashboard loaded faster within 5-6 seconds with default filters. However, changing date filters to months, still caused us to wait long and get a timeout eventually. Challenge accepted.

Pre-computing percentiles

The first thing come to my mind was using timeseries or similar kind of db extensions that auto pre-compute and store the percentiles for different time intervals. For now 1m and 1hr buckets would be enough. Then based on time range I just need to do some average or median of these pre-computed percentiles to get an approximate result.

There was a problem, It's not a postgres db. So what, we can build around tables by ourselves and manage them just like timeseries extensions do, by creating and maintaining pre-aggregated tables for different time intervals and updating them as new data comes in.

Only mistake was that I didn't touched the percentile math at all. Thankfully, I went to brainstorm the idea first with claude.

Percentiles are not additive, they don't work like count, sum, avg, min/max where you can combine pre-aggregated values to get the overall result. A percentile is a rank position in a sorted distribution. If a minute bucket has 10 requests, but another minute bucket has 100 requests, simply averaging the percentiles of these buckets will not reflect the true percentile of the combined 110 requests. The distribution of values within each bucket matters, and ignoring it leads to incorrect results.

Deciding tradeoffs and considerations

  1. We don't want exactly accurate percentiles, if we can get appproximate results which are deviating within 5% of the actual value, thats fine. what it means?

    • if the p95 is 100ms, getting a result between 95ms and 105ms is acceptable.
    • if the p95 is 55s, getting a result between 52.2s and 57.7s is acceptable. This would seem huge, but for high-latency operations, a 5% deviation is tolerable and still provides meaningful insights preventing false alerts.

  2. We are ok with reducing some filters, which are hard to support efficiently at scale, as long as the core insights and critical metrics remain accurate and actionable.

  3. We don't want to remove minute level granularity in the date range filters, simply because we are lazy to redesign the date component to allow user to select finer intervals.

  4. It's still a MVP and we don't want to move the data to a separate BI system or introduce complex ETL pipelines at this stage. We aim to keep the solution simple and maintainable within the existing infrastructure.

The approach for efficiently calculating percentiles

The key idea is to pre calculate the counts and distributions of the values within time buckets along with filters.

Instead of storing individual request times, we can store a histogram of latencies for each minute or hour bucket. Each histogram will capture the distribution of latencies within that time interval. When a query comes in for a larger time range, we can merge the histograms of the relevant buckets and then calculate approximate percentiles from the combined histogram. This allows us to efficiently compute percentiles over large datasets without scanning every individual record. Don't worry, I will explain it with example later on.

Our requests usaully have latencies in range of 5s to 1m, after which they get a timeout. we decided to use 1000ms buckets for the histograms, which gives us a good balance between accuracy and storage efficiency. we reduced down these filters:

  • response code - we only care about successful requests, any 4xx or higher status usually returns very early. not contributing to the percentiles.
  • user and other high cardinality attributes, because they are not suitable for histograms.

after this, we are left with the 3 filters and fixed 30×2×3=180 values. still high but manageable, if it's skewed.

so now we have 2 tables representing histograms over time buckets of 1m and 1h, looking like this:

time filter_1 filter_2 filter_3 b0_1s b1_2s b2_3s ... b59_60s total
2026-12-01 12:00 Abc a true 0 0 22 ... 0 590
2026-12-01 12:01 Def b false 1 0 18 ... 0 483

so now we have count of requests that fall under each latency bucket and filter.

calculating percentiles for the date range 12:00 to 12:01, with the filter combination filter_1 = Abc, filter_2 = a, filter_3 = true looks like this:

  • merge the histograms for the relevant time buckets (12:00 and 12:01) for each filter combination.
  • sum the counts for each latency bucket and the total column across the rows from 12:00 to 12:01 that matches the filter combination.
  • results:
b2_3sb3_4sb4_5sb35_36stotal​=22+18=40=18+39=57=0+48=48…=78+29=107=40+57+48+107=252​
  • calculate percentile range:
p50p90​=0.5×252=126=0.9×252=226.8​
  • That means p50 is the 126th request in the sorted order of latencies, and p90 is the 227th request.
  • commulative count of requests by latency bucket:
b2_3s+b3_4sb2_3s+b3_4s+b4_5s​=40+57=97=40+57+48=145​
  • so p50 lies somewhere in b4_5s time range:
126−97=29
  • so the 126th request lies 29 requests into the b4_5s bucket.
  • b4_5s has 48 requests in total, assuming they are evenly distributed into the b4_5s bucket. so the p50 latency is approximately:
4829​×1000ms≈604ms 4s+604ms≈4.604s

Even if it's not perfectly uniform distribution, with this bucket range, the maximum error will be within 1s range, while we accepted the error at around 2.2s in our tradeoffs. so practically, we can increase the bucket size to 2s for better storage efficiency without significantly affecting the accuracy.

The math looks terrible here, lot's of operations, but this is still significantly more efficient than sorting all individual request latencies, especially at scale.
We can do this all computation directly in SQL using queries too, saving a lot of memory and processing time compared to fetching and sorting all individual request latencies.

Scaling further

  • We can improve storage and computation by increasing the bucket size.
  • We also can add another level of aggregation, such as daily or weekly histograms, to further reduce storage and computation requirements for larger date range queries.
  • We can improve the date range filters by restricting to 5minute granularity, which reduces the number of time buckets we need to process.

Note: AI is only used to format the Katex(Latex math) in this document because Dev.to Latex support is terrible
