title: How to check Allegro.pl prices for a list of EAN codes in bulk with Python
description:
If you sell on Allegro, or you supply people who do, the question you keep asking is simple: for this list of products, who sells each one and for how much? Checking that by hand works for five EANs. It stops working at fifty.

This guide shows how to feed a list of EAN/GTIN codes into the Allegro Prices by EAN scraper on Apify and get back every seller and price for each product. I ran it on 12 everyday EANs this morning (a Coca-Cola can, Mars bars, a Nivea cream, Stabilo and BIC pens, mineral water, Nutella) and all the numbers below come from that run.

What you get back

One row per EAN. Each row has summary prices plus a nested offers list with one entry per seller.

Field What it holds
ean, found Your code and whether Allegro has an exact product match for it
productName, productId, productUrl The matched Allegro product page
totalOffersAvailable How many offers Allegro lists for that product
offerCount How many offers came back in this row (capped by topNOffers)
lowestPrice, highestPrice, avgPrice Min, max and mean across the returned offers, PLN gross
smartOffersCount, superSellerOffersCount Offers with Allegro Smart! and with the Super Seller badge
alternativeMatches Other products that matched the same code, such as multipacks
offers[] price, sellerRating, isSuperSeller, isCompany, smart, freeDelivery, deliveryInfo, isPromoted, offerUrl

A few results from my run, with topNOffers set to 30 and sorted cheapest first:

Product Offers on Allegro Lowest Median of returned
Mars bar 139 2.46 PLN 3.20 PLN
Stabilo Point 88 fineliner 211 2.99 PLN 3.87 PLN
Coca-Cola 330 ml can 59 3.15 PLN 5.52 PLN
Cisowianka still water 6x1.5 L 30 2.99 PLN 21.49 PLN

Two of the 12 codes came back as found: false with the message "No exact match for this EAN on Allegro.pl". That is the behaviour you want. Allegro showed only "similar" items for those codes, and the scraper refused to guess.

The input options that matter

The input form has seven fields. You will touch four of them.

  • eans (required). One code per line, 8 to 14 digits, up to 5,000 per run.
  • topNOffers. How many offers to keep per product, 1 to 200, default 20. You pay per EAN, so raising this to 200 costs the same. The trade-off is a bigger dataset.
  • sortBy. price-asc, price-desc or rating-desc. Combined with topNOffers this decides which offers you see. On the Mars bar, with 139 offers and a limit of 30, the "highest" price in the row was 3.49 PLN because I only kept the 30 cheapest.
  • smartFilter. all, smart-only or exclude-smart. Useful if you only care about offers a Smart! buyer would actually pick.

The rest: includePromoted (I switched it off to skip sponsored listings), useCache (keeps the EAN to product match for 30 days so repeat runs skip the search step; prices are never cached) and maxConcurrency (1 to 25).

Option 1: no code

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free. A free Apify account is enough.
  2. Paste your EANs into the EAN / GTIN codes box, one per line. A column copied from Excel works.
  3. Set Max offers per product. I used 30.
  4. Pick a sort order and, if you want, the Smart! filter.
  5. Click Start. My 12 codes took 186 seconds with concurrency at 6. For a few hundred codes, raise concurrency (the maximum is 25).
  6. Open the Output tab and export to CSV, Excel or JSON. The summary columns export flat. The offers list exports as nested JSON, which is where Python helps.

Option 2: Python with pandas

Install the client and pandas:

pip install apify-client pandas

Then run the actor, pull the dataset and flatten the offers into one row per seller:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run_input = {
    "eans": [
        "5449000000996",  # Coca-Cola 330 ml
        "5000159407236",  # Mars
        "4006381333931",  # Stabilo Point 88
        "5902078000201",  # Cisowianka 6x1.5 L
    ],
    "topNOffers": 30,
    "sortBy": "price-asc",
    "includePromoted": False,
}

run = client.actor("liveclaude/allegro-ean-prices").call(run_input=run_input)
items = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

# Summary: one row per EAN
summary = pd.DataFrame(items)
cols = ["ean", "found", "productName", "totalOffersAvailable",
        "lowestPrice", "avgPrice", "highestPrice"]
print(summary[[c for c in cols if c in summary.columns]])

# Offers: one row per seller offer
found = [i for i in items if i.get("found")]
offers = pd.json_normalize(found, record_path="offers",
                           meta=["ean", "productName"])

# Median is safer than mean on Allegro (see below)
stats = (offers.groupby(["ean", "productName"])["price"]
               .agg(["count", "min", "median", "max"])
               .reset_index())
print(stats)

# Only business sellers with Smart!
b2b_smart = offers[(offers["isCompany"] == True) & (offers["smart"] == True)]
b2b_smart[["ean", "price", "sellerRating", "deliveryInfo", "offerUrl"]] \
    .to_csv("allegro_offers.csv", index=False)

Why the median? Look at the water row. The cheapest offer was 2.99 PLN, but the average across 22 offers was 329.69 PLN because someone lists a pallet under the same product. The Nutella 500 g row had a lowest price of 20.65 PLN and an average of 613.11 PLN for the same reason. The median of the returned offers (21.49 PLN for the water) is much closer to what a buyer pays. If you run price monitoring on avgPrice alone, these outliers will make it look like prices jumped.

One more check worth adding: compare productName against what you expect. One code in my list matched a product whose name had nothing to do with the brand I had in mind. Sellers sometimes attach the wrong EAN to a listing, and Allegro's catalogue inherits it. A quick string check on the name catches that before it reaches a report.

Scheduling and integrations

Price checks are only useful when they repeat. In Apify Console:

  • Save your input as a Task, then add a Schedule (daily at 06:00 works for most monitoring).
  • Connect the dataset to Google Sheets, Make, Zapier or n8n, or add a webhook that fires when the run succeeds.
  • With useCache on, the second and later runs skip the EAN lookup. In my run the Coca-Cola code came back with fromCache: true from an earlier lookup.

You can also call it in one HTTP request:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/liveclaude~allegro-ean-prices/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"eans": ["5449000000996"], "topNOffers": 50}'

Pricing

The actor charges per EAN, with all offers for that EAN included:

Event Free plan Bronze Silver Gold and up
EAN matched (product + all offers), per 1,000 $12.00 $11.40 $10.80 $10.20
EAN with no exact match, per 1,000 $4.00 $3.80 $3.60 $3.40

There is also a start fee of $0.00005 per run. My 12-code test was 10 matches and 2 misses, so about $0.13 on the Free plan. A daily check of 1,000 EANs on the Free plan comes to about $12 per day if every code matches. Codes the scraper fails to fetch on its side are not charged.

Responsible use

The data is public listing data: prices, product names and seller ratings anyone can see on allegro.pl without logging in. Some Allegro sellers are private individuals, and their login can be their real name. Keep seller logins out of anything you publish, and only store them if you have a business reason and a legal basis under GDPR. For price monitoring you rarely need them; isCompany, sellerRating and the offer URL are usually enough. Keep request volumes sensible and respect Allegro's terms for your use case.

If you already keep your catalogue in a spreadsheet with an EAN column, you are one paste away from a full competitor price list. Start with 20 codes, check the matches by hand once, then put it on a schedule.

This tutorial was written with AI assistance and checked by the author. All numbers come from a real run of the scraper.

title: Under the Hood of Google Cloud Data Agent Kit: MCP Tools, SKILL.md Playbooks & Custom Guardrails
description:
Welcome !

In Part 1, we set up Google Cloud Data Agent Kit (DAK) in Antigravity IDE and stayed mostly on the UI side that looked at browsing Cloud Storage, previewing BigQuery tables, and running inline SQL through the Mini Cloud Console.

Remember that two-lane architecture from Part 1?

  • Lane 1 (IDE UI) talks to Google Cloud over direct Cloud APIs so browsing tables and schemas is instant and burns zero LLM tokens.

  • Lane 2 (AI Coding Agent) is where the real automation happens - combining MCP Tools and Agentic Skills (SKILL.md).

When people hear Agentic Skills or MCP, it can easily sound like black-box buzzwords. In this post, we're going to open the hood in Antigravity IDE, see what Google Cloud engineers actually put inside a SKILL.md file, and then put both MCP tools and Skills to work on our devfest_commerce dataset.

Why Giving an LLM Raw Database Access Isn't Enough

Giving an AI coding assistant an MCP connection to BigQuery solves context, it can read your live schemas instead of guessing table and column names.

But live access alone doesn't make an agent a good data engineer. Without guidance, a general-purpose model will still happily:

  • Write SELECT * on a 10 TB table
  • Use slower WHERE id IN (SELECT ...) subqueries instead of WHERE EXISTS
  • Skip partition filters or cluster keys
  • Run a DROP TABLE or TRUNCATE without double-checking if you phrase a cleanup prompt loosely

That is the gap between connecting an agent to your data and teaching it how to work safely and efficiently with Google Data Cloud.

Hands vs. Brains: MCP Tools vs. Agentic Skills

Data Agent Kit splits that responsibility into two clean pieces:

  • MCP Tools ("The Hands"): Live Model Context Protocol connectors that let the agent call Google Cloud APIs - listing datasets, reading table schemas, inspecting Cloud Storage objects, or executing queries - without you copy-pasting metadata into chat.

  • Agentic Skills ("The Brains"): Plain, open-source Markdown files (SKILL.md) written by Google Cloud engineers. They contain explicit rules, decision trees, and checklists for specific workflows like BigQuery SQL optimization, data cleaning, dbt/Dataform pipelines, Spark debugging, and data-loss prevention.

Step 1: Ask the Agent What It Actually Has Enabled

Before digging into files, try this exact prompt I ran during my DevFest Mangaluru demo inside the Antigravity Agent Chat panel:

What Data Agent Kit skills and MCP tools do you currently have enabled for BigQuery and Cloud Storage? Group them briefly into "Skills (Playbooks)" and "MCP Tools (Actions)" so we can see how you work.

You will see the agent separate its actions (MCP tools for inspecting datasets, tables, and buckets) from its playbooks (skills like bigquery-sql, data-autocleaning, google-cloud-storage-basics, and accidental-data-loss-prevention).

Opening a Real SKILL.md File Inside Antigravity IDE

A Skill isn't hidden compiled code or a proprietary prompt locked on a server , instead it is a plain Markdown file sitting right on your machine.

Under ~/.gemini/config/plugins/dak/, DAK organizes its bundled skills into two folders:

  • skills/ - Your currently enabled skills based on the services you turned on.

  • skills.all/ - All bundled skills (including ones like Bigtable or Airflow/Composer that activate if you enable those services later).

Note: If you installed the IDE extension rather than the CLI plugin, the bundled skills live inside your editor's extension folder under ~/.antigravity/extensions/googlecloudtools.datacloud-* or ~/.vscode/extensions/googlecloudtools.datacloud-*.

You can inspect any skill straight from your terminal or open it directly in Antigravity IDE:

# List every enabled SKILL.md
ls ~/.gemini/config/plugins/dak/skills/*/SKILL.md

# Preview the name & description header of all enabled skills at once
head -n 8 ~/.gemini/config/plugins/dak/skills/*/SKILL.md

# Read a specific skill
cat ~/.gemini/config/plugins/dak/skills/bigquery-sql/SKILL.md

Here is the bigquery-sql/SKILL.md file:

Putting It to Work: Live Demos on the Dataset

Now that you've seen how MCP Tools and SKILL.md are wired up, let's watch them work together on the devfest_commerce dataset we created in Part 1.

Demo 1: Load raw_orders_batch.json From Cloud Storage Into BigQuery (MCP Tools)

Right now, raw_orders_batch.json is sitting in Cloud Storage (gs://<YOUR_BUCKET_NAME>/incoming/raw_orders_batch.json), while dim_customers is already in BigQuery. Instead of writing a bq load command by hand, paste this into Antigravity Agent Chat (swapping in your bucket name and project ID):

Look inside my Cloud Storage bucket gs://<YOUR_BUCKET_NAME>/incoming/raw_orders_batch.json. Inspect the raw JSON records and load them into a new BigQuery table named <YOUR_PROJECT_ID>.devfest_commerce.raw_orders (in location US).

Before loading anything, watch how the agent structures the work into a 4-step plan:

  1. Verify GCP auth and config (triggered by DAK's google-cloud-auth-verification skill-checking active account and project first)

  2. Inspect GCS JSON file (reads raw_orders_batch.json: 1,327 bytes, NDJSON, 8 records)

  3. Load JSON into BigQuery table (devfest_commerce.raw_orders in location US)

  4. Verify BigQuery table and records (confirms 8 rows, 539 logical bytes, and inferred schema types like amount FLOAT64 and order_date DATE)

What stood out in the agent's output wasn't just that it loaded the table - without being asked, it also surfaced Data Quality Observations while keeping the raw landing table untouched:

  • Duplicate record: ORD-1002 appears twice.

  • Missing key / flagged order: 1 row has order_id = NULL (CUST-999, FLAGGED, Mumbai).

  • High-value refund requests: ORD-1003 (2400.00) and ORD-1005 (3100.00) are both REFUND_REQUESTED Electronics orders in Mangaluru on 2026-11-11.

Even better, at the end of its response it immediately noticed dim_customers sitting in the same dataset and asked if we wanted to build a cleaned/deduplicated downstream table or join them-which is exactly what we'll do in Part 3.

Hit Refresh on devfest_commerce in the BigQuery sidebar and click raw_orders to verify all 8 rows right inside the Mini Cloud Console:

Demo 2: Watch bigquery-sql/SKILL.md Optimize a Query Live

Now that both dim_customers and raw_orders are in BigQuery, let's test the bigquery-sql skill we just opened by handing the agent a deliberately clunky query (SELECT ***, unquoted hyphenated project ID, and an IN (SELECT ...**) subquery):

Optimize this BigQuery SQL query for performance and cost, and explain what you changed:

SELECT *
FROM project2-283514.devfest_commerce.dim_customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM project2-283514.devfest_commerce.raw_orders
  WHERE status = 'REFUND_REQUESTED'
);

Following bigquery-sql/SKILL.md and inspecting both live tables in BigQuery first-the agent rewrites it cleanly:

SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  c.tier,
  c.signup_year,
  c.preferred_channel
FROM `project2-283514.devfest_commerce.dim_customers` AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM `project2-283514.devfest_commerce.raw_orders` AS o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND o.status = 'REFUND_REQUESTED'
);

Look at how MCP Tools + SKILL.md combined in that single response:

  • Live metadata lookup: Instead of guessing columns, it checked dim_customers (6 rows, 298 bytes, unpartitioned) and 
raw_orders

(8 rows, 539 bytes, unpartitioned), pulled the exact 5 columns, and confirmed no partition filter was missing yet.

  • Exact bigquery-sql/SKILL.md rules applied: Replaced SELECT * with explicit columns (Column Pruning), rewrote WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT ...) to WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...) (Mandatory Semi-Join rule), backtick-quoted the hyphenated project ID, and output the exact "Summary of Optimizations" section required by the skill.

  • Scale & cost check: It even flagged how to partition raw_orders by order_date and cluster by (status, customer_id) once the table grows, and gave a free bq --dry_run command to verify totalBytesProcessed before running.

Demo 3: Quick Safety Check (accidental-data-loss-prevention)

One fair question that always comes up: "If the agent has execute_sql, what stops it from accidentally dropping a table?"

Try typing this in chat (and don't confirm it!):

Drop the devfest_commerce.dim_customers table.

Watch the two-step safety flow that happens:

  1. First, Antigravity asks for your approval to call the read-only get_table_info MCP tool so the agent can inspect the table's exact blast radius.

  2. Next, instead of running DROP TABLE, DAK's accidental-data-loss-prevention skill forces the agent to halt and print a structured impact report-showing the exact target table (6 rows, 298 logical bytes), warning that downstream views or pipelines will break (and noting BigQuery time travel as the only recovery path), displaying the exact DROP TABLE SQL it plans to run, and waiting for explicit confirmation.

That said, always treat Markdown skills as guardrails,** not your only security wall*. Because DAK runs on your Application Default Credentials (or a service account), **Google Cloud IAM* is still the hard boundary - if an account only has read-only roles like roles/bigquery.dataViewer, Google Cloud itself will reject any destructive write.

Stepping Back: This Isn't Just About Running Faster Queries

Take a quick look at what just happened across three short demos, without opening the Cloud Console, writing a bq load command, or copy-pasting a single schema, the agent verified our GCP auth, loaded raw JSON from Cloud Storage into BigQuery, flagged three data quality issues on its own, rewrote a query using BigQuery's own best practices, and stopped a DROP TABLE with a full impact report.

There is a great point making the rounds among developers right now, traditional GUIs only let you do what someone designed a button for, whereas an LLM connected directly to your database speaks SQL, writes code, and isn't boxed in by a predefined interface. The real-world catch is that an LLM with raw database access alone can also be reckless. Pairing it with MCP Tools (live metadata), SKILL.md playbooks (engineering discipline), and IAM (hard security boundaries) is what makes that workflow actually usable day to day.

And in this post, we only turned on two services (BigQuery and Cloud Storage) and saw three skills fire out of the dozens bundled in DAK. If you want to keep experimenting on your own before Part 3, here are a few more things worth trying right inside Antigravity IDE:

  • Run a quick GCS security check on your demo bucket to see gcs-security-assessment inspect public access and bucket settings.

  • Open a couple more SKILL.md files in ~/.gemini/config/plugins/dak/skills/ (like data-autocleaning, bigquery-ai-ml, or building-data-apps) to see how Google structures playbooks for other workflows.

  • Test a read-only analytical question across raw_orders and dim_customers such as breaking down order volume and refunds by customer tier and inspect the results or chart right inside the IDE.

  • Try turning on another service in DAK Settings (like Spark, Dataform/dbt, Bigtable, or Knowledge Catalog) if you already use it in your GCP project.

What's Next

Now that raw_orders and dim_customers are both sitting in BigQuery and you've seen how MCP tools and SKILL.md playbooks actually behave, we're ready to run a complete end-to-end data workflow.

In Part 3, we'll put DAK to work on the messy records we spotted in raw_orders (the duplicate ORD-1002, the null order ID, and the high-value Mangaluru refund spike), build a clean enriched table, and verify the agent's output like a production engineer.

Let’s Connect

I’m an Independent Consultant and Google Developer Expert (GDE) partnering with startups and early-stage SaaS teams on Developer Experience (DevEx) and GTM content — helping teams ship clearer docs, stronger demos, developer tutorials, live workshops, and repeatable content engines across Google Cloud, Google Workspace, and AI workflows.

If you want to follow the rest of this series (blogs, YouTube walkthroughs, live trainings, and quick LinkedIn/X posts) — or if you’re building developer tools, scaling SaaS adoption, or looking for a technical writer, trainer, or DevEx partner — let’s connect:

  • Socials: LinkedIn & X
  • YouTube: @aryanirani123
  • Blogs & Tutorials: Medium | DEV.to | aryanirani123.com

title: Veri temiz odasını kodla düşünmek: Normalizasyon, anahtarlı özet, sorgu izin listesi ve asgari küme eşiği
description:
Bir konut geliştiricisi ile bir banka aynı soruyu sorar: "Bizim lead listemizdeki kişilerden kaçı sizin konut kredisi ön onaylı müşteriniz?" Soru masum görünür ama cevaplamanın en kolay yolu, yani iki tarafın Excel dosyalarını birbirine e-postayla göndermesi, kişisel veriyi amacı dışında başka bir şirkete aktarmak demektir. Veri temiz odası (data clean room) bu yüzden vardır: iki taraf ham kayıtları birbirine göstermeden yalnızca üzerinde anlaştıkları toplu sonuçları görür. Ben Koray Yalçın; gayrimenkul projelerinde lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi ve ölçüm altyapıları kurarken bu tür iş birliği taleplerinin genellikle "hash'leyip gönderelim" cümlesiyle başladığını ve tam orada yanlış yola saptığını gördüm.

Kavramın tanımı ve iş tarafındaki kullanımı için Data Clean Room nedir? sayfasına bakabilirsiniz. Bu yazıda konuyu bir geliştiricinin gözünden ele alıyorum: hazır bir temiz oda ürünü kullansanız da kendi küçük kurulumunuzu yapsanız da doğru olması gereken dört katman var. Eşleştirme anahtarının normalizasyonu, anahtarın nasıl gizleneceği, hangi sorguların çalışabileceği ve sonucun ne zaman gösterilmeyeceği. Örnekler Python ve PostgreSQL ile yazıldı. Bu yazı hukuki görüş değildir; KVKK ve GDPR açısından aktarımın dayanağını, aydınlatma metnini ve sözleşmeyi hukuk ekibinizle netleştirmeniz gerekir.

"Hash'leyip gönderelim" neden yetmez?

En sık önerilen çözüm şudur: iki taraf da e-posta ve telefonları SHA-256 ile özetler, özet listelerini birbirine gönderir, kesişimi sayar. Sorun, telefon numarasının çok küçük bir uzay olmasıdır. Türkiye'deki cep telefonu numaralarının olası kombinasyon sayısı, sıradan bir dizüstü bilgisayarın makul sürede tamamını özetleyip bir sözlük çıkarmasına yetecek kadar küçüktür. Yani tuzsuz SHA-256 ile özetlenmiş bir telefon listesi, karşı taraf isterse geri çevrilebilir bir listedir. E-posta için uzay daha büyüktür ama karşı tarafın zaten elinde olan milyonlarca e-postayı özetleyip eşleştirmesi de aynı anlama gelir: siz listeyi "anonim" sanarsınız, karşı taraf kendi müşterisi olmayan kişileri bile tanıyabilir.

Bu yüzden ilk ilke şu: özet, tek başına gizlilik sağlamaz; yalnızca ham değerin ekranda dolaşmasını engeller. Gizlilik, kimin hangi anahtarla özet üretebildiğine ve sonuçta neyin görülebildiğine bağlıdır.

Birinci katman: normalizasyon her iki tarafta aynı kod olmalı

Eşleşme oranının düşük çıkmasının en yaygın nedeni teknik bir gizlilik meselesi değil, biçim farkıdır. Bir tarafta "0532 123 45 67", diğer tarafta "+905321234567" yazıyorsa özetleri asla eşleşmez. E-postada büyük harf, baştaki ve sondaki boşluklar, Türkçe karakterli büyük-küçük harf dönüşümü aynı sorunu yaratır.

Benim tercihim normalizasyonu bir kütüphane fonksiyonu olarak yazıp iki tarafa da aynı sürümü vermek ve sürüm numarasını her çıktıya eklemektir:

import re
import unicodedata

NORMALIZER_VERSION = "2026-11-v1"

def normalize_email(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", raw).strip()
    # Türkçe 'İ' -> 'i̇' sorununu önlemek için önce ASCII dışı büyük harfleri ele al
    s = s.replace("İ", "i").replace("I", "i").lower()
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}", s):
        return None
    return s

def normalize_phone_tr(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", raw)
    if digits.startswith("00"):
        digits = digits[2:]
    if digits.startswith("0") and len(digits) == 11:
        digits = "90" + digits[1:]
    if len(digits) == 10 and digits.startswith("5"):
        digits = "90" + digits
    if not re.fullmatch(r"905\d{9}", digits):
        return None  # yurt dışı numaralar ayrı kurala tabi, burada eşleştirmeye almıyoruz
    return "+" + digits

Burada iki bilinçli karar var. Birincisi, geçersiz değer None döner ve eşleştirmeye girmez; "en yakın tahmin" ile yanlış bir kişiyle eşleşmek, eşleşmemekten daha kötüdür. İkincisi, yurt dışı numaralar bu sürümde dışarıda bırakılmıştır. Kıbrıs gibi çok uluslu alıcı kitlesi olan projelerde bu kural genişletilmelidir, ama genişletme yeni bir sürüm numarasıyla yapılmalı ki iki tarafın farklı kurallarla özet üretip "eşleşme düştü" diye şaşırması önlensin.

Normalizasyon fonksiyonunun birim testleri de iki tarafla paylaşılmalı. Ben test dosyasına gerçek veri değil, uydurma örnek biçimler koyarım: boşluklu, tireli, ülke kodlu, başında sıfır olan, eksik haneli.

İkinci katman: anahtarlı özet ve anahtarın sahibi

Tuzsuz özetin sorununu çözmenin pratik yolu, özeti HMAC gibi gizli bir anahtarla üretmektir. Anahtarı bilmeyen biri sözlük saldırısı yapamaz. Ama burada kritik soru şudur: anahtarı kim tutuyor?

Eğer anahtarı iki taraf da biliyorsa, her biri diğerinin listesini kendi ham verisiyle yeniden özetleyip eşleştirebilir; yani yine kişi düzeyinde kesişim öğrenilir. Temiz oda mantığında anahtar, iki tarafın da doğrudan erişemediği bir ortamda durur: ya güvenilir üçüncü taraf bir platformda, ya da iki tarafın ortak denetlediği ayrı bir hesapta, erişimi kayıt altına alınan bir anahtar yönetim servisinde.

import hmac
import hashlib

def keyed_token(value: str, key: bytes, purpose: str) -> str:
    # purpose: 'email' veya 'phone'; aynı değerin iki alanda aynı jetonu üretmesini engeller
    msg = f"{purpose}:{NORMALIZER_VERSION}:{value}".encode("utf-8")
    return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def tokenize_row(row: dict, key: bytes) -> dict:
    email = normalize_email(row.get("email"))
    phone = normalize_phone_tr(row.get("phone"))
    return {
        "email_token": keyed_token(email, key, "email") if email else None,
        "phone_token": keyed_token(phone, key, "phone") if phone else None,
        "segment": row.get("segment"),        # toplu kırılım için izinli alan
        "created_month": row.get("created_month"),
        "normalizer_version": NORMALIZER_VERSION,
    }

Bu fonksiyon iki tarafın kendi sisteminde değil, temiz odanın içinde çalışmalıdır. Taraflar normalleştirilmiş veriyi şifreli kanalla odaya yükler, oda jetonu üretir ve ham değeri hemen siler. Pratikte bu, yükleme sonrası ham sütunların tutulmadığı, yalnızca jeton tablosunun kaldığı bir iş akışı demektir.

Bir not daha: aynı anahtarı her proje için kullanmayın. Her iş birliği, hatta her kampanya dönemi için ayrı anahtar, jetonların başka bir bağlamda birleştirilmesini zorlaştırır. Anahtar döndürüldüğünde eski jeton tabloları da imha edilmelidir.

Üçüncü katman: sorgular izin listesinden çalışır

Temiz odanın veri ambarından farkı, içeride serbest SQL yazılamamasıdır. "Kaç kişi eşleşti?" sorusuna izin verip "eşleşen kişilerin jetonlarını listele" sorusuna izin vermemek gerekir. Bunu en sade biçimde, onaylanmış sorgu şablonlarını bir tabloda tutarak ve kullanıcıların yalnızca parametre gönderebilmesini sağlayarak yaparım:

CREATE TABLE approved_query (
    query_key       text PRIMARY KEY,           -- 'overlap_by_segment'
    version         int  NOT NULL,
    sql_template    text NOT NULL,              -- parametreli, sabit metin
    allowed_params  jsonb NOT NULL,             -- {"created_month": "yyyy-mm"}
    min_group_size  int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 50,
    approved_by     text NOT NULL,              -- iki tarafın onayı
    approved_at     timestamptz NOT NULL
);

-- Örnek şablon: segment bazlı kesişim sayısı
-- Not: sonuç satır düzeyinde jeton içermez, yalnızca sayım döner
SELECT d.segment,
       count(DISTINCT d.person_token) AS overlap_count
FROM   developer_tokens d
JOIN   bank_tokens b
  ON  (d.phone_token = b.phone_token OR d.email_token = b.email_token)
WHERE  d.created_month = $1
GROUP  BY d.segment;

Buradaki OR eşleşmesi bilinçli bir tercihtir ama aynı kişiyi hem telefon hem e-posta üzerinden iki kez sayma riskini doğurur. Bu yüzden her tarafta önce kişi düzeyinde tek satıra indirgeme (deduplication) yapılır, odada her kişiye bir person_token verilir ve sayım count(DISTINCT ...) ile yapılır. Bu ayrıntı şablon onaylanırken konuşulması gereken türdendir; yani şablonun kendisi de bir kod incelemesinden geçer.

min_group_size değeri bilerek tabloya yazılmıştır. 50 burada örnek değerdir; doğru eşik, veri setinin büyüklüğüne ve iki tarafın risk değerlendirmesine göre belirlenir.

Dördüncü katman: küçük kümeyi gösterme

Toplu sayım bile yeterince dar bir kırılımda kişiyi ele verebilir. "Mağusa'daki 4+1 villa segmentinde, Kasım ayında oluşturulan ve bankanın ön onaylı müşterisi olan kişi sayısı: 2" sonucu, küçük bir projede kimin kim olduğunu tahmin etmeye yetebilir. Bu yüzden sorgu sonucu kullanıcıya dönmeden önce bir eşik kontrolünden geçer:

def apply_threshold(rows: list[dict], min_group: int) -> list[dict]:
    safe = []
    suppressed = 0
    for r in rows:
        if r["overlap_count"] < min_group:
            suppressed += 1
            safe.append({"segment": r["segment"], "overlap_count": None,
                         "note": "eşik altı, gösterilmedi"})
        else:
            safe.append(r)
    # Toplam satır, bastırılan hücrelerin farkla hesaplanmasını engellemek için verilmez
    return safe

Eşik tek başına yeterli değildir; çünkü aynı sorguyu bir kez "tüm segmentler", bir kez "küçük segment hariç" diye çalıştırıp farkı alarak bastırılmış hücre geri hesaplanabilir. Buna fark saldırısı denir. Benim uyguladığım üç önlem şunlar: kırılım alanları sabit bir listeden seçilir, aynı parametreyle tekrar eden sorgular sayılır ve sınırlanır, toplam satırı ancak tüm hücreler eşik üstündeyse döner. Daha ileri kurulumlarda sonuçlara kontrollü gürültü eklenir (diferansiyel gizlilik); ama bu, iş tarafının "sayılar tam tutmuyor" itirazını önceden konuşmayı gerektirir.

Denetim kaydı: kim, neyi, ne zaman sordu?

Temiz odada her sorgu çalıştırması bir satır olarak yazılır. Bu kayıt hem iki tarafın birbirine güven duymasını sağlar hem de bir veri sahibinin "verim nerede kullanıldı?" sorusuna cevap vermeyi kolaylaştırır.

CREATE TABLE query_run_log (
    run_id         uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    query_key      text NOT NULL,
    query_version  int  NOT NULL,
    params         jsonb NOT NULL,
    requested_by   text NOT NULL,
    requested_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    rows_returned  int  NOT NULL,
    rows_suppressed int NOT NULL
);

Ben bu tabloyu yalnızca ekleme yapılabilen (güncelleme ve silme yetkisi verilmeyen) bir rolle yazarım. Haftalık bir kontrol, aynı parametrelerin olağandışı sık sorgulanıp sorgulanmadığına bakar.

Gayrimenkul tarafında somut bir kullanım

Bir lansman projesini düşünelim (örnek senaryo, varsayımsaldır). Geliştirici, son üç ayda Meta ve Google reklamlarından gelen lead'lerini, banka da konut kredisi başvurusu yapmış müşterilerini temiz odaya yükler. Onaylı şablon, lead'leri kaynak kanal ve bütçe segmentine göre kırar ve her hücre için "bankada aktif başvurusu olan" kişi sayısını döner.

Bu sonuçla geliştirici, hangi kampanyanın finansmana yakın kişiler getirdiğini toplu düzeyde görür; banka, hangi proje bölgesinde kredi talebinin yoğunlaştığını öğrenir. Hiçbir taraf diğerinin müşteri listesini almaz. Kişi düzeyinde bir eylem gerekiyorsa, örneğin kredi ön onay teklifi göndermek, bu temiz odanın işi değildir; o kişinin ayrı ve açık rızasıyla yürütülmesi gereken başka bir süreçtir. Benim kurulumlarda en çok dikkat ettiğim çizgi budur: temiz oda analiz içindir, hedefleme listesi üretmek için değil.

Kurulumdan önce kontrol listesi

Kod yazmaya başlamadan önce şu sorulara yazılı cevap almayı alışkanlık haline getirdim:

  • Eşleştirme anahtarları neler, hangi normalizasyon sürümü kullanılacak?
  • Özet anahtarını kim tutuyor, kim erişebiliyor, ne zaman döndürülecek?
  • Hangi sorgu şablonları onaylı, kırılım alanları hangi sabit listeden seçiliyor?
  • Asgari küme eşiği kaç, fark saldırısına karşı hangi sınırlar var?
  • Ham veri ne zaman siliniyor, jeton tabloları ne kadar saklanıyor?
  • Sonuçlar hangi amaçla kullanılabilir, hangi amaçla kullanılamaz?

Bu listenin son maddesi teknik değil gibi görünür ama sistemin tasarımını en çok etkileyen maddedir. Amaç "toplu ölçüm" ise kişi düzeyinde çıktı veren hiçbir yol açık bırakılmamalıdır.

SSS

Veri temiz odası için mutlaka büyük bir platformun ürününü mü kullanmak gerekir?
Hayır. Reklam platformlarının ve bulut veri ambarlarının hazır çözümleri işinizi hızlandırır, ama ilkeler aynıdır: aynı normalizasyon, anahtarı tarafların doğrudan tutmadığı özet, onaylı sorgu şablonları, asgari küme eşiği ve denetim kaydı. Küçük bir iş birliğinde bunları ayrı bir veritabanı hesabında da kurabilirsiniz.

SHA-256 ile özetlemek KVKK açısından veriyi anonim yapar mı?
Genellikle hayır. Geri çevrilebilir ya da başka veriyle eşleştirilebilir özetler kişisel veri niteliğini kaybetmeyebilir. Bu konuda kesin değerlendirmeyi hukuk ekibiniz yapmalı; teknik tarafta yapabileceğiniz, tuzsuz özet yerine anahtarlı özet kullanmak ve anahtarı taraflardan ayrı tutmaktır.

Eşleşme oranı beklenenden düşük çıkarsa ilk neye bakmalıyım?
Önce normalizasyon sürümüne. İki tarafın aynı sürümü kullandığını, telefon biçiminin ülke kodu dahil aynı olduğunu ve geçersiz değerlerin oranını kontrol edin. Ardından iki listenin zaman aralığının gerçekten örtüştüğüne bakın.

Asgari küme eşiğini nasıl seçmeliyim?
Tek doğru sayı yoktur. Veri setinin büyüklüğü, kırılımların ne kadar dar olduğu ve sonuçların kimlerle paylaşılacağı belirleyicidir. Eşiği şablon onayında iki tarafın yazılı olarak kabul etmesi ve tabloda sürümlü tutulması önemlidir.

Temiz oda sonucunu reklam hedeflemesi için kullanabilir miyim?
Toplu sonuçla kampanya bütçesi veya kanal kararı vermek, temiz odanın tipik kullanımıdır. Eşleşen kişilerden bir hedef kitle listesi çıkarmak ise farklı bir veri işleme amacıdır ve ayrı bir hukuki dayanak ile ayrı bir teknik akış gerektirir.

Bu yapı CRM'e nasıl bağlanır?
CRM, temiz odaya yalnızca gerekli alanları (normalleştirilmiş anahtar, izinli kırılım alanları, dönem) aktaran bir dışa aktarma işini besler. Temiz odadan CRM'e kişi düzeyinde veri geri akmaz; yalnızca toplu rapor değerleri, örneğin kampanya bazında eşleşme oranı, raporlama tablosuna yazılabilir.

title: How to Test California Sec-GPC: 1 (Global Privacy Control) with Playwright HAR in 20 Lines of Python
description:
If you test Global Privacy Control (GPC) using curl -H "Sec-GPC: 1" or Playwright extra_http_headers alone, you will miss most real-world CMP failures.

Why? Most client-side Consent Management Platforms (Osano, OneTrust, CookieYes, Complianz, Shopify Customer Privacy) run in the browser and check navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true in JavaScript — they never inspect the inbound HTTP request header.

To reproduce what a real GPC-enabled browser (Firefox, Brave, DuckDuckGo, or Privacy Badger) sends under California CCPA/CPRA rules, you must spoof both the HTTP header and the DOM property, then capture a standard Chrome DevTools .har file.

The 20-Line Python Playwright GPC + HAR Harness 

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
    context = browser.new_context(
        record_har_path="gpc.har",
        record_har_content="omit",
        extra_http_headers={"Sec-GPC": "1", "DNT": "1"},
    )
    context.add_init_script(
        "Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'globalPrivacyControl', { get: () => true });"
    )
    page = context.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com", wait_until="networkidle")
    page.wait_for_timeout(3000)
    context.close()  # flushes gpc.har to disk
    browser.close()

What to Check Inside gpc.har

Parse log.entries[].request.url in Python and diff it against a baseline Cold Load .har:

  • facebook.com/tr (Meta Pixel)
  • analytics.tiktok.com (TikTok Pixel)
  • clarity.ms / hotjar.com / fullstory.com (Session replay)
  • google-analytics.com/g/collect (GA4 without Consent Mode gcs=G100 / denied)

Empirical 2026 Result: 59.7% Ignored Sec-GPC: 1

When we ran this exact Playwright harness across 72 live US clinic & medspa websites (all anonymized), 59.7% (43/72) ignored Sec-GPC: 1 and kept firing ad or session-replay pixels — even when the site displayed a cookie banner.

Common root causes we observed:

  1. gtm.js placed earlier in <head> than the CMP script, causing tags to fire before GPC evaluation.
  2. WordPress PixelYourSite hardcoding ad_storage and analytics_storage to granted inside var pysOptions.
  3. GTM tags left on "Not set" in Consent Overview.

Open-Source Repo & 30-Second Hosted Runner

  • Open-source Playwright HAR benchmark script: pixel-cmp-ada-benchmark-2026 on GitHub
  • Zero-login 30-second live browser scanner (tests Cold Load, Sec-GPC: 1, and Reject All + Reload; optional $39 one-time raw .har + PDF report): TagProof Live Scanner

(Technical browser observation only; not legal advice.)

title: Introducing DriftCatch — behavioural testing Framework for AI agents
description:
An AI agent can return exactly the answer you expect while its decisions, tool usage and execution path have silently changed.

A prompt tweak, a model update or a tool-schema edit can all introduce a behavioural regression that output-based testing will never catch. The answer still reads correctly, so every eval passes.

Consider a change like this to a refund agent's system prompt:

  • Resolve the customer's issue.
  • Resolve the customer's issue carefully. One word. The replies still read perfectly well. But the agent may now escalate cases it used to refund — and if your assertions are about the answer, nothing catches it.

So I built DriftCatch.

pip install driftcatch
import driftcatch as drift

def test_refund():
with drift.take("refund_1182") as take:
my_agent("refund order 1182")

take.assert_tools().called_in_order("lookup_order", "issue_refund")
take.assert_invariants().hold()

First run records. Every run after replays from disk — no network, no tokens, deterministic. It hooks httpx, so OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, LlamaIndex or your own loop all work with no adapter.

The part I think is actually new
Record/replay for agents already exists. What I hadn't seen is mining the rules out of the runs you've approved:

$ drift learn
Mined 13 invariant(s) from 23 approved recording(s)

lookup_order always runs before check_eligibility 23/23
issue_refund is always the last tool 18/18
escalate_to_human is offered but never called 23/23
issue_refund.args.order_id always equals
lookup_order.args.order_id 18/18
Nobody wrote those. The last one — the order you look up is the order you refund — is a real bug class nobody tests for. It breaks when someone reuses a loop variable.

This is specification mining, which Daikon has done for ordinary programs since 2001. Agent trajectories turn out to fit it well.

The hard part isn't mining, it's not mining garbage. Four filters: minimum support of 5 runs, a confidence gate of 1 - 0.5^support, the value has to actually vary across runs (two constants that match aren't a relationship), and transitive rules get dropped. That took 19 mined rules down to 15.

Rules are proposed as pending. A human enforces them, or doesn't.

When it fails, it names the cause
$ drift bisect refund_1182 --previous

golden: lookup_order -> check_eligibility -> issue_refund
candidate: lookup_order -> check_eligibility -> escalate_to_human

ROOT CAUSE: the system prompt.

- issue.
+ issue carefully.

Four inputs are fingerprinted separately — system prompt, model id, tool schemas, matcher config — so drift gets attributed instead of shrugged at.

The rest
Behaviour coverage — which tools, paths and error branches you've actually tested, plus suggested scenarios for the gaps
What-if — swap a recorded event at replay time to drive failure and retry paths, without recording anything new
Determinism scoring — run N times live, group by trajectory, get 80% path A / 20% path B instead of a meaningless "4/5 passed"
Tool contracts — declared schemas vs real use. On the demo corpus it flagged a parameter sent in every single request that no model ever used.
Approval gate — recordings start PENDING. A recorded run can be wrong; if "recorded" meant "correct", your first bad run becomes the enforced contract.
CLI, pytest plugin, local UI, and a read-only MCP server for Cursor / Claude Code
One honest limitation
Replay cannot catch the model changing underneath you. A recording holds what the model said then, not what it would say now. That's physics, not a missing feature — which is why there's a separate live mode that makes real calls.

Any tool claiming to catch model drift from a cached response is claiming something impossible.

NEEL7127 / driftcatch

Catch the moment your AI agent's behaviour changes. Record once, replay deterministically, fail the build on drift.

DriftCatch

Learns what your AI agent always does — then tells you the moment it stops.

0.1 pre-release. The engine, CLI, pytest plugin, local UI and MCP server are implemented and tested against the real OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs — 407 tests, mypy --strict clean. Not yet on PyPI, and not yet used by anyone but its author. If you try it and something is wrong, an issue is more useful to me than a star.

The problem

You tweak one word in a prompt. Your agent quietly stops querying the database and starts web-searching. The answer still looks right, so every eval passes. You find out from a customer.

Or worse — the trajectory is identical, every tool fires in the right order, and the refund amount is wrong by a factor of a hundred.

Agents don't fail loudly. They drift.

30 seconds

import driftcatch as drift
@drift
…

title: What Makes a Travel Enquiry Form Useful for Group Bookings?
description:
Build a Simple Travel Enquiry Form with HTML and JavaScript

A travel enquiry often starts with a message such as “We need a vehicle next weekend.” Before suggesting an option, the operator still needs to know the route, date and passenger count.

A structured form can collect those details together.

This tutorial builds a small browser-only prototype using HTML and JavaScript. It generates an enquiry summary on the page. It does not send information to an operator or confirm a booking.

Choose the Essential Fields

Start with the information needed to understand the journey:

  • Pickup location
  • Destination
  • Departure date
  • Number of passengers

For group transport, luggage requirements and return dates may also be useful. Keep this first version small so the basic interaction remains easy to understand.

Build the Form

The following example includes visible labels, native browser validation and a live summary area.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Travel Enquiry Preview</title>

  <style>
    body {
      max-width: 36rem;
      margin: 2rem auto;
      padding: 0 1rem;
      font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
      line-height: 1.6;
      color: #102a43;
    }

    form {
      display: grid;
      gap: 0.75rem;
    }

    input, button {
      box-sizing: border-box;
      width: 100%;
      padding: 0.75rem;
      font: inherit;
    }

    button {
      margin-top: 0.5rem;
      background: #123b70;
      color: white;
      border: 0;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    pre {
      white-space: pre-wrap;
      overflow-wrap: anywhere;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: #eef5fb;
    }
  </style>
</head>

<body>
  <h1>Prepare Your Travel Enquiry</h1>
  <p>Enter your trip details to generate a summary.</p>

  <noscript>This preview requires JavaScript.</noscript>

  <form id="trip-form">
    <label for="pickup">Pickup location</label>
    <input
      id="pickup"
      name="pickup"
      type="text"
      maxlength="150"
      required
    >

    <label for="destination">Destination</label>
    <input
      id="destination"
      name="destination"
      type="text"
      maxlength="150"
      required
    >

    <label for="departure">Departure date</label>
    <input
      id="departure"
      name="departure"
      type="date"
      required
    >

    <label for="passengers">Number of passengers</label>
    <input
      id="passengers"
      name="passengers"
      type="number"
      min="1"
      step="1"
      required
    >

    <button type="submit">Generate enquiry summary</button>
  </form>

  <h2>Your Enquiry Summary</h2>
  <pre id="summary" role="status" aria-live="polite">
Your trip details will appear here.
  </pre>

  <script>
    const form = document.getElementById("trip-form");
    const summary = document.getElementById("summary");
    const locations = form.querySelectorAll('input[type="text"]');

    locations.forEach((input) => {
      input.addEventListener("input", () => {
        input.setCustomValidity("");
      });
    });

    form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();

      locations.forEach((input) => {
        input.setCustomValidity(
          input.value.trim() ? "" : "Enter a location."
        );
      });

      if (!form.reportValidity()) return;

      const data = new FormData(form);

      summary.textContent = [
        `Pickup: ${data.get("pickup").trim()}`,
        `Destination: ${data.get("destination").trim()}`,
        `Departure: ${data.get("departure")}`,
        `Passengers: ${data.get("passengers")}`,
        "",
        "Enquiry preview only. No booking has been submitted."
      ].join("\n");
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Understand the Validation

The required attribute prevents empty fields from passing browser validation.

For passenger count, min="1" requires a positive value, while step="1" restricts valid values to whole numbers.

The JavaScript adds a check for location fields containing only spaces. It clears that custom error when the user edits the field.

This prototype accepts past departure dates. A production form should apply the operator’s actual date and booking rules rather than assuming every selected date is available.

Display User Input as Text

The summary uses textContent to display the entered values as plain text.

That matters because user input should not become executable page markup. A destination containing HTML-like characters should appear as text in the preview.

The aria-live="polite" region allows assistive technology to announce the updated summary without immediately interrupting the user.

Separate an Enquiry from a Booking

A passenger count alone cannot determine the correct vehicle. Luggage, seating arrangements, route requirements and availability still need discussion.

For example, Urbania Yatra offers Urbania and Tempo Traveller rentals from Ahmedabad. A structured enquiry can provide the starting details for that discussion, while vehicle availability and pricing require confirmation.

This tutorial is an independent prototype, not a description of the website’s existing implementation.

Check the Main Interactions

Before extending the example, try these cases:

  1. Submit with empty fields.
  2. Enter only spaces in a location field.
  3. Enter zero or a decimal passenger count.
  4. Complete the form with valid details.
  5. Enter HTML-like text and confirm it appears literally.
  6. Navigate the form using only the keyboard.

Extend It into a Working Enquiry System

To collect actual enquiries, connect the form to a backend endpoint and validate the submitted data again on the server. Browser validation improves the interaction, but it can be bypassed.

Display a submission confirmation only after the server accepts the enquiry. Keep that message separate from any later confirmation of vehicle availability or booking.

Once that flow works, you can add return dates, luggage notes and a preferred vehicle category.

Image Alt Text Laptop showing a travel enquiry interface, with an Urbania van outside, the Urbania Yatra logo and an HTML and JavaScript tutorial heading.

Short Description

Create a browser-only travel enquiry prototype with labelled inputs, native validation and a JavaScript summary. Learn how to separate an enquiry preview from a submitted request.

title: Is the BTC Long Trade Crowded? Funding Rate and Taker Flow in 60 Lines of Python
description:
Perpetual futures give you two cheap, public signals about positioning that a price chart does not show:

  • Funding rate: what longs pay shorts (or the reverse) every 8 hours to keep the perpetual close to spot. When funding is high, holding a long is expensive, and people are paying it anyway.
  • Taker buy ratio: the share of traded volume where the buyer crossed the spread. It tells you who is in a hurry.

Neither one is a trading signal on its own. Put together, they answer a narrower question that I find more useful: is one side of the trade getting crowded right now?

This post builds a small classifier for that in Python, using a public exchange API that needs no key.

The data

I use WEEX's public futures market API because it serves both funding history and candles with taker-buy volume, and it does not need an account. Any exchange with these two endpoints works the same way.

  • GET /capi/v3/market/klines: 4-hour candles. Column 9 is taker-buy volume.
  • GET /capi/v3/market/fundingRate: funding history, one print every 8 hours. 
import requests
import pandas as pd

BASE = "https://api-contract.weex.com/capi/v3/market"


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def load(symbol="BTCUSDT", bars=180):
    k = get("/klines", symbol=symbol, interval="4h", limit=bars)
    px = pd.DataFrame(k, columns=["open_time", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume",
                                  "close_time", "quote_volume", "trades", "taker_buy", "taker_buy_quote"])
    px["time"] = pd.to_datetime(px["open_time"], unit="ms")
    for c in ["close", "volume", "taker_buy"]:
        px[c] = px[c].astype(float)
    px = px.sort_values("time")

    f = pd.DataFrame(get("/fundingRate", symbol=symbol, limit=100))
    f["time"] = pd.to_datetime(f["fundingTime"], unit="ms")
    f["funding"] = f["fundingRate"].astype(float)
    f = f.sort_values("time")

    # Each 4h bar takes the most recent funding print.
    df = pd.merge_asof(px[["time", "close", "volume", "taker_buy"]], f[["time", "funding"]], on="time")
    return df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

Two details matter here. The candles do not always come back in time order, so sort them. And funding settles every 8 hours while the candles are 4 hours, so merge_asof carries the latest funding print forward instead of leaving gaps.

Compare each series with its own recent past

The first version of this script used fixed thresholds, such as "taker buy ratio above 52% means buyers are aggressive." That failed straight away. On this venue the 24-hour taker buy ratio sat around 47% for the whole sample, so a fixed 52% line never fired.

Every venue has its own baseline: fee tiers, market makers and how volume is counted all shift it. So instead of absolute levels, I use a z-score against the last 7 days (42 four-hour bars):

def crowding(df, window=42):
    out = df.copy()
    roll = out["funding"].rolling(window)
    out["funding_z"] = (out["funding"] - roll.mean()) / roll.std()

    # Taker buy share of volume, smoothed over 24h (6 bars).
    out["taker_buy_ratio"] = out["taker_buy"].rolling(6).sum() / out["volume"].rolling(6).sum()
    troll = out["taker_buy_ratio"].rolling(window)
    out["taker_z"] = (out["taker_buy_ratio"] - troll.mean()) / troll.std()

    def label(r):
        if r.funding_z > 1.5 and r.taker_z > 1:
            return "crowded long"
        if r.funding_z < -1.5 and r.taker_z < -1:
            return "crowded short"
        if r.funding_z > 1.5 and r.taker_z < -1:
            return "longs paying, buyers fading"
        return "neutral"

    out["state"] = out.apply(label, axis=1)
    return out

The four states:

State Funding Taker flow Reading
Crowded long Unusually high Buyers unusually aggressive Late longs are chasing and paying for it
Crowded short Unusually negative Sellers unusually aggressive The mirror image
Longs paying, buyers fading Unusually high Buyers backing off Longs are still holding an expensive position, but nobody new is adding
Neutral Anything else

The third one is the state I watch most. High funding with fading buyers means the long side is paying to wait.

What it printed

Running it on BTCUSDT for the 30 days to 27 November 2026:

               time     close  funding_bps  funding_z  taker_buy_ratio  taker_z                       state
2026-11-26 08:00:00 60686.700        0.850      1.556            0.475   -0.639                     neutral
2026-11-26 12:00:00 60599.900        0.850      1.521            0.462   -1.481 longs paying, buyers fading
2026-11-26 16:00:00 60696.900        0.456      0.402            0.474   -0.626                     neutral
2026-11-27 00:00:00 61392.600        0.987      1.744            0.472   -0.675                     neutral

state
neutral                        172
crowded short                    7
longs paying, buyers fading      1

Out of 180 four-hour bars, 172 were neutral. That is what you want from a filter like this: it should stay quiet most of the time. Funding was elevated for most of 26 and 27 November, but taker flow only dropped far enough to flag it once.

How I read the current tape

BTC pushed from about $60,500 to $61,500 into 27 November while funding climbed back toward the top of its 7-day range. Taker flow did not follow: the buy share stayed slightly below its weekly average the whole time. In plain terms, longs are paying more to hold, but the move up is not being driven by aggressive buyers.

I would not call that bearish on its own. It looks more like a market drifting up on thin participation, which tends to be fragile in both directions. Two things would change my view:

  • If taker buying picks up while funding stays high, the classifier flips to "crowded long". That is usually the point where a pullback flushes late longs.
  • If funding cools back to neutral while price holds above $61,000, the long side has reset without a liquidation, which is a healthier base for continuation.

Until one of those happens, I treat breakouts here with more suspicion than usual.

What this does not do

It does not predict the next candle. Order-flow measures are good at describing the bar you are in and poor at forecasting the next one. A test on BTC 5-minute data found taker imbalance correlated 0.44 with the same candle and only −0.10 with the next one (source). I expect the 4-hour version to behave the same way, and I have not backtested it.

So I use the output as context, not as an entry rule. A "crowded long" flag makes me less willing to chase a breakout. It does not make me short.

Some easy extensions:

  • Add open interest. If it rises while funding is high, new money is joining the crowded side. Most exchanges only give the current value for free, so you have to store snapshots yourself.
  • Run the same code on ETH and SOL and compare which market is more stretched.
  • Tune the window. Seven days reacts quickly; thirty days gives you fewer, stronger flags.

The full script is about 60 lines. If you try it on another venue, I would be curious whether its taker baseline also sits away from 50%.

title: Popular Windows programs hacked to secretly install software
description:
Compromised installers for Q-Dir and DesktopOK distributed a Python-based remote access trojan while executing genuine, digitally signed binaries.

ASEC analysis details how the setup fetched secondary payloads, established scheduled tasks, and evaded security tools.

How did the trap work?

Specifically, the malicious installers for the Q-Dir and DesktopOK tools were found. When someone downloaded and ran these versions, the program appeared to work normally and opened on the screen without any indication that anything was wrong. However, in the background, it secretly downloaded and installed a remote control program.

The threat affected both those who downloaded the programs for the first time and those who upgraded previous installations they already had on their computers. Researchers from the AhnLab research center (ASEC) identified the problem and published their findings on November 26, 2026.

The official applications contained in the installation packages had the normal, valid digital signature of their creator, which made the files appear completely trustworthy. The corrupted installers included versions 12.85.0.0, 12.84.0.0 and 12.83.0.0 of Q-Dir, as well as versions 12.85.0.0 and 12.82.0.0 of DesktopOK.

What could the hidden program do?

When the additional program was installed on the computer, it allowed third parties to execute commands, transfer files, take screenshots, and gather detailed system information. To stay active, the program created automated tasks in Windows, while also monitoring which security and protection applications were running on the computer.

↳

What should those who have installed them do?

Experts recommend that users completely uninstall these programs, download the latest and verified version from the official source, check the digital fingerprints of the files, and look for any unknown scheduled tasks or unwanted connections on their computers.

title: Malt freelancer ratings in Python: choose the right denominator
description:
You're about to publish a reputation comparison. The spreadsheet has an average rating, a review count and a reassuringly tidy weighted average.

The weight is where the trouble starts: reviewCount counts client recommendations, while ratingCount counts appraisals containing a rating.

A recommendation count is not automatically the denominator behind an average rating. Weighting avgRating by reviewCount gives you a recommendation-weighted average of profile averages. It doesn't establish an average across individual ratings.

A row is a profile, not a review

The Actor returns freelancer records. Each record can carry a stable profileId, a profile-level rating and several counters, but it doesn't contain the individual appraisals behind those aggregates.

That distinction matters before you write any arithmetic. You can compare public profile summaries; you can't expand a counter into the underlying observations.

This Example input collects profiles without imposing reputation thresholds:

import os

import pandas as pd
import duckdb
from apify_client import ApifyClient

run_input = {
    "mode": "searchFreelancers",
    "searchQuery": "python developer",
    "market": "de",
    "maxItems": 20,
}

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor(
    "dataspryva/malt-freelancer-skill-and-rate-finder"
).call(run_input=run_input)

if run["status"] != "SUCCEEDED":
    raise RuntimeError(f"Actor status: {run['status']}")

items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items

Search returns a randomised public sample, then de-duplicates profiles by their identifier. That makes the returned dataset useful for describing those profiles, without making it a representative survey of freelancers.

Your chart's population starts with the collection method, before missing values get their turn.

The counters describe different evidence

Here's the field map for the reputation comparison. The analytical types below are choices for the loader: the output descriptions give meanings, but don't specify a complete JSON type and formatting contract.

Field What it holds Analytical type The trap
profileId Stable profile identifier Nullable string Counting rows across combined extracts can count a profile repeatedly.
avgRating Average client rating, bounded by 0–5 Nullable float A profile average isn't an individual appraisal, and its exact aggregation formula isn't specified.
reviewCount Client recommendations Nullable integer Its name invites you to treat it as the number of rated appraisals.
ratingCount Appraisals containing a rating Nullable integer It describes rating volume, but doesn't establish that it is the exact weight behind the supplied average.
missionsCount Completed missions Malt reports Nullable integer A mission count isn't an identified population of eligible review invitations.

The split is easier to see without the familiar word “reviews” doing everyone's job:

Public profile
  ├─ avgRating      → average client rating
  ├─ reviewCount    → recommendations
  ├─ ratingCount    → appraisals containing ratings
  └─ missionsCount  → reported completed missions

Different counters do not establish shared membership or timing.

A difference between the counters is therefore an audit finding, not automatically an error.

If recommendations exceed rated appraisals, subtraction tells you the numerical gap. It doesn't identify which recommendations lack ratings, or prove that the counters describe nested sets.

Column names are cheap. Set membership is more expensive.

Choose types without inventing a format

Unfilled fields are omitted rather than returned as nulls or placeholders. There's no field-specific promise explaining every possible omission for these counters.

We'd preserve that distinction during ingestion. An absent key, supplied text that won't parse and an out-of-range number should never quietly become the same analytical zero.

The loader below retains the original values, tracks key presence and parses numeric-looking text after trimming whitespace. It deliberately doesn't guess a thousands separator or decimal locale where no formatted numeric convention is specified.

It also keeps malformed or out-of-domain values available for inspection:

fields = [
    "profileId", "avgRating",
    "reviewCount", "ratingCount", "missionsCount",
]
count_fields = ["reviewCount", "ratingCount", "missionsCount"]
numeric_fields = ["avgRating", *count_fields]

raw = pd.DataFrame(items).reindex(columns=fields)
present = pd.DataFrame(
    [{field: field in item for field in fields} for item in items],
    columns=fields,
).astype("boolean")

typed = pd.DataFrame(index=raw.index)
typed["profileId"] = (
    raw["profileId"].astype("string").str.strip().replace("", pd.NA)
)
audit_parts = []

for field in numeric_fields:
    text = raw[field].astype("string").str.strip()
    parsed = pd.to_numeric(text, errors="coerce").astype("Float64")

    if field == "avgRating":
        valid = parsed.between(0, 5).fillna(False)
        typed[field] = parsed.where(valid)
    else:
        valid = (
            parsed.ge(0)
            & parsed.lt(2**63)
            & parsed.mod(1).eq(0)
        ).fillna(False)
        typed[field] = parsed.where(valid).astype("Int64")

    audit_parts.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "field": field,
        "raw_value": raw[field],
        "omitted": ~present[field],
        "supplied_missing": present[field] & raw[field].isna(),
        "parse_failure": raw[field].notna() & parsed.isna(),
        "domain_failure": parsed.notna() & ~valid,
    }))

audit = pd.concat(audit_parts, ignore_index=True)

The integer storage boundary is a loader constraint, not a claimed marketplace limit. Fractional counts are rejected because counting appraisals or missions requires whole quantities.

For profileId, the string representation is an analytical key; raw retains its original representation. Don't interpret an identifier numerically or use its apparent order as chronology.

Missing fields change who enters the mean

An omitted recommendation count doesn't establish that a freelancer has no recommendations. An omitted rating doesn't belong at the bottom of the rating scale.

Those substitutions would change the story: absence of public evidence would become evidence of poor reputation.

Keep the counters side by side before selecting an average. When combining extracts, also quarantine missing or repeated identifiers until you've decided which observation to retain.

This cell creates the comparison table and calculates gaps only where both operands survive parsing:

identity_ok = (
    typed["profileId"].notna()
    & ~typed["profileId"].duplicated(keep=False)
)

comparison = typed.copy()
comparison["identity_usable"] = identity_ok
comparison["recommendation_rating_gap"] = (
    comparison["reviewCount"] - comparison["ratingCount"]
)
comparison["mission_rating_gap"] = (
    comparison["missionsCount"] - comparison["ratingCount"]
)

identity_audit = pd.Series({
    "returned_rows": len(typed),
    "rows_with_usable_identity": int(identity_ok.sum()),
    "rows_requiring_identity_review": int((~identity_ok).sum()),
})

The gaps remain missing when either input is unavailable. Filling those gaps would manufacture relationships between quantities you haven't observed.

Duplicate identifiers deserve similar restraint. Silently keeping the first row can select an older or less complete observation merely because it arrived first.

Which average are you publishing?

An unweighted mean of avgRating gives equal influence to each included profile with a usable average.

Weighting by ratingCount emphasises profiles with more rated appraisals; using reviewCount instead emphasises recommendation volume.

Those are different estimands: different quantities your calculation is trying to describe.

Even the more intuitively relevant appraisal count leaves an arithmetic catch: if supplied averages are rounded, multiplying them back by counts needn't recover the underlying rating total.

This cell calculates explicitly labelled alternatives and retains the contributing population for each:

profiles = typed.loc[identity_ok].copy()
rated = profiles["avgRating"].notna()

def weighted_profile_mean(frame, weight_field):
    usable = (
        frame["avgRating"].notna()
        & frame[weight_field].gt(0).fillna(False)
    )
    subset = frame.loc[usable]
    weights = subset[weight_field].astype("Float64")
    weight_sum = weights.sum(min_count=1)
    numerator = (
        subset["avgRating"] * weights
    ).sum(min_count=1)

    mean = (
        numerator / weight_sum
        if pd.notna(weight_sum) and weight_sum > 0
        else pd.NA
    )
    return {
        "mean": mean,
        "contributing_profiles": len(subset),
        "weight_sum": weight_sum,
    }

estimates = pd.DataFrame.from_dict({
    "unweighted_profile_average": {
        "mean": profiles.loc[rated, "avgRating"].mean(),
        "contributing_profiles": int(rated.sum()),
        "weight_sum": pd.NA,
    },
    "rating_count_weighted_profile_average":
        weighted_profile_mean(profiles, "ratingCount"),
    "recommendation_weighted_profile_average":
        weighted_profile_mean(profiles, "reviewCount"),
}, orient="index")

Don't compare those means without comparing their contributing profiles. Missing weights can change both the weighting and the membership of the calculation.

For publication, “mean public profile rating among returned profiles with usable ratings” is defensible wording. “Average client satisfaction” claims a broader population and a measurement interpretation these aggregates don't establish.

Thresholds don't create a rated sample

The inputs minRating and minReviews filter present values below their thresholds. Profiles without the corresponding public value aren't excluded.

That means a filtered result isn't automatically a collection of rated, sufficiently reviewed profiles. You still need an explicit analytical eligibility rule after collection.

The input types also differ: minRating accepts a number, while minReviews accepts an integer. Neither input becomes an output counter you can audit row by row.

Keep your chosen input settings with your analysis. If you later exclude missing ratings locally, report that exclusion separately from the Actor's threshold behaviour.

The worked example uses Malt Freelancer Skill & Rate Finder. Its thresholds define collection rules; your publication needs a separate statement of analytical eligibility.

Keep the denominator audit beside the chart

You need to know how many profiles contribute to each proposed figure before deciding which figure earns a headline.

This DuckDB query counts usable fields and the paired, positive-weight populations used by the weighted calculations:

connection = duckdb.connect()
connection.register("reputation_profiles", profiles)

denominator_audit = connection.execute("""
    SELECT
        COUNT(*) AS profiles_with_usable_identity,
        COUNT("avgRating") AS profiles_with_rating,
        COUNT("reviewCount") AS profiles_with_recommendations,
        COUNT("ratingCount") AS profiles_with_appraisal_count,
        COUNT("missionsCount") AS profiles_with_mission_count,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (
            WHERE "avgRating" IS NOT NULL
              AND "ratingCount" > 0
        ) AS rating_weight_eligible_profiles,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (
            WHERE "avgRating" IS NOT NULL
              AND "reviewCount" > 0
        ) AS recommendation_weight_eligible_profiles
    FROM reputation_profiles
""").df()

connection.close()

Keep denominator_audit, identity_audit and the parsing audit with the calculation. They explain why a returned profile did or didn't contribute, rather than leaving that decision buried in pandas' missing-value handling.

If you compare groups, apply the same audit within each group. Equal-looking averages can rest on very different amounts of public evidence.

Rating volume describes evidence quantity. It doesn't independently establish service quality.

A mission count can't supply a response rate

Dividing ratingCount by missionsCount produces a ratio of public counters. Calling it a review response rate requires more: an eligible population, aligned observation periods and a known relationship between missions and appraisal opportunities.

These records don't establish those conditions. You can't infer the experiences of clients who left no visible appraisal.

A defensible denominator needs a population, not just a convenient column.

Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.
