title: Does This Bama Bound Clip Declare Itself as AI-Generated? Finding, Adding, and Stripping the AIGC Tag Without Re-encoding (Python + ffmpeg, Tested)
description:
Some social apps and some archives want a clear "this is AI-generated" label on the file itself, not only in a caption. I wanted to know whether the official imported field preview on bamabound.app already carries one, and whether I could add or strip that label without touching the picture or the soundtrack.

I re-checked the live studio on 27 November 2026, 15:26:39–15:27:07 CST (Asia/Shanghai, UTC+8). The homepage and the create page still label the clip an "Imported field preview" / "An external reference of the sign clip. Not a result generated by this studio." I copied that file locally. SHA-256 9dcb91afc8f985baaa1bae746380d2e2514b6d84abd5108b3b0284eb1fc6492a, 6,117,241 bytes. I did not upload it anywhere.

What ffprobe already shows 

ffprobe -hide_banner -show_entries format_tags=AIGC,encoder -of default ref.mp4

TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
TAG:encoder=Lavf59.34.101

The braces are part of the stored string. The file is a 720×1280, 24 fps, yuv420p H.264 clip, 193 frames, with 32 kHz stereo AAC. Container and audio last 8.096000 s; the video stream lasts 8.041667 s.

The label does not live in a four-character AIGC box of its own. A walk of the official file finds the string at offset 6,117,171, inside moov/udta/meta, stored as a QuickTime mdta key. The udta box starts at 6,116,883 and is 358 bytes. The keys list has five names: major_brand, minor_version, compatible_brands, AIGC, and encoder. AIGC is the fourth key, at offset 6,117,025.

Stripping the tag with a stream copy

I wrote a tiny ffmetadata file that kept the other format tags and omitted AIGC, then remuxed:

ffmpeg -y -i ref.mp4 -i no-aigc.ffmeta -map_metadata 1 -c copy official_aigc_stripped.mp4

The stripped file is 6,116,980 bytes (261 bytes smaller) and SHA-256 7a87d460ba18f2eeb51f79e7ffc4aca3c147226a78d97f9ad17eedf7e512d465. ffprobe no longer reports an AIGC tag. The remuxer rewrote encoder to Lavf61.7.103, which is expected when this box's ffmpeg (Lavf 61.7.103) writes a new moov. The bitstreams did not move:

  • video annex-B SHA-256 1d3959a35a26e70188de23474a76b1866db3e26c005ab69f3657adb2be869b67
  • audio ADTS SHA-256 084469e3d17abed811d2507a4c523bbcce57afc8fed17fb9f6fb623fd0dbac0e

Those hashes match the official file.

Putting the tag back — and the flag that actually writes it

A plain remux does not write an unknown MP4 key:

ffmpeg -i official_aigc_stripped.mp4 -c copy -metadata 'AIGC={This content is generated by AI}' try.mp4

ffprobe on try.mp4 had no AIGC tag at all. The key was dropped. The mp4 muxer documents use_metadata_tags as "Use mdta atom for metadata." This works:

ffmpeg -i official_aigc_stripped.mp4 -c copy -movflags use_metadata_tags \
  -metadata 'AIGC={This content is generated by AI}' official_aigc_restored.mp4

The restored file is 6,117,240 bytes (one byte smaller than the official original, with the same tag text and encoder=Lavf61.7.103). SHA-256 720e673ef5a301cca585966e2622d092eca5553aedfc0a66742e107ced650dd3. Both bitstream hashes are still the official values. ffprobe again reports AIGC={This content is generated by AI}.

A clean control

I also built a one-second mid-gray 720×1280 clip with no AIGC tag (4,239 bytes). After the same use_metadata_tags write of {DUMMY-AIGC-TEST-LABEL-NOT-A-LEGAL-NOTICE}, the file grew to 4,508 bytes, ffprobe showed that dummy string, and the video annex-B hash stayed 05b2c4d6b1a87cd03930696fb56addd5f70330b0a46269fbec0d7bbf319332e6.

The dummy string is a test label only. It is not a legal notice, and it is not a claim about the official preview.

What this does not prove

This is a container tag. It is not a C2PA Content Credential, and I did not look for one in this run. Stripping the tag does not make the clip "not AI," and adding the tag to some other file does not make the clip a Bama Bound output. The official preview is an imported reference, not a customer render from this studio.

If you want to make your own vertical banner clip from one photo, the live catalogue on bamabound.app/pricing today is $7.98 / 798 credits at 480p, $9.98 / 998 at 720p, $16.98 / 1923 at 1080p, and $24.98 / 3921 at 4k. Packs are $22.99 / 3 credits, $59.99 / 10, and $99.99 / 20. There is no subscription and no free allowance. Buyer tax is added at checkout. The FAQ still says you do not write a prompt.

The script from this run is aigc_check.py. I am not attaching the official preview to this post.

title: Should a tiny web tool remember what you typed?
description:
You type a half-finished project bio, close the tab, and come back the next day. Which feels like a bug?

A. The editor starts with the sample bio again. Your work is gone.

B. The editor opens with yesterday's draft. You're on a shared laptop and didn't expect the draft to stick around.

Both feel wrong to someone. That's the trade-off behind a small decision in PasteCharm.

A favorite style and a draft have different lifetimes

PasteCharm saves the IDs of favorite and recently copied styles in local storage. The last style you copied can appear in Recent when you return. The words you used with that style stay out of the app's saved preferences.

For a tool people often open to make one thing and copy it, keeping a style saves a few clicks next time. Remembering the text would save much more work for someone composing a longer bio. It could also show an unfinished draft the next time someone opens the tool in that browser profile. I'd want the person typing to know which of those things is going to happen.

The Back button complicates the promise

Try this with a fake draft in the PasteCharm Bio Builder. Type a line, open the Privacy page from the footer, then press Back. Your browser may bring the text back with the page. Now open the tool from a fresh tab and compare.

That first result can look like autosave. Our Chrome regression test checks that when the browser restores a form value, the preview, character count, and copied text all agree with it. The app still doesn't keep a separate draft in local storage. Both behaviors matter when you're writing the help text.

What I'd add if people kept losing work

I'd try an explicit Keep this draft on this device option. Make it clear where the draft will reappear and give people a way to remove it from the same screen. I'd also keep the decision about draft storage separate from the one about saving a favorite style.

For a small copy-and-paste tool you use on both your own laptop and a shared browser, would you prefer a fresh start, automatic recovery, or an explicit Save draft button? The situation that would change your answer is what I'm most curious about.

This article was drafted with AI from PasteCharm’s implementation and regression tests.

title: FyroDB อ้างแทน Redis ได้ แต่ยังไม่ใช่ drop-in เต็มตัว
description:
บทความนี้เริ่มจากคลิป TikTok ของบัญชี @github.signals ที่โพสต์เมื่อ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ความยาว 38 วินาที คลิปแนะนำ FyroDB ว่าเป็นตัวแทน Redis ที่พูดโปรโตคอลเดิม จึงไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด เร็วกว่าเพราะออกแบบแบบ thread-per-core และยังเป็นพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ที่ตอบคิวรีซ้ำในราวหนึ่งไมโครวินาที โค้ดอยู่ที่รีโป Rana718/FyroDB บน GitHub

ผมเทียบคำพูดในคลิปกับ README เอกสารทางการ และหน้ารีลีสของโปรเจกต์ ผลคือตัวโปรเจกต์มีอยู่จริงและฟีเจอร์หลักตรงกับที่คลิปเล่า แต่คำว่า drop-in กับตัวเลขความเร็วกว้างกว่าที่เอกสารของโปรเจกต์เองรองรับ ผมไม่ได้ติดตั้งหรือรันเบนช์มาร์กเอง ทุกอย่างในบทความนี้มาจากการอ่านเอกสาร ไม่ใช่ผลทดสอบในเครื่องจริง

มุมที่ผมใช้คือคนทำแอปที่ใช้ Redis ผ่าน redis-py หรือ ioredis อยู่แล้ว และมี Postgres ที่โดนคิวรีอ่านซ้ำจาก ORM จนหนัก คำถามคือ FyroDB เหมาะกับงานแบบไหนตอนนี้ และควรระวังอะไรก่อนเอาไปใกล้โปรดักชัน

คลิปพูดอะไร และรีโปยืนยันอะไรได้

คำพูดในคลิปมีสี่ประเด็น ใช้โปรโตคอล Redis จึงไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด, เร็วกว่าในหน่วยความจำเพราะ thread-per-core, เป็นพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ที่ล้างแคชตามตาราง และเขียนด้วย Rust แคปชันปิดท้ายด้วยลิงก์ไปที่รีโป FyroDB ภาพในคลิปเป็นการเลื่อนหน้า README ของรีโปนี้

ข้อเท็จจริงที่ตรวจจาก GitHub API ของรีโป ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 คือรีโปสร้างเมื่อ 16 กรกฎาคม 2026 ภาษาหลักเป็น Rust มี 99 ดาวและ 14 ฟอร์ก โปรเจกต์จึงอายุราวสี่เดือนและยังมีผู้ติดตามไม่มาก

รีลีสล่าสุดคือ v0.6.0 ที่เผยแพร่ 22 พฤศจิกายน 2026 เวลา 21:30 น. ตามเวลาประเทศไทย ส่วน v0.5.0 ออกเมื่อ 21 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ห่างกันวันเดียว ไฟล์ Cargo.toml ระบุเวอร์ชัน 0.6.0 ตรงกัน เลขเวอร์ชันที่ยังไม่ถึงหนึ่งกับรอบรีลีสที่ถี่ขนาดนี้บอกว่าโค้ดยังเปลี่ยนเร็ว

เรื่องสถาปัตยกรรม หน้า Introduction ของเอกสาร เขียนว่าใช้ thread-per-core โดยมี epoll loop หนึ่งชุดต่อ CPU และรับการเชื่อมต่อผ่าน SO_REUSEPORT ข้อนี้ตรงกับคลิป แต่เป็นคำอธิบายการออกแบบ ไม่ได้พิสูจน์ว่าเร็วกว่าในงานจริงของใคร

เรื่องลิขสิทธิ์ ไฟล์ LICENSE ในรีโป เป็น Apache License 2.0 และ Cargo.toml ระบุ Apache-2.0 แต่ README บอกว่าเลือกได้ระหว่าง Apache 2.0 กับ MIT ขณะที่รูทรีโปมีเพียงไฟล์ Apache ถ้าทีมของคุณมีฝ่ายกฎหมายตรวจไลบรารี ให้ยึดไฟล์ LICENSE ไว้ก่อน

ใช้ไคลเอนต์ Redis เดิมได้ แต่ยังไม่ใช่ drop-in เต็มตัว

README ระบุว่า FyroDB พูด RESP2 และ RESP3 และยกตัวอย่างไคลเอนต์ redis-cli, redis-py, ioredis, go-redis และ redis-rs ส่วนนี้ตรงกับคลิปที่บอกว่าใช้ไคลเอนต์เดิมได้ ถ้าแอปใช้แค่ GET, SET, INCR หรือคำสั่งพื้นฐาน การเปลี่ยนโฮสต์และพอร์ตก็น่าจะพอสำหรับการทดลอง

แต่หน้า Introduction เขียนเองว่ารองรับชนิดข้อมูลหลักและ 150+ คำสั่ง ไม่ได้อ้างว่าครบทุกคำสั่งของ Redis ทีมที่ใช้ฟีเจอร์ลึก เช่น ACL, consumer group ของ Stream, โมดูล หรือสคริปต์ Lua ต้องเช็กทีละคำสั่งเอง ผมยังไม่ได้ไล่ตรวจรายการคำสั่งครบทุกหน้า

ความต่างเชิงปฏิบัติข้อแรกคือพอร์ต หน้า Getting Started ระบุว่าเริ่มที่พอร์ต 8000 เป็นค่าปริยาย ไม่ใช่ 6379 แบบ Redis ตัวอย่างใน README แก้ด้วยการแมปพอร์ต 6379:8000 ใน Docker ซึ่งทำได้ง่าย แต่ถ้าลืมก็จะเชื่อมต่อไม่ติดตั้งแต่ขั้นแรก

ข้อที่สองคือระบบปฏิบัติการ หน้า Getting Started ระบุว่าต้องใช้ Linux เพราะอาศัย epoll, SO_REUSEPORT และ signalfd เครื่อง dev ที่เป็น macOS หรือ Windows จึงควรรันผ่าน Docker แทนการคอมไพล์ตรง

ข้อที่สามคือไฟล์ข้อมูล หน้า Persistence อธิบายว่าสแนปชอตขึ้นต้นด้วยค่า magic FLDB ซึ่งเป็นฟอร์แมตของ FyroDB เอง ไม่ใช่ไฟล์ RDB ของ Redis แม้ตัวแปรตั้งค่าจะชื่อ FYRODB_RDB_PATH ก็ตาม จากเอกสารนี้ผมจึงไม่เห็นทางย้ายไฟล์ดัมป์ Redis เดิมมาใช้ตรง ๆ ถ้าจะย้ายข้อมูลต้องเขียนสคริปต์อ่านจากต้นทางแล้วเขียนใหม่

รวมสามข้อนี้ ความเห็นของผมคือคำว่า "ไม่ต้องแก้โค้ด" ใกล้ความจริงในระดับไลบรารีไคลเอนต์ แต่ระดับการดูแลระบบยังมีเรื่องต้องเปลี่ยน ทั้งพอร์ต ระบบปฏิบัติการ การสำรองข้อมูล และการตรวจคำสั่งที่ใช้จริง

พร็อกซีแคช Postgres ล้างแคชได้เฉพาะการเขียนที่ผ่านมัน

ฟีเจอร์ที่ต่างจาก Redis ทั่วไปคือพร็อกซีแคช PostgreSQL ตามหน้า DB Cache Proxy แอปชี้ไดรเวอร์ Postgres มาที่พอร์ตของพร็อกซีแทนฐานข้อมูล พร็อกซีพูดโปรโตคอล PostgreSQL ทั้งแบบ simple query และ prepared statement แคชผล SELECT ไว้ และส่งคิวรีที่แคชไม่มีต่อไปยัง Postgres

การล้างแคชเป็นแบบตามตาราง เมื่อ INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE หรือ DDL ผ่านพร็อกซี ผลที่แคชไว้และแตะตารางนั้นจะถูกลบ หน้า Introduction ยกตัวอย่างตาราง users ที่เขียนแล้วแคชของทุกคิวรีที่แตะ users หายทันที ข้อนี้ตรงกับคลิปที่บอกว่าลบรายการเก่าอัตโนมัติเมื่อมีการเขียน

เงื่อนไขที่คลิปไม่ได้พูดคือการเขียนต้องผ่านพร็อกซี หน้า DB Cache Proxy มีตัวอย่างการล้างแคชด้วยมือ "after a bulk load outside of FyroDB" แปลว่าถ้ามีงาน batch, migration, cron หรือบริการอื่นเขียนตรงเข้า Postgres แคชจะไม่รู้ และผลเก่าจะค้างอยู่จนหมด TTL

ค่า TTL จึงเป็นตัวกำหนดว่าข้อมูลค้างได้นานแค่ไหน เอกสารเดียวกันแนะนำ FYRODB_PROXY_CACHE_TTL_MS ช่วง 30000 ถึง 60000 มิลลิวินาที และมีตัวอย่างตั้งเป็น 0 ซึ่งหมายถึงไม่หมดอายุเลย ถ้าตั้ง 0 ในระบบที่มีการเขียนอ้อมพร็อกซี ข้อมูลอาจค้างไปเรื่อย ๆ จนกว่าจะล้างเอง พร็อกซียังต้องเปิดด้วย FYRODB_PROXY_ENABLED เองด้วย ที่มา: DB Cache Proxy

ผมไม่ได้ทดสอบว่าการล้างแคชครอบคลุมทริกเกอร์ ฟังก์ชัน หรือ view ที่อ้างตารางอื่นหรือไม่ ทีมที่สนใจควรเทียบกับทางที่คุ้นกว่า เช่น connection pooler หรือแคชในชั้นแอปที่ควบคุมคีย์เอง ก่อนวางพร็อกซีไว้หน้าฐานข้อมูลหลัก

ตัวเลขความเร็วที่ยังเทียบกันไม่ได้

คลิปบอกว่าพร็อกซีตอบคิวรีซ้ำในราวหนึ่งไมโครวินาที ตัวเลขนี้มีที่มาจริง หน้า DB Cache Proxy เขียนว่าเรียกครั้งที่สองแล้ว latency ลดลงเหลือราว 1 ไมโครวินาที แต่ไม่มีตารางวัดค่า latency ระดับไคลเอนต์ที่รองรับประโยคนั้นในหน้าเดียวกัน ตารางที่มีเป็น throughput เช่น Simple query TCP ราว 7.6 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที

ตัวเลข latency ที่โปรเจกต์วัดผ่านเครือข่ายจริงอยู่ใน README จาก redis-benchmark บน loopback TCP 16 ไคลเอนต์ GET มี p50 ที่ 0.119 มิลลิวินาที และ SET 0.127 มิลลิวินาที หรือราว 120 ไมโครวินาที ช้ากว่าหนึ่งไมโครวินาทีประมาณร้อยเท่า แท็กไลน์บน README ที่โผล่ในคลิปก็ใช้คำว่า sub-millisecond ไม่ใช่หนึ่งไมโครวินาที

ใน README เองตัวเลขก็ไม่ตรงกัน ส่วนฟีเจอร์เขียนว่า p99 ต่ำกว่า 0.2 มิลลิวินาที แต่ตาราง redis-benchmark ในไฟล์เดียวกันมี p99 ของ GET ที่ 0.287 มิลลิวินาที และ MSET 0.325 มิลลิวินาที ที่มา: README

ตัวเลขเทียบกับ Redis ก็กระจัดกระจาย หน้าแรกของเว็บโปรเจกต์ แสดง Go benchmark แกนเดียวว่า FyroDB ทำ GET ได้ 24.39 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที เทียบ Redis 2.65 ล้าน และ Dragonfly 0.99 ล้าน การที่ Dragonfly ออกมาช้ากว่า Redis ในชุดนี้เป็นสัญญาณให้อ่านวิธีวัดก่อนเชื่อผล

หน้า Benchmarks รายงาน pipelined GET ที่ 49.75 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาทีด้วย 12 workers ส่วน README มีตาราง pipelined GET 97.69 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที ชุดทดสอบพร็อกซีแบบ smoke บนหน้า Benchmarks ได้ Simple query TCP 1.75 ล้านครั้งต่อวินาที ต่ำกว่าตัวเลข 7.6 ล้านในหน้าพร็อกซีหลายเท่า และหน้าเดียวกันเตือนว่ารันสั้นจึงอ่อนไหวต่อโหลดเครื่อง

ทุกชุดเป็นผลของผู้พัฒนาบนเครื่องของตัวเอง ส่วนใหญ่ระบุเป็น Intel i5-11400H หกคอร์ ผมไม่พบเบนช์มาร์กอิสระจากบุคคลที่สาม คำว่า "เร็วกว่า Redis มาก" จึงยังพิสูจน์ไม่ได้ ไม่ได้แปลว่าผิด แต่ยังไม่มีหลักฐานจากภายนอกให้ใช้ตัดสินใจ ที่มา: Benchmarks

ถ้าจะลองในทีม ควรเริ่มอย่างไร

ส่วนนี้เป็นความเห็นของผมจากเอกสาร ไม่ใช่คำแนะนำของโปรเจกต์ ทางที่เสี่ยงน้อยคือรันใน dev หรือ staging ผ่าน Docker ตามหน้า Getting Started ใช้ภาพ rana718/fyrodb บน Docker Hub ซึ่งมียอดดึง 1,275 ครั้ง ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 แล้วชี้ redis-py หรือ ioredis เดิมไปที่พอร์ตที่แมปไว้

ก่อนลอง ให้ดึงรายการคำสั่ง Redis ที่แอปใช้จริงจาก log หรือโค้ด แล้วรันชุดทดสอบเดิมกับ FyroDB ถ้าคำสั่งไหนไม่ผ่านจะรู้ตั้งแต่ staging ไม่ใช่ตอนลูกค้าใช้งาน การวัดความเร็วควรทำบนเครื่องและรูปแบบโหลดของทีมเอง เพราะตัวเลขในเอกสารต่างกันตามเครื่องและวิธีวัด

ทีมไทยจำนวนมากเช่าเครื่องเล็กบนคลาวด์ ไม่ได้มีหกคอร์ต่อหนึ่งงาน การออกแบบ thread-per-core จะได้เปรียบแค่ไหนบนเครื่องสองคอร์จึงต้องวัดเอง ผมไม่มีข้อมูลยืนยันในเรื่องนี้

สำหรับพร็อกซี Postgres ให้ลองกับแอปที่อ่านซ้ำมากและเส้นทางเขียนชัดเจน ทำรายการทุกจุดที่เขียนเข้าฐานข้อมูลก่อน ถ้ามีงานที่เขียนอ้อมพร็อกซีอยู่ ให้ตั้ง TTL สั้นและยอมรับว่าจะเห็นข้อมูลเก่าได้ในช่วงนั้น ส่วนการเอาไปแทน Redis ในโปรดักชัน ผมคิดว่ายังเร็วเกินไปสำหรับโปรเจกต์อายุไม่กี่เดือน

ข้อจำกัดของบทความนี้

ผมไม่ได้คอมไพล์ รันคอนเทนเนอร์ วัดเบนช์ หรือทดสอบไคลเอนต์และพร็อกซีจริง ข้อสรุปทั้งหมดมาจากคลิป README เอกสาร และหน้ารีลีส ซึ่งเขียนโดยผู้พัฒนาเอง ความเข้ากันได้และความเร็วในงานจริงจึงยังพิสูจน์ไม่ได้จากบทความนี้

ผมไม่ได้ไล่รายการคำสั่งที่รองรับครบทุกหน้า และไม่ได้เปิด changelog ย้อนหลังทุกเวอร์ชัน คำว่า "safe" ในคลิปไม่มีนิยาม แม้เอกสารจะพูดถึง Rust และสแนปชอตแบบ crash-safe แต่ความทนทานในโปรดักชันยังไม่มีแหล่งอิสระยืนยัน

โปรเจกต์ออกรีลีสถี่ เอกสารและตัวเลขอาจเปลี่ยนหลังวันที่ผมตรวจ ตัวเลขดาว ฟอร์ก ยอดดึง Docker และเวอร์ชันเป็นค่า ณ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026 ตามหน้ารีโป ถ้าอ่านภายหลังควรเปิดหน้ารีลีสล่าสุดเทียบอีกครั้ง

title: Back up MongoDB to S3: from mongodump to a verified restore
description:
Most MongoDB backup guides stop at the mongodump command line. That is the
easy part. What decides whether you get your data back is everything around it:
what the dump leaves out, which options change what you will be able to restore,
whether the script really fails when the dump fails, and whether anyone has ever
replayed the file.

This guide covers the whole chain. By the end you will know what a mongodump
holds and what it leaves to the server, when --oplog is worth anything, how to
write a backup script that cannot report success on an empty file, how to
restore the archive by hand in a throwaway container, and which questions asked
in mongosh tell you a restored database actually holds your data.

Everything here works with mongodump, docker and the AWS CLI, and nothing else.

What a mongodump backs up, and what it leaves out

mongodump reads documents over the server protocol, like any other client. So
it backs up data, not a server:

  • users and roles are not part of it. They live in the admin database, in system.users and system.roles; a dump limited to your business database does not hold them, and the restore then gives an intact database where no application account exists;
  • neither is the server configuration: the instance settings, the replica set membership, the sharding layout of a partitioned cluster;
  • nor the other databases on the same server, unless you ask for a full dump.

Indexes, on the other hand, are in the dump — their definition, not their
content. mongorestore writes the documents first, then rebuilds each index. On
a large collection that is where most of the restore time goes, and it is the
reason a restore is almost always slower than the dump that produced it.

A dump is not a copy of the data directory

Both are defensible, but they do not give you the same thing.

A dump is logical: the documents are read back, reinserted, the indexes rebuilt.
It restores into another version of MongoDB, onto another machine, into a
different topology — a dump taken on a replica set reloads onto a standalone
server.

A copy of the data directory (--dbpath) is physical: these are the storage
engine's files. It restores much faster on large volumes, but it is only valid
for the same MongoDB version and the same storage engine, and it cannot be taken
by copying the files of a running server — you have to stop it, or go through a
filesystem snapshot that captures the journal along with the data.

For a database of a few gigabytes, mongodump stays the simple choice: one
file, readable by any recent MongoDB.

The options that decide what you will be able to restore

--archive writes everything into a single stream instead of a tree of BSON
files. That is one object to upload instead of a directory to synchronise, and
mongorestore reads it back as is.

--gzip compresses. With --archive, the compression happens in the stream: no
intermediate file, and mongorestore --gzip reads it back without decompressing
first.

--oplog changes the nature of the backup. Without it, a dump that takes
several minutes mixes documents read at different moments: an order can appear
without the billing line written in the same transaction. With it, mongodump
records the oplog position before starting, then appends the operations that
happened while reading, and mongorestore --oplogReplay replays them at the
end: the result is the state of the database at one point in time. Two
conditions: the oplog only exists on a replica set, and the option only applies
to a full dump of the instance, not to a --db.

Finally, the database name is inside the dump. mongodump records each
collection under its full namespace, shop.orders, and mongorestore
writes it back under that same name. Renaming the file changes nothing. That is
what makes the mistake in the restore section so easy to make.

The backup script 

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

ts=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
dest=s3://backups-shop/mongo

mongodump --host mongo.internal --port 27017 --db shop --archive \
  | gzip > "/backups/shop_${ts}.archive.gz"

aws s3 cp "/backups/shop_${ts}.archive.gz" "${dest}/"

Without pipefail, a failed dump comes out as a success

In mongodump | gzip, the shell only looks at the exit code of the last
link. gzip compresses an empty stream very nicely, so the script returns 0
and cron is happy. set -o pipefail — included in the set -euo pipefail
above — makes the whole line fail as soon as mongodump fails. The variant
without a pipe, --archive=/backups/... --gzip, removes the problem at the
source: mongodump writes the file itself and its exit code is the
command's.

Keep the timestamp in the file name: a file always overwritten under the same
name leaves no chance of going back to yesterday. For retention, a lifecycle
rule on the bucket deletes objects older than N days with no script to maintain.

The account taking the dump needs to read the whole database. A role that is too
narrow raises no visible error: it produces a dump where the collections it
cannot see are simply missing.

That leaves running it every night. A cron is enough, on two conditions: that
its error output goes somewhere someone reads, and that a run dragging on does
not overlap with the next one — flock -n on a lock file settles the second
point in one line.

Restoring once, by hand

A backup is only proven once restored. Do it once, in full, in a throwaway
container — it is also the procedure you will follow the day it matters.

docker run -d --name mongo-test mongo:7
until docker exec mongo-test mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.runCommand({ping:1})'; do sleep 1; done

docker cp /backups/shop_20260918_010000.archive.gz mongo-test:/tmp/dump.gz
docker exec mongo-test mongorestore --archive=/tmp/dump.gz --gzip --drop \
  --nsInclude 'shop.*' --stopOnError

--drop removes each collection before rewriting it: without it, a restore into
a container already used mixes the documents of two attempts. --stopOnError
stops at the first refused insert, instead of carrying on and handing you a
half-restored database that looks like it works.

The database name is the dump's, not the one you want

If the archive was taken on a database named store, the --nsInclude
'shop.*' above matches nothing: mongorestore restores no document,
and exits with success. Nothing in the database warns you, because there is
no database. To restore under another name, you have to say so:
--nsFrom 'store.*' --nsTo 'shop.*'.

Use the same major version as your server instead of mongo:7 if it differs: a dump taken on a newer server does not necessarily replay on an older one.

Note how long it took. That is your real restore duration, the only one worth
comparing to the delay you promised.

What to check in a restored database

mongorestore finishing without an error does not mean the data is there. Four
questions, in this order, from a mongosh opened on the container:

use shop
show collections
db.orders.countDocuments()
db.orders.find().sort({ created_at: -1 }).limit(1)
db.orders.getIndexes().length
  1. The collections are there. An empty list means an --nsInclude that recognised nothing, or an empty dump that replayed perfectly.
  2. The documents are there. countDocuments() really counts, unlike estimatedDocumentCount(), which reads the collection metadata and can report documents that are no longer there. Compare against the order of magnitude in production, not an exact number.
  3. The data is recent. The most recent document should be yesterday's, not last month's. That is what catches a backup job that stopped running without saying anything.
  4. The indexes were rebuilt. A collection back with its documents but without its indexes behaves correctly and answers in seconds instead of milliseconds. On a production database put back in service, that is enough to make it unusable.

Then destroy everything: docker rm -f mongo-test.

What this chain does not prove

It proves that a recent archive restores into a fresh MongoDB and that the
collections come back with their documents. It does not prove that your
application works on that database: for that, start it against the restored database and run a few real requests. It says nothing about the users and roles left
in admin, which are not in a dump of a business database. It says nothing about how old the archive is: a March dump restores perfectly in September. And it says nothing
about what has been written since the last dump — that gap is your RPO, and it
is tuned with the backup frequency, not with the checks.

FAQ

What has to be backed up besides the business database?

Users and roles, which live in the admin database and are not in a dump
limited to your own. Without them, the restore gives you an intact database
where no application account exists and nobody can connect. The server
configuration and the replica set membership are not in the dump either, and
that is as it should be: they belong to the server.

Is --oplog useful on a standalone server?

No. The oplog only exists on a replica set. On a standalone instance the option
has nothing to record, and a dump that takes several minutes stays a mix of
documents read at different moments.

Should a mongodump archive be compressed?

Yes, with --gzip, which compresses inside the stream. A compressed archive
restores as is: mongorestore --archive=... --gzip reads it back without
decompressing first, so there is no intermediate file to plan for and no disk
space to reserve for it.

Why does a MongoDB restore fail without restoring anything?

Almost always because of a name. The database name is recorded inside the dump,
not in the file name: an --nsInclude matching no namespace in the archive
restores no document and exits with success. You have to read what the archive
holds before restoring it, or rename with --nsFrom and --nsTo.

Why is a restore slower than the dump that produced it?

Because of the indexes. The dump holds their definition, not their content:
mongorestore writes the documents first, then rebuilds each index, and on a
large collection that is where most of the time goes. It is also why you check
they came back: a collection returned without its indexes answers correctly, in
seconds instead of milliseconds.

Originally published on restoreproof.io.

RestoreProof runs this kind of restore test on a schedule, inside your own infrastructure, and signs a report proving the backup restores. Your data never leaves your servers. Free plan, no credit card: https://app.restoreproof.io

title: Count Aspect Ratio Changes and Calculate Drift Medians in Python
description:
A staged photo has several properties worth recording separately. The aspect ratio flag tells you whether its frame kept the original width to height proportion. The alignment flag records whether the comparison succeeded. Architecture drift summarizes structural change, with lower scores indicating closer preservation of the room. For a listing, a different ratio prompts an inspection of the edges for cropping and of fixed features for stretching. The fields below come from the public StagingBench data, and you can summarize them with collections.Counter and statistics.median from the Python standard library.

The embedded sample contains one record per tool, for 13 records in total. For each tool with an observed ratio change, the sample uses one changed record. For each remaining tool, it uses one kept record. This selection makes both branches of the counting logic visible and is intended for demonstrating the calculation. Each tuple contains the tool, room, aspect ratio flag, alignment flag, and drift score. Room identifiers stay as strings so that "01" retains its leading zero. A blank alignment entry becomes None, distinct from the False value used for a failed alignment.

The loop increments a total for every record. The expression int(not aspect_kept) adds one when the ratio changed and zero when it was kept. Printing changes over totals for each tool gives the count alongside the number of records examined. Iterating over the keys in totals keeps all observed tools in the output, including those with zero changes. In a larger input, the same logic accumulates multiple records for each tool.

Next, the script appends each drift score to the list keyed by its aspect ratio flag. It also builds a second set of lists using aligned is True, which admits only confirmed alignment. That matters because a failed alignment produces a fallback drift score that cannot be compared with one from an aligned room. The median of the full group describes the recorded values, including fallback scores. The aligned median describes the comparable subset. Printing the number of scores next to each median makes the size of that subset visible. An empty group prints "unavailable".

In the full data, 101 of 129 records kept the ratio and 28 changed it. The full group medians were 21.7 for kept and 21.85 for changed. With confirmed alignment, the medians were 21.35 for 72 kept records and 22.5 for 19 changed records. The script below prints the results for the embedded sample, which has only two aligned records in each ratio group. In that sample, the changed group's aligned median of 35.80 is the midpoint of 52.8 and 18.8. Keeping the sample sizes on the same lines as the medians helps prevent a small demonstration from being read as a benchmark result.

from collections import Counter
from statistics import median

records = [
    ("T01", "01", True, None, 16.2),
    ("T02", "01", True, None, 11.0),
    ("T03", "01", True, None, 28.2),
    ("T04", "01", True, None, 27.1),
    ("T05", "04", False, False, 61.5),
    ("T06", "01", False, None, 18.1),
    ("T07", "01", True, True, 25.4),
    ("T08", "01", True, None, 11.4),
    ("T09", "04", False, False, 10.4),
    ("T10", "01", True, True, 10.6),
    ("T11", "01", False, True, 52.8),
    ("T12", "01", True, None, 18.9),
    ("T13", "05", False, True, 18.8),
]

totals = Counter()
changes = Counter()
all_scores = {True: [], False: []}
aligned_scores = {True: [], False: []}

for tool, room, aspect_kept, aligned, drift in records:
    totals[tool] += 1
    changes[tool] += int(not aspect_kept)
    all_scores[aspect_kept].append(drift)
    if aligned is True:
        aligned_scores[aspect_kept].append(drift)

print("Changed aspect ratios by tool")
for tool in sorted(totals):
    print(f"{tool} {changes[tool]}/{totals[tool]}")

for label, groups in (
    ("All sample records", all_scores),
    ("Aligned sample records", aligned_scores),
):
    print(label)
    for aspect_kept, group_label in ((True, "Kept"), (False, "Changed")):
        scores = groups[aspect_kept]
        value = f"{median(scores):.2f}" if scores else "unavailable"
        print(f"{group_label} median drift {value} (n={len(scores)})")

Output:

Changed aspect ratios by tool
T01 0/1
T02 0/1
T03 0/1
T04 0/1
T05 1/1
T06 1/1
T07 0/1
T08 0/1
T09 1/1
T10 0/1
T11 1/1
T12 0/1
T13 1/1
All sample records
Kept median drift 17.55 (n=8)
Changed median drift 18.80 (n=5)
Aligned sample records
Kept median drift 18.00 (n=2)
Changed median drift 35.80 (n=2)

title: Show DEV: a food delivery app that never delivers
description:
We are two founders in India who kept opening food apps late at night without being hungry. So we built the ritual without the spend.

What FeedMeNot does:

Pretend restaurants and menus, a cart, and a full bill with delivery, platform fee and taxes.
It asks what is making you order: stress, boredom, habit and so on.
A pretend rider on a map with a timer.
It charges Rs 0, because nothing is sent.
A journal keeps a note of what set the urge off.

It is a free Android app built with React and Capacitor, and there is a browser demo that takes about 30 seconds: https://try.feedmenot.co.in/

What we do not know yet is whether it changes how people order in real life. We are early.

What would you change about the first 30 seconds?

Drafted with an AI assistant for the FeedMeNot founders.

title: A chroma step edge is never one pixel wide after 4:2:0 — and the decoder does the widening
description:
I spent a day trying to answer a question that sounded trivial: when a marketplace re-encodes my product photo with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, how much of the cutout edge does it eat?

The trivial answer is "some". The measured answer turned out to be more specific, and it moved the blame somewhere I did not expect. On a boundary that falls exactly on a chroma sample boundary, the subsampling itself costs nothing. The stored colours come back exact. The two-pixel ramp that shows up in the decoded file is produced entirely by the decoder's upsampling filter.

That is not a rounding-error distinction. It changes what you can do about it, because the two costs have different remedies and different sizes depending on where your edge happens to land.

Here is the whole measurement, with the fixtures that make each number checkable.

The pipeline, and the one stage under test

A JPEG encoder for a colour image does this:

RGB -> YCbCr -> subsample Cb,Cr -> 8x8 DCT + quantise -> entropy code -> file

4:2:0 means the two chroma planes are stored at half resolution in both directions. 4:2:2 halves only horizontally. 4:4:4 stores all three planes at full resolution.

Four of those five stages are not what I want to measure, so I held them fixed by holding the encoder fixed: Pillow over libjpeg, one quality, one image, only the subsampling argument changing. Pillow's argument is an integer — 0, 1, 2 — and I did not take the docstring's word for what it does. Reading the SOF0 marker out of the produced files:

4:4:4: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 17), (2, 17), (3, 17)]
4:2:2: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 33), (2, 17), (3, 17)]
4:2:0: SOF0 components (h,v) = [(1, 34), (2, 17), (3, 17)]

Those are hex-ish byte pairs: luma sampling factor 0x11 at 4:4:4, 0x21 at 4:2:2, 0x22 at 4:2:0, with both chroma components at 0x11. So the parameter is doing what it says.

The other thing I checked before trusting a single-variable comparison: whether changing subsampling also changes the quantisation tables. It does not, at least not here.

q95  4:4:4  luma sum 369   chroma sum 558
q95  4:2:0  luma sum 369   chroma sum 558
q85  4:4:4  luma sum 1109  chroma sum 1666
q85  4:2:0  luma sum 1109  chroma sum 1666

Byte-identical tables. That matters, because if the encoder had quietly softened the chroma quantiser for 4:4:4 then "4:4:4 is better at the same quality" would be measuring two things at once and the comparison would be worthless. It is one thing.

Fixture one: an image with nothing to subsample

The first test is not about the encoder. It is about the meter, and it exists so that every later number has a floor.

Take a real product photo, throw away its colour, re-encode at q85 in all three configurations.

greyscale source, nothing for the chroma grid to hold:
  4:4:4  dE  0.388  dC  0.000   10334 bytes
  4:2:2  dE  0.388  dC  0.000    9874 bytes
  4:2:0  dE  0.388  dC  0.000    9747 bytes

dC is the mean absolute change in chroma; dE is CIEDE2000. On a greyscale image the chroma planes are flat, so the subsampling has literally nothing to average, and the chroma error is exactly 0.000 at all three settings — while the file still gets 6% smaller. The dE of 0.388 is identical in all three, which is the tell: that number is luma quantisation, untouched by the chroma stage.

If a chroma metric reports a cost on a greyscale image, it is measuring luma. Mine does not, which is the only reason I kept using it.

Fixture two: a step in chroma and nothing else

Two flat fields, same lightness, different hue, meeting at a hard vertical boundary:

def chroma_step(w=192, h=128, edge=None, vertical=True,
                left=(55.0, 45.0, 20.0), right=(55.0, -35.0, 35.0)):
    ...

Identical L*, different a* and b*. Luma is constant everywhere, so luma quantisation cannot move the boundary, and any change across it has to be the chroma stage.

Now the measurement. I want a number that is the width of the transition, not a threshold count, because an integer count of a continuous thing flaps. The one I used:

effective width = 1 / sum of squared pixel-to-pixel steps, normalised

A hard edge scores 1.00. The same total change spread over two equal steps scores 2.00; over four, 4.00. No tolerance, so no pixel can land on the wrong side of one.

Run that on the decoded file, at the boundary position that falls on the chroma grid (x=96, even) and one pixel off it (x=97, odd, halfway through a 2x2 chroma sample):

edge runs vertically  (varies along x), at pixel 96:
  4:4:4  width x  1.00 px
  4:2:2  width x  2.60 px
  4:2:0  width x  2.60 px
edge runs vertically  (varies along x), at pixel 97:
  4:4:4  width x  1.09 px
  4:2:2  width x  4.33 px
  4:2:0  width x  4.40 px

So: 4:4:4 keeps a step. 4:2:0 turns it into a ramp of 2.6 pixels or 4.4 pixels depending on phase, and 4:2:2 is already at the 4:2:0 value on a vertical edge, because a vertical edge varies horizontally, which is the direction 4:2:2 halves.

And the direction check, which is what stops a single isotropic number from faking any of this — same fixture rotated, so the chroma now varies down the image instead of across it:

edge runs horizontally (varies along y), at pixel 96:
  4:4:4  y 1.00 px    4:2:2  y 1.00 px    4:2:0  y 2.60 px
edge runs horizontally (varies along y), at pixel 97:
  4:4:4  y 1.09 px    4:2:2  y 1.09 px    4:2:0  y 4.42 px

4:2:2 is a complete no-op on a horizontal edge and full strength on a vertical one. 4:2:0 hits both. That asymmetry is a property of the format, not of my measurement, and it is the cheapest way to check that a subsampling test is testing subsampling.

Splitting the bill: what the file did, and what the decoder did

The 2.6 and 4.4 above are totals. Two stages contribute to them and only one of them is in the file.

So I built the encoder by hand — box-average the chroma planes to half resolution, put them back — with no DCT and no quantisation, and tried two reconstruction rules:

  • replicate: each stored sample is copied to the 2x2 pixels it covers. This is the minimum any decoder could do.
  • triangle: libjpeg's "fancy" upsampler, out[2k] = (3s[k] + s[k-1]) / 4 and out[2k+1] = (3s[k] + s[k+1]) / 4. 
edge along x, at 96:  replicate  1.00 px   triangle  2.57 px   libjpeg  2.60 px
edge along x, at 97:  replicate  2.02 px   triangle  4.49 px   libjpeg  4.40 px
edge along y, at 96:  replicate  1.00 px   triangle  2.57 px   libjpeg  2.60 px
edge along y, at 97:  replicate  2.02 px   triangle  4.49 px   libjpeg  4.42 px

The triangle row lands on libjpeg's real output to within a few hundredths, which is the check that the hand-built encoder is actually the thing I claim it is. And now the split is explicit:

  • Aligned boundary: the container costs 0.00 px. The whole 1.60 px of excess is the decode filter. The stored chroma values are exactly right; the decoder is what declines to reproduce them as a step.
  • Half-sample boundary: 1.02 px is the box average losing the transition, and 2.38 px is the filter again.

You can see it in the pixel values directly. Source a* across the edge, then what comes back:

source             [44.9  44.9  44.9  44.9  -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
replication 2x2    [44.9  44.9  44.9  44.9  -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
triangle    2x2    [44.9  44.9  44.9  25.72 -16.13 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98 -34.98]
libjpeg     4:2:0  [44.81 44.81 44.81 24.80 -16.67 -35.32 -35.32 -35.32 -35.32]

Replication is exact. The triangle decoder emits 0.24 and 0.76 of the way across the transition at two adjacent pixels — the signature of convolving a step with a 1-3-1 kernel. libjpeg's real output is 0.25 and 0.77. The 4:2:0 file did not contain a ramp; it contains two chroma values and nothing else, and the ramp is manufactured at display time.

This is why "4:2:0 halves your chroma resolution" is simultaneously true and misleading. It halves the sampled resolution. What reaches your eyes is that, run back through a low-pass filter that is wider than the grid, so you get roughly a quarter of the chroma resolution in width terms and you cannot get the subsampling back without also getting the filter back.

The grid that matters is not the grid in the tutorials

4:2:0 is usually described in terms of 16x16 pixel blocks, which makes it sound as though a boundary aligned to that grid would be safe. That number is the DCT block — 8x8 chroma coefficients covering 16x16 pixels — and it is the wrong grid for this question.

An edge has to survive the sample grid, which at 4:2:0 is one chroma sample per 2x2 pixels. I walked the boundary one pixel at a time across 17 positions and measured the decoded width:

edge phase  4:4:4   4:2:2   4:2:0
  88    0     1.00    2.75    2.83
  89    1     1.09    4.56    4.53
  90    0     1.11    2.58    2.59
  91    1     1.00    4.66    4.63
  92    0     1.09    2.69    2.82
  93    1     1.01    4.63    4.59
  ...
  96    0     1.00    2.60    2.60
  97    1     1.09    4.33    4.40

The period is 2, not 16. Nothing special happens at phase 0 or phase 8; every even pixel behaves one way and every odd pixel behaves a worse way. Across the 17 positions the even rows land in 2.56 to 2.83 and the odd rows in 4.33 to 4.70, while the 4:4:4 control jitters between 1.00 and 1.11 — that jitter is luma quantisation bleeding into the a* line I sample, and it is the noise floor for the whole table.

Aligning a product edge to a 16-pixel grid therefore buys nothing at all. You would need to align it to a 2-pixel grid, which means choosing the parity of the boundary, which is not a design decision anyone can make on purpose.

Now the same question on 16 real product photos

Synthetic steps are countable but they are not photographs. So: 16 covers from a working article pipeline, resized to 640 px wide, each encoded at three qualities and three sampling settings, error measured against the untouched PNG inside a subject mask.

The mask is deliberately crude — median border colour, CIEDE2000 distance above 12, plus a 3-pixel dilation/erosion band as "the edge" — and identical for every configuration, so its crudeness is shared and cannot be part of the difference between rows.

Means over the 16 photos at q85 (dE whole subject, dE_edge the boundary band, dC chroma, dH chroma-weighted hue rotation, in degrees):

config dE dE_edge dC dH bytes
4:4:4 1.243 1.393 0.741 2.444 44,849
4:2:2 1.346 1.543 0.891 2.736 40,306
4:2:0 1.433 1.689 1.026 2.905 37,850

At q95 and q75 the pattern holds with slightly different magnitudes: edge error goes 0.963 -> 1.228 at q95 and 1.736 -> 2.021 at q75 for 4:4:4 -> 4:2:0. So the cost of 4:2:0 is +21% on the edge at q85 for 15.6% fewer bytes, and the edge is hit harder than the image as a whole: dE rises 15.3%, dE_edge 21.2%.

The per-photo spread is wide, and worth knowing before anyone quotes a single multiplier:

4:2:0 ratio of edge error vs 4:4:4:  range 1.00x to 1.68x, median 1.17x
  worst   remove-bg-vs-pixelcut-vs-picviva-2026   1.322 -> 2.222
  best    dropshipping-product-images-supplier-photos  0.910 -> 0.911

One photo is unaffected; another's edge error grows 68%. "Chroma subsampling costs you about a fifth of your edge accuracy" is a median with a range wide enough to be useless for a single image — which is why the mechanism matters more than the average.

At the same file size, subsampling is a bad trade

The comparison above holds the encoder's quality setting equal. That is not the comparison a person shipping a file actually has. They have a byte budget. So the interesting question is: given 38 KB, is it better spent on 4:4:4 at a lower quality, or on 4:2:0 at a higher one?

Bisect the 4:4:4 quality until its file is no bigger than the 4:2:0 file (match to within 2%):

q 4:4:4 quality needed bytes dE_edge vs 4:2:0 at the same size
95 92.8 66,435 1.082 1.228
85 78.9 37,222 1.593 1.689
75 64.4 28,175 1.974 2.021

4:4:4 wins at every size. The price is a quality drop of 2.2 points at q95, 6.1 at q85 and 10.6 at q75 — the more you have already compressed, the more quality you have to surrender to buy the 15–17% of bytes back. Expressing it as a rate:

q95: subsampling is 2.23x as expensive per byte saved as lowering the quality
q85: 1.48x
q75: 1.20x

The trend is the interesting part. At high quality the chroma grid is the binding constraint and losing it is expensive; at q75 luma quantisation has already destroyed so much that the two options converge. If you are shipping at q85 or above, 4:2:0 is not a good deal. If you are already at q70 because the marketplace caps you at 100 KB, the argument mostly disappears — which is also why the folklore "4:2:0 is fine, nobody can see it" is sometimes true and never for the reason given.

Checking the mechanism without a mask

Everything above depends on a mask, and a mask is a place to hide a mistake. So here is the same damage measured with no mask, no boundary detection, and no threshold: bucket every pixel with meaningful chroma by how fast the chroma was changing in the original, and average the error per bucket.

If subsampling damages edges because a half-resolution grid cannot hold a fast change, the error has to rise with the gradient. If it is flat, my story is wrong.

bin (flattest 12.5% first):
  4:4:4             0.492  0.552  0.611  0.675  0.754  0.830  0.956  1.444
  4:2:0             0.645  0.726  0.811  0.906  1.044  1.173  1.385  2.305
  ratio 4:2:0/4:4:4  1.31   1.31   1.33   1.34   1.38   1.41   1.45   1.60

Both curves rise, because JPEG is lossy everywhere and steeper chroma is harder to code at any sampling ratio. The ratio is what isolates subsampling, and it rises monotonically: 1.31x on flat chroma, 1.60x on the steepest twelfth. The extra cost is concentrated exactly where the grid is thinnest.

That is the mechanism, confirmed on 15 of the 16 photos (one was excluded by the binning guard: only 4.1% of its frame is subject, too few high-gradient pixels to fill the last bucket).

The part I did not expect: the platform's re-encode dominates

Nothing in the previous sections decides what a buyer sees, because nobody ships one encode. A seller exports, the marketplace ingests and re-encodes, and that second file is the one on the page.

So: seven uploads, each pushed once through the same marketplace-style pass (q82, 4:2:0), error measured against the original PNG both before and after.

upload bytes dE_edge before dE_edge after the pass added
png 233 KB 0.000 1.786 —
4:4:4 q95 82 KB 0.963 1.806 +87%
4:4:4 q85 44 KB 1.393 1.867 +34%
4:2:2 q85 39 KB 1.543 1.894 +23%
4:2:0 q95 68 KB 1.228 1.854 +51%
4:2:0 q85 37 KB 1.689 1.890 +12%
4:2:0 q70 25 KB 2.143 2.274 +6%

Two things fall out of that table.

First, the losses are not additive, they overlap. The platform pass charges a pristine 4:4:4 q95 export 87%, and an already-4:2:0 q85 export only 12%, because most of what it would remove has already been removed. Uploading the best possible file does not get you the best possible output; it gets you 1.806, which is within 1.1% of what an untouched PNG would have produced (1.786) and 4.4% better than uploading a 4:2:0 q85 file, which is the file that would otherwise sit on the page.

Second, the choice you control is worth a few percent, and the choice you do not control is worth tens. Across all seven uploads the final edge error spans 1.786 to 2.274 — 27% — and six of those seven sit inside 6% of each other. Meanwhile the single re-encode in the middle of every chain, which you have no say in, is worth more than any of it.

The practical reading: stop optimising your export for a platform that is going to overwrite it, and check what the platform actually does instead, because that is the stage with the leverage.

Re-saving is nearly free, until you change a setting

The last thing I wanted to know is what happens on the second and third pass, because "every save loses quality" is repeated constantly and I wanted a number.

Same file, four passes, chroma error against the untouched PNG:

chain             pass 1   pass 2   pass 3   pass 4    total
82 x4              1.072    1.088    1.095    1.099     +2.5%
90 x4              0.943    0.967    0.982    0.991     +5.1%
82,90,75,82        1.072    1.120    1.287    1.320    +23.2%

Passes two to four at a fixed setting add 1.6% / 0.6% / 0.4% of the first pass's cost, converging. The quantised coefficients map onto themselves, so re-encoding at the setting that produced the file lands back on nearly the same coefficients. Four saves are not four times the loss; they are about 1.02 times it.

Change the setting between passes and it starts over. Pass three of 82, 90, 75, 82 — the one after the quality drops to 75 — adds 15.6% of the first pass's cost on its own.

So the folklore is wrong in its mechanism and right in its conclusion, which is the worst combination. Re-saving is not what accumulates. Re-saving differently is. A workflow that touches a file five times at one setting is fine. A workflow that touches it twice at two settings is not.

What I would actually do

Given all of the above, and being honest that it is calibrated on one encoder:

  1. Find out whether the platform re-encodes at all, and at what. If it does not, upload the best file you can and stop reading. If it does, its settings are the dominant term and your export is a rounding decision.
  2. Do not use 4:2:0 as a size lever at q85 or above. At equal bytes, 4:4:4 is better on the edge at every quality I tested, and the price is two to eleven quality points — cheap at the top of the range, expensive at the bottom. Subsampling is only competitive once you are already deep into low quality.
  3. If you must use it, know that the container is not the whole cost. At q85 the edge error goes from 1.393 to 1.689; the box average accounts for part of that and the decode filter for the rest, and on an aligned boundary the box average accounts for none of it. You cannot buy the filter's share back with more chroma samples — the only thing that removes it is 4:4:4.
  4. Do not bother aligning product edges to a block grid. The period is 2 pixels, not 16. Aligning to 2 pixels means controlling boundary parity, which nobody can do deliberately.
  5. Export once, at the setting you will keep. Repeated identical saves cost about 2%, repeated different saves cost 20%+.

What this does not cover

  • One encoder. Pillow over libjpeg(-turbo). mozjpeg, libvips/sharp, and the various CDN encoders pick their own upsampler and their own chroma quantisation, so the split between "container" and "decoder" will move — the aligned-edge result in particular is a property of the triangle filter, and a decoder using nearest-neighbour would show the 1.00 px figure instead.
  • One colour space. sRGB in, YCbCr out, no ICC handling. Wide-gamut input will hit different chroma quantisation.
  • A 640 px working width. At full marketplace resolution the 2-pixel grid is a smaller fraction of the subject, so absolute dE_edge values will move; the mechanism will not.
  • A coarse mask. CIEDE2000 > 12 from the border median is not a segmentation model. It is identical across every row of every table, which is what the comparison needs, and it is why I also report the mask-free gradient table.
  • dE_edge is not perceptual importance. A ramp on the outside of a product's outline is often less visible than the same ramp across a printed logo inside it. Everything here is measured on pixel neighbourhoods, not on what a person notices.

Reproducing it

Five files, all of them plain numpy and Pillow:

  • subsample.py — the fixtures, the hand-built encoder, and the instrument checks in validate(). Run it first; if the greyscale chroma error is not 0.000, or the triangle row does not land on libjpeg, nothing after it means anything.
  • subsample_run.py — the 16-photo matrix, pinned by name and sha256 in subsample_photos.json so the corpus cannot drift out from under the numbers.
  • subsample_cascade.py — the marketplace-pass comparison and the equal-bytes bisection.
  • subsample_chain.py — the repeated-save chains.
  • subsample_report.py — every figure quoted above, printed from the JSON.

The pinning is not fussiness. My first run of the matrix and my first run of the cascade picked different photos, because the cover corpus grew between them, and for a while two tables in this piece were describing two different sets of images.

I work on the image pipeline at PicViva, which is where I ran into this: the export-and-upload step is ours, the ingest-and-re-encode step belongs to the marketplace, and it took a while to work out which of the two was costing the edge. The short version is that it is usually not the one I can fix in our code.
