title: Scraper input from strangers: country names, 01.08.2026, and why I stopped throwing
description:
When you run your own scraper you type the input the way your code expects it. When strangers run it from a public listing, they type Germany into a field you documented as an ISO country code, 01.08.2026 into a date field, and "50 ads" into a number field. On the Apify Store a failed run also counts against your public success rate, which the Store uses for ranking. So I moved most input handling into one small module whose rule is: understand what the user meant, log a warning, and keep going.

Below is what's in it and the run that made me write it.

The run that started it

My LinkedIn Ad Library actor took a start date and a country. A user sent 01.08.2026 as the date. I passed it straight to LinkedIn, LinkedIn answered with HTTP 500, and the run failed. While fixing that I found a second problem in the same code: I sent the country as countryCode=DE, which LinkedIn silently ignores. The parameter it actually reads is countries=DE. For one advertiser that was the difference between 629 ads (Germany) and 9,530 (everywhere). Nobody had complained, because a list of ads from all countries looks like a valid result.

Dates

The parser takes YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY/MM/DD, DD.MM.YYYY, slash dates, Unix timestamps and anything Date.parse understands, and returns YYYY-MM-DD or null:

let m = str.match(/^(\d{4})[-/.](\d{1,2})[-/.](\d{1,2})/);
let out = m ? iso(m[1], m[2], m[3]) : null;
// DD.MM.YYYY is always European order
if (!out && (m = str.match(/^(\d{1,2})\.(\d{1,2})\.(\d{4})$/))) out = iso(m[3], m[2], m[1]);

iso() builds the string and checks it round-trips through Date, so 31.02.2026 comes back as null instead of March 3rd.

Slash dates are the hard part. 31/12/2026 can only be day first, 12/31/2026 can only be month first, and a part above 12 decides. 08/01/2026 could be either. My first version read those as day first, quietly, which changed the result for every US user who had been sending that format. The current version keeps the US reading for ambiguous dates and says so in the log:

Ambiguous startDate "08/01/2026" - reading it as MM/DD/YYYY (2026-08-01). Use YYYY-MM-DD to be sure.

Something that can't be parsed at all logs a warning and the filter is dropped. The run continues without it.

Countries

Hardcoding a country list felt wrong, and it turns out Node already has one. Intl.DisplayNames gives the English name for every region code, so I build a name-to-code map at startup:

const names = new Intl.DisplayNames(['en'], { type: 'region' });
for (let a = 65; a <= 90; a++) for (let b = 65; b <= 90; b++) {
    const code = String.fromCharCode(a, b);
    const name = names.of(code);
    if (!name || name === code || name === 'Unknown Region' || RETIRED.has(code)) continue;
    map[name.toLowerCase()] = code;
}

Two things to watch: ICU also names retired codes (UK, SU, YU and others), so those get skipped, and a few common inputs need aliases on top (uk, usa, deutschland, españa, türkiye, holland). Values like worldwide, all or any mean no filter. Anything unknown is a warning and no filter, not an exception.

Numbers and lists

Numbers come in as 50, "50", "1,000" or "50 ads". Strip spaces, commas and underscores, take the leading number, fall back to the default with a warning if there isn't one.

Lists come in as arrays, newline-separated strings, semicolon-separated strings, or arrays of { url } objects from the Apify request-list editor. One function flattens all of that into unique trimmed strings. It also accepts a few field names that aren't in the schema (someone sends urls instead of startUrls) and logs which one it used.

Where I do fail

Being tolerant inside the run doesn't mean starting runs that can't work. Two places where failing is still the right answer:

Empty input, before the run exists. The platform validates input against the schema before it starts anything. A required field with a prefill and minItems: 1 but no default makes an empty start return HTTP 400, and no run is created. If you add "default": [] next to required, that check never fires, the container starts, and you get a failed run in your stats. The prefill is what people see in the form, so they can still click Start and get a working run.

Nothing usable after parsing. If every entry was invalid, the run exits with code 1 and a status message that says what was wrong. On Apify that message is the only thing the user sees, and I don't see their run at all. In SDK 3.7.2, Actor.exit({ exitCode: 1, statusMessage }) sends the message and exits about 1 ms later without waiting, and on roughly 1 in 5 of my failed runs the message never arrived. Setting it first fixes that:

export async function fail(msg) {
    await Actor.setStatusMessage(msg, { isStatusMessageTerminal: true, level: 'ERROR' }).catch(() => {});
    await Actor.exit({ exitCode: 1, statusMessage: msg });
}

The whole module is about 400 lines and the only dependency is apify. Most of it is the parsing above. It's shared by every actor I publish, so a fix lands everywhere with one deploy.

The LinkedIn actor from the story above is here if you want to throw odd input at it: https://apify.com/pulsedata/linkedin-ad-library-scraper

title: ui-ux-pro-max in Claude Code: three flags that keep your design system from drifting
description:
Disclosure: we run Skillselion, an independent directory of Claude Code, Codex and Cursor extensions ranked by real installs. We have no tie to nextlevelbuilder. Quotes come from the skill's SKILL.md at commit 2de1134, the head of main on 21 November 2026.

Short answer: ui-ux-pro-max is most useful when you let it write a design system to disk once and make every later screen read from it. Three flags control that: --persist writes design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md, --output-dir decides where it lands, and --force is the only way to overwrite it. Get those right and the agent stops inventing a new palette on every page.

On 21 November 2026 Skillselion's catalog API recorded 463,481 installs for the ui-ux-pro-max skill listing (skills.sh registry data), and the nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill repo had 152,242 GitHub stars, MIT licensed.

What does ui-ux-pro-max actually do?

It gives Claude Code a local design database to query. The SKILL.md lists what is searchable:

Searchable local UI/UX guidance: 80 searchable styles (51 active), 194 product palettes and exact reasoning profiles, 74 font pairings, 130 UX guidelines, 105 curated icons, 17 GSAP presets, 25 chart types, and 22 technology stacks.

Source: nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, .claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/SKILL.md

The agent answers by running a bundled script, scripts/search.py, against that data. That is also why it is worth reading the script before you install the skill in a work repo: it is code that runs on your machine.

How do you install it in Claude Code?

The README offers two routes. As a Claude Code plugin:

/plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill
/plugin install ui-ux-pro-max@ui-ux-pro-max-skill

Or with the CLI, run from your project folder:

npm install -g ui-ux-pro-max-cli
uipro init --ai claude

The same CLI takes other agent names (cursor, codex, copilot, gemini and more), or --ai all for every supported agent at once.

How do you save a design system with --persist?

Ask for a design system once, with --persist and an explicit output folder. The skill's own example:

python "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/.claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/scripts/search.py" "<query>" --design-system --persist -p "Project Name" --output-dir "<project-root>"

That writes design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md, which the SKILL.md calls the "Global Source of Truth". Add --page "dashboard" and you also get pages/dashboard.md as a per-page override. Add --tokens dtcg to the same --persist command and it also writes tokens.json next to the master file.

Commit that folder. From then on, the useful instruction to the agent is "read MASTER.md first", not "make it look nice".

Why does --output-dir matter?

Because without it the files go wherever the script happened to run. The SKILL.md says to "always pass --output-dir pointed at the project root". If you skip it, you end up with a MASTER.md somewhere outside the repo, no one commits it, and the next session starts from nothing.

When should you use --force?

Almost never, and only on purpose. This is the rule from the SKILL.md:

If design-system/<project-slug>/MASTER.md already exists, --persist skips writing and leaves it untouched unless you also pass --force

Source: nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill, .claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/SKILL.md

The skip is the safety net. Your MASTER.md may hold decisions a teammate made by hand. The skill tells the agent to read the existing file before deciding whether --force is justified, and never to use it without the user's explicit OK. If you see --force in a command your agent proposes, read the current MASTER.md before you say yes.

Which ui-ux-pro-max should you install?

The nextlevelbuilder original. The repo is a bundle of seven skills (ui-ux-pro-max plus design-system, design, ui-styling, brand, banner-design and slides), and our catalog also lists other repos that carry a skill with the same name. The biggest of those on 21 November, inside nexu-io/open-design, had 5,636 installs against the original's 463,481. Stars can mislead here because they belong to the repository: open-design has 108,731 GitHub stars, and its copy of the skill 5,636 installs.

Our ui-ux-pro-max guide for Claude Code covers the rest of the setup and the common pitfalls.

Do you keep a design-system file in your repo for the agent, or do you prompt for style every time?

title: Errors, validation and structure: the service that holds
description:
You deploy. The old process gets the signal and dies on the spot, with three requests half-way inside. The clients don't get an error: they get nothing. Measured, with the curl that was waiting:

without handler → 000
process exit without handler: 143

000 is "no response", and 143 is 128 + 15, the signal. Now the same test with four extra lines:

with handler → 200
process exit with handler: 0

That's the difference between a service and a pile of routes. And it isn't the only one: the same project that loses requests on deploy is usually the one handing stack traces to clients and the one that can't tell which request failed because its logs are loose lines.

This is the lesson that turns what you know into something maintainable.

One place for errors

In the previous lesson every route picked its code. With twenty routes that's twenty different decisions and no policy. The pattern is a single error middleware, with four arguments, mounted last.

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, status = 500, code = "internal_error") {
    super(message);
    this.status = status;
    this.code = code;
  }
}

class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(resource) {
    super(`No such ${resource}`, 404, "not_found");
  }
}

A domain error carries its HTTP status and its business code. And the central handler does the only translation that should exist:

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  const known = error instanceof AppError;
  const status = known ? error.status : 500;

  res.status(status).json({
    error: known ? error.code : "internal_error",
    message: known ? error.message : "something broke",
  });
});

With three routes failing in three ways:

curl -s http://localhost:3311/boom
curl -s http://localhost:3311/async-boom
curl -s http://localhost:3311/crash

{"error":"not_found","message":"No such book 7"}
{"error":"not_found","message":"No such async book"}
{"error":"internal_error","message":"something broke"}

The first two are errors you threw and they describe what happened. The third is an unexpected TypeError, and the client sees neither the message nor the trace: it gets a generic one. The full detail goes to the log, which belongs to whoever programs, not to whoever calls.

That's the rule that never breaks: the client gets what it needs to act; the server keeps what it needs to debug. Answer with error.stack and you're publishing your server's layout and your file names.

A 404 is also an error, and it's also centralised

An error middleware doesn't catch "no route matched": that isn't an error, it's Express reaching the end without finding anything and answering with its own HTML page. If your API speaks JSON, that page is noise. You fix it with a normal middleware after every route and before the error one:

app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: "not_found", path: req.originalUrl });
});

curl -s http://localhost:3322/nope

{"error":"not_found","path":"/nope"}

req.originalUrl and not req.url: inside a mounted router, req.url is trimmed to the prefix, and the client needs to see the path it asked for.

async no longer needs help

In Express 4, an exception thrown inside an async function never reached the error handler: it stayed in a rejected promise and, with luck, in an unhandledRejection. That's where express-async-errors came from: it wraps your routes so the exception travels up.

Express 5 doesn't need it. Measured, the async route above returns the same as the synchronous one:

{"error":"not_found","message":"No such async book"}

Express forwards the rejection to the handler by itself. If you see express-async-errors in a new project, it's dead weight from an older version.

What is still yours:

  • try/catch where you actually recover. If the cache fails and you fall back to the database, that isn't an error: it's plan B, and it lives in the route.
  • Never call next(error) after responding. If the body is already sent, the handler tries to answer again and you get Cannot set headers after they are sent.

Validate at the boundary

Everything coming in through a request is hostile until proven otherwise: strings where you expected numbers, null where you expected an object, two megabytes of text where you expected an id. And validating inside the route means repeating it in every branch.

The boundary is a schema, and Zod turns it into code:

import { z } from "zod";

const BookSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1),
  pages: z.coerce.number().int().positive(),
  genre: z.enum(["novel", "essay"]).default("novel"),
});

const ok = BookSchema.safeParse({ title: "Emma", pages: "474" });
console.log("valid:", ok.success, "· data:", ok.data);

const bad = BookSchema.safeParse({ title: "", pages: -3 });
console.log("valid:", bad.success);
for (const issue of bad.error.issues) {
  console.log(" ·", issue.path.join("."), "→", issue.message);
}

valid: true · data: { title: 'Emma', pages: 474, genre: 'novel' }
valid: false
 · title → Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters
 · pages → Too small: expected number to be >0

Three things it does that hurt by hand: it coerces ("474" becomes 474, which is what arrives over HTTP), it applies defaults (genre: "novel"), and it collects every problem with its exact path instead of failing on the first. And what it returns isn't an exception: safeParse hands you a result you can turn into a 400 with the list of failures.

That response shape matters more than it looks. A 400 with { error: "invalid_input", details: [{ field, message }] } lets the client paint the error next to the right input. A 400 with the text "invalid input" tells nobody anything.

Structure: routes, controllers, services

With two routes, everything fits in app.js. With twenty, it doesn't. The split that works is the usual one, because each layer has a different reason to change:

  • Routes: which URL calls which controller. Changes when the API changes.
  • Controllers: translate HTTP into calls. They read req, write res, and nothing else. Change when the protocol changes.
  • Services: the business logic, unaware that HTTP exists. Change when the business changes, and they're the only thing you can test without starting a server.

And two files with similar names worth not confusing: app.js builds and configures the application; index.js (or server.js) starts it, listens on a port and worries about signals. That split is what lets you import app in a test and throw requests at it without occupying a fixed port.

Better still, a factory:

export function createApp({ repository, logger }) {
  const app = express();
  // …
  return app;
}

Dependencies come in as arguments. In a test you pass a fake repository and a silent logger; in production, the real ones. Nothing global, nothing hidden.

And a configuration module that validates at startup, like the one in the files lesson: if DATABASE_URL is missing, the process dies at the beginning, not on the third request.

Logs you can follow

A log line without an identifier is a sentence in a diary with no dates. With twenty simultaneous requests you need to join the four lines of one request.

pino writes JSON, one line per event, and takes structured fields:

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.id = req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? randomUUID();
  const t0 = Date.now();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    log.info({ id: req.id, method: req.method, path: req.url, status: res.statusCode, ms: Date.now() - t0 }, "request");
  });
  next();
});

{"level":30,"time":1794697598645,"pid":1132699,"id":"e5f5f3e3-…","method":"GET","path":"/books/7","status":200,"ms":13,"msg":"request"}
{"level":50,"time":1794697598656,"pid":1132699,"id":"02053e8e-…","err":{"type":"Error","message":"the service exploded","stack":"…"},"msg":"unhandled error"}

Two things: the same id appears on the error line and the request line, so you can rebuild the whole story; and the error carries its trace to the log, where it's useful, while the client gets the generic one.

The identifier is copied from the client when it sends one (x-request-id) and generated otherwise. So when the frontend reports a failing request, its identifier and yours are the same one and nobody has to guess.

And a classic logging trap: the IP. Behind a proxy, req.ip is the proxy's unless you say otherwise:

app.set("trust proxy", 1);

without trust proxy → {"ip":"::1"}
with trust proxy    → {"ip":"203.0.113.9"}

With X-Forwarded-For set, without that line every log says ::1 and every IP-based rate limit points at the same place. With it, the real address. The 1 means "trust the first proxy in front of me"; behind a chain of several, you raise the number.

Shutting down without dropping requests

A deploy doesn't kill a process: it sends SIGTERM and waits for it to leave. What you do with that signal decides whether you lose requests.

const server = app.listen(3000);

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(() => {
    log.info("closed cleanly");
    process.exit(0);
  });
});

server.close() stops accepting new connections and waits for the ones in flight. The test, with an 800 ms request running and the signal at 200:

with handler → 200
process exit with handler: 0

Against the 000 and 143 from the introduction. With one caveat: if a request gets stuck, the close never finishes, which is why almost everyone adds a timer that forces the exit at ten or thirty seconds.

And the piece that separates a correct close from one that hangs: a deadline. If a request never finishes, server.close() waits forever. The complete pattern gives a few milliseconds of grace and then aborts whatever is still alive, with the AbortController from the async lesson.

const control = new AbortController();

app.get("/slow", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    await sleep(2000, null, { signal: control.signal });
    res.json({ ok: true });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.name === "AbortError") {
      res.status(503).json({ error: "shutting_down" });
      return;
    }
    next(error);
  }
});

for (const signal of ["SIGTERM", "SIGINT"]) {
  process.on(signal, () => {
    server.close(() => {
      console.log("closed");
      process.exit(0);
    });
    setTimeout(() => control.abort(), 100);
  });
}

kill -TERM <pid>

in-flight request → 503
exit: 0
SIGTERM · stop accepting, 100 ms of grace
deadline reached · aborting what is left
closed

The in-flight request gets a 503 with a message that tells the truth — "I'm shutting down" — instead of a cut connection. And the process exits with 0, because it did what it had to do. SIGINT is the same story with Ctrl+C: you register both, because locally you kill with the keyboard and in production with a signal.

Exit codes say something and are worth using well: 0 is "I finished fine", 1 is "I failed", and 143 is "I was killed", which is what you'll see in the logs of a container that was sent the signal and ignored it. process.exitCode = 1 lets the process end by itself with that code; process.exit(1) cuts it on the spot, and it's only justified when there's nothing left to finish.

And the two safety nets, with judgement: unhandledRejection and uncaughtException. Their job is to record the error and exit; a process that has seen an uncaught exception is in a state you don't know, and serving requests from there is worse than falling over. Exiting lets the orchestrator start a clean one.

Common problems

Cannot set headers after they are sent

You responded and also called next(error), or the error handler tried to answer an already-sent request. Check res.headersSent before writing.

The error handler never runs

It has three arguments instead of four. Express doesn't warn.

The client receives the error's stack trace

You're sending error.stack or the whole object. Respond with a code and a message, and keep the rest in the log.

Logs don't let me follow a request

There's no identifier, or it isn't on every line. Add it in the first middleware and put it in every log for that request.

Requests are lost on deploy

There's no SIGTERM handler, or the process doesn't wait for server.close(). The orchestrator kills it a few seconds later.

Validation is scattered across routes

Move it to a middleware or the controller, with one schema per endpoint. Repeating if (!body.title) in every branch is how one gets forgotten.

What you take from this lesson

  • An error middleware with four arguments, last in line, decides the code for everything.
  • Domain errors carry their status and code; unknown ones become a generic 500.
  • The client gets what it needs to act; the trace stays in the log.
  • Express 5 forwards async rejections; express-async-errors is dead weight.
  • try/catch only where you recover, and never next() after responding.
  • Zod at the boundary: it coerces, applies defaults and collects problems with their path.
  • Routes, controllers and services, with app.js separate from index.js and a factory that takes dependencies.
  • JSON logs with one identifier per request; the real IP requires trust proxy.
  • A closing 404, after the routes and before the error handler, so the API never returns HTML.
  • SIGTERM and SIGINT with server.close(), a deadline and an AbortController: whatever doesn't finish in time gets a 503 instead of a cut connection. 143 means you didn't do it.
  • unhandledRejection and uncaughtException get logged and exited.

With this the service survives a deploy and a hostile request. There's one code lesson left before the close: the final project, where all of this gets assembled into a real API.

Never stop coding!

title: Your logger prints secrets after you redacted them
description:
A redaction hook sees values. The logger prints text. Errors, structs and printf arguments turn into text after the hook has run, so the secret inside them goes out as it came in. We found this in five of the six languages flare-redact supports and fixed it in 1.12.1. Here is the mechanism, the real output, and a test you can run against your own logger.

Short answer: redact what the logger will print, not only the values it is handed. A value the hook does not recognise (an error, a struct, a URL, a %s argument) has to be turned into text the way the logger would, and that text redacted. Then test with the real logger writing to a buffer, never with a fake of its hook.

How we found it

While checking code samples for a round of replies, we logged a database error through our own Go handler:

slog.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: connection refused", dsn))

The password came out in clear. The handler's tests were green, because none of them logged an error. The redactor walks strings, maps and lists. An error is none of those, so the handler passed it on unchanged, and slog's JSON handler called err.Error() when it wrote the line.

So we checked every logging integration the same way: the real logger, a known secret, the printed output. Eight integrations in five languages leaked in at least one path.

The mechanism

Every logger works in two steps:

  1. You hand it values: a message template, arguments, fields, bound context.
  2. Later, when it writes the line, it turns some of those values into text: Error(), String(), toString(), __str__, ToString(), printf's %s.

A redaction hook sits between the two, so it can only redact what is already text when it runs. An error object is not text yet. Neither is a dataclass, a Uri or a struct. If the hook returns unknown objects unchanged, which is the polite thing for a walker to do, the text is created after redaction and nothing looks at it again.

Go slog 

dsn := "postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod"
slog.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: connection refused", dsn))
slog.Info("config", "db", DB{Host: "db.internal", Password: "S3cret-canary-42"})

With flare-redact 1.12.0:

{"level":"ERROR","msg":"db down","err":"connect postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod: connection refused"}
{"level":"INFO","msg":"config","db":{"Host":"db.internal","Password":"S3cret-canary-42"}}

With 1.12.1:

{"level":"ERROR","msg":"db down","err":"connect postgres://app:***@db.internal:5432/prod: connection refused"}
{"level":"INFO","msg":"config","db":{"Host":"db.internal","Password":"***"}}

A key rule in ReplaceAttr, such as if a.Key == "password", would not have helped with the first line: the key is err. The secret is in the value, and the value is not text yet.

pino

pino adds two twists. It builds the message itself from the template and arguments, and passes only the merge object to formatters.log, so a formatter never sees msg. And child() with no options swaps the bindings formatter for one that returns its input, so child bindings skip it too.

log.info('connecting to %s', dsn);
log.error(new Error(`connect ${dsn}: refused`));
log.child({ dsn }).info('pool ready');

With 1.12.0 (stack trimmed):

{"level":30,"msg":"connecting to postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod"}
{"level":50,"err":{"type":"Error","message":"connect postgres://app:***@db.internal:5432/prod: refused"},"msg":"connect postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod: refused"}
{"level":30,"dsn":"postgres://app:S3cret-canary-42@db.internal:5432/prod","msg":"pool ready"}

Look at the middle line: the same string is masked in err.message and printed raw in msg right next to it. With 1.12.1 all three lines show app:***@db.internal.

Python logging

A logging.Filter sees record.msg and record.args. getMessage() runs later, in the handler, and calls str() on each argument.

log.info("config %s", DB("db.internal", "S3cret-canary-42"))

1.12.0  INFO config DB(host='db.internal', password='S3cret-canary-42')
1.12.1  INFO config DB(host='db.internal', password='***')

This one leaked only with RedactingFilter on its own. install() also wraps the handler's formatter, which redacts the final text, and that caught it. But the filter alone is a common setup, so it had to be right too.

The other five

  • winston: splat arguments and an Error's message and stack, when winstonRedact() runs before format.splat() or format.errors(). Those formats read the raw arguments kept under Symbol.for('splat') and the Error's non-enumerable properties.
  • console (wrapConsole() and --import flare-redact/register): an object with its own toString() printed through %s.
  • .NET Microsoft.Extensions.Logging and Serilog: a Uri, a class with its own ToString(), or a struct passed as a structured value or a scope.
  • Java Log4j2: object values in a MapMessage.

The Rust engine and the Fluent Bit filter only ever see JSON and msgpack values, so nothing is turned into text later. Logback and the Log4j2 pattern converters already redacted the formatted text.

Why our tests missed it

The old pino test called our formatters.log with a record that had a msg field in it. Real pino never puts msg there. The test checked the hook contract as we imagined it, not as the logger implements it, so it passed while the real path leaked. The Go, Python, .NET and Java tests had the same blind spot in a quieter form: none of them logged an error, a struct or an object with its own string form that held a secret.

The fix for the tests was the same everywhere: drive the real logger, write to a buffer, search the buffer for the secret. Every new leak test fails on 1.12.0.

What the fix does

One rule, applied per logger: redact what will be printed.

  • When the hook meets a value it does not walk, it turns it into text the way the logger would (Error(), String(), str(), ToString(), String.valueOf) and redacts that text. In Go, structs, typed slices and maps are redacted as their JSON, decoded with UseNumber so int64 ids stay exact, and a Password field is masked whole by the key rule.
  • Plain numbers and booleans keep their type, so dashboards and queries keep working.
  • Where the logger formats the message itself (pino), the integration hooks in earlier, at hooks.logMethod, to redact the template and its arguments. For a logger whose bound context holds something sensitive, it also redacts the finished line in hooks.streamWrite. That check runs once per logger, so loggers with clean bindings pay nothing extra.
  • If redaction itself fails, the field becomes [REDACTION FAILED]. Printing the original is the one outcome a redactor exists to prevent.

A test you can copy

This works whatever you use for redaction, including your own ReplaceAttr or a regex filter. Pick a canary secret, log it through every path your code uses, and search the printed output. The paths that matter: the message text, format arguments, errors (message, stack, traceback), objects with their own string form, child or bound context, and groups or scopes.

Go 

func TestLogsNeverPrintTheCanary(t *testing.T) {
    const canary = "S3cret-canary-42"
    dsn := "postgres://app:" + canary + "@db.internal:5432/prod"

    var buf bytes.Buffer
    policy, _ := flareredact.Compile(flareredact.Options{})
    log := slog.New(flareredact.NewSlogHandler(slog.NewJSONHandler(&buf, nil), policy))

    log.Info("connecting to " + dsn)                                    // the message
    log.Error("db down", "err", fmt.Errorf("connect %s: refused", dsn)) // an error
    log.Info("config", "db", struct{ DSN string }{dsn})                 // a struct
    log.With("dsn", dsn).Info("pool ready")                             // bound context
    log.Info("pool", slog.Group("db", "url", dsn))                      // a group

    if strings.Contains(buf.String(), canary) {
        t.Fatalf("secret printed:\n%s", buf.String())
    }
}

Node.js with pino 

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import pino from 'pino';
import { pinoRedact } from 'flare-redact/pino';

test('logs never print the canary', () => {
  const canary = 'S3cret-canary-42';
  const dsn = `postgres://app:${canary}@db.internal:5432/prod`;
  let out = '';
  const log = pino(pinoRedact(), { write: (line) => { out += line; } });

  log.info(`connecting to ${dsn}`);                // the message
  log.info('connecting to %s', dsn);               // a printf argument
  log.error(new Error(`connect ${dsn}: refused`)); // an error
  log.info({ db: { dsn } }, 'config');             // a field
  log.child({ dsn }).info('pool ready');           // child bindings

  assert.ok(!out.includes(canary), out);
});

Python 

import io
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass

import flare_redact.log as flare_log


@dataclass
class DB:
    dsn: str


def test_logs_never_print_the_canary():
    canary = "S3cret-canary-42"
    dsn = f"postgres://app:{canary}@db.internal:5432/prod"

    stream = io.StringIO()
    log = logging.getLogger("canary-test")
    log.addHandler(logging.StreamHandler(stream))
    flare_log.install(log)  # your redaction setup goes here

    log.warning("connecting to %s", dsn)  # a format argument
    log.warning("config %s", DB(dsn))     # an object with its own str()
    try:
        raise ConnectionError(f"connect {dsn}: refused")
    except ConnectionError:
        log.exception("db down")          # the traceback

    assert canary not in stream.getvalue(), stream.getvalue()

The Go and Node tests fail on flare-redact 1.12.0 and pass on 1.12.1. The Python test passes on both, because install() already redacted the formatted text in 1.12.0; the Python leak needed RedactingFilter on its own.

Upgrade 

npm install flare-redact@1.12.1
pip install -U flare-redact
go get github.com/flare-collection/flare-redact/sdk/go@v1.12.1

The Rust crate was not affected. Java and .NET are not on Maven Central and NuGet yet; until they are, build sdk/java with mvn install and sdk/dotnet with dotnet pack from the 1.12.1 tag.

What 1.12.1 still does not cover. A Python traceback is only redacted by the formatter, so use install() or add RedactingFormatter yourself; a filter never sees the rendered traceback. In pino, bindings added with setBindings() after a logger's first line are not checked again. A Node Buffer is printed as its byte values and is not scanned.

The code and every test are in the repository, and the full list of changes is in the changelog.

title: One Shared CSS File Across 8 Tool Pages: How I Keep Every Page in Sync
description:
My site has eight tool pages: TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, and a few more. Every one of them looks the same — same blue-and-white theme, same link box, same download button, same quality dropdown. That sameness is deliberate, and it comes from one decision: every page links to a single shared stylesheet.

It was not always like that. In the early days each page carried its own styles. That felt harmless when there were two pages. By page five it was a chore. I would change the button colour on the homepage and forget the TikTok page still had the old one. A visitor would jump from one tool to another and the site would look slightly different each time, like nobody was minding the shop.

So I pulled every shared rule into one file — assets/style.css — and linked it from all eight pages. The layout of the link box, the look of the download button, the spacing around the quality dropdown, the footer, the colours: all of it lives in that one file. When I change one rule, all eight pages change together. That is the whole point.

There are a few rules I keep to make this work in practice.

First, the shared file holds only shared rules. If a page genuinely needs something unique — say, the TikTok page has an extra slideshow layout — that rule goes in a small per-page stylesheet, loaded after the shared one. The moment page-specific rules creep into the shared file, it stops being shared and starts being a dumping ground.

Second, class names are boring and consistent. The link box is .link-box on every page. The download button is .download-btn. The quality dropdown is .quality-select. Boring names are the feature: any fix I make to .download-btn lands on every tool at once, and I never have to remember which page called it something different.

Third, I cache-bust it. A shared stylesheet is also a single point of failure for caching: if a visitor's browser holds the old file, they see the old design on every page. Every link to the stylesheet carries a version query string, like style.css?v=12, and I bump that number whenever I change the file. That is how the whole site changed from a dark theme to the blue-and-white one in a single afternoon — one CSS file, one version bump, and every page followed.

There is a real risk, and I will not pretend otherwise: one bad line in that file breaks the look of all eight pages at once. I manage it by keeping the file small and by testing a change on one page before I bump the version number for the rest. A small file is easy to read, and an easy-to-read file is hard to break by accident.

The payoff is quiet but constant. The site has no frameworks and no webfonts, and the homepage stays under 100KB. The shared CSS is a big part of that: eight pages, one download, cached once, reused everywhere. It also means a new tool page takes minutes to style instead of an afternoon, because the page arrives already dressed.

If you run a small site with several pages that should look like one site, start here. One stylesheet, boring class names, a version number you bump on every change. You can see the result on every tool page at ramrom.io — eight pages, one file, one look.

title: The FastAPI Bottleneck Nobody Tells You About Until Production
description:
Everyone benchmarks FastAPI with wrk on a single endpoint that returns {"ok": true} and calls it a day. Then it goes to production, traffic has real payloads and real I/O, and throughput falls off a cliff that the benchmark never showed.

Three things that actually move the needle, in the order we usually find them:

1. Worker count isn't 2 x cores + 1 once you have async I/O. That formula is for sync WSGI workers saturating CPU. With uvicorn workers running async handlers that spend most of their time awaiting a DB or an upstream call, you're often CPU-underutilized with "correct" worker counts. We've seen throughput improve 30-40% just by profiling actual CPU-busy time per request and sizing workers against that, not core count.

2. Gunicorn + Uvicorn workers vs. plain Uvicorn: the difference shows up under load, not at idle. A bare uvicorn process looks identical to gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker in a quick smoke test. Where it diverges is worker death/restart behavior under memory pressure and SIGTERM handling during rolling deploys — gunicorn's process management catches failure modes uvicorn alone doesn't surface until you're already paged.

3. The bottleneck that actually ate our throughput wasn't FastAPI at all — it was connection pool exhaustion on the DB driver. asyncpg's default pool size silently became the real concurrency ceiling, while CPU and worker metrics looked fine the whole time. If your latency graph has a hard ceiling that doesn't correlate with CPU, check your pool max_size before you touch anything else.

None of this shows up in a synthetic benchmark because synthetic benchmarks don't have a database. If you're chasing a req/s number, profile with your actual dependency graph in the loop, not a mocked handler.

We wrote up the full tuning process — including the exact pool-size math and the gunicorn config that stopped our rolling deploys from dropping requests — in a deeper breakdown of the worker-tuning math.

title: Two Records, One Card: Keeping the Vault and the Ledger in Agreement
description:
Every Braintree renewal is a meeting between two records that are supposed to describe the same card. The vault holds the credential — the token standing in for a number, an expiry, a billing address. The ledger holds the history — what was charged, what failed, what the failure claimed was wrong. When the two records agree, renewals are boring, which is the highest praise billing infrastructure can earn. When they disagree, the retry logic faithfully charges a card the vault already knows is dead, and the ledger records a mystery.

The most common disagreement is quiet. A customer replaces a card inside your product, or their bank issues a fresh one, and the vault learns the new credential through the account updater or a manual update. Meanwhile the subscription still points at the older payment method, or the retry was scheduled against the stale token before the update landed. Nothing errors. The charge simply goes to the wrong record, fails for a reason that sounds like the customer's fault, and starts a dunning sequence for a problem the business had already solved.

This is why Braintree recovery work is less about retry counts than about reconciliation. Before asking how many attempts a renewal deserves, ask which credential each attempt will use, and when that choice gets locked. A retry fired twelve hours after a failure may use fresher vault data than one fired twelve minutes after. Speed, usually a virtue, can be the mechanism that guarantees the stale card gets charged twice.

There is a second disagreement worth hunting: the descriptor and address record. Issuers weigh the details accompanying a charge, and a vault entry carrying an old billing postcode or a descriptor the customer no longer recognizes invites declines and disputes that look, in the ledger, like funding problems. Auditing the vault for stale addresses is unglamorous work with an outsized return, because it fixes failures before they are failures — the only truly free recovery there is.

For developers, the practical habit is a pre-retry check with teeth. At each attempt, re-read the payment method attached to the subscription rather than trusting the object captured when the case opened. Log which token was charged on every attempt, not just the outcome, so a post-mortem can distinguish "the card declined" from "we charged the retired card again." Those are different bugs with different owners, and blended logs make them indistinguishable.

The customer-facing side matters just as much. When a renewal fails despite a card on file, the message should never imply the customer did something wrong before the business has checked its own records. A surprising share of "please update your card" emails are sent to people whose new card is already sitting in the vault, attached to nothing. Each one teaches the customer that the business does not know what it holds — a lesson subscribers remember at cancellation time.

Braintree dunning read as a records problem — keeping the vault, the ledger, and the retry in agreement about which card is current walks through the platform specifics behind this, including where Braintree's native tooling helps and where the agreement has to be enforced by the layer above it.

None of this argues for more retries. It argues for retries that deserve to succeed: aimed at the current credential, carrying current details, and recorded precisely enough that a failure teaches you something. A ledger full of unexplained declines is usually a vault full of unexamined records, and the fix begins with admitting the two are one system.

That reconciliation habit is built into how Swipe Again watches for replaced cards across the renewal, so a Braintree retry never spends itself on credentials the vault has already retired — check the record first, then spend the attempt.

title: From Emulators to Physical Devices: Building a More Reliable Mobile Testing Strategy
description:
Every mobile team has lived through it. The build passes every check in the pipeline, the release goes out, and within hours the reviews start arriving: the app freezes on a particular Samsung model, the camera screen crashes on an older iPhone, checkout hangs on a slow 4G connection.

Nothing was wrong with the tests. They were simply running in the wrong place. Emulators and simulators are excellent tools, but they are approximations of a phone, not the phone itself. When a testing strategy leans on them too heavily, the gap between “passed in CI” and “works for customers” quietly widens.

This post looks at where emulators fit, what only physical hardware can tell you, and how to build a layered strategy that combines both without slowing your releases down.

Where emulators earn their place

Emulators (Android) and simulators (iOS) deserve credit. They are a big reason mobile teams can move as fast as they do today.

Speed. They spin up in seconds, run in parallel on ordinary CI machines and need no physical setup.
Cost. There’s no hardware to buy, charge, update or replace.
Debugging. Developers can inspect logs, set breakpoints and reproduce issues right from their IDE.
Early feedback. Unit tests, UI component checks and basic functional flows run well in a virtual environment.

For the first layers of testing, emulators are often the right choice. The trouble starts when they become the only choice, and the final word on whether a release is ready.

What only a physical device can tell you

An emulator runs your app on a desktop processor, with desktop memory, a stable network and a battery that never drains. Real phones live very different lives. Some of the bugs that only show up on physical hardware include:

  • OEM customisations. Android manufacturers modify the OS in ways that affect permissions, notifications, background tasks and battery optimisation. An app that syncs perfectly on a stock emulator can be silently killed in the background on certain brands.
  • Hardware features. Cameras, fingerprint and face sensors, GPS, NFC, Bluetooth and accelerometers either can’t be emulated or are only mocked.
  • Real performance limits. Mid-range and older phones have slower CPUs, less RAM and storage that fills up. Thermal throttling kicks in during long sessions. None of this shows up on a powerful build server.
  • Real networks. Moving between Wi-Fi and mobile data, weak signal, high latency and packet loss expose timeout and retry bugs.
  • Screens and input. Notches, punch-hole cameras, foldables, high-density displays and actual touch gestures behave differently from a mouse click on a virtual screen.
  • Interruptions. Incoming calls, low-battery warnings, OS update prompts and other apps competing for resources.

These aren’t rare edge cases. For many apps, they are the everyday conditions most users experience.

The device lab problem, and how the cloud solves it

Once teams accept they need physical devices, the next question is practical: how many, and who looks after them?

An in-house device lab sounds simple until you run one. Phones need buying, charging, updating and replacing every year. Someone has to track which tester has which device. Remote team members can’t reach them. And even a well-stocked drawer of 30 phones covers only a small slice of what your users actually own.

A real device testing cloud removes most of that overhead. Instead of owning the hardware, teams get on-demand access to hundreds or thousands of real phones and tablets hosted in managed data centres. Key benefits include:

  • Broad coverage. Test on current flagships, budget models, older OS versions and regional devices without buying any of them.
  • Parallel execution. Run the same suite across dozens of devices at once, so wider coverage doesn’t mean slower pipelines.
  • CI/CD integration. Trigger automated runs on every build with frameworks like Appium, Espresso and XCUITest.
  • Remote access for everyone. Developers, testers and support staff anywhere can open a live session on a specific device to reproduce a bug.
  • Rich artefacts. Videos, screenshots, device logs and network traces are captured automatically for every run.

When choosing a real device testing cloud, look at device availability and wait times, how quickly new models and OS versions are added, data security and device wiping between sessions, and whether devices are available in the regions and networks your users rely on.

Performance: where emulators mislead the most

Functional bugs are obvious when they happen. Performance problems are quieter. An app that takes four seconds to open, stutters while scrolling or drains the battery rarely triggers a crash report, but users notice, and many simply uninstall.

Emulators are especially poor at revealing these issues because they run on hardware far more powerful than a typical phone. Performance numbers measured on a virtual device can look healthy while real users on mid-range phones have a very different experience.

That’s why mobile performance testing tools are most valuable when they run on physical devices. The metrics worth tracking include:

  • App launch time, both cold and warm starts
  • Frame rate and dropped frames during scrolling and animations
  • CPU and memory usage, including memory leaks over long sessions
  • Battery drain and device temperature
  • Network request timing, payload size and behaviour on throttled connections
  • App size and storage use

When evaluating mobile performance testing tools, look for ones that capture these metrics on real hardware, simulate different network conditions, compare results across builds so regressions stand out, and plug into your pipeline so performance checks run automatically rather than once before a big launch. Many teams combine platform profilers such as Android Studio Profiler and Xcode Instruments for deep debugging with tools that run on a real device testing cloud for coverage across many models.

The key habit is setting performance budgets, for example a maximum launch time on your lowest-end supported device, and failing the build when they’re exceeded.

A layered strategy: the right test in the right place

The goal isn’t to abandon emulators. It’s to use each environment for what it does best, so you get fast feedback early and real-world confidence before release.

This approach keeps pipelines fast, because most runs still happen on cheap virtual devices, while making sure nothing ships without being checked on the hardware your customers actually hold.

Making the shift: six practical steps

  1. Build your device matrix from real data. Use your analytics to list the devices, OS versions and screen sizes your users actually have. Cover the top ones by usage, plus your oldest and lowest-spec supported models.
  2. Identify device-sensitive flows. Onboarding, login, payments, camera, location and push notifications are usually the first candidates for real-device coverage.
  3. Start small in the cloud. Move your smoke suite to a real device testing cloud first, prove the value, then expand to full regression.
  4. Add performance checks early. Pick one or two mobile performance testing tools, set baseline budgets for launch time and memory, and track them on every release build.
  5. Test under realistic conditions. Include throttled networks, low battery, background interruptions and different locales and accessibility settings.
  6. Review and adjust regularly. Device popularity shifts every year. Refresh your matrix each quarter and retire devices your users no longer use.

Conclusion

Emulators made mobile testing fast. Physical devices make it trustworthy. A reliable strategy needs both.

By running quick checks on virtual devices, using a real device testing cloud for broad hardware coverage, and making mobile performance testing tools part of every release, teams can close the gap between “it passed in CI” and “it works for our users.” Fewer surprises in production, fewer one-star reviews, and far more confidence every time you ship.

title: Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built
description:
Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built

Every designer has done it: you open a blank page, type a headline, and then freeze, because the words aren't written yet. So you paste in some lorem ipsum, the layout suddenly makes sense, and you can finally see what you're building.

That is exactly what placeholder text is for. It is not a shortcut or a sign of laziness. It is a tool that lets you judge a design on its own merits — typography, spacing, hierarchy, rhythm — before a single real sentence exists.

Why meaningless text makes better designs

Real copy is distracting. The moment a reviewer can read the words, they start editing the words. "Should this say 'customers' instead of 'clients'?" — and suddenly nobody is looking at the layout anymore.

Lorem ipsum solves this because it means nothing. The eye treats it as texture, not language, so attention stays where it belongs: on how the page holds together. Printers have used it since the 1500s for exactly this reason, and web designers inherited the habit because it still works.

How to use placeholder text properly

A block of dummy text is only useful if you use it the way a real page will be used. Here is the workflow I follow:

1. Match the amount to the real content. If the final article will be 800 words, don't test the template with two short paragraphs. Generate the same volume the real page will carry, so you see the true shape of the layout — where it gets long, where it breathes, where it breaks.

2. Test the extremes. Generate a very short version (a few words) and a very long one (many paragraphs) and drop both into the same template. Headlines wrap, cards stretch, buttons move. A layout that survives both extremes will survive real content.

3. Check every breakpoint. Placeholder text behaves differently at mobile width than on desktop. Paste the same block in, resize the browser, and watch for awkward orphans, cramped line lengths, and columns that collapse badly.

4. Vary the lengths. Real pages mix short intros, long bodies, and tiny captions. If every test block is the same size, you are testing one layout, not the design system.

A free generator that does the job in seconds

You don't need a plugin or a paid tool for this. FakeXLab's Lorem Ipsum Generator is free, needs no sign-up, and runs entirely in your browser. You choose paragraphs, sentences, or words, set the amount, click Generate, and copy the text straight into your mockup.

Because it generates by word and sentence count as well as paragraphs, you can build exactly the shape you need — a one-line button label, a three-sentence card description, or a full article's worth of body text for a long-form template.

Build a complete mockup, not just a text block

Placeholder text works best as part of a full fake page. Once the body copy is in place, fill the rest of the design with equally fictional data so the whole mockup feels real without exposing anyone's real information:

  • Add a byline with the Random Name Generator so author cards and profile blocks look finished.
  • Fill out sample forms and checkout screens with the Fake Address Generator — a complete fictional profile, address included, in one click.
  • Protect any test accounts you create along the way with a strong password from the Password Generator.

Everything on FakeXLab is fictional and for testing only, and nothing you generate is stored or sent anywhere — it all happens in your browser.

The mistakes to avoid

Placeholder text is a design tool, not content. Three mistakes turn it into a problem:

  • Shipping it live. Lorem ipsum on a published page looks unfinished and hurts trust. Replace every block with real copy before launch — run a quick search for "lorem" across the site as a final check.
  • Testing with one perfect block. If your test text is always the same length, your layout only works at that length. Real content is messy; test messy.
  • Using real copy too early. Drafting final words before the layout is settled means rewriting both when the design changes. Get the shape right first, then write into it.

The takeaway

Good layouts are built before the words arrive. Lorem ipsum lets you see the design clearly, test it honestly, and hand it over with confidence — and a free generator like FakeXLab's makes the whole thing take seconds instead of an afternoon of copy-pasting.

Next time you start a mockup, generate the text first, build around it, and let the design speak before the content does.

title: SQL Challenge : What Happens When You Insert a Duplicate PRIMARY KEY?
description:
Imagine you are working on an employee management system.

The company stores employee details in a database. Every employee has an employee ID, name, department and salary.

Now, a developer tries to insert a new employee using an ID that already exists in the table.

Will SQL accept the new record, replace the existing employee or return an error?

Let's understand this with a practical SQL example.

  1. Create an Employees Table

First, create an "employees" table with a PRIMARY KEY on "employee_id".

CREATE TABLE employees (
employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
employee_name VARCHAR(100),
department VARCHAR(50),
salary DECIMAL(10,2)
);

Here, "employee_id" is the PRIMARY KEY.

It means every employee must have a unique ID.

  1. Insert Existing Employee Records

Let's insert three employee records.

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES
(101, 'Rahul', 'IT', 65000),
(102, 'Priya', 'HR', 55000),
(103, 'Amit', 'Finance', 60000);

Employees Table:

employee_id| employee_name| department| salary
101| Rahul| IT| 65000
102| Priya| HR| 55000
103| Amit| Finance| 60000

So far, everything is working correctly.

  1. Try to Insert a Duplicate Employee ID

Now, a developer tries to insert another employee with "employee_id = 101".

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_id, employee_name, department, salary)
VALUES (101, 'Sneha', 'IT', 70000);

What will happen?

The INSERT statement will fail because employee ID 101 already exists as a PRIMARY KEY.

The database returns a primary key or unique constraint violation error. The exact error message depends on the database.

  1. What Will the Final Table Look Like?

The original records remain unchanged.

employee_id| employee_name| department| salary
101| Rahul| IT| 65000
102| Priya| HR| 55000
103| Amit| Finance| 60000

Sneha's record will not be inserted.

  1. Important Points About PRIMARY KEY

A PRIMARY KEY has two important rules:

  • It does not allow duplicate values.
  • It does not allow NULL values.

A PRIMARY KEY helps uniquely identify every record in a table.

For example, it is commonly used for:

  • Employee IDs
  • Customer IDs
  • Order IDs
  • Product IDs

These rules help maintain correct and reliable data in a database.

Your Turn: Test Your SQL Knowledge

Can a table have two PRIMARY KEY constraints?

A. Yes, every column can have a separate PRIMARY KEY.

B. No, a table can have only one PRIMARY KEY constraint, but it can contain multiple columns (a composite PRIMARY KEY).

C. Yes, but only when both columns have different data types.

D. No, a PRIMARY KEY can contain only one column.

Share your answer in the comments!

Learn More About SQL Constraints

If you want to learn more about SQL CREATE TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL and other database constraints, explore these practical SQL tutorials:

"Sankalan Data Tech – SQL DDL Commands and Database Constraints" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/ddl-manage-tables-relationships-sql-faq.html)

title: How to Design a Final Year Project Database: ERD and Normalization to 3NF in MySQL
description:
Most FYP database chapters fall apart in the viva for one simple reason: the student drew an ERD that looks nice, then built whatever tables felt right in phpMyAdmin. The first time an examiner asks "why is this field in this table?", there is no answer.

Here is the order that survives questioning, using a hostel management system as the example:

1. Entities come from the problem statement, not from screens.
Read your problem statement and underline the nouns your system must remember: Student, Room, Allotment, Payment, Complaint. If a noun never gets stored, it is not an entity. If it gets stored and changes over time, it probably is.

2. Draw the ERD before you create a single table.
For each pair of entities, write the relationship in a sentence: "One Room has many Allotments over time, but one Allotment belongs to exactly one Room." That sentence gives you cardinality, and cardinality tells you where the foreign key lives. Panels ask about relationships far more than about box shapes.

3. Normalise to 3NF on paper, in this order.

  • 1NF: no repeating groups. A student row with phone1, phone2, phone3 fails this instantly.
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. In an Allotment table with a composite key (student_id, room_id), the student's name depends only on student_id — it moves out.
  • 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Room rent depends on room type, not on the room number — so rent lives in a RoomType table, not repeated on every Room row.

4. Only now open MySQL.
Create tables in dependency order (the "one" side first), add foreign keys with the right ON DELETE behaviour, and seed each table with 5-10 realistic rows. Realistic data is what makes your demo and your test cases believable.

5. Write the viva answers while you design.
For every table, one sentence: "This table exists because…" If you cannot finish that sentence, the table is either missing or should not exist. This is also exactly the justification your Chapter 3 needs — the full chapter structure (methodology choice, use case diagram, DFD levels, and this database design sequence) is laid out in this Chapter 3 guide if you are writing yours now.

Design on paper first, and the database stops being the scary part of the viva.

Are you drawing your ERD before or after building your tables? I am curious how other students were taught this.

title: Avoiding Partially Written Export Files in GBase 8a with Python UDFs
description:
GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP database from GBASE, can export over ftp and sftp. When the export is large — tens of GB — the target file takes time to finish writing. If a downstream job picks it up mid-export, it reads an incomplete file, which shows up as inconsistent data or parse errors. This post uses Python UDFs to add ftp / sftp rename support so the file only becomes visible when it is complete.

The idea

Downstream consumers usually scan for files matching a rule, for example *.csv under a load directory. Making an unfinished file fail that rule can be done two ways, and they can be combined:

  • Name does not match — target is .csv, temporary file is .csv.tmp
  • Path does not match — write to a temporary directory first

Two steps

  1. Export to a temporary file (different suffix, or a temporary directory).
  2. Once the export finishes, use the protocol's rename to switch the temporary name to the final one — changing the suffix or moving across directories.

FTP rename UDF

Stored under gclusterdb, taking host, username, password, source name, target name. Port customisation is not implemented; extend it if you are not on the default ftp port:

use gclusterdb;
drop function if exists ftpRename;
create function ftpRename(server varchar(100),username varchar(100),password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))
returns varchar
$$
from ftplib import FTP
ftp = FTP(server)
ftp.login(username, password)
ftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)
ftp.close()
return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

Calling it:

gbase> select ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv')  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                             |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

SFTP rename UDF

The standard Python library does not speak sftp, so this example uses pysftp (pip install pysftp). Everything else matches the FTP version:

use gclusterdb;
drop function if exists sftpRename;
create function sftpRename(server varchar(100),v_username varchar(100),v_password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))
returns varchar
$$
import pysftp
with pysftp.Connection(server, username=v_username, password=v_password) as sftp:
    sftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)
    sftp.close()
return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

gbase> select sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                             |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

The full flow 

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';
Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.32)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv');
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv') |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.43)

The temporary file can live in a different directory, provided the account has write permission there. This example uses both a temporary tmp directory and a .tmp suffix:

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';
Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv');
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv') |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| OK                                                                                                            |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

Both the export and the rename run inside the gbase client, and the consumer's scan rule never matches a .tmp file. Handing atomic visibility to rename means even a tens-of-GB export no longer needs a sleep timer or a human "is it done yet" check — a small UDF turns the database's own export into a safe handoff.

title: How to Stop Guessing GPU Size: Checking VRAM & Memory Bandwidth Before Provisioning
description:
Most teams size bare metal GPU nodes by looking at parameter count (7B, 70B, 405B) and guessing a GPU SKU. That shortcut breaks in two predictable ways:

  1. You rent an H100 / H200 cluster when a single AMD Instinct MI300X (192 GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s) or FP8-quantized node would avoid multi-GPU tensor-parallel overhead.
  2. You rent a GPU for a sparse CFD/FEA workload like OpenFOAM that is actually memory-bandwidth bound and PCIe transfer bound, where a high-RAM EPYC or Xeon CPU node starting at ₹1,499/mo (~$16/mo) delivers better cost per run.

This guide gives you the exact back-of-the-envelope formulas we use at Hydenring before provisioning any node—and links to our live INR & USD calculator at hydenring.com/compare.

1. The 3-Part VRAM Formula (Weights + KV Cache + Overhead)

Before choosing between bare metal GPU servers (MI300X, H200, H100, B200) or multi-GPU pods, compute total required VRAM:

Total VRAM ≈ Model Weights + KV Cache + Runtime Overhead

A. Model Weights 

Weights (GB) ≈ Parameters (B) × Bytes per Parameter
Precision Bytes / Param 70B Dense Model
FP16 / BF16 2.0 140 GB
FP8 / INT8 1.0 70 GB
INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ) 0.5 35 GB

B. KV Cache (With Grouped-Query Attention) 

KV Cache per Token (bytes) = 2 × Layers × KV_Heads × Head_Dim × Bytes_per_Element

Take a 70B GQA model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, BF16 = 2 bytes):

  • 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes/token (320 KiB/token)
  • At 32,768 (32K) context for 1 concurrent sequence: 32,768 × 327,680 bytes = 10.0 GiB (~10.7 GB)
  • At 16 concurrent 32K sequences: ~160 GiB of KV cache alone

C. Why 141 GB vs 192 GB Changes Node Count (MI300X vs H200)

Add 140 GB (70B BF16 weights) + ~10.7 GB (single 32K KV sequence) + ~8–12 GB (CUDA/HIP workspace & activation buffers) = ~159–163 GB:

  • NVIDIA H200 (141 GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s): Too tight for unquantized 70B BF16 at 32K context on 1 GPU—you must either quantize to FP8 (~70 GB weights) or step up to TP=2.
  • AMD Instinct MI300X (192 GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s): Fits 70B BF16 + 32K KV cache + runtime overhead on 1 GPU (TP=1) with ~30 GB left for batching.

(Note: If your stack already depends on TensorRT-LLM or custom CUDA kernels, staying on NVIDIA H100/H200 often beats ROCm on engineering time. We cover those exact boundaries in our Workload-First Silicon Selection post.)

2. Checking the Decode Memory-Bandwidth Ceiling

Single-stream LLM token generation (decode) is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound. Every generated token must stream the active model weights from HBM into compute units:

Theoretical Max Decode Speed (tok/s) ≈ HBM Bandwidth (GB/s) / Active Weights (GB)

For a 140 GB BF16 70B model (batch = 1):

  • AMD Instinct MI300X (5,300 GB/s): 5,300 / 140 ≈ 37.9 tok/s hardware ceiling (~26.5 tok/s at 70% bus efficiency)
  • NVIDIA H200 (4,800 GB/s, if FP8 70 GB): 4,800 / 70 ≈ 68.6 tok/s hardware ceiling (halving active bytes doubles decode ceiling)

If your cloud GPU pricing quote compares GPUs purely on TFLOPs for a decode-heavy serving API, you are sizing the wrong bottleneck.

3. When to Skip GPUs Entirely (OpenFOAM & Sparse FEA)

The fastest way to waste compute budget is putting a sparse, memory-bound physics solver on an H100:

  • Steady-state OpenFOAM (simpleFoam, icoFoam under 10M cells, or cases with Arbitrary Mesh Interfaces / cyclic boundaries and custom C++/Fortran UDFs) saturates lduMatrix sparse-matrix memory bandwidth and hits PCIe host-to-device transfer bottlenecks when partially offloaded.
  • Implicit FEA (MOOSE, CalculiX) is similarly limited by sparse linear-solver memory latency and MPI synchronization.

For these workloads, a high-memory EPYC or Xeon node starting at ₹1,499/mo (~$16/mo) avoids idle GPU SMs and cuts total cost per simulation.

4. Two Pre-Provisioning Sanity Checks

Before running multi-GPU workloads on bare metal, verify interconnect topology and pin immutable Apptainer container digests:

# AMD Instinct: inspect XGMI / PCIe link topology before setting TP
rocm-smi --showtopo

# NVIDIA: inspect NVLink / PCIe topology matrix
nvidia-smi topo -m

# Pin an immutable @sha256:<digest> instead of mutable :latest tags
apptainer exec --rocm docker://rocm/vllm@sha256:<pinned-digest> python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --help

Compare Live TCO in INR & USD

  • Interactive comparison (no email gate): hydenring.com/compare — compare CPU, AMD Instinct, NVIDIA, and Intel Gaudi 3 economics side-by-side.
  • Submit your solver or model profile: hydenring.com/workload-review — get a bottleneck-first silicon recommendation across India, Europe, and North America (hydenring.com/regions) backed by transparent Mon–Fri 09:30–18:30 IST engineering support (hydenring.com/sla).

title: In a second test of Streamer, Defender recorded 659 non-notification events in the files examined
description:
SOCRadar’s report on Streamer, a Rust-written Windows malware sample, documents a change in detection between two controlled tests.

The revised version connected to its operators’ control system without an alert in the exported Defender log, though 659 events were recorded.

The report does not identify what changed or establish that the result would recur on another device.

This doesn't mean that the second test wasn't recorded. Defender recorded 659 events, including external system connections, data preparation, and account discovery attempts. None of these events in the log had an alert ID.

What did the two tests show?

Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar identified the program as Streamer. Its report, published on November 26, was based on files, screenshots, and Defender logs that connected to the infrastructure of the program's operators.

In the first test, Defender rated the incident as high severity. Four of the 10 alerts were for a program that unexpectedly loaded an extra file. Defender then isolated the computer from the network.

In the October 21 test, Streamer appeared as a security product component. Defender recorded it as an unknown program and marked it as more difficult to control. The device page did not show any known risks, but Defender continued to collect events.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Cyber ​​Attacks & Data Breaches

SAP confirms theft of employee digital keys and access to GitHub

↗

The report doesn't explain what change led to the different result. It also doesn't clarify whether the same version would have passed without notification to another device.

Items linked to other groups

SOCRadar found files for MetaEncryptor/LostTrust, a ransomware platform, on the same development machine. It also found similarities between the infrastructure associated with Streamer and a system called Eclipse, which had been examined by the Atos Threat Research Center. Among the similarities was the same tool and the same creator indication.

The researchers assessed with high confidence that the two infrastructures had a common creator and used common tools. However, they were unable to determine whether the names MetaEncryptor and LostTrust belonged to the same group.

The operator records named 17 organizations in four countries, 14 of which were in the United States. Among them were a federal agency, three energy cooperatives, and a healthcare provider. The records included confirmed activity, operator claims, and one case where only an acknowledgment was made. Therefore, the 17 organizations do not correspond to 17 confirmed breaches or ransomware installations.

For the federal agency's case, the report describes prolonged access and theft of files with the code of a program, as well as a private digital key used to access services.

SOCRadar reported that the researchers did not interfere with the organizations' systems and informed those affected, as well as the relevant authorities.
