title: AI Builds Clean CRUD for Proptech. It Breaks the Moment One User Has Two Roles on Two Properties
description:
Ask an AI coding tool to build a property management app and you'll get working auth, a clean CRUD admin panel, a Stripe checkout flow, and a dashboard that looks fine in a demo. All of that is generic SaaS scaffolding, and AI handles it well because it's been trained on thousands of examples of exactly that pattern. The part that breaks isn't the UI or the database schema for listings. It's permissions, specifically the assumption baked into almost every generated auth system that a user has one role. Real estate doesn't work that way. The same person can be a board member on one property and just an owner on another, in the same account, and most vibe-coded proptech has no data model for that at all.

Where the AI capability line actually sits

AI builds the generic SaaS layer reliably: authentication, basic create-read-update-delete admin panels, Stripe checkout, simple dashboards, landing pages with a waitlist form. A founder with some technical skill can extend that into listing display pages, inquiry forms, and basic tenant directories. What consistently breaks, regardless of how good the model is, falls into four categories: permission modeling tied to real-world structure, integrations with legacy systems that don't have clean APIs, financial workflows touching actual balances, and compliance-sensitive workflows. None of those are language-model problems. They're modeling problems that require someone to think through the real-world structure before any code gets written.

Why "one role per user" is the wrong schema

The default pattern almost every generated auth system produces is a single role column on the user record. That works for most SaaS. It fails immediately for property management, where the same person needs different permissions on different properties, sometimes owner on one unit and board member on another in the same association:

// Wrong: role lives on the user, can't vary by property
User { id, email, role }  // "owner" doesn't tell you which property

// Right: role is scoped to the relationship between a user and a property
UserPropertyRole {
  userId,
  propertyId,
  role,              // "owner", "board_member", "employee", "administrator"
  grantedAt,
}

function checkPermission(userId, propertyId, action) {
  const scopedRole = userPropertyRoles.find(userId, propertyId);
  if (!scopedRole) return deny(action, "no_role_on_property");
  return rolePermissions[scopedRole.role].includes(action);
}

That second pattern is the difference between a system that can actually model a real association and one that only works until the first user with a role conflict signs up. Support access needs the same discipline: a "view as this account" mode should be a logged impersonation event, not a shared admin login that leaves no trail of who looked at what.

What this looked like on a real build

Brocoders built exactly this pattern for C.I.A. Services' HOA management app, which runs five distinct access tiers, owners, multi-lot owners, board members, employees, and administrators, across roughly 150 associations and 50,000 properties. Registration itself is a verification problem: a community code, account number, and PIN get checked against live association records before an account is even created. Support staff get a scoped "view as this account" mode that logs every impersonation instead of sharing credentials. We run this on hard data isolation at both the database and API layer, so a permission bug in one association's records can't leak into another's, with two-factor authentication and audit logging on top. Internal tooling at bcboilerplates.com covers this kind of auth and tenancy scaffolding by default, so new builds start with scoped permissions instead of a single role column that has to be ripped out later.

Other builds hit the same category of problem differently. CondoGenie, a Canadian condo management platform, has needed this same board-versus-resident-versus-manager distinction since inception. Lake, a vacation rental platform, saw connected properties grow 80x with a 210% spike in site activity within three months of a rebuild that included fixing exactly this kind of access modeling. ShineUp's codebase needed a 2-3 week AWS migration at a fixed price with no rebuild required, evidence that not every legacy proptech problem needs a rewrite, some just need the infrastructure moved without touching the permission logic that already worked.

The four questions that tell you if this is a DIY problem or not

  1. Do multiple user types need different property access? A single owner-versus-admin split is DIY territory. Five tiers with overlapping scopes isn't.
  2. Does this integrate with a system you don't fully control? Legacy property management software and MLS feeds rarely expose clean APIs.
  3. Does a permission error carry real compliance or financial consequences? A wrong role assignment that exposes another owner's financial data is a different risk class than a cosmetic bug.
  4. Are there cross-property enforcement rules? Booking limits, amenity availability, and approval chains that span properties need real logic, not a checkbox.

Three or four "yes" answers means this needs a team that's modeled real-world property structures before, not just a capable coding assistant. One or two "yes" answers means DIY territory is probably still viable, at least for now.

Engineering checklist before you scale a proptech permission model

  • Role lives on the relationship, not the user: can the same person hold different roles on different properties without a schema change?
  • Impersonation is logged, not shared: does support access leave an audit trail, or does it use a shared login?
  • Isolation enforced at the data layer: can one association's records reach another's through any code path, even a bug?
  • Legacy integration scoped honestly: does the plan account for a PMS or MLS with no clean API, or assume one exists?
  • Financial workflows get extra review: does anything touching real balances get more scrutiny than a standard CRUD flow?
  • Compliance workflows are explicit: are they designed in from the start, or patched in after the first audit finding? If you're trying to figure out whether your proptech idea needs a real permission model before you keep building on AI-generated scaffolding, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.

title: How to choose a Bootstrap 5 admin template: a 10-point checklist
description:
Most admin templates look the same in the preview screenshot. The differences show up three weeks into a project, when you try to connect real data, add a language or ship the bundle to a slow phone. This is the checklist I use before committing to one. Every point has a test that takes a few minutes.

Disclosure: I make admin templates (Kova and Kova Lite, linked at the end), so I have opinions about what goes wrong. The checklist works for any template, including mine.

1. Which Bootstrap version, exactly?

"Bootstrap 5" can mean 5.0 from 2021 or the current 5.3. Version 5.3 added native dark mode through data-bs-theme; templates built on older versions usually implement dark mode with their own CSS overrides, which break when you add a Bootstrap component the author did not restyle.

Test: open the bundled bootstrap.min.css and read the version comment on line one.

2. What does it depend on besides Bootstrap?

Look at the <script> tags in the HTML. jQuery, Moment, a chart library, a date picker, a table plugin, an icon font: each is a separate update and a separate security surface. None of them is wrong, but you should know the number before you start.

Test: unzip the template and run grep -rho "<script[^>]*src=[^>]*>" . | sort | uniq -c. A long list is a maintenance bill.

3. How heavy is a single page?

Admin screens load on office laptops and on a phone in a warehouse. Open the dashboard page in Chrome DevTools, Network tab, disable cache, and look at transferred size and the number of requests.

Test: Lighthouse in mobile mode on the main dashboard. You are not chasing 100, only looking for surprises such as a 600 KB chart library to draw four charts.

4. Is the data hard-coded in the HTML?

Many templates ship tables with rows typed into the markup. That is fine for a screenshot and a rewrite for production. Look for templates where tables and charts read from JSON or a single API setting, because that is the part you will replace first.

Test: view source on the orders or users page. If the rows are in the HTML, plan to rebuild the table.

5. Do the interactive parts actually work?

Search boxes that do not search, filters that do not filter, "Export" buttons with no handler. Click everything on the demo, especially tables: sorting, pagination, bulk select, empty states.

Test: sort a numeric column and a date column. Wrong ordering ("100" before "20") means string sorting.

6. Dark mode and RTL, for real

Both are easy to claim and easy to get half right. Switch the demo to dark and open a page with a form, a modal and a chart. Switch to RTL and check the sidebar, dropdown menus and table alignment.

Test: in the demo, toggle dark mode, reload the page. It should stay dark without a flash of light theme.

7. Responsive down to 320 px

Resize the window to 320 px wide. The sidebar should collapse, tables should scroll inside their container rather than the whole page, and no horizontal page scrollbar should appear.

8. Is there a source, or only minified output?

If the template is built from partials or a build step, you will want the source. If it is plain HTML, check that headers and sidebars are not copy-pasted into 40 files by hand, because then every nav change is 40 edits.

Test: look for a src/ or partials/ folder, or a documented build script.

9. License and what it allows

Read the license before the code. Typical questions: can you use it in a client project, in a SaaS you sell, in multiple projects? Marketplace "regular" licenses usually cover one end product. If you are building for clients, check whether each client needs their own license.

10. Documentation and updates

Open the docs page. Good docs cover folder structure, theming, how to add a page, and how data is loaded. Then check the last update date and the changelog; a template untouched for two years will not follow the next Bootstrap release.

Quick scoring

Give each point 0, 1 or 2. Under 12 out of 20, keep looking. Above 16, you probably found something maintainable.

If you want to compare

I built two admin templates on these principles, so you can run the checklist against real ones:

  • Kova Lite: 8 pages, a starter edition. Demo: https://kova-lite.toolsy.pro. Item: https://www.codester.com/items/75045/kova-lite-admin-dashboard-starter-bootstrap-5?ref=toolsy
  • Kova: the full version, 35 pages. Demo: https://kova.toolsy.pro. Item: https://www.codester.com/items/74303/kova-e-commerce-admin-dashboard-bootstrap-5?ref=toolsy

Both use Bootstrap 5.3.3 and vanilla JavaScript with no jQuery, and the charts are a small custom library rather than a third-party package. The data is fictional sample data. I wrote them with AI assistance and tested them by hand. Test them the same way you test any other template, and tell me which points they fail.

title: A regex from examples: the must-not-match list
description:
Why the strings a JavaScript regex must reject define it more than the ones it accepts, with anchors, the u flag and \p{L} for non-English text.

A list of strings that a pattern must accept cannot define the pattern, because the loosest possible expression, one that matches everything, accepts all of them. What narrows a pattern down is the list of strings it has to turn away: the value with one digit too many, the value with text around it, the value in another alphabet. This guide shows how to build a JavaScript regular expression from examples with that in mind. It covers choosing the rejected strings, anchors and the m flag, the word-character trap that breaks patterns on Bulgarian or French text, the u and v flags, and a test harness that was checked against deliberately wrong patterns. Catastrophic backtracking is a different…

title: The Transactional Outbox Pattern in Postgres and NestJS: Ending Dual Writes Between Your Database and Your Queue — Field Notes
description:
Headline: Saving a row in Postgres and then publishing a message to a queue is a dual write, and it loses or invents events whenever the process dies between the two calls. The transactional outbox pattern fixes it by inserting the event into an outbox table in the same Postgres transaction as the business change, then letting a relay publish pending rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event ID.

For a long time my NestJS services created an order and then pushed an order.created job to a queue on the next line. It passed every test, because tests never kill the process between two awaits. Production does: SIGTERM during deploys, OOM kills, broker timeouts. These are my notes from replacing that code with a transactional outbox.

Key takeaways

  • A dual write is one operation that writes to two systems with no shared transaction, such as a Postgres row plus a Redis, RabbitMQ or Kafka message; a crash between the writes leaves the systems disagreeing.
  • The transactional outbox stores each event as a row in the same database transaction as the state change, so the commit makes both durable or neither.
  • A relay claims unpublished rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes them and marks them published; several relay instances never claim the same row.
  • The outbox gives at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so consumers record processed event IDs under a unique constraint and skip repeats.
  • Polling is the simplest relay; change data capture with Debezium removes polling latency but adds Kafka Connect and a replication slot to operate.

What is the dual-write problem, and why don't retries fix it?

The dual-write problem is that two independent writes cannot be made atomic from application code, so a failure between them produces an inconsistency that no retry can see. This is the code I used to ship:

// orders.service.ts — the dual write
async createOrder(input: CreateOrderDto) {
  const order = await this.ordersRepo.insert(input);             // write 1: Postgres commits here
  await this.queue.add('order.created', { orderId: order.id });  // write 2: Redis
  return order;
}

It fails in two directions:

  • Lost event: Postgres commits, then the process dies or the queue call times out. The order exists, but no confirmation email, invoice or stock reservation ever follows.
  • Phantom event: the message is published first, or inside the transaction before COMMIT, and the transaction rolls back. A consumer receives order.created for an order that does not exist.

A retry loop cannot fix the dual write, because the process that would retry is the process that crashed. Publishing inside the transaction only swaps lost events for phantom events while holding a transaction open across a network call. Two-phase commit (XA) would solve it on paper, but Redis, Kafka and most managed brokers cannot join a Postgres transaction.

How does the transactional outbox pattern work?

The transactional outbox pattern turns "publish a message" into "insert a row", which Postgres commits atomically with the business change. A separate relay reads committed rows later and does the actual publishing. This is my table:

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id              uuid        PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type  text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. 'order'
  aggregate_id    text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. the order id
  event_type      text        NOT NULL,              -- e.g. 'order.created'
  payload         jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at    timestamptz,
  attempts        int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_error      text
);

-- The relay only ever reads pending rows; a partial index keeps that scan cheap
CREATE INDEX outbox_pending_idx ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

The write side is one Drizzle transaction in the NestJS service, so the order and its event commit together or not at all:

// orders.service.ts — the outbox write
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

async createOrder(input: CreateOrderDto) {
  return this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const [order] = await tx.insert(orders).values(input).returning();
    await tx.insert(outbox).values({
      id: randomUUID(),
      aggregateType: 'order',
      aggregateId: order.id,
      eventType: 'order.created',
      // Snapshot what consumers need now; a later read could see a newer state
      payload: { version: 1, orderId: order.id, customerId: order.customerId, totalCents: order.totalCents },
    });
    return order;
  });
}

The same shape works with Prisma's interactive prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => …) and TypeORM's dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => …). I put a version field in every payload because the outbox row outlives the code that wrote it.

How does the relay publish outbox rows safely with several workers?

The relay claims a batch of pending rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes each one, and marks the successes as published before committing. FOR UPDATE locks the claimed rows; SKIP LOCKED makes a second relay skip those rows instead of waiting, so I run the relay in every API replica.

// outbox.relay.ts — DB, Database, EventPublisher and the outbox table come from this app's own modules
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';
import { and, asc, eq, inArray, isNull, lte, sql } from 'drizzle-orm';

@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelay implements OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OutboxRelay.name);
  private running = true;

  constructor(@Inject(DB) private readonly db: Database, private readonly publisher: EventPublisher) {}

  onApplicationBootstrap() { void this.loop(); }
  onApplicationShutdown() { this.running = false; } // requires app.enableShutdownHooks()

  private async loop() {
    while (this.running) {
      const claimed = await this.drainBatch().catch((err) => { this.logger.error(err); return 0; });
      if (claimed === 0) await sleep(500); // idle: poll every 500 ms; a busy relay loops immediately
    }
  }

  private drainBatch(): Promise<number> {
    return this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      const rows = await tx.select().from(outbox)
        .where(and(isNull(outbox.publishedAt), lte(outbox.nextAttemptAt, sql`now()`)))
        .orderBy(asc(outbox.createdAt))
        .limit(50)
        .for('update', { skipLocked: true });

      const sent: string[] = [];
      for (const row of rows) {
        try {
          // The outbox row id travels with the message as the deduplication key
          await this.publisher.publish(row.eventType, { eventId: row.id, payload: row.payload });
          sent.push(row.id);
        } catch (err) {
          // Back off this row only: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … capped at 5 minutes
          await tx.update(outbox).set({
            attempts: sql`${outbox.attempts} + 1`,
            nextAttemptAt: sql`now() + least(power(2, ${outbox.attempts}), 300) * interval '1 second'`,
            lastError: String(err),
          }).where(eq(outbox.id, row.id));
        }
      }
      if (sent.length > 0) {
        await tx.update(outbox).set({ publishedAt: new Date() }).where(inArray(outbox.id, sent));
      }
      return rows.length;
    });
  }
}

Three details took me more than one attempt:

  • Per-row error handling. My first version let one failing publish roll back the whole batch, so one poison row blocked everything behind it. Now a failure only bumps that row's attempts and next_attempt_at, and a broker outage delays delivery without losing anything.
  • Publish timeouts. The claim transaction stays open while the relay talks to the broker, so the publisher needs a short timeout. For slow targets such as third-party webhooks, I use a lease instead: set locked_until, commit, publish outside the transaction, then mark the rows published.
  • Ordering. Postgres now() returns the transaction's start time, so an event whose transaction commits late can be published after a newer one. The relay never skips that row, because it re-queries every pending row, but several relays remove global ordering entirely. For per-aggregate order I run one relay or shard relays by aggregate_id, and consumers discard stale versions.

Why is outbox delivery at-least-once, and how do consumers deduplicate?

Outbox delivery is at-least-once because the relay can crash after the broker accepts a message but before published_at commits, so the next run publishes that row again. The fix lives in the consumer: an inbox table keyed by event ID, written in the same transaction as the consumer's work.

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
  event_id     uuid        PRIMARY KEY,
  processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

// invoice.consumer.ts — the handler's work runs once per event ID, however often it is delivered
async handleOrderCreated(event: OutboxMessage<OrderCreatedV1>) {
  await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const fresh = await tx.insert(processedEvents)
      .values({ eventId: event.eventId })
      .onConflictDoNothing()
      .returning();
    if (fresh.length === 0) return; // duplicate delivery: already handled

    await tx.insert(invoices).values({ orderId: event.payload.orderId, totalCents: event.payload.totalCents });
  });
}

INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING returns no row for a known event ID, so a duplicate becomes a no-op. For side effects outside the database, such as charging a card, I pass the event ID as the provider's idempotency key; Stripe's Idempotency-Key header is the standard example.

Should the relay poll, use LISTEN/NOTIFY, or use change data capture?

Polling is the right default; change data capture pays off when you already run Kafka or need sub-second latency at high volume:

Relay strategy Latency Extra infrastructure Main catch
Polling with SKIP LOCKED Up to one poll interval None beyond a worker Constant small query load, even when idle
Polling plus LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-ups Near-immediate One dedicated session connection Notifications are not durable, so keep the poll as a fallback; transaction-mode PgBouncer does not support LISTEN
CDC with Debezium's outbox event router Near-immediate, in commit order Kafka Connect or Debezium Server, wal_level=logical, a replication slot An abandoned replication slot retains WAL until the disk fills

Change data capture (CDC) reads row changes from the Postgres write-ahead log through logical replication instead of querying the table; Debezium ships an outbox event router transform for this table shape. NOTIFY is transactional, delivered only if the sending transaction commits, so it is a safe wake-up signal for a poller.

How do I keep the outbox table healthy in production?

Keep the outbox small and alert on its lag. A scheduled job deletes published rows older than a few days, in batches; at higher volumes, partitioning by created_at and dropping old partitions is cheaper. The alert I would not ship without tracks the oldest pending row:

SELECT count(*)                                         AS pending,
       coalesce(max(now() - created_at), interval '0')  AS oldest_pending_age,
       coalesce(max(attempts), 0)                       AS max_attempts
FROM outbox
WHERE published_at IS NULL;

A growing oldest_pending_age means a stuck relay, a down broker or a poison row. None of these is visible from the API, which keeps returning 201 because the order itself was saved.

FAQ

Q: Do I still need an outbox if my queue is BullMQ on Redis?

A: Yes. Writing a Postgres row and enqueuing a BullMQ job in Redis is a dual write. The alternative is a Postgres-backed queue such as Graphile Worker, whose graphile_worker.add_job() SQL function enqueues a job inside your own transaction, making the job table the outbox.

Q: Does the transactional outbox give exactly-once delivery?

A: No. The transactional outbox gives at-least-once delivery; exactly-once processing comes from consumers that deduplicate by event ID.

Q: Can I write to the broker first and to the database second?

A: No. Reversing the order still leaves two independent writes and turns lost events into phantom events for rows that never commit.

Q: Should the outbox payload contain the full entity or only its ID?

A: A versioned snapshot of the fields consumers need. An ID-only event forces every consumer to call back to the producer, which may already hold a newer state.

Originally published on devya.dev. Also on eng-ahmed.com. Built by Devya Solutions.

title: The Check That Catches the Loop Misses the Fixation
description:
Six times. A small triage helper I run on my laptop listed the same five GitHub issues six times in a row, burned 10,063 tokens doing it, and never answered the question. The right answer was issue 397, an enhancement. The helper never got there. It just kept asking for the same list, getting the same list, and asking again.

That job sat in my saved run logs for a week before Dr Srinivas Padmanabhuni left a note on my last piece. His shopping helper had done the same shape of thing, worse: it called the same search URL more than ten times and came back with an empty answer. His suggestion was a check from agentest, an open-source checklist of 165 tests for agent traces. Test T5-009 flags the same tool called with the same arguments more than three times in a row. Simple idea. I pointed it at my own logs to see what it would have caught: 41 saved trace files, 429 jobs, 1,074 tool calls, 1,255,700 prompt tokens counted turn by turn.

Here is what came back, and why I am not sure the storm is the thing to guard.

1. The check works. It caught the loop, and fifty others.

T5-009 failed 13 of the 41 files. The six-turn loop tripped it three times over. Across the whole set, 51 of the 429 jobs contain a run of four or more identical calls, 129 such windows in total. Cutting every storm off at the fourth identical call would have saved 103,452 prompt tokens, about 8% of everything the jobs spent. On the six-turn job alone, stopping at the fourth call saves 4,087 of its 10,063 tokens. So the check does what it says on the tin, and the loop that started this whole thing would have been stopped cold at turn four.

2. The storm is the small bill. The second call is the big one.

Here is the number that changed my mind about what to guard. Counting every repeat, not just runs of four: 96 of the 429 jobs repeat an identical call at least once. 276 repeat calls in total. The turns carrying them cost 341,116 prompt tokens, 27% of the whole set. And the most common repeat in the entire corpus is not a storm at all. It is the second call. The helper lists the issues, lists them again, and only then starts working. Two identical calls, then it moves on. T5-009 waves that straight through, because its bar is four.

So the check catches the dramatic failure and misses the ordinary one. 45 jobs repeat a call without ever reaching four in a row, worth 43,327 tokens the check never sees. If I cut at the first repeat instead of the fourth, the saving jumps from 103,452 to 341,116 tokens. But that cut would also kill the double list most triage jobs open with, and I have no evidence that double list is waste. It might be the helper double-checking before it commits. The honest saving is the storm tail, 8%. The 27% is the number I cannot claim without first knowing which second calls are habit and which are doubt.

3. The check is blind to the failure that actually cost us answers.

The six-turn loop is dramatic, but it is not the expensive failure in these logs. That one is the crash report. Issue 412, a crash on launch, is the loudest issue in the set, and the helper answered 412 with the label "bug" on 101 jobs across the triage traces, including jobs where the right answer was a different issue entirely. Five failed jobs in the first full run alone ended on 412. An answer is not a tool call, so no tool-call check can flag it. T5-009 would have passed those jobs as clean while the helper gave the same wrong answer again and again. A check that watches calls will never catch a helper that is stuck on an answer.

4. Shorter results storm less, and the storming jobs solve worse.

The pattern across the arms is hard to ignore. The trimmed arm, which sees five short fields per issue instead of the full dump, never stormed once in 52 jobs. The full arm stormed 3 times in 50. In a later experiment, the diary arm never stormed in 36 jobs and solved 18 of 24. The sender arm stormed on 24 of 36 jobs and solved 2 of 24. That is a correlation across arms, not proof of cause, and I will not dress it up as more. But it points the same way twice: the jobs that loop are the jobs that fail, and the shapes that keep the result short are the shapes that do not loop.

So where does that leave the check? I am keeping it. A test that catches 51 storms in 429 jobs for free is worth running, and the six-turn loop is exactly the failure it was built for. But I am not going to pretend it covers the problem. It guards the fourth repeat and misses the second, and it watches calls while the real fixation lives in answers. The next check I want is the one I do not have yet: something that flags the same answer given twice for different questions, the way T5-009 flags the same call made twice for the same question.

What does the loop look like on your side? Do you cut at the second repeat or the fourth, and has anyone here caught a helper stuck on an answer rather than a call? I would rather steal a check that already works than build another one that watches the wrong thing.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: SaaS Dashboard UX: How to Turn Complex Product Data Into Better User Decisions
description:
A SaaS dashboard can display dozens of metrics, charts, reports, and activity logs. But none of that matters if users still struggle to understand what is happening inside their product.

This is one of the most common problems in SaaS product design. Teams invest heavily in analytics, reporting capabilities, and backend functionality, yet the interface often makes users work harder than necessary to find meaningful information.

The real challenge isn't displaying more data. It's designing an experience that helps users interpret that data, identify what needs attention, and decide what to do next.

Effective dashboard UX starts with understanding user workflows, organizing information around real tasks, and reducing the cognitive effort required to make decisions.

Here are the practical design considerations that make a SaaS dashboard genuinely useful.

  1. Design Around User Workflows, Not Available Features

A common mistake in dashboard development is starting with a list of available features.

The product team asks:

Which analytics can we display?

How many charts should we include?

Which filters should be available?

What information can we pull from the database?

These are implementation questions, not UX questions.

A better starting point is understanding what users actually want to accomplish.

For example, consider a marketing analytics platform. A marketing manager might open the dashboard to answer three questions:

Which campaigns are performing below expectations?

Where is the advertising budget being wasted?

Which campaigns need immediate attention?

These questions should influence the dashboard structure.

Instead of presenting every metric with equal importance, the interface should prioritize campaign performance, budget efficiency, and actionable alerts.

Practical approach: Map the primary user journeys before creating dashboard components. Identify the decisions users make most frequently, then organize the interface around those activities.

  1. Establish a Clear Information Architecture

Information architecture determines how dashboard content is grouped, prioritized, and accessed.

Without a logical structure, even a visually attractive dashboard becomes difficult to navigate as the product grows.

A useful SaaS dashboard usually separates information into meaningful layers:

Overview layer: Key performance indicators, account summaries, and important notifications.

Analysis layer: Detailed charts, historical comparisons, trends, and performance breakdowns.

Action layer: Tasks, alerts, approvals, and operational controls.

Detail layer: Individual records, customer information, transactions, and supporting data.

This structure allows users to move from a high-level understanding to detailed investigation without overwhelming the initial screen.

For larger SaaS applications, navigation should also reflect how users mentally categorize their work. For example, billing, team management, reporting, and account settings should not be mixed into an unpredictable menu structure.

The objective is simple: users should understand where information lives without having to explore the entire application.

  1. Make Every KPI Explain Something

A dashboard KPI should provide context, not just a number.

Displaying revenue as $48,500 might look informative, but users cannot determine whether that performance is positive or negative without additional information.

A more useful KPI includes:

The current value.

A comparison against a previous period.

The percentage or absolute change.

A clear definition of the measurement.

The relevant reporting timeframe.

For example:

Monthly Recurring Revenue

$48,500

+12.4% compared with the previous month

This provides a much stronger understanding of business performance.

However, comparison periods must be consistent. Comparing the last seven days with an entire previous month can produce misleading conclusions.

Also, avoid presenting every KPI as equally important. Identify the metrics that directly influence user decisions and give them appropriate visual priority.

  1. Treat Data Visualization as a Communication Problem

Charts are useful when they make relationships easier to understand.

They become unnecessary decoration when users need additional effort to interpret them.

Choose chart types according to the question being answered:

User question

Suitable visualization

How has revenue changed over time?

Line chart

Which product category performs best?

Bar chart

How is the budget distributed?

Stacked bar or carefully used pie chart

How do conversion rates compare?

Bar chart

Where are operational bottlenecks?

Funnel visualization

A few additional considerations matter:

Avoid using too many colors without a consistent meaning.

Label axes and measurement units clearly.

Do not truncate scales in ways that exaggerate differences.

Provide tooltips for additional context.

Make important data points accessible without relying exclusively on hover interactions.

A chart should reduce interpretation time. If users need to study the visualization before understanding its message, reconsider the design.

  1. Design for Different Data States

One of the most overlooked aspects of SaaS dashboard UX is what happens when data is unavailable.

Designers frequently focus on the ideal scenario, where all information loads correctly and every account has sufficient data.

Real applications are not that predictable.

A production-ready dashboard needs carefully designed states for:

Empty state: The user has not generated any data yet. Explain what belongs here and provide a useful first action.

Loading state: Information is being retrieved. Use appropriate skeletons or progress indicators rather than leaving unexplained blank spaces.

Error state: A request has failed. Communicate what happened and provide a recovery option.

Partial data state: Some metrics are available while others are still processing. Make the limitation clear instead of presenting incomplete information as final.

These states are not secondary UI details. They directly influence whether users trust the application.

For example, an empty revenue chart should not simply display a blank area. It should explain that revenue data will appear after the first transaction and guide the user toward the relevant setup step.

  1. Build Responsive Dashboards Around Real Usage

Responsive design for SaaS dashboards requires more than shrinking desktop components.

The information density, interaction patterns, and navigation requirements can change significantly between devices.

A desktop dashboard might comfortably display:

Multiple KPI cards.

A detailed analytics chart.

A sidebar navigation.

Several data tables.

On a smaller screen, displaying everything simultaneously creates unnecessary complexity.

A better responsive strategy prioritizes information based on user needs.

For mobile layouts:

Keep the most important KPI visible early.

Stack cards according to their importance.

Simplify navigation.

Make filters accessible through compact controls.

Avoid horizontal scrolling for essential information.

Preserve readable chart labels and interactive targets.

It is also important to test actual interactions, not just visual breakpoints. Date pickers, dropdowns, tables, and chart tooltips can behave differently on touchscreens.

  1. Make Accessibility Part of the Design System

Accessibility should be considered during component design rather than added after development.

Dashboard interfaces often contain dense data, small labels, status indicators, and complex interactions. These elements can create usability barriers if accessibility is ignored.

Important considerations include:

Color contrast: Ensure text and graphical elements remain distinguishable against their backgrounds.

Color-independent communication: Do not use red and green as the only indicators of failure and success. Add labels, icons, or other visual cues.

Keyboard navigation: Users should be able to navigate menus, filters, dialogs, and interactive components using a keyboard.

Readable typography: Maintain appropriate text sizes, spacing, and hierarchy.

Accessible data tables: Use meaningful headings and logical reading order.

WCAG 2.2 provides useful accessibility criteria for evaluating these experiences, including keyboard accessibility, contrast, and non-text visual information.

Accessibility improves the overall usability of a product because it encourages more predictable and understandable interactions.

  1. Validate Dashboard UX With Actual Product Usage

A dashboard can look excellent in a design presentation and still perform poorly in real-world usage.

The difference becomes clear when actual users start interacting with it.

Instead of relying exclusively on internal opinions, evaluate the interface through usability testing and product analytics.

Some useful measurements include:

Time required to complete a common dashboard task.

Number of interactions needed to find a specific metric.

Filter usage and abandonment.

Frequency of report exports.

Errors during important workflows.

Feature discovery and adoption.

User feedback about confusing or unnecessary information.

For example, if users repeatedly export a report because they cannot understand the information displayed on the dashboard, the problem might not be missing functionality. It could be poor information hierarchy or unclear data presentation.

Use these observations to identify friction points, redesign individual components, and measure the impact of each change.

A Practical SaaS Dashboard UX Review Checklist

Before releasing a dashboard, review the following:

Does the main screen answer a clear user question?

Are the most important KPIs visually prioritized?

Do metrics include meaningful comparisons and timeframes?

Are charts appropriate for the information being communicated?

Are filters understandable and predictable?

Do empty, loading, and error states provide clear guidance?

Does the layout work across desktop, tablet, and mobile?

Can users navigate essential interactions with a keyboard?

Are status indicators understandable without color?

Have real users tested the most important workflows?

This checklist can help teams identify design issues before they become recurring usability problems.

Final Thoughts

A successful SaaS dashboard is not defined by how many charts it contains or how sophisticated its interface looks.

Its value comes from how effectively it helps users understand information and complete important tasks.

Good dashboard UX requires a combination of information architecture, interaction design, data visualization, accessibility, and continuous usability testing.

For a deeper look at the design principles behind effective data presentation, read this guide on SaaS Dashboard UI/UX Design: 8 Principles for Clear Data.

It explores practical ways to organize dashboard information, establish KPI hierarchy, improve empty states, and make complex product data easier to understand.

Ultimately, the best dashboards don't simply show users what is happening. They help users understand what matters and what to do next.

title: Supabase PGRST116 "Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object": what it means and how to fix it
description:
You call .single() in supabase-js and get this back:

{"code":"PGRST116","message":"Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object","details":"The result contains 0 rows","hint":null}

Older PostgREST versions say "JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned". The HTTP status is 406.

What it means
You asked for exactly one row. The query returned zero rows or more than one. PostgREST refuses to guess.

Why it happens

  1. The filter matched nothing: wrong id, the row was not created yet, or Row Level Security hides it from this user.
  2. The filter matched several rows because the column is not unique.
  3. You ran .insert(...).select().single() but your SELECT policy does not let the user read the row they just inserted.

How to fix it

  1. If "no row" is a normal state, use .maybeSingle() and handle null: 
const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('profiles')
  .select('*')
  .eq('id', user.id)
  .maybeSingle()
if (!data) { /* create the profile or show onboarding */ }
  1. Filter on a primary key or another unique column.
  2. If the row is in the table but not returned, the problem is RLS. Add a SELECT policy scoped to the owner.

"But I can see the row in the dashboard"
The dashboard bypasses RLS. Your app's role does not. Test the query as the user, not as the admin.

The fix to avoid
Do not "solve" it by making the SELECT policy using (true). Then every user can read every row in that table. PGRST116 itself is not a security problem. That shortcut is.

Check it is fixed
Test as a brand-new user with no row and as an existing user. Neither should throw PGRST116.

Full reference with the same steps: https://proofforge.live/errors/pgrst116 . If you are not sure whether your tables are open to the public, run the free outside check at https://proofforge.live

title: Kagelin v1.54.0: a keyboard-first focus timer and pickers that survive midnight
description:
Kagelin is a local-first task, habit and calendar app built on Next.js 16 with Supabase for sync. v1.54.0 removes friction from three common actions: starting a focus session, picking a date, and editing offline. Most of the work is only visible when it is missing.

Three changes are worth a closer look.

Focus mode should behave like a timer, not a page

The focus screen used to have one large play button and a lot of empty space. It now has a full shortcut set, handled by one window-level listener:

if (e.code === "Space" || e.key === " ") {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (state.isRunning) pause();
  else start();
  return;
}

if (e.key.toLowerCase() === "s" && !e.shiftKey) {
  e.preventDefault();
  skip();
  return;
}

if (e.key.toLowerCase() === "r" && e.shiftKey && isSessionActive) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setStopConfirmOpen(true);
  return;
}

if (e.key === "," && !e.shiftKey) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setSettingsOpen(true);
}

The handler bails out when focus is inside an input, textarea, select, or contenteditable, and when a dialog or popover is open. Space also yields to a focused button so it does not double-fire. The rest is conventional: s skips, Shift+R opens a stop confirmation, , opens settings, Esc leaves focus mode.

The bigger bug was how the timer calculated its total duration. Progress was computed from the current settings:

const totalSeconds = {
  focus: settings.focusDuration,
  shortBreak: settings.shortBreakDuration,
  longBreak: settings.longBreakDuration,
}[state.mode] * 60;

That works until someone changes the focus duration while a session is paused. The finish line moves, the progress bar jumps, and a paused session can look like it has more time left than it started with. The store now stamps the session length when the session starts:

sessionDurationSeconds:
  s.state.sessionDurationSeconds ??
  getDurationForMode(s.state.mode, s.settings),

and every consumer reads that stamp:

const totalSeconds =
  state.sessionDurationSeconds ?? getDurationForMode(state.mode, settings);

const isPausedMidSession =
  !state.isRunning &&
  (state.sessionDurationSeconds != null ||
    state.remainingSeconds < totalSeconds);

Settings changes now only adjust the displayed duration when the timer is genuinely idle. A paused mid-session timer keeps its original length, shows a PAUSED badge, and gets a muted progress fill instead of the brand colour.

The countdown also moved into the tab title. Running sessions show the remaining time and mode; paused sessions get a prefix:

if (isPausedMidSession) {
  document.title = `Paused (${formatMmSs(state.remainingSeconds)}) · Kagelin`;
}

The tab title makes the timer usable from another tab. Accessibility was the bigger gap: the old screen had no live region, so a screen reader user could not tell when a session started or when five minutes remained. There is now a polite live region that announces start, pause, five minutes left, one minute left, and completion. It deliberately does not announce every tick.

A date picker should not make you choose a date before choosing a time

The old picker disabled the Time tab until a date was selected. That is backwards for the common case: you know you want 3pm, and the date is the easy part. The Time tab is now always available, and opening it without a date defaults to noon today:

if (nextStep === "time" && !tempDate) {
  const todayNoon = new Date();
  todayNoon.setHours(12, 0, 0, 0);
  setTempDate(todayNoon);
}

The date step also gained four presets in a 2x2 grid, each with the weekday or time printed on the button: Today, Tomorrow, Next Week, Evening. The hint is generated, not hard-coded, so it stays correct as the week rolls over:

{ label: "Today", hint: format(new Date(), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Tomorrow", hint: format(addDays(new Date(), 1), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Next Week", hint: format(addDays(new Date(), 7), "EEE"), onClick: ... },
{ label: "Evening", hint: "6pm", onClick: ... },

On phones, the calendar event editor now uses a responsive dialog instead of a popover. The same DateTimeWizard component renders in both, but the mobile path gets a bottom sheet with a real title for assistive tech. A popover anchored to a field near the bottom of a phone viewport fights the virtual keyboard. The sheet does not.

Two smaller correctness fixes came with it. Changing an event's start date now preserves its duration instead of resetting the end to an hour later. And an end date before the start is clamped at submit time, so a bad range cannot be saved:

const clampedEndDate =
  safeEndDate.getTime() < safeStartDate.getTime()
    ? getDefaultEndDate(safeStartDate)
    : safeEndDate;

The time picker itself was rebuilt around accessible spinbuttons. Arrow keys increment and decrement hours and minutes, typing a digit moves focus between fields, and AM/PM is a real focus target. The old control was two styled boxes that looked like inputs but were not.

Offline replay needs order and identity

The offline queue was the least visible change and the one most likely to lose data. Mutations were persisted and replayed as a loose pool. A create and an edit of the same row could run in either order, so the edit could hit a row that did not exist yet, or the create could overwrite the edit.

TanStack Query already has the primitive for this: mutation scopes. Each mutation now declares a scope, and replays within a scope are serialized:

client.setMutationDefaults(["createTask"], {
  mutationFn: taskMutations.create,
  scope: { id: "tasks" },
});

The same is done for habits and calendar events. Creates also stamp a stable client ID at the moment the user acts, not when the network returns:

const tempId = input._clientId || crypto.randomUUID();
input._clientId = tempId;

That ID is reused as the row ID, so a retried create is idempotent. Without it, a create that succeeded on the server but failed on the response would be retried and produce a duplicate.

The second bug was dates. Habit start dates used to be filled in inside the mutation function:

start_date: input.start_date || new Date().toISOString().split("T")[0]

Two problems. toISOString() is UTC, so a local evening in a negative-offset timezone can already be tomorrow in UTC. And the value was computed at replay time, so a habit created at 23:55 and replayed at 00:05 got the wrong day even in UTC. The date is now captured when the mutation is enqueued, using the local calendar:

const today = format(new Date(), "yyyy-MM-dd");
input.start_date = input.start_date ?? today;

Tasks, habits, habit entries and calendar events all have regression tests that create and edit offline, cross midnight, reconnect, and assert the original local date survived. The tests matter as much as the fix. The next person to touch the queue will otherwise reintroduce the bug.

Smaller changes

Vim selection used to be a border that vanished against some surfaces. It is now an inset ring plus a lighter row background, applied consistently to list rows and board cards.

There is a branded 404 page instead of the framework default (but needs more work), and production responses now send Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains. Telemetry consent and any queued events are cleared on sign-out and account switch, so a shared device does not inherit the previous person's choice.

Try to break it

The focus shortcuts are the part I most want stress-tested: Space while a button is focused, s inside an input, Esc with a dialog open, a paused session across a reload. The offline queue is the other: create something offline, edit it, cross midnight, reconnect. If the order or the date is wrong, I want the reproduction.

  • App: app.kagelin.app (guest mode works, no account needed)
  • Source: Achyuth072/kagelin
  • Full changelog: Settings, then What's new

title: GDOM: A Browser-Based Operations Console for GBase 8a
description:
GDOM (GBase Database Operation Manager) is the B/S-architected operations tool that GBASE ships for its China-domestically developed GBase 8a MPP database. Its goal is full-lifecycle operations coverage: visual monitoring plus cluster management, host management, health checks and alerting, so that running a cluster 7×24 costs less and breaks less often.

Most everyday gcadmin commands are available inside GDOM — running SQL, cluster locks, events and failover included. The notes below are based on GDOM 3.2Build2 from early December 2024, monitoring a local single-node setup; newer releases may differ.

From commands to a console

GDOM feature Equivalent command Notes
Cluster start / stop / restart gcware_services all start + gcluster_services all start Covers all three layers: gcware (management), gcluster (scheduler) and gnode (data)
Running SQL show processlist But across all coordinator nodes; click View SQL to see what a given connection is executing
Locks gcadmin showlock Direct equivalent
Inconsistent events gcadmin showdmlevent, showddlevent, showdmlstorageevent All three event types in one place
Failover gcadmin showfailover Direct equivalent

The original post also includes screenshots of the multi-cluster home page and the single-cluster monitoring view; only the extractable text is kept here.

The point of a console is not to replace the CLI but to aggregate across nodes. show processlist only shows the coordinator you are connected to, whereas GDOM presents every coordinator at once; DML, DDL and storage events, along with failover state, no longer require logging into each host to run gcadmin. When you are watching several gbase clusters at the same time, that aggregated view is usually the fastest route to the actual problem — and it is why a gbase cluster with many coordinators benefits more from GDOM than a single-node lab does.

title: I planted 15 bad pull requests to test my AI code reviewer. Here is what broke.
description:
An AI code reviewer told me "Merge After Fixes."

My tests said the PR was broken.

That gap is why I built CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted pull-request reviewer for Java and Spring Boot. The idea is simple: an AI opinion is not evidence.

  • Every finding is labeled: verified by rule, rule-based heuristic, AI finding with the code located, or AI inference.
  • An unverified AI claim cannot score above 60/100, however confident the model sounds.
  • The merge verdict comes from a policy you configure, not from the model.
  • With sandbox validation on, it runs the project's tests in Docker on the PR head and the base branch, so a failure is labeled "new in this PR" or "already there."

This post is not a sales pitch. It is about what happened when I stopped adding features and tried to break it.

The lab

I wrote 15 pull requests against a small Java project: SQL injection, command injection, path traversal, SSRF, XXE, a broken build, fake tests, and a few pieces of safe code that must not be flagged (a prepared statement, a path guard, a hardened XML parser). Then I ran every one through the real app, with a real AI provider and real Docker.

It found more problems in my own work than months of reading my own code. Here are five.

1. The AI contradicted its own verdict

The policy said Do Not Merge. The AI's summary, written before the policy ran, still said "Safe to Merge." Both were technically correct. Together they were useless.

The fix was a small reconciler: when the final recommendation is stricter than the AI's, the summary gets a line saying so and why.

CodeGuard decision: Do Not Merge. 5 finding(s) meet the blocking policy
(severity >= High, confidence >= 80, VERIFIED, category in [Security, Bug, Team Rule]).
The AI's own summary, written before the policy check and not a verdict: ...

Lesson: when a model and a rule engine both speak, the user needs to know who has the last word.

2. A regex silently skipped a bad test

One rule flags tests that assert a value the test itself stubbed:

PriceService prices = mock(PriceService.class);
when(prices.total(10.0, 2)).thenReturn(20.0);
assertEquals(20.0, prices.total(10.0, 2)); // can never fail

The analyzer first collects fields and locals that are mocks. To avoid counting a mock that is later reassigned to a real object, it used a "shadow" pattern roughly like this:

"\\s*=\\s*(?!(?:Mockito\\.)?mock\\s*\\()"   // assigned to something that is not a mock

Look at = mock(. The greedy \s* can backtrack and give back the space, so the lookahead then sees mock( (with a leading space), which is not mock(, and the negative lookahead passes. The mock was classed as shadowed and dropped. The tautology went unflagged.

The fix is one character:

"\\s*=\\s*+(?!(?:Mockito\\.)?mock\\s*\\()"  // possessive: no backtracking

I only found this because I had planted that exact test and it did not fire. A happy-path demo would never have shown it.

3. Every review re-downloaded Maven

Most of a four-minute review was the sandbox downloading dependencies, because each review starts a fresh docker run --rm. I added an opt-in named volume:

codeguard.validation.dependency-cache-volume=codeguard-deps

which becomes -v codeguard-deps-maven:/root/.m2 for maven: images (and the Gradle equivalent). Typical review time dropped to roughly one to two minutes.

It is opt-in on purpose: a shared cache means code in one PR could influence the dependencies of a later run. That is a trust decision for the person running it, not for me.

4. A 422 with no explanation

A review failed with a generic message. The log showed a 413 from the AI provider: on Groq's free tier, input tokens plus the reserved output tokens count against a per-minute cap. A big diff plus a 4,500-token reservation blew past 8,000.

Two fixes: the real cause now appears in the review message, and the docs explain the limit and the knobs (a smaller input budget, another model, or a paid tier). Errors that name their cause are a feature.

5. "Build failed" is not an answer

When a PR does not compile, the finding now quotes the compiler output, parsed from Maven's [ERROR] lines: file, line, and the missing symbol.

src/main/java/com/lab/CheckoutService.java:12: cannot find symbol (symbol: variable taxRate)

Keeping it fixed: a benchmark with a gate

Fixing five bugs is easy to undo by accident, so I added a frozen benchmark: 73 cases, split into a development set, a held-out set and a set of known gaps. A JUnit test replays the real pipeline (diff parser, deterministic checks, security flow analysis, test-quality rules, ranker, merge policy) with no AI and no Docker, and fails the build if a rule regresses or a compliant case gets blocked.

When I added the new security cases, it immediately caught a false positive of mine: "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM " + TABLE was flagged as SQL concatenation even though only a constant was joined. Fixed the same day, with a test.

Honest limits

  • The analysis is static and name-based, so it can miss indirect cases.
  • The benchmark uses planted cases. It proves the rules behave as designed. It does not measure accuracy on real-world code.
  • AI findings and fixes are advisory.
  • It is a source-code product you run yourself, not a hosted service.

What I would tell anyone building a dev tool

  1. Plant known-bad cases and known-good ones. False alarms get a tool muted.
  2. Test through the real app at least once. My unit tests passed while the product contradicted itself.
  3. Freeze a benchmark and make the build fail on regression, so improvement cannot quietly undo itself.
  4. Make failures explain themselves.

CodeGuard AI is self-hosted Java 21 and Spring Boot with full source. There is a public preview (README, screenshots, one real module with tests) on GitHub: https://github.com/ISabiTech16/CodeGuard-AI

If you review Java PRs: what would you want an AI reviewer to prove before you trusted it?

title: One rules engine, two languages
description:
CheX runs the rules of chess twice: once in TypeScript in your browser, once in Rust on the game's server. Both must agree on every move, every capture and every checkmate, down to the last byte. This post is about how the game keeps two engines in two languages saying exactly the same thing.

Why write the rules twice

Online chess has a trust problem. If only your browser knew the rules, anyone could open the dev tools and teleport a queen. So the server has to be the referee: it checks every move and decides what the game looks like.

But a referee that lives 200 ms away makes the game feel slow. Every tap would wait for a round trip before a piece moved. So the browser needs to know the rules too, so it can show legal moves instantly and play your move the moment you make it.

The browser runs on TypeScript and the server on Rust, for speed and safety. So the game has one set of rules in two languages, and they must never disagree. If they did, the board you see and the game the server records would quietly drift apart.

One engine, designed to be copied

The trick is not clever translation. It is designing the engine so that a faithful copy is easy to write and easy to check. Three choices did most of the work.
1. The game is a pure function. The whole engine boils down to one function: gameReducer(state, action) → state. Same state and same move in, same new state out. No clocks, no randomness, no hidden globals. A pure function is easy to port, because there is nothing around it to port.
2. Every move is a list of small effects. A move does not change the board directly. It produces effects such as relocate, remove, transform (promotion) and spawn, and one small function applies them. Castling is two relocates. En passant is a relocate plus a remove. Both engines only need to agree on six effect types, not on every special case in chess.
3. Variants plug in as rule modifiers. CheX mods, like the knight that can leap like a camel, are not forks of the engine. A mod adds movement rules to a piece kind through one hook, and the engine treats them like the piece's own rules for moves, attacks and check. Charges and cooldowns live in the game state as plain data.
The result is about 1,300 lines of TypeScript and 1,700 lines of Rust, with the same files, the same functions and the same names on both sides. Reading them side by side feels like reading a translation with the original on the facing page.

Keeping them honest: TypeScript records, Rust replays

A copy is only as good as the test that checks it. The game's test is simple: TypeScript plays a game and writes down everything, and Rust has to reproduce it exactly.


A small script plays a game with the TypeScript engine and saves three things to a JSON fixture: the starting state, every action, and the full game state after each one. Each state is everything: the board, every piece, castling rights, the event log, even the mod charges left on each knight.
On the Rust side, a test loads that file, feeds the same actions through the Rust reducer and serializes each result back to JSON. Then it demands an exact match with what TypeScript wrote. Not "same position". The same JSON: the same fields, the same order of events, the same piece ids. If anything differs, the test fails and prints both versions side by side at the exact move where they split.
The test suite keeps two of these recorded games:

  • A classic game of 29 moves, checked at every single step.
  • A knight-camel game of 90 moves, ending with a rematch. The script picks camel leaps 70% of the time when one is legal, so charges, cooldowns and "used up" knights all get exercised. It is checked every 15 moves to keep the file small.

The moves come from a seeded random generator, so the same script always records the same game. When a rule changes, both engines change with it, the game is re-recorded, and the Rust test shows whether the copy is still faithful.

Parity only proves the two engines agree, not that they are right. For that, the Rust engine also runs perft, chess programmers' standard correctness test: count every legal position a few moves deep and compare with known answers. From the starting position that is 20, 400, 8,902 and 197,281 positions at depths 1 to 4. Four more tricky test positions, full of castling, en passant and promotions, are checked too.

What two identical engines do for the gameplay

Moves that never wait for the network. When you move a piece online, your browser runs the move through its own engine and shows it at once, before the server has even heard about it. Because the server runs the same rules, its answer lands on an identical state and silently replaces the browser's. In tests, your move appeared in about 18 ms, even with 600 ms of simulated lag. If the server ever disagrees, the browser rolls back to the server's version.

One message format for both sides. The browser and the server send each other the same game state JSON that the parity test compares. There is no translation layer to go wrong, because the format is the very thing the parity test checks.

Mods ship on both sides at once. Adding the knight-camel mod meant adding one movement rule to each engine and recording a new parity game. The day the Rust test went green, the browser and the server agreed on every camel leap, check and cooldown.

The cost is real: every rule change is written twice, and the fixture has to be re-recorded. For a game where trust and speed both matter, that is a good trade.

If you are building something similar

  • Make the core a pure function of state and action. It is the easiest code in the world to port and to test.
  • Shrink the surface the two sides must agree on. Small effects beat special cases.
  • Test the copy against the original, not against your idea of the original. Record real runs from one engine and replay them in the other, comparing the exact output.
  • Keep a separate correctness test like perft, so both engines are not just agreeing on the same mistake. Next time: how your move shows up before the server even knows about it.
