title: Which permission is missing, and what does it switch off? A pure function that keeps an Android app from ever feeling dead
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code. QuickDial is not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

QuickDial adds shortcuts around chat and phone calls on Android: open a chat from a typed number, a call button inside a chat, a chat button while a call is on. Those shortcuts need up to six things from the user, spread across system dialogs and Settings pages. The early complaint was blunt: users did not know they had to allow anything.

The fix was not more screens. It was one pure Kotlin object that answers three questions, and a rule that the app is never "dead".

A snapshot in, a plan out

No Android classes go in. A Snapshot is six booleans read by the permission checker elsewhere:

data class Snapshot(
    val canPostNotifications: Boolean,
    val hasOverlay: Boolean,
    val accessibilityEnabled: Boolean,
    val notificationAccessEnabled: Boolean,
    val hasContacts: Boolean,
    val backgroundRestricted: Boolean,
)

Because it is plain data, the order, the reduced mode and the reminder rule are all unit-testable on the JVM with no emulator.

The order is a design decision, so it lives in code 

fun items(s: Snapshot): List<Item> = buildList {
    add(Item(Kind.ALERTS, s.canPostNotifications, essential = false))
    add(Item(Kind.CONTACTS, s.hasContacts, essential = false))
    add(Item(Kind.ACCESSIBILITY, s.accessibilityEnabled, essential = true))
    add(Item(Kind.OVERLAY, s.hasOverlay, essential = true))
    add(Item(Kind.CALL_ACCESS, s.notificationAccessEnabled, essential = true))
    if (s.backgroundRestricted) add(Item(Kind.BACKGROUND, granted = false, essential = true))
}

Each choice has a reason that would otherwise be lost:

  • Notifications first. It is a single system dialog, and it is what lets the app tell the user later that something else is still off. Without it, a missing permission is silent for ever.
  • The two in-app dialogs next, then the accessibility service before the two Settings pages. Once the service is running it can bring the app back to the foreground after the user visits those Settings pages, so the guided flow does not strand them there.
  • The battery item is conditional. It is only listed when the system has actually restricted the app in the background. Testing showed that the Play install ran fine without an exemption; asking for one anyway adds a scary dialog for no benefit. The list is built from evidence of a real problem, not from a general worry.

Nothing is a gate

The most important function is the shortest:

fun workingFeatures(s: Snapshot): List<Feature> = buildList {
    add(Feature.OPEN_CHAT_FROM_NUMBER)
    if (s.hasOverlay && s.accessibilityEnabled) add(Feature.CALL_BUTTON_IN_CHATS)
    if (s.hasOverlay && s.notificationAccessEnabled) add(Feature.CHAT_BUTTON_DURING_CALLS)
}

With nothing granted, the list still has one entry: opening a chat from a typed number needs none of the six. That gives the UI an honest sentence for every state. Instead of "permissions required", the card can say which shortcut is on and which is off, and what to tap to turn the next one on. Each missing item switches off one shortcut, never the whole app.

Two features each need the overlay permission plus one other thing, which is why the conditions are combined rather than one flag per feature. If the user grants the overlay but not accessibility, the call button in chats stays off and the chat button during a call does not depend on it.

Reminders only for things that matter 

fun needsReminder(s: Snapshot): Boolean = missing(s).any(Item::essential)

Notifications and contacts are marked essential = false. A user who declines contacts is not nagged: they lose name matching, not a shortcut. A reminder goes out only while something that actually switches a shortcut off is missing, and it stops by itself the moment the last essential item is granted.

Tests worth writing

Because the object is pure, the useful tests are small tables:

  1. All six granted: missing is empty, needsReminder is false.
  2. Nothing granted: workingFeatures is exactly one item, never empty.
  3. Overlay granted but accessibility off: the call button in chats is absent.
  4. backgroundRestricted false: the list has five items; true: six.
  5. Order is stable: alerts first, accessibility before overlay.

The pattern is portable to any app with a permission ladder: a snapshot of booleans, a pure ordered plan, a "what still works" function that can never return empty, and a reminder rule that looks only at essential items.

QuickDial is not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

title: One tap from the notification shade: a Quick Settings tile that opens a photo picker, and the Android 14 API change it hides
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code.

Auto UPI QR reads a UPI QR from a picture and hands the link to the UPI app you already use. The usual way in is to open the app and press "Choose QR image". That is two steps too many for something you do while standing at a counter, so the app also ships a Quick Settings tile: pull down the shade, tap, and the photo picker is already open.

The tile is about thirty lines. Two things in it are worth writing down.

The service does almost nothing

A TileService is a service Android binds to when your tile is visible. It is the wrong place for real work, so the tile only forwards a tap to the Activity that already knows how to scan:

class PickTileService : TileService() {
    override fun onClick() {
        super.onClick()
        val intent = Intent(this, MainActivity::class.java)
            .setAction(MainActivity.ACTION_PICK_QR)
            .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP)
        // start the Activity and close the shade (see below)
    }
}

The manifest entry needs the BIND_QUICK_SETTINGS_TILE permission, an icon, a label and the QS_TILE intent filter. The user adds the tile themselves from the edit screen of Quick Settings; the app cannot place it for them.

The action string, ACTION_PICK_QR, is not special to the tile. The launcher long-press shortcut "Choose QR image" uses the same action. One entry point, three doors.

The Android 14 change: startActivityAndCollapse(Intent) is deprecated

A tile that starts an Activity also has to close the notification shade, or the Activity opens behind it. TileService.startActivityAndCollapse does both. On Android 14 (API 34) the Intent overload is deprecated and a PendingIntent overload takes its place, so the call has to branch:

if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 34) {
    startActivityAndCollapse(
        PendingIntent.getActivity(
            this, 0, intent,
            PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
        )
    )
} else {
    @Suppress("DEPRECATION")
    startActivityAndCollapse(intent)
}

FLAG_IMMUTABLE is required for a PendingIntent you hand to the system on current Android versions, and it is the right choice here because nobody needs to fill in extras later. The deprecated branch keeps older phones working; it is the only place in the app where the suppression lives.

The Activity side: cold start and warm start are different paths

The same tap reaches MainActivity in two ways. If the app is not running, the intent arrives in onCreate. If it is already open, CLEAR_TOP brings the existing instance forward and delivers the intent to onNewIntent. Both must open the picker:

// onCreate
if (savedInstanceState == null && intent?.action == ACTION_PICK_QR) {
    launchPicker()
} else if (firstLaunch) {
    showOnboarding()
}

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    if (intent.action == ACTION_PICK_QR) launchPicker()
}

The savedInstanceState == null check matters. When Android recreates the Activity after a rotation or after the process was killed, it replays the original intent. Without the check, the picker would pop open again every time the screen turned, for a user who had already chosen a picture.

Note also that the first-launch onboarding is an else if: someone who reaches the app through the tile on day one goes straight to the picker rather than past a tutorial they did not ask for.

The picker needs no permission

launchPicker() uses the system photo picker (PickVisualMedia, images only). The app never asks for access to the whole gallery; it receives the one picture the user selects. The tile only opens a chooser, nothing more, and what happens next is the ordinary scan and hand-off.

What I would tell myself before building it

  1. Keep the TileService a dumb forwarder; put the behaviour in an Activity action you can reach from other doors.
  2. Branch on API 34 for startActivityAndCollapse and keep the deprecated call in one suppressed spot.
  3. Handle both onCreate and onNewIntent, and guard the cold-start path with savedInstanceState == null.

Auto UPI QR is not a payment app: it finds the link in the picture and passes it to your UPI app. Always check the payee name before entering your UPI PIN.

title: I Built an Open-Source App Store on Top of GitHub Releases Using Rust and Tauri 2.0
description:
Installing great open-source desktop software usually means jumping from blog post to GitHub repository, scrolling past source tarballs in the Releases tab, guessing which .AppImage, .deb, .dmg, or .exe matches your CPU architecture, and repeating the whole routine manually when an update drops.

I wanted a single interface for that workflow, so I built Open Source Store: a cross-platform desktop app (100% Rust backend with Tauri 2.0 and a vanilla JavaScript + Vite frontend) that treats GitHub Releases as an app store catalog, complete with a live web demo you can open directly in the browser.

  • GitHub Repository: marlonferreira1800-hue/open-source-store
  • Live Web Demo (GitHub Pages): marlonferreira1800-hue.github.io/open-source-store
  • Desktop Installers (v0.1.3): GitHub Releases (Windows .exe/.msi, Linux .AppImage/.deb/.rpm, macOS .dmg)

Why build this instead of using an existing package manager?

Tools like winget, brew, apt, and flatpak are great once you already know what you want to install. They are less helpful when you want to browse visual apps by category, compare project activity and license metadata side by side, or grab the latest release of a smaller GitHub project that hasn't made it into a distro repo yet.

Open Source Store focuses on visual discovery plus direct release installs:

  1. Curated catalog (204 apps): Starts immediately with vetted projects across categories (Development, Utilities, Internet, Multimedia, and more), such as yt-dlp, uv, LocalSend, Logseq, and Ollama.
  2. Live GitHub Search: Searches any public repository on GitHub in real time and applies the store's safety checks before showing an install button.
  3. Local lifecycle tracking: Tracks downloaded apps in installed.json so you can see installed vs. available apps, check for newer GitHub Releases, launch, update, or uninstall them from one tab.

Architecture and Technical Decisions

I kept the stack intentionally lean. The Rust backend (src-tauri/) compiles with opt-level = "s", LTO, and stripped symbols (the Windows NSIS setup binary in v0.1.3 comes out to 2.4 MB), while web/ uses Vite and plain JavaScript modules without a heavy UI framework.

1. Selecting the right release binary across OS and CPU architectures

GitHub Releases do not enforce a naming standard. One project publishes App-linux-amd64.AppImage, another publishes app_0.4.0_x86_64.deb, and both include .sha256 sidecar files and source archives in the same asset list.

In src-tauri/src/platform.rs, asset_score inspects every asset name, filters out source archives and checksum/signature files (.sha256, .sha1, .sha512), rejects mismatched operating systems and architectures (x64 vs. arm64), and scores native installers by preference (for example .msi/.exe on Windows, .AppImage/.deb/.rpm on Linux, .dmg on macOS).

2. Enforcing a 5-gate curation and safety policy

Pointing a downloader at arbitrary GitHub search results carries obvious risks. Every repository and release goes through rules defined in data/curation-policy.json and enforced in src-tauri/src/catalog.rs:

  • Activity and adoption thresholds: Curated entries require at least 3,000 stars, 180 days of repository history, 365 days of owner account age, 3+ releases, and 5,000+ release downloads. Live search uses lighter thresholds (1,000+ stars, 90+ days, 500+ downloads).
  • License allowlist: Accepts recognized open-source licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-*, LGPL-*, BSD-*, MPL-2.0, ISC, etc.).
  • Repo, keyword, and non-app filters: Excludes awesome-lists, documentation-only repos, blocked keywords, and repos without matching platform binaries.
  • Dangerous asset checks: Rejects unsafe asset extensions before offering a download.
  • Strict host allowlisting: Download URLs and HTTP redirects must stay on HTTPS github.com or githubusercontent.com domains.

3. Safe redirects, streaming progress, and SHA-256 checks

GitHub Release downloads bounce through CDN redirects on githubusercontent.com. Rather than letting reqwest follow arbitrary external redirects, src-tauri/src/downloader.rs uses a custom redirect policy that checks every hop, streams bytes to disk while emitting Tauri download-progress events (with cancellation via tokio::sync::watch), and verifies the SHA-256 digest when GitHub reports one on the release asset:

let client = reqwest::Client::builder()
    .user_agent("open-source-store/0.1")
    .redirect(reqwest::redirect::Policy::custom(|attempt| {
        if attempt.previous().len() > 8 {
            attempt.error("Excesso de redirecionamentos")
        } else if is_safe_redirect_url(attempt.url()) {
            attempt.follow()
        } else {
            attempt.error("Redirecionamento bloqueado para domínio externo ao GitHub")
        }
    }))
    .build()?;

4. Handling GitHub API rate limits and the web preview

Unauthenticated requests to the GitHub API cap at 60 requests per hour per IP. Polling 200+ repositories on startup would hit that wall immediately.

To keep startup snappy without requiring a token:

  • The app bundles an embedded snapshot (data/catalog-seed.json) so the initial catalog loads instantly in both desktop and GitHub Pages web mode.
  • The desktop backend caches fetched API responses locally in catalog_cache.json with a 30-minute TTL.
  • Users who do heavy live searching can optionally save a personal GitHub token (save_github_token) in the sidebar settings.

The GitHub Pages deployment reuses the exact same web/ interface with a browser API fallback: you can browse the seeded catalog, inspect security scores and metadata, and run live GitHub searches without installing anything. Only downloading, installing, and updating local apps require the desktop Tauri binary (and the UI tells you when an action is desktop-only).

Try it and help shape what comes next

You can explore the catalog in your browser right now at marlonferreira1800-hue.github.io/open-source-store or download the v0.1.3 installer from GitHub Releases.

The project is MIT-licensed and very early (v0.1.3). I would especially love feedback on:

  • Linux and macOS testing: I develop primarily on Windows, so real-world test reports for the .AppImage, .deb, .rpm, and .dmg packages (and platform.rs asset matching edge cases) are super helpful.
  • Catalog curation: Are there essential open-source desktop apps missing from data/curated.json?
  • Security model: Ideas for tighter signature verification or sandboxed installs.

If this looks useful to you, check out CONTRIBUTING.md, open an issue, or drop a comment below with what you'd expect from a GitHub-powered open-source app store.

title: Why CSS 1in = 96px Is Not 1 Physical Inch (Building a True 1:1 Screen Ruler in React)
description:
If you have ever tried setting width: 1in; or width: 10cm; in CSS and held a physical ruler up to your monitor, you probably noticed something frustrating: it is almost never 1 physical inch.

On a 27-inch 4K monitor, a 13-inch MacBook Air, and a 6.7-inch Android phone, 1in in CSS can be off by 15% to 45%.

Here is why browsers cannot reliably report physical millimeters out of the box, and how we built a true 1:1 actual-size online ruler and ring sizer in React using ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit-card PPI calibration.

Why 1in, 1cm, and window.devicePixelRatio Cannot Give True Physical Size

According to the W3C CSS Values and Units specification, 1in is locked to exactly 96 CSS pixels (1cm = 37.795px, 1mm = 3.7795px).

Wait - what about window.devicePixelRatio?
devicePixelRatio only tells you how many hardware pixels map to 1 CSS pixel (for example, 2 on Retina displays or 2.75 on high-DPI phones). It still does not tell JavaScript the physical diagonal size of the monitor or phone glass in inches!

Browsers deliberately omit raw physical display dimensions (EDID data) to reduce browser fingerprinting. As a result:

Display CSS 1in Real Physical Size of 96 CSS px Error
Standard 24" 1080p Monitor 96px ~1.04 in +4%
13.3" MacBook Retina (2x) 96px ~0.84 in -16%
6.5" Smartphone (3x) 96px ~0.66 in -34%

So if you build a browser ruler using static CSS cm or in units, it will be visibly wrong on almost every laptop and smartphone.

The Reliable Fix: ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 Credit-Card Calibration

Almost every person on Earth has a globally standardized physical reference object in their wallet: a standard bank card, debit card, or ID card.

Under the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 international standard, every standard payment card has the exact same physical width:

  • Width: 85.60 mm (8.56 cm / 3.370 inches)
  • Height: 53.98 mm (5.398 cm / 2.125 inches)

Instead of guessing the user's screen PPI, let the user hold a bank card flat against the screen and drag a slider until an on-screen card box matches the physical card edge-to-edge.

Once cardWidthPx matches 3.37 physical inches, calculating the exact effective CSS Pixels Per Inch (PPI) takes one line of math:

const STANDARD_CARD_INCHES = 3.37; // 85.60 mm (ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1)

export function calculateEffectivePpi(cardWidthPx: number): number {
  return cardWidthPx / STANDARD_CARD_INCHES;
}

From that single calibrated ppi number, every physical unit becomes exact on that display:

export function pxToPhysical(px: number, ppi: number) {
  const inches = px / ppi;
  return {
    inches: Number(inches.toFixed(2)),
    cm: Number((inches * 2.54).toFixed(2)),
    mm: Number((inches * 25.4).toFixed(1)),
  };
}

Persist that calibrated ppi in localStorage, and the user only ever has to calibrate once per device:

const STORAGE_KEY = "omnitools_ruler_ppi";

export function loadSavedPpi(): number {
  try {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    const parsed = saved ? parseFloat(saved) : NaN;
    return Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed >= 40 && parsed <= 300 ? parsed : 96;
  } catch {
    return 96;
  }
}

(Clamping between 40 and 300 prevents corrupted storage values from breaking the UI.)

Bonus Use Case: An On-Screen Ring Size Finder (US, UK, and India Sizes)

Once you know the true ppi of a screen, you can measure more than straight lines. You can render a calibrated circle where the user places an existing ring directly onto their phone or laptop glass and adjusts the circle diameter until it aligns with the inside edge of the ring:

interface RingSizeEntry {
  mm: number;
  us: string;
  uk: string;
  india: string;
}

const RING_SIZES: RingSizeEntry[] = [
  { mm: 14.9, us: "4", uk: "H", india: "8" },
  { mm: 15.7, us: "5", uk: "J 1/2", india: "10" },
  { mm: 16.5, us: "6", uk: "M", india: "12" },
  { mm: 17.3, us: "7", uk: "O", india: "14" },
  { mm: 18.2, us: "8", uk: "Q", india: "17" },
  { mm: 19.0, us: "9", uk: "S", india: "19" },
  { mm: 19.8, us: "10", uk: "T 1/2", india: "22" },
  { mm: 20.6, us: "11", uk: "V 1/2", india: "25" },
];

export function matchRingSize(diameterPx: number, ppi: number) {
  const diameterMm = (diameterPx / ppi) * 25.4;
  const closest = RING_SIZES.reduce((prev, curr) =>
    Math.abs(curr.mm - diameterMm) < Math.abs(prev.mm - diameterMm) ? curr : prev
  );
  return { diameterMm: Number(diameterMm.toFixed(1)), closest };
}

3 Frontend Edge Cases to Watch Out For

  1. Browser Zoom (Ctrl + / Ctrl -): Remind users to keep browser zoom at 100% during calibration and measurement, because zooming scales CSS pixels without changing localStorage.
  2. Prevent Accidental Text Selection While Dragging Markers: Add select-none (user-select: none) and touch-action: none on draggable measurement handles so mobile Safari/Chrome does not scroll the viewport while dragging a marker.
  3. Sub-Pixel Rendering for 1mm Ticks: On standard displays, 1mm is roughly 3.78px. Always compute tick positions from mm * (ppi / 25.4) instead of rounding each step cumulatively, otherwise rounding drift compounds to 2-3mm across a 15cm ruler!

Try the Live Browser Implementation

We built this full calibrated ruler, dual red/blue measurement markers (horizontal and vertical), and US/UK/India ring sizer completely client-side with zero tracking or app downloads:

  • Online Ruler (Actual Size 1:1 + Ring Size Finder): https://omnitools.net/tools/online-ruler
  • Unit Converter (Length, Weight, Temp & Storage): https://omnitools.net/tools/unit-converter

Have you ever run into CSS physical-unit bugs on HiDPI screens or print stylesheets? Drop your experience in the comments!

title: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production
description:
Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier and ESLint with a single Rust-powered formatter and linter, but the migration exposes formatting edge cases that break diffs, missing rule coverage for React and accessibility plugins, and configuration translation pitfalls that stall teams mid-sprint. Developers who switch without mapping these gaps face silent behavior changes, thousands of lines of formatting churn in pull requests, and broken CI pipelines that reject commits the old tooling accepted.

A migration starts, hits formatting drift, and fails with broken diffs and CI rejections

The correct approach maps the differences before the migration starts, documents the missing plugins, and stages the rollout to isolate formatting changes from functional commits.

A migration maps gaps first, stages formatting changes, and completes cleanly

Key Takeaways

  • Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier's formatter and a subset of ESLint's rules, but React-specific linting (like eslint-plugin-react) and accessibility checks (like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y) remain gaps as of late 2026.
  • Edge-case formatting differences between Biome and Prettier include line-break decisions in complex JSX expressions, trailing-comma placement in function parameters, and quote-escaping in template literals, all of which surface as thousands of changed lines in the first formatting commit.
  • Configuration translation from .prettierrc and .eslintrc to the configuration file requires manual mapping of formatter options and an audit of which ESLint rules Biome does not yet cover, with the remainder staying in a minimal ESLint config.
  • Performance benchmarks show Biome running 2-5x faster than Prettier alone and 10-15x faster than ESLint plus Prettier combined on codebases over 100,000 lines, but the speed gain matters only if the missing rules do not force teams to keep both tools running in parallel.
  • Production readiness depends on the project: greenfield TypeScript projects with no React-specific linting needs are safe to migrate immediately, while existing React codebases require a dual-tool setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for the React-specific rules) until Biome's plugin ecosystem catches up.

What Biome 2.0 Actually Replaces (And What It Does Not)

Biome 2.0 is a formatter and a linter, not a complete ESLint replacement. The formatter matches Prettier's output on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation, but the remaining 5% consists of edge cases that produce different line breaks, indentation, or quote usage. The linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules (unused variables, missing return types, dangerous equality checks) but omits the ecosystem-specific rules that ESLint plugins provide.

What Biome replaces:

  • Prettier's formatter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, and JSON
  • ESLint's core rules for syntax errors, unused bindings, and code smells
  • Import sorting (Biome includes a built-in import organizer)

What Biome does not replace as of version 2.0:

  • React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react (prop types, hooks rules, JSX accessibility)
  • Accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y (alt text enforcement, ARIA usage)
  • Testing library rules from eslint-plugin-testing-library (async utility usage, screen queries)
  • Framework-specific linters for Next.js, Vue, or Angular

The gap means teams migrating from a full ESLint setup will keep a minimal .eslintrc for the plugin rules Biome cannot cover, running both tools in CI.

Biome covers formatting and core linting but not React-specific or accessibility plugins

Formatting Differences Between Biome and Prettier: The Edge Cases That Break Your Diffs

The migration from Prettier to Biome produces a formatting commit that touches thousands of lines because the two tools handle edge cases differently. The differences cluster in four areas: JSX expression wrapping, trailing commas, quote escaping, and import sorting.

JSX Expression Line Breaks

Prettier wraps long JSX expressions at the opening brace when the expression exceeds the print width. Biome keeps the opening brace on the same line as the tag attribute and breaks at the first operator inside the expression.

Prettier output:

<Component
  disabled={
    user.role !== "admin" && user.permissions.length === 0
  }
/>

Biome output:

<Component
  disabled={user.role !== "admin" &&
    user.permissions.length === 0}
/>

The difference surfaces in every JSX file with complex boolean expressions.

Trailing Commas in Function Parameters

Prettier adds trailing commas to multi-line function parameters when the target is ES5 or higher. Biome omits the trailing comma in arrow function parameters unless the function has type annotations.

Prettier output:

const handler = (
  event: Event,
  context: Context,
) => {
  // ...
};

Biome output:

const handler = (
  event: Event,
  context: Context
) => {
  // ...
};

Quote Escaping in Template Literals

Prettier escapes quotes inside template literals when the string contains both single and double quotes. Biome leaves the quotes unescaped unless the template literal contains an expression.

Prettier output:

const message = `Error: "value" can't be null`;

Biome output:

const message = `Error: "value" can't be null`;

The difference appears identical in this example because Biome matches Prettier's default, but in strings with mixed quotes and expressions, Biome escapes differently.

Import Sorting Order

Biome sorts imports alphabetically within three groups: external dependencies, internal modules, and relative imports. Prettier does not sort imports unless a plugin like prettier-plugin-organize-imports is installed. Teams migrating from Prettier without the plugin will see every import block reordered.

Formatter JSX line break Trailing comma Quote escaping Import sorting
Prettier At opening brace Always in ES5+ Escapes mixed quotes Plugin-dependent
Biome At first operator Omits unless typed Escapes in expressions Built-in alphabetical

The migration strategy isolates the formatting commit in a separate pull request with a title like "chore: migrate to Biome formatter" and no functional changes. Reviewers skip the diff and verify the build still passes.

A migration run exposes formatting drift, isolates changes in a formatting PR, and merges cleanly

Migration Gotchas: Configuration Translation, Git History, and CI Pipeline Changes

The migration from Prettier and ESLint to Biome requires translating configuration files, updating pre-commit hooks, and changing CI commands, all of which introduce points of failure.

Configuration Translation

Prettier stores options in .prettierrc as a flat object. Biome groups formatter options under a formatter key in the configuration file and uses different names for some settings.

Prettier config:

{
  "printWidth": 80,
  "semi": true,
  "singleQuote": false,
  "trailingComma": "es5"
}

Biome equivalent:

{
  "formatter": {
    "lineWidth": 80,
    "indentStyle": "space"
  },
  "javascript": {
    "formatter": {
      "semicolons": "always",
      "quoteStyle": "double",
      "trailingCommas": "es5"
    }
  }
}

The printWidth option becomes lineWidth, and the quote and semicolon settings move into a nested javascript.formatter object. ESLint rules translate to Biome's linter.rules object, but only the rules Biome supports. Teams must audit their .eslintrc and extract the unsupported rules into a separate minimal ESLint config.

Git History Preservation

A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs. Without this step, every line's last edit shows the formatting commit instead of the functional change.

Create .git-blame-ignore-revs:

# Migrate to Biome formatter
a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0

Configure git to use the ignore file:

git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

CI Pipeline Changes

CI pipelines running prettier --check . and eslint . must switch to biome ci or split into biome check and a minimal eslint command for the remaining rules.

Before migration (GitHub Actions):

- name: Check formatting
  run: npx prettier --check .

- name: Lint
  run: npx eslint .

After migration:

- name: Check formatting and lint
  run: npx @biomejs/biome ci

- name: Lint React rules
  run: npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json .

The biome ci command runs the formatter check and linter in a single pass, failing if either finds an issue.

A pipeline translates config, updates hooks, adds blame ignore, and switches CI commands

Rule Gaps and Missing Plugins: What Biome Still Cannot Cover in 2026

Biome's linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules but misses the ecosystem-specific checks that ESLint plugins provide. The gaps fall into three categories: React-specific rules, accessibility checks, and testing library rules.

React-Specific Rules

The eslint-plugin-react package enforces prop types, hooks dependencies, and JSX best practices. Biome does not replicate these rules as of version 2.0. Teams relying on hooks dependency checks (like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps) must keep ESLint installed.

Missing rules include:

  • react/prop-types: enforces prop type validation
  • react-hooks/rules-of-hooks: enforces hooks are called in the correct order
  • react-hooks/exhaustive-deps: warns when effect dependencies are incomplete
  • react/jsx-key: requires keys in list items

Accessibility Checks

The eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y package enforces ARIA roles, alt text on images, and keyboard navigation. Biome does not include these checks. Projects with accessibility requirements must run ESLint with the jsx-a11y plugin in parallel.

Missing rules include:

  • jsx-a11y/alt-text: requires alt text on images
  • jsx-a11y/aria-role: enforces valid ARIA roles
  • jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events: requires keyboard handlers alongside click handlers

Testing Library Rules

The eslint-plugin-testing-library package enforces best practices for React Testing Library, such as using screen queries and avoiding waitFor with side effects. Biome does not cover these rules.

Missing rules include:

  • testing-library/await-async-queries: requires await on async queries
  • testing-library/no-wait-for-side-effects: disallows side effects inside waitFor
Plugin Rules Biome covers Rules requiring ESLint
eslint-plugin-react None All React-specific
eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y None All accessibility
eslint-plugin-testing-library None All testing rules

The workaround is a dual-tool setup: Biome handles formatting and core linting, ESLint handles the plugin rules.

A codebase runs Biome for core checks and ESLint for React-specific rules

Real Migration: Step-by-Step Conversion Without Breaking Your Team's Workflow

The migration follows a staged rollout: install Biome, run the formatter once, translate the config, and update CI.

Step 1: Install Biome

Install Biome as a dev dependency:

npm install --save-dev @biomejs/biome

Step 2: Run the Formatter Once

Run the formatter to see the diff:

npx @biomejs/biome format --write .

Commit the formatting changes in a separate pull request with no functional changes.

Step 3: Translate Configuration

Create the configuration file from .prettierrc and .eslintrc:

{
  "formatter": {
    "lineWidth": 80
  },
  "javascript": {
    "formatter": {
      "semicolons": "always",
      "quoteStyle": "double",
      "trailingCommas": "es5"
    }
  },
  "linter": {
    "enabled": true,
    "rules": {
      "recommended": true
    }
  }
}

Extract the unsupported ESLint rules into .eslintrc.react.json:

{
  "extends": ["plugin:react/recommended"],
  "rules": {
    "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps": "warn",
    "jsx-a11y/alt-text": "error"
  }
}

Step 4: Update Pre-Commit Hooks

Replace Prettier and ESLint in pre-commit hooks with Biome:

Before:

{
  "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}": [
    "prettier --write",
    "eslint --fix"
  ]
}

After:

{
  "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}": [
    "biome check --apply .",
    "eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json --fix"
  ]
}

Step 5: Update CI Commands

Replace Prettier and ESLint in CI with Biome:

- name: Check formatting and lint
  run: npx @biomejs/biome ci

- name: Lint React rules
  run: npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json .

Step 6: Add Git Blame Ignore

Add the formatting commit hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs and configure git to use it:

git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

The staged rollout isolates failures to individual steps, making rollback straightforward.

Migration workflow diagram

Performance Benchmarks: Does Biome 2.0 Actually Save Time in Large Codebases

Biome's Rust implementation runs faster than Prettier's JavaScript and ESLint's Node.js runtime, but the speed difference matters only if the team is not forced to run both tools in parallel.

Benchmark Setup

The benchmark uses a TypeScript monorepo with 120,000 lines of code across 400 files. The machine is a MacBook Pro M2 with 16GB RAM. Each tool runs three times, and the median time is recorded.

Tool Median time Relative speed
Prettier alone 4.2s 1x
ESLint alone 12.8s 3x slower
Prettier + ESLint 17.0s 4x slower
Biome (format + lint) 1.1s 3.8x faster
Biome + ESLint (React) 13.9s 1.2x faster

Biome alone is 3.8 times faster than Prettier alone and 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint. When teams keep ESLint for React rules, the combined time drops to 13.9 seconds, only 1.2 times faster than the original setup.

The speed gain is real when Biome replaces both tools, but projects with React-specific linting needs see a smaller benefit because ESLint still runs.

A benchmark compares Prettier alone, ESLint alone, both together, Biome alone, and Biome with ESLint

Performance benchmark chart

Production Readiness Verdict: When to Migrate and When to Wait

Biome 2.0 is production-ready for projects that do not depend on ESLint plugins, specifically greenfield TypeScript codebases and backend services. React projects or any codebase requiring accessibility checks must run Biome alongside ESLint, which reduces the speed benefit.

Migrate immediately if:

  • The project is TypeScript-only with no React or framework-specific linting needs
  • The team can tolerate a one-time formatting commit that touches thousands of lines
  • CI performance matters and the team is willing to maintain the configuration file instead of .prettierrc and .eslintrc

Wait if:

  • The codebase relies on React-specific rules like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps or accessibility checks from jsx-a11y
  • The team cannot isolate a formatting commit or preserve git blame history
  • The CI pipeline is already fast enough that saving 10-15 seconds per run does not justify the migration effort

For teams in the middle, the hybrid setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for plugin rules) works as a stepping stone until Biome's ecosystem catches up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Biome 2.0 produce identical output to Prettier?

Biome matches Prettier on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation, but edge cases like JSX line breaks, trailing commas, and import sorting differ. The first formatting commit shows the differences.

Can Biome replace ESLint entirely in a React project?

No. Biome does not cover React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react or accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y. React projects must keep ESLint running with a minimal config for the missing rules.

How much faster is Biome than Prettier and ESLint combined?

Benchmarks on a 120,000-line codebase show Biome running 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint when it replaces both. When ESLint stays in the pipeline for React rules, the combined time is only 1.2 times faster than the original setup.

What happens to git blame after a formatting commit?

A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs. Configure git to use the ignore file with git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs.

Is the Biome configuration format stable?

The configuration schema is stable as of version 2.0 according to the Biome configuration documentation, but the nesting structure differs from Prettier's flat .prettierrc. Teams must translate the config manually.

Biome 2.0 delivers on the speed promise but not the full ESLint replacement. Greenfield TypeScript projects gain a faster, simpler toolchain. React projects gain faster formatting but keep ESLint for the gaps. The migration is a tradeoff: less tooling complexity and faster CI in exchange for maintaining a dual-tool setup until the ecosystem catches up. Projects that can live with the gaps should migrate now. Projects that cannot should wait for the React plugin support or accept the hybrid setup as the new baseline.

title: How to Build Unified Bid Request Mapping Systems for Multiple DSP and SSP Integrations
description:
Here's the specific trap every AdTech platform integrating multiple partners walks into. The spec says OpenRTB 2.6. The integration docs from 15 SSPs and 40 DSPs all cite OpenRTB 2.6 compliance. You code against the spec, ship the integration, and discover that every single partner interprets the spec slightly differently. Content taxonomy versions drift, impression ID formats clash, user ID arrays arrive in four different shapes, geo fields contradict each other, and video placement types mean different things on different exchanges.

Modern OpenRTB Development teams building unified bid request mapping systems solved this years ago. The engine normalizes incoming requests from every SSP into a canonical internal schema, enriches with missing fields, routes to DSPs in each DSP's preferred dialect, and handles version drift per integration. Platforms running on "spec compliant" integrations without a proper mapping layer burn impressions on field mismatches and lose fill every single day.

That's not a documentation problem. That's a specific engineering problem. The 2026 reality is that OpenRTB 2.6 is the live spec across most exchanges, OpenRTB 3.0 adoption is slow-rolling, and every major partner carries protocol extensions, deprecated field handling, and custom interpretations. Platforms engineering proper mapping middleware integrate 50+ partners cleanly. Platforms treating OpenRTB as a universal translator eat integration bugs quarterly.

Why OpenRTB Isn't a Universal Translator

The OpenRTB spec is a specification document. It is not a wire protocol validator, not a field dictionary enforcer, not a behavior guarantee. Every partner's implementation sits somewhere inside the spec's permissible interpretations, and the overlap between any two implementations is smaller than engineers expect.
The commercial cost shows up at scale. A field a DSP requires that your SSP doesn't send drops that DSP's bids entirely. A video placement type you send wrong gets filtered pre-auction. A deal ID formatted differently from the partner's expectation doesn't match. Each of these failures looks like "low fill" in the dashboard; the actual cause is mapping, not demand.

The Specific 5 Mapping Challenges

IAB Content Taxonomy Version Drift
IAB Content Taxonomy 1.0 (categories like IAB2-3), 2.0 (hierarchical with underscore separators), and 2.2 (current stable) all live in parallel across partners. Some SSPs send 1.0 codes, some send 2.2, some send both in different fields. The mapping layer maintains a translation table across versions and normalizes to the canonical internal version before routing to buyers.

IAB Taxonomy 1.0, 2.0, 2.2 all live in parallel:Translation table per direction.
Canonical internal version normalization: One schema inside, dialects at the edges.

Impression ID Normalization

OpenRTB imp[0].id is the standard. Some SSPs put correlation IDs in bid request ext fields, some use their own impression identifiers for post-auction reconciliation. The mapping layer preserves the original SSP-side ID for win notification, stores the canonical internal ID for cross-partner tracking, and maps both directions for billing reconciliation.

User ID Mapping Across EIDs Array**

Post-cookie, user identity flows via the OpenRTB EIDs array carrying UID2, ID5, LiveRamp RampID, EUID, Google PPID, and dozens of proprietary identifiers. Each DSP accepts different EIDs, with different hashing expectations, different source field requirements, and different fallback behavior when IDs are missing. The mapping layer normalizes incoming EIDs, enriches via ID bridges where available, and formats outgoing EIDs per DSP expectations.
EIDs array carries UID2, ID5, RampID, EUID, Google PPID: Each DSP accepts a subset.
Enrichment via ID bridges fills gaps: Where deterministic links exist.

Geo Enrichment and Field Discrepancy

Country codes arrive as ISO 3166 alpha-2 (US) or alpha-3 (USA) depending on partner. Postal codes come as 5-digit, 9-digit, or alphanumeric international. DMA codes versus metro codes versus city names versus lat/long coordinates all show up. The mapping layer standardizes to a canonical geo schema, enriches missing fields via MaxMind GeoIP2 or IP2Location where the request is under-specified, and formats per DSP preference.

Video Spec Translation and Placement Semantics

OpenRTB video objects carry mimes, protocols, playbackmethod, placement (deprecated in 2.6), plcmt (the 2.6 replacement), api frameworks (VPAID 2.0, OMID 1.0), and dozens of other fields. The placement vs plcmt transition is still mid-rollout across exchanges. Some SSPs send only placement, some send only plcmt, some send OpenRTB DSP Integration both with conflicts. The mapping layer handles both, normalizes to plcmt semantics internally, and sends whichever the target DSP expects.

Schema Registry and Version Management

The schema registry maintains canonical schema definitions, per-partner version tracking, and field deprecation warnings. Named tools: Confluent Schema Registry for Avro or Protobuf schemas, custom JSON Schema stores, or OpenAPI specs managed in version control. The registry becomes the source of truth for every adapter's input and output expectations, with automated contract testing catching integration drift before production.
Adapter-per-integration keeps mapping encapsulated: 5-10 days per onboarding vs 30-60 scattered.
Schema registry with contract testing catches drift: Confluent, custom JSON Schema, or OpenAPI.

title: Accept crypto payments in Spring Boot
description:
How to connect Moonvex to a Spring Boot 3 app: RestClient creates a checkout and returns the link to the page where the customer picks the coin, and the webhook controller receives the body as byte[], verifies the signature with javax.crypto.Mac and marks the order in a transaction.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. In Spring Boot inject them into application.properties from environment variables.

# application.properties — values come from environment variables
moonvex.secret-key=${MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY}
moonvex.webhook-secret=${MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET}

2. Create a checkout with RestClient

A RestClient (Spring Framework 6.1+) with the base URL and the Authorization header is built once. The request has no network, so Moonvex creates a checkout where the customer picks the coin and network. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl (https only) is where the Back buttons lead. The amount is BigDecimal.toPlainString(), never a double. The controller responds 303 with Location set to paymentUrl.

// MoonvexClient.java
@Service
public class MoonvexClient {
    private final RestClient http;

    public MoonvexClient(@Value("${moonvex.secret-key}") String secretKey) {
        this.http = RestClient.builder()
                .baseUrl("https://api.moonvex.org")
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, "Bearer " + secretKey)
                .build();
    }

    public JsonNode createCheckout(long orderId, BigDecimal amount, int attempt) {
        return http.post()
                .uri("/v1/payments")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "order-" + orderId + "-" + attempt)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(Map.of(
                        "orderId", String.valueOf(orderId),
                        "amount", amount.toPlainString(), // BigDecimal → "25.00", not a double
                        "currency", "USD", // no network: the customer picks the coin on the checkout page
                        "description", "Order #" + orderId, // shown as “You are paying for”
                        "returnUrl", "https://shop.example.com/orders/" + orderId)) // the Back buttons
                .retrieve()
                .body(JsonNode.class); // {"object": "checkout", "id": "inv_…", "paymentUrl": …}
    }
}

// PayController.java
@RestController
public class PayController {
    private final MoonvexClient moonvex;
    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public PayController(MoonvexClient moonvex, OrderRepository orders) {
        this.moonvex = moonvex;
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @PostMapping("/orders/{id}/pay")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> pay(@PathVariable long id) {
        Order order = orders.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
        JsonNode checkout = moonvex.createCheckout(order.getId(), order.getTotal(), 1);
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SEE_OTHER)
                .location(URI.create(checkout.get("paymentUrl").asText()))
                .build();
    }
}

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook.

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. A @RequestBody byte[] parameter receives the body without Jackson getting involved, and those are exactly the signed bytes. Signatures are compared with MessageDigest.isEqual and hex is parsed with HexFormat (Java 17+).

// MoonvexWebhookController.java
@RestController
public class MoonvexWebhookController {
    private final ObjectMapper json;
    private final OrderService orders;
    private final byte[] secret;

    public MoonvexWebhookController(ObjectMapper json, OrderService orders,
                                    @Value("${moonvex.webhook-secret}") String secret) {
        this.json = json;
        this.orders = orders;
        this.secret = secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    // byte[] gives the body as is, without Jackson conversion
    @PostMapping("/moonvex/webhook")
    public ResponseEntity<String> webhook(@RequestBody byte[] raw,
                                          @RequestHeader(name = "Moonvex-Signature", required = false) String signature) throws Exception {
        if (!verify(raw, signature)) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body("bad signature");
        }
        JsonNode event = json.readTree(raw);
        String type = event.path("type").asText();
        if (type.equals("payment.confirmed") || type.equals("payment.overpaid")) {
            orders.markPaidOnce(event.path("id").asText(), event.path("data").path("orderId").asText());
        }
        // payment.cancelled also arrives when the customer switches coins: do not cancel the order on it
        return ResponseEntity.ok("ok");
    }

    private boolean verify(byte[] raw, String header) throws Exception {
        if (header == null) return false;
        String ts = null;
        List<String> sigs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String part : header.split(",")) {
            String[] kv = part.split("=", 2);
            if (kv.length != 2) continue;
            if (kv[0].equals("t")) ts = kv[1];
            else if (kv[0].equals("v1")) sigs.add(kv[1]);
        }
        if (ts == null || !ts.matches("\\d+")) return false;
        if (Math.abs(Instant.now().getEpochSecond() - Long.parseLong(ts)) > 300) return false;

        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
        mac.update((ts + ".").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        byte[] expected = mac.doFinal(raw);
        for (String s : sigs) {
            try {
                // MessageDigest.isEqual is a constant-time comparison
                if (MessageDigest.isEqual(expected, HexFormat.of().parseHex(s))) return true;
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException ignored) {
                // not hex, skip it
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open. @Transactional plus INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: jdbc.update returns 0 on a redelivery.

// OrderService.java
// CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id text PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public OrderService(JdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void markPaidOnce(String eventId, String orderId) {
        int fresh = jdbc.update("INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", eventId);
        if (fresh == 0) return; // a redelivery
        jdbc.update("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = ? AND status <> 'paid'", Long.parseLong(orderId));
    }
}

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • With Spring Security, exclude /moonvex/webhook from CSRF (csrf.ignoringRequestMatchers) and allow it without authentication (permitAll).
  • Do not bind the webhook body to a DTO or a Map: after Jackson the bytes differ and the signature will not match.
  • Money is BigDecimal only; send toPlainString() in JSON so you never get 2.5E+1.
  • Move heavy work to @async or a queue: the webhook response must go out within 10 seconds.
  • Need one fixed coin instead of the customer's choice? Add network (and asset when currency is USD) to the same request, for example "network", "TRON", "asset", "USDT" in Map.of: that is the classic payment in one coin. The checkout above is the recommended flow.

FAQ

Can I use WebClient or OkHttp instead of RestClient?

Yes, the protocol is plain: POST /v1/payments with JSON and the Authorization: Bearer and Idempotency-Key headers. The example uses RestClient as Spring's own synchronous client.

Why is amount in the webhook higher than the order price?

The checkout returns your price as is in amount and currency. The payment the customer starts (data in webhooks) is in the chosen coin, and its amount is the total due including the Moonvex fee on top. Your price stays in pricing.amount, and what you receive on a full payment is in merchantAmount. Reconcile orders by orderId and pricing.amount.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

title: How Do You Pace Authorized Web Scrapers So You Stay Within a Site's Fair-Use Limits?
description:
Short answer

Pace an authorized scraper by making the client polite by default: one shared rate limiter, a concurrency cap, retries that honor Retry-After and exponential backoff, a cache so you do not refetch unchanged pages, and a hard stop when the site returns 429, 403, or a terms/robots disallow. Build this in Python around Playwright or HTTPX; use Rust only if you need a fast shared limiter or cache keyed on normalized URLs. Fair-use pacing is about staying inside the site’s published limits and your written authorization — not about looking like a human or bypassing a block.

Scope

This article is for sources you are allowed to collect: public APIs, official bulk downloads, or sites you have permission to access. It is not a guide to evading bot detection, rotating identities to dodge blocks, or ignoring robots.txt and terms of use.

If a target suspends or blocks you, stop and review the authorization and the rate. Do not add an automatic “recover and continue” path.

The pieces that matter

  1. A single limiter for the whole process, not a sleep() in one function and a free-for-all in another.
  2. Concurrency limits. Two or four workers are often enough. More workers can mean more 429s, not more throughput.
  3. Cache first. If you already have a fresh enough copy, do not hit the network.
  4. Backoff that listens. Honor Retry-After. Back off on 429 and 5xx. Give up after a fixed number of attempts and record the failure.
  5. A budget. Max requests per minute and per hour, with a default that is conservative. Make the cap configurable, and log when you hit it.

A shared limiter in Python 

import random, threading, time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, per_minute: int = 20, per_hour: int = 400):
        self.per_minute = per_minute
        self.per_hour = per_hour
        self._hits: list[float] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self) -> None:
        while True:
            with self._lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self._hits = [t for t in self._hits if now - t < 3600]
                last_min = sum(1 for t in self._hits if now - t < 60)
                last_hour = len(self._hits)
                if last_min < self.per_minute and last_hour < self.per_hour:
                    self._hits.append(now)
                    return
                wait = 60.0 if last_min >= self.per_minute else 3600.0 - (now - self._hits[0])
            time.sleep(min(wait, 30) + random.uniform(0, 0.5))

The jitter is only there to avoid a thundering herd when several workers wake at once. It is not a disguise.

Honor Retry-After and stop on a hard refusal 

import time
import httpx

def fetch(client: httpx.Client, limiter: RateLimiter, url: str, attempts: int = 5):
    for n in range(attempts):
        limiter.acquire()
        r = client.get(url, timeout=20, headers={"User-Agent": "ExampleCollector/1.0 (+contact@example.com)"})
        if r.status_code in (401, 403, 451):
            raise RuntimeError(f"stopped: HTTP {r.status_code} for {url}")
        if r.status_code == 429 or r.status_code >= 500:
            retry_after = r.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** n
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2 ** n
            time.sleep(min(delay, 120))
            continue
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r
    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts: {url}")

Identify your client honestly. Include a contact address in the user-agent if the project is long-running. Caching (ETag / If-None-Match, or a local table of URL plus fetched-at) belongs in front of fetch.

Check robots and your written scope before the first request

  • Read the site’s robots.txt and any published API limit. If a path is disallowed, skip it and log the skip.
  • Stay on the documented API or the pages you were authorized to use. Official bulk files (for example an FMCSA census download) are usually a better first choice than a page scrape.
  • Store a run log: start time, request count, 429 count, and when the limiter paused. That log is how you show the job was paced, and how you tune the cap downward if needed.

A small Rust helper can sit behind this if you want a process-wide counter that several Python workers share through a file or Redis-compatible store. The policy still lives in one place: requests per minute, requests per hour, and “stop on 403.”

When the site says no

Pause the job. Alert the operator. Do not rotate IPs, accounts, or sessions to continue. Recovery, if it happens at all, is a manual review of authorization, rate, and the site’s current terms.

FAQ

What default limits should I use?

There is no universal number. Start from the site’s documented cap if it has one. If it does not, start low (for example tens of requests per minute, not hundreds) and only raise the cap when the run log stays clean. This article does not publish a “safe” rate that will keep a site unblocked.

Is a random delay the same as fair use?

No. A random sleep does not replace a real budget, a concurrency cap, or Retry-After. Random delay is not a way to look like a person.

Should I use Playwright or a plain HTTP client?

Use a plain HTTP client when the data is in the response HTML or JSON. Use Playwright when the authorized source actually requires a browser. A browser is heavier; it still must go through the same limiter.

Can Rust help here?

Yes, as a shared limiter or a cache keyed on normalized URLs, especially if several workers run on one host. Python can still own the crawler, the parsers, and the run log.

What about personal data?

Collect only what you are allowed to store, keep a retention limit, and do not log raw personal fields in world-readable run files.

What this is not

This is not advice on bypassing access controls, CAPTCHAs, or blocks, and it does not claim that pacing will keep a SIM, IP, or account unblocked.

I'm Muhammad Afzal, a Rust and Python automation engineer at INDUS Web Agency.

title: A Developer's Quick Checklist for Messy Java Installs on Windows 11
description:
If you have ever switched between a university project, a Minecraft modding tool and a work codebase on the same Windows machine, there is a good chance you have more than one Java on it. Most of the time nobody notices. Then a build fails with a strange class version error, or a security advisory lands and you need to know exactly what is installed. Here is a short checklist to get a clear picture.

1. Find out which java actually runs

Open Terminal and run:

java -version

The first line is the version Windows uses when anything calls plain java. The next line usually names the vendor (Oracle, Microsoft, Temurin, Zulu and so on). Write down both the major version and the vendor.

Remember the two numbering styles: 1.8.0_xxx is Java 8 in the old format, while 11.0.x, 17.0.x or 21.0.x lead with the major version.

2. List every java.exe on your PATH 

where java

This prints every java.exe Windows can find on PATH, in the order it would use them. If you see three entries, the first one wins, and the other two are just sitting there. This is the single most useful command for "why is my terminal running the wrong JDK?"

3. Check JAVA_HOME separately

Many build tools and IDEs look at the JAVA_HOME environment variable instead of PATH. That means your terminal and your build can quietly use different JDKs. Check it with:

echo %JAVA_HOME%

(in Command Prompt) or $env:JAVA_HOME in PowerShell. If it points to a folder that no longer exists, or to a different major version than java -version reports, fix that first.

4. Cross-check Installed apps

PATH only shows part of the story. In Settings > Apps > Installed apps, search for "Java", "JDK", "OpenJDK", "JRE", "Temurin" and "Microsoft Build of OpenJDK", because each vendor names it differently. Older Oracle installs may show up as "Java SE" or "Java Runtime Environment".

5. Don't forget bundled runtimes

Some applications ship their own private Java. Those copies often don't appear in Installed apps and aren't on PATH, so neither command above finds them. You can't safely swap them yourself; the app's maker has to ship an update.

6. Decide what stays

A simple rule set:

  • Nothing needs it? Uninstall it. You can reinstall later if something complains.
  • A project needs a specific major version? Keep that one and keep it updated from the same vendor you installed it from.
  • Several versions you no longer use? Remove the extras from Installed apps.

After installing or removing anything, open a fresh Terminal window before re-running java -version. An old window can keep reporting stale results.

7. Update only from the vendor

Get updates from the vendor's own site: java.com for Oracle Java 8, Microsoft's download page for the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and adoptium.net for Temurin. Never trust a pop-up or ad saying "your Java is out of date".

This matters right now because of Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), which the OpenJDK advisory of 17 November 2026 lists for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds up to specific versions. TechGuide HQ's guide on how to check which Java versions are installed on Windows 11 includes the affected-version table and the vendor fixed builds, so you can compare your output against it instead of guessing.

Quick recap

java -version, where java, JAVA_HOME, Installed apps, bundled runtimes, then clean up and update from the right vendor. Five minutes, and your machine stops surprising you.

title: UI UX Design & App Development Services in Chicago
description:
Chicago has always been a city of builders. It rebuilt itself after the Great Fire, turned its rail yards into the crossroads of the country, and set prices for the world's grain from its trading floors. Today, a lot of that building happens on screens.

A bakery in Logan Square takes pre-orders through an app. A logistics company near O'Hare tracks its drivers in real time. A clinic in the Loop lets patients book a visit in three taps. Behind each of those experiences is a set of decisions about design, code, and how people will find the product in the first place.

What separates the apps people keep from the ones they delete after a week rarely comes down to a single feature. It comes down to how well three disciplines fit together: thoughtful design, solid engineering, and marketing that brings the right people through the door. This guide walks through how those pieces connect, what each one should include, and how to plan a digital product that earns a permanent spot on someone's home screen.

Why So Many Apps Struggle Before They Ever Launch

The most common mistake businesses make is treating design, development, and marketing as three separate purchases. One vendor designs the screens. Another builds them. A third gets hired after launch to "get the word out." Nobody talks to each other until something breaks.

Here is how that plays out. The designer delivers beautiful screens that turn out to be expensive to build. The developers cut corners to stay inside the budget. Then the marketing team arrives and discovers that no one ever defined who the app was for. Every team did good work on its own, and the product still struggles.

The fix is easy to describe and harder to execute: plan all three together from the very first conversation. When the people who will market your app join the discovery phase, they raise audience questions early. When developers review wireframes, they spot the feature that would double the timeline. When designers understand the acquisition plan, they build onboarding that actually converts the traffic marketing sends. Each discipline makes the others better, and that connection is the thread running through everything below.

What UI UX Design and Development Services Really Include

People often use "UI" and "UX" as if they mean the same thing. They don't. UX (user experience) is about how the product works: the flow from opening the app to finishing a task, and how easy or frustrating that journey feels. UI (user interface) is about how it looks and responds: the colors, type, buttons, spacing, and motion that make each screen clear.

Good UI UX design and development services treat these as one continuous process rather than a hand-off. Here is what that process should cover.

Research that shapes the product

Before anyone opens a design tool, someone should be talking to real users. That means short interviews, a look at competing apps, and a clear map of the main jobs your customers are trying to get done. A restaurant app, for example, might discover that regulars care far more about reordering a favorite meal in one tap than about browsing the full menu. That single insight changes the home screen, the navigation, and even the marketing message.

Prototypes you can test before you build

Changing a design in a clickable prototype takes hours. Changing it after the code is written can take weeks. That is why strong teams build interactive prototypes and put them in front of a handful of target users first. Watching five people try to sign up will reveal more problems than a month of internal meetings.

A design system developers can actually use

This is where design and development meet. A design system is a shared library of colors, type styles, and reusable components such as buttons, cards, and forms. When designers and developers build from the same library, the app stays consistent, new features ship faster, and future updates cost less. It is one of the clearest signs that a partner offers true design and development, not two separate services stapled together.

Accessibility from day one

According to the CDC, up to one in four adults in the United States lives with some type of disability. Designing for readable contrast, screen readers, larger text sizes, and simple navigation isn't a niche concern. It widens your market, improves the experience for everyone, and reduces legal risk, since accessibility claims tied to the ADA have become common for digital products. Building it in from the start costs far less than retrofitting it later.

What Strong Mobile App Development Services in Chicago Look Like

Once the design is tested and approved, the engineering work begins. This is where quality differences between providers become very visible, usually a few months after launch.

Choosing the right technology

You will typically choose between native apps (built separately for iOS and Android) and cross-platform apps (one shared codebase using a framework such as Flutter or React Native). Native development offers the best performance and deepest access to device features. Cross-platform development can reduce cost and speed up launch for many business apps. A trustworthy partner explains the trade-offs in plain language and recommends what fits your goals, not what their team happens to prefer.

Security and Illinois privacy rules

This is one area where hiring locally pays off. Illinois has the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), one of the strictest biometric privacy laws in the country. If your app uses fingerprints, face scans, or voice recognition, you need clear consent and careful data handling. Health apps also need to account for HIPAA, and any app that takes payments needs secure processing. Experienced mobile app development services in Chicago will raise these issues before they become expensive problems.

Building for growth

The back end, meaning the servers, databases, and APIs behind the app, needs to handle growth. If marketing succeeds and your user count jumps tenfold, the app should stay fast. That means planning cloud infrastructure, caching, and monitoring from the start rather than patching them in during a crisis.

Testing, launch, and life after launch

Real-device testing, app store submission, and review guidelines all take time. And launch is not the finish line. Apple and Google release major operating system updates every year, so apps need regular maintenance to stay compatible and secure. Ask any partner what their support looks like for the first year after launch.

Why a Chicago partner makes sense

Working with a team in your time zone makes collaboration easier. In-person workshops are possible when a big decision needs a whiteboard. A local team also understands the industries that power the Midwest economy, including logistics, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and food service, along with the customers they serve.

Getting Found: Where Digital Marketing Agency Services Fit In

An app no one can find is an expensive hobby. With millions of apps across the major stores, visibility has to be planned as carefully as the product itself. This is where digital marketing agency services connect directly to design and development work.

A strong marketing plan for an app usually includes:

  • App store optimization (ASO): writing titles, descriptions, and keywords, and designing screenshots so your listing ranks and converts in the App Store and Google Play.
  • Search engine optimization (SEO): building a fast, well-structured website and helpful content so people searching on Google find your product and your brand.
  • Paid campaigns: search ads, social ads, and app install campaigns aimed at clearly defined audiences, with budgets tied to real results.
  • Local visibility: for Chicago businesses, a complete Google Business Profile and neighborhood-focused content help you show up when nearby customers search.
  • Email and push notifications: thoughtful, permission-based messages that bring people back without annoying them.
  • Analytics: tracking that shows where users come from, what they do inside the app, and where they drop off.

Notice how much of this depends on design. App store screenshots are design work. Landing page speed is development work. Onboarding that turns a download into a loyal user is UX work. Marketing can send people to the door, but design and development decide whether they walk in and stay.

The Feedback Loop That Ties Everything Together

The real power of combining these services shows up after launch, when data starts flowing. Think of it as a loop that keeps improving the product:

  1. Design a focused experience based on user research.
  2. Develop it on a stable, secure, scalable foundation.
  3. Market it to the audience defined during research.
  4. Measure what users actually do, using analytics and reviews.
  5. Refine the design and code based on what the data shows, then repeat.

Say analytics show that half of new users quit on the third signup screen. A marketing-only agency would simply buy more traffic. A connected team asks a better question: why are people leaving? Maybe that screen asks for too much information too soon. The designer simplifies it, the developer ships the change, and the marketing budget suddenly goes much further. That is the difference between spending money on growth and building growth into the product.

What to Look For Before You Hire a Partner

Whether you are a startup with a first idea or an established company modernizing an old app, a few checks will save you time and money:

  • Look at their process, not just their portfolio. Ask how they research users and test designs before writing code.
  • Check that design and development share one roadmap. A shared design system and a single project lead are good signs.
  • Ask about privacy and compliance. They should bring up BIPA, HIPAA, or payment security on their own if your app needs them.
  • Make sure marketing is part of the plan. Launch strategy should be discussed before development is finished, not after.
  • Clarify ownership. You should own your code, designs, and accounts.
  • Understand post-launch support. Get maintenance, updates, and response times in writing.
  • Expect clear communication. Regular demos and plain-language updates matter more than technical jargon.

How InstaaCoders Brings It All Together

At InstaaCoders, we built our approach around the idea that design, development, and marketing work best as one team. Our UI UX designers, mobile developers, and digital marketers plan together from the first discovery session, so the app we design is the app we can build well, and the app we build is ready to be found.

We start with your users and your business goals. We prototype and test before we code. We build secure, scalable apps for iOS, Android, and the web. Then we help you reach the right audience and use real data to keep improving. Whether you need full mobile app development services in Chicago, focused UI UX design and development services, or digital marketing agency services to grow an existing product, our goal stays the same: build something people genuinely want to use.

Ready to Build Something Chicago Will Use?

Every great app starts with a clear conversation about who it serves and what it needs to do. If you have an idea, an outdated app, or a product that isn't growing the way it should, now is a good time to plan the next step.

Reach out to the InstaaCoders team to talk through your goals. We'll help you map out a design, development, and marketing plan that fits your budget and turns your idea into a product your customers come back to again and again.
