title: Track your brand in Google AI Overviews with Limelit Open and your own Apify account
description:
Limelit Open is an open-source, self-hosted tracker for "AI visibility": it asks ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI surfaces your prompts, and records whether your brand is named and which sites are cited. Each engine is reached through a provider you choose.

I added one more provider for Google AI Overviews: apify. It runs an Apify Actor on your own Apify account, so you pay Apify directly and the scraping capacity is yours. The pull request is limelit-co/open#72. It is not merged yet, so this post builds Limelit from my fork. When the PR is merged, the normal release works the same way.

Disclosure: I built the Actor this provider runs (Google AI Overview Scraper on Apify). It is a paid Actor; prices are on the Actor page. It returns US English results only.

1. Build Limelit from the fork

You need Go 1.25 or newer.

git clone --branch provider-apify https://github.com/krammer0/open limelit-open
cd limelit-open
go build -o ~/limelit/limelit ./cmd/limelit
cd ~/limelit && ./limelit serve

Open http://localhost:1515. The first visit starts the setup wizard.

2. Set up with only an Apify token

The wizard asks for your domain, competitors and prompts, then for one key.

  1. Brand: I used nerdwallet.com as an example.
  2. Prompts: I kept four:
    • best high yield savings account
    • best credit card for beginners
    • how to improve credit score fast
    • is a roth ira worth it
  3. Key: pick Apify and paste your Apify API token (Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations). Then press Connect and finish.

Connecting the key also adds the target ai_overview:apify. Every prompt becomes one Actor run.

3. Press Run

The server log for my run:

level=INFO msg="run finished" evaluation=1 completed=4 failed=0 took=33s

Four prompts, four AI Overviews, no failures, 33 seconds.

4. What came back

./limelit export writes everything as JSON. This is a summary of my export (2026-11-27):

prompt                               | sources | nerdwallet.com cited at | NerdWallet named
best high yield savings account      |    7    | position 1              | 2 times
best credit card for beginners       |    6    | -                       | 0
how to improve credit score fast     |   11    | -                       | 0
is a roth ira worth it               |   11    | position 10             | 0

For "best high yield savings account", NerdWallet's guide is the first source, and the answer names NerdWallet in the text:

... and NerdWallet highlights Capital One 360 Performance Savings (3.20% APY) for in-person branch/cafe access.

The other cited sources for that prompt were bankrate.com, usnews.com, everbank.com, sofi.com, marcus.com and ally.com. For the two credit prompts, NerdWallet is not cited at all. That is the kind of gap Limelit is built to show.

Each answer is stored with its full text and its sources, so the Answers and Citations pages show the evidence behind every number.

5. Ask Claude about it

Limelit has an MCP server. With Claude Code:

claude mcp add limelit -s user -e LIMELIT_DATA_DIR=$HOME/limelit/data -- $HOME/limelit/limelit mcp

Then ask: "How visible is my brand in AI answers, and which prompts am I losing?"

Notes

  • The provider sends each prompt as one query. Line breaks in a prompt become spaces.
  • A query where Google shows no AI Overview is stored as "no answer surface". Limelit leaves it out of every percentage instead of counting it as an answer that missed your brand.
  • The Actor covers US English only. Limelit returns an error before any request for other countries or languages.
  • The token stays in Limelit's encrypted settings store, or in the APIFY_TOKEN environment variable. It is sent only as a bearer header.

title: Multiple Brands: Why I Tie DNS Zone Ownership to Mail Reputation
description:
Give each media brand its own DNS zone when it has a separate team or sending-domain reputation; keep one zone when the names belong to the same product. During a move away from a registrar-specific API, the deciding constraint is whether published records still match each brand's approved intent. A long hostname list alone doesn't justify a split.

Short answer: use separate zones for independently operated publications and one zone for alternate names of the same product. I favor explicit brand-to-zone configuration and an inventory comparison before migration approval. That trades extra verification and rotation work for clearer ownership and an easier future brand sale.

Consider a publisher moving its newsletter and account-verification records away from a registrar-specific integration. This is a proposed architecture decision, not a production migration report. The homepage is only part of the review: an inventory that omits the records supporting mail leaves the most delivery-sensitive part of this move outside the acceptance decision. The useful evidence is a comparison of approved and observed records, attached to a brand, its responsible team, and an explicit zone identifier.

Should multiple brands share one DNS zone for mail reputation?

Mail reputation attaches to the sending domain. Creating a separate DNS zone establishes an administrative boundary; it doesn't itself establish a separate sending-domain reputation. That distinction matters when deciding between many hostnames in one zone and a zone per brand. Brands that send mail independently need their sending identities considered separately, with DNS ownership arranged to support that separation. Counting hostnames answers a different question.

I would separate zones for independently operated publications because their teams need clear ownership and because a publication may eventually be divested. A brand sale should not require someone to infer record ownership from naming conventions. For one publication marketed under several names, a shared zone can remain the better choice: the same team accepts the same mail responsibilities, and splitting adds verification and rotation work without a matching ownership benefit.

Budget that work.

The compliance concern is specific. Handover evidence should show which team approved the intended records and which zone was checked. A matching inventory establishes agreement between two inputs. It isn't a compliance certification or a promise that a newsletter or OTP will reach an inbox. DMARC, described in RFC 7489, belongs in the mail-authentication review; a zone-count decision can't substitute for that review.

The invariants that make drift reviewable

The first invariant is explicit zone configuration.

Never derive the zone identifier from a brand's display name. A rebrand should not silently change the destination of a DNS operation. When replacing a registrar-specific integration, changing the provider binding must be an intentional configuration change too. Keep the approved inventory attached to that binding so reviewers can identify what was checked, rather than reconstructing it from a later configuration.

The second invariant is that intended and observed inventories refer to the same brand and zone. A clean comparison against the wrong zone offers false reassurance. The third is that differences block approval until a responsible person reconciles them. Missing records, changed values, and unexpected records all deserve review; automatically deleting an unexpected entry would turn detection into an unreviewed change. Retain the comparison with the decision so a later owner can understand why the migration was approved.

Use 3 local review outcomes: missing, unexpected, and changed. These are application categories, not provider response fields.

The failure boundary is narrow. A comparison cannot prove that the observed inventory was collected correctly, that every resolver sees the same answer, or that mail authentication and delivery behave as intended. Those require separate checks. Treating matching TXT inventories as a complete deliverability test would leave a gap in both the newsletter and account-verification workflow.

Compare the integration boundary before choosing the provider

Record the zone decision separately from the API decision. A different DNS API does not determine whether two publications are one product. I would evaluate these real options against the same acceptance evidence. The table gives selection conditions, rather than claims about relative mail reputation or performance.

Option When I would shortlist it Trade-off and required evidence
Amazon Route 53 The intended owner wants DNS aligned with its AWS operating model. A direct integration accepts that provider dependency; require explicit brand-to-zone configuration and an inventory mapping.
Cloudflare DNS The intended owner chooses Cloudflare as its DNS administration boundary. Review the direct integration against the same drift check; the provider choice does not settle the brand split.
Google Cloud DNS The intended owner wants DNS administration aligned with Google Cloud. Cloud alignment is a selection condition, not a delivery guarantee; require the same ownership and record evidence.
Common capability API Swapping the vendor behind a capability keeps the application contract stable, without changing application code. One REST API uses plain HTTP, with no SDK to install. Public discovery requires no key and supplies request and response schemas. Runnable examples in 10 languages help the team review an inventory collector in its own runtime; adapter mapping and migration approval remain application responsibilities.

Direct-provider integrations are reasonable when the organization deliberately accepts that dependency. A common capability contract is useful when replacing the dependency is part of the requirement. The additional advantage here is discoverable request and response schemas: reviewers have a concrete contract to examine before approving an inventory adapter. Neither approach decides who owns a publication's records.

These are conditional recommendations. This comparison doesn't establish which provider has the best delivery, latency, or migration success rate. It asks which integration boundary the publisher wants to maintain, then requires every candidate to produce the same reviewable record evidence.

Infrai supplies one API key and one bill across backend services, with 295 routes across 20 modules. Its single REST API uses plain HTTP with no SDK required, so the publisher can keep a Python inventory collector without installing another vendor SDK. Swapping the provider behind a capability keeps the application code unchanged. For newsletter and account-verification flows maintained alongside DNS, the shared credential also reduces the separate keys and invoices the team must administer. The public, self-describing API and runnable examples in 10 languages address a different friction: a reviewer can inspect request and response schemas before granting access. That reduces the setup needed to assess an adapter; it does not remove the need to verify what its inventory means.

Keep approval separate.

Put the comparison on the approval path

This runnable Python example uses only the standard library. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS v1 API base. The read-only domain-list call prints its JSON without assuming an undocumented response shape. It uses 5 attempts and a 30-second request timeout as example settings, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, and surfaces other HTTP errors. No records are written.

The subsequent comparison uses illustrative local inventories, not the printed API response. An inventory adapter must translate the source and destination records into this local contract before the comparator can be used for an actual move. The TXT strings below are review markers, not SPF, DKIM, or DMARC configuration.

The example contains 2 intended records and 1 changed value. Those are fixture sizes, not production measurements. Its zone identifiers are application configuration placeholders, not provider-issued identifiers.

from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def read_domains():
    base = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
    if not base.startswith("https://"):
        raise ValueError("Use the documented HTTPS v1 API base")
    request = Request(
        base + "/dns/domain/list",
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
    )
    for attempt in range(5):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            delay = float(2 ** attempt)
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    requested = float(retry_after)
                except ValueError:
                    deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    requested = (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
                delay = max(delay, requested)
            time.sleep(delay)


def inventory(records):
    grouped = defaultdict(list)
    for record in records:
        key = (record["name"], record["type"])
        grouped[key].append(record["value"])
    return {key: tuple(sorted(values)) for key, values in grouped.items()}


def compare(brand, observed_zone, intended, observed):
    if brand["zone_id"] != observed_zone:
        raise ValueError("Observed inventory belongs to a different zone")
    wanted = inventory(intended)
    actual = inventory(observed)
    differences = []
    for key in sorted(wanted.keys() | actual.keys()):
        if key not in actual:
            differences.append(("missing", key))
        elif key not in wanted:
            differences.append(("unexpected", key))
        elif wanted[key] != actual[key]:
            differences.append(("changed", key))
    return differences


brand = {"name": "Culture Desk", "zone_id": "example-zone-culture"}
intended = [
    {"name": "culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "migration-review=approved"},
    {"name": "news.culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "owner=newsletter-team"},
]
observed = [
    {"name": "culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "migration-review=approved"},
    {"name": "news.culture.example", "type": "TXT",
     "value": "owner=previous-team"},
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(read_domains(), indent=2))
    differences = compare(
        brand, "example-zone-culture", intended, observed
    )
    for category, (name, record_type) in differences:
        print(f"{category}: {record_type} {name}")
    print("HOLD" if differences else "READY FOR FURTHER CHECKS")
    raise SystemExit(1 if differences else 0)

The fixture exits with status 1 and reports the changed newsletter marker. Replace the observed value with the intended value to exercise the matching path. A match means the local comparison passed; further checks still have to pass before approval.

The grouped values preserve multiple records under the same name and type. A dictionary that kept only one value per pair could hide a difference by overwriting an earlier entry. That's the quiet inventory error I want this approval path to expose.

This small comparator checks names, types, and values exactly as supplied; it does not normalize provider-specific representations or examine TTLs. Establish adapter rules before using it for approval, and extend the local contract if TTLs are acceptance criteria. For mail records, explicitly review how the adapter represents their values. A normalization rule that conceals a meaningful change defeats the reason for comparing inventories. The local fixture demonstrates the gate, not a complete registrar migration tool.

The rejected option and when it belongs

For separately operated publications, I would reject a single shared zone organized only by hostname prefixes. That makes naming conventions carry ownership information that belongs in explicit configuration. It also leaves a future divestiture dependent on untangling records. A shared zone remains valid when those names represent the same product, the same team owns the records, and the additional verification and rotation work of separate zones has no corresponding benefit.

My acceptance rule is concrete: select the zone boundary from team and sending-domain responsibilities, store its identifier in brand configuration, and withhold migration approval when the intended and observed inventories differ. Then perform the separate mail-authentication and delivery checks. For a media publisher moving off a registrar-specific API, this keeps the decision centered on accountable record ownership instead of hostname volume or a provider's marketing.

References

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/Welcome.html
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation: https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/overview

title: Cloud Storage for User Uploads: Signed Document Access Boundaries and Deletion Deadlines
description:
Cloud Storage for User Uploads: Signed Document Access Boundaries and Deletion Deadlines

For user uploads, comparing Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and Amazon S3 is useful only after a fintech system states the boundary it must enforce. For signed documents with an explicit deletion deadline, the durable record is a retention decision: who may retrieve the object, under which authorization, and when the system must make retrieval impossible. Direct client uploads are acceptable only when the service signs a narrowly scoped request and records the same decision in an audit trail.

This is the decision rule I use for the storage comparison: keep authorization and retention state in the application-owned ledger, keep bytes in object storage, and treat a provider-issued signed URL as a delivery capability rather than as proof of entitlement. The design tolerates retries, makes reconciliation possible, and leaves the provider-specific URL mechanism behind one interface.

The boundary comes first.

Auditability wins.

What must remain true after a retry or a deadline?

The workflow has four invariants. A document has one immutable object identity, one tenant and case association, one retention deadline, and a state transition that can be explained later. An upload retry must not create a second logical document. A download retry must not extend authorization. A deletion retry must be safe after the object has already disappeared.

Those statements sound operational until a signed contract is involved. Then the failure boundaries matter. The database can commit metadata while an upload is still in flight; an object can be present while its metadata row is missing; a client can retain a URL after its intended lifetime; and a lifecycle rule can remove bytes without producing the business audit event required by the compliance process. Object storage supplies useful primitives, but it does not know that a particular PDF is the document that settled a particular payment.

I therefore separate three clocks:

  • The authorization clock controls how long a user may obtain a delivery URL.
  • The retention clock controls the deletion deadline recorded for the document.
  • The reconciliation clock controls how quickly an operator investigates a mismatch between metadata and bytes.

The first clock may be minutes. The second may be years or a precisely stated business deadline. The third is an operational service-level objective. Confusing them is a common source of accidental retention: a long-lived object lifecycle policy is mistaken for a legal retention decision, or a short-lived URL is treated as if it revoked every previously issued copy. Once bytes have been delivered, a storage service cannot recall a downloaded file.

How should cloud storage handle user uploads and signed document delivery?

The three major object-storage families can all support this pattern, but their request-signing and policy vocabulary differ. The comparison below is deliberately narrow; it is about the boundary between an application authorization decision and a client delivery request, not a ranking of providers.

Service family Delivery mechanism to isolate Useful engineering boundary Important limitation
Amazon S3 Presigned URL A URL can authorize a specific object operation for a bounded period; the application can keep the bucket private and issue it after an authorization check. The URL is a bearer capability. It does not replace application authorization, and a downloaded copy cannot be revoked.
Azure Blob Storage Shared access signature (SAS) A SAS can constrain resource scope, permissions, and validity for a client-facing transfer. The token is also a bearer capability; its delegation policy and revocation model must be designed explicitly.
Google Cloud Storage Signed URL A signed request can provide time-bounded access to a named object without exposing broad bucket credentials to the client. The URL is a bearer capability, and the application still owns the document-to-user authorization decision.

This leaves a real choice. Provider-native direct delivery is operationally simple and usually reduces proxy bandwidth, while an application proxy gives the service more direct control over response headers, authorization checks, and emergency blocking. Neither choice changes the retention invariant.

For a small document, a proxy may be the clearer boundary because the service can check status immediately before streaming. For large uploads, a direct transfer with a one-object, one-operation capability may be the better delivery path. The decision should be driven by the sensitivity of the content, expected object size, network topology, and the strength of the audit requirement. “The browser has a URL” is not an authorization model.

The critical path is a state machine, not a URL generator

The application should create the logical document before it asks a client to upload, then accept the object only if its identity and checksum match the record. The following Go sketch shows the important ordering without binding the design to a commercial SDK. The interfaces are intentionally small: an adapter can implement them for S3, Blob Storage, or Cloud Storage while the business service remains testable. That separation is more than a portability exercise; it lets the test suite force a timeout, duplicate callback, mismatched digest, or deletion race without pretending that a provider request has exactly-once semantics.

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Document struct {
    ID        string
    TenantID  string
    ObjectKey string
    Digest    string
    DeleteAt  time.Time
    State     string
}

type Repository interface {
    CreatePending(ctx context.Context, d Document) error
    MarkUploaded(ctx context.Context, id, digest string, size int64) error
    MarkDeleteRequested(ctx context.Context, id string) error
}

type ObjectStore interface {
    IssueUpload(ctx context.Context, key string, expires time.Duration) (string, error)
    Head(ctx context.Context, key string) (size int64, digest string, err error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

func PrepareUpload(ctx context.Context, repo Repository, store ObjectStore, d Document) (string, error) {
    if d.ID == "" || d.ObjectKey == "" || d.DeleteAt.IsZero() {
        return "", errors.New("incomplete document identity")
    }
    if err := repo.CreatePending(ctx, d); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return store.IssueUpload(ctx, d.ObjectKey, 10*time.Minute)
}

func ConfirmUpload(ctx context.Context, repo Repository, store ObjectStore, d Document, body []byte) error {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
    want := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    if want != d.Digest {
        return errors.New("content digest mismatch")
    }
    size, got, err := store.Head(ctx, d.ObjectKey)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if got != d.Digest || size != int64(len(body)) {
        return errors.New("stored object does not match document")
    }
    return repo.MarkUploaded(ctx, d.ID, got, size)
}

The example keeps the business state transition in the repository and makes the object check explicit. In production, the digest should be computed from the exact bytes being transferred, and the upload confirmation should be idempotent: repeating a successful confirmation must return the same logical result, not append another document event. A real implementation also avoids holding a full document in memory; the sketch is a compact illustration of the ordering, not a streaming upload implementation.

The deletion worker follows the same discipline. It selects records whose deadline has passed, records a delete intent with an idempotency key, requests object deletion, and then verifies the outcome with a bounded retry policy. A “not found” result is normally a successful terminal state for deletion, but the audit record must distinguish “deleted” from “never observed” so reconciliation can investigate an earlier metadata mismatch.

Exactly-once execution is not a property to assume from a queue or a cron job. It is a business result assembled from an idempotency key, durable state transitions, and reconciliation. The worker may execute twice; the document deletion decision must still be represented once.

What breaks when access control is delegated to delivery?

The rejected option is to put a long-lived public object URL in a database and rely on the storage platform’s lifecycle policy to delete the object later. It is attractive because there are few moving pieces. It also collapses two different questions: “may this principal read the document now?” and “has the retention deadline passed?”

That option is valid for genuinely public, non-sensitive assets where revocation and per-user authorization do not matter. It is a poor fit for signed financial documents. A lifecycle policy is a useful backstop, but the application still needs a deadline in authoritative metadata, a deletion event, and a way to find objects that violate the expected state. Compliance requirements also vary by jurisdiction and record type; a retention field is not legal advice, and the system should not encode a universal period merely because a storage policy accepts one.

The simpler direct-delivery option has a different failure mode: a client receives a valid capability, then the user’s account is disabled or the document is placed under legal hold. A short expiry limits exposure, but it does not perform immediate revocation for a URL already issued. If immediate blocking is material, route retrieval through an authorization-aware service or maintain a revocation control that is checked before every delivery. That adds latency and operational work. It is the price of the stronger boundary.

How do I test and operate the deadline?

Test the state machine with provider adapters replaced by a fake store, then run a smaller set of contract tests against each selected service. The important cases are repetitive and unglamorous: the upload callback arrives twice; the object has the wrong checksum; the database commit succeeds while the signed-request call fails; deletion is retried after a timeout; a deadline is exactly equal to the worker’s current time; and a previously issued URL is used after the application has denied access. Time must be injectable so a test can place an object precisely on either side of the deadline.

Observe counts and states, not just HTTP failures. Useful signals include pending documents older than the upload window, objects without matching metadata, deletion intents past their retry budget, and successful URL issuance for documents already expired or blocked. Include tenant and document identifiers in structured audit fields only when the logging policy permits it; never turn the document body or a signed capability into a log message.

The deployment procedure should version bucket/container policy separately from application code, review changes as security-sensitive, and make a rollback unable to extend expired retention accidentally. A policy change that broadens read access deserves the same review as an authorization code change. Periodic inventory is essential because object stores and relational databases fail independently, and a clean application metric cannot prove that no orphaned bytes exist.

The final architecture is therefore intentionally unexciting: private objects, application-owned document state, narrowly scoped delivery capabilities, explicit deadlines, idempotent workers, and an audit trail that records decisions rather than only HTTP responses. The storage service affects adapter details and delivery ergonomics. It does not own the business meaning of a signed document.

References

  • AWS, “Amazon S3 presigned URLs”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Microsoft Learn, “Grant limited access to Azure Storage resources using shared access signatures (SAS)”: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview
  • Google Cloud, “Signed URLs”: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • NIST, “Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management (SP 800-63B)”: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html
  • OWASP, “Logging Cheat Sheet”: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Pipeline Error Logs: Detect Backend Failures With Attributable Polling Evidence
description:
Detect backend failures in a nightly fintech pipeline by polling structured error logs, then attach account usage before sending a Slack webhook alert; choose this design when the notification needs both failure evidence and an accountable owner, and resist turning account totals into a bill for an individual failed job.

TL;DR: Poll structured error logs, attach an account-usage snapshot, and let a worker own deduplication, cooldowns, retries, and Slack delivery. For a Node.js backend, this is a separate operational worker; the runnable example below uses Python. Search can establish that a failure was observed. Account usage supplies billing context. Neither fact, by itself, establishes what a particular pipeline run cost.

The decision here is about evidence provenance: what can a notification actually justify? A payment failure recorded during an import, a repeated job failure, and a pipeline that never started demand different evidence, even if the same team receives all three alerts. Keep them distinct.

Record the decision before choosing the notification transport

Use a scheduled worker to search recent structured logs for error status, job failures, or payment failures, then deliver a compact notification to Slack or email through a transport the application owns. Keep a durable delivery ledger outside the worker process. A notification should identify the pipeline run and the relevant evidence, with an explicit distinction between measured account usage and any allocation calculated locally.

This is a proposed design, not a benchmark. Its acceptance criteria are concrete: an observed failure produces one incident identity, overlapping searches do not create a fresh incident every time, and a successful account read does not erase an unsuccessful log read. The schedule, search window, and cooldown belong to the deployment configuration. They are not universal constants.

Infrai's self-describing REST API needs no SDK and puts account and observability calls behind one key and one bill, so the collection worker doesn't need separate account and log credentials. Its public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so adding a capability starts with reading one capability description rather than learning another SDK; per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata give the worker useful attribution evidence, although those records still need a local association with the pipeline run.

That association is the architectural work. A shared credential does not invent it.

How should polling error logs detect backend failures without misattributing usage?

The first invariant is that an error observation and a delivery acknowledgment are separate records. Consider a proposed polling interval of 60 seconds and a 300-second cooldown: a restart inside that cooldown must not reset the delivery ledger, and a second observation of the same incident should update its evidence rather than acquire a new identity. These numbers illustrate a policy to test, not a service guarantee. Use a stable event identity where the actual response schema provides one; otherwise define the incident identity from application-owned fields and accept the grouping trade-off explicitly.

A useful application log contract includes a pipeline run identifier, a job name, an operational region label, an owner, and an event classification such as payment failure. These are proposed producer fields, not promised API response fields or search parameters. Keep raw payment credentials and customer identifiers out of the notification. A region label in a record describes the workload; it does not prove where a provider stores that record, so a US or EU SaaS deployment needs a separate residency decision.

The second invariant is that search completeness has to be demonstrated. Pagination, late arrivals, event timestamps, and cursor behavior must be taken from the actual schema before advancing a durable checkpoint. Do not call a partially consumed response a complete interval. Re-reading overlapping intervals is a reasonable worker policy only when the delivery ledger can recognize previously observed evidence.

Failure boundaries matter.

A log with trace_id or span_id offers correlation, not a distributed span tree. A job that never starts may emit no error at all, which calls for a heartbeat tool such as Healthchecks. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, and session replay are separate investigative requirements. Likewise, operational search should not serve as the system of record for erasure, bulk export, retention, or cold-storage policy; those requirements need a separately evaluated data lifecycle, including the obligations described in GDPR Article 17. None of these boundaries should be hidden behind a green Slack delivery acknowledgment.

Compare the evidence each option contributes

The useful comparison is the investigation each choice supports. Notification transport comes afterward.

Option Evidence or role in this decision Trade-off and acceptance boundary
Shared REST account and log capabilities Places account usage and operational search behind the same credential; discovery describes how to call each capability The worker still owns incident identity and delivery state. Account usage alone cannot allocate cost to a run.
Sentry Event grouping and fingerprint mechanics give a concrete basis for grouping repeated errors Evaluate the grouping against the application's incident identity; grouping errors does not establish account-cost attribution.
Datadog Logs plus a vendor console Separates log investigation from the vendor account used for billing context In this proposed two-service arrangement, plan for two service enrollments and two credential sets, then write the join and its ownership rules.
Grafana Loki A log-oriented alternative to evaluate when retaining a separate investigation stack Validate the run-to-record association before adopting it; account reconciliation and notification identity still need explicit ownership.
Healthchecks Covers the missing-run question through a heartbeat-oriented workflow Pair it with error evidence when both silence and explicit failures matter; a missing heartbeat does not identify the failing payment operation.

Sentry's grouping documentation is particularly useful because it makes the grouping mechanism something an engineer can inspect. For Datadog, the relevant alternative here is specifically the vendor-console-plus-logs arrangement, not a claim that every deployment needs exactly two human signups. An organization may already have both accounts. It still needs a way to connect the account evidence, log evidence, incident owner, and delivery state across them.

The trade-off is less credential glue because both capabilities share authentication, at the cost of concentrating dependency risk. Consolidation has a cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Accept that deliberately.

Make the account-to-search handoff explicit

The following Python program is a runnable, read-only collection step for the polling worker. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL in the environment, with the latter pointing to the platform's HTTPS API base ending in /v1, then run it with Python 3. It reads account usage first, carries that response into the collection context, and passes the same context into log collection using the same key and base URL. Both API responses are preserved without assuming undocumented payload fields. No server-side filter parameters are invented.

The handoff is deliberately local: account usage becomes the billing context for the subsequent search result, not an undocumented search filter. The program prints one JSON evidence bundle and exits. It does not claim that fetching two responses implements a complete alerting service. Run it under a scheduler, then build the schema-aware selection and durable delivery stage around that bundle.

import json
import os
import random
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]

def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    if value:
        try:
            return max(0.0, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            try:
                deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
                if deadline.tzinfo is None:
                    deadline = deadline.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
                now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
                return max(0.0, (deadline - now).total_seconds())
            except (ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError):
                pass
    return (2 ** attempt) + random.random()

def read_json(path):
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers={
                "Authorization": "Bearer " + API_KEY,
                "Accept": "application/json",
            },
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Retry budget exhausted")

def collect_logs(context):
    bundle = dict(context)
    bundle["log_search_response"] = read_json("/logs/search")
    bundle["collection_finished_at"] = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    return bundle

def main():
    context = {
        "collection_started_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "account_usage_response": read_json("/account/usage"),
    }
    print(json.dumps(collect_logs(context), indent=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The two response names and collection timestamps are local bundle fields. Collection start and finish bound the worker's activity, not the time range of the returned events, and the two reads are not an atomic account-and-log snapshot. Restrict access to the output as operational data. An HTTP failure terminates collection with its status and response body; route that diagnostic to a protected worker log rather than copying it wholesale into Slack. The example retries rate limits with exponential backoff and honors Retry-After when present. Its four-attempt budget is an example worker policy.

Before adding Slack delivery, inspect the response schemas and implement the actual interval selection, pagination, and incident grouping. Retain the source request metadata where available so a local attribution record can point back to the calls that produced it. An account-usage response can support reconciliation, but dividing an account total by the number of error records would confuse observation volume with consumption. A failed payment may create repeated observations without representing repeated billable work.

Slack delivery needs its own state transition: persist an intent, attempt delivery, then record the acknowledgment. If the process loses the acknowledgment after sending, a retry may duplicate a message; marking it delivered before sending creates the opposite failure mode, a lost notification. Choose and document the acceptable behavior, include the stable incident identity in the message, and retain the uncertain delivery state. A local idempotency key cannot force a remote webhook to deduplicate.

Reject the all-in-one incident ledger for the right reason

The rejected option is treating searchable operational logs as an authoritative ledger for incident delivery, allocated cost, and customer-data lifecycle. It is attractive because one query appears to answer everything. It cannot justify those conclusions without separate invariants: a log match is evidence of an observation, a billing record concerns consumption, and a delivery acknowledgment concerns a transport action. Joining them is useful; treating them as interchangeable is where the design fails.

That smaller operational-search approach still has a valid use case. Choose it for a nightly pipeline whose team needs recent failure evidence and can operate a durable notification worker, with account usage attached as context. If missing runs dominate, add heartbeat evidence; if grouping semantics dominate, evaluate the specialist grouping workflow; if the organization already investigates in a separate log platform, compare the cost of maintaining that join before moving it.

The acceptance test should replay an overlapping search, restart the worker inside its cooldown, and simulate a lost delivery acknowledgment. Each case must preserve incident identity and attribution provenance. Only then does a Slack alert about a nightly failure mean more than a successful HTTP request.

References

  • Sentry, event grouping and fingerprint mechanics
  • Datadog, Log Explorer
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Slack, incoming webhooks
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure

title: Roll forward storage unit balances and gate supervisor release in TypeScript
description:
Unit B12 opens with $150 past due. A $50 fee and a $75 payment leave $125. In this example, an active dispute or missing certified-mail delivery proof blocks the supervisor release step even with that positive balance.

Replay the unit ledger in posting order

The ledger takes already-posted fees and payments, each with a stable ID and a positive amount in bigint cents. Apply the sign according to the posting type and carry the resulting balance to the next row. A duplicate ID fails the import before a second copy can change the balance.

Ledger row Change Running past-due balance
Opening balance $150
Fee FEE-01 +$50 $200
Payment PAY-01 −$75 $125

Check dispute status and delivery evidence independently

The fixture checks for a positive closing balance, a cleared dispute hold, and certified-mail delivery evidence tied to the same unit and current notice. A mailing record can carry a tracking ID while delivery is still pending. The delivered record in this example carries both a tracking ID and a separate evidence ID. Proof for a prior notice or a different unit leaves the delivery check open.

Dispute status Certified-mail evidence Supervisor release check
Active Matching delivery proof Blocked by dispute
Cleared Mailing record only Blocked by missing delivery proof
Active Missing Blocked by both reasons
Cleared Matching delivery proof Eligible for the supervisor step

The gate returns every active reason so a reviewer can see both problems in one pass. The ELIGIBLE result is scoped to the fixture's checks. Keep the facility's jurisdiction-specific auction requirements and the actual supervisor decision in the broader workflow.

Run the benchmark

Save the block as storagedelinq-benchmark.ts and run node --experimental-strip-types storagedelinq-benchmark.ts with Node.js 24. The script needs no packages. Node.js TypeScript documentation

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

type Posting = {
  id: string;
  kind: "fee" | "payment";
  amountCents: bigint;
};

type UnitLedger = {
  unitId: string;
  openingCents: bigint;
  postings: readonly Posting[];
};

type CertifiedMail = {
  unitId: string;
  noticeId: string;
  trackingId?: string;
} & ({ status: "mailed" } | { status: "delivered"; deliveryEvidenceId?: string });

type NoticeReview = {
  noticeId: string;
  disputeHold: boolean;
  certifiedMail?: CertifiedMail;
};

function rollForward({ unitId, openingCents, postings }: UnitLedger) {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  let balanceCents = openingCents;
  const rows = postings.map(({ id, kind, amountCents }) => {
    const postingId = id.trim();
    assert(postingId, "Posting ID is required");
    assert(!seen.has(postingId), `Duplicate posting ID: ${postingId}`);
    assert(amountCents > 0n, "Posting amount must be positive");
    seen.add(postingId);

    const deltaCents = kind === "fee" ? amountCents : -amountCents;
    balanceCents += deltaCents;
    return { id: postingId, deltaCents, balanceCents };
  });
  return { unitId, openingCents, rows, closingCents: balanceCents };
}

function evaluateRelease(
  ledger: ReturnType<typeof rollForward>,
  { noticeId, disputeHold, certifiedMail }: NoticeReview,
) {
  assert(noticeId.trim(), "Current notice ID is required");
  const reasons: string[] = [];
  if (ledger.closingCents <= 0n) reasons.push("NO_PAST_DUE_BALANCE");
  if (disputeHold) reasons.push("ACTIVE_DISPUTE_HOLD");
  if (certifiedMail?.status !== "delivered" ||
    certifiedMail.unitId !== ledger.unitId ||
    certifiedMail.noticeId !== noticeId ||
    !certifiedMail.trackingId?.trim() ||
    !certifiedMail.deliveryEvidenceId?.trim()) {
    reasons.push("MISSING_CERTIFIED_MAIL_DELIVERY_PROOF");
  }

  return { supervisorReleaseEligible: reasons.length === 0, reasons };
}

const unit: UnitLedger = {
  unitId: "UNIT-B12",
  openingCents: 15_000n,
  postings: [
    { id: "FEE-01", kind: "fee", amountCents: 5_000n },
    { id: "PAY-01", kind: "payment", amountCents: 7_500n },
  ],
};
const ledger = rollForward(unit);
assert.deepEqual(ledger.rows, [
  { id: "FEE-01", deltaCents: 5_000n, balanceCents: 20_000n },
  { id: "PAY-01", deltaCents: -7_500n, balanceCents: 12_500n },
]);
assert.equal(ledger.closingCents, 12_500n);
assert.throws(() => rollForward({ ...unit, postings: [...unit.postings,
  { ...unit.postings[1], id: " PAY-01 " },
] }), /Duplicate posting ID/);

const mail = { unitId: unit.unitId, noticeId: "NOTICE-02", trackingId: "TRACK-02" };
const review = { noticeId: mail.noticeId, disputeHold: false };
const delivered = { ...mail, status: "delivered", deliveryEvidenceId: "POD-02" } as const;
const scenarios = [
  { label: "Active dispute + delivery proof", review: { ...review, disputeHold: true, certifiedMail: delivered } },
  { label: "Cleared dispute + mailing record", review: { ...review, certifiedMail: { ...mail, status: "mailed" } } },
  { label: "Active dispute + no proof", review: { ...review, disputeHold: true } },
  { label: "Cleared dispute + matching delivery proof", review: { ...review, certifiedMail: delivered } },
] satisfies { label: string; review: NoticeReview }[];
const decisions = scenarios.map((scenario) => evaluateRelease(ledger, scenario.review));
const missingProof = "MISSING_CERTIFIED_MAIL_DELIVERY_PROOF";
assert.deepEqual(decisions, [
  { supervisorReleaseEligible: false, reasons: ["ACTIVE_DISPUTE_HOLD"] },
  { supervisorReleaseEligible: false, reasons: [missingProof] },
  { supervisorReleaseEligible: false, reasons: ["ACTIVE_DISPUTE_HOLD", missingProof] },
  { supervisorReleaseEligible: true, reasons: [] },
]);

for (const certifiedMail of [
  { ...delivered, noticeId: "NOTICE-01" },
  { ...delivered, unitId: "UNIT-B13" },
  { ...delivered, deliveryEvidenceId: " " },
  { unitId: mail.unitId, noticeId: mail.noticeId, status: "delivered", deliveryEvidenceId: "POD-02" },
  { ...mail, status: "delivered" },
] satisfies CertifiedMail[]) {
  assert.deepEqual(evaluateRelease(ledger, { ...review, certifiedMail }),
    { supervisorReleaseEligible: false, reasons: [missingProof] });
}
const paid = rollForward({ ...unit, postings: [...unit.postings,
  { id: "PAY-02", kind: "payment", amountCents: 12_500n },
] });
assert.equal(paid.closingCents, 0n);
assert.deepEqual(evaluateRelease(paid, { ...review, certifiedMail: delivered }),
  { supervisorReleaseEligible: false, reasons: ["NO_PAST_DUE_BALANCE"] });

const [fee, payment] = ledger.rows;
console.log(`${ledger.unitId} opening + fee - payment (cents): ${ledger.openingCents} + ${fee.deltaCents} - ${-payment.deltaCents} = ${ledger.closingCents}`);
for (const [index, { label }] of scenarios.entries()) {
  const { supervisorReleaseEligible, reasons } = decisions[index];
  const outcome = supervisorReleaseEligible ? "ELIGIBLE" : `BLOCKED (${reasons.join(", ")})`;
  console.log(`${label}: ${outcome}`);
}

Verified Node output 

UNIT-B12 opening + fee - payment (cents): 15000 + 5000 - 7500 = 12500
Active dispute + delivery proof: BLOCKED (ACTIVE_DISPUTE_HOLD)
Cleared dispute + mailing record: BLOCKED (MISSING_CERTIFIED_MAIL_DELIVERY_PROOF)
Active dispute + no proof: BLOCKED (ACTIVE_DISPUTE_HOLD, MISSING_CERTIFIED_MAIL_DELIVERY_PROOF)
Cleared dispute + matching delivery proof: ELIGIBLE

Save the ledger cutoff, notice ID, dispute state, and evidence reference used in each review. Replay the checks against current records before recording the supervisor's decision.

StorageDelinq past-due unit workflow · B2B Ops and FinOps Benchmarks

title: Audit kitchen exhaust scope and photo evidence in TypeScript
description:
The crew marks a duct section cleaned, but the photo index contains only its before photo. The same job records a rooftop fan as inaccessible. Both records need follow-up. One needs an after photo and the other needs an access plan.

Bind each photo to its system and component

Use the pair (systemId, componentId) as the scope key. Two kitchens can both have a HOOD-01. Each photo ID resolves to one system, component, and capture phase. A reference to P-06, the after photo for KITCHEN-B/HOOD-01, fails when attached to KITCHEN-A/HOOD-01. An unknown photo ID or a duplicate index entry also fails before the audit issues a queue.

System / component Reported status Attached photos Follow-up
KITCHEN-A/HOOD-01 cleaned P-01 before, P-02 after
KITCHEN-A/DUCT-02 cleaned P-03 before MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO
KITCHEN-A/ROOF-FAN-01 inaccessible P-04 before INACCESSIBLE
KITCHEN-B/HOOD-01 cleaned P-05 before, P-06 after

Freeze the follow-up queue for each audit

The fixture asks for both phases when a component is marked cleaned. For an inaccessible component, the access status itself creates a follow-up. The audit sorts the queue for stable review and freezes the array and each row. When the correct after photo P-07 arrives for the duct, a new audit returns only the rooftop fan. The original two entries remain available in the previous snapshot.

Run the benchmark

Save the block as hoodcert-benchmark.ts and run node --experimental-strip-types hoodcert-benchmark.ts with Node.js 24. The script needs no packages. Node.js TypeScript documentation

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

type ComponentKey = { systemId: string; componentId: string };
type ScopeRow = ComponentKey & {
  status: "cleaned" | "inaccessible";
  photoIds: readonly string[];
};
type Photo = ComponentKey & { id: string; phase: "before" | "after" };
type FollowUp = ComponentKey & {
  reason: "INACCESSIBLE" | "MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO" | "MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO";
};

function auditScope(scope: readonly ScopeRow[], photos: readonly Photo[]) {
  const photoIndex = new Map<string, Photo>();
  for (const photo of photos) {
    assert(photo.id.trim(), "Photo ID is required");
    assert(!photoIndex.has(photo.id), `Duplicate photo ID: ${photo.id}`);
    photoIndex.set(photo.id, photo);
  }

  const seenComponents = new Set<string>();
  const followUps: Readonly<FollowUp>[] = [];
  for (const { systemId, componentId, status, photoIds } of scope) {
    assert(systemId.trim() && componentId.trim(), "System and component IDs are required");
    const key = JSON.stringify([systemId, componentId]);
    const label = `${systemId}/${componentId}`;
    assert(!seenComponents.has(key), `Duplicate scope component: ${label}`);
    seenComponents.add(key);

    const attached = new Set<string>();
    const phases = new Set<Photo["phase"]>();
    for (const id of photoIds) {
      assert(!attached.has(id), `Duplicate photo reference: ${id}`);
      const photo = photoIndex.get(id);
      assert(photo, `Unknown photo ID: ${id}`);
      assert(photo.systemId === systemId && photo.componentId === componentId,
        `Photo ${id} belongs to ${photo.systemId}/${photo.componentId}, expected ${label}`);
      attached.add(id);
      phases.add(photo.phase);
    }

    const addFollowUp = (reason: FollowUp["reason"]) => {
      followUps.push(Object.freeze({ systemId, componentId, reason }));
    };
    if (status === "inaccessible") {
      addFollowUp("INACCESSIBLE");
    } else {
      if (!phases.has("before")) addFollowUp("MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO");
      if (!phases.has("after")) addFollowUp("MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO");
    }
  }

  return Object.freeze(followUps.sort((left, right) => {
    const a = JSON.stringify([left.systemId, left.componentId, left.reason]);
    const b = JSON.stringify([right.systemId, right.componentId, right.reason]);
    if (a === b) return 0;
    return a < b ? -1 : 1;
  }));
}

const scope: readonly ScopeRow[] = [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", status: "inaccessible", photoIds: ["P-04"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-01", "P-02"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-03"] },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", status: "cleaned", photoIds: ["P-05", "P-06"] },
];
const photos: readonly Photo[] = [
  { id: "P-01", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-02", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "after" },
  { id: "P-03", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-04", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-05", systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "before" },
  { id: "P-06", systemId: "KITCHEN-B", componentId: "HOOD-01", phase: "after" },
];

const queue = auditScope(scope, photos);
const expected = [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", reason: "MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO" },
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "ROOF-FAN-01", reason: "INACCESSIBLE" },
];
assert.deepEqual(queue, expected);
assert.deepEqual(auditScope(scope.toReversed(), photos.toReversed()), expected);
assert(Object.isFrozen(queue) && queue.every((entry) => Object.isFrozen(entry)));
assert.equal(Reflect.set(queue[0], "reason", "INACCESSIBLE"), false);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-01", "P-06"] }], photos),
  /belongs to KITCHEN-B\/HOOD-01, expected KITCHEN-A\/HOOD-01/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-03"] }], photos),
  /belongs to KITCHEN-A\/DUCT-02, expected KITCHEN-A\/HOOD-01/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-99"] }], photos), /Unknown photo ID/);
assert.throws(() => auditScope(scope, [...photos, photos[0]]), /Duplicate photo ID/);
assert.deepEqual(auditScope([{ ...scope[1], photoIds: ["P-02"] }], photos), [
  { systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "HOOD-01", reason: "MISSING_BEFORE_PHOTO" },
]);

const newPhoto: Photo = { id: "P-07", systemId: "KITCHEN-A", componentId: "DUCT-02", phase: "after" };
const updatedScope = scope.map((row) => row.systemId === newPhoto.systemId && row.componentId === newPhoto.componentId
  ? { ...row, photoIds: [...row.photoIds, newPhoto.id] }
  : row);
const nextQueue = auditScope(updatedScope, [...photos, newPhoto]);
assert.deepEqual(nextQueue, [expected[1]]);
assert.deepEqual(queue, expected);

console.log(`Audited components: ${scope.length} | indexed photos: ${photos.length}`);
for (const { systemId, componentId, reason } of queue) {
  console.log(`${systemId}/${componentId}: ${reason}`);
}
console.log(`After attaching ${newPhoto.id}: ${nextQueue.length} follow-up | original queue: ${queue.length}`);

Verified Node output 

Audited components: 4 | indexed photos: 6
KITCHEN-A/DUCT-02: MISSING_AFTER_PHOTO
KITCHEN-A/ROOF-FAN-01: INACCESSIBLE
After attaching P-07: 1 follow-up | original queue: 2

Keep the scope and photo index with each audit snapshot. That gives the reviewer the exact references behind a missing-evidence flag and preserves the access exception when the rest of the job is documented.

HoodCert kitchen exhaust reporting · B2B Ops and FinOps Benchmarks

title: Freeze marina haul-out and storage rates in TypeScript
description:
A 30-foot boat rings up $845 for haul-out, prep, and four months of storage. Apply the $200 deposit and the balance is $645. The marina later changes all three rates. Open the approved revision again and the same $645 is still due.

Price the work order at approval

Length overall (LOA) is the billable length for the haul-out in this example. The fixture takes whole billable feet and whole storage months as inputs. If a marina bills fractional lengths, establish the billable quantity under its pricing terms before approval.

Work-order line Calculation Amount
Haul-out 30 ft × $4 per foot $120
Prep One flat charge $125
Seasonal storage 4 months × $150 per month $600
Approved total $845
Applied deposit Receipt DEP-200 −$200
Balance $645

Use bigint cents for rates, charges, and deposits. At approval, copy the live rates and freeze the copied rates, calculated charges, and revision record. Those nested freezes matter because Object.freeze operates on one object at a time. Editing the live card to $5 per foot, $150 for prep, and $170 per month produces a $980 second approval and leaves revision 1 at $845.

Replay the applied deposits

The example ledger contains one row per applied receipt for the work order. Each row carries its receipt ID, work-order ID, and amount applied. Before subtracting the credits, reject duplicate receipt IDs, receipts attached to another order, and totals above the approved price. Replaying the same deposit entries against the saved approval reproduces the balance without reading the live rate card.

Run the benchmark

Save the block as boathaul-benchmark.ts and run node --experimental-strip-types boathaul-benchmark.ts with Node.js 24. The script needs no packages. Node.js TypeScript documentation

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

type RateCard = {
  haulPerFootCents: bigint;
  prepCents: bigint;
  storagePerMonthCents: bigint;
};

type WorkOrderRevision = {
  workOrderId: string;
  revision: number;
  loaFeet: bigint;
  storageMonths: bigint;
};

type DepositApplication = {
  receiptId: string;
  workOrderId: string;
  appliedCents: bigint;
};

function approve(draft: WorkOrderRevision, rateCard: RateCard) {
  const { workOrderId, revision, loaFeet, storageMonths } = draft;
  assert(workOrderId.trim(), "Work order ID is required");
  assert(Number.isSafeInteger(revision) && revision > 0, "Invalid revision");
  assert(loaFeet > 0n && storageMonths >= 0n, "Invalid LOA or storage term");

  const rates = Object.freeze({ ...rateCard });
  assert(rates.haulPerFootCents >= 0n && rates.prepCents >= 0n &&
    rates.storagePerMonthCents >= 0n, "Rates must be nonnegative");

  const haulCents = loaFeet * rates.haulPerFootCents;
  const storageCents = storageMonths * rates.storagePerMonthCents;
  const charges = Object.freeze({
    haulCents,
    prepCents: rates.prepCents,
    storageCents,
    totalCents: haulCents + rates.prepCents + storageCents,
  });
  return Object.freeze({ workOrderId, revision, loaFeet, storageMonths, rates, charges });
}

function reconcileDeposit(
  approval: ReturnType<typeof approve>,
  applications: readonly DepositApplication[],
) {
  const usedReceipts = new Set<string>();
  let appliedCents = 0n;
  for (const entry of applications) {
    const receiptId = entry.receiptId.trim();
    assert(receiptId, "Deposit receipt ID is required");
    assert.equal(entry.workOrderId, approval.workOrderId, "Deposit belongs to another work order");
    assert(!usedReceipts.has(receiptId), `Duplicate deposit receipt: ${receiptId}`);
    assert(entry.appliedCents > 0n, "Applied deposit must be positive");
    usedReceipts.add(receiptId);
    appliedCents += entry.appliedCents;
  }

  const { totalCents } = approval.charges;
  assert(appliedCents <= totalCents, "Applied deposits exceed approved total");
  return { appliedCents, balanceCents: totalCents - appliedCents };
}

const draft = { workOrderId: "WO-030", revision: 1, loaFeet: 30n, storageMonths: 4n };
const rateCard = { haulPerFootCents: 400n, prepCents: 12_500n, storagePerMonthCents: 15_000n };
const deposit = { receiptId: "DEP-200", workOrderId: draft.workOrderId, appliedCents: 20_000n };

const approved = approve(draft, rateCard);
const expectedR1 = {
  ...draft,
  rates: { ...rateCard },
  charges: { haulCents: 12_000n, prepCents: 12_500n, storageCents: 60_000n, totalCents: 84_500n },
};
assert.deepEqual(approved, expectedR1);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved, "revision", 2), false);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved.rates, "haulPerFootCents", 999n), false);
assert.equal(Reflect.set(approved.charges, "totalCents", 0n), false);
const originalBalance = reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit]);
assert.deepEqual(originalBalance, { appliedCents: 20_000n, balanceCents: 64_500n });

rateCard.haulPerFootCents = 500n;
rateCard.prepCents = 15_000n;
rateCard.storagePerMonthCents = 17_000n;
const revisedApproval = approve({ ...draft, revision: 2 }, rateCard);
const reopened = reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit]);

assert.deepEqual(approved, expectedR1);
assert.deepEqual(reopened, originalBalance);
assert.equal(revisedApproval.charges.totalCents, 98_000n);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [deposit, { ...deposit, receiptId: " DEP-200 " }]),
  /Duplicate deposit receipt/);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [{ ...deposit, workOrderId: "WO-031" }]),
  /another work order/);
assert.throws(() => reconcileDeposit(approved, [{ ...deposit, appliedCents: 84_501n }]),
  /exceed approved total/);

const { workOrderId, revision, charges } = approved;
console.log(`${workOrderId} r${revision} haul + prep + storage (cents): ${charges.haulCents} + ${charges.prepCents} + ${charges.storageCents} = ${charges.totalCents}`);
console.log(`Applied deposit / balance (cents): ${originalBalance.appliedCents} / ${originalBalance.balanceCents}`);
console.log(`After rate-card edit, r${revision} total / balance (cents): ${charges.totalCents} / ${reopened.balanceCents}`);
console.log(`New approval r${revisedApproval.revision} total (cents): ${revisedApproval.charges.totalCents}`);

Verified Node output 

WO-030 r1 haul + prep + storage (cents): 12000 + 12500 + 60000 = 84500
Applied deposit / balance (cents): 20000 / 64500
After rate-card edit, r1 total / balance (cents): 84500 / 64500
New approval r2 total (cents): 98000

Persist approved snapshots under the work-order ID and revision number. Keep applied receipts with the work order so a marina can trace both the original price and the credits behind a balance.

BoatHaul marina work orders · B2B Ops and FinOps Benchmarks

title: Rust Anything: Port to Rust and Verify Behavior
description:
title: "Rust Anything: Port your code to Rust and check that it still behaves the same"
published: false
description: "An open-source tool that records how your code behaves and replays those cases against a Rust port."

tags: rust, opensource, tooling, ai

When you port a piece of software to Rust, getting it to compile is just the beginning. The harder question comes next: Does it still behave like the original?

I came across Rust Anything, an open-source project by Erkam Yaman that helps you answer that question by migrating one component at a time and using the original implementation as a baseline.

How it works

  1. Rust Anything runs the original code and records inputs and outputs.
  2. A coding agent writes the Rust implementation.
  3. Rust Anything replays the recorded cases against the port and flags any differences.

The project reports matching results for all 3,414 recorded cases in its Fuse.js port. It also documents a port of PEAR XML_Util, a PHP library that calls into Rust through PHP’s ext-ffi extension.

Where I’d start

In a PHP or TypeScript backend, I’d start with a component whose inputs and outputs are easy to reproduce, such as a parser or file transformer. I’d include malformed inputs and edge cases in the comparison, then benchmark both implementations with a representative workload to see whether the port is worth keeping.

If you already have Cargo, you can install the tool and set up integrations with coding agents such as Codex, Claude Code, or OpenCode:

cargo install rust-anything
rust-anything setup
  • Rust Anything website and documentation
  • Source code on GitHub

What part of an application you maintain would you try porting to Rust first?

title: Full-Page Motion Blueprints vs Component Kits: Choosing Between MovaUI, 21st.dev, Magic UI & Aceternity UI
description:
Disclosure: I build and maintain MovaUI (movaui.com). This is an honest scoping guide based on where our approach helps—and where I'd still reach for 21st.dev, Magic UI, or Aceternity UI first. (Note: MovaUI at movaui.com is unaffiliated with mova-ui.com or movavi.com.)

TL;DR: If you already have a React + Tailwind design system and just need an animated card, marquee, or button, 21st.dev, Magic UI, or Aceternity UI will get you shipped faster. If you are using Claude Code or Cursor to generate a cohesive full-page 60FPS landing page—especially across Next.js, Vue, Astro, or Vite, with looping video backgrounds and frame-budget guardrails—a full-page blueprint system like MovaUI avoids the glue-code mess.

At a glance: five engineering dimensions

Dimension MovaUI (movaui.com) 21st.dev / Magic UI / Aceternity UI
Core deliverable 900+ full-page and section motion blueprints, 218 60FPS looping video backgrounds, and 21 cloud Agent Skills Individual React, Tailwind, and Framer Motion component snippets
Framework support Framework-portable blueprints adapted to Next.js, React, Vue, Astro, Nuxt, and Vite via MIT stack-adapter-skill Primarily bound to React + Tailwind CSS (shadcn ecosystem)
Coding agent MCP Zero-auth Streamable HTTP MCP at /mcp/catalog (Official MCP Registry, Glama Grade A, mcpservers.org, mcptry 99/100 Security Grade A) Component-discovery MCP on some platforms (e.g., 21st.dev Magic) focused on single snippets
60FPS looping backgrounds 218 watermark-free 60FPS seamless loop video backgrounds with responsive React/HTML embed code No dedicated looping video background catalog
Pricing model One-time period plans with zero auto-renewal, plus non-expiring pay-per-prompt Boost Credits Free open-source primitives plus recurring Pro plans or template packs

Why stitching single-component kits breaks down on full-page AI builds

Component kits solve local UI problems cleanly. The trouble starts when you ask Claude Code or Cursor to assemble an entire landing page by pulling five unrelated animated snippets together:

  • Conflicting motion physics: One section runs a stiff spring, the next uses linear CSS keyframes, and the hero uses an uncapped requestAnimationFrame loop.
  • GPU & WebGL budget bloat: Stacking two shader backgrounds and a particle canvas without a devicePixelRatio cap or off-viewport pause turns mobile devices into hand warmers.
  • Framework friction: Copying React + Tailwind v3 shadcn snippets into a Tailwind v4, Next.js App Router ("use client" boundary), Vue, or Astro repo often triggers hydration warnings or broken styling tokens.

A full-page motion blueprint flips the direction of work. Instead of pasting isolated widgets and hoping they harmonize, you hand the coding agent one structured specification covering visual tokens, typographic rhythm, motion curves, and hard 60FPS constraints up front.

Even if you never use MovaUI, adding these four lines to your own system prompt eliminates most AI animation regressions:

- Cap canvas/WebGL pixel ratio to Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2) and dispose GPU resources on unmount.
- Pause continuous loops and shaders when off-viewport using IntersectionObserver + document.visibilitychange.
- Animate compositor-only properties (transform, opacity, clip-path); never use transition-all.
- Honor @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) with a clean static fallback and zero debug/FPS HUDs in DOM.

Choose by delivery granularity

Work backwards from what you are actually shipping this week:

  • 1–2 animated widgets inside an existing design system: Go straight to Magic UI, Aceternity UI, or 21st.dev. Dropping in a single React primitive is faster and adds zero extra workflow overhead.
  • A full landing page or 3D portfolio from 0 to 1 with Claude Code / Cursor: Use a full-page blueprint plus stack detection (stack-adapter-skill) so visual hierarchy, scroll pacing, and 60FPS limits stay consistent from Hero to Footer.
  • Hero atmosphere without shipping a 150KB+ WebGL runtime: Pair a compressed 60FPS looping video background (autoPlay muted loop playsInline + WebP poster + contrast scrim + motion-reduce:hidden) instead of forcing Three.js on every page.
  • Non-React stacks (Vue, Nuxt, Astro, vanilla Vite): Check framework portability before component count—blueprints translate cleanly across stacks, whereas React-coupled component snippets require manual rewrites.

When NOT to use MovaUI

Skip MovaUI if:

  • You just want a single copy-paste React button, bento card, or modal snippet.
  • You want a visual drag-and-drop no-code builder (MovaUI is built for developers and AI coding agents).
  • You want an npm install UI component dependency rather than prompts, backgrounds, and Agent Skills.
  • Your site is purely content/documentation with no need for hero motion or looping video backgrounds.

The lightest tool that matches your delivery scope is always the right pick.

Quick FAQ

Can Vue, Astro, or plain Vite projects actually use MovaUI blueprints?

Yes. The blueprints describe structure, tokens, motion physics, and performance budgets independently of React. Our MIT open-source stack-adapter-skill ships a zero-dependency Node script (detect-project-stack.mjs) that inspects your repo first—router mode, Tailwind v3 vs v4, installed animation libraries—so your coding agent adapts the implementation to your real stack.

Can I test the workflow without creating an account?

Yes—both the interactive prompt builder and the read-only MCP discovery layer work anonymously:

  • Free 60FPS Motion Prompt Builder (zero login): movaui.com/tools/motion-prompt-builder
  • MIT Open-Source Starter Skills (4 skills + Node validators): github.com/beautifulboy9527/movaui-skills
  • Zero-auth Remote Catalog MCP: https://movaui.com/mcp/catalog (setup spec at movaui.com/skill.md) 
# Connect read-only MovaUI Cloud Catalog MCP in Claude Code (no auth needed for public discovery)
claude mcp add --transport http movaui https://movaui.com/mcp/catalog

How are you handling motion consistency when building full pages with Claude Code or Cursor—sticking to single component libraries, custom system prompts, or MCP servers? Curious what's worked (or broken) for your stack.
