Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.

title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
description:
arXiv:2611.33896v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.

title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33962v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.

title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
description:
arXiv:2611.34092v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.

title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
description:
arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

title: SOLO: Towards Sample-Faithful and Detectable LLM Watermarking under Repeated Sampling via Content-Anchored Single-Owner Contexts
description:
arXiv:2611.34190v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Providers watermark the outputs of large language models, while applications sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, and uncertainty estimation. We show that deployed configurations of distortion-free watermarks, which deduplicate keyed contexts only within a response, couple the responses of a request: answer templates make all responses query the watermark with the same context before the answer, so collisions across responses, usually assumed rare, become the norm. Key pools reduce or avoid the coupling at the cost of multiple testing, and the exact remedy of a context history shared across the request leaves many positions unwatermarked. We propose SOLO, which keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so that siblings rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses, each detectable with a single key. On five language models from three families and three benchmarks, SOLO preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, also after randomly editing 10% of the tokens, and more than the context history on most clean tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhongliangGuo/solo-watermark.

title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.34250v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.

title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
description:
arXiv:2611.34363v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql

title: How RAG Beats Fine-Tuning: Building a Node.js Company Handbook Simply
description:
A healthtech handbook changes more often than its prose suggests. Product indications, training notes, escalation rules, and approved wording all move on different schedules. That operational constraint changes the answer: retrieve the current, permitted passages at question time instead of teaching those passages to a model through fine-tuning.

TL;DR: RAG usually beats fine-tuning for a company handbook because knowledge stays outside the model. You can replace, delete, date, and permission each source passage, then show the passages used for an answer. Fine-tuning changes model behavior; it is a poor substitute for a mutable content store. Explained simply, RAG looks up changing facts while fine-tuning teaches patterns. For a one-person SaaS, that separation protects the scarce resource: engineering hours that should ship product every week.

The key cost question is not "How many documents do we have?" It is "How many chunks do we embed, retain, search, and re-embed after each edit?" Start with retrieval, measure answer support, and fine-tune later only if repeated behavioral errors remain.

Why doesn't fine-tuning solve a changing handbook?

Fine-tuning and retrieval change different parts of the system. Fine-tuning adjusts a model's parameters from examples. RAG retrieves external text and supplies it as context before generation. The original RAG paper describes this as combining parametric memory with explicit non-parametric memory. That distinction matters more than either acronym.

Facts move.

Suppose an internal healthtech handbook says which product-content claims have completed review. On Tuesday, an editor replaces one approved paragraph. With retrieval, the ingestion job can remove the old chunks, index the new revision, and attach its review state. The generator never needs to memorize that paragraph. With fine-tuning, producing another training set still does not create a reliable document database, a deletion primitive, or a citation trail.

Freshness is only half the issue. Access is part of correctness. A contractor, a support employee, and a clinical reviewer may be allowed to see different passages. Retrieval can filter candidates by authorization metadata before any text enters the model context. Training shared restricted text into model weights makes that boundary harder to reason about. This is an architectural consequence, not a claim that retrieval automatically provides security. The application must enforce it.

I use a simple decision rule: if an editor must be able to change an answer without retraining, the fact belongs in retrieval. If examples are intended to change tone, response shape, or stable task behavior, fine-tuning may be relevant. Many systems eventually use both. They should not use one as a vague replacement for the other.

That is the split.

Build the smallest useful retrieval loop

The first implementation needs four operations: split approved content, embed each chunk, retrieve permitted candidates, and construct a grounded prompt. Keep those boundaries generic. Outsource the undifferentiated embedding and generation work behind interfaces; retain ownership of content state, authorization, and evaluation.

This runnable TypeScript example uses an in-memory index and a deterministic toy embedder. The embedder is deliberately weak, but the retrieval contract, metadata filter, and prompt construction are real. Replace the implementation behind embed when moving beyond the build log.

type Access = "all-staff" | "clinical-review";

type Chunk = {
  id: string;
  documentId: string;
  revision: number;
  access: Access;
  text: string;
  vector: number[];
};

const embed = (text: string): number[] => {
  const vector = Array<number>(64).fill(0);
  for (const token of text.toLowerCase().match(/[a-z0-9]+/g) ?? []) {
    let hash = 0;
    for (const char of token) hash = (hash * 31 + char.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0;
    vector[hash % vector.length] += 1;
  }
  const norm = Math.hypot(...vector) || 1;
  return vector.map((value) => value / norm);
};

const cosine = (left: number[], right: number[]): number =>
  left.reduce((sum, value, index) => sum + value * right[index], 0);

const source = {
  documentId: "product-content-policy",
  revision: 7,
  access: "all-staff" as const,
  paragraphs: [
    "Publish product content only after its review state is approved.",
    "Archive superseded wording when a new revision becomes active.",
    "Send unresolved medical questions to the clinical review queue."
  ]
};

const index: Chunk[] = source.paragraphs.map((text, position) => ({
  id: `${source.documentId}:r${source.revision}:${position}`,
  documentId: source.documentId,
  revision: source.revision,
  access: source.access,
  text,
  vector: embed(text)
}));

function retrieve(question: string, allowed: Set<Access>, limit = 2): Chunk[] {
  const query = embed(question);
  return index
    .filter((chunk) => allowed.has(chunk.access))
    .map((chunk) => ({ chunk, score: cosine(query, chunk.vector) }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, limit)
    .map(({ chunk }) => chunk);
}

function groundedPrompt(question: string, chunks: Chunk[]): string {
  const context = chunks
    .map((chunk) => `[${chunk.id}] ${chunk.text}`)
    .join("\n");

  return [
    "Answer only from the supplied handbook passages.",
    "If they do not support an answer, say that the handbook does not answer it.",
    "Cite passage IDs in the answer.",
    `Question: ${question}`,
    `Passages:\n${context}`
  ].join("\n\n");
}

const question = "What happens to superseded product wording?";
const chunks = retrieve(question, new Set<Access>(["all-staff"]));
console.log(groundedPrompt(question, chunks));

No model call is needed to test this boundary. Inspect the selected IDs first. Generation can hide bad retrieval behind fluent prose, so debugging both at once wastes time.

Start there.

Paragraphs are an acceptable starting unit, not a universal chunking rule. Headings, lists, and tables carry structure that a fixed character window can destroy. Preserve the document ID, revision, section path, access class, and stable chunk ID. Those fields earn their keep during deletion and incident review.

Make index cost an explicit budget

Index growth is multiplicative. Let D be active documents, C the average chunks per document, V the number of separately indexed variants, and R the retained revisions. The stored vector count is approximately D × C × V × R. That equation is intentionally plain. It exposes expensive habits before a vendor bill or a slow rebuild does.

Consider 8,000 active product-content documents averaging 14 chunks. One current variant produces 112,000 vectors. Keeping four complete revisions in the live index produces 448,000. These are arithmetic examples, not benchmark results. The useful decision is to keep one active revision searchable, put history in ordinary archival storage, and delete superseded vectors by stable document and revision identifiers. Do not duplicate the same vector for every role if access can be represented as filterable metadata with identical text. Do create separate chunks when the text itself differs. Measure both choices: heavy metadata filters can reduce the candidate pool available to approximate search, while duplicate indexes increase storage and update work. The right boundary depends on the retrieval engine and permission model. Chunk overlap deserves the same scrutiny. A 20% overlap can create roughly 25% more chunks for long sliding-window documents because each new chunk advances by 80% of its width. That may preserve sentences across boundaries, but it is not free. My initial default would be no overlap for structurally parsed handbook sections; I would add it only where evaluation queries expose boundary misses. This is an explicit trade: lower recurring index work now, with evidence deciding whether more context is worth its permanent storage multiplier.

Track three numbers per ingestion run: active source chunks, inserted vectors, and deleted vectors. Also record the source revision attached to every answer. When those counts disagree with the content system, stop publishing the new index generation. Quiet duplication is a bad use of revenue-per-hour because it raises recurring cost while making freshness ambiguous.

Test the failure modes before adding polish

A demo question is not an evaluation set. Build a small set from real handbook jobs: exact policy lookup, paraphrased lookup, a question spanning two sections, an unauthorized question, a superseded statement, and an unanswerable question. Store expected source IDs or an explicit expectation of no answer.

For retrieval, measure whether an expected passage appears in the first k results. For the final response, verify each material claim against the retrieved passages. A grounded prompt helps, but instructions alone do not guarantee grounded output. Test abstention separately. The correct response to missing evidence is a refusal to invent handbook policy.

Deletion needs a test too. Insert revision 7, replace it with revision 8, and ask the question whose answer changed. Fail the deployment if revision 7 remains retrievable from the active alias. This catches a more dangerous class of bug than an awkward sentence.

Test deletion.

Keep logs useful but sparse: query ID, authorized scope, index generation, retrieved chunk IDs, scores, latency, and answer outcome. Avoid logging raw restricted passages by default. Health information and employee data require their own governance; a semantic-search project does not relax those duties.

Ship the narrow loop. Weekly releases make evaluation drift visible sooner, while a grand ingestion platform can consume a month before anyone learns whether employees ask answerable questions.

What I would change at scale

Move ingestion off the request path first. Content updates should produce an immutable index generation, run retrieval tests against it, and switch an alias only after those tests pass. If the switch fails, the previous generation remains available. The serving path stays boring.

Next, replace the linear scan with an index appropriate to the measured corpus and latency target. Exact search is valuable as an evaluation baseline even after approximate nearest-neighbor search enters production. Approximation trades some recall for speed; compare it against the exact baseline using the same questions and permission filters.

I would also cache embeddings by normalized content hash. An unchanged paragraph should not be embedded merely because an adjacent paragraph changed. The cache must include the embedding configuration in its key, since vectors from incompatible configurations do not belong in the same comparison space.

The trade-off remains clear. Retrieval adds an ingestion pipeline, an index, access filters, and evaluation work. Fine-tuning adds dataset construction, training lifecycle work, and a harder path for changing factual content. For a mutable company handbook, retrieval's operational burden maps directly to the job: find the current allowed text. That is why it wins here. Fine-tuning is still available later for stable behavior that prompt and retrieval evaluation cannot fix.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/
  • https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/index.html

title: Node.js SMS OTP Recovery — Carrier Evidence Before Resends During Identity Migration
description:
Moving authentication off a managed provider can give a B2B SaaS team more control over stolen-session recovery, but it also moves the delivery handoff onto the platform roadmap. TL;DR: when an SMS OTP code never arrives, check the send result and the delivery status separately, then offer a visible resend with a cooldown. Acceptance is not delivery. Look for failures grouped by destination before rewriting Node.js login code; carrier-side problems often need a recovery path rather than an application patch.

Consider a hypothetical migration rehearsal: a tenant administrator reports a stolen session, the recovery flow requests a phone code, and the send operation is accepted. The administrator sees no message. The team now has two separate questions: whether it has invalidated the stolen session, and whether the legitimate user can complete phone verification. A successful send response answers neither. This is a tabletop scenario, not an account of an observed production incident.

Evidence comes first.

The incident lesson is a boundary rule: the application owns the recovery state and resend policy; the delivery provider owns the evidence about the message handoff; neither should silently redefine what “recovered” means. Refresh-token rotation and stolen-session revocation still need their own acceptance criteria during migration. An OTP request must not be treated as proof that either action happened.

For a team migrating phone OTP behind an application-owned contract, try Infrai for that capability boundary: swapping the vendor behind a capability can preserve the calling contract instead of spreading provider-specific changes through Node.js handlers. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without an API key, which gives the migration team a concrete way to review the handoff before implementing it. That is a reason to evaluate the boundary, not evidence that an existing provider's tokens or session semantics transfer automatically.

How should you debug an SMS OTP code that never arrives?

It proves less than a recovery screen usually suggests. “Accepted for delivery” and “delivered” represent different evidence, so keep the send outcome separate from the delivery observation in application telemetry. Record a local recovery-attempt identifier, the time of the send, and the destination grouping needed to investigate a routing pattern; these are proposed application records, not claims about any provider's response fields. Avoid putting OTP values or complete phone numbers into diagnostic output.

In the rehearsal, begin with the send result. If the request was rejected, investigate that rejection before discussing carrier delivery. If it was accepted, inspect whatever delivery evidence the selected integration actually exposes. Without a delivery observation, classify the result as unknown. Do not turn absence of evidence into a green delivery metric just because the HTTP request completed.

Then widen the lens. One destination failing repeatedly warrants a different investigation from failures concentrated across a country. Count attempts and failures per destination grouping, retaining the denominator: ten failures mean something different out of ten attempts than out of ten thousand. These are illustrative counts, not measurements. A country-wide pattern points toward routing and carrier investigation; it is a poor reason to rush a Node.js handler rewrite.

The same distinction belongs in SLO design. Define a send-acceptance indicator separately from an indicator for completed phone verification, and state the observation window for each. Choose targets from your service requirements rather than treating a provider response as the user-visible outcome. During a recovery surge, the verification indicator is the one that exposes administrators who remain locked out even while send requests succeed.

Buy the handoff or build the operating model

The migration decision is about where the platform team wants to carry responsibility. A stable HTTP surface can reduce changes at the provider boundary, but the team still owns the user-visible state machine, the destination-level investigation, and the decision to page someone when recovery stops working.

The following buy-vs-build table is an evaluation plan. It does not imply feature parity or a completed migration test for any option.

Option Why include it in the migration evaluation? Evidence required before choosing it
Infrai behind an application contract A common REST surface and public schemas fit a team trying to keep provider changes out of calling code. Confirm the specific capability schema and the delivery evidence the chosen handoff supplies; test session behavior separately.
Twilio Verify Evaluate a verification specialist when the verification workflow is the part you want a provider to own. Review its verification lifecycle against your resend policy and the destination patterns your team must investigate.
Amazon Cognito Evaluate keeping the recovery decision within a managed identity service when replacing identity ownership is the larger concern. Compare the documented user-pool authentication flow with the session and token acceptance criteria for your migration.
Auth0 Evaluate retaining a managed identity boundary when the application would otherwise inherit too much authentication lifecycle work. Review the documented refresh-token rotation behavior and test the stolen-session recovery outcome you require.
Keycloak Evaluate a self-hosted identity boundary when control over the deployment is a requirement. Budget upgrades and on-call ownership, and validate recovery behavior before replacing a managed service.
Application-owned policy with direct integrations Build when the team needs explicit control over recovery transitions and can staff the operating work. Demonstrate cooldown enforcement, delivery classification, and revocation acceptance tests under concurrent requests.

The linked documentation in References provides starting points for those reviews. There is no measured reliability ranking here, and a single API shape does not establish equivalent carrier visibility, token handling, or operational support across providers.

A verification specialist such as Twilio Verify is the better evaluation starting point when provider-owned verification behavior is the main requirement. A managed identity option such as Cognito or Auth0 deserves priority when the team wants to keep lifecycle responsibility with that service. The common-contract approach fits a different decision: the application deliberately owns the recovery policy and wants a cleaner handoff around it.

Infrai is not a good fit for a team that expects an API contract alone to eliminate recovery operations; choose a managed identity boundary such as Auth0 when retaining that ownership is the priority. Its advantage for an application-owned boundary is one REST API, using plain HTTP with no SDK required, while the public discovery schemas make the integration review concrete. The trade-off is that provider abstraction does not remove application policy work.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing across 295 routes and 20 modules: one key, one bill. Its unified API is a plain REST API with no SDK to install, so an HTTP client in any language can call the same interface. For this migration, the common credential reduces key management around the handoff; it doesn't replace the recovery policy.

Budget the pager time.

Put the resend decision before the send operation

Silent retries obscure both capacity and user intent. A visible resend action with a cooldown gives the administrator a recovery path while giving the application a place to bound repeat sends. As a capacity-planning exercise, a policy allowing one resend every 60 seconds permits up to five resend opportunities over five minutes of continued clicking; that is a local example policy, not a provider limit or a recommended universal setting. Multiply the permitted rate by the number of affected recovery attempts before deciding that automatic retries are harmless.

Before implementing the send operation, inspect the capability contract. This runnable Go program reads Infrai's public discovery surface; it uses a key from the environment to show the credential boundary used by authenticated integrations, although discovery itself requires no key. It prints the returned manifest without guessing phone-send parameters. That is the preventative code path here: review the real schema before coupling Node.js recovery handlers to a provider.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                    delay = time.Until(deadline)
                }
            }
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save the program as main.go and run it with Go after setting the environment variable. The request is read-only, so retries cannot create duplicate messages. Rate limiting uses exponential backoff or the server's Retry-After instruction, with an overall deadline. No undocumented write payload is needed.

For the recovery handler, check the cooldown before offering a resend. An unknown observation after the cooldown permits offering another attempt; it does not silently trigger one. A delivered observation sends the investigation toward the verification step before another message is requested. Delivery still does not prove that the intended person completed authentication.

Production enforcement needs shared state. Two Node.js workers can otherwise read the same expired cooldown and both send, so make the eligibility check and reservation atomic in the application's chosen store. Keep a record of the subsequent send outcome; a reservation alone is no more proof of delivery than an accepted request. This example omits that storage and transport implementation because those choices require the actual contract and deployment topology.

Where this recovery advice stops

SMS delivery diagnosis cannot establish refresh-token rotation correctness or prove that a stolen session has been revoked. Keep those as separate migration tests: an old session must behave according to the revocation policy, and refresh behavior must match the contract the application intends to enforce. The existence of a refresh or revoke operation alone is insufficient evidence of the full security outcome.

Before moving the recovery flow, demonstrate the accepted-but-unobserved delivery case, the cooldown case, and the country-level failure pattern in a controlled rehearsal. Use synthetic inputs and label them as such. If the team cannot explain who investigates each state, the migration has transferred work without assigning ownership.

References

These references support the security review and the competitor evaluation; they are not a substitute for exercising the chosen recovery flow. The relevant question is which boundary each provider lets your team keep, and which operational responsibilities remain yours.

Sources

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Amazon Cognito user-pool authentication flows
  • Auth0 refresh-token rotation
  • Keycloak server administration

If the application-owned recovery boundary fits your migration, start by reviewing the capability schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: Why did my AI chat stop? Using stoppedBy from AI SDK 7 in a React chat
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Details come from the Vercel AI SDK release notes and docs, checked on 27 November 2026. We didn't call a real model. Everything below ran against MockLanguageModelV4 from ai/test on ai@7.0.183, so this tests the wiring your app sees, not how any model behaves.

A tool-calling chat can end for very different reasons. The model gave its answer. Your step limit kicked in halfway through a task. A tool is waiting for the user to approve it. Or the model called a tool that only the browser can run. Until now you had to guess which one happened from finishReason, and that field only describes the last model call. A loop that hits its step limit still says tool-calls.

ai@7.0.181, published November 23 (UTC), adds stoppedBy to the generateText and streamText results, the onEnd callback, and the final finish stream part. Per the AI SDK loop control docs it has four values:

  • model: the model finished without tool calls that keep the loop going. Check finishReason to tell stop from length.
  • stop-condition: a stopWhen condition was met, such as isStepCount(3).
  • tool-without-execute: a tool call needs a result from a tool with no execute function.
  • approval: a tool call needs approval.

The same release adds a per-call onWarning callback. The docs say WorkflowAgent and HarnessAgent don't report stoppedBy yet.

Getting it to the browser

stoppedBy lives on the server-side stream. The UI message stream's finish chunk that useChat reads carries finishReason and messageMetadata, but not stoppedBy. So pass it through message metadata:

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
import {
  streamText, convertToModelMessages, tool, isStepCount,
  type UIMessage, type StoppedBy, type FinishReason,
} from 'ai';
import { z } from 'zod';

export type ChatMessage = UIMessage<{ stoppedBy?: StoppedBy; finishReason?: FinishReason }>;

const tools = {
  searchDocs: tool({
    description: 'Search the docs',
    inputSchema: z.object({ query: z.string() }),
    execute: async ({ query }) => ({ hits: [`result for ${query}`] }),
  }),
  deleteDraft: tool({
    description: 'Delete a draft',
    inputSchema: z.object({ id: z.string() }),
    needsApproval: true,
    execute: async ({ id }) => ({ deleted: id }),
  }),
  askUser: tool({
    description: 'Ask the user a clarifying question',
    inputSchema: z.object({ question: z.string() }),
    // no execute: the browser answers this one
  }),
};

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages }: { messages: ChatMessage[] } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: openai('gpt-6.2-sol'),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    tools,
    stopWhen: isStepCount(3),
    onWarning: ({ warnings }) => console.warn('model warnings', warnings),
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse<ChatMessage>({
    messageMetadata: ({ part }) =>
      part.type === 'finish'
        ? { stoppedBy: part.stoppedBy, finishReason: part.finishReason }
        : undefined,
  });
}

On the client, useChat<ChatMessage>() gives you message.metadata.stoppedBy on the last assistant message. Only two cases need new UI:

export function LoopStatus({ message, onContinue }: { message: ChatMessage; onContinue: () => void }) {
  const { stoppedBy, finishReason } = message.metadata ?? {};
  if (stoppedBy === 'stop-condition') {
    return <p>Paused after the step limit. <button onClick={onContinue}>Keep going</button></p>;
  }
  if (stoppedBy === 'model' && finishReason === 'length') {
    return <p>The answer hit the length limit and may be cut off.</p>;
  }
  return null; // approval and client-side tools already show up as tool parts
}

We wire onContinue to sendMessage({ text: 'Continue where you left off.' }). The approval and client-side tool cases already appear as tool parts in approval-requested and input-available states, so those parts can render their own buttons.

What the test showed

We ran six scripted scenarios through the route handler above (with the mock model swapped in) and read each response the way useChat does, using parseJsonEventStream and readUIMessageStream.

Scenario Model calls stoppedBy finishReason
Plain answer 1 model stop
Cut off by max tokens 1 model length
Three searches, limit of 3 3 stop-condition tool-calls
Delete needs approval 1 approval tool-calls
askUser (no execute) 1 tool-without-execute tool-calls

The last three rows are the point. finishReason is the same in all three, while stoppedBy tells them apart. The metadata arrived on the client every time.

The sixth scenario had the mock return a provider warning. With onWarning set, the callback got {"type":"unsupported","feature":"temperature"} and nothing was printed. Without it, the same warning went to the global warning logger. That matches the streamText reference, which says warnings skip that logger when onWarning is set.

The other change: a 64 MiB cap per streamed event

@ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.84 (November 25, UTC) fixed a crash risk. Before, parseJsonEventStream buffered a server-sent event with no size limit, so a stream that never finished an event could use up memory. Now a single event is capped at 67,108,864 characters. Per the release notes, this cap also covers the streams useChat and useCompletion read. 5.0.85 a day later let the OpenAI and xAI Responses models accept events of up to 512 MiB, because response.completed repeats every output item, including base64 images.

We pushed one SSE event through parseJsonEventStream with the UI message chunk schema:

  • A 10 MiB text delta parsed fine.
  • A 70 MiB delta failed with ParseError: Buffered data exceeded max buffer size of 67108864 characters.
  • The same 70 MiB delta passed with maxEventSize raised to 128 MiB.

For a chat app, the practical rule is to keep big payloads out of single events. If a tool returns a generated file, send a URL in the tool output instead of base64. In ai@7.0.183, we found no maxEventSize option on DefaultChatTransport, so you can't raise the cap from useChat.

Honest limits

  • No real model. These results show what the SDK sends and reports. They don't show how often a real model hits your step limit.
  • The browser UI wasn't exercised. The route and the React components type-check against @ai-sdk/react@4.0.188, and the stream was read with the same parser useChat uses. We didn't click through a rendered page.
  • "Keep going" is a new turn. It sends another user message, which costs another model call with the full history.
  • Patch-level features. stoppedBy is optional in the types, so treat undefined as "unknown" if you share code with older versions or agents that don't report it yet.

Sources

  • ai@7.0.181 release notes (stoppedBy, onWarning)
  • Loop control: Why the loop stopped, AI SDK docs
  • streamText reference (onWarning), AI SDK docs
  • @ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.84 release notes (64 MiB event limit)
  • @ai-sdk/provider-utils@5.0.85 release notes (512 MiB for OpenAI and xAI Responses)
  • OpenAI API changelog (gpt-6.2-sol model ID)

If you'd rather not build the message list and tool-status rows yourself, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style AI chat components that fit this setup.

title: How to Scrape Twitter (X) with Go: Advanced Search Operators, Account Timelines, and a Cron Watcher (2026)
description:
"Twitter advanced search" gets about 18,100 US searches a month, and another 1,900 people a month search for how to "search twitter without account". Both groups want the same thing: type from:golang released min_faves:500 -filter:retweets and get a clean list of posts back, ideally in a script that can run every hour. In 2026 that is harder than it looks. The search page needs a login, the official API bills per post returned, and none of the logged-out tricks that used to work are left.

This post builds xsearch, a small Go tool (standard library only) that does it the other way around: it fetches candidate posts as JSON and then applies X's advanced-search operators locally, in about 800 lines of Go you can read and test. It has three commands:

  1. explain shows how a query is split between "what to fetch" and "what to filter"
  2. search prints matching posts as a table
  3. watch remembers what it has already reported and appends only new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron

Everything below ran on November 27, 2026 (04:10-04:45 UTC) with Go 1.27.3 on a Linux server.

Read this first: X's Terms of Service prohibit scraping. The X Terms of Service (effective October 9, 2026) say that "crawling or scraping the Services in any form, for any purpose without our prior written consent is expressly prohibited", and that you may not access or search the Services "by any means (automated or otherwise) other than through our currently available, published interfaces". The catch-all group in x.com/robots.txt is User-agent: * / Disallow: /. Review the terms and the legal risk for your use case and location before you run anything here. If the official X API covers your job, use it: recent search (last 7 days) and full-archive search are both there, billed pay-per-use (X's pricing page listed $0.005 per post read in November 2026). Keep volumes small, and don't republish other people's posts or build profiles of individuals. The tables below mask the handles of private persons.

Step 1: What a logged-out Go client gets

Before writing a parser, check what X sends to a plain HTTP client:

// probe: what X answers to a logged-out client in 2026. Go standard library only.
package main

import (

    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        // Show redirects instead of following them.
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error { return http.ErrUseLastResponse },
    }
    urls := []string{
        "https://x.com/search?q=golang%20min_faves%3A100&f=live",
        "https://api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent?query=golang",
        "https://syndication.twitter.com/srv/timeline-profile/screen-name/golang",
        "https://x.com/robots.txt",
    }
    for _, u := range urls {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/131.0 Safari/537.36")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {

Four doors, four answers:

  • x.com/search answers with a 307 to the login flow. The advanced-search form just builds a /search?q=... URL like this one, so it is behind the same wall.
  • api.x.com/2/tweets/search/recent is the official API. Without a bearer token you get 401. With one you pay per post returned.
  • The old syndication timeline (what embedded profile timelines used) is rate-limited to death: 429 on the first request from this machine.
  • robots.txt lists rules for named search crawlers and then closes everything else with Disallow: /.

So "just scrape the search page" is out, and I'm not going to show login automation or cookie reuse. That is exactly what the terms forbid, and the accounts get locked anyway. What's left is to fetch posts from a data source and do the search part yourself.

Step 2: Where the candidate posts come from

The tool reads X through ScrapeAtlas*, using two endpoints:

  • /v1/twitter/user-tweets?handle=golang&trim=true returns an account's latest posts (14-20 per account in my runs) with views, likes, retweets, replies, quotes and the full legacy object. since and until narrow it down, but only inside that latest window: asking @golang for September 2026 returned zero posts with the warning latest_window_limited, even though the account posted in September. It costs 1 credit.
  • /v1/twitter/search/posts?query=... finds posts by keyword through a web index, not through X's own search. Results come back in relevance order, a handful per page, with a cursor like atlas:2 or serper:3 for the next page. It costs 2 credits per page. In my runs the cursor ran out after 3-4 pages, at roughly 10-20 unique posts per keyword. Operators are not supported there: from:golang since:2026-11-01 came back with zero posts.

That split decides the design. A from: query is answered precisely from timelines. Everything else is discovery: the web index proposes posts, the local filter decides. You will not get "every post that mentions X". You'll get a relevant sample that is filtered exactly.

Every response also has a coverage object (complete, order, warnings). The tool prints the warnings on every run, because "0 matches" means something different when the source says complete: false.

Step 3: A client with a disk cache

While you tune a query you run the same fetches over and over. Each response is cached on disk for 30 minutes, keyed by the full URL, so re-running a filter costs nothing. 429 and 5xx are retried with backoff (2s, 4s, 8s). Other errors stop the run instead of being silently skipped.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha1"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.scrapeatlas.com"

type Client struct {
    key      string
    http     *http.Client
    cacheDir string
    cacheTTL time.Duration
    Calls    int // paid requests actually sent (cache hits are free)
}

// envelope holds the fields every ScrapeAtlas twitter response shares.
type envelope struct {
    Success  bool            `json:"success"`
    Status   string          `json:"status"`
    Cursor   *string         `json:"cursor"`
    Posts    []rawTweet      `json:"posts"`  // /search/posts
    Tweets   []rawTweet      `json:"tweets"` // /user-tweets
    Error    json.RawMessage `json:"error"`
    Coverage struct {
        Source   string   `json:"source"`
        Order    string   `json:"order"`
        Complete bool     `json:"complete"`
        Warnings []string `json:"warnings"`
    } `json:"coverage"`
}

func NewClient() (*Client, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    }
    return &Client{key: key, http: &http.Client{Timeout: 60 * time.Second},
        cacheDir: "cache", cacheTTL: 30 * time.Minute}, nil
}

func (c *Client) Get(path string, params url.Values) (*envelope, error) {
    u := apiBase + path + "?" + params.Encode()
    sum := sha1.Sum([]byte(u))
    cacheFile := filepath.Join(c.cacheDir, hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8])+".json")
    if st, err := os.Stat(cacheFile); err == nil && time.Since(st.ModTime()) < c.cacheTTL {
        if b, err := os.ReadFile(cacheFile); err == nil {
            return decode(b)
        }
    }
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if attempt > 0 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second) // 2s, 4s, 8s
        }
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("x-api-key", c.key)
        resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        c.Calls++
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == 429 || resp.StatusCode >= 500 {
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d", path, resp.StatusCode)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != 200 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d: %.300s", path, resp.StatusCode, b)
        }
        env, err := decode(b)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", path, err)
        }
        os.MkdirAll(c.cacheDir, 0o755)
        os.WriteFile(cacheFile, b, 0o644)
        return env, nil
    }
    return nil, lastErr
}

func decode(b []byte) (*envelope, error) {
    var env envelope
    if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &env); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if !env.Success {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("success=false: %.300s", env.Error)
    }
    return &env, nil
}

Calls counts requests that actually went out, so the summary line can tell you what a run cost. A search page is 2 credits, so a 4-page search is 8 credits.

Step 4: Normalizing a tweet

Both endpoints return X's own GraphQL tweet shape. Some details matter for searching:

  • Retweets are shells. The retweet object has favorite_count: 0 and text cut at 140 characters (RT @resend: We rebuilt our email API to Go.\n\nIt took 7 weeks and 140 PRs, and we've been running in production for weeks at roughly half th…). The real text and media are in retweeted_status_result.
  • Long posts live in note_tweet. legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters. In the saved @golang timeline, 5 of 17 posts were longer than that. If you match keywords against full_text, a word in paragraph two never matches. And not every long post has a note: one of NASA's posts ended mid-sentence at 277 characters ("NASA stands ready to") with no note_tweet at all.
  • Text is HTML-escaped. > and & show up in full_text, so unescape before matching.
  • Timeline items have no author object with trim=true. The url field (https://x.com/NASA/status/...) still has the handle in its original case. 
package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "html"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// Tweet is the flat shape the filter and the reports work on.
type Tweet struct {
    ID        string    `json:"id"`
    Author    string    `json:"author"`
    Created   time.Time `json:"created"`
    Text      string    `json:"text"`
    Lang      string    `json:"lang"`
    Faves     int       `json:"faves"`
    Retweets  int       `json:"retweets"`
    Replies   int       `json:"replies"`
    Quotes    int       `json:"quotes"`
    Views     int       `json:"views"`
    ReplyTo   string    `json:"reply_to,omitempty"`
    IsRetweet bool      `json:"is_retweet,omitempty"`
    IsQuote   bool      `json:"is_quote,omitempty"`
    HasMedia  bool      `json:"has_media,omitempty"`
    URLs      []string  `json:"urls,omitempty"`
    URL       string    `json:"url"`
}

type rawUser struct {
    Result struct {
        Core struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"core"`
        Legacy struct {
            ScreenName string `json:"screen_name"`
        } `json:"legacy"`
    } `json:"result"`
}

type rawLegacy struct {
    CreatedAt     string `json:"created_at"`
    FullText      string `json:"full_text"`
    Lang          string `json:"lang"`
    FavoriteCount int    `json:"favorite_count"`
    RetweetCount  int    `json:"retweet_count"`
    ReplyCount    int    `json:"reply_count"`
    QuoteCount    int    `json:"quote_count"`
    IsQuoteStatus bool   `json:"is_quote_status"`
    InReplyTo     string `json:"in_reply_to_screen_name"`
    Entities      struct {
        URLs []struct {
            ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
        } `json:"urls"`
    } `json:"entities"`
    ExtendedEntities struct {
        Media []json.RawMessage `json:"media"`
    } `json:"extended_entities"`
    RetweetedStatus *struct {
        Result rawTweet `json:"result"`
    } `json:"retweeted_status_result"`
}

type rawTweet struct {
    TypeName string    `json:"__typename"`
    Tweet    *rawTweet `json:"tweet"` // TweetWithVisibilityResults wraps the real tweet
    RestID   string    `json:"rest_id"`
    Core     struct {
        UserResults rawUser `json:"user_results"`
    } `json:"core"`
    Views struct {
        Count string `json:"count"`
    } `json:"views"`
    Legacy    rawLegacy `json:"legacy"`
    NoteTweet *struct { // posts longer than 280 characters
        Results struct {
            Result struct {
                Text      string `json:"text"`
                EntitySet struct {
                    URLs []struct {
                        ExpandedURL string `json:"expanded_url"`
                    } `json:"urls"`
                } `json:"entity_set"`
            } `json:"result"`
        } `json:"note_tweet_results"`
    } `json:"note_tweet"`
    URL string `json:"url"`
}

// normalize turns one ScrapeAtlas tweet object into a Tweet. Timeline items
// (trim=true) carry no author object: read it from the post URL, else use
// the handle the caller asked for.
func normalize(r rawTweet, fallbackAuthor string) (Tweet, error) {
    if r.Tweet != nil {
        r = *r.Tweet
    }
    l := r.Legacy
    created, err := time.Parse(time.RubyDate, l.CreatedAt)
    if err != nil {
        return Tweet{}, err
    }
    author := r.Core.UserResults.Result.Core.ScreenName
    if author == "" {
        author = r.Core.UserResults.Result.Legacy.ScreenName
    }
    if author == "" && strings.HasPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/") {
        author, _, _ = strings.Cut(strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL, "https://x.com/"), "/")
    }
    if author == "" {
        author = fallbackAuthor
    }
    views, _ := strconv.Atoi(r.Views.Count)
    t := Tweet{
        ID: r.RestID, Author: author, Created: created.UTC(),
        Text: html.UnescapeString(l.FullText), Lang: l.Lang,
        Faves: l.FavoriteCount, Retweets: l.RetweetCount, Replies: l.ReplyCount,
        Quotes: l.QuoteCount, Views: views, ReplyTo: l.InReplyTo,
        IsQuote: l.IsQuoteStatus, HasMedia: len(l.ExtendedEntities.Media) > 0,
        URL: r.URL,
    }
    for _, u := range l.Entities.URLs {
        t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
    }
    if n := r.NoteTweet; n != nil && n.Results.Result.Text != "" {
        // legacy.full_text stops near 280 characters; the note has the whole post.
        t.Text = html.UnescapeString(n.Results.Result.Text)
        t.URLs = nil
        for _, u := range n.Results.Result.EntitySet.URLs {
            t.URLs = append(t.URLs, u.ExpandedURL)
        }
    }
    if rt := l.RetweetedStatus; rt != nil {
        // The retweet shell has favorite_count 0 and a truncated "RT @x: ..." text.
        // Keep the shell's id and time, but read text and media from the original.
        orig, err := normalize(rt.Result, "")
        if err == nil {
            t.IsRetweet = true
            t.Text = "RT @" + orig.Author + ": " + orig.Text
            t.HasMedia, t.URLs = orig.HasMedia, orig.URLs
        }
    }
    if t.URL == "" {
        t.URL = "https://x.com/" + t.Author + "/status/" + t.ID
    }
    return t, nil
}

Step 5: Parsing advanced-search operators

This is the core. The parser supports the operators people actually type into advanced search:

Operator Meaning
word, "exact phrase" whole-word match, case-insensitive (golang also matches #golang)
a OR b either term
-word, -"phrase" exclude
#tag, @name the hashtag or mention specifically
from:, to: author, reply-to account
lang: X's language code
since:, until: YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, until exclusive
min_faves:, min_retweets:, min_replies: engagement floors
filter:replies, filter:retweets, filter:quote, filter:media, filter:links, url: post type, prefix - to exclude

Anything else (near:, within:, list:) fails loudly instead of being ignored. A silently dropped operator gives you a wider result set than you asked for, and you won't notice.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
    "unicode"
)

// Atom is one search term or operator, e.g. golang, "go 1.27", from:golang, -filter:replies.
type Atom struct {
    Neg   bool
    Op    string // "" for plain words and phrases
    Value string
}

// Query is an AND of clauses; each clause is an OR of atoms.
type Query struct {
    Clauses [][]Atom
    Since   time.Time // inclusive, UTC day
    Until   time.Time // exclusive, UTC day
    MinFav  int
    MinRT   int
    MinRepl int
}

func tokenize(s string) []string {
    var out []string
    for i := 0; i < len(s); {
        switch {
        case s[i] == ' ' || s[i] == '\t':
            i++
        case s[i] == '"' || (s[i] == '-' && i+1 < len(s) && s[i+1] == '"'):
            start := i
            if s[i] == '-' {
                i++
            }
            end := strings.IndexByte(s[i+1:], '"')
            if end < 0 {
                out = append(out, s[start:])
                return out
            }
            out = append(out, s[start:i+1+end+1])
            i += end + 2
        default:
            end := strings.IndexAny(s[i:], " \t")
            if end < 0 {
                end = len(s) - i
            }
            out = append(out, s[i:i+end])
            i += end
        }
    }
    return out
}

func ParseQuery(s string) (*Query, error) {
    q := &Query{}
    orNext := false
    for _, tok := range tokenize(s) {
        if tok == "OR" {
            if len(q.Clauses) == 0 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("query starts with OR")
            }
            orNext = true
            continue
        }
        a := Atom{}
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, "-") && len(tok) > 1 {
            a.Neg, tok = true, tok[1:]
        }
        if strings.HasPrefix(tok, `"`) {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(strings.Trim(tok, `"`))
        } else if k, v, ok := strings.Cut(tok, ":"); ok && v != "" && !strings.Contains(k, "/") {
            a.Op, a.Value = strings.ToLower(k), strings.ToLower(v)
        } else {
            a.Value = strings.ToLower(tok)
        }
        // Numeric and date operators become fields, not atoms.
        handled, err := q.setField(a)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if handled {
            orNext = false
            continue
        }
        if orNext {
            last := len(q.Clauses) - 1
            q.Clauses[last] = append(q.Clauses[last], a)
            orNext = false
        } else {
            q.Clauses = append(q.Clauses, []Atom{a})
        }
    }
    if orNext {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("query ends with OR")
    }
    return q, nil
}

func (q *Query) setField(a Atom) (bool, error) {
    if a.Neg && a.Op != "" && a.Op != "filter" && a.Op != "from" && a.Op != "to" &&
        a.Op != "lang" && a.Op != "url" {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("cannot negate %s:", a.Op)
    }
    switch a.Op {
    case "since", "until":
        t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", a.Value)
        if err != nil {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want YYYY-MM-DD, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        if a.Op == "since" {
            q.Since = t
        } else {
            q.Until = t
        }
        return true, nil
    case "min_faves", "min_retweets", "min_replies":
        n, err := strconv.Atoi(a.Value)
        if err != nil || n < 0 {
            return false, fmt.Errorf("%s: want a number, got %q", a.Op, a.Value)
        }
        switch a.Op {
        case "min_faves":
            q.MinFav = n
        case "min_retweets":
            q.MinRT = n
        default:
            q.MinRepl = n
        }
        return true, nil
    case "", "from", "to", "lang", "filter", "url":
        return false, nil
    }
    return false, fmt.Errorf("unsupported operator %s:", a.Op)
}

// words lowercases text and splits it on anything that is not a letter, digit,
// '_', '#' or '@', so "Go 1.27!" -> [go 1 27].
func words(s string) []string {
    return strings.FieldsFunc(strings.ToLower(s), func(r rune) bool {
        return !(unicode.IsLetter(r) || unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '_' || r == '#' || r == '@')
    })
}

func containsSeq(hay, needle []string) bool {
    if len(needle) == 0 {
        return false
    }
outer:
    for i := 0; i+len(needle) <= len(hay); i++ {
        for j := range needle {
            if hay[i+j] != needle[j] {
                continue outer
            }
        }
        return true
    }
    return false
}

func (a Atom) match(t *Tweet, raw, bare []string) bool {
    switch a.Op {
    case "":
        if strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "#") || strings.HasPrefix(a.Value, "@") {
            return containsSeq(raw, words(a.Value)) // #golang must be a hashtag
        }
        return containsSeq(bare, words(a.Value)) // golang also matches #golang
    case "from":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.Author, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "to":
        return strings.EqualFold(t.ReplyTo, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
    case "lang":
        return t.Lang == a.Value
    case "url":
        for _, u := range t.URLs {
            if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(u), a.Value) {
                return true
            }
        }
        return false
    case "filter":
        switch a.Value {
        case "replies":
            return t.ReplyTo != ""
        case "retweets", "nativeretweets":
            return t.IsRetweet
        case "quote":
            return t.IsQuote
        case "media":
            return t.HasMedia
        case "links":
            return len(t.URLs) > 0
        }
    }
    return false
}

// Match applies the whole query to one normalized tweet.
func (q *Query) Match(t *Tweet) bool {
    if !q.Since.IsZero() && t.Created.Before(q.Since) {
        return false
    }
    if !q.Until.IsZero() && !t.Created.Before(q.Until) {
        return false
    }
    if t.Faves < q.MinFav || t.Retweets < q.MinRT || t.Replies < q.MinRepl {
        return false
    }
    raw := words(t.Text)
    bare := make([]string, len(raw))
    for i, w := range raw {
        bare[i] = strings.TrimLeft(w, "#@")
    }
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        ok := false
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.match(t, raw, bare) != a.Neg {
                ok = true
                break
            }
        }
        if !ok {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

// Handles returns the accounts of the first clause made only of from: atoms
// (from:a OR from:b), or nil when no clause pins the author.
func (q *Query) Handles() []string {
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var hs []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            if a.Op != "from" || a.Neg {
                hs = nil
                break
            }
            hs = append(hs, strings.TrimPrefix(a.Value, "@"))
        }
        if hs != nil {
            return hs
        }
    }
    return nil
}

// Keywords returns plain search strings for the web-index search endpoint: the
// positive words and phrases, one string per alternative of the first OR clause.
func (q *Query) Keywords() []string {
    var base []string
    var alts []string
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        if len(clause) == 1 && clause[0].Op == "" && !clause[0].Neg {
            base = append(base, quoteIfSpace(clause[0].Value))
            continue
        }
        if alts == nil {
            plain := true
            for _, a := range clause {
                plain = plain && a.Op == "" && !a.Neg
            }
            if plain {
                for _, a := range clause {
                    alts = append(alts, quoteIfSpace(a.Value))
                }
            }
        }
    }
    if len(alts) == 0 {
        if len(base) == 0 {
            return nil
        }
        return []string{strings.Join(base, " ")}
    }
    var out []string
    for _, alt := range alts {
        out = append(out, strings.TrimSpace(strings.Join(base, " ")+" "+alt))
    }
    return out
}

func quoteIfSpace(s string) string {
    if strings.Contains(s, " ") {
        return `"` + s + `"`
    }
    return s
}

Three decisions worth explaining:

  • Whole words, no stemming. release does not match "released", and api does not match "APIs". X's search doesn't stem either, so the tool behaves the same, and you get used to writing release OR released.
  • OR binds to its neighbours, like X's search: golang OR #go -hiring means "(golang or #go) and not hiring". There are no parentheses, which keeps the parser tiny and covers most real queries.
  • Keywords() fans out OR groups. The web index doesn't understand OR, so scraping OR scraper OR crawler becomes three keyword searches. That's three times the credits, and explain shows it before you pay.

The tests pin down that behaviour, including the cases people get wrong:

package main

import (
    "testing"
    "time"
)

func TestMatch(t *testing.T) {
    day := func(s string) time.Time { v, _ := time.Parse("2006-01-02", s); return v }
    base := Tweet{ID: "1", Author: "golang", Created: day("2026-11-10"), Lang: "en", Faves: 968,
        Retweets: 160, Text: "🎊 Go 1.27.4 and 1.26.11 are released! #golang"}
    reply := base
    reply.ReplyTo, reply.Faves = "someone", 3
    rt := base
    rt.IsRetweet, rt.Faves = true, 0

    cases := []struct {
        q    string
        t    Tweet
        want bool
    }{
        {`released`, base, true},
        {`release`, base, false}, // whole words, like X
        {`"1.27.4 and"`, base, true},
        {`golang`, base, true},     // plain word also matches the hashtag
        {`#released`, base, false}, // a hashtag query needs the hashtag
        {`from:GoLang min_faves:500`, base, true},
        {`from:golang min_faves:1000`, base, false},
        {`released -filter:replies`, reply, false},
        {`released filter:replies to:someone`, reply, true},
        {`released -filter:retweets`, rt, false},
        {`security OR released lang:en`, base, true},
        {`security OR patch`, base, false},
        {`released since:2026-11-10 until:2026-11-11`, base, true},
        {`released until:2026-11-10`, base, false}, // until is exclusive
        {`released -lang:en`, base, false},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        q, err := ParseQuery(c.q)
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatalf("%s: %v", c.q, err)
        }
        if got := q.Match(&c.t); got != c.want {
            t.Errorf("%-45s got %v want %v", c.q, got, c.want)
        }
    }
}
