Step 6: Fetch, filter, report, watch

collect picks the source: timelines when the query pins from:, web-index search otherwise, plus any -watch accounts. watch keeps a state file of already-reported IDs (written to a temp file and renamed, so a crash mid-write can't wipe it) and appends new matches to JSONL.

// xsearch: X (Twitter) advanced-search operators, applied locally to posts
// fetched through the ScrapeAtlas API. Go standard library only.
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "text/tabwriter"
    "time"
)

type source struct {
    fetched  int
    warnings map[string]bool
}

// collect fetches candidate posts: timelines when the query pins from:,
// web-index search pages otherwise, plus any extra -watch accounts.
func collect(c *Client, q *Query, pages int, watch []string) (map[string]Tweet, *source, error) {
    seen := map[string]Tweet{}
    src := &source{warnings: map[string]bool{}}
    add := func(env *envelope, list []rawTweet, handle string) {
        for _, w := range env.Coverage.Warnings {
            src.warnings[env.Coverage.Source+":"+w] = true
        }
        for _, r := range list {
            t, err := normalize(r, handle)
            if err != nil || t.ID == "" {
                continue
            }
            src.fetched++
            seen[t.ID] = t
        }
    }
    handles := append(q.Handles(), watch...)
    for _, h := range handles {
        p := url.Values{"handle": {h}, "trim": {"true"}}
        if !q.Since.IsZero() {
            p.Set("since", q.Since.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        if !q.Until.IsZero() {
            p.Set("until", q.Until.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
        env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/user-tweets", p)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("timeline @%s: %w", h, err)
        }
        add(env, env.Tweets, h)
    }
    if len(q.Handles()) > 0 {
        return seen, src, nil // from: is answered by the timelines alone
    }
    kws := q.Keywords()
    if len(kws) == 0 && len(handles) == 0 {
        return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("query needs at least one word, phrase or from:")
    }
    for _, kw := range kws {
        cursor := ""
        for page := 1; page <= pages; page++ {
            p := url.Values{"query": {kw}}
            if cursor != "" {
                p.Set("cursor", cursor)
            }
            env, err := c.Get("/v1/twitter/search/posts", p)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("search %q page %d: %w", kw, page, err)
            }
            add(env, env.Posts, "")
            if env.Cursor == nil || *env.Cursor == "" {
                break
            }
            cursor = *env.Cursor
        }
    }
    return seen, src, nil
}

func filterSort(all map[string]Tweet, q *Query, order string) []Tweet {
    var out []Tweet
    for _, t := range all {
        if q.Match(&t) {
            out = append(out, t)
        }
    }
    sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool {
        if order == "top" && out[i].Faves != out[j].Faves {
            return out[i].Faves > out[j].Faves
        }
        return out[i].Created.After(out[j].Created)
    })
    return out
}

func printTable(ts []Tweet, mask bool) {
    w := tabwriter.NewWriter(os.Stdout, 0, 0, 2, ' ', 0)
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "CREATED (UTC)\tAUTHOR\tLANG\tLIKES\tRTS\tREPLIES\tVIEWS\tTEXT")
    for _, t := range ts {
        text := strings.Join(strings.Fields(t.Text), " ")
        if r := []rune(text); len(r) > 60 {
            text = string(r[:57]) + "..."
        }
        author := t.Author
        if r := []rune(author); mask && len(r) > 2 {
            author = string(r[:2]) + strings.Repeat("*", len(r)-2) // for reports you share
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "%s\t@%s\t%s\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%s\n", t.Created.Format("2006-01-02 15:04"),
            author, t.Lang, t.Faves, t.Retweets, t.Replies, t.Views, text)
    }
    w.Flush()
}

func explain(q *Query) {
    fmt.Println("local filters:")
    for _, clause := range q.Clauses {
        var alts []string
        for _, a := range clause {
            s := a.Value
            if a.Op != "" {
                s = a.Op + ":" + s
            }
            if a.Neg {
                s = "NOT " + s
            }
            alts = append(alts, s)
        }
        fmt.Println("  ", strings.Join(alts, " OR "))
    }
    if !q.Since.IsZero() || !q.Until.IsZero() {
        day := func(t time.Time, zero string) string {
            if t.IsZero() {
                return zero
            }
            return t.Format("2006-01-02")
        }
        fmt.Printf("   created in [%s, %s)\n", day(q.Since, "start"), day(q.Until, "now"))
    }
    if q.MinFav+q.MinRT+q.MinRepl > 0 {
        fmt.Printf("   likes>=%d retweets>=%d replies>=%d\n", q.MinFav, q.MinRT, q.MinRepl)
    }
    if hs := q.Handles(); hs != nil {
        fmt.Println("fetch: timelines of", strings.Join(hs, ", "))
    } else {
        fmt.Printf("fetch: web-index search for %q\n", q.Keywords())
    }
}

// watch keeps the IDs it has already reported in a state file and appends
// new matches to a JSONL file, so it can run from cron.
func watch(matches []Tweet, statePath, outPath string) ([]Tweet, error) {
    state := map[string]string{} // tweet id -> first seen (RFC 3339)
    if b, err := os.ReadFile(statePath); err == nil {
        if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &state); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", statePath, err)
        }
    }
    f, err := os.OpenFile(outPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    bw := bufio.NewWriter(f)
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)
    var fresh []Tweet
    for _, t := range matches {
        if _, ok := state[t.ID]; ok {
            continue
        }
        state[t.ID] = now
        fresh = append(fresh, t)
        line, _ := json.Marshal(struct {
            SeenAt string `json:"seen_at"`
            Tweet
        }{now, t})
        bw.Write(append(line, '\n'))
    }
    if err := bw.Flush(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    b, _ := json.MarshalIndent(state, "", " ")
    tmp := statePath + ".tmp"
    if err := os.WriteFile(tmp, b, 0o644); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return fresh, os.Rename(tmp, statePath) // atomic: a crash never truncates state
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: xsearch explain|search|watch [flags] 'query'")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    cmd := os.Args[1]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    pages := fs.Int("pages", 3, "max search result pages per keyword (2 credits each)")
    watchList := fs.String("watch", "", "comma-separated handles whose timelines are also checked")
    order := fs.String("sort", "top", "top (likes) or latest")
    statePath := fs.String("state", "state.json", "watch: ids already reported")
    outPath := fs.String("out", "matches.jsonl", "watch: new matches are appended here")
    mask := fs.Bool("mask", false, "print authors as go*** in the table")
    fs.Parse(os.Args[2:])
    q, err := ParseQuery(strings.Join(fs.Args(), " "))
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "query:", err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if cmd == "explain" {
        explain(q)
        return
    }
    c, err := NewClient()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    var extra []string
    if *watchList != "" {
        extra = strings.Split(*watchList, ",")
    }
    all, src, err := collect(c, q, *pages, extra)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    matches := filterSort(all, q, *order)
    var ws []string
    for w := range src.warnings {
        ws = append(ws, w)
    }
    sort.Strings(ws)
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "fetched %d posts (%d unique), %d match, %d paid requests; coverage warnings: %s\n",
        src.fetched, len(all), len(matches), c.Calls, strings.Join(ws, ", "))
    switch cmd {
    case "search":
        printTable(matches, *mask)
    case "watch":
        fresh, err := watch(matches, *statePath, *outPath)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%d new since last run\n", len(fresh))
        printTable(fresh, *mask)
    default:
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "unknown command", cmd)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

A post that crosses min_faves:1000 later is reported on the first run where it qualifies. A post that was already reported is never reported again, even if its likes triple. Pitfalls, in one place

  • Logged-out search is gone. x.com/search redirects to login, the API needs a token, the syndication timeline returns 429. Don't build on any of them, and don't automate a logged-in session.
  • Search-by-keyword is discovery, not a firehose. The web index gives about 10-20 relevant posts per keyword, in relevance order, across months. Treat the results as a sample and say so in anything you report.
  • Operators sent to the search endpoint don't work. from:golang since:2026-11-01 returned nothing. Send words, filter locally.
  • Timelines are a window, not an archive. About 20 latest posts. since/until filter inside that window and return nothing outside it (latest_window_limited).
  • Retweet shells have 0 likes and truncated text. Read the original from retweeted_status_result, or exclude retweets.
  • Use note_tweet for long posts. full_text stops near 280 characters, and some long posts have no note at all.
  • Whole-word matching is strict. api doesn't match "APIs". Write the variants with OR.
  • Counts move between runs. The same post had 6,605 likes in one response and 6,606 in the next. Store snapshots with a time if you want trends. Don't compare across runs as if they were exact.
  • Language codes include art, zxx, und and qme. lang:en silently drops emoji-only and link-only posts. A two-word English post can also come back as da (one @golang post did).
  • Credits add up with OR. Every alternative in the first OR group is a separate search, and every page is 2 credits. Run explain first.
  • The official X API doesn't support min_faves. If you move this tool to the official API later, keep the local filter: engagement floors stay client-side there too.

Wrapping up

  • Advanced search can be split in two: fetch candidates, then filter with operators you implement yourself. In Go that's a ~290-line parser plus a table of tests.
  • from: queries are precise; keyword queries are a sample. Print the coverage warnings next to every result, so nobody reads "14 matches" as "14 posts exist".
  • explain before search saves credits and surprises, and watch with a state file turns the whole thing into a cron job.
  • X's terms ban scraping. Read them, prefer the official API where it fits, keep volumes small, and keep individual people's handles out of anything you publish.

*I build it.

title: Enterprise Software Development: Building Scalable Business Systems
description:
Large organizations often depend on multiple applications to manage finance, operations, customer relationships, inventory, and internal communication.

When these systems operate separately, data becomes fragmented and business processes become difficult to manage.

Enterprise software solutions address these challenges by connecting business operations through integrated, scalable applications.

What Is Enterprise Software Development?

Enterprise software development involves designing and building applications that support the complex operational requirements of organizations.

Unlike smaller standalone applications, enterprise systems often need to support multiple departments, large user groups, extensive integrations, and strict security requirements.

Common examples include:

  • Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems.
  • Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platforms.
  • Human Resource Management Systems (HRMS).
  • Business intelligence platforms.
  • Supply chain management applications.
  • Enterprise workflow automation systems.

Key Components of Enterprise Software Architecture

A typical enterprise application may include:

1. Presentation Layer

Provides interfaces for employees, administrators, customers, and other users.

2. Application Layer

Contains business logic, validation rules, and application services.

3. Integration Layer

Connects internal applications and external services through APIs and messaging systems.

4. Data Layer

Manages databases, reporting systems, and data access.

5. Security Layer

Handles authentication, authorization, encryption, and audit logging.

A modular architecture helps development teams maintain these components as business requirements evolve.

Technologies Used in Enterprise Development

The technology stack depends on system complexity and organizational requirements.

Common technologies include:

  • Java, Python, and .NET: Backend development.
  • React and Angular: Enterprise frontend applications.
  • PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server: Database management.
  • REST APIs: Application integration.
  • Docker and Kubernetes: Containerization and orchestration.
  • Cloud platforms: Infrastructure and deployment.
  • CI/CD tools: Automated testing and delivery.

Challenges in Enterprise Software Development

Enterprise projects introduce challenges that require careful architectural planning:

  • Integrating legacy systems with modern applications.
  • Managing large volumes of business data.
  • Maintaining consistent access permissions.
  • Supporting high availability and performance.
  • Meeting compliance and security requirements.
  • Coordinating changes across multiple teams.

Developers should address these challenges through clear service boundaries, standardized APIs, automated testing, and effective monitoring.

Best Practices for Building Enterprise Applications

Start with business requirements and identify the systems that need to communicate.

Use modular architecture, documented APIs, centralized identity management, and role-based access controls. Establish automated testing and deployment pipelines to improve release consistency.

Also, monitor application performance and maintain audit trails for important operations.

Final Thoughts

Enterprise software development helps organizations connect systems, streamline workflows, and manage complex operations through integrated digital platforms.

The right architecture should balance scalability, security, maintainability, and actual business requirements.

Explore enterprise software solutions to learn more about building connected business applications.

For more software development insights, visit Invertio Solutions.

title: Support Report SMS Timeouts: 4 Checks for Idempotent Retries and Status Polling
description:
For SMS event notifications, a timeout should trigger reconciliation before a retry can create duplicate sends. The page to design for is a customer-support report notification whose submission outcome is still unknown. The on-call view should identify the support case, generated report revision, notification job, template revision, and last reconciliation attempt. This is a proposed alert design, not an incident account. Don't trust a green send-rate dashboard to explain that particular customer's message. What page fired?

Short answer: persist the notification job before sending an SMS, preserve its idempotency identity across timeout retries, and poll status or events before deciding to resend. For a generated report sent as an email attachment, give the email and its companion SMS separate job identities, with one accountable owner for each template. An SMS update cannot establish that the report attachment reached the customer.

The four checks are job identity, submission evidence, reconciled status, and template ownership. They support a postmortem question that a successful-request counter cannot answer: which customer-visible action was justified by the evidence available at that moment?

How should idempotency govern an SMS retry after an event notification timeout?

A timeout establishes that the caller stopped waiting. It does not establish whether the downstream service accepted the notification, which means an automatic fresh send can turn a communication delay into duplicate customer messages. The earlier signal should therefore describe an unresolved notification job and its age, rather than treating every timeout as either a definitive failure or an invitation to send again.

Keep uncertainty visible.

Consider a design example: support case CS-157 has generated report revision 3, an email job carrying that report, and a separate SMS job announcing its availability. These are illustrative application identifiers, not provider request fields. A support editor owns the customer-facing wording; engineering owns delivery policy and the durable job transition. If an editor revises the SMS while submission is unresolved, that edit must not silently create a second notification identity. Conversely, a genuinely new report revision may justify a new notification, subject to the team's communication policy. Those two decisions need separate review paths because one changes wording and the other changes what the customer receives.

The trap is using the attempt identifier as the notification identifier. Every network retry then looks like a new business action. Store both: one durable logical job identity and separate attempt records, including the template revision actually selected for submission. Freeze that revision while reconciling an uncertain result. It makes the eventual postmortem about an identifiable message instead of whatever template happens to be current when someone opens the dashboard.

Reconstruct the send before authorizing another one

Start with the stored job. Record submission intent durably before the request, save the provider identifier when one is returned, and retain the evidence used to authorize every later action. Where a provider supports idempotency for that operation, reuse the same key for the same logical notification; verify its scope and retention before treating it as a recovery guarantee. Local uniqueness still matters because it governs your worker's decisions outside the provider's deduplication window.

Then reconcile. A provider identifier gives a polling worker something concrete to inspect. Without that identifier, the job remains ambiguous: do not invent an identifier, assume the message was rejected, or generate a fresh idempotency key to get past the uncertainty. A request-level deduplication contract can help with a retry of the original submission, but it is different from proof of delivery. An application cannot promise exactly-once customer delivery merely because it stored a key.

For this workflow, Infrai combines one API key and one bill with a self-describing REST API whose public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a capability begins with inspecting its contract instead of learning another SDK. That single-key model reduces credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation between the report-email worker and SMS reconciliation worker. Its specified idempotency convention adds a useful supporting mechanism, with an Idempotency-Key header and a default 24-hour deduplication window; check the chosen capability's idempotency declaration before relying on that convention. Delivery reconciliation uses status or event polling, so include a polling worker in the design.

The application owns the decision.

Use bounded exponential backoff for retryable requests, honor Retry-After when supplied, and distinguish polling retries from sending retries. A rate-limited status check should not create a new customer message. Exhausting a polling budget should escalate an unresolved job for review, rather than convert uncertainty into permission to resend. For a Node.js Express application, the request handler can persist intent and return control while a worker performs this reconciliation; the lifecycle matters more than which language hosts it.

This Go status probe is deliberately read-only. Save it as main.go and run it with Go after setting SMS_API_BASE to the HTTPS API base ending in the version segment, INFRAI_API_KEY to your key, and SMS_ID to the identifier already stored on the job. It prints the actual response without guessing undocumented status fields; a production reconciler must interpret those fields against the response schema and persist its observation. There are 3 attempts, each with a 10-second HTTP timeout. A timeout exits with an error and never sends another message.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("SMS_API_BASE"), "/")
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" || key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set HTTPS SMS_API_BASE, INFRAI_API_KEY, and SMS_ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+"/sms/status/"+url.PathEscape(id), nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("status unresolved: %w", err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if proposed := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; proposed > delay { delay = proposed }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if proposed := time.Until(deadline); proposed > delay { delay = proposed }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("status unresolved after retry budget")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Put template ownership in the comparison

Choose the system in which the responsible team can review a template revision and reconstruct its use. The following are evaluation boundaries, not claims that every product supplies the same delivery semantics. In particular, an email template feature should not be scored as an SMS recovery guarantee.

Option Relevant template surface to inspect Fit and boundary for the support workflow
Twilio Messaging Content templates and messaging documentation Evaluate for the SMS notification leg; review its status callbacks as an alternative to a polling design. Establish separately who owns the report email and its attachment.
SendGrid Dynamic transactional email templates Evaluate when support needs ownership of the report email's wording. Verify attachment handling and how a template revision is associated with an application job; assess the SMS leg separately.
Amazon SES Email templates and sending documentation Evaluate when engineering can own the email integration and template lifecycle. Review the attachment sending contract, and make the SMS ownership decision separately.

Each is a real candidate for a different part of the communication path. None earns a complete workflow recommendation merely by appearing in a table. The referenced documentation is the place to validate the selected integration; this article does not present an authenticated comparison test or measured delivery results.

There is a trade-off here: an editor-facing template workflow can reduce engineering involvement in copy changes, while application-managed revisions can make deployment review and job reconstruction more direct. Decide which team is allowed to change customer-facing text during an active support incident. Then require the integration to preserve evidence of that choice. For the attachment itself, validate the selected email API's actual request schema before implementation; an SMS send contract says nothing about attachment fields or limits.

Instrument the decision the responder needs to make

Add application-level records for job creation time, logical notification identity, template revision, attempt time, provider identifier when available, and the last successful reconciliation. These are suggested internal fields. They are not an invented vendor payload. Track unresolved-job age separately from request duration, and distinguish a worker that cannot poll from a job whose latest observed state remains inconclusive. Otherwise a stalled reconciler can masquerade as a healthy system simply because it produces no new send errors.

One practical handoff record should answer all four checks: is this the original logical job; what submission evidence exists; when was its state last reconciled; and which template owner can explain the submitted revision? Keep customer message content out of routine alert text where a case reference and revision are sufficient. The responder needs a decision trail, not an attachment copied into a pager notification.

Scheduled communication adds another policy decision. Reconcile the outcome of an SMS cancellation before assuming a delayed notification has been suppressed. Treat scheduled report email cancellation as a separate contract requirement, and use an application-owned scheduling policy if that requirement cannot be established. Email fallback codes likewise need an explicit application design; do not assume a messaging integration supplies a managed email OTP flow.

Scope the evaluation to email and SMS. If the support workflow requires SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, make those independent selection criteria rather than implying that a shared messaging interface covers them. Country restrictions and geographic abuse controls also belong in the application's policy review. Record per-job accounting information internally when the team needs reporting by support category, and keep an application template inventory so recovery does not depend on discovering mutable template state during an incident.

Close the postmortem with the cost of a noisy threshold

Set the unresolved-job age threshold from the support team's acceptable notification delay and the polling schedule it can actually sustain. No measured delivery-time distribution is established here, so a universal timeout number would be false precision. Start with an explicit service expectation, inspect the resulting alerts, and revise it using observed outcomes.

Page on actionable uncertainty.

A threshold shorter than ordinary reconciliation can page repeatedly for jobs that resolve without intervention, consuming the same responder attention needed for a stalled worker or a report that never gets its notification decision resolved. A threshold set too generously can leave support waiting on an ambiguous message while the dashboard remains green. The useful postmortem action is to connect the threshold to a named owner, a known template revision, and a safe next action. If the alert cannot explain why another send is justified, its default action should remain investigation.

Further reading

References for validating the alternatives and the recovery model:

  • Twilio Message resource and delivery status callbacks
  • Twilio Content templates
  • SendGrid dynamic transactional email templates
  • SendGrid Mail Send API, including attachment parameters
  • Amazon SES email templates
  • Amazon SES attachments
  • RFC 9110, idempotent methods and retry semantics

title: Your commit says Tuesday. It might be lying.
description:
A commit can say it was made on Tuesday night when it was really made on Thursday morning. Git will happily write that date for you.

I ran into this while building Vigilante, a browser game where your real GitHub pushes open the next day of the story. If you build anything that counts "coding days" (a streak bot, a #100DaysOfCode tracker, a team dashboard), you hit the same question sooner or later:

Someone pushes at 12:03 am. Which day does it count for?

Keep that question in your head. I'll answer it at the end, and the answer isn't the one I started with.

First, the boring but necessary parts. Here's how I'd take a GitHub push webhook and turn it into "yes, this person coded today", in plain Java, no framework.

Step 1: prove the request really came from GitHub

A webhook endpoint is just a public URL. Anyone can POST JSON to it. If your "verified day" logic trusts whatever lands there, it isn't verified.

When you set a secret on the webhook, GitHub sends an X-Hub-Signature-256 header. It's sha256= followed by the HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the request body, keyed with your secret. You compute the same thing and compare.

Two details matter:

  1. Hash the raw body bytes, before any JSON parsing. Parse first and re-serialise, and the bytes change, so the signature won't match.
  2. Compare in constant time. GitHub's docs say outright never to use a plain ==. 
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public final class GithubSignature {

    public static boolean isValid(byte[] rawBody, String header, String secret) {
        if (header == null || !header.startsWith("sha256=")) return false;
        try {
            Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), "HmacSHA256"));
            String expected = "sha256=" + HexFormat.of().formatHex(mac.doFinal(rawBody));
            // MessageDigest.isEqual is a constant-time comparison
            return MessageDigest.isEqual(
                    expected.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                    header.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;
        }
    }
}

GitHub's docs publish a test vector, which makes a nice unit test. The secret It's a Secret to Everybody and the body Hello, World! should give:

@Test
void matchesGithubTestVector() {
    byte[] body = "Hello, World!".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    String header = "sha256=757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17";
    assertTrue(GithubSignature.isValid(body, header, "It's a Secret to Everybody"));
}

If that test passes, your HMAC code is right. If production still fails, something between GitHub and you (a proxy, a body parser) is changing the bytes.

Step 2: don't count the same push twice

Every delivery carries an X-GitHub-Delivery header, a unique ID for that event. Store it and ignore any ID you've already seen. In a real app that's a unique column in your database, not an in-memory set:

// sketch: in production, a UNIQUE constraint on delivery_id does this job
if (!seenDeliveries.add(deliveryId)) {
    return Response.ok("already processed");
}

The commit IDs deserve the same treatment. Push the same commit to main and then to a release branch, and it shows up in two push events. The payload's commits array marks each commit with a distinct flag for exactly this case. I'd still keep my own set of counted commit SHAs as a backstop.

One more limit to know: the commits array holds at most 2048 commits. Nobody pushes that many in a normal day, but if they do, you'll need the Commits API for the rest.

Step 3: decide what a "real" commit is

This is where streak apps quietly break. An empty commit is a commit. So is a lockfile bump that a bot made. If those count, the streak means nothing.

Each commit in the push payload lists the files it added, modified and removed. That's enough to drop the obvious noise without ever reading the code:

private static final Set<String> NOISE = Set.of(
        "package-lock.json", "yarn.lock", "pnpm-lock.yaml",
        "Gemfile.lock", "poetry.lock", "Cargo.lock");

static boolean looksLikeRealWork(JsonNode commit) {
    if (!commit.path("distinct").asBoolean(true)) return false;

    List<String> files = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String key : List.of("added", "modified", "removed")) {
        commit.path(key).forEach(f -> files.add(f.asText()));
    }
    if (files.isEmpty()) return false;              // empty commit

    return files.stream()
            .map(path -> path.substring(path.lastIndexOf('/') + 1))
            .anyMatch(name -> !NOISE.contains(name)); // not lockfile-only
}

Merge commits are trickier, because the push payload doesn't list a commit's parents. You can ask the Commits API, or filter on the Git side. I wrote a separate post about sorting merge, empty and lockfile noise with a git script, so I won't repeat it here.

Notice what this code never touches: the diff. File names and commit IDs are enough to say "this person changed real files today". You don't need anyone's code to verify their effort, and I think you shouldn't ask for it.

Step 4: the question from the top

Now the fun part. You have a valid, deduplicated push with real commits in it. Which day is it?

The obvious answer is the commit's timestamp. It's right there in the payload, and it's when the person actually wrote the code. Feels honest.

It isn't. That timestamp comes from the committer's own machine, and Git lets you set it to anything:

git commit --date="2026-11-24T21:00:00" -m "totally did this on Tuesday"
# or for the committer date too
GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-11-24T21:00:00" git commit --amend --no-edit

Missed Tuesday? Backdate a commit on Thursday, push it, and a tracker that trusts commit dates gives you Tuesday. People build whole GitHub contribution graph "art" this way.

So the commit date is a claim. The only clock you control is your own: the moment your server received the push. Bucket that into the user's time zone and you get the day:

static LocalDate countedDay(Instant receivedAt, ZoneId userZone) {
    return receivedAt.atZone(userZone).toLocalDate();
}

Which brings back the 12:03 am push. The commits were written at 11:58 pm, the push landed five minutes after midnight, and this rule says it counts for the next day.

At first that feels unfair to the person coding late.

Then I flipped it around. A commit sitting on your laptop hasn't shipped anything. Your work becomes real for everyone else the moment you push it. So the honest rule is simple: the day you pushed is the day you shipped. If you want it to count for tonight, push before midnight. That's a better habit anyway.

Recap

  • Verify X-Hub-Signature-256 against the raw body, in constant time.
  • Deduplicate on X-GitHub-Delivery, and on commit SHAs.
  • Count commits by what files they touch, never by reading the code.
  • Trust your server's clock, not the commit's. Commit dates are self-reported.

If you're doing #100DaysOfCode and want days checked this way instead of by screenshot, Vigilante has a free 100 Days of Code tracker (full disclosure, I built it): vigilante.ocix.in/100-days-of-code

And if you've built a streak counter yourself: which clock did you trust?
