title: Kong Plugins for Authentication and Traffic Control
description:
Meta description: Secure and throttle your APIs with Kong: key-auth, Basic auth, JWT, ACL, rate limiting, request size limiting and IP restriction.

What you'll learn

  • How plugins work and where they apply
  • Authentication vs authorization
  • Ways to authenticate
  • How to limit traffic fairly

What is a plugin?

A plugin adds behavior to the request/response flow without changing your backend code. You can attach it at different scopes:

Scope Applies to
Global Every request through Kong
Service All routes of one service
Route Only one route
Consumer Only one caller

When scopes overlap, the more specific one wins.

Part 1: Authentication, "who are you?"

Key authentication (key-auth)

The simplest approach. The client sends a secret key in a header.

# 1. Enable on a service
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins --data name=key-auth

# 2. Create a key for the consumer
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/key-auth --data key=asha-secret-key

# 3. Call
curl -i http://localhost:8000/alpha/hello                                # 401
curl -i http://localhost:8000/alpha/hello -H 'apikey: asha-secret-key'   # 200

Without a key, Kong answers 401 and your backend never sees the request.

Basic authentication (basic-auth)

Username and password in the Authorization header. Simple and widely supported, but use it only over HTTPS.

JWT authentication (jwt)

The client sends a signed token: Authorization: Bearer <token>.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins --data name=jwt
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/jwt     # returns key + secret

Kong checks the token's signature with the consumer's secret and checks it hasn't expired. The token's iss claim must equal the consumer's JWT key.

Method Best for
key-auth Simple service-to-service or partner access
basic-auth Quick internal tools (over HTTPS)
jwt User sessions, stateless tokens with expiry

Part 2: Authorization, "what may you do?" (acl)

Authentication identifies the caller. Authorization decides what they can access. Kong's ACL plugin uses groups:

# put the consumer in a group
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/consumers/asha/acls --data group=shoppers

# allow only admins on a route
curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/routes/alpha-write/plugins \
  --data name=acl --data 'config.allow=admins'

The ACL plugin needs an authentication plugin on the same route, because it has to know who the consumer is.

401 vs 403. 401 means "I don't know who you are". 403 means "I know you, but you may not do this."

Part 3: Traffic control, "how much?"

Rate limiting

Protects your service from abuse and accidental loops.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins \
  --data name=rate-limiting \
  --data config.minute=30 \
  --data config.policy=local

Responses include headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining-Minute. After the limit, Kong returns 429 Too Many Requests.

Which policy?

  • local: counters in each Kong node's memory (fast, but each node counts alone)
  • redis: shared counters across nodes (accurate across a cluster)

You can also attach a rate limit to a consumer, so a premium customer gets 1000/min and a free one gets 30/min.

Request size limiting 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/services/alpha-service/plugins \
  --data name=request-size-limiting \
  --data config.allowed_payload_size=1 \
  --data config.size_unit=megabytes

Oversized bodies are rejected with 413 before they reach your backend.

IP restriction

Allow or deny by address, handy for admin routes:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8001/routes/alpha-write/plugins \
  --data name=ip-restriction --data 'config.allow=10.0.0.0/8'

A typical policy for one API

Route Plugins
GET /items auth, group readers or admins
POST /items auth, group admins only
/orders auth, ACL, rate limit 30/min
everything request size limit 1 MB

Common mistakes

  • Adding acl without an authentication plugin.
  • Using rate-limiting with local policy on several Kong nodes and expecting a global total.
  • Committing real secrets and keys to git. Use environment variables or a secret manager.
  • Confusing 401 and 403 when debugging.

Key takeaways

  • Plugins give you security and limits without touching backend code.
  • Authenticate first, authorize second.
  • Rate limits and size limits are cheap protection; set them early.
  • Attach plugins at the narrowest scope that makes sense.

Next: Transformations and observability.

title: Building huge go repo
description:
I came across an interesting problem recently when building AzureRM: due to a massive refactoring, the repo now have a lot more files and packages

Ran out of tmp space

First, my WSL box throw tons of write /tmp/go-build123456789/...: no space left on device error. The tmp file system ran out of space.

This can be fixed be mapping another larger volume for compilation: export GOTMPDIR="$HOME/.cache/go-tmp" although I suspect this makes the build slower?

Slow compilation time

A cold build with no cache hit took 12 minutes. A common daily main pull require 5 - 7 mins depending on how much are changing.

I learned that go keep local build cache in $HOME/.cache/go-build and the morning ritual of pulling latest main to warm up the cache is really useful to speed up subsequent build throughout the day.

Stripping debugging info cuts down my build time to 10 minutes, it's not much, but why not if we don't need it? go build -ldflags="-s -w" ..

What about a more powerful machine? In my 16vCPU/64GB devbox (cloud VM), the cold build took 6 minutes, which is half the time, not bad!

Which got me thinking.. wouldn't it be great if devbox and my local can share the cache?

gobuildcache

I found this gobuildcache library which is pretty close to what I want: it allows me to upload the build cache to a blob store. Let's give it a try!

First I installed the binary: go install github.com/richardartoul/gobuildcache@v1

Then I created the blob store that will hold the remote cache:

RESOURCE_GROUP=my-azurerm-buildcache
LOCATION=australiaeast
STORAGE_ACCOUNT=myazurermbuildcachev1
CONTAINER=go-build-cache

az group create --name "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --location "$LOCATION"

az storage account create --name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --kind BlockBlobStorage --sku Premium_LRS \
  --allow-blob-public-access false --allow-shared-key-access false \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2
STORAGE_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" --query id -o tsv)

# Grant the signed-in user data-plane access to create the container.
USER_ID=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$USER_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type User --role 'Storage Blob Data Contributor' \
  --scope "$STORAGE_ID"

az storage container create --account-name "$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
  --name "$CONTAINER" --auth-mode login --public-access off

Drop a few environment variables to tell go to use gobuildcache (hint use direnv to automate this 😉):

export GOCACHEPROG=/path/to/go/bin/gobuildcache

export GOBUILDCACHE_BACKEND_TYPE=azblob
export GOBUILDCACHE_AZURE_ACCOUNT=myazurermbuildcachev1
export GOBUILDCACHE_AZBLOB_CONTAINER=go-build-cache
export GOBUILDCACHE_READ_ONLY=false
export GOBUILDCACHE_PRINT_STATS=true
export GOBUILDCACHE_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/.cache/gobuildcache/cache
export GOBUILDCACHE_LOCK_DIR=/path/to/.cache/gobuildcache/locks
export GOBUILDCACHE_DEBUG=false

Ran the build again in devbox to warm up my remote cache. And look at how warm and cozy my blob store is now with all the cache populated 😛:

And now for the moment of truth, jumping back to my local, I forced a cold build by clearing the cache: "$GOCACHEPROG" clear-local, then ran a built which hopefully hits these remote cache.

Drumrolls...

Backend cache hits: 6526 (65.8% of GETs)

Promising.. but total time is 10 min 44 second, there's no speed benefit although CPU compute is swapped with 7148 HTTP GET requests 🤣.

So I guess local cache is still the way to go. Maybe I'll setup some cron job that pull and compile daily before I start in the morning.

title: webhook-relay: receive webhooks on a server, handle them on your laptop
description:
Webhooks are awkward to develop against. The sender, whether it is a payment provider, GitHub or a chat platform, needs a public URL to call. Your handler runs on localhost:3000, behind a home router. The usual answer is a tunnelling service, which gives your laptop a public address for a while.

A tunnel gets the request to your machine, and then it is gone. If your handler crashed on it, you have to trigger the event again on the sender's side, which can mean making another test payment or pushing another commit. If two deliveries behaved differently, you compare them by scrolling through logs. And if your laptop was closed when the webhook fired, the delivery simply failed.

webhook-relay is a self-hosted alternative to tunnelling services, built for webhook development. A small server on a public machine receives the webhooks, records every one, and relays them over a websocket to a CLI on your laptop, which calls your local app. Because every request is stored, you can look at it later, replay it after fixing your handler, and diff two deliveries to see what changed.

Stripe/GitHub/… ──POST──► relay-server /h/stripe ══websocket══► relay (CLI) ──► http://localhost:3000
                               │  stores every request                          (your app)
                               └─ inspector UI: list, detail, replay, diff

What it does

Capture first. The endpoint /h/{channel}/{rest...} reads the body up to a limit, strips hop-by-hop headers, and stores the request in SQLite before doing anything else. A delivery is never lost, even when no client is listening. In that case the sender gets 202 Accepted with the request ID, and the request waits in the inspector.

Relay with the real response. Each channel has at most one connected client, and a newer client replaces the older one. The server sends a JSON request frame over the websocket with a random correlation ID, then waits for the matching response frame or the timeout. The response from your local app goes back to the sender, so signature checks and status-code retries behave as they would in production.

Paths are kept. Anything after the channel name is preserved: /h/stripe/v1/events?x=1 arrives at http://localhost:3000/v1/events?x=1.

Failure is visible. If the local target is unreachable, the sender gets a 502 and the error is stored with the request. The client performs the local HTTP calls concurrently, so one slow handler does not block the others.

A connection that stays up. The server pings every 25 seconds to keep proxies from dropping the websocket. The client reconnects with exponential backoff, but it stops on 401 or 403, because a bad token will not fix itself.

Inspector. Server-rendered html/template pages embedded in the binary, with no JavaScript. You get a list per channel and a detail page per request. Replay re-sends a stored request as a new request linked to the original. Diff renders both requests as text (request line, sorted headers, pretty-printed JSON body) and shows a line diff computed with LCS.

JSON API. GET /api/channels/{c}/requests, GET /api/requests/{id} and POST /api/requests/{id}/replay, with a Bearer token.

Storage. The pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite driver, with no cgo, in WAL mode with one connection. Old requests are pruned per channel on insert.

How to use it

Install both binaries with Go:

go install github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/webhook-relay/cmd/...@latest

The README also lists prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows (amd64 and arm64) on the GitHub releases page. Each archive contains relay-server and relay, and checksums.txt has the SHA-256 sums.

On a server with a public URL, build and start the relay server:

go build -o relay-server ./cmd/relay-server
RELAY_TOKEN=change-me ./relay-server -addr :8080 -db relay.db

On your machine, start the client and point it at your local app:

go build -o relay ./cmd/relay
RELAY_TOKEN=change-me ./relay -server https://relay.example.com -channel stripe -to http://localhost:3000

Then set the webhook URL on the sender's side to https://relay.example.com/h/stripe. The inspector is at https://relay.example.com/, behind HTTP Basic auth: any user name, the token as password.

The server has five flags:

flag default meaning
-addr :8080 listen address (put TLS in front, for example Caddy or nginx)
-db relay.db SQLite file
-keep 500 requests kept per channel
-max-body 1048576 bytes stored and forwarded per request
-timeout 25s how long a webhook waits for your local answer

RELAY_TOKEN protects the websocket, the inspector and the JSON API. The /h/… endpoints are public by design, since the sender has to be able to reach them without your token.

A typical session then goes like this. The provider sends an event and your handler returns a 500. You open the inspector, read the stored headers and body, fix the code, and press Replay. The same request goes through the relay again, and you never have to trigger a new event on the sender's side. If a later delivery behaves differently, Diff shows which headers or JSON fields changed between the two.

Things to know

  • One client per channel. There is no fan-out to several developers. A second client on the same channel replaces the first, so give each developer their own channel name.
  • A single shared token. There are no per-channel credentials and no user accounts.
  • Bodies are capped. A body over -max-body is truncated when stored and when forwarded. Streaming and very large payloads are not supported.
  • It is for webhooks, not general tunnelling. Websocket passthrough is not supported.
  • Single instance. The server keeps waiting clients in memory. Scaling horizontally would need a shared pub/sub.
  • No TLS termination built in. Run it behind a reverse proxy.
  • The UI shows the latest 200 requests per channel. There is no pagination beyond that.
  • What was tested. go test -race ./... includes end-to-end tests that start the relay server and a real client over a websocket in-process, with an httptest server acting as the local app. They cover forwarding (method, path, query, headers, body, status, response headers), storing while no client is connected and then replaying, Bearer and Basic auth, the client giving up on a bad token, invalid channel names, the 502 when the target is down, the inspector pages including the diff output and the replay redirect, and a newer client replacing an older one. There are also unit tests for the store (pruning, round trips) and for the diff.

Why I built it

A generic tunnel solves reachability, and reachability is only the first problem in webhook work. The problems that take the time come after it: reproducing a delivery, understanding why two deliveries differ, and not losing an event that arrived while nothing was listening.

All three have the same answer, which is to keep the request. Once every delivery is stored before anything else happens, replay and diff are small features on top of it, and a closed laptop turns from a failed delivery into a pending one.

Hosting it yourself is the second half of the idea. Webhook payloads can contain customer and payment data, and with this tool they stay in a SQLite file on a server you control. The pieces are deliberately few: one server binary, one client binary, one token, and no JavaScript in the inspector.

Sending the local app's real response back to the sender was also important. A relay that always answers 200 hides bugs, because the sender never retries and a signature failure looks like a success.

Get the code

The server, the client, the inspector and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/webhook-relay. It is MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode needed an object boundary
description:
Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode needed an object boundary

Template engines are often described as presentation layers, but a server-side template can call objects, read properties, and invoke application services. Thymeleaf's restricted expression mode exists to limit that power when a template is not fully trusted. CVE-2026-136410 concerns a bypass that used expression objects to perform actions that restricted mode should have blocked.

The GitHub advisory and VulnCheck describe the issue in Thymeleaf before 3.1.6.RELEASE. The public scoring reaches roughly CVSS 9.0 in some feeds because an unauthenticated remote attacker may influence a template expression. The practical risk depends on whether the application exposes user-controlled expressions, how the expression context is built, and which objects are available to the template.

Restricted mode is a policy, not a sandbox

Thymeleaf evaluates expressions against a context. A restricted expression mode can reduce the set of methods, types, and objects that a template may access. The control is only as strong as the boundary between the template and the application objects. If a permitted object exposes a method that returns a more powerful object, the template may reach functionality outside the intended set.

Expression objects are useful because they provide reusable helpers for formatting, links, and data access. They also enlarge the surface. A bypass may not look like a raw Java call. It may be a chain of property reads and method calls that begins with an object the application intended to expose.

Identify applications that evaluate untrusted templates

Inventory services that use Thymeleaf and allow users, tenants, integrations, or lower-privileged administrators to supply templates or expression fragments. Examples include email templates, report builders, notification editors, CMS integrations, and workflow configuration screens. A template supplied only by developers in a reviewed repository has a different risk profile from a template saved through a web form.

Check the Thymeleaf version and the application's expression context. Search for custom expression objects, utility beans, SpringTemplateEngine, TemplateEngine, and code that constructs variables from request data. Review whether the application enables restricted mode and whether it also passes a broad root object into the evaluation.

Upgrade to 3.1.6.RELEASE or later through the dependency-management path used by the service. A transitive dependency may require an explicit version constraint. Rebuild the image and confirm the runtime classpath. A stale cached artifact can make a source change look successful while the deployed application still uses the old library.

Do not rely on a single template flag

Restricted mode is one layer. Applications should separate developer-controlled templates from user-controlled content. If business users need configurable output, prefer a constrained data model and a small set of safe formatting operations. Avoid exposing service beans or arbitrary object graphs to the expression context.

Apply least privilege to the process that evaluates templates. A template service should have only the credentials and network reach needed for its job. Keep secrets out of the context unless the template truly needs them. Review custom dialects and utility objects for methods that can load classes, access files, execute commands, or make network requests.

Run regression tests with representative malicious expressions in a safe test environment. The tests should assert that restricted mode blocks access to forbidden classes and methods, and they should verify that an application error is not being mistaken for a policy denial. Test chained calls and object properties because that is where a type check can be incomplete.

Detection and response

Review application logs for template compilation or evaluation from unexpected users, repeated render failures, suspicious property names, and template changes outside the normal workflow. Correlate those events with outbound network requests, filesystem access, and process creation by the application server. A template vulnerability can be used as a data read or as a step toward command execution.

If the application evaluates untrusted templates, temporarily disable that feature or restrict it to trusted administrators while the upgrade is completed. Preserve the submitted template and the application context for analysis. Remove stored templates that are no longer approved.

The patch fixes the known bypass. The durable control is a smaller expression context with a clear trust model. CVE-2026-136410 should prompt teams to ask which objects a template can reach and why each one is necessary.

References

  • Thymeleaf, GHSA-2wmw-5fmc-m25v
  • Thymeleaf, 3.1.6.RELEASE
  • CVE Program, CVE-2026-136410
  • VulnCheck, Restricted expression mode bypass advisory

title: Secure MERN JWT Authentication: Beyond Simple Login
description:
Originally published on PEAKIQ

Source: https://www.peakiq.in/blog/stop-treating-jwt-authentication-as-just-a-login-secure-mern-auth

Stop Treating JWT Authentication as Just a Login — Secure MERN Auth in 2026

Most tutorials teach authentication as a simple three-step process:

  1. User submits email and password.
  2. Server validates credentials.
  3. Server generates a JWT and returns it.

That works for a demo.

But production authentication is not just about verifying credentials and generating a token. It is about protecting sessions, handling expired credentials, managing concurrent requests, preventing token theft, revoking access, and keeping the application secure without breaking the user experience.

In 2026, building authentication for a MERN application means thinking beyond the login endpoint.

You need an authentication architecture that can handle:

  • Access token expiration
  • Refresh token rotation
  • Secure token storage
  • Session revocation
  • Multiple devices
  • Concurrent API requests
  • XSS and CSRF risks
  • Logout and account security
  • API scaling

This is the architecture I would use for a production MERN application.

1. The Authentication Stack

For this architecture, we are using a modern MERN stack with a clear separation between authentication, session management, and application APIs.

Frontend

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Axios
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit
  • React Router
  • TanStack Query

Backend

  • Node.js
  • Express
  • TypeScript
  • MongoDB
  • JWT access tokens
  • Refresh token sessions
  • HttpOnly cookies
  • Zod validation
  • Rate limiting

The goal is not to add more dependencies.

The goal is to make authentication predictable, secure, and easy to maintain.

2. The Three Problems Most JWT Tutorials Ignore

Before writing code, we need to understand the real problems.

Problem 1: Token Exposure

If you store long-lived authentication tokens in localStorage, any JavaScript running within your origin that is compromised through XSS may be able to read those tokens.

A stolen token can become a stolen session.

Problem 2: Session Lifecycle

JWTs are stateless, but production applications still need state.

You need to know:

  • Is the user logged out?
  • Is this device still authorized?
  • Has the refresh token been rotated?
  • Has the session been revoked?
  • Has the account been disabled?

Problem 3: Concurrent Requests

Imagine a user opens the dashboard and 10 API requests start simultaneously.

The access token expires.

All 10 requests receive a 401 Unauthorized.

If every request independently calls the refresh endpoint, you can end up with:

  • 10 refresh requests
  • Refresh token rotation conflicts
  • Some requests succeeding while others fail
  • Unexpected logout
  • Duplicate retries

This is why authentication needs to be designed as a system rather than a single endpoint.

3. Stop Storing Long-Lived JWTs in localStorage

The most common implementation looks like this:

localStorage.setItem("token", accessToken);

And then:

const token = localStorage.getItem("token");

This is convenient, but it creates a major security trade-off.

JavaScript can access localStorage. If an attacker executes JavaScript through an XSS vulnerability, they may extract the stored token.

Instead, separate the responsibilities.

Token Storage Purpose
Access token In-memory state Authenticate API requests
Refresh token HttpOnly cookie Renew authentication
Refresh token hash MongoDB Validate and revoke sessions

The access token should be short-lived.

The refresh token should be protected by the browser and managed by the server.

The server should store a hash of the refresh token rather than the raw token.

This reduces the impact of a database leak.

4. Authentication Architecture

The authentication lifecycle looks like this:

flowchart TD
    A[User Login] --> B[Validate Credentials]
    B --> C[Create Session]
    C --> D[Generate Access Token]
    C --> E[Generate Refresh Token]
    D --> F[Return Access Token]
    E --> G[Set HttpOnly Cookie]
    F --> H[React Stores Token in Memory]
    H --> I[API Request]
    I --> J{Access Token Valid?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Return API Response]
    J -->|No| L[Refresh Endpoint]
    L --> M[Validate Refresh Session]
    M --> N[Rotate Refresh Token]
    N --> O[Issue New Access Token]
    O --> P[Retry Original Request]

The important difference is that the refresh token is never returned inside the JSON response.

The browser stores it in a protected cookie.

5. Short-Lived Access Tokens

Access tokens should not remain valid for days.

For most applications, a short lifetime such as 10–15 minutes is a reasonable starting point. The exact duration depends on the application's threat model and usability requirements.

Example JWT payload:

{
  "sub": "user_123",
  "sid": "session_456",
  "iss": "api.peakiq.in",
  "aud": "peakiq-client",
  "iat": 1764200000,
  "exp": 1764200900
}

The token contains:

  • sub — user ID
  • sid — session ID
  • iss — issuer
  • aud — intended audience
  • iat — issued at
  • exp — expiration

Do not put sensitive user data into JWT payloads.

JWT payloads are encoded, not encrypted.

Access token generation 

import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

export function createAccessToken(
  userId: string,
  sessionId: string
) {
  return jwt.sign(
    {
      sid: sessionId,
    },
    process.env.ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET!,
    {
      subject: userId,
      issuer: "api.peakiq.in",
      audience: "peakiq-client",
      expiresIn: "15m",
      algorithm: "HS256",
    }
  );
}

In production, keep signing secrets outside your source code and use strong, separate secrets for access and refresh token mechanisms.

6. Refresh Tokens Are Sessions

The refresh token is what keeps the user logged in after the access token expires.

Instead of treating refresh tokens as permanent credentials, treat them as sessions that can be:

  • Rotated
  • Revoked
  • Expired
  • Audited
  • Associated with a device

I prefer using a cryptographically random opaque refresh token instead of a long-lived JWT refresh token.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export function createRefreshToken() {
  return crypto.randomBytes(64).toString("hex");
}

export function hashRefreshToken(token: string) {
  return crypto
    .createHash("sha256")
    .update(token)
    .digest("hex");
}

The refresh token itself is sent to the browser.

The hash is stored in MongoDB.

7. MongoDB Session Model

A session collection gives us control over authentication beyond JWT expiration.

import { Schema, model } from "mongoose";

const authSessionSchema = new Schema(
  {
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      ref: "User",
      required: true,
      index: true,
    },

    refreshTokenHash: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      unique: true,
    },

    deviceName: String,
    ipAddress: String,
    userAgent: String,

    expiresAt: {
      type: Date,
      required: true,
    },

    revokedAt: {
      type: Date,
      default: null,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
  }
);

authSessionSchema.index({ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 });
authSessionSchema.index({ userId: 1, revokedAt: 1 });

export const AuthSession = model(
  "AuthSession",
  authSessionSchema
);

This gives us a foundation for:

  • Logout
  • Device management
  • Session expiration
  • Revoking individual devices
  • Revoking all sessions
  • Security audit trails

The TTL index is cleanup automation. It is not a substitute for checking session expiration in the authentication logic.

8. Login: Create the Session

When the user successfully authenticates, create:

  1. A session ID
  2. An access token
  3. A refresh token
  4. A hashed refresh token stored in MongoDB
  5. An HttpOnly cookie containing the refresh token 
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { AuthSession } from "../models/auth-session";
import { createAccessToken } from "../utils/access-token";
import { createRefreshToken, hashRefreshToken } from "../utils/refresh-token";

export async function createAuthSession(
  userId: string,
  res: any
) {
  const sessionId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const refreshToken = createRefreshToken();

  const refreshTokenHash = hashRefreshToken(refreshToken);

  await AuthSession.create({
    userId,
    refreshTokenHash,
    expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
  });

  const accessToken = createAccessToken(userId, sessionId);

  res.cookie("refreshToken", refreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
    maxAge: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });

  return {
    accessToken,
  };
}

Notice what we return.

{
  "accessToken": "..."
}

We do not return the refresh token.

The refresh token is delivered through the cookie.

The cookie configuration must match your deployment topology. If your frontend and backend are cross-site, you may need SameSite=None with Secure, plus appropriate CSRF protections.

9. Refresh Token Rotation

A refresh endpoint is one of the most important parts of authentication.

When a refresh token is used:

  1. Validate the existing token.
  2. Hash it.
  3. Find the matching session.
  4. Reject expired or revoked sessions.
  5. Generate a new refresh token.
  6. Replace the stored hash.
  7. Issue a new access token.
  8. Update the browser cookie. 
import { Request, Response } from "express";
import { AuthSession } from "../models/auth-session";
import { hashRefreshToken, createRefreshToken } from "../utils/refresh-token";
import { createAccessToken } from "../utils/access-token";

export async function refreshSession(
  req: Request,
  res: Response
) {
  const currentToken = req.cookies.refreshToken;

  if (!currentToken) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Authentication required",
    });
  }

  const currentHash = hashRefreshToken(currentToken);

  const session = await AuthSession.findOne({
    refreshTokenHash: currentHash,
    revokedAt: null,
    expiresAt: { $gt: new Date() },
  });

  if (!session) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Session expired or invalid",
    });
  }

  const nextRefreshToken = createRefreshToken();
  const nextHash = hashRefreshToken(nextRefreshToken);

  const updated = await AuthSession.findOneAndUpdate(
    {
      _id: session._id,
      refreshTokenHash: currentHash,
      revokedAt: null,
    },
    {
      $set: {
        refreshTokenHash: nextHash,
      },
    },
    {
      new: true,
    }
  );

  if (!updated) {
    return res.status(401).json({
      message: "Session no longer valid",
    });
  }

  const accessToken = createAccessToken(
    session.userId.toString(),
    session._id.toString()
  );

  res.cookie("refreshToken", nextRefreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
    maxAge: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  });

  return res.json({
    accessToken,
  });
}

Why rotation matters

If a refresh token is stolen and then reused after the legitimate user has rotated it, that reuse can be a signal of token theft.

A production implementation should consider refresh token reuse detection and session-family revocation. It should also handle refresh requests that race with one another, because strict rotation can cause legitimate concurrent requests to fail if coordination is missing.

10. React: Keep the Access Token in Memory

The frontend only needs the access token to make API requests.

You can store it in Zustand:

import { create } from "zustand";

type AuthState = {
  accessToken: string | null;
  setAccessToken: (token: string | null) => void;
};

export const useAuthStore = create<AuthState>((set) => ({
  accessToken: null,

  setAccessToken: (accessToken) => {
    set({ accessToken });
  },
}));

This token disappears when the application reloads.

That is intentional.

On application startup, the frontend calls the refresh endpoint. The browser sends the HttpOnly cookie automatically, and the backend issues a new access token if the session is still valid.

11. Axios: Handle Expired Tokens Automatically

A production application cannot ask users to log in again every 15 minutes.

Axios interceptors can handle token expiration automatically.

The architecture needs to:

  • Add the access token to outgoing requests.
  • Detect authentication failures.
  • Refresh the session.
  • Retry the original request.
  • Prevent multiple simultaneous refresh calls.

Axios client 

import axios from "axios";

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  withCredentials: true,
});

Request interceptor 

import { useAuthStore } from "../store/auth-store";

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = useAuthStore.getState().accessToken;

  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }

  return config;
});

The access token remains in memory and is attached to requests only when needed.

12. Prevent Multiple Refresh Requests

This is where many applications become unreliable.

If 10 requests fail simultaneously, they should not trigger 10 refresh requests.

Instead, use a single shared refresh operation within the current JavaScript runtime.

let refreshPromise: Promise<string> | null = null;

async function refreshAccessToken() {
  if (!refreshPromise) {
    refreshPromise = api
      .post("/api/auth/refresh")
      .then((response) => {
        const accessToken = response.data.accessToken;

        useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(accessToken);

        return accessToken;
      })
      .finally(() => {
        refreshPromise = null;
      });
  }

  return refreshPromise;
}

This ensures requests in the same tab share one refresh operation.

It does not coordinate refresh requests across multiple browser tabs. Multi-tab coordination may require an additional mechanism such as BroadcastChannel, shared state, or server-side handling of rotation races.

13. Retry the Original Request

Once the refresh completes, retry the original API request with the new access token.

api.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,

  async (error) => {
    const originalRequest = error.config;

    if (
      error.response?.status === 401 &&
      originalRequest &&
      !originalRequest._retry &&
      !originalRequest.url?.includes("/auth/refresh")
    ) {
      originalRequest._retry = true;

      try {
        const accessToken = await refreshAccessToken();

        originalRequest.headers.Authorization =
          \`Bearer \${accessToken}\`;

        return api(originalRequest);
      } catch (refreshError) {
        useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

        return Promise.reject(refreshError);
      }
    }

    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

The _retry flag prevents infinite retry loops.

Without it, a failed retry could trigger another refresh indefinitely.

14. Application Startup Authentication

When React starts, it does not know whether the user has an active session.

The access token is stored only in memory, so the application needs to restore authentication.

export async function restoreSession() {
  try {
    const response = await api.post("/api/auth/refresh");

    useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(
      response.data.accessToken
    );

    return true;
  } catch {
    useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

    return false;
  }
}

Use this during application bootstrap.

While session restoration is in progress, show a loading state instead of briefly rendering the login screen.

This prevents unnecessary redirects and improves the user experience.

15. HttpOnly Cookies, CORS, and CSRF

Using HttpOnly cookies solves one problem.

It does not solve every authentication security problem.

Cookie configuration 

res.cookie("refreshToken", refreshToken, {
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: true,
  sameSite: "strict",
  path: "/api/auth",
});

What these options do

Option Purpose
HttpOnly Prevent JavaScript from reading the cookie
Secure Send the cookie only over HTTPS
SameSite Restrict cross-site cookie behavior
Path Restrict where the cookie is sent

CORS configuration 

import cors from "cors";

app.use(
  cors({
    origin: "https://app.peakiq.in",
    credentials: true,
  })
);

Do not use a wildcard origin with credentialed requests.

Your frontend and backend deployment configuration must agree about cookie domain, SameSite, and HTTPS requirements.

CSRF protection

Because cookies are automatically sent by browsers, cookie-based authentication needs a CSRF strategy.

Depending on your deployment, use:

  • Strict origin validation
  • Appropriate SameSite settings
  • CSRF tokens for state-changing requests where required
  • Avoid state-changing GET requests

Do not assume HttpOnly prevents CSRF.

It protects cookie confidentiality from JavaScript, not the browser's automatic cookie sending behavior.

16. Logout Means Revoking the Session

A frontend logout that only clears Zustand is incomplete.

useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

That removes the access token from memory, but the refresh session may still be active.

The backend should revoke the session and clear the cookie.

export async function logout(req: Request, res: Response) {
  const refreshToken = req.cookies.refreshToken;

  if (refreshToken) {
    const hash = hashRefreshToken(refreshToken);

    await AuthSession.updateOne(
      {
        refreshTokenHash: hash,
      },
      {
        $set: {
          revokedAt: new Date(),
        },
      }
    );
  }

  res.clearCookie("refreshToken", {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
    sameSite: "strict",
    path: "/api/auth",
  });

  return res.status(204).send();
}

Then clear frontend state:

await api.post("/api/auth/logout");

useAuthStore.getState().setAccessToken(null);

This creates a real logout.

The refresh session is no longer valid, and the browser cookie is cleared.

For a production application, users should also be able to see and revoke their active sessions from their account security page.

17. Modular Monolith Architecture

Authentication should not be mixed into controllers and utility files randomly.

Keep it inside a dedicated module.

src/
├── modules/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.ts
│   │   ├── auth.service.ts
│   │   ├── auth.routes.ts
│   │   ├── auth.validation.ts
│   │   ├── auth.middleware.ts
│   │   ├── session.service.ts
│   │   └── auth.types.ts
│   │
│   ├── users/
│   │   ├── user.controller.ts
│   │   ├── user.service.ts
│   │   ├── user.model.ts
│   │   └── user.routes.ts
│   │
│   └── projects/
│       ├── project.controller.ts
│       ├── project.service.ts
│       ├── project.model.ts
│       └── project.routes.ts
│
├── middleware/
│   ├── error-handler.ts
│   ├── rate-limit.ts
│   └── validation.ts
│
├── utils/
│   ├── jwt.ts
│   ├── crypto.ts
│   └── logger.ts
│
├── config/
│   ├── database.ts
│   ├── cors.ts
│   └── environment.ts
│
└── app.ts

The auth module owns authentication.

The user module owns user data.

The middleware layer owns reusable request behavior.

This structure is easier to test, audit, and maintain.

18. MongoDB Indexes That Matter

Authentication queries should not become slow as sessions grow.

At minimum, consider indexes for:

authSessionSchema.index(
  { refreshTokenHash: 1 },
  { unique: true }
);

authSessionSchema.index({
  userId: 1,
  revokedAt: 1,
});

authSessionSchema.index(
  { expiresAt: 1 },
  { expireAfterSeconds: 0 }
);

These support:

  • Refresh token lookup
  • Session management by user
  • Cleanup of expired session records

Do not rely only on TTL cleanup to validate sessions.

Every refresh operation must explicitly verify expiration and revocation.

19. Scaling Authentication

You do not need microservices to build secure authentication.

A modular monolith is usually enough to start.

Phase 1 — MVP

  • Login and registration
  • Short-lived access tokens
  • Refresh sessions
  • HttpOnly cookies
  • Logout
  • Rate limiting
  • Password hashing

Phase 2 — Production Traction

  • Device sessions
  • Refresh token rotation
  • Session revocation
  • Reuse detection
  • Security audit logs
  • Multi-tab coordination
  • Email verification
  • Password reset

Phase 3 — Scale

  • Centralized session management
  • Redis for distributed coordination if needed
  • Dedicated security monitoring
  • Risk-based authentication
  • MFA
  • Suspicious login detection
  • Session policy enforcement

The architecture should evolve based on actual traffic and security requirements.

20. Authentication Gotchas

These are the mistakes I would watch closely during implementation.

1. HttpOnly does not prevent XSS

It prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie.

XSS can still perform actions as the authenticated user.

2. Refresh rotation creates race conditions

Multiple refresh requests can invalidate each other if the backend uses strict single-token rotation.

3. Never return refresh tokens in JSON

Use protected cookies instead.

4. Access tokens and refresh tokens should have different purposes

Use different secrets or signing keys if JWTs are used for both, and validate token type, issuer, audience, and expiration.

5. Logout should revoke server-side state

Clearing frontend memory alone is not enough.

6. Cookies require CSRF consideration

HttpOnly is not a CSRF defense.

7. Never log tokens

Avoid logging:

  • Authorization headers
  • Refresh cookies
  • Passwords
  • Authentication request bodies

8. A JWT is not a complete session management system

You still need to manage the session lifecycle.

21. Before Calling Authentication Production-Ready

Here is the checklist I would use before shipping.

  • [ ] Passwords are hashed with a suitable password hashing algorithm
  • [ ] Access tokens are short-lived
  • [ ] Refresh tokens are securely generated
  • [ ] Refresh tokens are hashed before database storage
  • [ ] Refresh token rotation is implemented
  • [ ] Refresh reuse detection is considered
  • [ ] Session revocation is implemented
  • [ ] Logout revokes the server session
  • [ ] Refresh cookie uses HttpOnly
  • [ ] Secure cookies are enabled in production
  • [ ] SameSite policy is explicitly configured
  • [ ] CORS uses an explicit origin allowlist
  • [ ] CSRF protections are in place
  • [ ] Login and refresh endpoints are rate-limited
  • [ ] Concurrent refresh requests are handled
  • [ ] Token secrets are not committed to source control
  • [ ] Tokens are never logged
  • [ ] Session expiration is validated server-side
  • [ ] Authentication failures do not leak sensitive information

Conclusion

JWT authentication is easy to implement.

Secure JWT authentication is much harder.

The difference between a tutorial implementation and a production implementation is not the JWT library. It is how you handle the entire session lifecycle.

A production MERN authentication system needs to think about:

  • Token security
  • Refresh rotation
  • Session persistence
  • Concurrent requests
  • Device management
  • Revocation
  • Cookie security
  • CSRF
  • XSS
  • Scalability

The biggest mistake is treating authentication as a login endpoint.

Authentication is a lifecycle.

If you design that lifecycle correctly from the beginning, your application becomes safer, easier to maintain, and much more predictable as it grows.

title: devnet-fixtures: funded wallets, mints and token balances from a YAML file
description:
An end-to-end test for a Solana app needs a starting state before it can check anything. There must be a wallet with some SOL to pay fees, a second wallet to receive, a mint with known decimals, token accounts, and balances the test can assert on. Most projects build that state with a setup script: a few airdrops, a mint creation, some mintTo calls, then a list of addresses copied into environment variables.

Those scripts tend to break in the same places. Devnet airdrops are rate limited and fail at random. Running the script twice creates a second mint or doubles the balances. And the addresses change on every run, so the test config has to be regenerated each time.

devnet-fixtures is a small CLI for CI pipelines and local end-to-end tests that replaces the script with a description. You write the wallets, mints and token balances you need in YAML. It creates them on a cluster, then prints their addresses as .env lines or JSON.

Two warnings from the README come first. The project is not audited, and it is for devnet, testnet and localnet only: it refuses mainnet, both by URL and by checking the RPC's genesis hash. It also writes throwaway keypairs to disk, so never fund them with real assets, and keep keysDir out of git.

What it does

The spec is one YAML file:

cluster: ${FIXTURES_CLUSTER:-localnet}   # localnet | devnet | testnet | URL
keysDir: .fixtures                        # keypairs saved here (0600), gitignored
# funder: ./funder.json                   # used when airdrops fail (devnet rate limits)
airdrop: { retries: 5, delayMs: 1000, maxSolPerRequest: 2 }
accounts:
  - { name: alice, sol: 2 }
  - { name: bob, sol: 1 }
  - { name: carol }
mints:
  - name: usdc
    decimals: 6
    authority: alice
    mintTo:
      - { owner: alice, amount: 1000 }
      - { owner: bob, amount: 12.5 }
    atas: [carol]
  - name: points
    decimals: 0
    token2022: true
    authority: bob
    mintTo: [{ owner: carol, amount: 42 }]

Running it against a local validator prints the result:

$ devnet-fixtures examples/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899 --prefix e2e
E2E_RPC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8899
E2E_ALICE_PUBKEY=FnJm4NKB…
E2E_ALICE_KEYPAIR=/…/.fixtures/alice.json
E2E_USDC_MINT=93g3h43j…
E2E_USDC_DECIMALS=6
E2E_USDC_TOKEN_PROGRAM=TokenkegQfeZyiNwAJbNbGKPFXCWuBvf9Ss623VQ5DA
E2E_USDC_ATA_BOB=AFjfVXrH…
E2E_POINTS_MINT=2egvfGXW…
...

It never prints secret keys. The output contains public keys and keypair file paths only. A test that needs to sign as alice loads the file at E2E_ALICE_KEYPAIR.

It is idempotent. Keypairs are reused from keysDir. Mints are remembered per cluster genesis hash in keysDir/state.json, and reused while they still exist. SOL balances and token balances are topped up to the target, never added on top. A second run against the same cluster makes no transactions, except to top up SOL that was spent on fees.

Airdrops are handled with care. Each request is split into chunks of maxSolPerRequest and retried with exponential backoff (delayMs × 2^n). If airdrops still fail and a funder keypair is configured, the tool sends a System transfer from the funder instead. Token operations, meaning mint creation, ATAs and minting, are retried in the same way.

Amounts are exact. Values in mintTo are UI amounts, such as 12.5, and they are converted exactly to base units with no float drift.

SPL Token and Token-2022. A mint is created with the classic token program by default, or with Token-2022 when the spec says token2022: true. The output tells the tests which program owns each mint.

How to use it

You need Node.js 20 or later. Clone and build:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/devnet-fixtures
cd devnet-fixtures
pnpm install && pnpm build

Then run it from the checkout:

node dist/cli.js examples/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899   # with solana-test-validator running
node dist/cli.js spec.yaml --format json --out fixtures.json
node dist/cli.js spec.yaml --github-env                               # also append to $GITHUB_ENV

The first command needs solana-test-validator running locally. The second writes JSON to a file instead of .env lines on standard output. The third also appends the variables to $GITHUB_ENV, so later steps of a GitHub Actions job see them without any glue code.

In GitHub Actions, the job has three steps. This is the README's sketch, adapted to a tool that was cloned and built into devnet-fixtures/ in an earlier step:

- run: solana-test-validator --reset --quiet &
- run: node devnet-fixtures/dist/cli.js test/fixtures.yaml --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899 --github-env
- run: pnpm test:e2e      # reads E2E_* env vars

The cluster field accepts localnet, devnet, testnet or a URL, and it supports ${VAR:-default} expansion. That lets the same spec run against a local validator on a laptop and against devnet in CI, with one environment variable to switch.

Things to know

  • Not audited, and never for mainnet. The tool refuses a mainnet URL, and it also refuses when the RPC answers with the mainnet genesis hash, so pointing a custom URL at mainnet does not get around the check.
  • The keypairs are throwaway. They are saved in keysDir with 0600 permissions. Treat them as test material: never send real assets to them, and add the directory to .gitignore.
  • One mint authority per mint, no freeze authority. Token-2022 extensions are not configurable.
  • A harmless warning. @solana/spl-token prints "bigint: Failed to load bindings" when its optional native build is disabled. The README says this can be ignored.
  • What was tested. The 14 unit tests never touch the network. They cover spec parsing and validation, ${VAR:-default} expansion and refusing mainnet by URL. They run the main logic against an in-memory FakeChain to check chunked airdrops, backoff timings, the funder fallback, failure without a funder, idempotent re-runs, refusing a mainnet genesis hash, 0600 keypair files, and env output that contains no secrets. The RPC layer is tested against a mocked JSON-RPC fetch.
  • One manual run. The example spec was also run by hand against solana-test-validator (Agave 4.2). It created 3 funded wallets, an SPL mint and a Token-2022 mint, 4 ATAs and the balances, and a second run reused everything. The README reports no run against public devnet.

Why I built it

Test setup for a Solana project is repetitive, and the usual script has three weak points. It depends on airdrops that fail under rate limits. It is not safe to run twice. And it leaves the test code to find out which addresses were created.

A declarative spec answers all three. Because the tool knows the target state, it can compare it with the cluster and do only what is missing, which is what makes a second run free. Because it owns the airdrop step, it can chunk, back off and fall back to a funder in one place instead of in every project's script. And because it prints addresses under stable names, the tests read E2E_USDC_MINT and do not care how the mint came to exist.

The mainnet refusal and the rule about never printing secret keys come from the same idea. A tool that creates keypairs and runs inside CI logs should be hard to misuse by accident.

Get the code

The CLI, the example spec and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/devnet-fixtures. It is MIT licensed. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Frontend Performance Is an Architectural Decision
description:
A page can have memoized components, compressed images, and a good bundle report—and still feel slow.

Sometimes the delay was decided before any of those optimizations: the application waits for JavaScript before requesting essential data, unrelated features ship together, or one global update causes too much work.

Performance is partly a matter of implementation. Architecture determines how much work the implementation has to do and when that work can begin.

Draw the critical path

Consider a product page that loads like this:

  1. Fetch the HTML shell.
  2. Download and execute the application JavaScript.
  3. Fetch the product.
  4. Read the product's category and fetch recommendations.
  5. Render the complete page.

Some dependencies are real. Recommendations may need information from the product. But the customer may not need recommendations before seeing the product title, image, and purchase controls.

That distinction changes the architecture. Essential content can render independently. Secondary work can happen later. Data available earlier in the request lifecycle can sometimes be fetched before browser execution begins.

The important exercise is identifying what must happen sequentially, what can happen concurrently, and what should not block the primary task.

Moving code into a smaller component will not remove a data waterfall on its own.

Rendering strategy changes where the work happens

Client rendering, server rendering, static generation, and streaming distribute work differently.

A mostly static article and a highly interactive trading interface have different requirements. Applying the same strategy to both can create avoidable work or unnecessary infrastructure.

Server rendering can deliver useful HTML before client code runs, but it also introduces server work and may still require substantial hydration. Static output can avoid request-time rendering for suitable content, but freshness needs a plan. Streaming can expose ready content earlier when the framework and application support it, but loading states must remain usable.

Choose based on content freshness, personalization, interaction needs, and measured user experience. The label of the rendering strategy is not a performance result.

Data ownership determines request behavior

If every widget independently fetches the same account record, the page may duplicate requests. If a root loader fetches everything, it may delay the entire route for data needed only by a hidden panel.

Neither extreme is universally right.

Put request coordination at the narrowest level that understands the shared need. Deduplicate equivalent requests where appropriate. Keep essential and optional data distinguishable. Define cache freshness around how the product uses the data.

Caching is a correctness decision as well as a speed decision. A stale avatar and a stale stock availability indicator have different consequences.

Avoid treating one global cache duration as a complete policy.

Dependencies are a recurring budget

A dependency adds more than downloaded bytes. Depending on how it is delivered and used, it can add parsing, execution, initialization, and maintenance work.

A charting library might be justified on an analytics route and unnecessary on the sign-in page. A route boundary gives you a place to defer it. A shared module imported everywhere can accidentally pull it into a broader loading path.

Define budgets for meaningful entry points, then inspect the generated output. Source-level imports do not always tell you exactly what users download.

Treat a budget as a review trigger. If a dependency exceeds it, assess the user benefit and alternatives rather than mechanically rejecting useful functionality.

State boundaries affect interaction cost

A keystroke should not require the application to reconsider unrelated screens.

Broad subscriptions, expensive derived work, and large synchronous updates can make interaction slow even after the page has loaded.

Keep rapidly changing state close to its consumers. Subscribe to the values a view needs. Profile actual interactions before adding memoization: caching a calculation does little if network delay or layout work dominates the experience.

Architecture creates opportunities for local work. Profiling confirms whether the implementation uses them.

Make performance part of ownership

Assign responsibility for the whole user journey as well as individual features.

Track loading, responsiveness, and visual stability in representative conditions. Use controlled checks to catch regressions and production measurements to understand the range of real experiences. Segment results when device or network differences hide important failures.

When a regression appears, connect it to a decision: a new dependency, a request dependency, a rendering change, or a wider update boundary.

Performance work becomes more effective when teams can change those decisions. The strongest optimization is often arranging the system so that unnecessary work never enters the user's critical path.
