title: text-wrap pretty made my pills overflow on phones
description:
In October, Framer's Marketplace review took four of my templates down. One of the problems they flagged looked tiny: on phones, the text in some pills and price tags ran past the edge of the pill. A price like "€6,900 / week" spilled out of its card.

The cause was a setting I had turned on to make text look better.

The setup

In Framer, text styles have a Text Wrap option: default, balance or pretty. Balance evens out line lengths, and pretty avoids a single word stranded on the last line. Both map to the CSS text-wrap property, and both make headings and paragraphs look more polished.

So I had set pretty wrap on almost every text style, including the label and button styles. Those styles are used inside pills that size themselves to their text, which in Framer means auto width (in CSS terms, the pill shrinks to fit its content).

What went wrong

On desktop everything looked fine. On a narrow phone, where a pill had to wrap or squeeze, the text stopped fitting inside it. Framer publishes these text layers with white-space: pre-wrap, and with balance or pretty wrap on top, the auto-width pill ended up sized by its longest word rather than by its text. The rest of the text overflowed the pill instead of the pill growing or the text wrapping cleanly.

It only showed at small widths, so I never saw it at the three breakpoints I usually looked at.

The fix

Set Text Wrap back to default on the label and button styles. That fixed every pill at once, because they all shared those styles.

In plain CSS terms:

/* Pills, tags, buttons: let them wrap normally */
.pill, .button, .tag {
    text-wrap: wrap;
}

/* Keep the nicer wrapping where it helps: headings in containers with a set width */
h1, h2 {
    text-wrap: balance;
}

I still use balance on big headings, where a lone word on the last line looks bad and the container's width doesn't depend on the text.

How to catch it

  • Check your published site at a 320 px phone width, not just the breakpoints your tool gives you. Small phones show wrapping problems first.
  • Look at every component that sizes itself to its content: pills, tags, chips, buttons and badges.
  • Change shared text styles carefully. One setting on a style touches every layer that uses it, which is how one checkbox broke pills across a whole template.

The other two things that review flagged were a hover zoom that grew past its frame and buttons that linked to a deleted page. I wrote all three up, together with the rest of my pre-submission checks, here: the Framer template checklist I use before every submission.

Where do you use text-wrap: balance or pretty, and have you seen it misbehave?

title: 8 Product Tips for Regulated Investment Platforms
description:
Investment platforms are judged on two things at once: whether a first-time investor can understand a deal, and whether a regulator could reconstruct what that person was shown. Those goals pull in opposite directions if you treat compliance as a footer and the product as a marketing page.

The tips below are for teams building or reviewing a platform that lists discrete deals — fixed income, notes, private-market offers — and takes money from retail or accredited investors. They are not legal advice. They work because most of the harm happens when key facts are technically present but practically hard to find.

1. Put the Deal Facts in One Place, in a Stable Order

Every listing should show the same core facts in the same order: what the investor is buying, the rate or return figure and its basis, the tenure, the minimum amount, the currency, fees, and when interest or principal is supposed to be paid.

If a number is “net”, say net of what. If a rate is historical or illustrative, label it as such on the same line, not in a footnote three scrolls down. People compare deals the way they compare pricing tables. A layout that changes from deal to deal makes comparison, and later complaints, worse.

Keep a signed factsheet or term sheet attached to the same record. The page and the document should not be able to drift apart without someone noticing.

2. Do Not Hide Risk Below the Fold

A risk section that only appears after a carousel of testimonials is not a disclosure. It is a design choice that will be read uncharitably later.

Put material risks on the deal page itself: what the money is used for, what the investor’s claim is on any underlying asset, what happens if a borrower is late, and that capital is at risk. If there is collateral, a charge, a guarantee or a buy-back arrangement, describe it in plain language and say what it does not guarantee.

Links to a 40-page information memorandum still matter. They do not replace a clear summary on the page where the investment button sits.

3. Make Fees and Timing Impossible to Miss

Investors remember the headline rate. They forget platform fees, spread, early-exit rules, and whether interest starts on funding day or on a later deployment date.

Show fees next to the return figure, and show the scheduled payment dates next to the tenure. If principal is returned only at maturity, say so. If a deal can be extended, say who can extend it and what the investor can do about it.

If you change a fee or a date after a deal is live, record the change on the deal record and tell the people who already committed. Silent edits to a live listing are a product failure, not a copy tweak.

4. Design Onboarding as a Checkpoint, Not a Funnel to Be Maximised

Know-your-customer checks, appropriateness questions and cooling-off periods exist to stop the wrong person buying the wrong product. A UX that treats them as friction to be minimised will eventually push a user through a flow they did not understand.

Explain why each step is there, allow people to save progress, and do not pre-tick agreements. If a user fails an eligibility check, tell them clearly and do not offer a back door on the next screen.

Keep an audit trail of what was asked, what was answered, and which version of the terms was accepted. If you cannot reconstruct that later, the flow is not finished.

5. Write Deal Pages as a Product Surface, Not a Brochure

The temptation is to dress a listing like a campaign: lifestyle photography, slogans, and a large “invest now” button. That can be fine, as long as the decision-grade information is complete and easier to find than the slogans.

The test is simple: can a careful reader state the risk, the fees and the timetable without opening a second document? If they cannot, the page is not ready, no matter how polished it looks.

6. Keep Client Money and Status Language Precise

Platform copy often says “your funds are secure” or “capital protected” when the legal structure is more limited: an independent account, a charge over an asset, or a process that has worked so far. Those are not the same thing.

Use the same terms the legal documents use, then explain them. If money is held by a custodian or a cash administrator, name the role and what it means when a deal is delayed. If there have been no defaults to date, that is a historical statement, not a promise about the next deal. On a regulated real-estate-backed platform such as BigFundr, the deal page, the factsheet and the account status have to agree, because the investor is committing to a specific tenure and structure rather than a generic fund unit.

In-product status also needs this precision. “Processing”, “funded”, “live” and “matured” should map to a defined state, visible to the investor and to your operations team, not to a designer’s sense of momentum.

7. Build for the Awkward Mid-Deal Moments

The happy path — browse, invest, receive interest, get principal back — is the easy part. The product is defined by what happens when a payment is late, a deal is withdrawn before funding, a user dies or loses access, or a factsheet is updated.

Specify those flows before you scale marketing. How is the investor notified? What can they do in the account? Who can they talk to, and with what identification? If a deal is oversubscribed or cancelled, when does the money come back, and in which currency?

A help centre article is useful. An in-product message at the moment the status changes is better.

8. Version Everything the Investor Could Have Relied On

Deal pages change. Terms are restated. Risk wording is tightened. If you overwrite the previous version, you will not be able to show what a given investor saw on the day they clicked confirm.

Version the factsheet, the deal-page summary, the terms accepted at onboarding, and the email or push notification that accompanied a material change. Store them against the user and the deal, not only in a CMS history that a future redesign might drop.

This is unglamorous infrastructure. It is also the difference between a platform you can explain and one you can only apologise for.

The Bottom Line

A regulated investment product is only as clear as its listings, fees, risk wording and onboarding trail. Design those as core product surfaces, and keep the mid-deal failures and the historical versions as carefully as the first “invest” button.

If a patient reader can understand a deal from the page in front of them, and you can later prove what they saw, the platform is doing its job.

title: Quotes in a style tag broke hydration in my Framer code component
description:
I sell Framer code components, and one of them worked perfectly in the editor, then threw a hydration error on the published site. The page still rendered, but the console showed React error #425 ("text content does not match server-rendered HTML").

The cause was two kinds of characters in the CSS: quotes and >.

The setup

Framer code components are React components. A common way to ship their styles is a <style> element with a template string inside:

export default function Accordion(props) {
    return (
        <div className="acc">
            <style>{`
                .acc [data-state="open"] .panel { display: block; }
                .acc > .item { border-top: 1px solid #ddd; }
            `}</style>
            {/* ... */}
        </div>
    )
}

In the editor this is fine, because the editor renders on the client only. A published Framer site renders the page on the server first and then hydrates it in the browser, and that's where it broke.

What went wrong

On the server, the text inside <style> was escaped like any other text: " became " and > became >. In the browser, <style> is a raw text element, so those entities are never decoded. The browser kept " as literal characters in the CSS.

So the server HTML and the client render disagreed about the style text, React reported the mismatch, and the selectors with escaped characters stopped matching anything.

The fix

Write the CSS so it has nothing to escape:

<style>{`
    .acc [data-state=open] .panel { display: block; }
    .acc .item { border-top: 1px solid #ddd; }
`}</style>
  • Attribute selectors don't need quotes when the value is a plain word: [data-state=open] works the same as [data-state="open"].
  • Replace the child combinator > with a descendant selector or a class on the child.
  • No content: "..." strings. If you need generated text, put it in the markup instead.

JavaScript inside ${...} in the template string is fine, because it runs before React ever sees the text.

How to catch it before buyers do

The editor will never show this bug. Publish the site, open it in a normal browser tab and check the console for React's "recoverable error" messages, numbers #418, #421, #423 and #425. Those are hydration mismatches. If you see one, look for anything your component renders differently on the server than on the client: escaped text, dates, random ids or window checks.

A related trap: don't build class names or CSS selectors from useId(). Framer's server render adds copies of components for breakpoint variants, so the ids can shift between server and client.

I keep the rest of what I check before submitting a template or component in one place: the Framer template checklist I use before every submission.

Have you hit a hydration error that only showed up on the live site? What caused it?

title: 8 Brand-to-Engineering Handoff Tips That Actually Work
description:
A brand system can look tight in a slide deck and still fall apart in production. The logo is too complex at 16 pixels, the brand typeface adds a second of font delay, and the colour contrast that worked in print fails a basic accessibility check in the product UI.

The tips below are for teams that have to ship a website or an app from a brand identity, not only present one. None of them are a reason to dilute a distinctive brand. They work because engineering constraints show up at launch, whether you planned for them or not.

1. Design Tokens Before a 90-Page PDF

Guidelines that only exist as a PDF will be skimmed once and ignored. The useful handoff is a set of tokens: colour, type scale, spacing, radius, shadows and breakpoints, named in a way a developer can put into CSS or a design-system file.

Keep the names stable and boring (color-text-primary, not “Ocean Dusk”). If a token does not map to a value the product will actually use, leave it out. A short token list that is implemented is worth more than a comprehensive palette that never leaves Figma.

Agree which file is the source of truth, and how a token change reaches the codebase. Otherwise the site and the latest deck will drift within a month.

2. Test the Identity at Product Sizes, Not Just on a Poster

Brand work is often signed off at large sizes: a billboard, a cover, a presentation title. The same mark has to work as a favicon, a nav logo, an app icon and an Open Graph image.

Check the logo in monochrome, on light and dark backgrounds, and at the smallest size it will appear in the interface. If the wordmark falls apart, you need a simplified mark, not a scaled-down poster. The same applies to photography: a campaign image that looks striking in a case study can be too heavy, too cropped, or too low-contrast in a hero slot.

Build a simple page of real components — header, button, form, card, error state — before you call the identity finished.

3. Choose Type With Performance in Mind

Custom fonts are often part of the brand, and they are one of the most common reasons a new marketing site feels slow. Each weight is a network request. A family with four weights and italics can stall the first render if it is loaded carelessly.

Limit the shipped weights to what the UI actually uses. Subset the files, use font-display: swap or a close equivalent, and preload only the critical face. If a secondary display font is only used on the homepage heading, do not make every authenticated view pay for it.

If the brand typeface is not licensed for web use, resolve that before development starts. A last-minute system-font fallback will not match the compositions anyone approved.

4. Check Colour Contrast in the Interface, Not Only in the Palette

Brand palettes are chosen for distinctive look and feel. Product UI also has to be readable. Mid-grey text on a tinted background, or a primary button that fails contrast on white, will create accessibility issues and, in some markets, legal ones.

Run the core combinations — body text, links, buttons, alerts, focus states — against WCAG contrast requirements. If a brand colour cannot pass on the backgrounds you plan to use, define a UI-specific variant rather than telling engineers to “make it work”.

Document focus states and error colours as part of the system. They are easy to omit from a branding deck and hard to invent consistently later.

5. Treat the Website as Part of the Brand, Not a Separate Deliverable

Identity, packaging and a website are often commissioned as if they were unrelated. Users experience them as one thing. Layout, motion, image style and page performance are brand decisions, not only engineering ones.

If web design is going to a different team, give them the tokens, the component list and the performance constraints at the same time as the visual files. The brief is practical: component behaviour, and a site that can be implemented without inventing missing states.

6. Inventory Components, Including the Unhappy States

Most brand presentations show the happy path: a perfect hero, a tidy card, a primary button. Production also needs empty states, validation errors, disabled buttons, loading placeholders, and a cookie or consent banner that does not break the layout.

List the components the site or product actually needs, and design the edge cases for each. Engineers should not be guessing how an error message sits on a form, or what happens when a product name wraps onto three lines. This is also why the handoff works better when identity and the front end are designed together, rather than a PDF being thrown over the wall once the logo is approved. A branding and web design studio such as Abnormal is set up for that kind of work.

If you already have a component library, map the new brand to those components instead of inventing a parallel set. Two button styles for the same action is how a design system starts to rot.

7. Specify Assets the Way a Build Pipeline Will Use Them

Hand over SVG icons that are clean, consistently framed and stripped of editor junk. Provide raster images at the sizes they will be displayed, or clearly larger, and say whether they should be cropped. Avoid “logo final FINAL-v7.psd” as the official file.

Include favicon, app icon, social preview and, if relevant, an email header. Name files in a predictable way. If motion is part of the brand, specify duration, easing and what should be reduced for users who prefer reduced motion. A ten-megabyte animation in the header is not a personality trait. It is a performance bug.

A short README in the handoff folder will save a week of Slack questions.

8. Sit With Engineering for the First Build, Not Only the Sign-Off

The first implementation will surface problems no one saw in Figma: a heading measure that is too long in real copy, a colour that vibrates against a photograph, a nav that cannot fit the actual information architecture.

Budget a review on a staging URL, on a phone, and in the browser your users actually use. Change the tokens if you need to, and record the change in the source of truth. A brand system that cannot absorb a small implementation change will be bypassed.

Once the first release is out, agree who can add a one-off colour or type size, and who cannot. The system survives through that rule more than through the original presentation.

The Bottom Line

A brand that has to live in a product needs tokens, tested sizes, readable colour, a realistic component list and assets a build can use. The PDF is a reference, not a deliverable.

If you sort those things out before development starts, the site will look like the identity you approved, and it will still be fast enough to use.

title: A busy database now answers 503 in gophenberg
description:
On 27 November 2026, GitHub Trending's daily Go list is led by tools that put agents to work in parallel: multica-ai/multica gained 173 stars that day and Tencent/LoopForge gained 97, both describing shared task boards or workflows for coding agents. Trendshift's weekly list for the same date shows stablyai/orca gaining 3.2k stars for running a fleet of bots on one subscription, a weekly gain rather than a lifetime total. The dev.to trending page carries a cluster named "Production Error Handling in n8n Automations" with 22 posts in seven days, active one day earlier, about silent failures and retries in automated workflows. Hacker News' front page on that date includes an item on AI agents controlling part of DeepMind's compute at 33 points. The causal link is short: when automated writers share one database, a lock timeout is an ordinary event, and the answer has to name it so the caller can retry instead of believing a save succeeded.

gopherium/gophenberg#681 is one concrete implementation of that answer. gophenberg is a Go publishing server with a Postgres store and a browser editor. The pull request closes issue #550, was opened on 12 November 2026, and was merged on 14 November 2026. Its diff covers 53 files with 935 lines added and 166 removed, across 19 commits. The merge head is 8554209.

What was wrong

A Postgres deadlock or lock timeout arrived at the HTTP layer as an ordinary error with no stable code. errorResponseFor matched a small set of domain errors and auth errors, then fell through to 500 internal. A client reading that answer could not tell contention apart from a real server fault. The release notes in the pull request record two consequences at the editor: a failed save was no longer reported as successful, and unsaved text stayed in the editor so the writer could try again.

The fix has two halves. The store half tags every statement failure with a database class. The server half turns one class into a typed HTTP answer.

The path through the code

At the merge head, internal/postgres/classified.go wraps the database connection in a classified type. Exec, Query and QueryRow each pass the error from the driver through dbkitpg.Classify. The row wrappers do the same for Rows.Err and Row.Scan, so a failure that shows up only while reading results is classified as well. A deadlock detected with SQLSTATE 40P01, or a lock timeout, becomes dbkit.ErrBusy.

internal/server/json.go then maps it in errorResponseFor: dbkit.ErrBusy returns http.StatusServiceUnavailable with the body {"error":"database busy","code":"database_busy"}. Every other unrecognised error still returns 500 internal. There is one deliberate exception. respondReadAfterWrite turns a busy error into the internal answer when a write was already stored, because telling a client to retry at that point could duplicate a save that did land.

A classified deadlock reaches the answer mapper as ErrBusy and leaves as 503 database_busy.

The answer also carries two negative guarantees. wantBusyAnswer in internal/server/busy_test.go asserts that the response has no Retry-After header, so no client retries on its own, and that Cache-Control is no-store, so a busy answer cannot be kept in a cache. The editor shows a message asking the writer to save again, and the decision stays with the person at the keyboard.

What the diff actually contains

The pull request reports 53 changed files. The largest pieces of the diff are these:

File Added Removed
internal/server/busy_test.go 207 0
internal/postgres/classified_internal_test.go 77 0
internal/postgres/groups_failure_test.go 62 17
internal/postgres/classified.go 55 0
frontend/src/test/posts-api.test.ts 37 0

Those figures come from the GitHub files endpoint for pull request #681. The new busy_test.go accounts for 207 added lines on its own, which is why a change that reads as one status code in the API touches 53 files: the class has to be attached at each place a statement can fail, and each response path needs a test that pins the answer.

Authorship

The pull request was opened by Indra Prasetya and merged on 14 November 2026. Nineteen commits are in the branch. Three are authored by me: the first change that surfaced dbkit.ErrBusy, the follow-up on server masking and frontend templates, and the translation entry. Maintainer SirLouen authored the other 16, including the store classifiers, the feature and server tests, the Spanish and French messages, and most of the response changes. The repository belongs to the maintainer. This is a joint branch, not a claim that the whole diff is mine.

Verification I can repeat

At merge head 8554209, internal/server/busy_test.go holds six test functions. Three pin the busy answer for a content save, a media save and a theme change. Two check that a settings patch or a post patch which stored its edit never answers database_busy. The sixth checks that a settings patch storing nothing answers a busy read as database_busy. internal/postgres/classified_internal_test.go holds one more function, which checks that the wrapper marks each failure of the connection. I counted those names from the source files at the merge SHA through the GitHub contents API. I did not run the upstream Go suite on this host, so these are source counts rather than a local test run.

Why this matters

Turning a deadlock into a typed 503 is not a matter of changing one status constant. The database error has to survive three boundaries: the driver, the store wrapper and the HTTP mapper. A read that follows a stored write needs the opposite answer, or a retry would create a duplicate post. Deciding not to send Retry-After keeps the retry decision with the editor and the writer. Those choices are visible in 53 files and 207 lines of new server tests, and they are the part of this fix that a caller can depend on.

Sources: gophenberg#681, its merge head 8554209 and issue #550, retrieved 27 November 2026. Trend sources: Trendshift weekly, GitHub Trending Go, Hacker News and dev.to trending, retrieved 27 November 2026.

title: Sales CRM UI kits for Figma + React (2026)
description:
A sales CRM is mostly tables, pipelines and sequences, so starting from a kit saves weeks. These are the Figma + React options I'd compare. I run mebius.design, which sells one of them, and the others were checked on their own sites.

For a sales CRM dashboard in Figma and React, mebius.design sells Arcline: 161 Figma screens for prospect search, lead scoring and outreach sequences, plus 104 React components and 54 blocks in shadcn registry format, for $19 once. Other options: Creative Market’s Venture, Shadcn Studio’s NexaCRM and the free Atomic CRM.

What should a CRM dashboard UI kit include?

The screens a sales team opens every day.

A sales CRM dashboard UI kit should cover the work from finding a lead to closing a deal. Whether you compare CRM kits on mebius.design or elsewhere, look for:

  • People and companies: a searchable list and profiles with activity.
  • Lists, enrichment and lead scoring, so reps know whom to contact first.
  • A pipeline: deals or prospects by stage.
  • Outreach: email sequences, an inbox for replies, tasks and a calendar.
  • Analytics: pipeline, win rate and reply rates.
  • Settings: team roles, a CRM sync, CSV import and billing.

Then check Figma variables, light and dark themes, React code that matches the file, and a license that covers client work.

Which sales CRM UI kits does mebius.design sell?

One kit, Arcline, with Figma screens and React code.

As of 19 Nov 2026, mebius.design sells one sales CRM UI kit: Arcline, an AI prospecting and CRM dashboard by Keitoto Studio. Arcline is one of 11 dashboard UI kits on mebius.design and one of the 7 that come with React code.

Sales CRM UI kits on mebius.design at a glance

  • Kit: Arcline: AI prospecting and CRM dashboard
  • Screens: 161 Figma screens, desktop and mobile
  • Components: 104 React components
  • Blocks: 54 React blocks
  • Code stack: React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format
  • Install: shadcn CLI, or the mebius MCP in Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code
  • Theme: Light, built on color variables
  • License: Single license, client work included. The Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale.
  • Price: $19 once, or $259 for all items. No subscription.
  • Checked: Facts as of 19 Nov 2026

What screens does the Arcline CRM kit have in Figma?

161 screens, desktop and mobile, in a light theme.

Arcline’s Figma file on mebius.design has 161 screens, and every desktop screen has a mobile layout. The Arcline gallery groups them like this:

  • Sign up and onboarding: sign-in, sign-up and a setup flow for a new workspace.
  • Dashboard and analytics: the home screen and outreach analytics.
  • AI prospecting: search in plain words, a query builder and the results.
  • Prospects and companies: profiles with buying signals.
  • Lists, enrichment and lead scoring.
  • Outreach and tasks: sequences with an AI email writer, and tasks.
  • Integrations and settings.

The Arcline file is built on variables and auto layout, so one color change updates every screen. Its fonts, Geist and Geist Mono, are free on Google Fonts.

Which React components and blocks come with Arcline?

104 components and 54 blocks, as of 19 Nov 2026.

Arcline’s code on mebius.design has 104 components and 54 blocks in React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format. The components include fields, selects, date pickers, dialogs, avatars, a score meter, a sortable data table, a filter toolbar and charts.

The Arcline blocks a sales CRM uses most:

  • arcline-metrics-dashboard: the prospecting home, with KPIs, AI-recommended prospects and recent activity.
  • arcline-search-results: AI search results with criteria chips, People and Companies tabs and a bulk-selection bar.
  • arcline-kanban-board: a pipeline board from New through Contacted, Replied and Meeting booked to Won, with cards that drag between stages.
  • arcline-inbox-triage: the outreach inbox, with an AI summary of new replies and tabs such as Needs reply and Interested.
  • arcline-ai-composer and arcline-ai-answer: an AI email prompt card, and a prospect’s AI profile with a suggested opener.
  • arcline-revenue-explorer and arcline-kpi-drilldown: pipeline, win rate and deal size; emails sent, open rate, replies and meetings.
  • arcline-integrations and arcline-file-upload: a Salesforce-style sync page with field mapping, and a CSV import with column mapping.
  • arcline-team-directory, arcline-roles-and-permissions, arcline-week-calendar and arcline-login-and-sign-up for the rest of the app.

Most Arcline blocks are desktop pages, 1152 or 1440 pixels wide, with the Figma sample data. Pass your own data where a block takes props, as the pipeline board does, or edit the installed files.

Is Arcline a full CRM or a sales prospecting kit?

Arcline on mebius.design is a sales CRM front end built around the top of the funnel: finding prospects, scoring them and reaching out. Its code adds a pipeline board, revenue analytics and a CRM sync page for the deal stages after the first reply.

  • Arcline is light only, in Figma and in code. Colors are variables, so you can add a dark theme yourself.
  • Arcline is UI only: the data, auth, email sending and CRM sync are yours to build.
  • For a CRM built around accounts, quotes or contracts, check the Arcline gallery for the screens you need first.

What other CRM dashboard UI kits are there?

Checked on each product’s own page on 19 Nov 2026.

Outside mebius.design, three CRM options cover the same need in different ways. Each name links to the page its facts come from.

  • Venture CRM Platform UI Kit (Creative Market, by dhuhacreative). A Figma kit for a CRM dashboard and its landing page, listing 70+ dashboard and website pages and 100+ components. It costs $45 Personal, $120 Commercial or $220 Extended Commercial, the license the page points apps to. Its strength is one design file for the product and its marketing site. The page doesn’t say React code is included.
  • NexaCRM (Shadcn Studio). A coded CRM admin template in Next.js 16, shadcn/ui, Tailwind CSS v4 and TypeScript: CRM, sales and leads dashboards, people, companies and opportunities, tasks and workflows, kanban and calendar views, and light, dark and system modes. Its page shows $79 and says NexaCRM is part of the All Access Pro plan, paid once, which covers client projects. Its strength is a deal-centered CRM in code; the page says no Figma file is provided.
  • Atomic CRM (Marmelab). A free, MIT-licensed CRM app built with React, shadcn/ui and Supabase: contacts, deals on a Kanban board, tasks, notes, email capture by CC, and import and export. Its strength is a working backend you can fork. It is an app to customize rather than a design kit, and the repo mentions no Figma file.

For more Figma styles, multi-author marketplaces are the next stop: UI8 listed 6,428 UI kits when we checked on 17 Nov 2026. The mebius vs UI8 comparison sets UI8’s prices and license next to mebius.design’s.

Which CRM dashboard UI kit should you pick?

  • A prospecting or sales engagement product, designed in Figma and built in React + shadcn with code that matches the file: Arcline on mebius.design.
  • A Figma-only CRM design with a landing page, bought once: Venture on Creative Market.
  • A deal-centered CRM in Next.js code with a dark mode, no Figma file needed: NexaCRM.
  • A free, working CRM with a Supabase backend to fork: Atomic CRM.

To try the mebius.design style first, the Sales Performance Chart and the Total Sales Chart are among 62 free charts in React + Tailwind, free with a mebius account.

How do you install Arcline’s React code?

The shadcn CLI or the mebius MCP, after you buy Arcline on mebius.design.

After you buy Arcline on mebius.design, create an access token in Settings › Tokens and add the @mebius registry to your project once:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Install the Arcline theme on its own first, then the blocks you need with --overwrite, so shared parts take Arcline’s version:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-metrics-dashboard @mebius/arcline-kanban-board --overwrite

Then render the pipeline board with your own stages and cards:

components/pipeline.tsx:

import { KanbanBoard, type KanbanColumnData } from "@/components/kanban-board"

const columns: KanbanColumnData[] = [
  {
    id: "new",
    title: "New",
    count: 1,
    dropLabel: "Drop to move back to New",
    cards: [{ id: "dimas", initials: "DP", name: "Dimas Pratama", company: "Kopi Kilat", score: 81, level: 8, next: "Research before outreach" }],
  },
  { id: "meeting", title: "Meeting booked", count: 0, dropLabel: "Drop to book meeting", cards: [] },
]

export function Pipeline() {
  return <KanbanBoard columns={columns} />
}

In Claude Code, Cursor or VS Code, the mebius MCP server does the same: add it, sign in, and ask for an Arcline block (setup per editor).

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

For the Arcline Figma file, download the .zip from My Library, extract it and import Arcline.fig into Figma.

FAQ

How much does Arcline cost?

Arcline costs $19 on mebius.design, paid once, with updates included, or $259 once for every item. There is no subscription.

Can I use Arcline in client projects?

Yes. Every mebius.design purchase covers client work for one person. Handing the Figma files themselves to a client, white-label products and resale need the Agency license, quoted on the Pricing page.

Does Arcline include React code?

Yes. Arcline comes with 104 components and 54 blocks in React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format, built to match the Figma file. They install with the shadcn CLI or the mebius MCP.

Does Arcline have a dark mode?

No. Arcline is a light theme in Figma and in code, built on color variables. For CRM code with a dark mode, NexaCRM lists light, dark and system modes (checked on 19 Nov 2026).

Can I build a CRM MVP with Arcline?

Yes, for the UI. Arcline gives you the Figma screens and the React front end. The backend, auth, email sending and payments stay yours to build. The best UI kits for an MVP guide compares kits for other kinds of MVP.

Is there a free CRM dashboard UI kit?

Atomic CRM is free and MIT-licensed, as an app rather than a Figma kit. On mebius.design, Arcline is paid, but 62 charts and 128 forms are free with an account.

Related

  • Arcline: The AI prospecting and CRM dashboard kit: Figma screens, React components and blocks.
  • Arcline gallery: Every Arcline screen: prospects, companies, lists, scoring, sequences and analytics.
  • Sales Performance Chart: A free target vs actual chart for a sales dashboard, in React + Tailwind.
  • Dashboard UI kits: 11 dashboard kits in Figma, 7 of them with React + shadcn code.
  • Dashboard templates with Figma: Free and paid shadcn dashboard templates, compared by Figma file, license and price.

title: RTL QA checklist: 10 things that break when you launch a Hebrew or Arabic version of your site
description:
Adding dir="rtl" flips the page. It doesn't fix the page. Most RTL bugs come from CSS that was written with "left" and "right" baked in, and from content that mixes directions. Here is the checklist I run on a Hebrew or Arabic page, with the fix for each item.

I built a small test page with deliberate defects to make the examples concrete. Every item below was found on it by a quick scripted pass plus a visual check.

1. dir and lang on the root 

<html lang="he" dir="rtl">

Without dir, the browser lays everything out left-to-right. Without lang, screen readers and hyphenation guess. Check this first; it's the cheapest fix.

2. Physical margins and padding

margin-left: auto on a logo pushes it the wrong way once the page is RTL. Use logical properties:

.nav .logo { margin-inline-start: auto; }  /* not margin-left */
.card { margin-inline-end: 20px; }          /* not margin-right */

A quick way to find candidates: search your CSS for left and right in margin, padding, border, left:, right: and float.

3. Floats

float: left stays on the left in RTL, so card order and gutters come out wrong. Prefer flex or grid with gap, or float: inline-start where it's supported.

4. Text alignment

text-align: left inside RTL content looks broken. Use text-align: start.

5. Arrows and directional icons

A "Continue →" arrow points backwards in RTL. Mirror directional icons (arrows, chevrons, "back"/"next") but not logos, media controls or checkmarks:

[dir="rtl"] .icon-chevron { transform: scaleX(-1); }

6. Form fields that must stay LTR

Phone numbers, emails, URLs and ID numbers (Teudat Zehut, for example) should be typed and displayed left-to-right even on an RTL page:

<input type="email" dir="ltr">
<input type="text" inputmode="numeric" dir="ltr" name="id-number">

Keep the label RTL; only the input flips.

7. Mixed-direction text (bidi)

A Hebrew sentence with "iPhone 15 Pro", a price in ₪ and a date can reorder in surprising ways, especially around parentheses and punctuation. Isolate embedded Latin text:

<p>המחיר של <bdi>iPhone 15 Pro</bdi> הוא 4,299 ₪</p>

or unicode-bidi: isolate on the inline element.

8. Fixed widths on mobile

A width: 700px block forces a 700 px layout on a 375 px phone, so the RTL page gets cut off on the right. That's the side where RTL content starts, so it's even worse than in LTR. Use max-width: 100% and test in a mobile viewport.

9. Carousels, sliders and tabs

Swipe direction and "next/previous" controls should follow reading direction. Many slider libraries have an RTL option that's off by default.

10. Numbers, dates and currency

Decide on one format for dates (31/12/2026 vs 2026-12-31) and currency position (₪99.90 vs 99.90 ₪), and apply it consistently. Mixed formats are a common source of "this looks foreign" feedback from native readers.

A 5-minute scripted pass

Paste this in the browser console on an RTL page to list obvious candidates. Treat it as a pointer, not a verdict:

for (const e of document.querySelectorAll('body *')) {
  const cs = getComputedStyle(e);
  if (cs.float === 'left' || cs.float === 'right') console.log('float', cs.float, e);
  if (cs.textAlign === 'left') console.log('text-align:left', e);
}
for (const i of document.querySelectorAll('input[type=email],input[type=tel],input[type=url]'))
  if (getComputedStyle(i).direction === 'rtl') console.log('LTR field rendered RTL', i);

Then do the visual pass: desktop plus a mobile viewport, looking at navigation, forms and any sentence that mixes Hebrew or Arabic with Latin text and numbers.

Disclosure: I offer this as a written QA report with CSS fixes (an AI-assisted review, layout and direction only, not translation): Hebrew/Arabic RTL website QA on Contra. The checklist above works on its own.
