title: What kept breaking in my AI counselor. It was never the prompt.
description:
For the last month I've been building 予安 (Yu An), an AI counselor inside iYarrow, a small divination site I run alone. She talks with a guest about whatever is weighing on them, and when a reading would help she picks a tradition (I Ching, Zi Wei Dou Shu, tarot, a few others) and the guest draws the cast. She is openly an AI. There's a daily free allowance, and past it, talking with her costs credits.

Every change to her goes through a written proposal that says what was wrong, usually with numbers from production. That gives me something most side projects don't have: a record of what kept breaking. I went back through all of it, 25 days and a few dozen changes, expecting to find a lot of prompt fixes.

There were a few. But the bugs that came back, the ones I fixed three or five times, were not prompt bugs. They were places where the architecture let one decision live in two places, or happen in the wrong order. Here are the five patterns, and where each decision lives now.

1. Safety was a branch in the paywall chain

If a guest writes that they don't want to live, she must answer with care and point to a helpline, whatever their balance. That sounds like one rule. It took five fixes, all on the same day, each closing a gap the previous one left:

  1. A text turn ran the credit check before the crisis reply, so a guest with no credit who wrote 「我不想活了」 got an "out of credits" error. Voice calls already skipped the check; text didn't.
  2. The keyword backstop only knew Traditional Chinese. 「我想自殺」 was caught, 「我想自杀」, the same sentence in Simplified, was refused. And a guest who could pay was charged for the crisis turn.
  3. On a day the house spend cap was hit, every crisis turn got a canned paragraph instead of a real reply.
  4. Fixing that made a new path that was unreachable: a guest with no credit couldn't even open a sitting on a capped day, so they never got far enough to be in crisis.
  5. The helpline numbers followed the screen language, so a Chinese-speaking guest abroad was told to dial a Taiwanese number.

None of these was a bad prompt. The root cause was structural: safety was one more branch inside the billing flow, so every new billing rule could get in front of it. The fix was to make it a precondition. The crisis check now runs before the guard is ever asked:

if st.Crisis || (!acted && crisisKeyword(content)) {
    // A guest in crisis never meets a paywall, and the house pays for
    // every crisis turn: the guard is not asked.
    in.crisisHouse, in.crisisFixed = true, h.crisisCapped(ctx, uid)
} else if in.dec, err = h.guard.CheckSitting(ctx, uid, st.freePass()); err != nil {
    // ... (one more house-paid branch and paywall bookkeeping elided)
    return chat.GateError(err, h.logger, uid)
}

Once a sitting is flagged, every later turn runs with an empty toolkit. Not a prompt saying "don't do readings now", but no tools at all. A prompt is a request; an empty toolkit is a fact.

One gap is still open, and I'd rather say so. A crisis line that contains none of the keywords is only a crisis once the model flags it, and the model only sees the line if the guard lets it through. A guest with nothing left who writes something the keyword list misses still gets the ordinary refusal. The credit dialog in her room carries one helpline line for that case. It's a mitigation, not a fix.

2. The gate and the meter lived in different places

Every model call costs money and has to be charged to someone: the guest, or the house. The file that decides this is the most-changed file in the project, 33 commits. Most of those commits are the same bug in new clothes:

  • Free regenerations of a chart essay never checked the cap and never recorded the spend.
  • Regenerating an unlocked reading built a billing decision with no price, so it recorded $0.
  • Changing your birth details gave unlimited free rewrites.
  • Unheard call audio and repeated opening lines weren't counted at all.

The pattern: checking ("may this call happen?") and recording ("this call cost X") were two separate steps in two separate places, so any new code path could do one and skip the other. The spend cap's meaning also changed twice, from "all spend" to "only spend the house pays for". Credit-paid usage is sold above cost, yet a few paying guests on voice calls could use up the cap and lock everyone out, paying guests included.

What it looks like now: the check returns a decision, and the main recording functions take that decision as an argument, so the price comes from the check rather than from whoever is recording. It isn't airtight. The $0 bug was a decision built by hand without a price, and there's still a side door for auxiliary costs that takes no decision at all. But the default path now makes skipping the check awkward instead of easy.

3. State was written before the gate said yes

Three bugs with the same shape:

  • A guest past their daily limit could cast a hexagram. The cast was saved and shown, and then interpreting it failed with a 429. Every one of the 19 unanswered casts in production came right after a guest hit the limit.
  • That refused cast also left behind a conversation thread named after a question nobody answered.
  • If a reply failed and the guest retried, the cards were drawn again. A tarot reading where the cards change on retry isn't a reading.

Each time, something durable (a cast, a thread, a draw) happened before the step that could refuse it. The fix is ordering: a read-only check before anything is written, and the first draw is pinned in the sitting's state before the model runs, so a retry replays the same cards.

4. One decision, several detectors

"What language is the guest speaking?" got decided in at least three places: the reply prompt, the greeting and status lines, and the crisis resources. Each had its own heuristic and its own thresholds.

So they disagreed. Replies followed the UI locale instead of what the guest typed, and 153 of 161 questions written in Simplified Chinese got answers in Traditional. Later, inside a single sitting, the greeting could be in one language and the reply in another. The voice gate nearly billed Mandarin text-to-speech for a Vietnamese guest.

The fix was boring and complete: one function decides the reply language from what the guest wrote, and everything in the room calls it. If you find yourself writing a second "detect X" helper with slightly different rules, that's the bug, before it has a symptom.

5. Rules with a number in them leaked out of the prompt

Some behavior started in the prompt and had to move to code, because the model couldn't see the state the rule depends on:

  • Openers. Her opening line came from a deterministic rule, and I got the identical sentence two visits in a row. Asking the model to "vary your openers" can't work, because it has no idea what it said last time. Code now picks one of 22 opening moves by weight, excluding the last two used, and the prompt gets only the chosen move.
  • Follow-ups. She asked about the same unfinished matter every visit. Now a ledger caps it: 
// The thread caps. They are product rules, not tuning: reference last time
// once, keep the guest's agenda central, never pursue.
const (
    maxThreadAsks      = 2
    ignoredSkipOpeners = 2
    ignoredCooldown    = 7 * 24 * time.Hour
)
  • Reading style. A prompt rule banning one technical term made her drop it even when it mattered. Production showed 34% of replies still opened with cast metadata, and 15 of 40 follow-up replies re-read the whole cast. The fix there stayed in the prompt, but it came with a script that measures reply health on real traffic, because until then nothing measured any of it.

The test I ended up with: if a rule has a number in it ("at most twice", "within seven days", "30 a day"), the prompt can know the rule exists, but code has to hold the count.

The pattern behind the patterns

What broke Symptom Where the decision lives now
Safety inside billing Guest in crisis got "out of credits" Precondition before the guard
Check and record split Calls recorded at $0, or not at all One guard decision, recorded as-is
Write before gate Cast shown, then refused; cards redrawn Read-only check first; draw pinned in state
Many detectors Reply language disagreed with greeting One function, every caller
Counts in the prompt Same opener twice; same question every visit Code picks, ledger counts, prompt writes

Looking at all of it together, the model was rarely the problem. It writes almost everything she says, and it does that well. What broke was everything around it: the order of operations, where a decision was made, and how many places made it. Those are ordinary software bugs, and they recur for the ordinary reason: the architecture allows them.

Not everything that changed was a bug. The "how did it go?" feedback ask was rebuilt three times in three days (a card, then an email, then a line she says in her own words), but that was me not knowing what I wanted, not a structure that made it fail.

Yu An is live at iYarrow, still in beta. If you're building something conversational and drew these lines somewhere else, I'd like to hear where.

title: Print a Web Page to PDF in Go: chromedp and IronPDF
description:
A shipment tracking page has to become a PDF, filed by a Go service as proof of delivery. One route drives a browser, and in Go that browser can be controlled by chromedp, an MIT-licensed module that speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol with no external driver.

Our IronPDF for Go is coming soon, with early-access sign-up. The chromedp print path comes first here, then the parts of that path that fall to the service team, and then what the Go edition is designed to put in its place.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

How does chromedp print a page to PDF after v0.19.0?

It navigates to the page and then runs one PrintToPDF action, which returns the file as a byte slice. That action arrived in v0.19.0, released on October 4, 2026, on top of the generic API from v0.17.0, in which chromedp.Run takes one action and returns its value along with an error, while chromedp.Do runs actions that return nothing. Three names belong to the earlier API, page.PrintToPDF().Do(ctx), chromedp.ActionFunc and chromedp.Tasks, so a snippet that contains any of them predates the generic API.

The listing below prints the tracking page on A4 paper with custom margins and backgrounds.

// The first action run on this context starts the browser, and cancel stops it.
ctx, cancel := chromedp.NewContext(context.Background())
defer cancel()

url := "https://track.example.com/shipments/48213"
if err := chromedp.Do(ctx, chromedp.Navigate(url)); err != nil {
    return err
}

// Since v0.17.0, Run takes one action and returns its value with the error.
buf, err := chromedp.Run(ctx, chromedp.PrintToPDF(
    chromedp.PDFPaper(chromedp.PaperA4),
    chromedp.PDFMargins(0.9, 0.6, 0.9, 0.6),
    chromedp.PDFPrintBackground(),
))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
return os.WriteFile("delivery-proof-48213.pdf", buf, 0o644)

With no options, PrintToPDF produces Letter paper in portrait, 1 cm margins, no header or footer and no backgrounds. Letter paper and missing backgrounds come from the browser's own print behavior, so a tracking page with a colored status banner loses its color until the call asks for backgrounds.

Where does the browser come from in a container?

It has to be installed in the image, because chromedp drives a browser that must already exist on the host. On Unix-like systems the package searches at start-up for an executable by name, beginning with headless_shell and headless-shell, moving on to chromium, google-chrome and their variants, and falling back to the name google-chrome when nothing turns up. A machine that already has Chrome or Chromium installed passes that search. A bare container image fails it until a browser is added.

The project publishes a chromedp/headless-shell container image, a slimmed-down Chrome built to support the package, and the documented route for headless environments is to run the Go program inside it. The package also sets container-friendly defaults. It sends shared memory to the temp directory, because /dev/shm is small in many containers, and it adds --no-sandbox when the process runs as root unless that default is turned off.

Each of those settings is a decision the service team makes about a browser, and the shared-memory default trades away some speed and can let memory grow.

Who looks after the Chrome process once it runs?

The service does, under rules that the project's FAQ spells out. The first Run on a context starts the browser and ties its life to that context. A timeout on that context stops the browser when it expires, so the working pattern is a long-lived parent context with no timeout and a derived, timed context for each print. Concurrent requests follow the same shape, with one parent browser context and a child per goroutine.

When the connection to the browser drops, chromedp cancels the context and the caller sees context canceled. That happens when the browser is closed or its process is killed, and if the process died on its own, the error includes its exit error. A browser that never comes up reports chrome failed to start: followed by Chrome's own output. In containers, the headless-shell image should run with --init so that zombie processes are reaped.

The print options and automation chromedp offers

The print options in chromedp go well past the listing above, with header and footer templates, page ranges, scale, CSS page size, tagged output for screen readers and a streaming mode in which the browser sends a large file in pieces. The same package handles clicks, waits and screenshots when a page needs interaction before it prints, and the project's migration document lists every renamed and removed name.

What does IronPDF for Go put in place of the browser?

An in-process engine, by design. According to the IronPDF for Go page, the edition will run IronPDF Universal, the IronPDF engine rebuilt as WebAssembly, inside the application itself, with no server, no remote call and nothing extra to deploy next to the app. The engine is designed to run in a Wasmtime sandbox, with one pair of modules for every operating system and architecture, and the page says one package update will deliver a security patch.

For the tracking page, a design with nothing extra to deploy would leave no Chrome binary to add to the image. The page lists HTML conversion from strings, files and URLs, with HTML, CSS and JavaScript rendered to PDF. Beyond conversion, it lists document assembly, page edits such as headers, footers, watermarks and bookmarks, forms and digital signatures, extraction and comparison, and security work such as passwords, redaction, compression and PDF/A.

Where should a Go service start the move?

Start with a list of every endpoint that prints a web page to PDF in Go, and mark the ones where Chrome exists only to print. Those endpoints are the first candidates for the Go edition, because they gain the most when the browser leaves the image.

  1. Pick the hardest page: choose the tracking page with the colored status banner, its scripts and its web fonts, and keep a reference PDF from the current endpoint.
  2. Stabilize the current endpoint: remove any timeout from the context that starts the browser, move timeouts to per-print child contexts, and run the container with --init.
  3. Sign up for early access: register the team so the reference page can be rendered with IronPDF for Go as soon as a build is available, then compare the two PDFs side by side.
  4. Move endpoint by endpoint: if the reference page matches, point the next print-only endpoint at the Go edition and remove its share of the browser setup.

The chromedp details in this article come from the project's repository, documentation and migration notes. Sign-ups for the Go edition's early access go through the IronPDF for Go page on ironpdf.com, and the first page we would try with it is the one that has given the team the most trouble.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the chromedp calls and defaults were checked against the chromedp source at tags v0.20.0 and v0.24.0, its README and its migration notes, the release history against its tags and release notes, and the IronPDF for Go claims against its product page.

chromedp, Chrome, Chromium, Google, Go and Wasmtime are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the chromedp repository, its documentation and release notes and the IronPDF for Go page on ironpdf.com.

title: HTML Template to PDF in Scala: OpenHTMLtoPDF and IronPDF
description:
A Scala service turns an order into order-confirmation.pdf from a template and a handful of values. Then the order form gains a delivery note field, customers type whatever they like into it, and that text lands in the same template. The question for the renderer changes from how it lays out a page to what exactly reaches it.

Our released IronPDF for Java already runs in Scala services, and IronPDF for Scala is coming soon, with early-access sign-up. Before either of them, the same template goes through OpenHTMLtoPDF.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

How does OpenHTMLtoPDF render a template from Scala?

It renders through a builder that takes a source and a target and then runs once. OpenHTMLtoPDF is a pure-Java library that lays out a reasonable subset of well-formed XML or XHTML, and some HTML5, with CSS 2.1 and later standards. Output goes to PDF through Apache PDFBox, and the library can also produce images. It grew out of Flying Saucer, and Scala calls it like any other Java dependency.

import java.io.FileOutputStream
import com.openhtmltopdf.pdfboxout.PdfRendererBuilder

// The builder takes a well-formed XHTML file and an output stream.
val out = new FileOutputStream("order-confirmation.pdf")
val builder = new PdfRendererBuilder()
builder.withUri("file:///srv/templates/order-confirmation.xhtml")
builder.toStream(out)

// One call lays out the document and writes the PDF.
builder.run()
out.close()

That render stays inside what the project recommends, because the file is well formed and nobody outside the team wrote a character of it.

What changes when the template takes user text?

The renderer starts to receive input that a customer wrote. The delivery note reaches the page through one line.

// The customer's note goes straight into the template string.
val note = order.deliveryNote
val page = template.replace("{{deliveryNote}}", note)

OpenHTMLtoPDF expects strict XML by default, so an HTML5 template with an unclosed <br> needs converting first. The documented route parses the page with Jsoup, converts it with the fromJsoup method of W3CDom and hands the result to builder.withW3cDocument(doc, url). Every HTML5 template therefore carries a conversion step that the team owns.

The project's position, repeated across its changelog, is that untrusted SVG and XML are strongly advised against. A note passed through as markup, tags and all, is user-supplied XML arriving at the renderer, which is exactly the input the project advises against. A note that is escaped first, so that a typed <b> prints as three visible characters, stays a data value in a fixed template.

Which dependency fixes has OpenHTMLtoPDF shipped?

Its changelog records CVE fixes in its dependencies and one fix in its own code marked as security. The dependency entries name Apache Batik, which draws SVG, PDFBox, which writes the file, and xmlgraphics-commons, which is also used in SVG rendering. Batik moved to 1.14 and PDFBox to 2.0.24 in version 1.0.9, and xmlgraphics-commons moved in 1.0.10. The fix in the library's own code stopped an almost endless loop on deeply nested content with page-break-inside: avoid, also in 1.0.10.

Version 1.0.10, the last release under the com.openhtmltopdf group on Maven Central, is dated September 13, 2021, and the last commit on the project's default branch is dated April 1, 2022. On those artifacts, any dependency version newer than the ones 1.0.10 pulls in is a line the team adds to its own build.

OpenHTMLtoPDF strengths on a JVM back end

Several of its features suit server-side JVM code. It runs on Java 8 or later with no native binary to ship, and it generates accessible PDFs under Section 508, PDF/UA and WCAG 2.0, as well as PDF/A. Its README also lists footnotes, font fallback, CSS3 transforms and built-in SVG and MathML plugins, and the project runs automatic visual regression tests across many end-to-end cases.

How does IronPDF for Java handle the same template in Scala?

It renders the HTML5 template as web content, with no XHTML conversion in front. IronPDF for Java is a released library that supports Java, Scala and Kotlin on Java 8 or later, and a Scala service calls it as it would any Java library.

import com.ironsoftware.ironpdf.PdfDocument

object OrderConfirmation {
  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = {
    // The HTML5 template renders as written, with its stylesheet and scripts.
    val confirmation = PdfDocument.renderHtmlFileAsPdf("order-confirmation.html")
    confirmation.saveAs("order-confirmation.pdf")
  }
}

Rendering an HTML file also loads the stylesheets, scripts and images that the file references by relative path. In the PDF from that listing, the layout follows the stylesheet, the total is the figure that the template's script computed, and the delivery note prints its <b> tags as text.

IronPDF for Java also handles the steps that usually follow a confirmation, including running headers and footers and digital signatures. According to its product page, the dedicated IronPDF for Scala edition will let Scala code produce and edit PDFs.

Which Scala template should switch to IronPDF first?

The template that takes user text should switch first, since it carries the conversion step and the input question together.

  1. Escape the note in the current renderer: until the move is done, print the delivery note as text so the template stays inside what OpenHTMLtoPDF asks for.
  2. Render the HTML5 version with IronPDF for Java: use the template as written, without the Jsoup conversion, and compare it with the current PDF page by page.
  3. Move the remaining templates: point each one at IronPDF for Java once its output matches, and remove the conversion step from the build.
  4. Register for the Scala edition: use the sign-up form on the IronPDF for Scala page on ironpdf.com to try that edition when it opens.

Everything said here about OpenHTMLtoPDF traces to its repository, README and changelog. In our run on November 26, 2026, the IronPDF for Java listing compiled with Scala 2.13.10 against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 and turned the HTML5 confirmation, stylesheet and script total included, into a one-page PDF. We would start with the template behind the delivery note, rendered in the existing sbt project with IronPDF for Java under a 30-day trial key.

Drafted with AI. On November 26, 2026, the IronPDF for Java listing was compiled with Scala 2.13.10 on Java 17 and run against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3. The OpenHTMLtoPDF listing and the Jsoup route were compiled against openhtmltopdf-pdfbox 1.0.10, the other OpenHTMLtoPDF claims were checked against its repository, README and changelog, and the IronPDF for Scala claims against its product page.

OpenHTMLtoPDF, Flying Saucer, Apache PDFBox, Apache Batik, Jsoup, Scala and Java are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above come from the OpenHTMLtoPDF repository, README and changelog, the IronPDF for Java documentation, our run of the IronPDF for Java listing and the IronPDF for Scala page on ironpdf.com.

title: Building a Zero-Library Interactive 2D CAD Canvas in TypeScript: Cursor Zoom, Ortho/T-Junction Snapping & Layered Hit-Testing
description:
When teams start building an interactive floor-plan editor, diagramming canvas, or architectural CAD viewport in the browser, the default instinct is to pull in Fabric.js, Konva, or PixiJS.

For general-purpose drawing boards, a retained-mode scene graph makes sense. For an architectural CAD studio where every wall has a physical thickness in inches, doors live along wall centerlines, rooms are solved dynamically from a planar graph, and dragging one wall slides an entire collinear chain, a generic canvas scene graph quickly becomes a second source of truth you spend half your week fighting.

In PlanCaliber, our 2D CAD editor runs directly on a single HTML5 <canvas> element in pure TypeScript with zero canvas dependencies. All state lives in world inches (1 ft = 12 in), and rendering is a pure function of (solvedPlan, panX, panY, zoom, selection).

Here are the four core interaction primitives that make a raw HTML5 <canvas> feel like native desktop CAD.

1. World-to-Screen Math & Cursor-Anchored Zoom

Every wall vertex, opening offset, and fixture coordinate stays in world inches (+x East, +y South). The camera is just three numbers: panX, panY (in CSS pixels), and zoom (screen pixels per world inch).

interface Point2D {
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

function worldToScreen(wx: number, wy: number, panX: number, panY: number, zoom: number): Point2D {
  return {
    x: panX + wx * zoom,
    y: panY + wy * zoom
  };
}

function screenToWorld(sx: number, sy: number, panX: number, panY: number, zoom: number): Point2D {
  return {
    x: (sx - panX) / zoom,
    y: (sy - panY) / zoom
  };
}

When a user scrolls the wheel or pinches on a trackpad, the single most important invariant is cursor-anchored zoom: the exact world inch under (cx, cy) before zooming must remain under (cx, cy) after zooming.

function zoomAroundScreenPoint(
  factor: number,
  cx: number,
  cy: number,
  state: { panX: number; panY: number; zoom: number }
) {
  const before = screenToWorld(cx, cy, state.panX, state.panY, state.zoom);
  const nextZoom = Math.max(0.2, Math.min(10, state.zoom * factor));
  state.zoom = nextZoom;
  state.panX = cx - before.x * nextZoom;
  state.panY = cy - before.y * nextZoom;
}

Notice we never accumulate rounding error inside panX/panY — each step solves cx = panX + before.x * nextZoom directly. Combined with a ResizeObserver on the canvas wrapper and window.devicePixelRatio backing-store scaling, lines stay crisp at both 0.25 px/in whole-house view and 8.0 px/in cabinet-clearance zoom.

2. Zoom-Aware Snapping: Ortho-First Angle Lock + T-Junction Wall Capture

Raw pixel grids feel terrible in residential drafting. When a user draws a partition wall, they want a strict priority hierarchy:

  1. Existing corner capture (Math.max(13 / zoom, 7) inches): screen-constant pixel magnet so you can close a room reliably whether zoomed out or zoomed in.
  2. Architectural ortho-first angle lock: strongly prefer 90° (±26° capture window) with a lighter 45° detent (±7°), snapping wall length to 1/2" increments unless Shift unlocks free angle.
  3. Cross-plan guide alignment: snap x or y to existing vertices within 4" so opposite walls align effortlessly across hallways.
  4. T-junction centerline snap: project the candidate point onto every existing wall segment (t ∈ (0.02, 0.98)) so interior partitions terminate cleanly on an existing wall centerline instead of stopping 2 inches short and breaking room closure. 
function distPointToSegment(
  px: number, py: number,
  ax: number, ay: number,
  bx: number, by: number
): { dist: number; t: number; projX: number; projY: number } {
  const dx = bx - ax;
  const dy = by - ay;
  const lenSq = dx * dx + dy * dy;
  if (lenSq < 1e-6) {
    return { dist: Math.hypot(px - ax, py - ay), t: 0, projX: ax, projY: ay };
  }
  const t = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / lenSq));
  const projX = ax + t * dx;
  const projY = ay + t * dy;
  return { dist: Math.hypot(px - projX, py - projY), t, projX, projY };
}

function snapVertexPoint(
  wx: number,
  wy: number,
  zoom: number,
  vertices: { id: string; x: number; y: number }[],
  walls: { id: string; startId: string; endId: string; start: Point2D; end: Point2D }[],
  excludeVertexId?: string,
  anchorOther?: Point2D | null,
  freeAngle = false
): { x: number; y: number; snappedVertexId?: string; snappedWallId?: string } {
  // 1. Existing vertex magnet (constant ~13px screen radius, floor 7")
  const snapRadiusIn = Math.max(13 / zoom, 7);
  for (const v of vertices) {
    if (v.id === excludeVertexId) continue;
    if (Math.hypot(wx - v.x, wy - v.y) <= snapRadiusIn) {
      return { x: v.x, y: v.y, snappedVertexId: v.id };
    }
  }

  let sx = Math.round(wx);
  let sy = Math.round(wy);

  // 2. Ortho-first 90 deg / 45 deg polar snap from anchor vertex
  if (anchorOther && !freeAngle) {
    const dx = wx - anchorOther.x;
    const dy = wy - anchorOther.y;
    const len = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
    if (len > 3) {
      const deg = (Math.atan2(dy, dx) * 180) / Math.PI;
      const orthoDeg = Math.round(deg / 90) * 90;
      const diagDeg = Math.round(deg / 45) * 45;
      const snappedLen = Math.round(len * 2) / 2;

      if (Math.abs(deg - orthoDeg) <= 26) {
        const rad = (orthoDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
        sx = anchorOther.x + Math.cos(rad) * snappedLen;
        sy = anchorOther.y + Math.sin(rad) * snappedLen;
      } else if (Math.abs(deg - diagDeg) <= 7) {
        const rad = (diagDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
        sx = anchorOther.x + Math.cos(rad) * snappedLen;
        sy = anchorOther.y + Math.sin(rad) * snappedLen;
      }
    }
  }

  // 3. Cross-plan alignment to existing vertex axes
  for (const v of vertices) {
    if (v.id === excludeVertexId) continue;
    if (Math.abs(sx - v.x) <= 4) sx = v.x;
    if (Math.abs(sy - v.y) <= 4) sy = v.y;
  }

  // 4. T-junction snap onto an existing wall centerline
  const wallSnapTol = Math.max(14 / zoom, 9);
  let bestWall: { x: number; y: number; wallId: string; dist: number } | null = null;
  for (const sw of walls) {
    if (excludeVertexId && (sw.startId === excludeVertexId || sw.endId === excludeVertexId)) {
      continue;
    }
    const hit = distPointToSegment(sx, sy, sw.start.x, sw.start.y, sw.end.x, sw.end.y);
    if (hit.t > 0.02 && hit.t < 0.98 && hit.dist <= wallSnapTol) {
      if (!bestWall || hit.dist < bestWall.dist) {
        bestWall = { x: hit.projX, y: hit.projY, wallId: sw.id, dist: hit.dist };
      }
    }
  }
  if (bestWall) {
    return {
      x: Math.round(bestWall.x * 4) / 4,
      y: Math.round(bestWall.y * 4) / 4,
      snappedWallId: bestWall.wallId
    };
  }

  return { x: Math.round(sx * 4) / 4, y: Math.round(sy * 4) / 4 };
}

Quantizing every returned coordinate to 1/4" (Math.round(v * 4) / 4) aligns the interactive canvas directly with our imperial dimension formatter and planar-graph room healer.

3. Priority-Layered World Hit-Testing (Including Rotated Fixtures & Openings)

Without a retained DOM or scene-graph hit buffer, clicking the canvas calls a deterministic hitTestWorld(wx, wy) function in strict architectural Z-order:

  1. Electrical symbols (small targets on walls/ceilings — highest priority so outlets never get trapped behind cabinets)
  2. Doors & windows (tested in each wall's rotated local frame)
  3. Cabinets & furniture fixtures (rotated bounding boxes)
  4. Walls (point-to-segment distance <= wall.thicknessIn / 2 + tolIn)
  5. Enclosed rooms (ray-casting point-in-polygon fallback)

Checking rotated doors, angled islands, and furniture takes 8 lines by rotating the pointer into the object's local coordinate frame:

function pointInRotatedBox(
  px: number, py: number,
  cx: number, cy: number,
  w: number, d: number,
  rotDeg: number,
  padIn = 2
): boolean {
  const rad = (-rotDeg * Math.PI) / 180;
  const cos = Math.cos(rad);
  const sin = Math.sin(rad);
  const dx = px - cx;
  const dy = py - cy;
  const lx = dx * cos - dy * sin;
  const ly = dx * sin + dy * cos;
  return Math.abs(lx) <= w / 2 + padIn && Math.abs(ly) <= d / 2 + padIn;
}

For a residential floor plan (30–120 walls, 15–60 fixtures), a linear priority pass runs in under 0.05 milliseconds per pointer move — fast enough for live hover highlights without maintaining an R-tree or duplicate hit-canvas. And when the user activates the 1-Wall Calibrate tool, hitTestWorld short-circuits immediately to walls only so clicking a wall behind a countertop never accidentally selects the cabinet.

4. Typing Every Drag Gesture as a Discriminated Union

Canvas interaction bugs almost always come from tangled boolean flags (isDragging, isPanning, draggingWall, draggingVertex). Replacing those booleans with a single discriminated union makes illegal states unrepresentable:

type DragState =
  | { kind: 'pan'; startScreen: Point2D; origPanX: number; origPanY: number; moved: boolean }
  | { kind: 'vertex'; vertexId: string; anchorOther: Point2D | null }
  | {
      kind: 'wall';
      wallId: string;
      startWorld: Point2D;
      normX: number;
      normY: number;
      chainVertices: { id: string; orig: Point2D }[];
      moved: boolean;
    }
  | { kind: 'opening'; openingId: string; wallId: string }
  | { kind: 'fixture'; fixtureId: string; offsetX: number; offsetY: number }
  | { kind: 'electrical'; electricalId: string; offsetX: number; offsetY: number };

Look closely at the kind: 'wall' variant: when you grab a wall segment and slide it perpendicular to its normal (normX, normY), chainVertices stores the original positions of every vertex in its collinear wall chain captured on pointerdown. Moving the pointer computes total offset from startWorld rather than incremental frame deltas — eliminating drift and keeping adjacent corners square even at 120 Hz trackpad rates.

Try the Live 2D/3D Studio

You can test the zero-library 2D CAD canvas, orthogonal/T-junction wall snapping, and instant 3D cutaway sync live in your browser (no signup required to draw) at PlanCaliber.

title: Before You Merge an AI-Built Landing Page: A 15-Minute Core Web Vitals Review
description:
Disclosure: I work on VibUI, a paid catalogue of website prompts. It appears once, near the end. The review below needs only a browser and whichever AI tool you already use.

Short answer: an AI-built landing page can look finished in the preview and still fail on speed: an oversized hero image delaying the main content, elements that jump as fonts and images load, and scripts that make taps feel slow. Spend fifteen minutes on three metrics (Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift and Interaction to Next Paint), write each finding back into the prompt as a constraint, and regenerate only the section that failed. This applies to output from v0, Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Replit, GitHub Copilot, Framer AI, Google Stitch, Readdy, Aura.build and OpenAI Codex.

The gain is small and concrete: a page you can hand to a client or ship without a "why is it slow on my phone?" follow-up. It is not a promise of any ranking or conversion change.

Why do AI-built pages pass the eyeball test and fail the speed test?

A preview shows a fast laptop on a good connection. The problems are invisible there:

  • Heavy hero media. A full-bleed image or video is requested at original size, so the biggest element on screen is also the slowest to arrive.
  • No reserved space. Images, embeds and web fonts load without width, height or fallback metrics, so text and buttons move after the reader has started reading.
  • Decorative JavaScript. Scroll effects, particle backgrounds and animation libraries are added "for polish" and run on the main thread.
  • Third-party tags nobody asked for. Chat widgets, font loaders and analytics snippets get pasted in by habit.

Which three metrics should you read first?

Metric What it measures Common AI-built cause Constraint to add to the prompt
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) How quickly the main content appears. Google's "good" line is 2.5 s or less. Unoptimised hero image or video, render-blocking fonts "Hero image: modern format, explicit width and height, no autoplay video; preload only the hero asset."
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) How much content jumps during load. "Good" is 0.1 or less. Images without dimensions, late-loading fonts, injected banners "Reserve space for every image and embed; use font-display: swap with a similar fallback."
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) How fast the page responds to taps and clicks. "Good" is 200 ms or less. Heavy scripts, large animation loops, re-rendering widgets "No animation library; CSS transitions only; no script on the main thread that is not needed for the first screen."

How do you run the review in fifteen minutes?

  1. Open the page in a private window and run Lighthouse in DevTools with mobile emulation and throttling on.
  2. Write down LCP, CLS and the biggest items in the "opportunities" list. Do not average runs you have not repeated.
  3. Open the Network panel, sort by size, and look at the top five requests. If one of them is a decorative asset, that is your first fix.
  4. Scroll the page slowly on a throttled profile and watch for jumps.
  5. Tap every button and menu on a real phone, not only in emulation.

Treat these as lab numbers. Real-user (field) data only exists after real visitors arrive, so do not quote a lab score as a result.

What should the performance constraints in the first prompt look like? 

Build the [PAGE] section by section. Performance rules (apply to every section):
- Hero: one optimised image, explicit width/height, no autoplay video, no background animation loop.
- Fonts: at most two families, font-display: swap, system fallback with similar metrics.
- Images: lazy-load everything below the first screen; always set width and height.
- JavaScript: none unless a feature needs it; no animation or carousel library; no third-party tags.
- Layout: reserve space for embeds, forms and images so nothing moves after load.
- Report back: list every external request the page makes.

Ask the tool to list every external request. That one line catches most of the surprise scripts before you open DevTools.

Where does a prompt catalogue fit in a performance workflow?

If you build one page a quarter, keep the block above in a snippets file and skip any paid library. A catalogue earns its place only when you repeat the same section types often and want starting briefs that already carry constraints like these.

If you want to inspect one: The library I work on is VibUI. It has 2,852 website prompt templates (775 full pages, 1,100 sections, 817 components and 160 animated backgrounds), and about 1,000 of them include source code. Payment is one-time with no auto-renewal: $48 quarterly, $99 yearly, or $179 lifetime (listed down from $384). The yearly and lifetime plans also include 2,407 AI video prompts. There are 60 free samples, and a free account can copy 2 prompts. Try a free sample on a real section, run it through the review above, and only consider paying if it saves you setup time on pages you will actually build.

FAQ

Is a perfect Lighthouse score the goal?

No. Use it to find the largest problems. A page that scores a little lower but loads its main content quickly on a phone is better than one tuned to the test.

Should I remove all animation?

Not necessarily. Keep it cheap (CSS transforms and opacity), keep it away from the first screen, and respect reduced-motion settings.

Can the AI tool fix these issues by itself?

It can, if you hand it the specific finding ("LCP element is the hero image, no dimensions") and ask it to change only that section. Vague requests like "make it faster" rarely help.

Do I need to pay for a library to follow this review?

No. Everything above works with free tools and the AI builder you already use.

title: Fitting a resume to the page automatically, without breaking it for ATS parsers
description:
This is a layout problem, not an AI problem. Every HTML-to-PDF generator eventually runs into it: the last page that holds only a couple of lines. I'll cover how we hit it, the options we weighed, why predicting page breaks is a dead end, and the trick we ended up using, which is to let the browser measure the layout instead of guessing it. If you generate PDFs from HTML, some of this should be directly reusable.

The situation

I'm the founder of CV by JD. We rewrite resumes for specific job descriptions, and when you're happy with the result, you download it as a PDF.

A resume PDF has two readers. One is a person, often a recruiter skimming a stack of applications. The other is an ATS (applicant tracking system), the software employers use to pull the text out of a resume and search it. A good PDF has to look finished to the first reader and stay easy to parse for the second.

How we got here

We render PDFs on our server with headless Chrome, a copy of the Chrome browser with no window, controlled by code (puppeteer-core with a serverless Chromium build). The PDF uses exactly the same HTML and CSS as the preview in the app, so what you see is what you download:

 In your browser                     On our server
 ───────────────                     ─────────────
 Resume preview      ── "Download" ─▶ The same HTML and CSS, opened in
 (HTML + CSS)                         headless Chrome and printed to PDF
                     ◀── resume.pdf ──

We offer five templates, each with its own fonts, spacing and margins.

The templates were designed for a "typical" resume. Real resumes aren't typical. Some are half a page, some are four pages, and they almost never end neatly at the bottom of a page.

The problem

My own resume was the test case. In one template it ran to four pages, and page four held two lines from the education section followed by white space all the way down.

Nothing was wrong with the content. It just looked unfinished, and that's the first impression a reader gets. The usual fix is manual: open the file in Word, use "Shrink One Page", nudge the margins, and export again. We wanted every export to fit its pages well, automatically, for every template, without ever looking cramped and without changing what an ATS reads.

What we researched

We started by looking at how existing tools handle this. Word's "Shrink One Page" reduces font sizes until the document loses a page. Some resume builders give you sliders for spacing, margins and font size, and leave it to you. Both approaches confirmed the same toolbox: vertical spacing, line height, margins and font size. Both also showed the risk. Shrink too far and the page looks crammed, and text at 8pt is hard to read.

Thinking through how to do this automatically, three constraints narrowed the design:

  1. Free knobs can combine badly. If spacing, line height, margins and font size can each move freely, some combinations fit the page but look wrong, like tiny text inside wide margins.
  2. Word counts don't predict page breaks. Headings that won't sit alone at the bottom of a page, list items that won't split and long URLs all move where a page ends. Two resumes with the same word count can end on different pages.
  3. Rendering real PDFs to search for a setting is slow. The first PDF render after a serverless function starts up takes a few seconds. Trying many settings for every download would keep users waiting.

The options we found

For what to adjust:

Option Problem
Shrink only the font, as Word does Gets small quickly, and does nothing for a page that's too empty
Search four independent knobs Finds strange combinations, and is hard to test or explain
One "fit level" that moves all four together, within limits Fewer possible outcomes, but every one of them looks designed

For how to decide:

Option Problem
Estimate from word count Wrong too often, because page breaks depend on layout
Render real PDFs at several settings and pick one Accurate, but takes many seconds per download
Have the browser lay the document out as pages and measure it, without printing Needs a clever setup, but it's accurate and fast

What we chose, and why

One number per document

Each document gets one fit level, a whole number from −8 to +8. Think of it as a single dial: negative values tighten the layout, positive values loosen it. Level 0 is the template exactly as designed. Each other level is a fixed mix of small changes:

  • vertical spacing, between 70% and 130% of the original
  • line height, within fixed bounds
  • side margins, between 0.35 and 0.58 inches
  • font size, never below 9.5pt for body text

The four settings change together in a fixed order, so none of them runs out of room before the others. When shrinking, spacing tightens first and font size changes last. When growing, margins widen last, because wider margins frame a short page well. If a template's text is already small, we never shrink it further.

We chose this because 17 levels is a small, testable set, and every level looks like a deliberate design rather than an accident.

Let the browser measure the pages

This is the part I'd most like other people to reuse.

Printing and CSS columns split content the same way. Content flows down a box of fixed height, and when the box is full it continues in the next one. In Chrome, both use the same layout engine. So if you put the resume in a hidden container whose columns are exactly the size of one printed page's content area, Chrome breaks it into "pages" for you, side by side on screen:

 ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
 │ page 1 │ │ page 2 │ │ page 3 │ │ page 4 │
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██     │  ◀ 4 columns = 4 pages,
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │        │    and the last one is
 │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │        │    only about 10% full
 └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘

The CSS is short:

/* simplified */
.measure {
  column-width: var(--page-content-width);
  height: var(--page-content-height); /* one page's content area */
  column-fill: auto;
}

Count the columns and you have the page count. Measure how far the content reaches down the last column and you know how full the last page is. This happens in an ordinary layout pass, with no PDF rendering. Most documents are settled by measuring level 0 alone. When they aren't, a small script inside the page applies each of the 17 levels' styles in turn, lets Chrome lay the document out again, and reads the page count and fill each time, which still takes a fraction of the time of a single PDF render.

One detail matters a lot here. Chrome rounds the printed page's content height up to a whole pixel. On US Letter paper with our margins, the content area works out to 979.2 CSS pixels tall, but Chrome prints it as 980. If you measure with 979.2, a nearly full page gets predicted as spilling onto the next one, and you pick the wrong level. Round up the same way and the predictions match.

A simple rule for choosing the level

With the page count and the fullness of the last page measured at level 0:

What we see What we do
One page Leave it alone
More than four pages Leave it alone. The content needs cutting, not squeezing
Last page 30% full or less Shrink just enough to remove that last page, picking the mildest level that does it. The new last page must stay under about 97% full, so it doesn't look crammed, and shrinking mustn't leave a big blank at the bottom of an earlier page because a block that can't be split, such as a job entry, got pushed onto the next page. If no level qualifies, leave it
Last page between 30% and 60% full Grow slightly so the pages fill more evenly, but only if it keeps the same page count and actually helps
Fuller than that Leave it alone

The thinking behind the thresholds: below 30%, the leftover content is small enough that a modest shrink usually absorbs it. Between 30% and 60%, losing the page would need too much squeezing, so evening out the pages looks better. We tuned these thresholds by rendering 150 test resumes of different lengths at every level as real PDFs and comparing the results.

For my resume, that turned four pages, the last one almost empty, into three pages with the last one nearly full.

Check the real output

In the user's browser, the preview runs the same measurement and picks a level, so what you see matches what you'll download. When you click Download, the server measures again in headless Chrome, prints the PDF, and then counts the pages in the actual file. If the count doesn't match the prediction, it prints again at level 0. We'd rather send the template as designed than a surprise.

Protect the second reader

Fitting must not change what an ATS extracts. Two rules guarantee that:

  1. A document at level 0 is byte-for-byte unchanged. At level 0 we don't add the fitting styles at all, so Chrome receives exactly the HTML it did before this feature existed.
  2. The extracted words never change. Our tests render every template at every level, extract the text with pdftotext, and check that the words match level 0 exactly.

That second test caught a real bug. One template used letter-spacing in em units on its uppercase section headings. At a larger font size the spacing grew enough that pdftotext read "SUMMARY" as "S U M M A R Y", seven one-letter words. An ATS could read it the same way, and a keyword search for "summary" would miss it. We now set heading letter-spacing in pixels.

What you can take from this

  • If the browser can lay it out, the browser can measure it. Multi-column layout makes a surprisingly good page simulator, and it's far faster than rendering PDFs.
  • One bounded setting beats several free ones. It's easier to test, easier to explain, and it can't produce strange combinations.
  • Match the browser's rounding, or your predictions will be off on exactly the pages that matter most: the nearly full ones.
  • Check the real output and keep a safe fallback for when the prediction is wrong.
  • If machines read your documents, test what they extract, not just what people see.

Have you used CSS layout as a measuring tool for something else? I'd like to know what else it's good for.

title: Nothing Shopify Plus Teardown (Part 2): Mid-to-Late Funnel UX, Community Drop Flows, and High-AOV Checkout Engineering
description:
Many consumer electronics DTC brands survive their initial single-SKU launch only to hit a frustrating conversion plateau in year two. As the catalog expands from one hero product to six or eight variants, storefront conversion rates often drop: shoppers open five tabs trying to compare specs, give up from decision fatigue, and abandon $300–$600 carts in the final ten seconds before checkout.

In Part 1 of our Nothing (nothing.tech) architecture teardown, we examined how sub-brand isolation (CMF by Nothing) and a two-step Story-to-Buy funnel protect top-of-funnel speed. In Part 2, we break down the mid-to-late funnel systems that actually close high-AOV hardware orders: subtractive comparison matrices, lightweight hardware micro-interactions, community co-creation with three-state Drop CTAs, and late-stage checkout trust engineering.

1. Ending Decision Fatigue: The 6-Row Upsell Comparison Matrix

Engineering-led hardware brands frequently copy 40-row factory spec sheets onto their comparison pages. On mobile screens, wide horizontal tables quickly break visual hierarchy and push shoppers to exit.

Nothing's comparison flow (such as across Ear, Ear (a), and Ear (open)) applies strict subtraction—surfacing only the 5 to 7 tangible differences that justify a higher price tier (fit style, ANC depth, wireless charging, high-res audio codecs, battery life, and price).

White Ear and yellow Ear (a). Identify the models before comparing their features. GPT editorial illustration. Source

UX Dimension Typical 3C Spec Sheet Nothing Comparison Pattern Conversion Impact
Row Density 30–40 raw engineering specs 5–7 high-impact buyer differentiators Eliminates choice overload in under 15 seconds
Mobile Layout Wide horizontal scroll table 2-column fixed view + dropdown selector + sticky Buy Now Enables one-handed comparison and immediate upsell
SEO / GEO Readability Flattened comparison JPEG Clean semantic HTML table with highlighted diffs Crawlable by Google and AI answer engines (GEO)

In multi-SKU hardware catalogs, a comparison table is not a user manual—it is an upsell engine. When a shopper immediately sees why an extra $50 unlocks wireless charging and stronger ANC while the sticky Buy Now bar sits at the top of the screen, AOV rises without aggressive popups.

2. Lightweight Hardware Micro-Interactions Without Hurting Core Web Vitals

Selling hardware online means buyers cannot feel chassis weight or tactile buttons. Embedding heavy 3D WebGL viewers directly onto product pages frequently pushes mobile LCP past 5 seconds and degrades INP.

Nothing protects storefront speed by separating storytelling from configuration:

  • Macro imagery and short lazy-loaded loops handle industrial design storytelling on the Story Page.
  • Minimal DOM and pre-fetched swatches keep the Buy Page fast and responsive when shoppers toggle storage tiers and colorways.

The rear Glyph light on the Phone (2a) Plus, from the official product page. Source

3. Beyond Paid Ads: Community Co-Creation & Three-State Drop Flows

Relying purely on paid social creates a fragile linear funnel where orders collapse whenever ad spend pauses. With its 2024 Phone (2a) Plus Community Edition, Nothing turned product development into a four-stage public co-creation cycle—inviting fans to submit and vote on glow-in-the-dark hardware design, wallpapers, packaging, and launch marketing, followed by regional registration flows (including Europe and Japan).

Community members contributed hardware, wallpaper, packaging and campaign designs. GPT editorial illustration. Source

At the storefront level, this pairs with a three-state Drop CTA (Teaser -> Live -> Sold Out Waitlist) so high-intent review traffic never hits a dead-end grey Sold Out button.

WESWOO Reference Implementation (12-Line Shopify Liquid Pattern):

{%- comment -%} WESWOO Example: Three-state Drop CTA driven by Metafield + Variant Stock {%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign stage = product.metafields.custom.drop_stage.value | default: 'live' -%}
{%- assign v = product.selected_or_first_available_variant -%}

{%- if stage == 'teaser' -%}
  <button type="button" data-open-waitlist="early_access">Notify Me — Early Access</button>
{%- elsif v.available -%}
  <button type="submit" name="add">Add to Cart — {{ v.price | money }}</button>
{%- else -%}
  <button type="button" data-open-waitlist="restock" data-variant-id="{{ v.id }}">
    Out of Stock — Notify When Back
  </button>
{%- endif -%}

4. Closing the Final 10 Seconds on $300–$600 Hardware Orders

Before clicking checkout on high-ticket electronics, buyers hesitate over three concerns: upfront sticker shock, accidental damage, and post-purchase support reliability.

Nothing lists Klarna at checkout. Options vary by region. GPT editorial illustration. Source

  1. Upfront Installment Clarity: On key regional storefronts (such as the UK store), Klarna installment messaging appears directly beside pricing rather than hiding at the final payment screen.
  2. One-Click Protection Plans & Accessories: Offering accidental damage coverage or official chargers inside the slide-out cart addresses durability anxiety while adding high-margin AOV.
  3. Top-Navigation Support Transparency: Placing Support, warranty lookup, and software updates prominently in the main header signals long-term brand accountability.

WESWOO Reference Implementation (10-Line Cart Drawer Guard):

{%- comment -%} WESWOO Example: Prevent duplicate or out-of-stock protection plan upsells {%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign plan = all_products['official-protection-plan'] -%}
{%- assign plan_v = plan.first_available_variant -%}
{%- assign in_cart = cart.items | where: 'product_id', plan.id -%}

{%- if plan_v != blank and in_cart.size == 0 -%}
  <div class="ws-cart-upsell">
    <span>Add {{ plan.title | escape }} ({{ plan_v.price | money }})</span>
    <button type="button" data-quick-add="{{ plan_v.id }}">+ Add</button>
  </div>
{%- endif -%}

Practical Engineering Checklist

  1. Lock mobile model comparisons to 2 columns with dropdown switchers, sticky Buy Now bars, and semantic HTML tables.
  2. Keep heavy media on story pages and strip configuration pages down to fast-responding DOM components.
  3. Replace dead-end Sold Out states with variant-aware restock waitlists.
  4. Surface regional installment options, guarded protection-plan upsells, and top-level Support links across the checkout path.
