title: Query Single Record with SelectList In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import static net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqFields.*;

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

TableList and SelectList

  • JooqFields.TL(...) builds a TableList: accepts multiple tables and supports aliases, e.g. TL("user_table u", "dept_table d").
  • JooqFields.SL(...) builds a SelectList: specifies the columns to query and supports the "tableAlias.field outputAlias" syntax, where the output alias maps automatically to the Bean property (d.name dept_name → deptName).

v Methods (Recommended, More Concise)

The v-suffixed loadv / loadRecordv / loadLowerCaseRecordv pass all conditions and ordering directly as varargs — the most concise style. The following sections describe the equivalent Condition-list style for side-by-side reference:

TableList tl = JooqFields.TL("order o", "user u");
SelectList sl = JooqFields.SL("o.id", "o.order_no", "o.amount", "u.name user_name");

// Conditions + ordering all as varargs: u.name = 'John', ordered by o.id ascending
OrderView order = jt.loadv(tl, OrderView.class, sl, "u.name", "John", "o.id:asc");

// Record / LowerCaseRecord versions
Record record = jt.loadRecordv(tl, sl, "u.name", "John", "o.id:asc");
LowerCaseRecord lr = jt.loadLowerCaseRecordv(tl, sl, "u.name", "John");

// Mix in a jOOQ Condition (join conditions are built with F(...))
OrderView r = jt.loadv(tl, OrderView.class, sl,
        "u.name", "John",
        JooqFields.F("o", "user_id").eq(JooqFields.F("u", "id")));

Single-Table Query with SelectList 

TableList tableList = JooqFields.TL("product");
SelectList selectList = JooqFields.SL("id", "name", "price", "category_id");

Condition condition = DSL.field("name").eq("Smartphone");

Product product = jt.load(tableList, Product.class, selectList, Arrays.asList(condition));

When fetching a single field, receive it directly as a String / Integer:

String name = jt.load(tableList, String.class, JooqFields.SL("name"), Arrays.asList(condition));

Multi-Table Join Query

Pass multiple aliased tables in the TableList and qualify fields with their aliases in the conditions to perform a JOIN query (mirroring the test example that joins user_table with dept_table to fetch the department name):

TableList tableList = JooqFields.TL("order o", "user u");
SelectList selectList = JooqFields.SL("o.id", "o.order_no", "o.amount", "u.name user_name");

Condition joinCond = DSL.field("o.user_id").eq(DSL.field("u.id"));
Condition nameCond = DSL.field("u.name").eq("John");

OrderView order = jt.load(tableList, OrderView.class, selectList,
        Arrays.asList(joinCond, nameCond));
// order.getUserName() is mapped from "u.name user_name"

Condition List + Ordering

The non-v variants accept a List<Condition> together with ordering (the ...ConditionOrderBy / ...ConditionsOrderBy overloads):

List<Condition> conditions = Arrays.asList(
        DSL.field("category_id").eq(2),
        DSL.field("name").like("%Lee%"));

Product product = jt.load(tableList, Product.class, selectList, conditions);

loadv: Varargs Style

loadv(TableList, Class, SelectList, fieldValuePairs...) passes conditions and ordering as varargs, with operators embedded in field names; jOOQ Condition objects can be mixed in:

// dept_id = 2 and name like '%Lee%', ordered by id ascending
UserEntity result = jt.loadv(tableList, UserEntity.class, selectList,
        "dept_id", 2, "name%", "Lee", "id:asc");

// No conditions at all: returns the first record
UserEntity first = jt.loadv(tableList, UserEntity.class, selectList);

// Mix in a jOOQ Condition (join condition)
UserEntity r = jt.loadv(tl, UserEntity.class, sl,
        "u.name", "John",
        JooqFields.F("u", "dept_id").eq(JooqFields.F("d", "id")),
        "d.name", "Finance Department");

loadRecordv / loadLowerCaseRecordv

The v variants that return a Record / LowerCaseRecord — no Class argument:

Record record = jt.loadRecordv(tableList, selectList, "name", "Smartphone", "id:asc");
String name = record.get("name", String.class);

LowerCaseRecord lr = jt.loadLowerCaseRecordv(tableList, selectList, "name", "Smartphone");
Object price = lr.get("price");

Behavior Notes

  • Returns null when no record matches.
  • Empty varargs do not throw; they are equivalent to an unconditional query and return the first record.
  • The % operator means a contains-match (name% + "John" → name like '%John%').
  • Output aliases in the SelectList (d.name dept_name) map automatically to the Bean's camelCase properties.

title: How to choose Java collection types: List, Set, Map
description:
Originally published at Shipped Code.

Most backend Java code gets by with ArrayList and HashMap, until a method returns a list nobody can add to or a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. How you choose a Java collection comes down to 3 questions. Do you need duplicates and positions? Use a List (ArrayList by default). Do you need uniqueness? Use a Set (HashSet, or LinkedHashSet to keep insertion order, TreeSet to keep it sorted). Do you look things up by key? Use a Map (HashMap, or LinkedHashMap/TreeMap when order matters).

Return List.copyOf(...) from methods so callers cannot change your data, keep LinkedList for the rare case you have measured, and switch to ConcurrentHashMap once several threads write to the same map. The classic trap is removing elements inside a for-each loop, and removeIf fixes it.

This post is for developers who write Java every day. If you are here for a specific exception, jump to Common traps.

Decision table

Need Pick Main trade-off
Ordered items, duplicates allowed, access by index ArrayList Inserting or removing in the middle shifts the elements after it
A fixed list you hand to callers List.of / List.copyOf Throws on any change, rejects null
Unique values, order irrelevant HashSet Iteration order looks random
Unique values in the order they arrived LinkedHashSet A bit more memory than HashSet
Unique values, sorted, range queries TreeSet O(log n) instead of O(1)
Lookup by key HashMap No order; not thread-safe
Lookup by key, keep insertion order LinkedHashMap A bit more memory than HashMap
Lookup by key, sorted, "next key after X" TreeMap O(log n); keys must be comparable
A map shared between threads ConcurrentHashMap No null keys or values

The Java backend roadmap puts collections in stage 1, modern core Java, and lists what to learn next.

Blocks titled Main.java are complete files that run with java Main.java on JDK 21.0.11. The others are excerpts that need imports and a main method.

Lists

ArrayList is the right default for nearly every list in a backend, such as DTOs for a response, rows from a query or items in a cart. It stores elements in one array, so reading by index is O(1), and iterating walks one contiguous block of references.

LinkedList looks better on paper for inserts in the middle, but you first have to walk to that position node by node, and each node is a separate object scattered across the heap. For typical backend lists it rarely beats ArrayList, and this post does not try to prove that with timings. The one job it does well is a queue, and ArrayDeque does that job too, without the per-node objects.

The interesting choice is how to make a list read-only. Java gives you 4 ways, and they behave differently.

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> source = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));

        List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
        List<String> copy = List.copyOf(source);
        source.add("c");

        System.out.println("view = " + view);   // sees the new element
        System.out.println("copy = " + copy);   // snapshot

        List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList("x", "y");
        fixed.set(0, "z");                      // allowed
        System.out.println("fixed = " + fixed);

        try {
            copy.add("d");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("copy.add -> " + e);
        }
    }
}

view = [a, b, c]
copy = [a, b]
fixed = [z, y]
copy.add -> java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

The view changed after it was created, because Collections.unmodifiableList only blocks writes through the wrapper. Anyone holding source can still change what your caller sees. List.copyOf takes a snapshot, and List.of builds an immutable list from values. Arrays.asList is the odd one, because you can replace elements but cannot add or remove them. The last line shows copy.add failing with an empty exception message, which makes the error hard to search for.

For a method that returns a list, return List.copyOf(items); is the safe default, as long as the list holds no null (see Common traps).

Sets

A common use for a Set in a backend is cleaning up ids from a request, for example ?ids=42,7,42,19,7. All 3 implementations remove the duplicates. They differ only in the order you get back.

List<Long> requested = List.of(42L, 7L, 42L, 19L, 7L);

System.out.println("HashSet       " + new HashSet<>(requested));
System.out.println("LinkedHashSet " + new LinkedHashSet<>(requested));
System.out.println("TreeSet       " + new TreeSet<>(requested));

HashSet       [19, 7, 42]
LinkedHashSet [42, 7, 19]
TreeSet       [7, 19, 42]

The HashSet order comes from hash buckets, and the specification does not promise it. If those ids end up in a JSON response or a cache key, use LinkedHashSet so the output is stable and matches what the client sent. Use TreeSet when the result should be sorted anyway.

Hash-based sets decide "same element" with equals and hashCode. A record generates both from its fields, so 2 records with the same values count as one. A plain class without those methods compares by identity.

record SkuKey(String sku, String warehouse) {}

static class SkuClass {             // no equals/hashCode
    final String sku, warehouse;
    SkuClass(String sku, String warehouse) { this.sku = sku; this.warehouse = warehouse; }
}

// add new SkuKey("TSHIRT-M", "HN") twice to one HashSet, then SkuClass twice to another

records: 1
plain class: 2

That second line is how duplicate rows sneak into a "unique" set. Records are the simplest fix for composite keys like this one.

For JPA users, entity collections (Set versus List in Hibernate) have their own rules, which the post on N+1 queries covers.

Maps

The most common map in a service is a lookup by id. You build it once from a list, then each get is O(1) instead of a scan through the list.

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    record User(long id, String name, String team) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<User> users = List.of(
            new User(1, "An", "mobile"),
            new User(2, "Binh", "backend"),
            new User(3, "Chi", "mobile"));

        Map<Long, User> byId = new HashMap<>();
        for (User u : users) byId.put(u.id(), u);
        System.out.println(byId.get(2L).name());
        System.out.println(byId.getOrDefault(99L, new User(0, "unknown", "-")).name());

        Map<String, List<String>> byTeam = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (User u : users) {
            byTeam.computeIfAbsent(u.team(), t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(u.name());
        }
        System.out.println(byTeam);
    }
}

Binh
unknown
{mobile=[An, Chi], backend=[Binh]}

computeIfAbsent creates the list the first time a team appears and returns the existing list after that, which replaces the usual if (!map.containsKey(...)) block. The grouping map is a LinkedHashMap, so teams come out in the order they first appeared. Streams can do the same with Collectors.toMap and groupingBy; the next post in this series covers them.

Reach for TreeMap when the question is "what is the next key after X?". Free appointment slots are a good example.

TreeMap<LocalTime, String> slots = new TreeMap<>();
slots.put(LocalTime.of(9, 0), "room 1");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(10, 30), "room 2");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(14, 0), "room 1");
slots.put(LocalTime.of(16, 15), "room 3");

LocalTime now = LocalTime.of(10, 5);
System.out.println("next slot:   " + slots.ceilingKey(now));
System.out.println("before noon: " + slots.headMap(LocalTime.NOON));
System.out.println("from 14:00:  " + slots.tailMap(LocalTime.of(14, 0), true));

next slot:   10:30
before noon: {09:00=room 1, 10:30=room 2}
from 14:00:  {14:00=room 1, 16:15=room 3}

With a HashMap you would sort the keys or scan all of them for each of these questions. headMap excludes its bound by default, while tailMap(key, true) includes it.

For enum keys, EnumMap and EnumSet are worth knowing. They are backed by an array or a bit vector indexed by the enum's ordinal, and they iterate in declaration order.

Sequenced collections (Java 21)

Java 21 added SequencedCollection and SequencedMap (JEP 431). They give every ordered collection the same methods for the first and last element. That covers List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap.

List<String> events = new ArrayList<>(List.of("created", "paid", "shipped"));
System.out.println(events.getFirst() + " .. " + events.getLast());
System.out.println(events.reversed());

SequencedSet<Long> recentIds = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of(42L, 7L, 19L));
System.out.println(recentIds.getLast() + " " + recentIds.reversed());

SequencedMap<String, Integer> steps = new LinkedHashMap<>();
steps.put("validate", 1);
steps.put("charge", 2);
steps.put("notify", 3);
System.out.println(steps.firstEntry() + " " + steps.lastEntry());
System.out.println(steps.pollFirstEntry() + " -> " + steps);

created .. shipped
[shipped, paid, created]
19 [19, 7, 42]
validate=1 notify=3
validate=1 -> {charge=2, notify=3}

Before Java 21, the last element of a LinkedHashSet meant iterating the whole set. reversed() returns a view, not a copy, and it keeps the original's rules, so calling removeFirst() on List.of("a", "b").reversed() still throws UnsupportedOperationException. I compiled the same file with JDK 17 to check the floor, and it fails with cannot find symbol ... method getFirst().

Sharing a collection between threads (Advanced)

You can skip this section if your collections live inside one request. HashMap is not thread-safe, and when several threads write to it the failure is usually silent. Here, 8 threads each count 100,000 hits into one map.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Main {
    static int count(Map<String, Integer> hits) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) {
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) hits.merge("GET /users", 1, Integer::sum);
                });
            }
        } // close() waits for all tasks
        return hits.get("GET /users");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("expected          800000");
        System.out.println("HashMap           " + count(new HashMap<>()));
        System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap " + count(new ConcurrentHashMap<>()));
    }
}

expected          800000
HashMap           139374
ConcurrentHashMap 800000

The HashMap number changed on every run. Across 13 runs it landed between 126,637 and 367,392, never close to 800,000. My first suspicion was that some tasks had died with an exception that submit swallowed into its Future. I wrapped the loop in a try/catch and nothing was thrown, so these are plain lost updates.

ConcurrentHashMap makes merge and computeIfAbsent atomic per key, which makes it the usual pick for an in-memory cache or counter shared across requests. Collections.synchronizedMap also works, but it puts one lock around the whole map. Queues, executors and async composition belong to the concurrency cluster.

Common traps

Removing inside a for-each loop. This one surprised me while preparing the example. My first version removed "expired-2" from ["ok-1", "expired-2", "ok-3"] and did not throw at all.

List<String> tokens = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ok-1", "expired-2", "expired-3"));
for (String t : tokens) {
    if (t.startsWith("expired")) tokens.remove(t);
}
System.out.println(tokens);

[ok-1, expired-3]

Removing the second-to-last element makes the iterator think it has finished, so the loop ends and expired-3 is never checked. With the expired token first, you get the exception everyone knows:

Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
    at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification(ArrayList.java:1095)
    at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.next(ArrayList.java:1049)

The fix is tokens.removeIf(t -> t.startsWith("expired"));, which prints [ok-1] for the list above. The silent version is the worse bug, because nothing crashes; only a test that checks the resulting list catches it.

List.of rejects null. An optional field from a request is enough to trigger it.

String middleName = null;
List<String> parts = List.of("Vu", middleName, "Duong");

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
    at java.base/java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.java:233)

Even List.of("USER", "ADMIN").contains(null) throws the same NullPointerException, while an ArrayList would return false. Filter nulls first, or use new ArrayList<>() if null is a legal value.

A mutable field in hashCode. The Cart class below defines equals and hashCode from couponCode, and the code changes that field after adding the cart to a HashSet.

Set<Cart> carts = new HashSet<>();
Cart cart = new Cart("SALE10");
carts.add(cart);

cart.couponCode = "SALE20";               // field used by hashCode changes
System.out.println(carts.contains(cart)); // same object!
System.out.println(carts.size());

false
1

Warning: the set still holds the cart, but it looks in the bucket for the new hash and finds nothing. The same happens with HashMap keys. Keep fields used by hashCode immutable (a record does this for you, as long as its fields are immutable types too), or remove the object, change it, and add it again.

Arrays.asList is fixed-size. It wraps the array, so set works and add does not.

String[] fromCsv = {"a@x.dev", "b@x.dev"};
List<String> emails = Arrays.asList(fromCsv);
emails.add("c@x.dev");

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
    at java.base/java.util.AbstractList.add(AbstractList.java:155)

Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(fromCsv)) when the list must grow.

Next step

Most of these collections end up feeding streams, through toMap, groupingBy or an Optional from findFirst. The next post in the series covers the patterns worth keeping there and the traps. Other posts on lists, sets and maps are collected under Java collections. For the official overview of every interface and implementation, see the Java Collections Framework guide.

title: Charge Once, Retry Forever: Idempotency Keys in Spring Boot
description:
A client sends POST /payments. The network hiccups, the client times out and sends the same request again. Did the customer just pay twice?

Without protection, yes. Retries are not a corner case: mobile apps retry on flaky connections, API gateways retry on 5xx, users double-click "Pay", and message consumers redeliver. Every one of those can turn into a second charge if the server treats each request as new.

The standard answer is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it in a header. The server promises that the same key produces the same effect once, no matter how many times it arrives. Stripe, Adyen and PayPal all work this way.

The idea is simple. The details are where duplicate charges sneak back in: two requests racing with the same key, a key reused for a different amount, or a provider that fails halfway. I built a small Spring Boot project, idempotency-demo, that handles those cases and proves them with tests. This article walks through what it contains and why each piece is there.

  • Source: https://github.com/josesaid/idempotency-demo
  • Project page: https://josesaid.github.io/idempotency-demo/
  • Diagrams: English · español

What the repo contains

Item Value
Language Java 21
Framework Spring Boot 3.3.5 (Web, Data JPA)
Database H2 in memory, table idempotency_record
Endpoints POST /payments, GET /payments/executions
Tests 3 integration tests, including 8 concurrent requests 
com.mx.development.jose.said
├── idempotency/
│   ├── IdempotencyRecord.java      entity: UNIQUE key, request hash, status, stored response
│   ├── IdempotencyRepository.java  findByKey
│   └── IdempotencyReserver.java    reserve / complete / release, each in its own transaction
└── payment/
    ├── PaymentController.java      POST /payments
    ├── PaymentFacade.java          the idempotency logic
    └── PaymentService.java         simulated provider (2 s latency, counts real charges)

PaymentService sleeps two seconds on purpose, so concurrent requests really overlap, and counts how many times it actually ran. GET /payments/executions exposes that counter, which makes "did we charge twice?" a question you can answer with one curl.

The contract

Every request ends in exactly one of these answers:

Situation Answer Provider called?
New key 201 Created Yes, once
Same key, same body, already completed 200 OK with the stored response No
Same key, same body, still processing 409 Conflict No
Same key, different body 422 Unprocessable Entity No
Provider throws Key released, error returned Retry may charge

Only the first row ever reaches the provider.

The record: a key, a hash and a status 

@Entity
@Table(name = "idempotency_record")
public class IdempotencyRecord {

    public enum Status { PROCESSING, COMPLETED }

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    // The database, not the application, guarantees one row per key
    @Column(name = "idem_key", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 100)
    private String key;

    // SHA-256 of the request body: detects a key reused for another payment
    @Column(name = "request_hash", nullable = false, length = 64)
    private String requestHash;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Status status;

    // What retries get back once the payment is done
    @Column(name = "response_body", columnDefinition = "TEXT")
    private String responseBody;
}

Three fields carry the whole design:

  • unique = true on the key is the real lock. More on that below.
  • requestHash lets the server tell "the same request again" from "a different request with a recycled key".
  • status + responseBody let the server say "still working" (409) or replay the original answer (200).

Reserve before you charge

The facade's main method is short:

public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> createPayment(String key, PaymentRequest request) {
    String hash = requestHash(request);

    Optional<IdempotencyRecord> existing = repo.findByKey(key);
    if (existing.isEmpty()) {
        try {
            reserver.reserve(key, hash);            // try to be first
        } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
            // Another request with the same key won the race: answer from its row
            return handleExisting(repo.findByKey(key).orElseThrow(), hash);
        }
        return process(key, request);
    }
    return handleExisting(existing.get(), hash);
}

The key step is reserve. Before calling the provider, the facade inserts a row with status PROCESSING and commits it. That commit is what lets every other request see "someone is already charging this key".

@Service
public class IdempotencyReserver {

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void reserve(String key, String requestHash) {
        // saveAndFlush forces the INSERT now; a duplicate key throws right here
        repo.saveAndFlush(new IdempotencyRecord(key, requestHash));
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void complete(String key, String responseJson) {
        IdempotencyRecord record = repo.findByKey(key).orElseThrow();
        record.setStatus(IdempotencyRecord.Status.COMPLETED);
        record.setResponseBody(responseJson);
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void release(String key) {
        repo.findByKey(key).ifPresent(repo::delete);
    }
}

Two details matter here:

  1. REQUIRES_NEW: each method commits on its own. If the reservation lived inside one big transaction that also wrapped the two-second provider call, no other request could see the PROCESSING row until the end. That is exactly the window where duplicates happen.
  2. A separate bean: @Transactional works through a Spring proxy. If PaymentFacade called its own @Transactional method, the proxy would be bypassed and the annotation silently ignored. Moving these methods into IdempotencyReserver makes them go through the proxy.

The common mistake

This version looks fine and is wrong:

// ❌ Check-then-act: both concurrent requests pass the check
if (repo.findByKey(key).isEmpty()) {
    PaymentResponse r = paymentService.process(request);   // charged twice
    repo.save(new IdempotencyRecord(key, hash, r));
}

Two requests that arrive together both see "no row" and both charge. The lookup is only an optimization. The protection is the UNIQUE constraint plus inserting before charging.

Who wins a race? The database

Scenario D in the repo sends two (in the test, eight) requests with the same new key at the same time:

  1. Both run findByKey and both get Optional.empty().
  2. Both call reserve. Request A's INSERT commits first.
  3. Request B's INSERT hits the unique index; H2 raises error 23505, Spring translates it to DataIntegrityViolationException.
  4. B catches it, reads A's row, sees PROCESSING and answers 409 Conflict.
  5. A charges, stores the response and answers 201.
  6. When B retries later, it finds COMPLETED and gets 200 with A's paymentId.

The full step-by-step diagram is on the project page: Scenario D · Concurrent requests.

Hash first, then status 

private ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> handleExisting(IdempotencyRecord record, String hash) {
    if (!record.getRequestHash().equals(hash)) {
        return ResponseEntity.unprocessableEntity().build();        // same key, different body
    }
    if (record.getStatus() == IdempotencyRecord.Status.PROCESSING) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).build();  // still running
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(fromJson(record.getResponseBody()));   // replay stored response
}

The order matters. If a client reuses pago-001 for a 999.00 payment, replaying the stored 150.00 response would hide a client bug and the customer would never be charged the 999.00. Checking the SHA-256 of the body first turns that bug into a clear 422, even while the original request is still PROCESSING.

The hash is computed over the JSON that Jackson produces for PaymentRequest:

private String requestHash(PaymentRequest request) {
    byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
            .digest(mapper.writeValueAsBytes(request));
    return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest);
}

When the provider fails: release the key 

private ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> process(String key, PaymentRequest request) {
    try {
        PaymentResponse response = paymentService.process(request);
        reserver.complete(key, toJson(response));
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(response);
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        reserver.release(key);   // free the key so the client can retry
        throw e;
    }
}

Without release, a failed payment would leave its row in PROCESSING forever, and every retry would get 409. Deleting the row, again in its own transaction, makes the key usable again.

One honest caveat: releasing is only safe when you know the provider did not charge. After an ambiguous timeout, a production system should ask the provider for the payment status (ideally passing the same idempotency key downstream) before releasing.

Proving it with tests

The integration test fires eight requests with the same key and counts real charges:

@Test
void peticionesConcurrentesMismaClave_cobranUnaSolaVez() throws Exception {
    String key = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    int before = executions();
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);

    List<Callable<ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse>>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        tasks.add(() -> post(key, request("250.00")));
    }
    List<Future<ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse>>> futures = pool.invokeAll(tasks);

    // ... collect status codes ...
    assertThat(executions() - before).as("real charges").isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(statuses.stream().filter(s -> s == HttpStatus.CREATED).count()).isEqualTo(1);
}

The other two tests check that a retry returns the same paymentId with a single charge, and that a reused key with another body gets 422. When the suite runs you will see seven Unique index or primary key violation lines in the log: those are the seven losers of the race, which is exactly what should happen.

Try it yourself 

git clone https://github.com/josesaid/idempotency-demo.git
cd idempotency-demo
mvn spring-boot:run

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Idempotency-Key: pago-001" \
  -d '{"accountFrom":"ACC-1","accountTo":"ACC-2","amount":150.00,"currency":"MXN"}'
# 201 the first time, 200 with the same paymentId on every retry

curl http://localhost:8080/payments/executions
# {"executions":1}

The diagrams

The project page has an overview (the path of one request, the decision flow and the states of a row) plus one sequence diagram per scenario, in English and Spanish:

Scenario English Español
A · First request (201) Diagram Diagrama
B · Retry with the same key (200) Diagram Diagrama
C · Same key, different body (422) Diagram Diagrama
D · Concurrent requests (201 + 409) Diagram Diagrama
E · Provider failure (500 → 201) Diagram Diagrama

Best practices checklist

  • ✅ Let the database enforce uniqueness of the key; never rely on a read-then-write check.
  • ✅ Reserve before calling the external system, and commit the reservation in its own transaction.
  • ✅ Store a hash of the request and reject reused keys with a different body (422).
  • ✅ Store the response and replay it; the retry must look like success to the client.
  • ✅ Answer 409 while the first request is in flight, so clients back off and retry.
  • ✅ Release the key only when you are sure nothing was charged.
  • ⚠️ Add a TTL or cleanup job; the demo keeps records forever.
  • ⚠️ Scope keys per client or account in multi-tenant systems, so two clients cannot collide.

Performance notes

The happy path costs one indexed SELECT, one INSERT and one UPDATE, each a short transaction. Retries cost a single SELECT and never touch the provider. The losers of a race fail fast on the unique index instead of waiting on a lock. In production, keep idem_key indexed (the UNIQUE constraint does that), keep the stored response small, and purge old rows on a schedule.

Takeaways

Idempotency keys are not about the header; they are about where the guarantee lives. In this repo it lives in a UNIQUE constraint, a reservation committed before the charge, a hash that catches misuse, and a stored response that makes retries boring. Clone idempotency-demo, run mvn test, and watch eight concurrent requests produce exactly one charge.

If you read my previous article on the transactional outbox, this is the other half of the story: the outbox makes sure events are delivered at least once, and idempotency makes sure "at least once" never becomes "charged twice".

title: When is a 2.5 KiB Korean web font enough?
description:
The heading on an order confirmation page stays the same. The customer's name and order number do not. Can both use a tiny subset of the same Korean typeface? We kept only the characters in the fixed heading and got a 2.5 KiB font, but it could not cover the name and number directly below it. Give fixed copy and dynamic data separate font strategies.

01 · Keep the typeface and format constant

We made four WOFF files from Noto Sans CJK KR Regular 2.004: the full face, the fixed phrase 주문 내역 저장 완료 (“Order details saved”), the fixed phrase plus a synthetic 박봄 203, and that sample plus digits 0–9. The font face and container stayed constant; the requested character set changed.

Figure 1. WOFF bytes on disk: full 13,608,420; fixed text 2,592; fixed plus sample 3,356; fixed plus sample and all digits 4,352.

2,592 bytes is about 2.53 KiB. These are file sizes, not transfer times. The full face re-encoded as a single WOFF is a control, not an estimate for a production WOFF2 service with range splitting.

02 · A passing fixture can hide the next missing glyph

We reopened every output and inspected its character-to-glyph mapping, or cmap. The table lists distinct missing code points, so a repeated digit appears only once.

Build Bytes Fixed phrase Included fixture: 박봄 203 Independent holdout: 최솔 999
Full face 13,608,420 None None None
Fixed copy 2,592 None 박봄203 최솔9
Sample added 3,356 None None 최솔9
All digits added 4,352 None None 최솔

Figure 2. For the holdout 최솔 999, adding all ten digits restores 9, but the syllables 최 and 솔 are still missing.

Adding the demo name made the fixture pass. It did not cover another synthetic name. The digit problem was different: 0–9 is a bounded domain that we could explicitly include. Passing a finite number of arbitrary names does not give you comparable coverage.

03 · Audit the output, not just the build exit code

Create an empty directory and install fonttools==4.61.1. The run used the KR Regular face at index 1 in Noto Sans CJK Regular TTC 2.004, with NFC input and WOFF output. Adjust the path; if using another distribution, verify the font face instead of assuming the same index. Two runs in the same environment returned identical results. The input SHA-256 was b76b0433203017ca80401b2ee0dd69350349871c4b19d504c34dbdd80541690a; the selected family was Noto Sans CJK KR, style Regular.

from pathlib import Path
from unicodedata import normalize
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
from fontTools import subset
SRC = "/usr/share/fonts/opentype/noto/NotoSansCJK-Regular.ttc"
FIXED = "주문 내역 저장 완료"
DYNAMIC = "박봄 203"
MIX = FIXED + "\n" + DYNAMIC
for label, chars in [("full", None), ("fixed", FIXED), ("with-sample", MIX), ("with-digits", MIX + "0123456789")]:
    with TTFont(SRC, fontNumber=1, recalcTimestamp=False) as face:
        if chars is not None:
            opts = subset.Options()
            opts.ignore_missing_unicodes = False
            sub = subset.Subsetter(opts)
            sub.populate(text=normalize("NFC", chars).replace("\n", ""))
            sub.subset(face)
        face.flavor = "woff"
        face.save(label + ".woff", reorderTables=False)
    with TTFont(label + ".woff") as face:
        cmap = face.getBestCmap()
        missing = lambda s: "".join(dict.fromkeys(c for c in s if ord(c) not in cmap))
        print(label, Path(label + ".woff").stat().st_size, len(cmap),
              repr(missing(FIXED)), repr(missing(DYNAMIC)),repr(missing("최솔 999")))
print([f"U+{ord(c):04X}" for c in DYNAMIC if c!=" "])

With ignore_missing_unicodes=False, the build rejects characters you requested but that the source does not contain. It cannot know which characters future users will enter. Reopen the generated font and test both known copy and an independent holdout. This experiment reads code point mappings; it did not benchmark browser loading, fallback metrics, layout, or WOFF2.

Including spaces, the heading has 11 code points in NFC and 23 in NFD. The build normalizes text to NFC; the coverage helper checks its input as supplied. If your app accepts decomposed input, test both forms separately. These counts do not predict browser rendering. The previous ZIP experiment shows why the same distinction matters for filenames.

At 390 CSS pixels, the name and digits switched fonts separately

On November 27 we rebuilt WOFF and WOFF2 from the same Noto Sans CJK KR source. Both formats used fontTools 4.57.0 and Brotli 1.1.0; the 4.61.1 WOFF experiment above is separate. The heading-only subset shrank from 2,488 to 1,920 bytes (22.8%). With digits included, it went from 4,284 to 3,608 bytes (15.8%). Neither change added missing glyphs.

  • Heading-only WOFF2 for both lines: The name and 999 used the serif fallback. Only the space used the web font.
  • Digit-inclusive WOFF2 for both lines: The name used the serif fallback; 999 and the space used the web font.
  • WOFF2 for the heading, separate system stack below: The name and number both used the installed Korean sans serif.

We rendered one fixture in a mobile viewport in Chromium 140 on Linux and checked the browser’s rendered-font data. The first two runs deliberately used installed Noto Serif CJK KR as a visible fallback; another device can choose a different face. This was not a test of real phones, load time, or layout shift.

Figure 3. Chromium at 390 CSS pixels. Top: heading-only subset. Middle: digit-inclusive subset. Bottom: separate heading and dynamic fonts.

04 · Use the tiny font where the text contract is closed

  • Fixed headings: Extract characters from the actual localized strings and rebuild when the wording changes.
  • Bounded numbers: Include all decimal digits and any grouping, decimal, negative or currency symbols the formatting code can emit.
  • Names, addresses and CMS copy: Do not make a small title subset the global default. Give these fields a Korean system font or a broader web-font strategy, then check representative and out-of-sample values on narrow layouts. Browser fallback may keep text legible while mixing typefaces within a word.

Before shipping, try a string you did not use to create the subset. It tells you where the design still holds, not just where yesterday’s fixture passed.

Sources: Noto CJK project · fontTools subset options · CSS font matching and fallback

title: Breakfast Special: showing a voice UI through two mascots and one real meal log
description:
Teddy orders two eggs and a latte. Brulee logs breakfast. Then Teddy asks the question that made this worth showing on screen: “How much protein did I get?”

Brulee and Teddy are two of the eight Live Voice mascots in Fud AI. For this short, I wanted the mascots to introduce the feature without asking viewers to take a cartoon’s word for what the app did.

Why the cut to the diary matters

A spoken “logged” is easy to miss. In the iPhone recording you can see which foods landed in the diary, then read the same protein total Brulee gives Teddy: 20 grams for this sample breakfast. That gives the follow-up question a purpose: it connects the conversation to something you can inspect.

The café exchange is scripted and voiced with ElevenLabs. The screen recording uses sample data, and the dialogue is captioned so the demo still makes sense on mute. If you’re making a demo of a voice interface, try watching yours with the sound off: can you still tell what changed?

title: Secure AI Apps on Spring Boot: Typed Prompts with AISL, Apps as Pimi with pim-core
description:
Unlike OpenClaw, Knoden PIM is built to be secure. Its skills aren't instructions written as informal text. Each one is a typed Java interface, so what goes to the model and what comes back is checked like any other code. Agents aren't let loose: they ask before using any tool that isn't on their allowed list. PIM is never given root access, and it only loads pimi whose checksum or signature checks out.

The architecture is built on a stack developers already trust: Java, Spring, Spring AI and Ollama. And PIM is designed with developers in mind, to be extended. Its engine, pim-core, is a set of Spring Boot libraries: an event bus, storage, security and an AI layer. Apps plug into it as pimi, modules with their own data, logic and AI skills. The fifteen apps that come with PIM are pimi too, written to show what can be built.

Every prompt in PIM goes through a small library of ours: AISL. It turns a prompt into a Spring bean you inject and call like any other. It's LGPL-3.0, so you can use it in any application, open or closed.

This article has two parts. The first is a walk-through: from an empty project to a typed Java record filled in by a model on your own machine, then the bug that the types didn't catch and the two ways we fix that kind of bug. The second is what pim-core adds when one prompt becomes an app, and how that app is packaged and loaded as a pimi.

What you need

  • Java 25 and Gradle (or the wrapper).
  • Ollama, with the default model pulled: ollama pull gemma4.

AISL is in a public GitLab package registry, so there's no token to set up, but it isn't on Maven Central yet, so Gradle needs one repository block:

// settings.gradle.kts
rootProject.name = "aisl-demo"

dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        exclusiveContent {
            forRepository {
                maven { url = uri("https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/86960067/packages/maven") }
            }
            filter { includeGroup("com.knoden.aisl") }
        }
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

// build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    java
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
}

java { toolchain { languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(25)) } }

dependencies {
    implementation(platform(org.springframework.boot.gradle.plugin.SpringBootPlugin.BOM_COORDINATES))
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("com.knoden.aisl:aisl-runtime:0.8.1")
}

That's every dependency. aisl-runtime brings Spring AI and its Ollama starter.

A prompt is an interface

We want to turn "Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm" into an appointment. First the shape of the answer, as a plain record:

public record Appointment(String title, String date, String start, String end) {
}

Then the prompt. It's a method on an interface: the system prompt goes on @AislPrompt, a {placeholder} is filled from the parameter marked @AislParam, and the first plain parameter is what the user typed:

public interface AppointmentSkill {

    @AislPrompt(system = "Today is {today}. Turn the user's request into one appointment. "
            + "Dates as YYYY-MM-DD, times as HH:MM in 24-hour time.")
    Appointment parse(String request, @AislParam("today") String today);
}

There's no implementation. @EnableAislSkills finds the interface and registers a bean for it:

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableAislSkills
public class DemoApp {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApp.class, args);
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner run(AppointmentSkill skill) {
        return args -> System.out.println(skill.parse(
                "Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm",
                LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 25) + " (a Wednesday)"));
    }
}

Because the method returns a record and not a String, the call goes through Spring AI's structured output: the model is asked for JSON matching the record, and the reply is mapped onto it. ./gradlew bootRun:

Appointment[title=Dentist, date=2026-11-30, start=15:00, end=16:00]

It compiled, it ran, every field is filled in, and the times are right. And November 30, 2026 is a Monday.

The bug the types didn't catch

We ran it five times with gemma4, the default. It said Friday the 27th twice. The other three times it said Monday the 30th (twice) and Friday, December 4, a week late. The record only guarantees the shape of the answer. A small model is good at language and bad at calendar arithmetic, and "this Friday, given that today is Wednesday the 25th" is arithmetic.

We've seen this before: in our own model tests, a small Gemma 4 put an appointment on the wrong Friday in all five runs (how we test the models). There are two ways out.

1. A bigger model for just this skill. Every skill is a bean with a name (the interface's name, first letter lower-cased), and one property moves that skill alone to another model:

aisl.skill-models.appointmentSkill=gemma4:26b

With gemma4:26b it was Friday the 27th, five out of five. Everything else in the application stays on the small, fast model. That's the point of the setting: you don't move your whole application to an 18 GB model for one prompt that needs it.

2. Don't ask the model to do arithmetic. Ask it for what it's good at, which day the person meant, and let Java compute the date. The record can use real Java types; Spring AI maps them:

public record Booking(String title, DayOfWeek day, LocalTime start, LocalTime end) {
}

public interface BookingSkill {

    @AislPrompt(system = "Turn the user's request into one appointment: what it is, the day of the week, "
            + "and the start and end time.")
    Booking parse(String request);
}

Booking b = skill.parse("Dentist this Friday from 3pm to 4pm");
LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 25).with(TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(b.day()));

Booking[title=Dentist, day=FRIDAY, start=15:00, end=16:00] -> 2026-11-27

Five out of five on the small model, and the prompt got shorter: it no longer needs today's date. DayOfWeek is an enum, so the model can only name one of seven days; there's no date left for it to get wrong.

We use both in PIM. The second one is the better habit: types tell you the answer has the right shape, so make the shape carry as little of the reasoning as you can.

When you have more than a few prompts

For a larger set of skills there's a second way to write them: .aisl files, a short declarative format that a build-time compiler turns into the same kind of bean. An output_schema block in the file also generates the Java records, and a skill can record its own model and whether a thinking model should think. The user guide has the format and the Gradle setup for the compiler. The interfaces above need no build step, so start there.

From a skill to an app: pim-core

AISL handles one prompt. An app needs more: somewhere to keep its data, a way to talk to the rest of the system, and limits on what it and its AI may do. That is pim-core, PIM's engine, published as Spring Boot libraries (com.knoden.pim.core, AGPL-3.0). You take only the modules you need:

  • Event bus (pim-events-core). Modules work by sending each other messages, not by calling each other. The kernel has no AI dependency.
  • Storage (pim-storage-core). Data is kept per person. Other modules store data by sending storage a message over the bus; only storage touches the database or the disk. A file goes into the person's own folder under the app's name, and a path that could leave that folder is refused.
  • Security (pim-security). Credentials (PBKDF2/BCrypt, lockout), crypto, an optional key store, and the encrypted backup format (AES-256-GCM).
  • AI (pim-ai-core), the only module that carries Spring AI: conversations, retrieval, memory, and agents. An agent has a list of tools it may run freely. Any other tool pauses the run until the person says yes or no, and that answer covers only that one call. By default a run stops after 6 tool calls or 3 minutes.
  • The pimi loader (pim-workspaces), below.

The same registry block as above, with pim-core's registry added, gets you any of them; the pim-core page has it.

An app is a pimi

A pimi is an app packaged as a plain jar: its own classes in its own package, its own tables as Flyway migrations, and its own AISL skills. Here is Notes, PIM's simplest app:

pimi.properties
db/pimi/notes/V1__notes.sql
db/pimi-grants/notes/R__notes_grants.sql
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesPimiConfiguration.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/DefaultNotesEventService.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesPersistenceEventService.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesRecord.java
com/knoden/pim/pimi/notes/NotesRepository.java
...

# pimi.properties
id=notes
name=Notes
type=Journal
description=Quick, freeform notes for anything you want to remember.

At startup pim-core's loader puts the workspace's pimi on the class path before Spring scans, so a pimi's beans are ordinary Spring beans. Nothing loads on trust:

  • A pimi loads only if its SHA-256 matches the one configured for it (pim.workspaces.trusted.notes=<sha256>) or a publisher-signed catalog vouches for that exact build (ECDSA P-256).
  • The loader accepts only classes in the pimi's own package (com.knoden.pim.pimi.notes) and its generated skills. A library the pimi brings is relocated into its package at build time, so two pimi can't clash over a library's version.
  • The app's code never depends on the AI stack. Its skills are .aisl files, and pim-core's AI module runs them on request over the bus, on whatever model the application is configured with.

The fifteen apps that come with PIM, from Notes and Calendar to Mail and Finance, are built exactly this way, in pim-apps. They are there to show what a pimi can do. Calendar books "dentist Friday at 3" for real, and it avoids the bug from part one in a third way: it gives the model the dates of the next two weeks with their weekdays, so the model looks the date up instead of working it out.

Rough edges

  • Pre-1.0: APIs can still change between minor versions.
  • Not on Maven Central yet, hence the repository block.
  • Built around Ollama: the per-skill model and thinking settings are Ollama options.
  • A method can't return List<Appointment> directly; wrap the list in a record.
  • pim-core is pre-1.0 too (0.64), and its agents are for PIM's own apps so far, not yet for pimi.

Links

  • AISL, code at gitlab.com/knoden/aisl-core (LGPL-3.0)
  • pim-core, code at gitlab.com/knoden/pim-core (AGPL-3.0)
  • PIM's apps as pimi: gitlab.com/knoden/pim-apps (AGPL-3.0)
  • Both on one page: For developers

Questions and bug reports are welcome as GitLab issues.

title: I built a swinging lanyard badge in React with no physics library. Here is the whole method
description:
I wanted an ID badge that hangs from a strap, swings when you grab it and flies when you throw it. Every example I found pulled in a physics engine and a 3D renderer for it. That is a lot of code to ship for one card.

It turns out the whole thing is a rope, a weight and one spring. Here is how it works. You can try the finished badge here first: grab it and throw it.

1. The strap is 14 links

A rope is a chain of points that are not allowed to drift apart. I store each point with its current and its previous position:

type Pt = { x: number; y: number; px: number; py: number }

There is no velocity field. The velocity is the difference between the two positions. This is Verlet integration, and it is why throwing works without any extra code: when you let go, the last two positions already contain the speed of your hand.

Each step moves every point by its own velocity, plus gravity:

const vx = (p.x - p.px) * 0.99   // a little air drag
const vy = (p.y - p.py) * 0.99
p.px = p.x
p.py = p.y
p.x += vx
p.y += vy + GRAVITY * dt * dt

2. Then pull the chain back together

After that step the points are too far apart. So for each neighbouring pair, measure the distance and move both points toward the right length. Repeat a few times:

const dx = b.x - a.x
const dy = b.y - a.y
const dist = Math.hypot(dx, dy)
const pull = (dist - segment) / dist
a.x += dx * pull * wa
a.y += dy * pull * wa
b.x -= dx * pull * wb
b.y -= dy * pull * wb

wa and wb decide who gives way. Normally both are 0.5. Three cases are different:

  • The top point is fixed, so it never moves (wa = 0).
  • The card is heavy, so on the last link the rope does most of the moving (0.88 against 0.12). This one number is what makes it hang straight and swing like a pendulum instead of flapping like a ribbon.
  • While you hold the card, it does not give at all.

Ten passes per step are enough for 14 links.

3. The card over-swings on its own spring

If the card simply took the angle of the last link, it would look glued to the rope. A real badge lags behind and overshoots. So the card has its own angle and its own angular speed, pulled toward the rope's direction by a spring:

const want = -Math.atan2(end.x - prev.x, end.y - prev.y)
spin += ((want - angle) * 90 - spin * 9) * dt
angle += spin * dt

The card also leans in 3D with its horizontal speed (rotateY), and a band of light moves across it by the same amount. Both are one line each and they sell the effect more than anything else.

4. Dragging, and the two bugs I hit

While dragging, the last point follows the pointer. Two things went wrong at first.

The rope stretched forever. The top is fixed and so is your hand, so the constraints cannot be satisfied. The fix is to limit the hand: past the strap's length the card only follows 12% of the extra distance. It feels like the strap going taut.

A fast flick launched the card into orbit. Verlet keeps whatever speed the last two positions imply, and a mouse can move very fast between two frames. I cap the release speed.

5. Do not run when nothing moves

A physics loop that runs forever drains batteries. This one counts frames in which the card is slow, the spin is near zero and nobody is holding it. After half a second of that it stops, and a pointer event starts it again. It also stops off screen (IntersectionObserver) and in a hidden tab.

With prefers-reduced-motion the simulation never starts: the badge hangs straight and still flips on click.

What it costs

About 500 lines in one file, styles and markup included, with an SVG path for the strap and a div for the card. The physics uses no library at all. The only import besides React is one hook from Motion that reads the reduced-motion setting.

The finished component, with a flip side and keyboard control, is part of goodui, a React component library I am building. 133 of the components are free and MIT licensed, installed as source through the shadcn CLI. The lanyard badge is in the paid set.
